Level W

1. A Grand Ship Lost in the Cold Sea

1Contents. A Grand Vessel. Out on the Open Sea. The Ship Goes Down. People Brought to Safety. The Wreck Is Located. What the Sinking Changed. Word List. Topic List. People of that time called the new ship the finest vessel ever to sail. Others said it was the biggest ship on the water. Some people even said it could not be sunk. Disaster came on Sunday, April 14, 1912. The time was just before midnight. Within hours, the Atlantic had swallowed the Titanic. In its own time, it was the most magnificent ship afloat. The full name of this ship was the R.M.S. Titanic. The letters R.M.S. stand for Royal Mail Ship. On the night of the sinking, the ship carried 3,500 bags of mail. Workers built the Titanic in Northern Ireland. The ship was meant to carry people. It was also meant to carry cargo. The route crossed the Atlantic Ocean. In 1912, airplanes were still new and strange machines. A trip between Europe and the United States required a boat.

2Passengers began to come aboard on Wednesday, April 10. The port was Southampton, England. They were excited to be on the ship. People said it was the finest ship in the world. The Titanic had never sailed this route before. A first trip is also called a maiden voyage. The voyage to New York would take one week. The crew numbered 900 people. The passengers numbered 1,300 people. Wealthy travelers rode in comfort. They had fancy rooms for meals. They had elegant rooms for sleep. First-class rooms were high up, near the ship's upper decks. Those rooms gave the best views. They also let in fresh air. The Titanic had four elevators. It had a lavish staircase too. A careful copy can show that grand staircase. People with little money stayed in smaller rooms. Those smaller rooms sat low in the hull. That area was called steerage. The rooms were tight. The rooms were crowded. Passengers in steerage were not allowed on the upper levels.

3A person's class was that person's rank in society. Class was based on how much money the person made. People in the upper class earned a great deal of money. Lower-class people had little money. In 1912, the classes were kept apart. The price of a ticket depended on the class. First class cost $4,350.00 for one person. Second class cost $65.00 for one person. Third class cost $35.00 for one person. A map of the North Atlantic Ocean uses a dotted line. That line shows the Titanic's route. The route was the ship's first voyage. It was also the ship's only voyage. Southampton was behind them. The next harbor was in France. The ship stopped in Ireland next. A few more passengers came aboard at those stops. On Thursday, April 11, the ship set out again. It headed into the cold, open water of the North Atlantic Ocean. The Titanic must have been an amazing sight. It glided across the ocean. No other ship of that time was larger.

4It was 269 meters long, or 883 feet. That length is about the same as 55 cars parked end to end. The ship was as tall as a building with ten stories. That height was 32 meters, or 104 feet. Its four tall smokestacks rose 19 meters, or 62 feet. Picture fifteen fourth-graders stacked one above another. The smokestacks were taller than that stack. Three days after Southampton, the ship was far from land. By then the ship was far out on the North Atlantic. Icebergs were common in that part of the sea. The ship's workers had to watch for those dangerous chunks of floating ice. On Sunday evening the water stayed smooth. No white-capped waves broke on the rough ice. Foam from those waves would have shown where the ice was. The night was dark in an ominous way. The sky had no clouds. With no moon, the quiet open water stayed dark. At 11:40 pm a hard thud shook the crew. Passengers felt it too.

5The thud struck the side of the ship. The Titanic had hit an iceberg. No one panicked. They believed the Titanic could not sink. One person on board knew that belief was wrong. An iceberg is bigger below the water than above it. The blow missed the ice that rises into the air. It hit the larger part that sits under the surface. One picture shows passengers crowded into a lifeboat. The ship had few boats like that. The person who understood the danger was Thomas Andrews. He had helped design the Titanic. He watched the way the ship was acting. He soon knew the ship was in grave danger. Crew members woke the passengers as calmly as they could. The passengers did not yet suspect the truth. Someone told them to wear life jackets. Women and children from first class were led into lifeboats. Crews let the boats down a long drop toward the sea. People waited their turn with patience. They still did not understand the danger.

6A famous painting shows the Titanic in its last moments. Very soon, the danger was clear to everyone on board. The ship that people called unsinkable was going down. The trouble was dire. There were not enough lifeboats for everyone. Musicians in the ship's band did not leave the deck. The musicians played so the people would stay calm. Some people prayed quietly. They waited for the worst. Others grabbed objects in a frantic way. They hoped the objects would help them float. Still others held on to the deck. The deck was lifting into the air. In the radio room, the operator sent an urgent message. The message said the ship had struck an iceberg. It also said the ship was badly damaged. A second message carried the distress signal SOS. The closest ship to answer was the Carpathia. The Carpathia would need several hours to arrive. That was not soon enough. Two and a half hours after the iceberg strike, the Titanic sank. The icy North Atlantic closed over the ship, and it was gone.

7Some people still suspect that another ship was nearby. Nobody has proved that suspicion past every doubt. The other ship may have been the Californian. Five miles may have been all that lay between the ships. It was surely no more than 19 miles from the Titanic. The Californian's crew said they had not seen the distress flares. Nobody aboard the Californian was listening, because its radio was off. So the crew never received the SOS. Rescue came in the early morning hours of Monday, April 15. The Carpathia arrived for the survivors. The survivors were exhausted. They were full of grief. About 700 people had lived through the night in the few lifeboats. About 1,500 people had died. Most of the dead had not drowned. They had been floating in their life vests. The extreme cold of the North Atlantic killed them. Newspapers gave their front pages to the story of the Titanic. People around the world felt shock at the loss.

8People asked how such a magnificent ship could go down so fast. People had called the ship unsinkable. Several decades later, many of the questions were answered. A picture shows the rescue ship, the Carpathia. A picture shows the bow of the Titanic. The bow lies on the floor of the North Atlantic. In 1985, something extraordinary happened. Searchers found the Titanic about four kilometers down, or 2.5 miles. The wreck sat on the North Atlantic seafloor. Scientists could finally seek answers. They wanted to know why the ship sank so quickly. They sent robotic devices to the wreck. The devices explored it and recorded video. On the video monitors, the ship's form looked ghostly. The front railing could still be recognized. Seventy years underwater had not erased it. Scientists proved the hull had split in two. People also asked about the hole from the iceberg. Sand on the ocean floor buried that hole. The hole could not be seen. Scientists had to use sonar.

9Sonar uses waves of sound. Those waves bounce off surfaces. The sound waves showed that the old idea was wrong. The iceberg had not cut one huge gash in the side. That huge gash is what people had first suspected. The ice had made several small holes instead. Added together, the holes equaled only about the area of a doorway. People had expected those holes to be lower. They were higher than expected. Each compartment had an open top. Water could flood from one compartment into the next. These smaller holes sat higher on the hull. They made the compartments fill very quickly. That fast filling is what made the ship sink. The sinking of the Titanic taught many lessons. New rules were put in place so ships would be safer. Today every passenger must have a place in a lifeboat. Crews must hold lifeboat drills. A drill shows each person what to do if trouble starts. A ship's radio must stay on for 24 hours of every day.

10The International Ice Patrol was established. That organization keeps track of where icebergs are. A picture shows lifeboats on a modern ship. People still call the Titanic a grand ship. The story of that ship is grand as well. People remember the lives that were lost. People remember the lessons of the tragedy. People remember the changes the tragedy brought to travel by sea. That memory is the legacy of the Titanic. A contraption is an interesting device that seems unfamiliar. Dire means terribly bad. Frantically means acting in a wild way because of strong feeling. Magnificent means beautiful and grand in a way that impresses people. Ominously means in a threatening way, as if something bad is coming. Steerage is the lowest area of a ship, where the poorest passengers stayed. Topics in this book include Thomas Andrews. They include the Carpathia. They include the iceberg. They include the International Ice Patrol. They include New York. They include the North Atlantic Ocean. They include Southampton.

2. A Joyful Day for the Dead

1Many places hold large celebrations for Día de los Muertos. A map of them can mark Montana, Oregon, and Wisconsin. It can mark California, New Mexico, Arizona, and Texas. It can mark the United States and Mexico. San Jose, California, is one city where a Day of the Dead parade fills the streets. Up ahead, a giant puppet shaped like a skull floats high in the air. Skeletons dance in the street. Drummers march along. Children wear masks. They also wear angel wings that glitter. People on stilts move through the crowd and perform tricks. You stop a woman and ask what is going on. Her face is painted in a beautiful way. She says this is a special parade. The parade honors friends who have died. It honors relatives who have died. You are taking part in Día de los Muertos. Día de los Muertos is celebrated in many parts of the world.

2Those Spanish words mean Day of the Dead. In Mexico, people have celebrated some form of this day for thousands of years. In the United States, parades and celebrations happen in many states. California, Arizona, and New Mexico are among them. Texas, Oregon, Montana, and Wisconsin are among them too. The dates are not the same everywhere. November 1 and November 2 are the usual days for these events. Each celebration honors people who have died. Sometimes pets are honored as well. A boy in Lima, Peru, dances the traditional scissors dance for this holiday. In Mexico City, Mexico, an Aztec dancer performs. Yearly harvest festivals were already a Native American custom in Mexico before Europeans arrived. The festivals came around early November. During them, people often gave food as offerings to their ancestors. A drawing can show an Aztec harvest festival.

3Halloween may be the first holiday this day reminds you of. The two holidays are not the same. Halloween is often built around scaring people. Joy, not fear, is the feeling of this holiday. In certain cultures, people believe something special happens. Loved ones who have died are believed to visit home as spirits. Those who have died are remembered. They are honored. They are celebrated. In Mexico, a family may visit a loved one's grave and decorate it. Each year, San Francisco, California, stages its own Day of the Dead procession. About 15,000 people take part. They carry candles. Along the route, people carry pictures of the dead they loved. A grand procession is Austin, Texas, way of marking the day. The city also holds a costume contest. Tucson, Arizona, has a huge parade. You can say Tucson as TOOsawn. The marchers in Tucson number more than 30,000.

4The best part of most of these parades is open to all. Anyone can join. Growing up in Mexico, Lidia Terán-Cooper marked Día de los Muertos every single year. November 2 always found Lidia and her family at the cemetery. The family brought flowers. They brought a picnic. Stories of relatives who had died were part of the day. Special songs came from musicians known as mariachis. The songs were in honor of the dead. Dancing filled the day for Lidia and the other children. They played all day too. A picture can show mariachis playing in a Mexican cemetery for this day. In the Tucson, Arizona, procession, puppets stand above the crowd. The day was always a happy one for Lidia. She spent it remembering the people she loved. These days, the United States is where Lidia lives.

5The Tucson parade includes Lidia and her family every year. They march to honor their ancestors. Her colorful Mexican dress is one she stitched with her own hands. She also wears a mask of a grinning skeleton. When people visit the cemetery, some of them clean the graves of loved ones. They decorate those graves too. Overnight stays at the cemetery are a custom in parts of Mexico. Extra blankets and extra pillows are laid out for the night. The spirits of loved ones can rest on them. Bowls of water are set out by some families too. They set out soap and towels. The spirits can wash up after a long journey. One family in Mexico left those washing things at a grave they had decorated. In San Antonio, Texas, dancers show off painted skull masks at the parade. Lidia builds special masks during the days leading up to the parade.

6Children and adults will decorate them. Newspaper is torn into bits and left to soak. Flour and glue go into the soaked newspaper. The mix becomes paper pulp. Lidia shapes that pulp into masks. After the masks dry, people paint them. Some masks look like skeletons. Others look like different creatures. Some painters add sparkles and flowers. Then they wear the masks in the parade. Children get a Día de los Muertos celebration of their own in some cities. The children decorate cardboard wings and wear them in their own parade. They make loud noisemakers. They learn circus tricks. Face paint and special costumes are part of the children's day. Adults dress up as angels and stand on very tall stilts. Those adults lead the children through the parade. A picture can show children in different costumes walking in Tucson, Arizona.

7Remembering loved ones who have died can happen outside a parade too. Old traditions fill this holiday from end to end. People take part in them in order to honor the dead. Some people build special altars inside their homes. The altars welcome the spirits of loved ones. An altar is one of the day's most important projects. Fabric covers the beautiful altars. Photos of the person who died decorate them. A favorite piece of clothing might rest on an altar. It might include an item that person treasured. Inside a family home, an altar may be prepared for someone who has died. Candles go around the altars, and the family lights each one. They also bake a special bread called pan de muertos. That name means bread of the dead. Spirits of relatives receive other treats as well. Candy is one favorite food.

8Tamales are another. A family may leave a favorite juice on the altar. Another drink may be left there too. Marigolds or other flowers decorate the altars. Skeleton toys decorate them. Dolls decorate them as well. Pan de muertos and other foods may cover an altar. People have long believed that the scent of marigolds does a special job. Loved ones' spirits are said to follow that scent back home. Some people scatter marigold petals along a path. The path runs from the graves to the family's front door. In a cemetery in Mexico, a woman may scatter marigold petals on a grave. Colorful sugar skulls are a yearly project for some people who keep this holiday. White sugar is pressed into molds to form the skulls. Colorful frosting goes on once the skulls have dried. Children in Mexico love to eat the sweet skulls.

9Children in the United States love them too. A market in Mexico may display handmade sugar skulls. Art made for this day often shows skeletons. Bright colors fill that art. Skeletons appear in colorful paintings that some artists make for the holiday. The paintings show grinning skeletons as they dance. They show skeletons playing guitars. They show skeletons celebrating. Friends who have died are celebrated through this art. It is also a way to celebrate family members who have died. People who have lost someone they love can turn to this holiday in many ways. Marching can bring back memories of time shared with that special person. Decorating an altar can help in the same way. Painting a picture can help too. Honoring the generations who came before can be both fun and creative. Those ancestors are the generations who came before. No other holiday is quite like this one.

10It is full of fun, costumes, and life. It is full of masks, joy, memories, and love. Los Angeles, California, hosts a festival for this holiday where children perform. An altar is a table or another raised surface used for a religious or spiritual purpose. Ancestors are family members from long ago. Dead people are buried in a place called a cemetery. A culture is the ideas and customs of a certain group of people. A generation is everyone born and living at about the same time. The word can also cover other animals alive then. To honor someone is to show respect or to think well of that person. A procession is a formal parade. In some beliefs, spirits are supernatural beings, souls, or essences. Traditions are beliefs or customs passed from year to year and from generation to generation.

3. A Leader Named Martin Luther King Jr.

1During the March on Washington, King lifts a hand to the crowd. This book has these parts. Childhood in the South. King Goes to School. The Montgomery Bus Boycott. The Birmingham Protests. The Fight Continues. King's Memorial. Words to Know. Childhood in the South Each January brings Martin Luther King Jr. Day in the United States. A great leader is honored that day. He fought so all people could have equality. Who was the man behind a national holiday? Birth came on January 15, 1929, for Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Atlanta, Georgia, was the city. A Baptist minister was his father. His mother was a teacher. King grew up in the South. White leaders there wrote unfair laws. The laws were known as Jim Crow laws. They took many rights away from Black people. Chances in every part of life were taken away. Black people and white people had to stay apart. Segregated means kept apart. A family photo places King at the front right. A young man drinks at a water fountain. The sign on it says Colored. People now see that word as offensive. Segregation reached many places. Schools were separate. Restaurants were separate. Bathrooms and parks were separate.

2Waiting rooms for buses and trains were separate. Even drinking fountains were separate. Places set aside for Black people were often less nice. They were often less clean than places for white people. Black people could not live in white neighborhoods. They could not marry a white person. Certain jobs were closed to them. Pay for the same job was lower than the pay white workers received. In one state, speaking out in public for equality was against the law. Support for equal standing of Black people with white people was against that law. Growing up, King watched the harm. These racist laws hurt Black people. Justice for Black people was his aim. Full equality was the goal. School Years As a student, King was gifted. He entered Morehouse College at age fifteen. In college he chose to become a minister, as his father was. Religion study took him north, to Boston University. There he learned about Mohandas Gandhi. India knew Gandhi as a great leader. Gandhi trusted nonviolent protest as a way to fight injustice. King chose peaceful methods for his own work. After school he moved to Montgomery, Alabama. His wife, Coretta, went with him. He became a minister in that city.

3About Coretta Scott King Leadership and civil rights work both marked Coretta Scott King. The year 1968 was when her husband was killed. She then started the Martin Luther King Jr. Center for Nonviolent Social Change. Some programs are local. Some are national. Some are international. The programs train people in nonviolent ways to protest. In the 1980s she led a campaign. The goal was a national holiday on her husband's birthday. Travel around the world filled her remaining years. She backed efforts for human rights. She died in January 2006. Buses in Montgomery May 1954 brought a ruling from the United States Supreme Court. Race could no longer decide who sat in which school. Black people hoped the ruling would spread. They hoped other public places would be desegregated too. Desegregation had opponents among many white Southerners. The name for them was segregationists. December 1955 found Rosa Parks, a Black woman, on a Montgomery city bus. She was on her way home. The bus was segregated. The back of the bus was the only legal place for Black riders. A white person could expect a Black rider to stand up and give over a seat. Parks knew the rule was unfair.

4Her seat was requested by a white man. She stayed where she was. Police arrested her. A photo shows her fingerprinting after the arrest. The arrest upset Black residents of Montgomery. Local Black activists quickly set up a boycott. It protested segregation on the city buses. They formed a group to run the boycott. They elected King president. Most riders on those buses were Black. Fares stopped coming in, and the city lost heavily. The boycott lasted more than a year. White city officials resisted what the protestors asked. At last, in June 1956, a Montgomery court ruled. The court said Montgomery buses had to end segregation. Officials of the city still did not want that change. They carried the case to the United States Supreme Court. A picture shows King talking with the people who organized the boycott. The first court's decision stood when the Supreme Court spoke on December 20, 1956. The next day, Montgomery ended segregation on its buses. The boycott drew notice across the nation. It showed that a nonviolent protest could bring change. King's leadership during the boycott made him widely known. People across the nation saw him as a leader in the civil rights movement.

5Women of the Boycott Black women were central in opening Montgomery buses to every rider. The Women's Political Council was a group of Black women activists in that city. Jo Ann Robinson led it. For many years, members had opposed segregation in that city. The call for a boycott came from them before anyone else. Meetings were one job they handled during the protest. They arranged carpools. They stayed in touch with protestors. Their work helped the boycott last. It lasted until the demands were met. A photo shows women walking to work while the boycott went on. The Birmingham Protests Segregation went on across the South. So did violence against Black people. Segregationists bombed several Black churches. They bombed homes of Black leaders, including King's home. King did not quit. A civil rights organization took shape in 1957, with King and other leaders. As its president, King traveled the country. He spoke about peaceful protest. He spoke about civil rights. April 1963 took King and other leaders to Birmingham, Alabama. At that time it was one of the most segregated cities in the country. They came to organize a mass protest. Marches were part of it. A boycott of businesses was part of it.

6Arrests swept up hundreds of people who had protested in peace. King was one of them. Black leaders raised money so the protestors could be released. The next month, another march met police force. Fire hoses were turned on peaceful protestors. Attack dogs were used. Many people were badly hurt. A lot of them were children. Hundreds were arrested. News of the attack spread across the country. People grew angry. A week later the two sides reached an agreement. President John F. Kennedy helped. Black civil rights leaders took part. White leaders of the city took part. Birmingham agreed to end segregation. People Who Shaped His Ideas Dr. Benjamin Mays lived from 1894 to 1984. Morehouse College had him as president. Ministry and civil rights activism were both his work. King found a mentor in him. Howard Thurman lived from 1899 to 1981. He was a minister. He taught King at Boston University. He brought King the ideas of Gandhi on nonviolent protest. Mohandas Gandhi lived from 1869 to 1948. He was an activist in India. He taught civil disobedience, which means peacefully refusing to obey unfair laws. His teaching inspired King. It inspired many other activists for human rights.

7Bayard Rustin lived from 1912 to 1987. Civil rights leadership was his role, and he mentored King. The famous 1963 March on Washington had his help in the planning. Martin Luther King Jr. delivers his famous speech. Its name is I Have a Dream. The Work Goes On Months after Birmingham, a march was planned by King and fellow civil rights leaders. The name was March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. The date was August 28, 1963. Washington, D.C., held a huge crowd. The number of people passed two hundred thousand. The protest challenged how Black people were treated in the United States. King spoke there. The speech is called I Have a Dream. He asked for justice for every person. He asked for equality for every person. Skin color should not decide a person's worth. President Lyndon B. Johnson put his signature on the Civil Rights Act in 1964. The law made segregation in public places illegal. That same year King received the Nobel Peace Prize. His guiding role in the civil rights movement was the reason for the prize. Many white people still fought desegregation. The struggle for civil rights went on. In 1965 violence broke out in Selma, Alabama.

8It broke out between segregationists and nonviolent protestors. Leaders from the civil rights fight wanted Black citizens there listed as voters. The vote already belonged to Black people by right. Blocks still came often from white officials at election time. The blocks took many forms. Violence was one of them. A march linking Selma with Montgomery was planned with King's help. It protested the treatment of Black voters. King was at the head of the protestors on March 7, 1965. They did not get far. Police blocked the road. The police attack stopped them. A second try came three weeks afterward. This time protection came with them. Soldiers of the United States Army guarded the march. The National Guard guarded it. President Johnson had sent those forces. The marchers reached Montgomery. Nearly fifty thousand supporters met them. One photo shows King walking with protestors in the Selma march. Another shows him as President Lyndon Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act and makes it law. President Johnson's signature made the Voting Rights Act law on August 6, 1965. The law protected the vote for all people of color. Who Could Vote The year 1920 had already given every Black person a legal vote.

9State laws still stopped many from using it. Local laws did too. Officials often made Black voters take unfair tests. They made them pay money. Some were told to recite the whole Constitution before a vote would count. White people in a community sometimes threatened Black voters. Attacks also met people who tried to cast a ballot. Congress created the Voting Rights Act as an answer to these problems. The act helped. A change in the law in 2013 opened a new gap. New barriers became easier for states to set up. Fresh laws about voting have been passed by some state lawmakers. The laws make voting harder for some people. Those lawmakers say the rules will help stop voter fraud. Other people point to a different fact. Voter fraud is rare. They say the new laws often hit Black voters hardest. They hit other voters of color hardest too. King's Memorial In 1968 King went to Tennessee. He came to support a protest by workers. A shot killed him during that visit. The accused shooter was a white man, James Earl Ray. King died on April 4. Age thirty-nine was the end of his life.

10Mourning spread around the world. Washington, D.C., opened a memorial in 2011. Forty-three years had passed since his death. The memorial honors him. Visitors come from every part of the world. They remember this great man. Work for justice goes on. Work for equality for all people goes on. The memorial built for Martin Luther King Jr. reaches 30 feet. That is 9 m. Words to Know A boycott is a refusal to buy something or to join in it. The refusal makes a point. It can also force a change. Civil rights are rights in law, in society, and in the economy. They promise freedom and equality to every citizen. Facilities are areas, buildings, or structures set aside for one purpose or task. Leadership is the skill of guiding other people and directing them. Marches are planned walks through the streets. The walkers support a cause or protest one. Mourned means felt grief or sadness, especially for a person who has died. Register means to enter a name in an official record. Voting is one reason. School is another. Resisted means pushed back against control or against change. Segregated means kept apart because of a group difference, such as race.

4. A Maya City Called Chichén Itzá

1A drawing shows a temple beside the ball court at Chichén Itzá. It suggests the temple's look in the distant past. This book has these parts. A City in the Jungle. The Maya Empire. A Monumental City. Styles of Building. Maya Science. The Maya Today. Visiting the City. More Mysteries. Words to Know. The stepped pyramid at Chichén Itzá rises ninety-eight feet. The temple on the summit is part of that height. City in the Jungle Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula holds an ancient jungle city called Chichén Itzá. Say the city name chee-CHEN eet-SAH. The Maya built it. They are a people native to this area. In the Mayan language the name points to a well of the Itzá people. It points to the mouth of that well. The wells were water sources inside the city. Daily life used them. Sacred life used them too. This city was once the largest in the Maya empire. Many Maya ethnic groups ruled it across thousands of years. People never fully walked away from it.

2Descendants of the builders still live nearby. Scientists have studied the city through the past 150 years. Historians have too. They want to understand its past. Huge stone buildings stand there. Paved roads run through it. A Wide Maya World Many large cities existed. Chichén Itzá was one of them. The Maya civilization raised them during a span of four thousand years. The empire covered land that is now five countries. Mexico is one of the countries. Belize is another. Guatemala belongs on the list. Honduras belongs on it. El Salvador belongs on it too. Related Mayan languages in the region numbered over thirty. They prayed to gods that were alike. In the third century they started cities of giant stone temples and palaces. A map of Maya territory labels the Gulf of Mexico. It labels Cancún, Uxmal, and Cozumel. It labels the Yucatán Peninsula, Belize, Mexico, and Guatemala. It labels the Pacific Ocean, Honduras, and El Salvador. Marks show places where Maya ruins are studied. The Temple of the Warriors holds a wall painting, shown here as a copy.

3A Maya village sits by the water in that scene. Warriors ride in canoes. The biggest cities began in lands that today are the south of Mexico, plus Guatemala. By about the year 1000, the heart of Maya life had shifted north. The new center was the Yucatán Peninsula. Say Yucatán as yoo-kah-TAHN. Too many people may explain the move. Too little rain may explain it. War may explain it. More people came to live at Chichén Itzá. Power and size both put it first in the empire. Today the peninsula is mostly jungle, forest, and farm. Only a few large cities stand in the region. Visitors come to see what the ancient Maya built. They visit Chichén Itzá. They visit Uxmal, said oos-MAHL. They visit Cobá, said koh-BAH. Chichén Itzá places its great stepped pyramid in the middle. A City of Huge Buildings This is one of the largest cities the Maya ever built. A great many buildings still stand.

4The stepped pyramid is the most famous. Restoration has brought it close to the look it had when new. The Great Ball Court is open for visitors as well. Players used a rubber ball. The court has the shape of a capital letter I. Temples fill the city. Priests led ceremonies inside them. An observatory stands there for watching the Sun and the stars. Two more sites mattered greatly. They are cenotes, said say-NOH-tayz, which means natural wells. One well supplied fresh water. The other was sacred. People brought offerings there for Chac, the rain god. A plan of the city names the Sacred Cenote and the Great Ball Court. It names the Venus Platform and the Stepped Pyramid. It names the Temple of the Warriors and the Ossuary. It names the Fresh Water Cenote. It names El Caracol, also called The Snail. It names Casa de las Monjas, also called The Nunnery. Probable building methods at this city are impressive. Each limestone block was cut out of the ground with stone tools.

5Workers carried every block. They set it by hand. Roads started as large blocks of stone. Finer layers of rock covered them, one layer after another. Sand was the last layer. Wall carvings of amazing skill were finished with stone tools as well. Sharp tools of volcanic glass may have been used too. One carving shows a jaguar. Maya belief made the jaguar a god. The realm was the Underworld. How the City Was Built Occupation ran from about 450 ce until about 1450 ce. Across those years, different groups from the Maya empire held power. Building styles blended as time passed. Rulers shaped the blend. Trading partners shaped it too. Earlier buildings used the Puuc style. Say Puuc as POOK. The Puuc region lies west of the city, still on the Yucatán Peninsula. Its buildings strongly influenced Chichén Itzá. Most Puuc buildings sit low and flat. Horizontal lines cross them. The lower walls are often plain. Rich carving gathers near the top.

6A photo shows one building in that style. Temples here have turned up a dozen of these Chacmool statues, or even more. This is one. In the tenth century a group from Central Mexico took Chichén Itzá. Historians still debate who they were. They may have been the Toltec, a people who were not Maya. They may have been Maya with close ties to Toltec culture. Afterward, new buildings mixed both traditions. Carvers put winged snakes on many later walls. They put jaguars on them too. Some temples hold statues called Chacmools, said chahk-MOOLZ. Each figure reclines. An offering dish rests on the stomach. Some buildings of the mixed style hide an older building inside. The stepped pyramid, for example, sits on a smaller and older pyramid. Columns crowd the Temple of the Warriors. An older structure sits inside it as well. Maya Science The buildings also show what the Maya understood about astronomy and about the seasons. Four staircases climb the stepped pyramid. Ninety-one steps form each staircase.

7Add the platform at the top. The total gives one step for every day of the year. That plan shows careful watching. The Maya studied patterns made as Earth orbits the Sun. The steps may stand for the ninety-one days between four markers. The markers are the winter solstice, the spring equinox, the summer solstice, and the fall equinox. A solstice is a day when the Sun sits farthest from the equator. At an equinox the Sun crosses the equator. Day and night then last the same time. Shadows on the pyramid may have worked as a calendar. People may have used them to time planting. They may have used them to time harvesting. The Snail Observatory Locals know the city's observatory as El Caracol, said EL kah-rah-KOHL. In Spanish the name means the snail. The building offers more clues. The Maya tracked how planets move and how stars move. The structure and its windows are angled with exact care. Venus can be seen there when it reaches the farthest north point of its path in the sky.

8A Maya woman walks with children through a traditional market in Guatemala. Maya People Now Maya people living in Central America number more than six million. Belize is one home country. El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras are others. Southern Mexico is another. Language count passes thirty. Some words sound almost alike in every Mayan language. Examples include the words for house and for sun. Time, mother, and corn match too. The match shows which ideas matter to all Maya people. A shared tie to corn runs through every Maya culture. Family matters in all of them. Community matters in all of them. A link to the sky remains important. It tells people when crops should be planted. Maya people take part in the wider world. Modern habits often mix with old traditions. Language carries the culture forward. Traditions carry it. So do ties to the land and to the sky. Visiting the City Tourists crowd Chichén Itzá more than ever.

9Each year, more than one million people come. Many buildings can be entered and explored. Some places are closed. Climbers, for example, may no longer go up the stepped pyramid. The rule saves the stone from the wear of feet. It also saves visitors from a fall. So many feet have used those steps that the stone is worn. It is slippery. A climb is no longer safe. An estimate says fifty thousand people once lived in the city or near it. The treasures they left still teach us. More Mysteries Archaeologists have answered many questions about Chichén Itzá. Some answers come from the city. Some come from descendants of the builders. Plenty of questions remain. When did the city's strongest era end? Why did most Maya leave in the 1400s? Historians still study this city and other ancient ones. Workers at the site keep uncovering structures. They keep uncovering artifacts. More objects may still lie in the ruins. Those objects may open buried secrets of the city's past.

10Words to Know Ancient means belonging to the distant past. Architectural describes the design of buildings and the way they are put up. Astronomy studies stars. It studies planets and comets. It studies other objects in space. A civilization is an organized society with a steady food supply, a government, a social structure, and a culture. It also has writing and a religion. Descendants are the offspring of a person or a group that lived earlier. An empire is a set of nations or peoples under one ruler or one government. Maya names both a people and a civilization. Their homeland is what we now call Central America, together with southern Mexico. Offerings are gifts. Worshippers give them to a god or to gods. A peninsula is a long stretch of land with water around almost all of it. Restored means put back into an earlier condition. A stepped pyramid stacks flat platforms, each one smaller than the one below. Temples are buildings used for worship.

5. A Park Shaped by Two Volcanoes

1A volcano leaks glowing red lava day after day. The volcano is on the island of Hawaii. It stands at the edge of the ocean. The lava is red-hot as it seeps out. Then the lava cools. Cooled lava turns into solid rock. Because of that rock, the island gains a little size. People call this volcano Kilauea. The name sounds like kee-luh-WAY-uh. Hawaii Volcanoes National Park includes the volcano Kilauea. Mauna Loa stands in the same park. These two volcanoes are famous. A border marks the edge of the park. Yearly visitors to this park number more than one million. A national park is an area of special land. People protect that land. Visitors can watch the lava beside the ocean. They can see hot lava become hard rock. The island of Hawaii grows a little from the new rock. The Pacific Ocean lies next to this island. Both famous volcanoes share this protected park. Fresh rock keeps adding a little land. The lava comes out day after day. Solid rock is what the cooled lava leaves behind. A visit can show lava turning into land.

2The shore changes as the rock builds up. This park is a wonderland of volcanoes. Hot lava and new stone meet the sea here. The protected land holds both great volcanoes. People come to watch a volcano build the island. Melted rock on the move is how a volcano gets its start. The melted rock comes from deep inside Earth. It comes out through a crack. The crack is in the surface of Earth. At the surface, the melted rock cools. It becomes solid rock. As time passes, that rock piles higher. The piled rock may form a mountain. The piled rock may even form an island. The Hawaiian Islands formed in this way. This park holds two volcanoes that rank among the most amazing on Earth. A drawing of the inside shows lava. The drawing shows the volcano. The drawing shows melted rock called magma. Kilauea is one of the two volcanoes. In Hawaiian, the name Kilauea means spewing. Few volcanoes on Earth stay as busy as Kilauea. Rivers of thick lava pour out of it.

3The flow has gone on almost all the time since 1983. Scientists think Kilauea began forming long ago. They place the start between 300,000 and 600,000 years ago. They think it probably showed up as an island later. They place that time between 50,000 and 100,000 years ago. Lava leaves Kilauea in a flow that looks like a river. Cooled rock from flows like these built the islands. A crack in the surface is where a volcano starts. Year after year, the rock can pile into a mountain. The same kind of pile can make an island. Kilauea has kept sending out thick lava since 1983. The lava in that long flow is thick. Melted rock deep in Earth is the start of the story. Hard rock at the surface is the end of each flow. A group of people posed for a photo at Kilauea. The photo is from the eruption in 1924. In 1790, Kilauea erupted. The number of people killed that year was at least eighty. More eruptions came in 1924. Huge rocks were flung all around the area by those blasts.

4Some rocks weighed as much as 8 tons (7,258 kg). In 1959, Kilauea sent lava high into the air. The stream of lava rose 1,900 feet (579 m). You would need about two Eiffel Towers, one above the other, to match it. Another volcano stands nearby. Its name is Mauna Loa. Say the name like MOU-nuh LOH-uh. In Hawaiian, Mauna Loa means long mountain. Earth has few mountains larger than Mauna Loa. Its base lies far beneath the ocean. From that base, it is more than 10 miles (16 km) high. Snow covers the top of Mauna Loa. People can see this snowy volcano from far away. The 1790 blast killed at least eighty people. The 1924 blasts scattered giant rocks. The 1959 stream leapt high above the ground. That tall stream is a picture of leaping lava. The people in the 1924 photo stand near the eruption. Ocean water lies over the lowest part of Mauna Loa. The full height counts the rock under the sea. Snow on the peak shows far across the land. The name long mountain fits this huge volcano.

5A weight of 8 tons (7,258 kg) is a very heavy rock. People remember the 1959 stream for that great height. Mauna Loa appears mid-eruption in a picture made in the 1870s. The view in the picture is from the ocean. Kilauea and Mauna Loa grew by a very similar process. Mauna Loa is giant. It stretches nearly 75 miles (121 km) across. It rises about 13,680 feet (4,170 m) above sea level. Half of the island of Hawaii lies under this volcano. Since 1843, dozens of eruptions have come from Mauna Loa. Earthquakes came along with an eruption in 1868. That eruption also caused lava flows. The shaking and the lava flows lasted four days. They destroyed nearly forty buildings. A crater holds a lava lake that is still active. The crater is at the top of Kilauea. People have visited Kilauea for hundreds of years. Hundreds of years of visits have been made to Mauna Loa. Early native people made offerings at the volcanoes. An offering is a gift. Visitors in the 1840s saw a giant lake of lava.

6Those visitors were amazed by the lake. The old picture looks in from the water. Half of Hawaii lies under this one volcano. Dozens of eruptions have come since 1843. The events of 1868 went on for four days. Nearly forty buildings were lost in that eruption. The lava lake at the top of Kilauea is active. Early native people left gifts at the volcanoes. The giant lava lake amazed people in the 1840s. Mauna Loa grew in a way much like Kilauea. Its width is nearly 75 miles (121 km). Its height above the sea is about 13,680 feet (4,170 m). People wanted to protect both volcanoes. They also wanted to protect the land around them. Under President Woodrow Wilson, the area became a national park. It was the thirteenth national park in the country. The date was August 1, 1916. 520 square miles (1,347 square km) is the area inside Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. From Mauna Loa, the park reaches all the way to the coast. Lava tubes run across the land. Some lava tubes lead into the sea.

7A lava tube is a big tunnel in the ground. Lava formed these tunnels long ago. People are able to walk inside because these tubes are very large. The Thurston Lava Tube is a tunnel that visitors walk inside. That tube is in the park. The new park guarded the volcanoes. It also guarded the land around them. August 1, 1916, is the day this park began. The park was number thirteen for the country. Its land runs from Mauna Loa out to the coast. The park's size is 520 square miles (1,347 square km). Old lava left the tunnels under the ground. Some of those tunnels reach the sea. A person can walk inside a lava tube. The Thurston Lava Tube is one tunnel visitors enter. The tubes are paths made by lava long ago. President Woodrow Wilson set this land aside. Protection was the reason for the new park. Walkers use the wide hollow left by old lava. The coast is one end of the park. Mauna Loa is the other end of that stretch.

8A volcano nearby does not stop animals from living here. The park shelters hundreds of animals under protection. Sea turtles live in the park. Bats live in the park. Unusual insects live in the park. The park has over twenty types of songbirds. The nene is one bird of the park. The apapane is another bird of the park. The Hawaiian happy-face spider lives here. The green grappler moth caterpillar lives here too. The park has many protected native plants. The park has many protected native trees. Hawaii is the only home for almost every plant growing in the park. For years, many plants have grown on and beside these volcanoes. The mamane is one of these plants. The ohia lehua is one of these plants. Tree ferns grow in the park. The silversword grows in the park. Animals stay even with a volcano close by. The protected animals number in the hundreds. Songbirds here include over twenty types. Plants found only in Hawaii fill almost the whole plant list. Some plants have grown near the volcanoes for years. The nene shares the park with the apapane.

9The happy-face spider is part of the park's animal life. The green grappler moth caterpillar is part of that life too. Mamane grows among the protected plants. Ohia lehua grows among the protected plants. Tree ferns are among the protected plants. Silversword is among the protected plants. Native plants and native trees are both protected here. The edge of the volcanoes is still full of life. A visitor can watch the land change while standing there. A visit to Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is wonderful. A person can drive along a volcano. A person can hike more than 150 miles (241 km) of trails. A person can bike along the paths of a volcano. A person can camp in the rainforest. People watch the volcanoes all the time for eruptions. Parts of the park close when lava flows are possible. Parts of the park also close when eruptions are possible. Quiet does not last long in this special place. Active means something is in a state of action. Erupt means a volcano threw out rock. The volcano also threw out lava.

10The volcano also threw out ash. That kind of blast comes from an active volcano. Lava is rock that has melted into liquid. The liquid rock flows from an opening. The opening is in the surface of Earth. A national park is land that the government protects. One reason for protection is the land's history. Another reason is the land's natural beauty. Native describes something natural to one area. Spewing means forcing out a lot of something. The material comes out fast. The material also comes out with force. A safe visit still offers a drive along a volcano. It still offers a long hike of more than 150 miles (241 km). It still offers a bike ride on a volcano path. It still offers a camp in the rainforest. Watch your step when a closing is in place. A lava flow can be the reason for a closing. An eruption can be the reason for a closing. Even then, this land does not stay quiet for long. People can watch the ground change on a visit.

6. A Stone Age Village by the Sea

1Skara Brae stands in the Orkney Islands, off Scotland, between the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. A location map also marks Northern Ireland, Wales, Ireland, and England within Europe. A wider view of the map marks Africa and the Indian Ocean. In February 1850, William Watt walked across the grounds of his estate in Scotland. A terrible storm had hit the Orkney Islands. The islands sit in the sea by Scotland, beside the northeast shore. People in Orkney were used to storms. This storm was especially rough. Winds that shrieked had changed the shape of the land. High tides had changed it too. Grass was torn off the earth. Sand was piled in the fields. As Watt checked the storm's harm, one sight grabbed his attention. Stone walls stuck out of a mound. Grass had been stripped from that mound. Watt was already familiar with stories told nearby. The legends told of old burial tombs hidden under the ground. He wondered whether those stories could be true. Curiosity pushed him to act. Watt brought in George Petrie, a scholar, to dig and to study the spot. Petrie was asked to excavate the site and to examine it. His work was the first step toward the secrets of a settlement.

2Today that settlement carries the name Skara Brae. Long-ago people set their homes into those stone mounds. At first, the site was called Skerrabra. It was also called Styerrabrae. Those names belonged to the mound that covered the whole village. People think the name Skara Brae is a later form of that older name. Nobody can say what name the residents used for their own home. Digging out Skara Brae was not an easy task. The island is flat, and it has no trees. It gave little shelter from strong breezes off the sea. Those breezes blow in from the west. The wind wears away the shoreline. It carries sand far inland. Petrie did his work in this blustery weather. Bit by bit, he uncovered what remained of four ancient buildings. Each building had stone walls that curved. The walls were nearly 2.4 meters thick. That thickness is 8 feet. Petrie was astounded by how well the structures had lasted. He was also astounded by the things inside them. Stone furniture suggested that people had once lived in the buildings. Hearths suggested the same thing. The sand that hid the ruins also helped keep them whole. The ruins are thought to be stone houses. Passages are part of the ruins too.

3One area may have been a workshop. A main passage linked parts of the village. Petrie spent more than ten years on the site. He dug with care. He wrote about what he found. He believed the stone houses belonged to a settlement from 500 bce. His scholarly write-up on Skara Brae appeared in 1868. After Petrie finished, years passed with the site left alone. Then several unlucky events took place. A thief raid struck the place around the year 1913. They stole artifacts of great value. In 1925, another terrible storm hit the area. Strong gusts harmed part of the stonework. The Watt estate gave guardianship of Skara Brae to the authorities. The goal was to protect the site from the weather. The authorities chose to build a seawall. The wall would help guard the ruins against wind and waves from the bay. Work on the seawall brought new interest to Skara Brae. Digging by Scottish authorities continued across the whole twentieth century. They uncovered four more buildings. The total then stood at eight. The digging revealed many interesting details. It seemed that people had buried part of each structure on purpose. Every house was backed into a rubbish pile known as a midden.

4A midden holds shells, bones, smashed pottery, and other rubbish. Building this way may look strange. It fit the climate of Orkney. A stone house set into the ground was sheltered from the wind. It was sheltered from the rain as well. Doorways of the homes all linked together. Passages covered in stone made the links. This feature also came from the environment. People could go from house to house without the wind striking them. Wind on the island almost never stops. The village had a system to drain water. It even had simple toilets indoors. Each home followed a similar plan. The houses had no windows. Solid walls helped keep out wind, rain, and cold. Midden soil, much like clay, rose over the walls and became the roof. The same soil made the roof. From a doorway set low, a person entered one big room. A hearth in the center gave off heat. It also gave off light. Smoke escaped by way of an opening overhead. Stone shelves stood on one wall. The shelves worked as a place to store things. A seat of stone sat in front of one object. Scientists think that object is a dresser. No one knows the full meaning of the dresser.

5People still think it mattered in every household. Beds made like stone boxes stood on both sides of the hearth. At the outer edge stood one building unlike the rest. Its hearth was larger. It had no beds. Experts suggest that building may have been where people met together. It may have been a workshop that people shared. Trees cannot grow on these islands. Because of that, the village contained no wooden objects at all. Builders chose the toughest stuff they could find. Those materials were sandstone and turf. Passageways joined the homes. Every house had its own door as well. A bar made of bone could lock the door. Combs, pins, and jewelry were among the artifacts. People had made them from the bones and teeth of animals. Sand preserved the stone structures across a long stretch of time. It also kept the objects inside whole. Those artifacts told a great deal about how people lived. Clumps of local grass served as cushions. Other plants served as cushions too. The cushions made hard beds of stone more comfortable. Tools showed how the people got food. Animal bones showed the same. These people fished. They raised sheep. They raised pigs. They grew wheat and barley.

6The site is so famous that even a fictional scientist took an interest. A 2008 film shows Indiana Jones speaking in a lecture on Skara Brae. Its title is Kingdom of the Crystal Skull. Villagers there showed real creativity. Pottery made with fine skill shows a love of beautiful things. Buttons show that love too. Jewelry shows it as well. Balls turned up among the ruins. Dice turned up too. Those finds suggest that people liked fun and games. What the ruins lack is just as interesting. Nothing found there was a weapon. Knives found there were tools only. The village appears to have lived in peace. It was a farming community. Nothing shows what finally became of the people. Nothing shows that a fight took place. Nothing in the ruins points to people fleeing an earthquake or a similar blow from nature. There is no sign that people ran for their lives. Experts have several theories about why the residents left. Some say a terrible storm drove them off. They compare that storm to the one in 1850. Others guess that blowing sand piled up on the land. The sand would have made farming harder. Another theory says the people simply moved. They may have gone to fields that produced more food.

7For now, most scholars share one conclusion. They simply do not know why the people left. People often call the ruins Scotland’s Pompeii. Skara Brae, like Pompeii, is an old village that remained well preserved. The two places differ in big ways. Disaster hit Pompeii in the year 79 ce. A volcano erupted. Thousands of people were buried quickly. Livestock was buried too. A carpet of thick ash covered them. Sand buried Skara Brae. The burial happened gradually. It did not come from one terrible event. That slow burial is the reason Skara Brae has yielded no complete skeletons. In the middle of the 1900s, scientists were not sure why the village was deserted. They did feel fairly sure about the date people first lived there. They thought Skara Brae began around 500 bce. By 1970, new technology had proved that date wrong. Scientists had found an accurate way to tell the age of some materials. The method is called carbon dating. An expert measures how much carbon is in an object. The measure can show how old the object is. Scientists tested plants that were buried at Skara Brae. They also tested fibers buried there. They learned that the settlement was far older than anyone had thought.

8The true date Skara Brae was put up is about 3200 bce. That time was the Neolithic period, also called the Stone Age. Egypt's great pyramids came after this village. Carbon dating also showed how long people stayed. People occupied the site across six centuries. An element called carbon is inside every living thing. Carbon-12 is a stable form of the element. Carbon-13 is stable too. A stable form stays the same across the years. Carbon-14 lacks that steadiness. As years pass, it breaks down. Carbon dating measures carbon-14. Skara Brae was a prehistoric village from the Stone Age. Its near-perfect condition gave experts a clearer view. They could see better how Neolithic people lived. In the Neolithic period, people began to grow crops. They also began to care for animals. Among the earliest human farms in Britain, this well-kept village is one. Its culture was strong. The culture could sustain itself. Orkney's Neolithic places are several, and this village is only a single example. The islands hold many structures from prehistoric times. The many-room tomb called Maeshowe stands on West Mainland. The tomb has many chambers. Not far off, stones known as the Standing Stones of Stenness rise in a circle. Two large slabs seem to work like a window.

9Through that opening, a person can see Maeshowe. The Neolithic village was an important find for history. In 1999, an agency of the United Nations gave it a classification. UNESCO is the short name for a United Nations body devoted to education, science, and culture. People often shorten that name to UNESCO. Skara Brae was placed on the World Heritage list by UNESCO. The name means the site was officially recognized. It was recognized as an important place in history. An international treaty protects it by law. Because the site matters so much, thousands of visitors come each year. They travel to the Orkney Islands of Scotland. Guided tours let them enter the homes. People lived in those homes fifty centuries ago. Historians keep studying the site. What historians learn here, they pass along to others. Perhaps one day they will learn why the people left. Those people abandoned a settlement beside the sea. Thousands travel here each year in hope of walking a prehistoric village at close range. A timeline can follow Skara Brae across the ages. Around 3200 bce, people built the Neolithic village. Around 2600 bce, the village was abandoned. A terrible storm later struck Orkney and uncovered the ruins.

10George Petrie later published his research on the site. In 1913, thieves raided Skara Brae. Scottish authorities took on the job of protecting the site. In 1925, a storm damaged the ancient ruins. In 1926, workers constructed a seawall. In the 1970s, carbon dating showed the true age of the village. Later, UNESCO gave Skara Brae the title of World Heritage Site. Accumulated means something has piled up as time has gone on. An artifact is an object that humans made or used long ago. Culture is a group's own ideas together with that group's own customs. To excavate means to uncover something or to dig it out. A hearth is the floor of a fireplace, or the area in front of it. Inhabited means lived in by people or by other animals. Materials are any kinds of objects used to make things. Protruding means sticking out, or reaching past an edge. A resident is a person or another animal that lives in a place. A scholar is a person with a great deal of knowledge, usually about one subject. A settlement is the home a community builds once people decide to stay. A site is simply the ground where a thing is found.

7. A Trip through Desert Latitudes

1Our expedition follows the line at twenty-five degrees north. It also explores twenty-five degrees south latitude. Those lines are written 25°N and 25°S. On the map, each of these lines circles Earth. Each one lies about 1,725 miles from the equator. That distance is also 2,775 km. One line is north of the equator. The other line is south of it. The two latitudes are far apart. Their climate is still similar. Each line sits equally far from the equator. How would you describe the climate along these lines? Here is a hint. Bring plenty of water. You will need it. The trip is called Expedition 25. You will go past the tropics. You will learn a recipe for making deserts. You will see deserts in the north. You will see deserts in the south.

2You will ask how a desert can sit beside an ocean. A closing and a word list come at the end. The subtropics hold a large share of Earth's great deserts. In Australia, a cowboy herds cattle. At 25°N and 25°S we are just outside the tropical zone. The tropics are the part of Earth closest to the equator. One edge of the tropics is the Tropic of Cancer. That line is at 23.5°N latitude. The other edge is the Tropic of Capricorn. That line is at 23.5°S latitude. The lands on this trip sit just past the tropics. They are in the subtropical zone. Near the equator, the tropical zone is hot. It is also rainy. The subtropics get very little rain. High pressure in the atmosphere is the cause. That pressure holds hot, dry air in place over the subtropics.

3The same high pressure keeps rain very low. In many places, less than ten inches fall in a year. These patterns make a band of deserts. The band circles Earth at these latitudes. People can predict where the band will be. Climb into the plane. Let us visit some of these deserts. Up high, air that is cool and dry travels outward from the equator. Rain falls in the tropics. Dry air comes back down in the subtropics. At the ground it warms up. Hot air then moves toward the equator. Along the way it picks up moisture. Moist air rises. It makes rain clouds in the tropics. Yearly rain in most of the tropics falls somewhere from 40 inches to 80 inches.

4A year of rain in many subtropical places totals under 10 inches. North Africa's Sahara is a huge sea of sand. You have been flying over northern Africa for hours. Your path is 25°N latitude. Below you is the Sahara, the largest desert on Earth. In Arabic, the word Sahara means desert. Arabic is spoken across much of North Africa. The Sahara matches the whole United States in size. Looking down from the plane, you can see dunes. Dunes are giant hills made of sand. They look like waves of gold on an ocean. Signs of people are few. The Nile River runs through the city of Cairo. Your plane lands at Cairo, Egypt. Cairo sits at 30°N latitude. As you step off the plane, grit fills your mouth. Dust stings your nose.

5Sand from the Sahara blows through the air. It covers everything. Several million people live in this large capital. The Nile flows through the middle of Cairo. For Egypt, the Nile is the main source of water. Because of the Nile, a great ancient civilization could thrive here. Its giant monuments can still be seen. They stand at the edge of Cairo. They are the Pyramids of Giza. More than four thousand years have passed since the pyramids were built. A huge stone figure called the Sphinx guards those pyramids. The Sphinx has the body of a lion. It has the head of a person. The next stop is Riyadh in Saudi Arabia. Say Riyadh as ree-ODD. Riyadh is at 24°N latitude. Like Cairo, it is hot. It is also dry. Egypt has a river.

6Saudi Arabia has no river. Much of the water here comes from wells under the ground. Some is pumped in from the sea. People in Riyadh use desalination. Desalination takes the salt out of seawater. The fresh water is used for drinking. It is also used to water crops. Arabic is spoken by most Saudi people. Most Saudi people follow Islam. Most people in Egypt speak Arabic. Most people in Egypt follow Islam. Riyadh is Saudi Arabia's capital. More than 4.8 million people live there. Ayers Rock is a large shape made of sandstone. You cross into the Southern Hemisphere. The landing is at Alice Springs, on the line of 23°S. Alice Springs sits in the heart of Australia's desert country. Aboriginal people were the first people to live in Australia.

7They settled in this area tens of thousands of years in the past. A jeep carries you over the flat red floor of the desert. The ride ends at Ayers Rock. The Anangu people call the rock Uluru. Say Uluru as oo-LOO-roo. Say Anangu as ON-ung-oo. To them, this place is sacred. Pictures on nearby rock walls tell their long history. Other people living here come from European families. They speak mostly English. Early in the 1900s, many ancestors of these families arrived at Alice Springs. They came to dig for rubies. They also came to dig for gold. Grasslands are home to most elephants. Namibia, in Africa, has some of the only elephants that live in a desert. You fly straight west across the Indian Ocean. Then you reach Namibia. The Namib Desert covers a large part of the country.

8Desert elephants live there. They walk great distances. They are looking for water holes that appear in certain seasons. You keep going west along 25°S latitude. You reach the Atacama Desert in Chile. In some parts of the Atacama, no rain has fallen for over ten years. Scientists have found mummies there. The mummies are of native people. They are nine thousand years old. Dry desert air kept them perfectly preserved. In the high Atacama, deep cracks open in the dry mud. Something may seem strange about two of these deserts. The Namib Desert lies next to an ocean. The Atacama Desert does too. In most places, ocean water would add moisture to the land beside it. That moisture would bring rain. In both of these places, cold currents run through the ocean.

9The cold stops water along the coast from evaporating. Because of that, rain clouds do not form. The Atacama Desert meets the Pacific Ocean. The Namib Desert meets the South Atlantic Ocean. In the subtropics, ocean waves crash onto shores of desert. Aboriginal people have lived well in subtropical Australia. Their life there goes back tens of thousands of years. On Expedition 25 you learned where most deserts of the world are found. Most of them lie between twenty degrees and thirty degrees of latitude. You learned some reasons these places stay dry. The reasons hold in the Northern Hemisphere. They also hold in the Southern Hemisphere. You visited cities that sit at these latitudes. I hope the trip was a good one. The path ran across subtropical lands that are desert.

10Civilizations are organized societies. Government in these societies is advanced. Religion, science, and language are advanced. Art is advanced. Learning is advanced. Climate means the weather in a place over a long time. Desalination means taking salt out of something. Seawater is the usual example. Descent means where a person comes from. It can mean family, nation, or culture. Evaporating is the change of water from a liquid into a gas. A rise in temperature causes it. On a globe, latitude lines stretch from the east toward the west. A latitude line tells the distance of a place from the equator, either to the north or to the south. Predictable means expected. It means you can tell what will happen. Preserved means kept from rotting away.

8. A Vast Land Called Russia

1Hikers walk in the mountains. Contents. Finding Russia. The People. The Land. The Past. Holidays. Meals. Closing. Word List. A map marks Europe and Asia. It marks the Arctic Ocean and the Bering Sea. It marks Estonia, Latvia, and Moscow. It marks the Sea of Okhotsk, Belarus, and Ukraine. It marks Kazakhstan, China, the Sea of Japan, and Mongolia. Russia covers a huge amount of land. The area is 16,377,742 square kilometers, or 6,323,500 square miles. No country on Earth is larger. The United States would fit into Russia almost two times. Several countries touch Russia's border. Finland and Ukraine are two neighbors in Europe. Mongolia, China, and Japan are neighbors in Asia. One more neighbor is the United States. Only 88.5 kilometers, or 55 miles, separate Russia's far eastern tip from Alaska's western coast. The Arctic Ocean lies along the north. Three seas lie along the east.

2Russia's capital is Moscow. More than twelve million people live in that city. One famous place there is the Kremlin. The Kremlin is not one building. It is a whole group. Palaces are part of the group. Government offices are part of it. Russia's president lives inside. A plaza just beyond the Kremlin is named Red Square. Visitors know both the Kremlin and Red Square. Saint Basil's Cathedral stands nearby. It is one of Russia's best-known sights. Russia's population is about 142 million. That makes it tenth in the world for number of people. Cities hold about three-fourths of the people. Moscow is one of those cities. Saint Petersburg is another. Many jobs away from the cities depend on natural resources. Coal, oil, and natural gas are found in large amounts. Energy work therefore fills a large role in the country. A large share of the world's oil comes from Russia.

3A large share of the world's natural gas comes from Russia too. Fishing matters deeply as well. Fish from Russia are sold in many countries. A great share of Earth's forests grows in Russia. Tree wood is made into lumber. Russia ranks among the top lumber countries. Cyrillic writing uses thirty-three letters. English writing uses seven fewer letters. The main language is Russian. Writers of Russian use the Cyrillic alphabet. Greek writing is the base of that alphabet. Some letters differ. Russian has sounds that Greek does not. Literature is a field where Russian people have excelled. The arts are another field. Sports are another. The Moscow Ballet is especially famous. Classical musicians are famous too. In Madrid, Spain, the picture shows the ballet rehearsing Swan Lake ahead of a show. Russian athletes stand out in several sports.

4Ice hockey is one. Soccer, gymnastics, and figure skating are others. A landform map marks the Arctic Ocean and the Bering Sea. It marks Saint Petersburg and the Kamchatka Peninsula. It marks Moscow and Oymyakon. It marks the Sea of Okhotsk and the Central Siberian Plateau. It marks the Ural Mountains, the Russian Plain, and the West Siberian Plain. It marks Lake Baikal, the Sayan Mountains, the Kulunda Steppe, and the Sea of Japan. Plains spread across the countryside. Mountains rise there too. Central Russia holds the West Siberian Plain. That plain is huge. Its area is over 2.6 million square kilometers, or 1 million square miles. The Ural Mountains rise in the west of the country. More ranges rise in the south and the east. Lake Baikal sits near the border with Mongolia. It is the world's oldest lake. It is the world's deepest lake too.

5About 20 percent of the planet's unfrozen fresh water is held in that lake. Landscapes in Russia are not all alike. The north is tundra. Tundra land is wide, flat, and frozen. South of that lies the taiga. The taiga is green forest made mostly of spruce and pine. Warmer parts of the country have other forests. Oak grows there. Maple and birch grow there too. The south has wide grasslands. Cold weather covers most of Russia. Much of the land sits as far north as Canada. The world's coldest settlement is in Russia. Winter there can fall to minus 71 degrees C, or minus 96 degrees F. Summer does come. In some places it lasts only two months. Lake Baikal's deepest point is 1,620 meters, or 5,315 ft. From 1682 to 1725, Peter the Great was Russia's czar. From 1762 to 1798, Catherine the Great led the country.

6For hundreds of years, czars, or emperors, were the rulers. Peter and Catherine are two of the best known. They were strong leaders. Under them, Russia grew into a modern power. In this same era, many farmers in Eastern Europe were serfs. Russian farmers were serfs as well. A serf worked land that belonged to someone else. Leaving was not allowed without the owner's permission. Marriage was not allowed without that permission either. Most crops had to be handed to the owner. An order from Alexander II set the serfs free. The government still treated them badly after that order. By the early 1900s, this unfairness angered many Russians. The czars lost their rule in a revolution in 1917. A new union was formed in 1922, after the revolution. Russia joined with other countries of Eastern Europe. Together they formed the USSR.

7Its full name was Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. The USSR had a plan. Government would help people become more equal. It would also face the problems that had sparked the revolution. The government grew too strong. Poverty spread because of economic trouble. Political trouble added to that poverty. December 31, 1991, was the union's last day. Russia's rulers now include a president chosen by voters, plus other leaders. Life has gotten better for many Russians. One picture shows the USSR flag. Another shows poor families in the 1920s Soviet Union. They stand in a line, waiting for loaves of bread. Christian holidays are celebrated by many Russians. Christmas is one of them. January 7, not December 25, is Christmas Day for some Russians. Easter brings shared baked goods. Hard-boiled eggs are painted. Muslim people live in Russia too, so Ramadan is a major holiday.

8Most Muslims fast during Ramadan. Fasting means no food and no drink. The fast runs from sunrise to sunset. It lasts every day for a month. June 12 is Independence Day. May 9 is Victory Day. Victory Day marks the close of World War II. Maslenitsa, said MOSS-leen-yit-sah, marks winter's end. People eat buttered pancakes called blinis, said BLEE-nees. Sleigh rides are part of the fun. Snowball fights are part of it too. A sack race for children also marks winter's end. A favorite soup is borscht. Beets give the soup its start. The soup may be hot. It may be cold. Cabbage goes in, along with other vegetables. Onions and carrots are two of them. Beets give the soup its red color. A traditional drink called kvass is made as well. Making kvass takes about two or three days. The drink tastes sour.

9Stale bread is what it is made from. Kvass is also the base of a soup called okroshka. Cucumbers are added. Sausages and salami are added. Boiled eggs are added. Summer is when people eat okroshka. It is served cold. Cities in Russia now sell many foods from other lands. Older foods remain popular. Moscow's buildings shine at night. Russia is vast. It is beautiful. Natural resources make it rich. Huge forests shape daily life. Oceans full of fish shape it too. Oil and coal under the ground matter as well. The country offers more than land and resources. Ballet is part of what it offers. Holidays are part of it. So are delicious foods. Tradition runs deep in this land. These facts come from the CIA World Factbook for 2016. The population is 142,423,773. The land covers 16,377,742 square kilometers, or 6,323,500 square miles.

10Moscow is the capital. Russian is the primary language. The primary religions are Russian Orthodox and Muslim. The currency is the ruble. Word List. Christian describes Christianity, a religion built on the life and the teachings of Jesus Christ. Czars were the men who ruled Russia before the 1917 revolution. Industry means businesses that make or sell one kind of product or service. Landscapes are the features you can see across a whole area of land. Muslim describes people who follow Islam. Natural resources are useful things found in nature, such as minerals and forests, that people value or turn into products. Revolution means a government is forced out and a different government takes its place. Settlement means a new place where people make a home, or where a community is set up. Traditional describes a custom that people have kept for a long time.

9. A Woods Map and How Maps Work

1The parts of this book come in this order. First, what maps do. Next, the key and what a map holds. Then scale. Then landmarks and symbols. Then the kinds of maps. Then physical maps, political maps, and data maps. Then a send-off for travelers. Then a map you make yourself. Last come a word list and a word finder. The woods beside my house are the place I drew. Trails appear on that drawing. Roads appear on it too. So do the buildings near my house. Read with a copy of that drawing in your hands. Think of a map as a picture someone drew of a place. The picture tells where each thing sits next to the others. The usual view is from high above, the way the ground looks from an airplane. That overhead view is also how map work is done now. A photograph may come from an airplane. It may come from a satellite instead. The person who turns that photo into a map is a cartographer (car-TOG-ra-fer). Planes did not exist yet. Spaceships did not exist yet. People drew maps anyway. Memory was their tool. They kept in mind the place of each thing. They kept in mind the distance between things. They kept in mind the direction from one thing to another. Surveying was another way to make a map. In surveying, math does the measuring. Distance is one thing those measures give. Direction is the other. Small maps are often still made that way. The result is an accurate map. Survey work on a wide region is slow. Memory and guessing were how I made my own map. The job was very hard. A few sizes on it may still be wrong.

2Even so, the trails by my house would not have to stay a maze. A lost walker could follow this map back out. In the picture, a surveyor takes measures with his equipment. Now, the key. A map is rarely a true-to-life picture. My trees do not look the way they would in a photo or a painting. My grass does not look that way either. My buildings do not look that way either. Symbols are what cartographers draw instead. A symbol is quicker to draw. A symbol is quicker to read. Look in a corner of most maps and you will find a box. People call that box the key. Each symbol is explained there. My key covers the woods. It covers my neighborhood too. Roads for cars are the double lines. Walking trails are the single lines. Buildings are the boxes.
