Water is the slanted lines. Inside the key is a star with four points. People call it the compass rose. North is one direction it marks. South is another. East is another. West is another. On most maps the top side is north. The bottom side is south. The right side is east. The left side is west. My rose does not follow that habit. The top of my map is northeast. I set it that way because northeast is the direction my house faces. That is the way I picture the neighborhood. Cities usually get their names written on a map. Roads get names too. Trails get names too. Rivers and oceans get names too. Every trail on my map has its name. Every road has its name. Every building has its name.

3Search the drawing for Hunter's Ravine Trail. Search it for the high school as well. GPS tracking rides on some airplanes. During the flight, that gear shows where the plane is. Two cities marked on the scale map are New York and San Francisco. Scale answers a size question. How big is the paper map next to the real ground? Two units are set side by side on most maps. The United States map here uses a bar for that job. Marks and numbers sit on the bar. Real-land distance is the upper row. Distance on the paper is the lower row. Centimeters are the unit of that lower row. One of those centimeters stands for nearly 500 kilometers on the real ground. Suppose the whole United States were drawn as large as my woods map. Every building in the country would have to appear. Every gap between those buildings would have to appear too. The sheet would stretch for hundreds of kilometers. A pocket could not hold it, even folded. A cartographer who draws a wide region chooses a smaller scale. The United States map here is a very small scale. Zoom the view onto a tighter area and the scale grows. One map does that for the northeast of the United States. My woods sit in that region. The region covers about one fourth of the country. The scale is about four times larger because of that. City names on that map include Augusta and Albany. They include New York and Detroit. They include Harrisburg and Columbus. Vermont is the state drawn next. After that comes the county where I live. A county is only one piece of a state.

4Watch the upper numbers on the scale. A smaller mapped area brings smaller numbers there. Pittsford is one name on the county map. Procter is another. Rutland County is named. Vermont is named. Here is a distance-and-area task. 1. On the United States map, measure the centimeters from New York across to San Francisco. 2. Learn how many kilometers belong to each centimeter. Multiply the measure you took by that number. 3. What distance separates New York from San Francisco? 4. On the Vermont map, measure the state's length in centimeters. Turn that measure into kilometers with the scale. 5. Measure how wide the state is. Width is not the same from the top edge to the bottom edge. Take the measure across the middle so you get an average. Turn that width into kilometers with the scale. 6. Multiply length by width. About how many square kilometers is Vermont? Landmarks and symbols come next. Important objects often get a place on a map. A landmark may be special. It may matter a lot. It may help a traveler find the way. It may simply be a thing the map user hopes to locate. My water tower is one landmark. Seeing it tells me that my road is close. City maps treat important buildings as landmarks. A school can be one. A hospital can be one. A courthouse can be one. Symbols stand in for most of those important objects. My water tower is a circle crossed by slanted lines. A hospital on a city map might be shown as a cross in blue. The cross might be red instead. A symbol can also mark an important area. It can mark an event.

5It can mark something no one can see. On a map about history, an explosion picture can mark a battle site. A gun picture can do that job too. On a weather map, colder air on the move is a blue line carrying triangles. Read the key when you need the meaning of a symbol. The key also helps you name the object. Weather keys use letters and marks. H can mean high pressure. L can mean low pressure. A cold front may be shown. A warm front may be shown. Precipitation may be shown. Use decides what a map includes. A boat trip needs rivers on the map. It needs lakes. It needs oceans. Land features are not required. A car trip needs roads. It needs towns. It needs cities. Farms are not required. Forests are not required. Hiking trails are not required. Physical, political, and data are the three basic map kinds. Natural features belong on a physical map. Rivers are one example. Mountains are another. Plants are another. Weather is another. People are the subject of a political map. Roads show up there. Cities show up there. Buildings show up there. Countries show up there. Other human-made things show up there. A single map can mix both kinds of facts. Pictures, not symbols, make a pictorial map. The next page has one of a ski area. That ski area sits atop a small mountain. Ski lodges are among the buildings it draws. It also draws woods that are unsafe for skiing. Skiers need the people-made facts. They need the natural facts too. Information is the job of the third kind, the data map. Numbers are a common form of that information.

6People call number-facts statistics. My own map will stand in for several kinds on the pages ahead. I will also show what each kind is for. One picture is a ski map for Killington and Pico. Physical maps are the next topic. A topographic map is a common physical map. Elevation is what it shows. Elevation means the height of the land, high or low. Neighboring lines differ by one unit. A meter can be that unit. Steep rise or steep fall packs the lines close together. Flat land spreads the lines far apart. Part of my map is now a topographic map. Rising ground shows on it. Falling ground shows on it. The small mountain under my woods starts to show its form. Wilderness travel is a good use for a topographic map. Roads may be missing out there. Signs may be missing too. Imagine being lost near Hunter's Ravine Trail. Could my map get you back to Pit Trail? North is hard to judge with no compass. A trail map by itself, with no compass rose, makes the choice of direction very hard. Land shape can be matched to the shape drawn on a topographic map. That match suggests where you are. The direction you have been walking is part of the clue. Elevation can be shown in other ways. Color does that job on a relief map. High ground is usually a light color. Low ground is usually a dark color. Shading on part of my map makes that part a relief map. A world relief map is a familiar sight. Major mountain chains appear on it. Some relief maps invent shadows. Those shadows seem to come from mountains.

7They seem to come from valley walls too. Plants are the subject of a vegetation map. Color can stand for each kind of plant. A pattern can stand for a kind of plant instead. My colored map marks grass. It marks shrubs and bushes. It marks evergreen trees. It marks blackberries. It marks trees that drop their leaves, and maples and birches are examples. The key tells the pattern apart from the others. Berry spots sit along Old Orchard Trail. Can the map help you find them? Crops appear on some other vegetation maps. Corn is one crop they may show. Apples are another. Birch Trail has trees along both sides. What kind are they? Political maps are next. Roads, and the places those roads reach, fill a road map. Getting from place to place is what it does best. Part of Auckland, a city in New Zealand, is drawn as a road map here. College Rifles Park is one park on it. Abbotts Park is another. How would a walker go from the first park to the second? How many turns would that walk need? Which way would the turns go? A visit to Auckland could be easier with this map in hand. My woods map works a bit like a road map. Its paths link one spot to another. Start at the water tower. Try to reach the field that belongs to Mister Taranovitch. Control of land, or ownership of land, is what a boundary map shows. On a world boundary map, each country is drawn. On a United States boundary map, each state is drawn. Counties can fill it too. I redrew my map as a boundary map on this page.

8Ownership is what it shows now. People can learn how the land may be used. They can also learn who might be on it. Mister Taranovitch owns parts of the woods. Hunting on his land is something he does not like. Hunters can read this boundary map. It shows the ground where hunting is not allowed. Numbers are the kind of information a data map carries. A news map of this sort can show how each area voted. A weather map of this sort can show the centimeters of rain that fell in each area. Nature can be the subject. Human life can be the subject too. I redrew the trails on one copy of my woods map. Walker counts are what the new lines record. A trail drawn with four lines has 30 to 40 people on it every week. A trail drawn with one line has 5 people or fewer every week. The key explains the rest of the trail marks. Heavy erosion is something you could guess from this map. A quiet walk, with few other people, is something you could plan from it. A newt picture is the mark on another copy. I use it for the red newts I notice in each area. Five red newts sit behind every one of those pictures. The copy can show whether that population is going up. It can show whether it is going down. It can also point you toward trails where many red newts can be seen. Almost any information can be drawn as a data map. Newspapers are one place to look. Magazines are another. The Internet is another. Read the key every time.

9Color gets its meaning there. So does each symbol. Finding the way is why this backpacker carries a map. Safe travels. A place you have never seen can still be known through a map. Finding the way is one gift of a map. Learning what you might see is another gift. Earth has many places, and maps come in just as many kinds. Things worth seeing are just as many. Look at the maps near you. A wonderful journey can be planned from them. The journey might be a real trip. It might live only in your mind. Your turn to make a map. Pick an important place and draw the way you go there from home. School could be that place. The snack bar could be that place. A friend's home could be that place. Gather graph paper. Gather a pencil that has an eraser. Gather a surface you can write on. 1. Put your home on the paper. A square can stand for it. A small drawing of the house can stand for it. 2. Walk toward the important place. From the home picture, draw a line that leaves in the same direction as your walk. 3. Distance can be guessed. Count steps along the first street. Minutes can be counted instead. A later street that takes twice the steps gets a line twice as long. The same rule fits a street that takes twice the minutes. A fresh sheet of paper is fine if you run out of room. 4. Corners come in different kinds. Copy the kind you turned. Copy the direction of that turn. 5. As you walk a street, write its name on the line.

10Add landmarks. A church can be one. A tree you know well can be one. A store you know well can be one. 6. When you arrive, draw the important place. 7. Color the map with markers and with crayons. Put in more detail. Hand the map to a friend. A person in your family can receive it instead. Ask that person to reach your important place by using only the map. Word list. Cartographer means the person who makes maps. A relief map lets color or shading stand for elevation. The compass rose is the pointed mark that places the directions on a map. Scale compares the size of one thing with the size of another. On a map, it compares the real area with the paper. Elevation means how high the land is. The key is the map part that tells the meaning of symbols. It tells the meaning of colors too. Surveying uses math to measure how far apart objects are and the angle between them. An object that guides you is called a landmark. A topographic map lets lines stand for elevation. A pictorial map uses pictures where other maps would use symbols. Word finder. Look through the book for these topics. Political maps. Relief maps. Road maps. Scale. Surveying. Topographic maps. Vegetation. Boundary maps. The cartographer, or mapmaker. The compass rose. Data maps. The key. Physical maps. Pictorial maps. The extra sheet titled My Map was drawn by Rachel Lawson. Keep that sheet apart from the book. Do not fasten the map into the pages. The woods drawing stays its own sheet while you read, and the book closes with that sheet still separate.

10. Animals That Stand on Hooves

1Contents. What Hoofed Animals Are. Ungulates With an Odd Number of Toes. Ungulates With an Even Number of Toes. A Closing Look. Word List. Topic List. Few creatures on Earth move with more grace than hoofed animals. They are large. They are powerful. Their bodies are built for speed. They are beautiful. They are fascinating. People admire them in the wild. People have also visited them in zoos. People have hunted them. People have kept them because they give milk. People have kept them for meat. People have kept them for wool. People have kept them for labor. People have kept them for transportation. People have kept them for companionship. A picture shows a gazelle. All hoofed animals belong to one group of mammals. That group is called ungulates. The word is said as UN-gyu-luts. An older group is the family line of every ungulate alive now. That older group of hoofed mammals is extinct. It lived 65 million years ago. Keratin is the material in an ungulate's hoof. The keratin covers their toes. A hoof is like a giant toenail. The hoof protects the foot. A picture shows horses at work. For thousands of years, humans have put horses to work. Most hoofed animals are herbivores. A herbivore is a plant eater. Many hoofed animals are food for carnivores.

2A carnivore is a meat eater. Getting away fast enough is one of their hardest jobs. They must avoid being killed by predators. Those predators include humans. They include lions. They include wolves. They include hyenas. Long legs help hoofed animals, since they must run. The legs are strong. Their feet are strong too. The skeletons of hoofed animals have a special shape. That shape helps them run quickly. Five separate bones sit in a human foot. Those bones connect the toes to the ankle. Many hoofed animals have one long bone instead. That bone is solid. It connects the toes, or the hoof, to the ankle. The solid bone is called a cannon bone. A cannon bone makes the legs longer. Longer legs help the animals run farther. They also help the animals run faster. Cannon bones make the legs more solid. They make the legs more stable. The legs can better support the animal's weight. Two different groups are how scientists sort hoofed animals. The groups are based on the toes. One group walks on an odd number of toes. The other group walks on an even number of toes. Each group will get its own look. Each group includes famous animals, and we will meet some of them. Odd-toed ungulates include rhinoceroses. They include horses, zebras, and donkeys.

3They include several other animals. Each rhino foot carries three toes. Ungulates that resemble horses put weight on a single toe per foot. That single toe is their hoof. Pictures show a rhino and a horse. Warm lands in many parts of the world are home to most of these animals. They live in forests. They live in grasslands. They live in deserts. Grasses are part of their food. So are other plants. That food is difficult to digest. Their stomachs have tiny bacteria. The bacteria help break the food down. Pictures show a zebra and a donkey. Horses are the first odd-toed animals to meet here. Dry grasslands hold the only horses alive today that are truly wild. Those grasslands are in Eurasia. Other horses live in North America. They live in South America. They live in Australia. People call those horses wild. They are actually domesticated breeds. They escaped human control. Then they grew wild. A horse can stay alive even when food is scarce. They can survive with little water. Even then, grazing takes most of their hours. They need enough grass to survive. They need enough nutrients too. Wagons were pulled by horses in the years before machines were common. They plowed fields. In modern times, people who love horses keep them for companionship. They keep them for riding.

4They keep them for racing. A picture shows racehorses. Their speed thrills us. Zebras come next. Africa is the home of every wild zebra. They mostly eat tall grasses. Without those famous stripes, a zebra would look much like a horse. Lions are the chief danger to zebras. Hyenas are enemies too. Wild dogs are enemies too. Humans also hunt zebras for their skins. Zebras come in three main kinds. They are plains zebras, desert zebras, and mountain zebras. Serious danger of extinction faces some zebra species. Bold stripes, black mixed with white, help a zebra mix into the herd. The blending works especially well when the whole herd is running. A predator has trouble picking one zebra out of that mix. A predator has a harder time choosing one zebra. No zebra's stripes match another zebra's, just as no human fingerprint matches another. No two zebras have stripe patterns that match. Rhinos are rare. They are unusual. A picture can show that. Parts of Africa are the rhino's native home. It is native to parts of Asia. Serious danger of extinction also faces the rhino, another ungulate. Wild land now holds only a small number of rhinos. Protected land is where most of them live now. That land includes national parks. It includes nature preserves.

5Rhinos live on plains. They live in forested areas. They live in swampy areas. There they eat grasses. They eat leaves. They eat other plants. Among land mammals, only one kind is larger than the rhino. Only elephants are larger. Rhinos are easy to recognize. They have horns on their noses. They have large heads. Dark, leathery skin covers their huge bodies. Keratin is what a rhino horn is made from. Hooves are made of that same material. One horn is enough for some kinds of rhinos. Other kinds have two horns. Deer belong to the even-toed ungulates. So do cattle, sheep, and goats. They include antelope. They include camels. They include hippos. They include giraffes. Two toes per foot are all that some even-toed ungulates have. Camels are one example. Four toes per foot show up on other animals in this group. Hippos are one example. A picture shows a camel. This even-toed group is among the biggest groups of mammals on Earth. Only two continents are outside their native range. Those two are Australia and Antarctica. Scientists call them successful animals. Successful means they have reproduced. They have spread out. Many kinds of environments have shaped how they live. A picture shows a hippo. Pigs and hogs are called swine. Swine are intelligent omnivores. An omnivore eats both plants and animals.

6They have round bodies. The bodies are stocky. They have long heads. The snout on that head can bend. They have tusks that point up. Four toes grow on each of their feet. The middle two toes are the largest. Europe was one of the first wild homes of swine. They lived in Asia. They lived in northern Africa. A picture shows a warthog. People now raise swine all over the world. They raise them as a food animal. People also hunt swine in the wild. Giraffes live in the grasslands of Africa. They have short horns made of bone. The horns are permanent. Furry skin covers the horns. That skin is never shed. Giraffes are famous for necks that are unusually long. They are famous for their pattern of spots. They are famous for long tongues. The tongues are blue-gray. Male giraffes test themselves against other males. They wrestle with their necks. They hit each other with their heads. Hippos are large animals. They are heavy. They live in Africa. Water is where they pass most of their hours. They do not really swim. Lake bottoms are where they walk. They walk on the bottoms of rivers. Their feet are slightly webbed. Each foot has four toes. They have huge teeth that point up. They eat grasses.

7They eat leaves. They eat fallen fruit. They eat other plants. Most of that food grows underwater. In a single day, an adult hippo may eat as much as 136 kilograms of plants. That amount is 300 pounds. Picture yourself eating over 1,200 veggie burgers before the day ends. The hippo's meal is that large. Camels are large herbivorous animals. They have long necks. The necks curve. A camel's back carries either one hump or two. They have two toes on each foot. Camels with one hump live in deserts. Those deserts are in the Middle East. They are in India. They are in North Africa. Deserts hold the two-humped camels. Windy grasslands hold them too. Those lands are in central Asia. Scarce food is a problem both kinds of camels can handle. They are well suited to scarce water. Fat is stored inside a camel's humps. This fat helps them survive long periods without food. Wild land now holds only a small number of camels. People keep most of them to carry packs. People also use one-humped camels for riding. Pronghorn antelopes are herbivores. North America's grasslands are their home. Males have permanent horns with one spike. Females have those horns too. Bone is the material inside the horns. A layer of fused hairs covers the horns. That layer is shed each year.

8Pronghorns are very fast. A healthy adult has no trouble running faster than a predator. The greatest danger arrives during the first two months after birth. In those months, coyotes kill many fawns. Inside the deer family, the moose is the largest member. Those antlers may reach the weight of a typical child of 11. In one day, those antlers may add as much as 25 millimeters. That growth is about 1 inch a day. Deer include elk. They include moose. They include caribou. Deer are herbivores. Some deer are grazers. A grazer eats mostly grass. Most deer are browsers. A browser eats leaves. A browser eats shoots. A browser eats twigs. A browser eats other plant parts. Deer are found in grasslands. They are found in forests. They are found in rainforests. They are found in tundra. They live in these places around the world. Many deer migrate when the seasons change. They move in order to find food. Most male deer grow antlers. Antlers are made of bone. While the antlers grow, furry skin covers them. That skin is called velvet. Antler growth starts ahead of the mating season. They fall off after the mating season. They grow again the following year. Female antlers appear on caribou, and on no other kind of deer.

9Horns come in many shapes. They come in many sizes. A set of pictures moves clockwise from the top left. The pictures show a Texas longhorn steer. They show a bighorn sheep. They show a kudu antelope. They show goats. Shape differs a great deal among cattle, sheep, goats, and antelopes. They vary widely in coloring. All of them grow permanent horns. Bone is the material inside the horns. A layer of keratin covers the bone. All the males in this group have horns. Some of the females have horns. Every horn in this group is one spike and nothing more. The horns can be simple in shape. They can be curved. They can be spiral. Antelopes often have horns with an elaborate shape. Milk is one reason people keep many tame animals from this group. They are kept for meat. They are kept for wool. Ungulates have bodies that let them live in many different places. Their ways of living help them do that too. People raise many ungulates in great numbers. Swine, sheep, and cattle provide food. They provide milk. They provide hides. Many wild ungulates are endangered. The rhino is one example. Some of these animals survive only in captivity. Others are at risk of the same fate. The risks include environmental destruction. They include hunting.

10They include other threats. Habitat preservation can help these amazing animals. Respect for life can help them too. Survival into later years becomes possible for them. A picture shows wild horses running free. That sight is becoming rare. A browser feeds on twigs, shoots, leaves, and other parts of plants. Hoofed animals have one long foot bone. That bone is the cannon bone. Carnivores are animals that eat only meat. An animal raised so people can use it is called domesticated. Fused means joined together. Grazers are animals that feed on grass. They also feed on other plants that grow near the ground. Herbivores are animals that eat only plants. Some animal bodies make a strong material called keratin. It makes up hair. It makes up hooves. It makes up claws. It makes up feathers. It makes up fingernails. An omnivore's meals include plants and also other animals. Successful means having the result that was wanted. It can also mean ending in success. Ungulates are animals with hooves. Topics in this book include antelope. They include camels. They include cattle. They include deer. They include donkeys. They include giraffes. They include goats. They include hippos. They include horses. They include the moose. They include the pronghorn antelope. They include rhinoceroses. They include sheep. They include swine. They include zebras.

11. Anime from Early Art to Today

1Hayao Miyazaki is a Japanese animator. He is also a director, a producer, and a screenwriter. He is an author and a manga artist. In 2014 he talks with the press at Studio Ghibli. He co-founded that studio. This book has these parts. Introduction. Art for All. From Curious Sketches to Comics. Cartoons Spring to Life. War Brings Sorrow and Lessons. Anime Today. Words to Know. Cave paintings at Lascaux, in France, tell old stories. Clay tablets from Mesopotamia tell old stories too. The cave art is the large picture. The tablets sit in a smaller inset. Introduction Pictures came long before words. Art was how early people told stories. They used it to pass along information. Cave paintings from ancient times did this. Stone carvings did it too. Each image showed the world as that artist understood it. Later, languages grew. Symbols carried ideas. Words carried ideas. Art still stayed central to storytelling. That remains true now. A story can sit in a still drawing. It can also move, through animated figures in cartoons and in video games. One storytelling art comes from Japan. Japan is an island nation in Asia. People call the art anime.

2It has grown popular all over the world. Pictures for Everyone The path toward anime began over two hundred years back. Large scrolls held most Japanese artwork before the nineteenth century. Scroll art demanded careful attention. The labor took time. The price climbed. Payment was possible only for people in Japan who were wealthy. A colored woodblock print needed a separate block for every color. Some pictures used twenty blocks to finish one image. A famous piece of manga art illustrates a well-known fable. The artist is Katsushika Hokusai. The fable's title is The Blind Men and the Elephant. A fresh kind of art arrived in 1814. People called it manga. Hands and paper were the tools for those sketches. A well-known artist used them to teach students. Students passed the sketches around. Clever drawings soon spread among the public. Manga could be made faster than a scroll. It could be made for less money. Art was open to everyone. Word Wise Manga joins two Japanese words. Man means curious. Ga means sketches. Side by side, they match the English word cartoon. Katsushika Hokusai was first to use the term.

3He used it for the comical drawings in his own sketchbooks. Sketches Turn into Comics By the late 1800s, manga had a path of its own. Trade at Japanese ports increased. British merchants arrived. American merchants arrived. Newspapers from their home countries came with them. Cartoon styles in those papers became a study for Japanese manga artists. They started using story panels set in a series. That layout entered their own art. Faces soon showed feelings that Western pictures had already used. As the twentieth century turned, many newspapers in Japan carried manga. Political cartoons poked fun at the news of the day. Comic strips amused children. They amused adults. The tales were simple and funny. Readers liked these pictures. A manga strip in a newspaper looks like a comic strip from the West. Cartoons Start to Move Another kind of media arrived with the new century. Motion pictures arrived. Studios in the United States began making movies. Studios in other Western nations did the same. Crowds packed theaters for the new show. Films soon reached theaters in more countries. Japan was one of them. The earliest movies were short. They were black and white.

4They were silent. No recorded speech played. Musicians in the theater played as the film ran. Words on the screen explained the action. They also explained what people in the story said. Actors could not be heard. They had to show feeling in other ways. Silent acting was still highly dramatic. Faces went wild. Actions went wild. In the 1917 film Patria, actors use gestures that are overly dramatic. The gestures carry the emotions of their characters. Cartoonists everywhere were fascinated by movies. Many wanted films of their own. American illustrators learned how to turn still sketches into pictures that moved. Walt Disney was one of them. Max Fleischer was another. Popular comic characters soon came alive on a big screen. The first animated movies lasted only a few minutes. The characters did not talk. Music played. Movement told the tale. Expressions told it too. Live actors in silent films had worked the same way. Manga artists in Japan soon made moving films of their own. Bold faces on manga characters suited the big expressions a silent story needed. People called the cartoons animēshon. The word comes from the English word animation.

5Later the word became anime. A Note on Music Live players made the music before sound tracks and recorded talk existed. Sometimes one player sat at a piano and followed the action. A full orchestra played at other times. Two jobs belonged to the music. First, it covered the loud noise of the projector. Second, it kept the crowd excited about the story on screen. Better technology brought color to Western cartoons. Sound tracks came too. Characters could speak. American cartoonists of the 1930s tried for human figures that looked more alive. New camera methods made backgrounds look almost real. That realistic style shows up in a Disney film. It was the studio's first animated movie at full length. Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs is the title. Sound reached Japanese anime not long after that film. It did not copy the realistic look of Western cartoons. Filmmakers borrowed a method from full-length Japanese movies. A long, still camera view would jump suddenly to a close-up. The fast switch felt very dramatic. Anime artists also kept drawing in the black-and-white style. Multiplane cameras added help. They made animated films look as if they had depth.

6A Look of Its Own The appearance of anime is distinct. Backgrounds carry a lot of detail. Characters often burst with energy. Expressions are exaggerated. Gestures are exaggerated. Action is often shown from angles that feel extreme. Western cartoons do not use those angles. Eyes matter most of all. Large eyes make a character seem childlike. They also make the character seem trustworthy. Smaller eyes pulled into a squint signal sneakiness. Tiny eyes signal evil. Eye shape and size do not stay fixed. Embarrassment brings a blush across the nose. Embarrassment looks stronger if the character scratches behind the head. Anger can show as blue lines across the face. It can show as narrowed eyes. It can show as bulging veins. It can show as drops of sweat. Hair has its own anime look. Color is often bright. Styles are unusual. The shape shifts to show movement. It shifts to show emotion. Picture labels mark the feelings embarrassed, happy, sad, and angry. War, Sorrow, and Lessons Cost helped freeze the anime look in place. New ways of filming were expensive. World War II was another reason. The war began in 1939.

7Leaders in Japan wanted support from everyone. They tried to build national pride. Movies from other countries were banned. Cartoons from other countries were banned. Only art that praised selected Japanese values was allowed. Refusal of those rules sent some animators out of the country. Other artists still made work and put it out where officials would not see. Capture meant punishment. Posters, including one shown in this book, pushed people to back their government against Japan's enemies. The war ended in a terrible way for Japan. Surrender came in 1945. Before that day, nearly two million Japanese people died. Atomic bombs destroyed the people and the city of Hiroshima. They destroyed the people and the city of Nagasaki. The events struck the Japanese people hard. They struck the art hard too. Lighthearted fun in anime gave way to serious themes. Manga artists sent messages through their work. Anime artists did the same. The messages spoke of peace. They spoke of justice. They spoke of freedom. A technology of the 1950s carried those messages farther. The technology was television. Anime reached a wider audience. Home became a place to watch cartoons.

8A manga comic book was the source of one beloved show. Osamu Tezuka drew it. The star was Mighty Atom, a robot boy. Rockets took the place of feet. Danger threatened the world, and the show sent him out to stop it. In Japan, Mighty Atom rose to stand among the most popular shows on television. The 1960s brought it to the United States as a hit, retitled Astro Boy. That success opened the door for more anime shows. The new shows were called mecha. Teens appeared in them. Giant robots appeared too. Monsters threatened the world, and the teens and robots fought to stop them. Popularity came to the mecha show Mazinger Z. Viewers in Japan saw it during the 1970s. Astro Boy first aired on New Year's Day in 1963. Anime Now One habit of modern anime matches manga. Characters and plots are built for a chosen audience. Shonen means young boy in Japanese. Its plots hold action. They hold comedy. Japan first showed the popular shonen series Dragon Ball Z during 1989. Stations around the world still show it. The run lasted from 1989 to 2003. Shojo means young girl in Japanese.

9Early shojo plots stayed on emotions. They stayed on relationships. The stories changed. Characters grew more active. Romance entered the plots. Adventure entered them. Sailor Moon, from the 1990s, is a classic shojo series. The artist is Naoko Takeuchi. Special powers come to a girl. Earth is what she guards, against forces that are evil. At least three films use the Sailor Moon character. She appears in thirty-nine video games. During the 1980s, studios in Japan began making anime films. The work continued in the 1990s. Hits in many countries followed. Hayao Miyazaki's 1984 release was Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind. The film did very well. A young princess has to rescue the planet she lives on. Theaters received the anime Spirited Away in 2001. A young girl enters the spirit world. Hayao Miyazaki directed it. Praise for the film was strong. The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature went to it later. Earnings since the 2001 opening have passed $396 million for Spirited Away. Anime also matters in the newest media of the twenty-first century. Favorite characters step into video games. Astro Boy is one.

10Digimon is one. Fighters from Dragon Ball Z are others. A player steers what the characters do. A button push sends them on missions. Long-ago figures acted out tales of adventure and daring. Images on a screen do that same work. Anime's lively characters push the art of modern storytelling to a new height. Words to Know Animated describes something made from drawings shown in a series so they seem to move. Lighthearted means cheerful, hopeful, or free of worry. Manga means comic books and illustrated novels from Japan. Anime is a Japanese style of animation for film and for television. Merchants are people who buy goods, trade them, or sell them. Banning means declaring that something is not allowed. Panels are the single boxes in a comic. People also call those boxes frames. Dramatic means sudden or exciting, or full of action or feeling. A scroll is a long roll. Paper or parchment can make it. People write on it or draw on it. Expressions are looks on a face that show feelings. Sketches are drawings made quickly and roughly. Illustrations are pictures or drawings that explain writing or decorate it.

12. April First, a Day for Pranks

1Contents. Pranking Fun. Why April First. Around the World. Famous Foolery. Company Tricks. Online Pranks. Closing. Word List. A loose lid on a saltshaker is a common joke for this day. Early spring has arrived. A bowl of chili looks delicious and ready. It needs only a pinch of salt. The shaker top is unscrewed, and you do not know it. Salt piles over the chili and buries it. An April Fools joke has made you its victim. Many countries mark April Fools Day. The date is the first of April, or a day close to it, every year. Practical jokes, called pranks, are treated as all right on this one day. Grease on a doorknob is a popular prank. Swapping salt into the sugar bowl is another. Friends may be talked into silly errands. One errand is a search for plaid paint. Another is a search for a screwdriver made for the left hand. Inventing fresh tricks is a large share of the enjoyment. Once the victim sees the trick, the old shout is April Fools.

2That shout is traditional. April 1 may bring a rude awakening, so plan for it. Nobody knows for certain why this fun sits on the first day of April. Historians think it began as a welcome to spring. Weather then is hard to predict. That shifting weather fooled many people. A second well-known idea places the start in the 1500s. The calendar most of us use now was brought in during those years. New Year's Day changed its place. It left the start of April. January 1 became the new date. People who kept celebrating on April 1 were labeled April fools, according to this idea. A legend puts another start in Gotham, a town in England. King John meant to take the villagers' land. He meant to take their property too. The villagers acted as if insanity had struck them. They hoped the act would drive the king off. Madness, in that time, was believed to spread from person to person.

3One trick tied a wheelbarrow to a tree. They called the wheelbarrow rabid. The point was to keep it from biting anybody. The 1700s and the 1800s saw a favorite prank at England's Tower of London. Posters announced a ceremony named Washing the Lions. No real lions were there, which was lucky. Days of foolishness near the opening of April appear in many older cultures. Ancient Romans kept a holiday called Hilaria until about ad 476. The holiday marked the seasonal return of longer spring days after a dark winter. People rejoiced in disguises. Games were played. Pranks were played. Late in the twelfth century, parts of medieval Europe kept the Feast of Fools. Revelers picked a Lord of Misrule. He was a pretend ruler who led the party. Followers dressed in disguise and joined in. People could poke fun at real leaders. The custom lasted into the sixteenth century. Bans were tried again and again. April Fools Day is not celebrated the same way in every land today.

4Only some of the celebrations are described here. Not every area of the United Kingdom lets jokes run past midday. Some people say the jokes must stop then. Scotland lets the fun run for two days. On the first day, a friend may be sent on a foolish errand. A sealed letter is handed over. The carrier thinks the letter asks for help. The words inside are Dinna laugh, dinna smile. Hunt the gowk another mile. A gowk is a cuckoo. In clearer words, the reader should not laugh and should not smile. The naive carrier should be sent yet another mile. That carrier is passed to the next person. The chain goes on until the trick is understood. Day two brings more practical jokes. The targets are innocent people. A map shows the Atlantic Ocean beside a cuckoo, or gowk. Other parts of Europe also keep April Fish. Canada keeps it too. France often calls its April 1 custom April Fish. The fish stands for someone easy to catch.

5That person is easy to fool. A paper fish is the tool. It is taped to a back when the joker is not seen. Some newspapers in France print a made-up story on this day. Clues are left so the story seems a little fishy. A map shows France, Canada, the United States, the Pacific Ocean, and Brazil. Tricks in the United States may fill the whole day. Telling a friend that class will not meet is a classic trick. Punching holes in a water bottle is another. Missing class earns the name April fool. A surprise shower earns that name too. Oil on a doorknob is another favorite. Food coloring may go into the milk in the refrigerator. Plastic bugs are a trick that stays fresh. They turn up in food and in beds. They turn up in ice cube trays and on chairs. Any spot where a reaction is likely will do. Brazil calls April 1 Dia da mentira, which means Lie Day.

6Jokes there are called brincadeiras, said breen-kah-DAY-rahs. People play them on one another. Mischievous lies last all day. A newspaper in Brazil is said to have begun this ritual in 1828. A false headline was printed. It claimed that Brazil's emperor had died. A major paper in Jordan ran a front-page story on April 1, 2010. Three spaceships, the story said, had come down in the desert. The spot was outside a town in the east of Jordan. April Fools tricks were new to some people there. Fear was real. The mayor thought about moving everyone out. The town held thirteen thousand people. An apology later came from the editor. A map shows Iran and Jordan. Iran and Afghanistan are the only places that use the ancient Iranian, or Persian, calendar. Day thirteen of that new year is Sizdah Bedar, said seez-DAH be-DAR. The name means getting rid of thirteen. The date lands near April 1. People have kept this tradition since 536 bc. Picnics fill Sizdah Bedar.

7Pranks and fun fill it too. It may be the oldest joke day anyone knows. A few April Fools events have also left a mark on history. In 1957, a BBC television program in the United Kingdom told viewers about a spaghetti tree in Switzerland. The show was Panorama. Most days it was a serious look at important world issues. This broadcast was different. Viewers watched people pull spaghetti down off trees. A Swiss family was shown at its yearly spaghetti harvest. Hundreds of viewers phoned the BBC after the show. They wanted to know how to grow spaghetti trees of their own. The advice was to set a small sprig of spaghetti into a tin of tomato sauce. Then they should hope for the best. Hoax stories are also printed by big companies and by the media, to fool the public. Taco Bell made a claim in 1996, on the first day of April. It said it had made a purchase. The purchase, it claimed, was the Liberty Bell.

8That bell is a famous treasure of the United States. A new name was planned: the Taco Liberty Bell. Lots of people believed it. A later statement had to correct the story. The bell was safe. It was not offered for sale. Burger King ran a full-page ad in 1998. The ad sold a burger for left-handed eaters. The design, the company said, was special. Food sat in the bun in a balanced way so a left hand could eat more easily. Some buyers ordered the new burger. Others demanded the usual burger for the right hand. Can you see any difference? Jokes for this day move fast online. Google has a name for these jokes. The Google Gulp, announced in 2005, is one of the best-known hoaxes. It was a drink. Drinking it was supposed to make a consumer smarter. Twitter made an announcement in 2013. Tweets that used vowels would cost users more. Vowels could be added back for an extra fee each month. A blog post explained the plan.

9The fee, it said, would push people toward more efficient communication. Pokémon Go itself started as an Internet hoax in 2014. A spoof tool was advertised on Google Maps. It would locate the greatest Pokémon Master in the world. The master had to be able to move through tall grass and capture wild creatures. The first April Fools version did not let the user and the character interact. Catching a creature took only a tap on the screen. Rules of safety belong with this celebration. Cruelty has no place. The jokes should feel fun. They should feel lighthearted. If someone asks whether a thing is a joke for this day, tell the truth at once. A trick can travel back to you. The return may be worse. Be ready to be the next target if you set a prank in motion. Fun without harm is the best kind. Each year, pranksters in many countries use their creativity. People who do not expect a joke get fooled.

10Only one day in 365 is set aside for this. A joke is shared. The funny side of life is celebrated. Keep it safe. Keep it simple. Above all, keep it fun. On this day, expect what you do not expect. Word List. A consumer is someone who pays for goods or services, or rents them, and then uses them. Disguises are clothes or other items worn so a person is not recognized. A hoax is a thing made to mislead or to trick. Media means ways of sending news to many people at once, such as papers, magazines, radio, television, and the Internet. Naive describes someone with little practice or weak judgment, or someone who is innocent. Pranks are tricks, or practical jokes. A spoof is a hoax, or a joke aimed at someone. Traditional describes a custom kept for a long time. A victim is a person or other animal hurt by an act or a condition, or someone who has been fooled.

13. Beasts and Heroes in Greek Myths

1A map shows the lands of ancient Greece around 750 BCE. It marks Macedonia and Troy. It marks Greece and Asia Minor. It marks Delphi, Athens, and Mycenae. It marks Europe and Italy. It marks Sparta, Africa, and Crete. It shows the Mediterranean. On a vase from the fifth century BCE, the hero Heracles greets Cerberus. Heracles is pronounced HAIR-uh-kleez. Cerberus is the dog that guards the underworld. The dog is shown with two heads or with three. People in many cultures tell myths. Myths are stories that explain important ideas in ways people can grasp. Good and evil are ideas of that kind. A myth can teach a lesson. It can tell about history. It can describe a wonder of nature. It can even give a warning. Religion in ancient Greece gave myths an important place. Fantastic creatures often stood at the center of Greek myths. Gods stood there too, along with goddesses and heroes.

2Another vase shows Athena, a goddess, helping Heracles as he attacks the Hydra. The Hydra is a monster formed from many snakes. A Centaur had a human head and a human chest. The rest of the body was a horse. The animal side was stronger than the human side. To the Greeks, Centaurs seemed like animals, pushed along by their feelings. The Greeks thought of themselves as civilized. A Greek king, Ixion, stands at the start of the Centaur story. Mount Olympus became Ixion's home because Zeus allowed it. Zeus then learned of Ixion's love for Hera. Hera was Zeus's own wife. Zeus set a test. He shaped a cloud so that it looked like Hera. Ixion fell in love with the cloud because he believed it was Hera. From that cloud came the first Centaur. Zeus then punished Ixion by making him spin forever on a burning wheel. Ancient Greeks painted and carved battles on many objects.

3The pictures showed Greeks fighting Centaurs. The objects ran from drinking cups to stone temples. Greek artists did not often picture events from their own day. They used myth pictures to show how they felt about the world around them. They linked one great enemy, the Persians, with the Centaurs. A sculpture on the Parthenon shows a Centaur fighting a Greek warrior who has fallen. The Parthenon is a temple in Athens from the fifth century BCE. In ancient Greek culture, the bond between a guest and a host was very important. The myth of Ixion and the first Centaur teaches that bond. Ixion failed to respect Zeus, who was his host. The punishment Zeus gave was a lesson about breaking this accepted custom. Sirens, like Centaurs, were hybrid creatures. They were women who had the wings, legs, and bodies of birds. They stood for how much self-control mattered. They lived on an island set in the middle of the sea.

4Beautiful songs from that island worked as a lure for sailors. Control of the ships would slip from the sailors. The ships would smash on the rocky shores of the island. The myth says the Sirens had once been human maids of the goddess Persephone. Her name is pronounced pur-SE-fuh-nee. One day the god of the underworld seized Persephone while she was picking flowers. Wings let the Sirens search for her. They never found her, so they settled on the island. Their songs pulled in many sailors. A few travelers still got past them. One traveler played music so loud that it covered the Sirens' song. Another traveler ordered his sailors to tie him tightly to the boat. Those sailors blocked their ears so the song could not reach them. Getting past that song stood for strength of will, a strength Greek people prized.

5Odysseus appears tied to his ship on a vase made in the fifth century BCE. Tied there, he can hear the Sirens and still stay alive. The creatures are tied to the word siren, a device that sends out a loud warning sound. They also shaped the idea of a siren song. A siren song is something so appealing that a person wants it even though it is dangerous. People knew the Sirens for beauty. People knew Medusa for a frightening look. Ancient Greek artists usually drew the Gorgons with large round heads and huge eyes. The Gorgons were Medusa and her two sisters. Snakes often took the place of their hair. They had pointed tusks, and their tongues stuck out. The sisters of Medusa were immortal, but Medusa herself was mortal. Because she was mortal, humans had a chance to defeat her. She still had a defense of her own. Anyone who looked straight into her eyes could be turned to stone.

6Her story begins with an evil king who loved the mother of a boy named Perseus. The king wanted Perseus out of the way. He tricked the boy into a promise to bring back anything the king asked for. The king then sent Perseus for the head of Medusa. He believed that task could not be done. Help came from gods and from goddesses. Perseus cut the head from Medusa. Her body released two creatures. Some people think her death stood for the end of a drought. The two creatures stood for the good that followed, which was crops and water. The Greeks believed a Gorgon face could protect them and keep evil away. They placed pictures of Gorgons in many spots, including on their shields. The Minotaur was another hybrid. It had the head of a bull and the body of a man. Fear of the monster led people to keep it in a maze.

7The maze was called the Labyrinth. The maze lay under the palace of Minos, home of the king of Crete. Boys from Athens killed the son of Minos, and the king wanted revenge. He began attacking Athens. Athens could end the attacks by sending seven boys. It also had to send seven girls. All of them would go to the Minotaur. Theseus, a brave boy of Athens, offered himself as one victim. When he reached Crete, he was locked in a cage with the other victims. Ariadne, the princess of Crete, saw him there and fell in love. Her name is pronounced ah-ree-AHD-nee. She did not want the Minotaur to harm him. She asked the builder of the Labyrinth how Theseus could get out. The builder told her to give Theseus a ball of yarn. Theseus was to tie that yarn to a door.

8Theseus was to unwind the yarn as he moved through the maze. She also handed him a sword. After he defeated the Minotaur, he followed the yarn trail back out. The myth grew popular after the Greeks took control of Crete. Just as Centaurs often stood for the Persians, bulls often stood for Crete. An important goddess on Crete held bulls as sacred. Some people read the fight as a picture of history. Theseus beating the Minotaur stood for the Greek takeover of Crete. Next to the giant Typhon, the Minotaur looked tiny. Typhon is pronounced TY-fon. This monster had wings. Snakes formed its legs. It had one hundred heads. One head was human, and the rest belonged to other creatures. Harmful forces in nature were what Typhon stood for. Only Zeus, king of the gods, was strong enough to face it. Their fight shook the whole world. Zeus set all one hundred heads on fire.

9He then shut Typhon inside the Earth. Ancient Greeks blamed Typhon for the fierce winds of great storms. Those winds raced over both land and sea. People took comfort from a single idea. They believed Zeus could beat the forces of weather that Typhon stood for. The ancient Greeks did not tell creature stories only to entertain an audience. They did not tell them only to cause fear. Each creature and each myth carried meaning. The meaning helped people of that time make sense of the world around them. Mythical creatures held an important place in ancient Greek culture. They are still popular now. Children still feel excitement at these amazing stories. Adults feel that excitement too. Some well-known companies use creatures from old Greek myths as logos. The fashion label Versace, pronounced vur-SAH-chee, uses the head of Medusa. Mobil Gas uses Pegasus, the winged horse of Perseus. Starbucks Coffee Company uses a Siren.

10Civilized describes a high level of social order and of cultural development. To lure is to draw someone toward a place or an action by offering something pleasant or rewarding. Creatures are animals, above all the ones that seem strange or unusual. Myths are stories that explain history, natural events, or customs. They often bring in supernatural parts. A culture is a particular society with its own ideas and its own customs. To defeat is to win a victory over someone else. Sacred means holy, or linked to a god, a religion, or a spiritual aim. A drought is a dry spell with little rainfall or with none. Symbolized means that an object, a picture, or a sign stood for an idea. Hybrid describes something made by mixing different things. Will, used this way, means strong determination to finish a task. Immortal describes a being that lives forever and does not die.

14. Benjamin Franklin, a Life of Many Works

1Sometimes a one-hundred-dollar bill gets a nickname, Benjamin. Ben Franklin's picture on that bill is the reason. The parts of this book follow his life. An opening comes first. Early years come next. Then he is a young apprentice. Then he is a printer who also runs a business. Family life and town work come after that. Inventions and science come next. His role as a founding father follows. A closing, a word list, and a topic list end the book. A public library near your home is one gift you can trace to Benjamin Franklin. Light for reading is another. Mail that arrives at the door is another. Summer evenings that stay bright, so outdoor play lasts longer, are another. A free country that stands on its own is another. One man did all of this. How? Early life is this part. Ben wrote that books took every small bit of money he ever held. January 17, 1706, is his birth date. Josiah Franklin was the father. Abiah Franklin was the mother. Boston, Massachusetts, was the family's town. Among the sons, Benjamin was the youngest. Seventeen children filled the family. Candles were the father's hard work. Soap was too. The big household was the mother's work to manage. School began for Ben at age eight. Learning pleased him. His subjects went well. Arithmetic did not. Years of school for all the children were more than Josiah and Abiah could pay. Wealthy families alone could manage that cost. Work beside his father began when Ben was ten. Wicks were cut by him. Candle molds were filled by him. Shop cleanup was his job. Errands were his job. Hours passed beside vats where tallow boiled. Tallow is fat. Sheep provide it. Cows provide it. The smell, to Ben, was awful. A pictured candle shop was probably close to the one where he worked for his father. A sailor's life was his dream.

2Water was a love of his. The local pond, with friends, got him swimming whenever a chance came. One day a kite went with him to that pond. The string stayed in his hand. Air did the pulling on the kite. He let his body relax. Across the pond he went, towed by the kite. A sailor's dangers on long ocean voyages made his parents say no. Bricklayers were people Josiah took him to see. Carpenters were next. Blacksmiths were next. A job Ben would like was the hope. Skills from those visits later helped in his own home. A job he wanted still did not appear. School was over for him, yet reading filled every possible hour. His father's books were all read. More books were bought with spending money that was meager. Love of books was plain to Josiah. James, a brother, had just opened a printing business. The right work for Ben was clear to Josiah at last. Boston Harbor in the 1700s appears in a painting. Metal letters, set by hand, were the work of apprentices like Ben. Each word in a document got its letters that way. Right to left was the direction of the work. Backward type was required, or the printed words would not read correctly. The young apprentice is this part. A saying he liked was short. Gain, if you hope for it, lessens pain. James took Ben on as an apprentice because Josiah arranged it. Twelve was Ben's age then. Work for James was the plan. Printing was the skill to learn. Twenty-one was the age when the plan would end. Eight of those years brought no pay. Food and a bed were the only return. A small salary arrived in the final year. Setting type became a skill he was good at. Letters for books are what type means. Letters for newspapers are too.

3Other apprentices became his friends quickly. Booksellers employed some of them. Books came to him on loan from those friends. Night hours went to reading. The next day, each book had to go back. A letter from Ben later reached the people of Philadelphia. Support for ending slavery was what he asked. Unfair treatment, while he was an apprentice, was how the work felt to him. Fairness toward other people became his aim because of that feeling. School chances for women were something he wanted. Abolition had his support too. Ending slavery is what abolition means. Meals were eaten alone. Study filled the time. Extra money, when he had it, bought books. Arithmetic got a second try. Skill followed. Writing began as well. An essay would be read. Then it would be set aside. Later the same essay would be written again, from memory alone. A few poems came from him too. Poets, his father said, earned nothing. Essays were the writing Ben should stick to. Pieces by Ben went into a newspaper James published. The New England Courant was its name. For a while, James had no idea. Pen names hid James and his friends. Articles in the paper were written that way. Letters to the editor were written that way too. A letter of his own was Ben's decision. James was not told. A middle-aged woman was the person Ben pretended to be. Silence Dogood was the name he chose. Under the print-shop door went that first letter. Silence Dogood was the signature. Into the paper it went. Readers liked it. More letters followed from Ben. The little brother, James learned, was the writer. Annoyance followed. Getting along had already failed between Ben and James. Arguments between them often needed Josiah to settle them. Seventeen was Ben's age when he left Boston at last. Work in some other place was the goal. One picture holds the New England Courant from the year 1723.

4Printer and businessman is the next part. Patience, Ben believed, lets a person gain what he wants. Another print shop gave him work. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was the city. Hard work was his habit. A shop of his own, someday, was still the dream. Great Britain, in this period, held control of the American colonies. Pennsylvania, Ben's home, was one colony. The year 1724 took him to London. Printing equipment for a business of his own was the plan. A new friend had promised the money. Governor William Keith was that friend. A printing press of the 1700s appears in a picture. London felt exciting to him. Two years was the length of the stay. More skill in printing was gained. Fun was part of the stay. Friends were made. Coffee shops were where he spent time. Ideas were discussed there. Ideas were debated there. An extra note belongs here. Readers in the 1700s read more than readers in the 1600s. Discussing issues was a skill they were learning. Logical thinking gained value for them. Traditions came under question. New ways of seeing the world were proposed. Government itself began to face a challenge. The Enlightenment is the name for this time. A young Ben at work in a print shop of his own appears in a picture. The promised money from his friend never arrived. Starting the business then was impossible. A kind merchant helped him travel home. Philadelphia received him again. The printing trade took him back. Twenty-two was his age. The year 1728 is when a print shop of his own finally opened in Philadelphia. The Pennsylvania Gazette was the newspaper he published. News for readers was one use. Speaking his mind was the other. Official printer for Pennsylvania is what he soon became. Family man and helper of his community is the next part. A rule for treating people mattered to him.

5Civility should go to all. A sociable manner should go to many. Familiar closeness should go to few. Real friendship should go to one. Enmity should go to none. Marriage to Deborah Read came in 1730. Help in the print shop came from her. Stationery was sold there too. Soap from his father was sold. Candles from his father were sold. William, a baby son, had come from an earlier romance. Raising William was work Ben and Deborah shared. Two more children followed. Sarah was one. Francis was the other. Smallpox took Francis at age four. Sally was the nickname for Sarah. Reading was her love, as it was her father's. Poor Richard's Almanack soon ranked among the publications readers liked most. Tides are one kind of fact an almanac holds. Sunset times and sunrise times are another. Weather is another. Many well-known sayings of Ben's filled this bestseller. One saying urges an early bedtime and an early rising. Health, wealth, and wisdom, he wrote, follow that habit. A desk holds Ben in one picture. Friends helped him organize the lending library where that desk stands. Other interests stayed with him, busy as the work was. Spare pennies once spent on books were still in his memory. The first lending library was organized by him and those friends. He also began the earliest fire company of volunteers anywhere in the colonies. A school was founded by him. The University of Pennsylvania is what that school eventually became. A hospital was founded with a friend. Doctor Thomas Bond was the friend. People saw that tasks got finished when Ben took them. Mail delivery was put in his charge by the government. Improvement followed. Sally, his daughter, sometimes rode beside him. The mail route was their path. Inventor and scientist is the next part. Success, he believed, should leave a person moderate.

6Twenty years went into building the printing business. Other cities held print shops of his as well. Much of the money was saved by Ben and Deborah. Early retirement became possible because of those savings. Passions of many kinds could then take his time. Everyday life was what he liked his inventions to improve. A stove had already been designed by him. More heat came from it than from the stoves most people used. Swim fins were his invention. Bifocals were his invention. An extension arm was his invention. High shelves and their books were what the arm could reach. Streetlights were improved by him. Daylight Saving Time was his suggestion. Saving money on lighting was the reason he saw. Two distances are easier to see with bifocals. A list of acts includes the swim fins. It includes America's first lending library, which he started. It includes a proposal that people use paper money. It includes the invention of swim fins again. The American Philosophical Society was founded by Ben. Scientists could gather there as a club. Study was one reason they came. Discussion was the other. Weather was a subject he wished to study. Electricity was another. Storms, he believed, traveled from place to place. Lightning, like other scientists, he took to be electricity. Proof was what he wanted. One afternoon took Ben and his son outdoors. William was the son. A meadow was the place. A storm had been seen coming. Silk and wood were the materials of a kite Ben had made. A stiff wire went onto the top. A silk ribbon was tied to the string. A key was tied to the ribbon. A dry ribbon was what Ben and William wanted. A shed was where they stood. The doorway was where the kite flew from. As the storm grew, loose threads on the string stood upright. A painting imagines the look of that kite-experiment day.

7A knuckle went near the key, with care. Ouch came next. A tiny shock was what he got. A spark was what he saw. Conviction followed. Lightning and electricity were the same thing. Fires often started from lightning. Protection for buildings was what he wanted to invent. Protection for people was wanted too. A lightning rod is the name of what he made. Use of it continues today. A patent was never something he applied for. A license is a fair comparison for a patent. A patent blocks other people from copying the invention unless you allow it. Anyone could use the inventions because he skipped the patent. Permission from him was not required. Here is the way a lightning rod works. Builders fix the rod at a building's topmost point. A wire is attached to the rod. The ground is where the wire leads. A lightning strike on the rod sends electricity along the wire. The ground receives it safely. Around the Empire State Building, that tower itself works the way a lightning rod works. Postmaster of Philadelphia is a role he took. Mail delivery improved under him. A volunteer fire company was organized by him. Founding father is this part. Liberty, for Ben, was not something to trade away. Basic liberty given up for a little safety that will not last leaves a person deserving neither liberty nor safety. Time was something he gave freely. Inventions were given freely too. Many years went to helping the colonies. An important role came later. Freedom from Great Britain was what the colonies sought. Uniting the colonies was a subject he talked about as early as 1754. Overseas trips happened many times. He worked to settle trouble that the colonies had with the government in Great Britain. Teaching the British about the colonies was his effort. Some British people were convinced by him. Self-government, he said, was something the colonists could manage.

8Lightning rods, as drawn in his own book, appear in a picture. Experiments were what that book described. The Franklin stove is one invention of his. One of America's first magazines is a publication of his. The lightning rod is an invention of his. A protest against pollution was led by him. Loyalty to Great Britain as a citizen had always been his stance. Independence from Great Britain was still what he wanted for the colonies. An ocean stood between them and Britain. Defense of themselves was something they could do better. In 1775 the Continental Congress gained him as a delegate. Colonists made up that group. Independence from Great Britain was their work. Constant argument was the delegates' habit. Peacemaker became his role. Negotiator became his role too. Independence from Great Britain was not wanted by some colonists. Unity for independence was what he urged. A political cartoon carried the point. The kite experiment is one act of his. Cleaner cities were a goal of methods he developed. Garbage was part of what those methods dealt with. Union of the colonies was his proposal. America's first political cartoon was printed by him. Ben joined the committee whose job was the Declaration of Independence. The colonies' independence is what that document proclaimed. Most of the writing was done by Thomas Jefferson. A few suggestions came from Ben. A reading by everyone in the Continental Congress followed, once the writing was finished. A change was offered by each member. A suggestion was offered too. Thomas sat down with Ben. Bother from all those changes was clear to Ben. A good friend is what Ben was. A funny story was told to Thomas. Cheer was the hope behind the story. A picture has Ben reading the Declaration of Independence. John Adams stands in the center. Thomas Jefferson is present too. Person-to-person spread of the common cold was Ben's theory.

9The glass armonica was his invention. Music is what that instrument makes. Daylight Saving Time was an idea he proposed. France held a reception to honor him, and a picture shows him there. His seventies were the age he had reached. An easier life was what he would have liked. The colonists asked him to travel to France. Help in the fight for independence was the aim. Love from the French, luckily, was what Ben received. Friendly was how they saw him. Funny was how they saw him. Down-to-earth was how they saw him. Great friends were made there. Help from France reached the colonies during the American Revolution. Their fight for independence gained that help. Writing the Declaration of Independence was work he shared. His signature went on it. Bifocals were invented by him. He invented an extension arm so books could come down off a high shelf. Peace after the revolution was something Ben helped establish. One side was the United States of America, new at that time. Great Britain was the other side. President of Pennsylvania is an office he was elected to. Three times is how often he held it. Public duties were almost over, but one more job came first. The Constitutional Convention included him in 1787. The U.S. Constitution is a document he helped create. Today's United States government rests on that foundation. A picture shows how the U.S. Constitution opens. He became president of the Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery. Creating the U.S. Constitution was work he shared. A closing follows. Long life, in a saying he liked, is what all people want. Being old is what none of them want. Bedridden is what his last years made him. Reading continued. Writing continued. Death had taken Deborah, his wife, many years earlier. Her family, with Sally, came to live there. Care for him was the reason.

10Family company was a pleasure. Grandchildren were a special pleasure. Spelling lessons arrived every afternoon with his granddaughter. Deborah was her name. Words were gone over by the two of them. A spoonful of jelly was his gift when she did well. Three months past his 84th birthday, death came for Benjamin Franklin. Among America's greatest writers, he stands. Among its greatest leaders, he stands. Among its greatest inventors, he stands. Among its greatest patriots, he stands. A word list follows. An apprentice learns a trade by working with a person already skilled at that work. Colonies are places such as towns or cities, and also groups of people, ruled by a different country. Contributed means something was done for a person or a cause, or something was given. Debate means a long, detailed talk about a subject that matters. A delegate stands in for other people. Electricity is energy that moving charged particles create, and it is used especially as power. An essay is short writing on a single subject. It holds what the writer thinks, feels, and believes. A foundation is the start, and the support, from which a thing develops. Freedom is being free, with the right and the power to act and to think as you wish. Meager means low, and too little to count for much. A merchant buys goods and sells them, and may sell products too. Passions are objects or activities that stir intense feeling or strong interest. Publications carry information out to the public, and printed materials are a common kind. A salary is a set sum of money paid for work, usually counted by the year. A topic list includes Boston and the Declaration of Independence. The Enlightenment, France, and Great Britain are on it. The lightning rod and newspapers are on it. Philadelphia, Deborah Read, and the U.S. Constitution are on it.

15. Black Regiments on the Western Frontier

1Black soldiers are honored by a memorial. It stands in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Their service covers every war the United States has fought. Great Britain lost control of the United States with help from thousands of Black soldiers. That conflict was the Revolutionary War. The Civil War ended in 1865, when the Northern Union Army won. More than 170,000 Black soldiers took part on the Union side. Black men could not enlist during peacetime until that war was over. The army formed its first peacetime Black regiments in 1866. Some of the new men had already fought for the Union Army. Others had lived as enslaved people. Among the first Black units were the 38th, 39th, 40th, and 41st Infantry Regiments. The 9th Cavalry and the 10th Cavalry were formed then as well. Infantry troops went into battle on foot. Cavalry troops rode horses. People native to the Great Plains chose a name for these soldiers. They called the men buffalo soldiers. A photograph from 1898 shows the 10th Cavalry. Sharecropping became the work of many Black people once the Civil War had ended.

2A sharecropper farms land rented from the owner, along with rented supplies. The owner takes part of the crop in return. White leaders in the South then passed new laws. Those laws cut into the freedom of Black people. The laws were racist, and people called them Black codes. Under the codes, Black people had to hold a job. The same codes limited which jobs they could take. They also had to sign work contracts that paid very little. A person who refused could be arrested. After arrest, that person could be forced to work without pay. One picture shows men who had fought for the Union Army in the Civil War. Starting in 1864, army pay was the same for every soldier. Race did not change the amount. At most other jobs, Black workers earned far less than white workers. A fair wage was rare. For many Black men, army service was among the few ways to earn one.

3Soldiers received food. They also received shelter. A soldier who could not read or write could learn both skills. Racism did not disappear inside the army. Most white soldiers believed Black men should not be allowed to serve. Some white officers refused to lead Black regiments. White townspeople did not want armed Black soldiers nearby. For that reason, most Black soldiers were posted to the West. Women were barred from the U.S. Army until 1943. Even so, Black women took an important part in every American war. Mary Jane Richards worked as a spy. Harriet Tubman did too. During the Civil War, both women sent useful information to the Union Army. Tubman also served as a guide and as a scout. She went with Union soldiers on raids against Southern plantations. Hundreds of enslaved people reached freedom because of those raids. Josephine Baker worked against the Nazis as a spy. She was an actress. The war was World War II. She carried information in secret notes written with invisible ink.

4In these wars, Black women worked as nurses, soldiers, guides, doctors, and spies. A photograph shows Maj. Charity A. Earley inspecting her troops. During World War II, she was the highest ranking Black woman officer. In the 1800s, the U.S. government wanted the nation to reach farther west. Decades of fighting followed. The army was on one side, and Native peoples were on the other. Year by year, the government drove more Native peoples off their homelands. Those nations had lived on the land for thousands of years. They were forced onto reservations. A reservation was only a small piece of land. It was usually the poorest ground for farming and for hunting. A photograph from 1891 shows members of the Lakota Nation. They are camped in South Dakota, near the Pine Ridge Reservation. A 19th century illustration shows a battle from 1868. In it, buffalo soldiers fight Native peoples of the Plains. Thousands of buffalo were killed after the government urged settlers and soldiers to do the killing. Officials knew that buffalo were a key food for Native peoples.

5Buffalo were also central to life on the Plains. On the reservations, hunger was common. Sickness spread quickly through the crowded camps. Many Native peoples refused to accept life on a reservation. Black soldiers were ordered west to fight them. Those soldiers were also ordered to guard white settlers. The West was so large that laws were hard to enforce. More white settlers kept arriving. Thieves stole cattle and horses. They robbed banks. They also robbed stagecoaches that carried needed supplies and mail. Guarding the settlers was one task for Black soldiers. Guarding those stagecoaches was another. The duties given to Black soldiers were the most dangerous ones. They rode many miles in search of water. They built roads. They mapped country that white settlers had not yet explored. Summers were burning hot. Winters were freezing. Their horses were old. Their supplies were poor. Some of the white settlers they guarded turned violent against them. That violence could kill. The troops still carried out their duties well.

6People came to know them as hardworking and talented. Buffalo soldiers is the name those Native opponents gave these troops. Those people may have been the Cheyenne. Many outsiders think the name honors courage in battle, like the courage of a buffalo. Nothing proves that idea. Many Native leaders today reject it. One picture shows a soldier in a coat made from buffalo hide. Only one woman is known to have been a buffalo soldier. Her name was Cathay Williams. The unit she joined in 1866 was the 38th Infantry Regiment. Women could not serve as soldiers then, so she pretended to be a man. She took the name William Cathay. Her service lasted nearly two years. During a hospital visit, a doctor discovered that she was a woman. She was discharged in 1868. An artist later made a picture of Williams. Buffalo soldiers remained in the West through the wars with Native peoples. Once the western fighting ended, the Spanish-American War became the next posting for many Black soldiers.

7The year was 1898. From 1870 to 1900, twenty-three buffalo soldiers earned the Medal of Honor. That medal is the highest award a U.S. soldier can receive. After the war, many of these soldiers went to California and worked as national park rangers. Roads were built under their direction. Trails were built under their direction too. They fought forest fires. They stopped people from hunting animals. Yosemite National Park is the setting of a picture of these buffalo soldiers. In the 1890s, the army tested whether bicycles could take the place of horses. Bikes cost less, and they were easier to care for. The ride covered 1,900 miles, equal to 3,057 km.
