It began in Missoula, Montana. It finished in St. Louis, Missouri. Mountains lay on the route. So did rivers. So did shifting sandhills. Even so, they still covered about 50 miles a day, which is 80.4 km. Motorcycles soon replaced the bikes. A photograph from 1896 shows the soldiers with their bicycles at Yellowstone National Park.

8Success did not end discrimination against Black soldiers. The year was 1906. In a small Texas town, white people blamed buffalo soldiers for a crime. They said the soldiers had killed one white man and hurt another. No proof supported the charge. Even so, 167 Black soldiers were forced out of the army. Only in 1972 were those soldiers found innocent. World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918. In Europe, Black soldiers were not permitted to fight beside white U.S. soldiers. They were placed under the French army instead. A picture shows Black soldiers coming home after that war. The United States joined World War II in 1941. By then, the old buffalo soldier regiments had already been reorganized. The last regiments made up only of Black troops were ended by the army in 1951. The troops were moved into white regiments, where racism continued. No Black student had graduated from West Point, the U.S. Military Academy, before Lt. Henry O. Flipper. He was also the first officer who was Black to take command of Black soldiers.

9Command of the 9th Cavalry passed to Lt. John Hanks Alexander in 1887. At that time, no other Black officer held a commission to lead troops in combat. One man who held command in the 9th Cavalry was Col. Charles Young. In 1903, a national park got its first superintendent who was Black, and that man was Young. Every important war in the history of America has included Black soldiers. Among those troops, the best known may be the buffalo soldiers who served in the 9th Cavalry and the 10th Cavalry. Writers have put their story into books. Filmmakers have put it into movies and television shows. Musicians have even put it into songs. Museums and memorials have been built in their honor as well. They met discrimination both inside the army and outside it. Even so, they were the soldiers least likely to desert their regiments. They showed bravery in fierce combat. They faced deadly violence. They endured hard living conditions.

10United States history includes their service as an important part. The Buffalo Soldier Monument at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, honors their memory. Bravery is the courage a person shows when something is scary, hard, or painful. To command is to hold control, or authority, over a person or a thing. A contract is a written agreement between two or more people, and it can be formal or legal. Discrimination means a person or a group is treated unfairly. The reason may be race, age, sex, religion, or another difference. Expand means to grow, or to cause growth. That growth may be in size, in amount, in volume, or in scope. Fierce describes something very powerful, very forceful, or very violent. A regiment is a unit in the military. It holds at least two large groups of soldiers. Native peoples were once forced by the U.S. government to live on certain lands. Those lands are called reservations. A stagecoach is a large covered vehicle with four wheels, pulled by horses.

16. Blue Whales: Earth's Largest Animals

1This book has these parts. Introduction. Blowholes and Blubber. A Whole Lot of Little. From Sea to Shining Sea. Those Big Baby Blues. Song of the Sea. Conclusion. Words to Know. See the Size A person in the comparison stands 6 feet (1.8 m) tall. That person weighs 175 pounds (79.4 kg). A blue whale can be 100 feet (30.5 m) long. Weight can reach 200 tons. The metric measure is 181.4 mt. The Search Scientists look along the horizon, far from shore. They are hunting the largest creature on Earth. An animal that enormous should be simple to spot. The oceans are vast. They are wide. All at once a thunderous roar breaks out. Water blasts upward in a tall column. The search is over. The animal is the mighty, magnificent blue whale. Its spout of water can climb higher than 30 feet (9.1 m). The size of a blue whale is hard to believe.

2Weight can reach 200 tons (181.4 mt). Length can reach about 100 feet (30.5 m). Set beside an elephant, the tongue is a match in weight. Main blood vessels of the heart are wide enough for a person to crawl through. The body matches a basketball court in length. What Makes This Whale a Mammal? Air goes in through blowholes. Those openings sit on top of the head. A fat layer called blubber helps the body stay warm. Baleen hangs inside the upper jaw. The pieces look like hair. Every mammal is warm-blooded. Every mammal breathes air. Every mammal has hair at some stage while the body develops. Every mammal makes milk to feed its babies. The body of a blue whale is mammoth. Under the water the skin looks blue. Seen from overhead, the color is blue-gray. Pale yellow sometimes shows on the belly. Tiny organisms often ride on the skin.

3They cause that yellow tint. A flap lies over the blowholes. It shuts water out during a dive. Breathing and Fat The sea is home to blue whales. Fish is the wrong group for them. Among mammals, no animal is larger than these graceful giants. Lungs do the breathing. The air is the same air humans breathe. Two blowholes handle each breath in and each breath out. They sit on top of the head. A breath requires a trip to the surface. The blowholes open. Air rushes out. A spout may climb 30 feet. That height is 9.1 m. Then a fast breath fills the massive lungs. The whole exchange takes under two seconds. Whale watchers scan the surface for circles. The circles show where a whale is. Several breaths happen at the surface before a dive begins. A flexible spine helps the whale move through the water.

4Wide tail flukes help it steer. Flukes are tissue. Bone does not form them. That is why they bend. A dive leaves circles on the surface. A usual cruise is 5 miles per hour. In metric terms that is 8 kmph. A fast swim can hit 20 miles per hour. The metric speed is 32 kmph. Time underwater can last about thirty minutes. These whales count as shallow divers. They rarely pass 700 feet (213.4 m) down. A sperm whale goes down about 3,280 feet. That depth is 1,000 m. That depth is more than four times greater. A cutaway shows four layers. The outside is skin. Under it lies an inner skin layer. Blubber comes next. Muscle lies beneath the blubber. Warmth is only one job of blubber. The fat also helps the whale float better. It helps the whale swim faster. Water at those depths can be frigid.

5Blue whales handle the cold. Like every sea mammal, they carry blubber. The fat sits just under the skin. It insulates the body. Chilly deep water cannot steal the heat. Krill is the main food. The tiny animals often swim near the surface. A small inset picture shows krill up close. A Whole Lot of Little A dive is a search for favorite food. The food is krill. Krill are tiny. They look a bit like shrimp. They travel in large groups. Some stay near the surface. Some krill live past a depth of 6,000 feet. The metric depth is 1,829 m. The pairing seems odd. Earth's biggest animal feeds on a creature near the smallest end of size. Even so, a blue whale is gargantuan. The throat is still very narrow. The esophagus is only inches wide. Nothing large can go down. Teeth for chewing are missing too. Each bite of food must be swallowed whole.

6Baleen lines the mouth. As many as eight hundred plates can grow there. Teeth are not present. Plates of baleen grow on the upper jaw instead. Keratin builds the baleen. The same material builds our hair. It builds our fingernails. The plates resemble a mustache. This mustache grows inside the mouth. Baleen acts as a filter. The mouth opens. One gulp pulls in ocean water crowded with krill that are swimming. The throat stretches. Thousands of gallons of seawater can fit. The mouth closes. The tongue pushes the water back out. Water passes through the baleen and returns to the sea. Krill cannot slip through. They stay trapped. Then they are swallowed whole. About forty million krill go down in a day. Where Blue Whales Live A world map names North America, Asia, Europe, and Africa. It names South America, Australia, and Antarctica. It names the Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, and the Indian Ocean.

7A mark shows the blue whale range. Every Ocean Deep water in each ocean on the planet carries gliding blue whales. Some travel alone. Some travel in pairs. They follow the places where krill live. Summer feeding happens in polar waters. Winter sends the krill toward the equator. The whales migrate that way too. One favorite meeting place is the Costa Rica Dome. The spot is near Central America's southern shore. Grooves run along the throat. The grooves spread open. A single gulp can take in as much as 17,000 gallons. That volume is 64,352 L. Those Big Baby Blues A female gives birth in warmer water. Gestation lasts about ten to twelve months. Birth comes every two or three years. The baby is called a calf. Birth weight passes 5,000 pounds. That is 2,268 kg. Within minutes the calf swims upward.

8The mother swims with it. They reach the air. Warm waters are the birthplace. A new calf has little blubber to insulate it. The tie between mother and calf is strong. Many months pass before they part. The calf drinks milk. Gain can pass 200 pounds (90.7 kg) in a day. About one year later, the young whale goes off alone. It lives on its own from then on. Whale songs sit too deep and too low for bare human hearing. Special equipment is required. Underwater Songs No animal on Earth is larger. They are also the loudest. Their sounds can top a jet engine. A song can travel for miles underwater. Loud as the sounds are, people cannot hear them without special gear. Some scientists think the whales use sonar. Sonar may guide them through dark water. Bats find their way in a similar style. Other scientists think the songs are messages between whales.

9One fact is certain. Only males sing. Songs shift a little from one region of the world to another. Conclusion Songs are one behavior scientists still hope to understand more clearly. Habits of these enormous animals still hold many unknowns. From early in the twentieth century through the middle of it, hunters killed blue whales in huge numbers. The species was nearly wiped out. Numbers have come back only a little since then. Blue whales are endangered. The International Whaling Commission protects them. Even with that protection, today's surviving number is thought to be about ten thousand at the low end and twenty-five thousand at the high end. Research goes on. The hope is fresh knowledge that can help these gentle giants. They want the whales to keep living for many years. At one time, more than three hundred thousand blue whales swam the oceans. The present count sits near ten thousand to twenty-five thousand.

10Words to Know Baleen is a mouth material in certain whales. It strains food out of ocean water. Insulates means it blocks heat from passing through. Keratin is a tough material that some animal bodies produce. It forms hair. It can form hair. It can form hooves and claws. Feathers and fingernails can be keratin too. Blubber is fat beneath the skin. It keeps sea mammals warm. The esophagus is a muscle-lined tube. Food travels through it on the way from throat to stomach. Krill are tiny crustaceans of the ocean. Many other animals feed on them. A whale tail splits into two flukes. Sonar sends sound waves of high frequency out through water. It notes the vibrations an object bounces back. Gestation is the stretch of time a baby develops inside the mother before birth. The word also names that development.

17. Bodies Kept for the Next Life

1What You Will Read. A Start. What a Mummy Is. Preparing the Body. Life After Death. The Burial. The Tomb of the Boy King. Animal Mummies. A Closing Look. Try This. Words to Know. Headstones in cemeteries today often give facts. A stone may show the name of the person who died. It may show the date of birth. It may show the date of death. Sometimes a stone adds a quote or a short phrase. The words may tell about that person's personality. They may tell about the person's place in the family. A Start. In many countries today, including Egypt, burial in a coffin is common after death. Sometimes the body is cremated instead. Loved ones may keep the ashes. The ashes may be spread over a place the person enjoyed, such as the ocean. People have not always treated the dead this way. Dead bodies were made into mummies by the ancient Egyptians. People know them for that work. They mummified everyone from kings to pets. They dried the bodies. They rubbed the bodies with spices. They wrapped the bodies in strips of cloth. Egyptians were not the only people to do this. Signs of mummification appear in many places around the world. What a Mummy Is. A mummy is a corpse that has been preserved. Most of the time, a dead body breaks down very fast. Bacteria in the air begin decomposing body cells at once after death. If nobody protects the body, scavengers and pests eat it. Vultures may come. Flies may come. In a mummy, that decay is stopped. The body can last for thousands of years.

2The earliest mummies formed on their own. They formed where it was too dry for bacteria to grow. They also formed where it was too cold. No person had to step in. Later, people learned how to preserve bodies on purpose. Peru is where a frozen mummy of a young Inca girl was discovered. She is 500 years old. She lay near the summit of a mountain that is 6,309.36 meters (20,700 ft.) high. A corpse left in the open soon decays and falls apart. Preparing the Body. The first Egyptian mummies were placed in hot desert sand. The sand was so dry that the bodies dried almost at once. The dryness saved them from decay. These dried bodies looked a lot like beef jerky. The flesh turned tough and hard. Jackals often ate any body left uncovered in the desert. Jackals like the taste of that human jerky. Egyptians tried to guard buried ancestors by piling rocks on the grave. Richer families used painted coffins. The coffins kept the jackals out. They also kept the hot sand out. Without the sand, the bodies inside decayed. Skilled Egyptians found a better plan. They learned how to preserve a body before it was buried. After a death, the body went to a team of embalmers. First they laid the body face up on an embalming table. The table was six feet wide. Their first task was to take out the soft organs. Those organs helped bacteria grow. An embalming hook pulled the brain out by way of the nose. They took care not to deform the face.

3The brain did not matter much to the ancient Egyptians. They believed the heart was the most important organ. They believed the heart was the center of thought and of feeling. A Fact to Know. The ancient Egyptians believed the god Osiris was the first mummy. His brother Set murdered him and cut him into pieces. His wife, Isis, used magic to put him back together. His nephew Anubis, who had the head of a jackal, embalmed him. Osiris then became god of the dead and god of the underworld. The chief embalmer made an incision on the left side of the stomach. Through that opening, the team removed the inner organs. They left the heart in place. The stomach, the liver, the lungs, and the intestines were each preserved alone. They went into special jars called canopic jars. Those organs traveled with the body at burial. They still mattered less than the heart. The heart stayed preserved inside the body. Embalmers washed the body, inside and outside, with palm wine. Alcohol in the wine killed bacteria. By then the body had likely started to stink, which was a sign of decay. Bags inside the body held sweet-smelling spices blended with natron. Natron is a special salt. They then covered the body and the inner organs with more natron. They left everything alone for 40 days. The lids of canopic jars were decorated. Each lid stood for a minor god who guarded what was inside the jar. The full process of mummification took seventy days. After the drying was finished, the embalmers took the salt away.

4The mummy was then very light. All the water was gone. Water had been over 65 percent of the body's weight. The embalmers packed the inside with linen stuffing. The stuffing made the body look strong and healthy instead of shriveled. Next they rubbed on more spices, mixed with wax and oil, so the body would smell sweet. Then they poured a sticky resin over the body. The resin was made from tree sap. When it hardened, it formed a thin shell that protected the body. The shell kept bacteria away. It also made the body darker. Workers stuff the body and then rub it with spices and oils. Embalmers often put makeup on the face so the mummy looked more alive. On a rich person's body, they added jewelry before the wrapping began. The wrap was soaked in resin. It was made of linen bandages as long as a football field. The wrap helped the body keep its shape. The finest linen was saved for the outer layer of bandages. Cheaper linen was used on the inside, where nobody could see it. Charms and talismans went between the layers. They were meant to keep the mummy safe in the realm of the dead. The talismans were carved from precious stones. A priest reads spells as the wrapping goes on. A papyrus scroll is set between the hands. The scroll carries spells from the Book of the Dead. The Steps of Mummification. 1. Lay the body face up on a large table. 2. Take the inner organs out through a cut in the abdomen.

53. Palm wine is used to wash the body. 4. Dry the body under piles of salt. 5. Take the salt off, and rub the body with sweet herbs. 6. Fill the body with linen and with bags of spices. 7. Coat the body with resin. 8. Add makeup and jewelry. 9. Wrap the body in bandages. Once the linen bandages are on, a cloth goes around the whole body. A picture of the god Osiris is painted on that cloth. A Fact to Know. In the Middle Ages, doctors in Europe ordered mummy powder as medicine. The powder was ground from mummies. They believed the dust would cure sick people. Most of the time, it only made the sick people worse. The Egyptian Book of the Dead shows scenes of daily life in ancient Egypt. It also shows rituals that belonged to death. Life After Death. The ancient Egyptians believed a person could live forever only with a well-preserved body. They believed that at the moment of death a person split into parts. One part was the ba. Another was the ka. The last was the physical body. The ka was a ghostly twin, identical to the person. It lived inside the mummified heart. It could not leave the tomb. The ba stood for personality and for spirit. It was a bird with a human head. By day, it could fly freely. The ba and the ka came together to form the akh, which was the person's soul. Ancient Egyptian belief sent the soul on a hard road. The soul crossed the dangerous realm of the dead.

6It traveled to a palace where judgment took place. The palace belonged to Osiris. On the way, the soul had to dodge monstrous snakes and crocodiles. It had to cross huge rivers of fire. Osiris, god of the dead, judged each person by weighing the heart on a scale. A heart heavy with sin was thrown to a hungry monster under the scales. That person would die for good. A heart lighter than a feather meant a different end. That person would stay alive forever inside the world of Osiris. When mummy-making first began, only very rich or very important people were mummified. People believed only pharaohs and nobles deserved an afterlife. A painting shows Osiris judging a soul and finding it worthy. Embalming grew easier as time passed. The ancient Egyptians also grew richer. More people were mummified. In time, they believed everyone deserved a chance at immortality. They believed the afterlife was exactly like ordinary life. So they buried mummies with favorite objects and with tools. Gold and gems went into the graves of wealthy nobles. Children were buried with favorite toys. Everyone was buried with clay copies of food and drink. Everyone was also buried with clay figurines called shabtis. Shabtis were servants who would work in the afterlife. Rank decided what a shabti was made of. The material might be clay, stone, wood, or even gold. The Burial. Mummies rested in decorated coffins. The coffins were usually made of papier-mâché and of beaten gold. Richer people might rest in a stone sarcophagus. They might rest in a coffin of wood brought from far away.

7A pharaoh might have as many as four gold-covered coffins, each nested inside the next. Painters put the person's face on the coffin. The face helped the ba find the right tomb when it came back at night. Hieroglyphs were painted or chiseled on the coffin. They told the story of the person's life. Spells in the writing were meant to protect the dead person below. The painted wooden sarcophagus of Lady Isis shows a lifelike image. She was the wife of Kabekehent. Many ancient Egyptians believed a mummy would curse anyone who disturbed the tomb and stole from the dead. Treasure still tempted thieves. They broke into even the best-guarded tombs. They often tore mummies apart while searching for gold and gems under the bandages. They would risk death and punishment for those riches. Robbers reached most tombs only a few years after burial. The treasure of King Tutankhamun included a game table. It also included game boards and game pieces. Archaeologist Howard Carter, on the left, studies a coffin with an Egyptian archaeologist, on the right. The coffin is that of King Tutankhamun. It was discovered in 1922. The Tomb of the Boy King. Pharaoh Tutankhamun is also called the Boy King. He died while he was still a teenager. His life in ancient Egypt is mostly a mystery. His rule is mostly a mystery too. Even so, no mummy in the world is better known. His tomb was opened in 1923. Robbers had entered it twice in ancient times. Great treasures were still inside. The thieves had reached the second room.

8That room held Tut's gold chariots and his statues. They took about a sixth of the gold in the tomb. They were probably stopped before they could finish. The mummy itself had not been touched. King Tut lay in three coffins, one inside another. The outer two were wood covered with bands of gold. The innermost coffin was solid gold and covered with gems. His beautiful burial mask was pure gold. Heavy jeweled bracelets circled his wrists. Golden amulets and necklaces lay around his neck. The gold mask belongs to the teenage pharaoh Tutankhamun. He ruled ancient Egypt more than 3,000 years ago. A Fact to Know. Egyptians stopped making mummies around 400 ce. By then, many Egyptians had been converted to Christianity by Christians who came from outside Egypt. Fewer people still believed a loved one must be mummified in order to have eternal life. Animal Mummies. Animals were mummified too, not only people. Cats were especially sacred. A cat stood for Bast, the cat-headed goddess of happiness. Families kept cats as pets. A dead cat brought grief to the whole family. They shaved their heads. They shaved their eyebrows. Some cat mummies lay with their owners. Others were placed at temples of Bast. Other animals sacred to the gods were mummified too. Crocodiles, ibises, and falcons were among them. The gods received those animals in the afterlife as gifts. This cat mummy comes from Abydos, in Upper Egypt. It dates to the Roman Period, around the first century ce. A Closing Look. Natural mummies have turned up around the world. Denmark has marshes of cold, acidic water where some of them lie.

9Some lie in the frozen depths of a glacier in the Alps. Some lie in the hot sand of a desert. Many cultures preserved their dead this way. Buddhist monks in Japan did so. Tribesmen in Papua New Guinea did so. The Incas of Peru, half a world away from Egypt, mummified their ancestors in much the same manner as the ancient Egyptians. Made mummies and natural mummies differ in some ways. They match in one important way. Every kind of mummification stops cell decay. The body can then last for hundreds of years, or even for thousands. Tollund Man, of Denmark, was preserved by nature. He was found in a bog in 1950. He lived in the iron age, from 300 to 400 bce. No prehistoric body in the world is preserved better. Mummies and the goods in their tombs can teach us about ancient civilizations. Scientists all over the world study mummies for that reason. They want to learn how ancient people lived and how they died. Peru is the find-spot of this young man's mummy. It is more than seven hundred years old. Where Mummies Have Been Found. AFRICA: Egypt, Nubia. ASIA: Japan (Honshu), China, Siberia, Indonesia. SOUTH AMERICA: Peru. EUROPE: the Alps (Italy/Austria), Denmark, Italy, Greenland. SOUTH PACIFIC: Australia, New Zealand, and Papua New Guinea. NORTH AMERICA: Canada, the U.S., Mexico. Try This. Make mummies of your own. 1. Divide an apple so you have twelve wedges. 2. Set half of the wedges on a baking sheet, with the skin side down.

103. Use low heat for an hour. Stop when the wedges are dry. Low heat is about 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees F). You could also leave the wedges in a warm, dry, sunny spot for several days. 4. Take the wedges off the heat after they have dried. 5. Set them beside the six wedges that were never dried. 6. Keep both groups inside at room temperature for several days. Notice how the two groups differ. Words to Know. Afterlife: the place of life that follows death. Akh: a person's soul and inner essence, made when personality joins the ghostly form. Amulets: charms worn on the body to guard against harm or evil. Ba: a human-headed bird formed from a person's personality after death. Cremated: burned a dead body down until ashes remained. Decomposing: breaking down by rot, or decaying. Embalmers: people who preserve the bodies of the dead. Embalming hook: a tool used while embalming to pull the brain from a mummy. Hieroglyphs: picture writing of ancient Egypt, with symbols that stand for syllables. Immortality: a life that never ends. Incision: a cut that goes deep. Mummified: turned into a mummy. Papier-mâché: a stiff material made from wet paper pulp that is later dried. It was used to form coffins for mummies. Resin: a sticky, fragrant material that comes from the sap of a tree. Sacred: holy, or linked to a god or to a religion. Shriveled: dried out and wrinkled. Talismans: magical objects that carry spells and prayers of protection. Tempted: pulled hard by a wish for something that is not allowed.

18. Bonfires on the Fifth of November

1Masks show the face of Guy Fawkes. A traditional rhyme in the United Kingdom tells people to remember a date. The date is the fifth of November. The rhyme names gunpowder. The rhyme names treason. The rhyme names a plot. It says there is no reason to forget this gunpowder treason. Every year on November 5, people gather in the United Kingdom. Adults gather. Children gather. They come for fireworks. They come for bonfires. Friends and families cheer. A dummy sits on top of the fire. People call the dummy a Guy. The dummy bursts into flames. This old festival is called Guy Fawkes Day. People also call it Bonfire Night. Guy Fawkes Day marks a day in 1605. James I and the people on his staff halted the plot on that date. The plot would have blown up Parliament. Lewes, England, holds the world's largest Bonfire Night celebration. A bonfire is a large fire built outside for a celebration. A dummy is a figure made to look like someone. A festival is a celebration. It can also be a set of cultural events. Treason is a crime of betrayal against one's government or ruler.

2Parliament is the lawmaking body of the United Kingdom. Commons and Lords are the two houses inside it. A plot is a plan. The cheering crowd watches the Guy burn. Fireworks and a bonfire mark the night. The memory goes back to a plot against Parliament in 1605. 1570 was the birth year of Guy Fawkes. He was born in York, England. Queen Elizabeth I ruled then. At that time, many countries in Europe were at war. Some of the countries were Catholic. Some were Protestant. They fought because of religious differences. England banned the Catholic religion while Elizabeth ruled. Catholics who were caught practicing were often fined. They were often killed. Guy Fawkes used the nickname Guido. Guy's grandparents were Catholic. His parents were Protestant. Guy's father died. After that, his mother took a Catholic husband. When Guy was a teenager, he decided to become a Catholic. Violence against Catholics in England made him angry. He was angry about the cruelty too. His early twenties were when Fawkes departed England. He traveled to the Netherlands. He joined the Catholic Spanish army. That army was fighting the Protestant Dutch army. Twelve years of his life were spent as a soldier for Spain.

3Explosives were a skill he picked up in that army. He used gunpowder. A picture shows the Gunpowder Plotters. Robert Catesby led them. In the picture he is second from the right. Queen Elizabeth I's death came in 1603. Her crown passed to King James I. He promised greater tolerance for Catholics. The laws he actually passed treated Catholics even more harshly. Loyalty to the king remained among many English Catholics. Other Englishmen serving Spain were people Fawkes met. Anger at violence toward Catholics in England filled them too. Robert Catesby asked Fawkes in April 1604 to join a revolt. The revolt was against the king. They needed his skill with gunpowder. Fawkes agreed right away. He was excited to help their cause. Tolerant means willing to allow beliefs different from your own. Loyal means faithful to a person, a government, or a cause. Fighting a government or another authority is what a revolt means. Back in London, Fawkes met the other plotters in May 1604. They met at a local inn. Secrecy was the promise they swore. Many women were part of the wider movement. Anne Vaux was one of them.

4This particular plot included men alone. Blowing up Parliament was the plotters' plan. Their chosen day was the official opening day. The king would be there. His entire staff would be there. Afterward, the plotters had another plan. They would make Princess Elizabeth queen. She was King James's daughter. Elizabeth's age then was only nine. They believed they could raise her Catholic. Then they could influence her reign. The sworn group numbered thirteen plotters. Robert Catesby had a house near Parliament. The house was just across the river. The plotters bought thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. They stored the barrels in Catesby's house. One plotter was Thomas Percy. A royal bodyguard job became his. A house close to Parliament became his home. A cellar rental was also within his reach. The cellar was beneath the buildings of Parliament. A rowboat carried the gunpowder for the plotters. They moved it at night. They crossed the river from Catesby's house. They brought it to the cellar under Parliament. A name that was not his own was what Guy Fawkes used. He called himself John Johnson. Thomas Percy's servant was the role he played. Inside Parliament's buildings, the disguise gave him free movement.

5Care of the hidden gunpowder was the task given to him. The gunpowder was in the cellar. The opening of Parliament was set for November 5, 1605. The plotters were ready. Some people think the gunpowder was too old. Age may have left it unable to explode, some people think. Thirty-six barrels waited under Parliament. A nine-year-old princess was part of the plan for a new queen. Lord Monteagle received a letter that was kept secret. He was a Catholic nobleman. He was loyal to the king. He was warned by the letter to stay away from Parliament on November 5. A terrible event, the letter said, was coming. The king's assistant was shown the letter. When the king heard the news, he gave an order. A full search of Parliament's houses was his order. Part of the letter had no name on it. Firewood turned up in the cellar during the search. A second search was ordered. This time they caught Fawkes. He had fuses. He had matches. They searched the cellar more carefully. The gunpowder was discovered on the second search. There were thirty-six barrels.

6Guy Fawkes tried to escape. He was caught. The king's chambers were where the guards took him. They questioned him there. Fawkes told the king's guards his plan. Blowing up the king was the aim he described. The plan was to blow up his government. He kept saying the act was his alone. Only one regret was what he offered the king. Failure of the plot was that regret. The Tower of London held Fawkes as a prisoner. His final confession carried his signature by November 9. Names of the other plotters came out in that confession. On November 5, during the morning, the remaining plotters learned of the arrest. They stole some horses. They rode away from London. A revolt against the government was still their plan. The king's men reached them on November 8. Robert Catesby was killed in a gunfight. That gunfight also took the lives of three other plotters. The rebellion had failed. A photograph shows the Tower of London. Fawkes was a prisoner there. A rebellion is a fight against authority. It is an uprising. The English courts found eight plotters guilty. These were the eight who had survived. The charge was treason.

7The courts sentenced each traitor to death. In January 1606, four of them were taken out to die. Guy Fawkes was one of the four. Three other plotters went with him. The place was the yard outside Parliament. They were executed there. The punishment was meant to warn others against a similar act. Later praise for Guy Fawkes came from King James I. He praised him for loyalty to his cause. Some experts suggest another idea about the Gunpowder Plot. They think it may have been an inside job. They think the king's staff may have planned it. The goal may have been harsher laws against Catholics. The king's top aide may even have written the warning letter. The letter went to Lord Monteagle. Otherwise, a question remains. How could the plotters work so close to the king's guards? Some ask if the plotters were only scapegoats. A scapegoat can raise support for a king who is not popular. Clear proof of that idea has not been found. Even so, the public felt relief when the plot was found. Relief spread because the king had survived. The king said his survival was a miracle.

8He said it proved his right to the throne. A law from Parliament came in that same year. November 5 became an official celebration under that law. An unpopular king became someone to celebrate. After the Gunpowder Plot, people celebrated King James I. Executed means killed as punishment for a crime. The yard outside Parliament was the place of the execution. Praise from the king came later, for Fawkes's loyalty to his cause. The inside-job idea has no clear proof. Gunpowder Treason Day was the holiday's first name. Church bells were rung in the seventeenth century. Bonfires were lit as a mark of the day. In England then, a custom was popular. Hated figures were represented by dummies burned on the fires. Evil spirits, they believed, would be driven off by the burning. A dummy made to look like Guy Fawkes began to go on the fire each November 5. The dummy went on the bonfire. Fireworks appear in Guy Fawkes's hands in modern art. More bright fireworks burst overhead in that picture. Parliament is in the background of that picture. Special Bonfire Night customs belong to some parts of Britain. In the town of Lewes, people wear costumes.

9Lewes is in the south of England. People carry torches through the streets. In some towns, the dummy is not Guy Fawkes. It is a famous person who is unpopular with the public today. That dummy is the one they burn. By the late nineteenth century, big firework shows became popular. Towns and cities also took up parades. People marched to the place of the bonfire. They marched to the firework shows. These days, local organizations usually arrange the bonfires. Spectacular means wonderful and impressive. Bells and bonfires were the early way to mark the day. A burning dummy was once thought to drive evil spirits away. Guy Fawkes became the figure on the fire. Lewes still uses costumes and torches. Some towns choose a modern unpopular figure instead. Fireworks and parades grew popular late in the nineteenth century. Local groups now set up most of the fires. Guy Fawkes Day marks a failure. England's king was not killed, because the Gunpowder Plot failed. More than four hundred years have passed since these events. Millions in the United Kingdom still join the day. They enjoy bonfires on November 5.

10They enjoy fireworks on November 5. Some people see Guy Fawkes in another way. To them, he was someone who defended his own beliefs. Parliament's houses get a guard search one time each year. They search before the official opening. They make sure no would-be plotters are hiding. They check the basements. Scientists have calculated the power of the hidden gunpowder. The amount was 2,500 kilograms (5,512 pounds). They say it would have exploded outward about 490 meters (536 yards). Guy Fawkes has an island named after him. The island is in the Galapagos Islands. The Galapagos Islands are in Ecuador. The island is called Isla Guy Fawkes. Guards prepare for their yearly search of Parliament. The celebration remembers a plot that did not succeed. Four centuries have passed since 1605. Bonfires and fireworks still fill November 5. The yearly search still checks the basements of Parliament. The old gunpowder is measured at 2,500 kilograms (5,512 pounds). The blast would have reached about 490 meters (536 yards). Far away, Isla Guy Fawkes carries his name. Some people remember a rebel. Others remember a plot that failed. The night still belongs to fire and fireworks.

19. Bowlers, Batters, and the Pitch

1Near the ocean in the West Indies, men take pleasure in a cricket match. A batter strikes the ball with a bat that is large and flat. The ball is about the size of a baseball. Cricket carries an honored history and a huge following in many countries. Players from many lands compete while crowds of adoring fans look on. Those fans can be found from India all the way to Jamaica. Practice asks little of a beginner. A bat is enough, with a ball, a few friends, and free time. Teams play on an oval field that holds a cleared rectangle called the pitch. Each of the two teams has eleven players. The sides switch between a turn at bat and a turn at bowling. Players name a turn at bat an inning. On the bowling side, one player is the bowler, the thrower. Another is the wicketkeeper, the catcher. The other nine players spread out in the oval.

2Two batters walk out and stand at opposite ends of the pitch. The first to bat is the striker. The other is the nonstriker. Behind the batter, the wicketkeeper gets ready to catch the ball. That job is much like the catcher's job in baseball. A field diagram labels the pitch, the bowling crease, the return crease, and the popping crease. It labels the boundary and the wicket. It shows the bowler, the striker, the nonstriker, and the field players. It shows the umpire and the wicketkeeper. Nine field players cover the ground. Fields are not all the same size. A standard field covers at least 16,000 square yards, or 13,378 square meters. The diagram marks a span of 22 yards, or 20.12 meters. It also marks a span of 12 feet, or 3.66 meters. The bowler bowls the ball, which means throwing it overarm. The arm stays above the head, and the elbow stays straight.

3Hitting the wicket is how the bowler hopes to put the batter out. Three small posts make a wicket. They stand in the ground and are called stumps. Two wooden pieces, the bails, rest on top. If the bowler knocks the bails off the stumps, the batter is out. A batter can stop the ball from striking the wicket by hitting it with the bat. A batter can also hit hard enough to score runs. A hit by the striker sends both batters running. The nonstriker runs too. Each heads for the far end of the pitch. A line just in front of each wicket is the popping crease. If both runners cross that crease and change ends, the team scores one run. Cricket gear includes a bat and padding for the legs, the chest, and the arms. It includes a face guard, gloves, bails, a wicket, a ball, and stumps. The stumps of the wicket are hammered down into the ground.

4The two batters run back and forth, scoring a run on every completed crossing. They must stay alert. The fielding side tries to run a batter out, which means to dismiss that batter. A fielder can end the stay if the batter has not reached safety past the popping crease. Knocking the bails off the stumps with the ball makes the batter out. A batter may stop behind the crease at any moment to avoid that out. A batter is also out if a player on the bowling side catches the hit ball before it bounces. After a running spell, the player now standing where the striker began becomes the new striker. A bowler may deliver the ball six times with no hit and no out. That bowler then swaps places with a teammate. The nonstriker becomes the striker for the next turn. Batters can add extra runs in other ways.

5If a hit ball crosses the boundary without bouncing even once, the team adds six runs. A match lasts for two innings, or it ends when the day ends. The team with more runs is the winner. If the day ends before both teams finish their innings, the match is a draw. Honesty is expected from players and from fans. Fair play is expected. Good manners are expected too. Many rules ask the two teams to agree on whether a player is out. No one argues, and no one waits for an umpire to make the call. Every player is held to this high standard of behavior. In one match, players from Bangladesh chase a hit ball against South Africa. An old picture shows people playing cricket in London in 1743. Fans and players both cherish the story of their sport. No one knows the exact year the game began. Children in England were already playing it by the 1500s.

6Adults soon joined them. By the early 1700s, some players took wages and fees. Those players became the first professionals. Around that same time, noblemen in London wrote down a set of rules. Those rules are still used hundreds of years later. Changes since that time have touched only a few rules. New rules have been few as well. People call the nineteenth century the Golden Age of Cricket. Bowlers began to bowl overarm, and batters learned to handle balls that came in faster. The game spread across the world. New teams appeared in the United States and in Canada. Others appeared in Australia, India, and South Africa. Still more appeared in New Zealand and across the Caribbean. Late in that century, the matches now seen as the first Test cricket were played. A Test match is long. It lasts for many days. It decides an international championship. Cricket is popular in many lands that were once colonies of England.

7It is not popular in the United States. The game did have a following in early America. Late in the 1800s, baseball grew quickly and pushed cricket aside. Baseball moved at a faster pace. Its games were shorter. It suited American taste better. By the early 1900s, cricket had nearly disappeared from the United States. The 1900 Olympic Games included cricket. Since that time, the sport has grown around the world. Teams from many countries now play the nations that led cricket in the Golden Age. The newer sides have added ideas of their own. One of those ideas is the fast bowling style made by players from the West Indies. A West Indies bowler releases the ball in a 2014 championship match against Australia. A cricket ball can fly at about 95 to 100 miles an hour. That speed is 152.8 to 160.9 kilometers an hour. Today the strongest sides play professional international Test matches.

8Twelve national teams compete at that level right now. Below Test cricket, many other levels of play exist. Women's teams compete both inside their own countries and against other countries. Leagues and special matches follow rules of their own. The twelve Test nations stand in this order. England is first, and Australia is second. South Africa is third, and the West Indies are fourth. New Zealand is fifth, and India is sixth. Pakistan is seventh, and Sri Lanka is eighth. Zimbabwe is ninth, and Bangladesh is tenth. Ireland is eleventh, and Afghanistan is twelfth. Players on the West Indies team come from sixteen separate countries, colonies, and protectorates. Many outstanding players have filled the game across the centuries. W. G. Grace, who lived from 1848 to 1915, changed the way cricket was played. He built a batting style that was smart and full of detail. That style could answer many different kinds of bowling.

9A wide public ranks him among the most important players the sport has known. Kumar Shri Ranjitsinhji, pronounced koo-MAR SHREE rahn-JEET-seeng-jee, was known as Ranji. He lived from 1872 to 1933. In India, his home country, he led as a royal. He first met the game in England, and he became one of its finest batters. India names its national championship the Ranji Trophy in his honor. Every year since 1889, five players are named Players of the Year. In 2009, Claire Taylor, born in 1975, became the first woman to receive that honor. A bat, a ball, and a wicket give young players a way to build skill. In northern India, boys start up a game of their own. Cricket has a rich past. Its future rests with the batters, bowlers, and fielders of tomorrow. New players should keep a few aims in mind. They should protect the wicket. They should watch the ball.

10They should keep the spirit of fair play and the spirit of respect. Good luck, and good game. Adapted means changed so something fits a new situation or a particular setting. Behavior is the way a person, or another animal, acts in a given situation. A boundary is a marker, such as a fence or a line, that shows where an area starts or stops. To cherish something is to treat it with love and care. It also means to hold that thing dear or to guard it. Complicated describes a thing with many parts or details that are hard to understand. A draw is a match that ends with no clear winner, which means a tie. Fielding means playing in the field during a baseball game or a cricket game. International describes something that concerns two or more nations. Umpires are the officials who rule on plays during a sporting event.

20. Building Pictures from Small Pieces

1An opening starts this book. A history of mosaics follows. Materials and supplies come next. Then the steps for making a mosaic appear. A closing and a word list finish it. One picture is a mosaic in the old style. Another is a mosaic made in a modern way. Pieces of different materials, set together, are what a mosaic is. The result is a design that is unique. Designs of this kind, like the project in this book, go back thousands of years. Simple tools and simple supplies can be enough. The materials change with the maker. Tile, glass, pottery, and china are the older choices. Stones, seashells, marbles, and bits of mirror are the more imaginative choices. History is this part. Early mosaics did a practical job and a decorative job at the same time. Turkey is where pebble mosaic floors turned up inside homes.

2The 700s BCE is when those homes were built. Wall mosaics belonged to some ancient Romans. Sacred images were what those walls showed. Early religious groups used wall displays of the same kind. Places of worship were what they decorated. One ancient mosaic was uncovered in the ruins of a worship place. By the 1400s, practical use was no longer the only role. An art form is what mosaics became. Whole walls received mosaic covers. Ceilings did too. Complex images filled those mosaics. The Renaissance is when mosaics mirrored paintings. Pictorial realism is the name for that. The 1700s and the 1800s brought mosaic miniatures from artists. Glass in very small bits, plus ceramic, was the material. Keepsake boxes, plaques, and jewelry were what the bits decorated. Late in the 1800s, Art Nouveau sparked interest again. Making mosaics was wanted once more.

3Formal designs are made by artists today. Abstract designs are made too. The top picture is an Art Nouveau example. The bottom picture is art of the 20th century. Tesserae is the label on one picture. Materials and supplies are this part. Complex is how the finished work looks. Simple is how the making really is. Inexpensive materials are common. A hardware store can supply many of them. Free is the cost of some. Five needs get a project started. Tesserae are the small pieces. A larger design is what they form when set together. Stone, glass, and ceramic tile are among the most common tesserae. A broken plate can supply pieces. A broken cup can too. Interesting stones can. Seashells can. Creativity should not be limited. Glue of some kind is needed. The job of the glue is to stick tesserae to your chosen surface for good.

4Several glue types exist. Mastic is one. Latex is its base. Thinset is another. Mortar is what thinset resembles. Grout is needed as well. Spaces between the tesserae are what grout fills. Portland cement is in every grout. Strength and durability come from that cement. Some grout is polymer-enhanced. Extra strength is the gain. Flexibility is a gain too. Cracks narrower than one-eighth inch call for non-sanded grout. Wider cracks call for sanded grout. Many colors are sold for both types. Pictures show grout and thinset adhesive. Tile nippers, rubber gloves, a dust mask, a trowel, safety glasses, and a spatula appear among the supplies. A hammer is what many people use to break big tesserae. Handheld tile nippers give more control. Pliers are what they resemble. Smoothing grout and glue may call for more tools.

5A trowel, a float, a palette knife, or a spatula can do that work. A sponge is needed at the end. Wipe the mosaic surface with it after the grout goes on. Safety always matters. Safety glasses belong on you when tesserae are broken or cut. A dust mask belongs on you too. Silica is in the powdered cement mortars. Silica is in the grouts. Eyes can be irritated by silica. Lungs can be irritated by it. Latex gloves, or rubber gloves, belong on your hands while grout is in use. Mortar calls for them too. Hands stay protected that way. Making the mosaic starts here. Choose the item you want to decorate before anything else. A garden stone you can step on is one simple item to begin with. A simple design is a good start too. Gather the tesserae next. Cut them so the pieces match in size.

6Tile nippers, if you use them, should have their cutting jaws overlapping the edge. The jaws should cover roughly one eighth inch of the edge. A firm squeeze of the handles comes next. A curve takes several small cuts. Nibble slowly. Trouble with the nippers usually means too much material sits in the jaws. Pick the first tessera. A small amount of glue goes on its back. Press that piece onto the surface you chose to decorate. Too much glue is a mistake. Enough to hold the piece is the right amount. Extra glue will squeeze up between the pieces. A palette knife can wipe the extra away. A finger can do it too. Repeat until tesserae cover the object. Leave gaps when you set the pieces. Grout needs those gaps. Design changes with the size of the grout lines.

7It changes with how often those lines appear. Stagger the cracks. Straight lines running through the design are what you avoid. Drying comes once the cover of tesserae is complete. Wait 24 hours or longer. Grout is the next step. Cut the top off a plastic milk jug that holds a gallon. The bottom becomes a bowl for mixing grout. Wipe the surface clean first. Any glue still sitting there should go. Rubber gloves go on. Safety glasses go on. A dust mask goes on. Mix a small batch. The package directions are the guide. Thick and smooth is the aim. Peanut butter is the texture to match. A spatula can do the mixing. A trowel can too. After mixing, let the grout sit. About ten minutes of curing should pass before you continue. An even coat of grout goes on the surface next.

8A spatula presses it down into the cracks. A rubber float can do that pressing too. Once every crack holds grout, the extra on the surface can come off. Wipe the whole mosaic thoroughly. The sponge should be only lightly damp. A bucket of clean water should sit nearby. Clean the sponge in that water. Wring it. Wipe again. Keep going until the face of the mosaic looks mostly clear, and smooth as well. Every tessera should stay visible. Thinner pieces sometimes get buried under grout. A haze may remain. A clean, soft cloth can take it off in about an hour, once the grout hardens. Do not send the rinse water down the drain during cleanup. Grout can settle inside a drainpipe. Hardening there can cause clogs later. After cement products such as grout, Vinegar on the hands should come first, and the soap wash after.

9Skin pH balance is what that rinse helps restore. Three days later, the grout is fully hard. Sealing can happen then. Sealing is not required. Outdoors, it is a good idea. Frequent contact with moisture makes it a good idea too. Stains stay out better once a seal is on. An extra tip follows. Now and then, mist the mosaic with water that is clean and cool. Do this for three days. Curing is helped by that mist. A simple plastic spray bottle is enough. The closing looks back. Sophisticated is how the finished piece looks. Complex is how it looks. Simple is how the making stays. The list of needed supplies stays short. Beautiful designs that last can come from beginners. They can come from professionals. Broken tiles can be the material. Pieces of broken dishes can be the material.

10Other unique objects can too. Those, plus a few common tools, let you make a mosaic of your own in no time. A word list follows. Art Nouveau is a decorating style of long curves that look like leaves and like blooms. Cure means a chemical process that preserves something. A float smooths plaster or cement. A palette knife is a small artist knife whose blade bends. Mixing, scraping, or applying paint is its use. pH balance is the right acid level. Illness follows if the body holds too much acid. Pictorial realism shows subjects as they are, not in an idealistic way and not in an abstract way. A polymer is large molecules linked in a chain, and those molecules add strength to other compounds. A trowel is flat, and it makes surfaces even.

21. Buildings That Face Strong Wind

1A typhoon struck in 2018. It damaged buildings in Hong Kong. More than four hundred people were injured. What You Will Read. Three Pigs and a Wolf. Wind That Pushes Hard. Storms with Several Names. How Wind Starts. Building for the Wind. Rows of Trees and Shrubs. Towers That Should Not Rock. Burj Khalifa in Dubai. Taipei 101 in Taiwan. Shanghai Tower in China. A Closing Look. Words to Know. Three Pigs and a Wolf. Think back to the tale of the three little pigs. A house was built by every pig. One house was made of straw. One house was made of sticks. One house was made of brick. Along came the big, bad wolf. He blew down the straw house. He blew down the stick house. The brick house stayed strong. In 2020, Storm Gloria struck Spain hard. Severe weather acts like that wolf. The wolf huffs and puffs and tries to blow houses down. Hurricanes create hazards. Tornadoes create hazards. Other severe storms create hazards too. Those hazards can destroy buildings. They can take lives. The number of severe weather events has grown over time. The hazards that come with them have grown too. People cannot stop these events. Like the three little pigs, people can still act. They can find ways to stop the harm from severe weather.

2They can find ways to control that harm. High winds are a common problem. High winds can be dangerous for many people around the world. Climate Change and Severe Weather. Some heat escapes from Earth. The Sun shines on Earth. Some heat stays trapped. Extra CO2, also called carbon dioxide, sits in the atmosphere. The picture on the right shows this extra gas. It traps more of the heat that rises off Earth's surface. The picture also shows a natural amount of CO2. It shows a large amount of CO2 beside that. A layer of gases surrounds Earth. The layer is called the atmosphere. The atmosphere protects the planet. It also traps heat from the Sun. A greenhouse holds heat inside in a similar way. People call this process the greenhouse effect. The greenhouse effect is one reason Earth is a comfortable place to live. Gas and oil are among the fuels people burn. Burning those fuels releases more carbon dioxide into the air. Over many years, CO2 has built up in the atmosphere. Other greenhouse gases have built up too. The gases make the atmosphere hold more heat from the Sun. The extra heat becomes trapped. It cannot escape into space the way it should.

3Earth's temperatures therefore continue to climb. That rise is called global warming. As Earth heats up, higher temperatures cause changes. The changes show up in the planet's weather. They show up in the planet's climate. Climate change has caused more severe weather events. For instance, warmer temperatures cause more water to evaporate from the ocean. More evaporation leads to stronger storms. Wind That Pushes Hard. Most of the time, wind is harmless. Wind is also a force of nature that we need. Strong winds, however, can cause danger. The U.S. National Weather Service describes one speed range. Winds at 30 to 45 miles (48 to 72 km) per hour can toss small objects. Tall vehicles become hard to drive. Semitrucks are one example. Gusts from ordinary thunderstorms can reach these speeds. The most dangerous winds come with severe storms. Winds faster than 50 to 60 miles (80 to 97 km) per hour cause damage. Severe thunderstorms can gust at more than 100 miles (161 km) per hour. A hurricane's winds may pass 200 miles (322 km) in a single hour. Scientists estimate the speed of tornadoes. They estimate 300 miles (483 km) per hour. These winds can tear up forests. They can destroy towns and cities. They can change the land itself.

4Hurricane Sandy struck the United States in 2012. It caused 70 billion dollars in damage. One Storm, More Than One Name. Hurricanes, cyclones, and typhoons are the same kind of storm. Each one is a severe tropical storm. The only difference is where they happen. Each name comes from the language of the place. People in that place use the name for the storm. Severe storms with high winds can happen anywhere on Earth. Early warnings are among the best ways to keep people safe. Education is among the best ways too. Scientists around the globe can predict severe weather. They can predict where high winds will strike. Governments can use that information to warn people. They can teach people how to prepare. They can tell people to leave dangerous areas. How Wind Starts. Wind begins when air pressure is not the same in every place. Differences in temperature also help. The Sun warms the air of Earth. The warmed air rises. The warmed air spreads out. Air that is more spread out has lower air pressure. Cooler air sinks toward the ground. Cooler air condenses, which means it packs closer together. That closer air has higher air pressure. Air always travels from a high-pressure place to a low-pressure place. The movement evens out the pressure in the atmosphere.

5Cooler air rushes in to take the place of warmer air that is rising. That rush is wind. Pressure may build up in one place. Then the air rushes toward another place where the pressure is lower. Building for the Wind. People have invented ways to limit damage from severe winds. The damage can hit homes. It can hit many other buildings. Some buildings stand where severe storms are common. Those buildings were designed to be stormproof. They have many features that guard them. The features protect against the different hazards a storm can create. To stand up to severe winds, many of these buildings use concrete. Concrete makes them stronger. Concrete helps them last longer. A box with four sides is the shape of many homes. Homes built against wind often have many sides. Some are even shaped like spheres. Wind slips around these shapes more easily. It does less pushing against the walls. This Florida home was built to stand through hurricanes. It has done so. Why Air Pressure Can Lift a Roof. Powerful winds may pass over a roof. The moving air is pushed upward. A low-pressure area forms above the roof. Wind may get inside the building. It may enter through the roof or through a window.

6Then a high-pressure area forms inside. Air indoors then moves toward the low pressure above the building. Many roofs are blown off in storms for this reason. Severe winds often damage roofs. They can blow a roof all the way off. Builders install metal ties where the roof meets the wall. They may install clips there instead. The stronger link helps keep the roof in place. In many older homes, those ties cannot be added easily. Workers would have to cut into the walls or the ceiling. That job can be expensive. Strong winds can smash windows and doors. Flying objects can smash them too. Special materials make glass hard to break. Special materials make doors hard to break. People may also install storm shutters. Shutters may be metal. They may be plastic. They may be some other material. Shutters come in many looks. They work in different ways. Every shutter makes a barrier over an opening. The barrier keeps flying objects out. It keeps wind out too. Poplars planted close together are a common windbreak on farms. Rows of Trees and Shrubs. Some places have few hills. They may have no mountains. They may have nothing else to slow the wind. In those places, people plant windbreaks.

7A windbreak is a line of trees or shrubs. The line forms a wall. Wind must pass through the wall or pass over it. Either path slows the air. Slower wind is one of the many benefits of a windbreak. A windbreak can take up a large area, though. It needs many years to grow. A windbreak is only as strong as its plants. Some storms can rip up even big, old trees. Towers That Should Not Rock. Wind often grows stronger as you go higher. Near the ground, plants slow the wind. Buildings slow the wind. Even the ground itself slows the wind. On an ordinary day, wind at the top of some skyscrapers is very fast. It can pass 100 miles (161 km) per hour. Skyscrapers will not fall over in high wind. They are amazingly strong. They do sway with the wind. The sway can make people feel sick. The buildings on the next pages have special features. The features keep people on higher floors comfortable when the wind is high. Burj Khalifa in Dubai. The Burj Khalifa stands in Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates. It is 2,716 feet (828 m) tall. Its shape keeps changing as it rises. The changing shape confuses the wind. The More than 160 stories rise inside the Burj Khalifa.

8The corners of the building are rounded for that same reason. As the building rises, it becomes narrower. A narrower top gives the wind less surface to push. Taipei 101 in Taiwan. Taipei 101 stands in Taipei, Taiwan. It does not have square corners either. It does not grow narrower on the way to its top. Its height is 1,667 feet (508 m). Instead, it uses a damper. The damper is a steel ball that weighs 728 tons (666 mt). Near the top, that ball is hung in place. When the building sways, the huge steel ball moves the other way. That opposite movement balances the building. The building sways less. The damper in Taipei 101 also cuts vibration from earthquakes. It cuts vibration from wind as well. Weights Set Against the Wind. New York City has a tower that is both very slim and very tall. The tower is at 111 West 57th Street. Its height is 1,428 feet (435 m). Near the top sits a damper that weighs 800 tons (726 mt). Wind pushes on the tower. The damper uses two weights. One weight, shown in green, hangs from the ceiling. A series of cables holds it. The other weight, shown in blue, is held up from the floor below.

9The weights sway the opposite way from the building. By doing that, they dampen the sway. They pull the building back toward the center when high winds blow. Shanghai Tower in China. The Shanghai Tower stands in Shanghai, China. A damper near the top weighs 1,200 tons (1,089 mt). The tower itself is 2,073 feet (632 m) tall. The building also twists as it rises. The twist lowers the force of the wind. Wind follows the twist around the building and then away. The wind does not strike the building straight on. A Closing Look. Severe weather events are happening more often because of climate change. The dangers that come with those events are also more common. Some methods already work well to prevent wind damage. People are also making amazing new designs to help control these hazards. Some new homes use the methods. Some skyscrapers use them. Many other homes and buildings will still need a new design. Science keeps advancing. Design keeps advancing. We will keep improving the ways we deal with wind. These designs will help save lives. They will make people safer when severe weather hits. They will make people more comfortable too. Getting Ready for High Winds. Pay attention to warnings about high wind.

10The warnings may be on the Internet, the radio, or the TV. Take away objects that might fly in high wind, or tie them down. Trash cans are one example. Lawn furniture is another. Close the doors, the windows, and the shutters. Make them secure. Go to a basement, or go to a room that has no windows. Leave a mobile home for a safer shelter before the storm gets there. If no safer shelter is near, leave the mobile home. Lie down in the lowest spot of ground close to you. Use your hands to cover your head. Words to Know. Concrete: a mix for building that turns hard as it dries. Cement, sand, broken rocks, and water are stirred together to make it. Damage: harm that has been done to a person or a thing. Dangerous: likely to cause harm, or able to cause it. Gusts: short blasts of strong wind. Hazards: dangers or risks that might occur. Install: to put equipment, furniture, or software in place so it is ready to use. Severe: very harsh, or very unpleasant. Shutters: solid covers over windows or doors. They give privacy, safety, and a shield from weather. Sway: to rock slowly from side to side, or forward and back.

22. Canada, From One Ocean to the Other

1Ranchers move cattle across land in Canada. Contents. Finding Canada. The People. The Land. Animals. The Past. Festivals. Closing. Word List. On the mainland of North America, Canada is the largest country. It is also the one farthest north. Ten provinces make up the country. Three territories make it up as well. The motto is From sea to sea. The words fit. The Pacific Ocean is one edge of the land. The Atlantic Ocean is the other edge. A big country often has many neighbors. Canada has a single neighbor. The neighbor is the United States. Ottawa holds the government buildings. It is the nation's capital. French and English are both spoken by most government workers. Those are the country's two main languages. Other languages are spoken too. Spanish is one. Chinese is another. Many cultures live side by side. Foods differ. Clothes differ. Ways of prayer differ. Winter in Ottawa is long.

2It is cold. People there still share something special. They skate on the Rideau Canal. That canal is the largest skating area in the world. They can also use one of 267 neighborhood rinks. A hill in Ottawa carries the offices of the national government. France and Britain helped form the nation. They did this on land that Indigenous Peoples had held for thousands of years. Three Indigenous groups now include less than 5 percent of Canadians. The Métis, said may-TEE, live mostly on the plains. The Inuit live in the far north. First Nations live in every part of the country. Many families trace their arrival to France or England long ago. No earlier group from Europe arrived and remained in such large numbers. Germans arrived later. So did Ukrainians, Italians, and others. People then began arriving from China and from India. Others came from more countries in Asia and from the Middle East.

3Nearly every part of the world is now represented. One Canadian in five was born outside the country. Many people say the mix makes the nation stronger. Inuit children are shown playing outside at school. The United States border is within 160 kilometers, or 100 miles, of nine out of ten Canadians. Large cities hold most of the people. Hotels, banks, and schools are common workplaces. Factories hire people too. Some areas drill for oil. Some mine copper or gold. Some people farm. Some cut forest trees. Canadian goods go to buyers around the world. The largest share is traded over the border with the United States. A farmer in Ontario pours corn seed so he can plant. Women sell garlic at a market for farmers. Seven main regions divide the land. The west holds the Cordillera.

4Tall mountain ranges fill that region. The Rocky Mountains are the highest. They reach 3,954 meters, or 13,000 ft. After that, the land falls and becomes flat. Grass covers much of the south. Trees cover much of the north. These flat lands are the vast interior plains. The Canadian Shield comes next, wrapping around Hudson Bay. It is huge. Heavy glaciers crept across this ground thousands of years ago. Melting glaciers left piles of rock. They left thousands of lakes. Endless forest grew afterward. Inside this region sit the frozen lowlands of Hudson Bay. The south holds the lowlands of the Great Lakes and the Saint Lawrence. People call this small area Canada's heartland. It matters a great deal. Half of all Canadians live there. Many cities are there too. The Appalachian region comes last. Its hills roll and carry forest. Farms are scattered on them. Rocky shores edge the land.

5Beyond all these regions, and beyond their forests, lies the Arctic. Trees cannot grow there because of the freezing cold. The coastline measures 202,080 kilometers, or 125,566 miles. It circles the huge mainland. It also circles 52,455 islands. No other nation has a longer coast. Niagara Falls drops 57 meters, or 188 ft, in the Great Lakes and Saint Lawrence lowlands. Horseshoe Falls is the part in Canada. It stretches 670 meters, or 2,200 ft. Six football fields set end to end would match that length. White fur helps many northern animals hunt or hide in the snow. Polar bears are huge animals. Black skin lies under their fur. The white coat lets them blend in. Harp seals are their main food. A young seal pup cannot swim at first. It stays stuck on the ice until it learns. White fur lets the pup blend in too.

6The white coat is shed as soon as the pup can swim. A dark coat grows in. Northern forests have snow on the ground for only part of the year. Snowshoe hares wear white in winter so they stay safer. After the snow melts, that white coat is shed. Brown fur grows. The brown coat matches the dark floor of the forest. A Rocky Mountain goat stands on steep stone. Sure feet help an animal in steep, rocky mountains. Jumping comes easily to a bighorn sheep because of its feet. Those feet also grip well on rock. Some animals across Canada move as the seasons change. Caribou walk for hundreds of miles. Their path runs from one part of the country to another. Other animals leave for warmer weather. Salmon leave. Geese leave. Butterflies leave too. Arctic terns hold the record for the longest trips. They fly from the Arctic to Antarctica.

7The distance is some 35,500 kilometers, or 22,060 miles. They fly the whole way back six months later. The first people to reach today's Canada came thousands of years ago. They crossed a land bridge out of Asia. First Nations cultures thrived for thousands of years. Inuit culture thrived too. The earliest Europeans sailed from Greenland. More than one thousand years have passed since then. Those sailors did not stay. John Cabot, an explorer, claimed land for England in 1497. France then sent explorers to claim land of their own. They found codfish and fur. Both were costly items in Europe. More communities grew up. Growing colonies pushed First Nations people aside. Colonial settlers took their lands. Some alliances were made with Indigenous Peoples. A wide trading network grew as well. France and England often fought each other. The wars happened in Europe.

8They also happened in Canada. France in time lost its Canadian lands. People still wanted freedom from English rule. Canada became a country in 1867, with a government of its own. Canada became free in 1931. Loyalty to England remained. July 1 is the country's birthday, marked with fireworks and parades. Calgary celebrates the Old West every summer. Bull riding is part of it. Steer wrestling and more are part of it too. Winter itself is celebrated in every part of Canada. Ice-skating fills some places. Dogsledding, skiing, and other sports fill others. Quebec holds the largest winter festival of this kind. A snow-carving contest is one activity. An ice castle can be visited. Guests can even sleep in a hotel built of ice and snow. Workers build that hotel each winter. It melts away each summer. A woman races barrels in Calgary. A guest slides down ice at a Quebec ice hotel.

9In Ottawa, skaters go to work or to school on the ice. Others skate only for fun. Earth has few countries as large as Canada. The land runs from sea to sea. Ice and snow cover some regions. Tall mountains rise in others. Endless forests and big cities fill still more. French may be the language a person speaks. English may be the language. Many other languages are spoken too. Every one of these people is Canadian. Pride in the country is shared. Ice hockey fits Canada so well that it was made a national sport in an official way. A Canadian wrote the rules used in the modern game. Canada is where the first modern games were played. The sport soon reached the United States. Most players in both countries are still Canadian. The player in the picture is Givani Smith. The Central Intelligence Agency in 2021 and the World Bank give these facts.

10The population is 38,000,000. The land covers 9,984,670 square kilometers, or 3,855,103 square miles. Ottawa is the capital. English and French are the official languages. The currency is the Canadian dollar. Word List. Cultures are the ideas and customs of particular groups of people. First Nations are the people living in what is now Canada before Europeans came, and the descendants of those people. Glaciers are huge bodies of ice and pressed snow that last all year and creep downhill. Interior describes the inner part of something. Inuit are an Indigenous people of the Arctic in North America. Métis are people whose ancestry mixes First Nations and European families. Provinces are the biggest sections some countries are split into. Regions are particular places or areas. Territories are areas of land or water that a country controls.

23. Cheers Beside the Game

1This book tells how a cheering spirit can lift a crowd. It tells how cheerleading began. It tells how the activity moved from the side of the field to the center. It tells how a person joins a squad. It tells what may come next for the sport. A list of hard words comes at the end. Cheerleaders from the University of Cincinnati stand beside fans. They support a player who is shooting a basket. A Spirit That Lifts Fans. Fifty thousand people fill one arena. They have come to watch a basketball team they love. The score is tied. The clock shows just a few minutes still to play. A ball rises through the air. From the sideline, a group urges the players on. At the same time, that group moves in step together. Their clothes match the clothes of the team on the court. They get fans to rise from their seats. The fans join in support of the players. The ball completes its curve. The wait grows strong. The ball then drops clean through the hoop. People along the side are clapping. People there are also yelling.

2People there are also jumping. Those people are cheerleaders. Cheerleaders help a large crowd feel united at a sporting event. They use simple motions while they chant short phrases. Fans in the stands can see the motions clearly. Those fans can then copy the motions. Jumping and clapping after a big play can feel natural to many fans. Cheerleaders can still help that crowd cheer with more force. Players try to carry out plays that matter. While they try, cheerleaders work to raise the crowd's energy. That energy, in turn, lifts the players. In Florida, a high school squad backs its team while play is going on. The sport of cheerleading includes school-age athletes. It also includes professional athletes. Some cheerleaders belong to squads that cheer for a sports team. American football is one such sport. Basketball is another. Other cheerleaders perform routines in front of judges. They also perform for their own fans. Those shows take place at competitions. How Cheerleading Began. Sports have been played for a very long time. Across that whole span, fans have rooted for athletes they love. Cheering in an organized way did not start until the 1880s.

3Football fans at Princeton University in New Jersey were the first. Few universities in the United States are older than this one. The fans spoke words together to back their team. People gave those words a name. The name was the Princeton Cheer. A person who had finished at Princeton took football-game cheers somewhere new. The new place was the University of Minnesota. Cheers became very popular there. The year was 1898. At a game played at home, Johnny Campbell stood up and led the crowd. He was a student at the University of Minnesota. He shouted, Rah, rah, rah! He also shouted, Get together, hoo-rah! Hoo-rah! He shouted, Varsity! Varsity! Varsity, Minn-e-so-ta! That shout gave him the title of the first cheer leader. Not long after that, an official squad took shape. It had six male students. Fans who followed other teams began using the cheers too. Schools across the country formed squads of their own. In the early years, cheer squads were open to men alone. Those groups were often called yell squads. The squad yelled the chants so the crowd could hear them.

4The fans then repeated the chants. Cheerleaders from Columbia University pose with their mascot. The picture is from New York in 1924. The 1920s brought women in the United States many rights that mattered. One right was the right to vote. Women could join cheer teams starting in 1923. Marion Draper stood in front of fans at Tulane University and led the cheers. The year was 1925. The school is in Louisiana. She was among the earliest women to lead cheers. Matching uniforms were what cheerleaders wore in the 1940s. The look was a long skirt and a sweater. A letter on the sweater stood for the school name. Their shoes were black and white. Pom-poms came into use among cheerleaders in the 1930s. A pom-pom is a stick with lengths of colorful paper on one end. A wave of those sticks pulled the crowd's attention. World War II was being fought in the 1940s. Large numbers of men were overseas in that war. Cheerleading then shifted away from yell squads. It became mostly women doing organized routines.
