The routines used clapping and dancing. As the years passed, women became the main force in cheerleading.

5A Fact to Know. Lawrence R. Herkimer led cheerleading education. In 1948 he invented the herkie. To do this classic move, one leg is thrust out parallel to the ground. The other knee bends backward toward the ground. A picture shows a cheerleader doing a herkie. By the 1960s, squads were a common sight at schools across the United States. Colleges showed the same sight. In the 1970s, cheerleaders began to add harder stunts to their routines. They did this in the 1980s as well. Dances were added too. Music was set under the routines. Soon, teams faced one another in official competitions. Many squads formed in Germany during the 1990s. Through the 1980s, cheerleading spread to other countries. The spread kept going in the 1990s. Cheerleaders in Norway began to entertain fans and support teams. Germany, Japan, and Chile saw the same change. The International Cheer Union is also called the ICU. Its athletes today number more than 3.5 million. They work to help cheerleading grow worldwide. Championship events are planned by the ICU. It also promotes education in cheerleading. From the Side to the Center.

6American football games may be where this activity first stirred a crowd. It has become a sport of its own. USASF is short for United States All Star Federation. That group now runs many contests in this country. The contests include cheerleading and dance. All-star cheerleading keeps growing in popularity around the world. A yearly event got its start under the USASF in 2004. The event is the Cheerleading and Dance World Championship. People also call it Worlds. Around eleven thousand cheerleaders competed at the 2018 Worlds. They were on top teams. The teams came from more than forty countries. A team must first win a national competition. Only then can it qualify. High school cheerleaders build a pyramid at the Japan Cup in 2008. All-star cheerleaders perform routines that last two and a half minutes. A routine includes acrobatics. It also includes tumbling, dancing, gymnastics, and stunts. Difficulty is one score the judges give. They score creativity. They score technique. They score the number of advanced moves. Squads perform many parts at the same time. Judges take points away if cheerleaders fall out of time with one another.

7One common stunt is the basket toss. Bases is the name for the pair of athletes underneath. The bases lock arms. They lift another squad member and toss that person. The tossed member is called the flyer. The flyer may do a toe-touch. The flyer may do a herkie. The flyer may do some other move. The bases form a cradle. On the way back to earth, the bases catch the flyer. Spotters stand in front of the bases. They may also stand behind the bases. Spotters step in to help the catch when a problem shows up. Young all-star athletes practice the basket toss as a group. A high school squad performs a pyramid. A pyramid matters a great deal in this sport as well. Connected stunts stacked in a line make a pyramid. At the finish, people standing on the ground hold other cheerleaders above them. Cheerleaders keep working to learn moves that are hard. They also work to perfect those moves. A newer part of cheerleading is called STUNT. STUNT puts two teams in a match against one another. Both teams do matching routines together. Play lasts for four quarters.

8The quarters cover partner stunts. They cover pyramids and tosses. They cover jumps and tumbling. They cover a team routine. Athletes carry out hard technical moves for judges. They also do those moves for fans. Joining a Squad. Cheer squads are part of many schools. Other squads exist only so members can enter competitions. Youth leagues often give young people a chance to join. Recreation centers often do the same. Some children start cheering at age three. A smile matters in cheerleading. So does a look of confidence. Cheerleaders need certain qualities if they are to succeed. They must be skilled athletes. Lifting teammates is a regular task. Strong muscles are important for that work. Many cheerleaders have trained in dance as well. A loud voice lets the crowd hear them clearly. Hard choreography stays in place when memory is strong. Crowd-leading cheerleaders need to know the rules of the sport they support. They also need good timing. They must answer at once to action on the field. The cheer they pick depends on the action in the game. If their own team is defending, they rally the people watching.

9The aim is to build confidence in the players. During a time-out, they entertain the fans. After a score, they lead short cheers of celebration. Midway through a game, a longer routine is common. Music plays with that routine. Athletes often must try out for a squad. Tryouts are common for high school squads. They are common for college, all-star, and professional squads too. A coach will want to see skills in action. A squad captain may want the same look. They decide whether the athlete will fit the team. Hard routines take training and practice. They also take flexibility and strength. Precision is important if a cheerleader is to master the work. Timing and focus matter too. School-age cheerleaders perform at a ceremony tied to the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. What May Come Next. Cheerleaders are athletes who are disciplined. They are skilled as well. They are also creative performers. They entertain fans. They impress judges with bright displays of acrobatics. Those shows also include dance. Gymnastics is included too. More athletes choose to train in the sport. As they do, cheerleading keeps spreading around the world.

10Cheer received the name of a sport in 2013 from the international group that decides official sports. Recognition came in 2016 from the International Olympic Committee. The group receiving it was the International Cheerleading Union. That recognition is the groundwork cheer needs to join the Olympic Games. Where does the sport of cheer go from here? Word List. Rally means to urge people on during hard times. Athletes are people trained for sports or games that need strength, speed, and skill. Routines are sets of actions made for people who watch. Chanting means saying or singing something again and again with a beat. Squads are small groups that take part in an activity together. Choreography is the order of moves in a dance or other show, often with music. Stunts are bold physical feats, often done to entertain. Competitions are events where people or teams oppose one another to win. Synchronized means arranged so the actions happen together. Inspire means to move a person to act. Unison is when actions or spoken words happen at one time. Qualify means to show enough skill to enter a hard event.

25. Cities the World Forgot

1Cliff Palace stands in Colorado. The legend of Atlantis reaches back to 360 bce. The Greek thinker Plato gave the first account of it at that time. In his telling, the people of an advanced nation made their homes on beautiful islands. In his account, Atlantis sank beneath the ocean. He said the disaster took only one day and one night. For thousands of years, people have tried to find the city. It has never been found. Plato's account of legendary Atlantis has been painted by many artists. A lost city is a human settlement that people nearly or fully abandoned. The sites of many such places have slipped from memory. Interest in them began even before Plato wrote about Atlantis. They still stir the imagination today. They open a window onto our own ancient past. They also offer the chance of secrets not yet found.

2Atlantis may still lie under the waves. Other lost cities have been located and explored. In Italy, the ruins at Pompeii are studied with great care by archaeologists. The word archaeology comes from Greek. It means the study of old things. Dr. Chip Colwell-Chanthaphonh explains the work of these scientists. He says they study how people lived in the past. They do it by examining what people left behind, and that is often trash. The study includes old houses. It includes broken bowls. It includes bones from animals that people ate. Scientists fit those scraps together like a giant puzzle. The finished picture shows what daily life was like long ago. Thousands of visitors come to Machu Picchu each year. Machu Picchu sits high in the Andes Mountains of Peru.

3About one thousand people, and no more, lived in the Inca place known as Lost City of the Incas. They were there from roughly 1450 ce until 1572. The Incas had no writing system, so nobody is sure how the city was used. Nobody is sure why the people left, either. Archaeologists still debate the purpose. It may have been an ordinary village. The ruler's family may have had their home there. It may have been a religious sanctuary. The Incas raised large buildings, walls, and ramps. They also shaped more than seven hundred terraces. They did all of this without iron, without steel, and without wheels. Many people who lived nearby already knew the city. The wider world noticed it only in 1911. A local guide led the American explorer Hiram Bingham to the site. Mount Vesuvius rises over the ruins of Pompeii.

4The volcano is still active. Today, over 3 million people have homes near the volcano. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius lasted two days. That was in 79 ce. Ash buried Pompeii to a depth of 20 feet, or 6 m. The city stayed hidden for almost 1,700 years. Its discovery came in 1748. Finds from the dig astonished people around the world. The ash layers preserved the city and showed daily life in the Roman Empire. Paintings, shops, and small pieces of ordinary life were still in place. The ash even hardened into casts around human bodies. Diggers have cleared only about two-thirds of Pompeii since it was found. Archaeologists still have many years of work ahead. As the bodies decayed, the hard ash around them turned hollow. Workers poured plaster into those hollows to form the shapes.

5Inside the Great Zimbabwe, the Great Enclosure ranks among the biggest buildings. Inside it were a shared open area and a row of homes. Southern Africa held a trading empire. The Great Zimbabwe stood at that empire's center. The empire's years ran from about 1100 ce until 1500. Evidence suggests that twelve thousand people, or more, lived there at the peak. Artifacts from the site include gold beads and bronze spearheads. Finds also included utensils made of iron and statues carved from sandstone. Skilled builders cut stones with care and stacked them. The walls climbed 32 feet, or 9.8 m, above the ground. Archaeologists believe the people drifted away slowly after the natural resources were used up. Angkor Wat matters so much to Cambodia that the country placed it on the national flag.

6Angkor, in Cambodia, once covered about 400 square miles, or 1,000 sq km. A large empire used Angkor as its capital. From 800 ce until 1400, the population was about a million. No city in the world was larger at that time. Angkor had an advanced network for storing water and moving it through the city. Evidence suggests that people left after this water system grew too large and broke down. Some archaeologists suspect that invaders attacked. No one can say for certain. The city never stood completely empty. People still live in Angkor. More than one thousand temples stand there. Angkor Wat is one of those temples. No religious monument in the world is larger. The Treasury has appeared in many movies. In Greek, petra means rock. The name suits a city carved, beautifully, from sandstone cliffs.

7The Nabataean people built it. Their name is said na-buh-TEEuhn. Experts cannot say when the building began. By 312 bce the city was already booming. Records from that year tell of an attack by the king of a neighboring land. The attack failed. Petra was a center of trade then. Because it stood in a desert, it needed a complex way to move water. Pipes, reservoirs, and waterways did that work. Archaeologists think an earthquake ruined the water system and forced people to leave. New trade routes that bypassed Petra may have pushed people away as well. Local people knew the city. Outsiders did not visit until 1812. Only a small share of Petra has been uncovered. Most of it is still buried. Kings and other important people were buried in amazing tombs.

8Later, some of those tombs served as churches. Archaeologists dig through the stacked layers of Troy. Scientists think the first city there was built around 3000 bce. The Iliad is an ancient Greek poem by Homer. It tells of the Trojan War. In the poem, Greek forces kept Troy under siege for ten years. Hunters looked for the real city for hundreds of years. Scholars believed Troy existed only in stories. Then, in 1871, a dig in Turkey uncovered a city that matched the old description. Deeper digging revealed nine cities, each built atop the one before it. The earliest Troy dates to about 3000 bce. Newer digs have uncovered huge walls like the ones in the Iliad. Most archaeologists agree that this site is ancient Troy. They still cannot tell which layer is the city from the poem.

9In 2000, archaeologist Franck Goddio found the ruins of Thonis-Heracleion. People had long treated that important Greek port as nothing but a legend. Goddio settled another puzzle at the same time. Thonis and Heracleion were two names for one city. Thonis was the Egyptian name. Heracleion was the Greek name. Several lost cities have been found. Angkor is in Cambodia. Cliff Palace is in Colorado. Machu Picchu is in Peru. Petra is in Jordan. Pompeii is in Italy. The Great Zimbabwe is in Zimbabwe. Thonis-Heracleion is in Egypt. Tikal is in Guatemala. Troy is in Turkey. Over the years, archaeologists and other searchers have located many lost cities. More may still be hidden. Countries around the world tell their own stories of cities that vanished. Atlantis remains the most famous of them all. The hunt for that legendary city goes on.

10It might be only a tale invented by a poet. Who can say? People once said the same of Troy. If something comes from times far in the past, it is ancient. Archaeologists are scientists who study what remains of ancient cultures. An artifact is an object that humans made or used long ago. Preserved means kept in its original condition, or shielded from harm. A sanctuary is a safe place, and the word can also mean the protection that place gives. A settlement is a new place where people make their homes. A siege is a long effort to surround an enemy, often with attacks, while cutting off food and other supplies. Terraces are level strips cut into a hillside and used for farming. Uninhabited means that no people live there.

26. Cooking a Bowl of Vegetable Soup

1Winter cold feels easier when a steaming bowl is in your hands. You sit down with the steam rising. The heat warms you from the inside. You feel satisfied. The best part is the huge choice. There are enough kinds for every person to find a favorite. Some soups are clear. Some soups are creamy. Some soups hold beef. Some soups hold chicken. Some soups hold fish. Some soups hold noodles. Some soups hold rice. Some soups are spicy. Some soups are plain. The list of soups almost never ends. Almost any food tastes wonderful in a soup. Vegetables taste especially good in a soup. Vegetables hold nutrients. They hold minerals. They hold vitamins. Your body needs those things every day. Vegetables still taste good in soup. Have you cooked vegetable soup at home before? The job is easier than you might think. The soup is wonderfully healthy. A strong recipe is written below. You need a large pot. You need a few foods. You need a small bit of patience. Would you like to try? Here is the list for homemade vegetable soup.

2Use 2 carrots. Chop the carrots. Use 2 celery stalks. Chop the celery. Use 1 leek. Chop the leek. Use 1 medium yellow onion. Chop the onion. Use 1 potato. Peel the potato. Cut the potato into cubes. Use 3 cups of tomato-vegetable juice cocktail. Use 2 cups of water. Use 1 cup of long-grain white rice. Use 1 can of diced tomatoes. The can holds 15 ounces. Drain the tomatoes. Use 1 can of peas. The can holds 15 ounces. Drain the peas. Use 1 can of whole-kernel corn. The can holds 15 ounces. Drain the corn. Use 2 cans of garbanzo beans. Each can holds 15 ounces. Drain the beans. Use 1 tablespoon of soy sauce. Use 1 teaspoon of dried dill weed. Use 1/2 teaspoon of ground black pepper. Use 1/4 teaspoon of dried thyme. Use 1/4 teaspoon of garlic powder. Wash the vegetables that need washing. Peel the vegetables that need peeling. A vegetable peeler can be sharp. Keep your fingertips away from the blade. Keep your knuckles away from the blade.

3The first cooking step is to gather the foods. You need fresh vegetables. Take two carrots. Take two celery stalks. Take one medium yellow onion. Take one potato. Take one leek. A leek is a long green vegetable. Its taste is a bit like an onion. The taste is milder than an onion. Scrub the celery well. Scrub the leek well. Peel the onion. Peel the carrots. Peel the potato. Someone chopping an onion may start to cry. Do not worry. The smell causes the tears. Juices from the cut onion make eyes water. Those juices make a nose run. Cooks know a useful trick. Chill the onion for at least one hour before you cut it. Many cooks say the chill keeps the onion from bothering your eyes. Ask an adult to cut the vegetables into bite-size pieces. Cut every piece to about the same thickness. Pieces of one thickness cook at an even rate. The vegetables are gathered. They are chopped. Now they go into the large pot. The pot can sit on the stove top. The counter is another place it can sit.

4Do not light the burner yet. When the adult finishes the cutting, pick up the pieces. Drop the pieces into the pot. Next, make the broth. Broth is the liquid base of the soup. Find a liquid measuring cup. It looks like a small glass pitcher. Marks run up the side. Measure 3 cups of tomato-vegetable juice cocktail. Pour the juice into the pot. Try not to spill. Measure 2 cups of cold water. Pour the water into the pot too. Measure 1 cup of uncooked long-grain white rice. Use a dry measuring cup for the rice. Shake the rice into the broth. Canned vegetables come next. Beans carry a lot of protein. Peas carry a lot of protein. Protein is a nutrient. It helps build strong muscles. It gives food a meaty taste. You will need a can opener for this step. A hand-cranked opener can be tricky. An electric opener can be tricky too. An adult may need to help. After some practice, open the can of diced tomatoes. Open the can of peas.

5Open the can of whole-kernel corn. Open the cans of garbanzo beans. A can opener can have a sharp blade. The lid can get a sharp edge. The rim of the can can get a sharp edge. Handle the metal with care. Open cans still need to be drained. A strainer is the simple tool for that job. A strainer looks like a bowl full of small holes. Solids stay in the strainer. Liquids run away. The sink is where the strainer should go. Dump the tomatoes into the strainer. Lift the strainer. Shake it gently over the sink. Let as much liquid as possible leave the tomatoes. Wait until drops no longer fall. Then bring the strainer across to the pot. Slide the tomatoes in. You may hold a palm under the strainer. The palm can catch the last drops. A puddle on the floor is a mess worth avoiding. Rinsing your hands is much easier than mopping. Do the same job with the peas. Do the same job with the corn. Do the same job with the garbanzo beans.

6Each time, set the strainer in the sink. Empty one can into it. Shake until the dripping stops. Then empty the food into the pot. The pot looks nearly full. You are almost done. The best foods were saved for the end. Those foods are the spices. Spices make food unique. Spices make food tasty. They give soup a flavor of its own. They are the secret foods in your masterpiece. Teaspoons measure spices. Tablespoons measure spices. These are not the spoons you eat with. You will need measuring spoons that come as a set. The set needs a tablespoon. The set needs a teaspoon. The set needs a 1/2 teaspoon. The set needs a 1/4 teaspoon. Soy sauce is the first spice to add. Soy sauce has a salty tang. It makes the vegetable flavor stronger. Measure 1 tablespoon of soy sauce. Pour that spoonful into the pot. Measure 1 teaspoon of dried dill weed. Sprinkle the dill into the pot. Dill weed has a wonderful smell. Cooks often use it in Mediterranean dishes.

7Measure 1/2 teaspoon of ground black pepper. Toss the pepper into the pot. Pepper wakes up almost any dish. Measure 1/4 teaspoon of dried thyme. Measure 1/4 teaspoon of garlic powder. Shake both into the pot. Thyme gives the soup a hearty flavor. Garlic powder gives the soup a hearty flavor. You are nearly ready. Now the soup can cook. Turn the burner under the pot to the highest setting. If you are unsure how the stove works, ask an adult. Stir everything with a large wooden spoon. Stirring mixes the foods in an even way. Do not mash the vegetables. Do not splash broth out of the pot. You want the soup to be as good as it can be. Hot liquid can burn skin. Do not spill hot liquid on yourself. At this point you can take a break you have earned. The soup needs time on the heat. You will probably want to clean the kitchen. You may have made a mess. That is all right. A mess is part of cooking. Leave the pot on the burner until the soup starts to boil.

8Fast bubbles in the liquid mean a boil has started. After the boil begins, turn the heat down until it is almost off. The soup should then start to simmer. A simmer barely shivers. Only tiny bubbles show. Put a lid on the pot. One picture shows a simmer. Another picture shows a boil. Let the soup simmer slowly. Keep the simmer gentle. Give it about half an hour. Soon you will smell an enticing aroma. The smell is wonderful. Every so often, stir with the large wooden spoon. Use a gentle stir. Stirring blends the foods. Stirring blends the flavors. The blend becomes one delicious soup. Stirring also keeps vegetables from burning on the bottom. After about thirty minutes, lift out one piece of vegetable with the wooden spoon. A chunk of carrot works well. Blow on the piece a few times. Cool it enough to taste. Bite it to test the texture. Tender means soft in a pleasant way. If the carrot is tender, the soup is done. If the carrot is still hard, keep simmering.

9A crunchy carrot needs more time. Wait several more minutes. Every few minutes, taste another vegetable. Stop when the tenderness seems right. Do not cook the soup too long. You do not want mushy vegetables. Turn the heat off once the soup seems right to you. Serve the soup with a ladle. What do you think of your soup? It turned out pretty well. You can serve it with a grilled cheese sandwich. You can serve it with bread and butter. You can serve it alone. Leftovers can go in the refrigerator. Heat them again on the stove. Heat them again in the microwave. You may have enough for warm lunches all week. Those lunches are healthful. If you liked this soup, follow the same steps with other vegetables. Try zucchini. Try broccoli. Try mushrooms. Try red peppers. Soup can make nearly every vegetable taste fantastic. You can enjoy a hot meal that you made at home. You can feel proud of the work. The vegetables are full of vitamins the body needs.

10The vegetables are full of nutrients the body needs. You cooked this soup the way a professional chef would. The work began with a large pot. Carrots went into the pot. Celery went into the pot. A leek went into the pot. An onion went into the pot. A potato went into the pot. Juice helped make the broth. Water helped make the broth. Rice went into the liquid. Drained tomatoes went in next. Drained peas went in next. Drained corn went in next. Drained garbanzo beans went in next. Soy sauce seasoned the soup. Dill weed seasoned the soup. Black pepper seasoned the soup. Thyme seasoned the soup. Garlic powder seasoned the soup. The soup came to a boil. Then the pot simmered under a lid. A soft carrot showed that the soup was ready. A ladle served the soup. Bread can sit beside the bowl. A grilled cheese sandwich can sit beside the bowl. Leftovers can wait in the refrigerator. A later pot can use different vegetables. A hot bowl made at home is a proud finish.

27. Curiosity Searches the Red Planet

1Curiosity's robotic arm was on test in 2010 while scientists watched at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. This story moves from the landing to a search for ET. It then looks at a science lab on wheels, at driving the rover, and at listening to it. A computer picture shows a landing NASA had never tried. A Sky Crane lowers Curiosity in a gentle way onto the surface of Mars. One watch took place at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Cupertino, California. The date was September 20, 2012, and the time was 7:20 in the evening. The wait would last about as long as boiling an egg until the yolk is firm. Some watching scientists held their breath. Others chewed their fingernails. All of them hoped the strange craft would set down safely on Mars. Curiosity is the craft's name. Mars is still its home. Its job is to hunt for signs of life from the past or from now. Curiosity is a machine rover bigger than a golf cart. No earlier robotic vehicle from NASA, the United States space agency, was larger than this 2012 rover.

2Curiosity tore through space at 13,000 miles an hour, or 20,921 kilometers an hour, as it broke into the planet's atmosphere. Next came a drop that lasted 7 minutes. For the rover team at NASA, those 420 seconds felt longer than any others in their lives. Mars has a thin atmosphere. Even so, the air dragged on the craft and slowed it to 1,000 miles an hour, which is 1,609 kilometers an hour. That was still much too fast for a landing. The team had planned for the moment. A parachute weighing 100 pounds burst open above the craft. The chute cut the speed to 200 miles an hour, or 321 kilometers an hour, about as fast as a top race car. A landing chart lists the steps in order. The craft enters. The back shell comes off. The hottest stretch of the fall comes next. The parachute opens. The Sky Crane finishes the job. Safe arrival on August 5, 2012, set off a reaction among scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

3Moments later the parachute let go. Seconds remained, and the ground was rushing up. The Sky Crane held Curiosity underneath and fired its rocket engines. The rockets slowed the fall even more. About 66 feet up, or 20 meters, cables from the crane set Curiosity softly on the ground. No one had tried to land a spacecraft this way before. Success was not guaranteed. The control room stayed quiet. Then the seven minutes ended. A voice cried out that touchdown was confirmed. The room filled with cheers. People wrapped one another in hugs. A few of them wept. The rover was safely down. For centuries, Mars has held people's interest. Ancient Romans named the planet for their god of war, and ancient Greeks did the same for theirs. The Greek war god was Ares. The Roman war god was Mars. An Italian astronomer in 1877 was sure the Martian surface was cut by canals. He was wrong. That error started the notion that somebody lived there. Later, people noticed how much Mars shares with Earth.

4The two worlds are the same age. Seasons change on Mars, just as they change on Earth. Mars has volcanoes, mountains, and valleys. One thing found on Earth is still missing on Mars, and that thing is life. As far as anyone knows, no other planet in our solar system has ever been a home for living things. Scientists hope the Red Planet has life, or that it once supported life. Red Planet is another name for Mars. NASA sent the craft to look for aliens, but not for little green men. The search is for tiny extraterrestrial life, short for ET. Those forms might hide under rocks or lie buried in the soil. They might be smaller than an animal made of one cell, or as small as a virus. Where could such critters have started? Long ago, water moved across Mars, and water is vital for life. A wet Mars might have let life grow on the rust-red ground. If life did bloom there, some proof might remain. Three rovers have gone to Mars, and scientists have posed with test models of each one.

5Curiosity went in 2012. Spirit and Opportunity went in 2004. Sojourner went in 1996. After Earth, Mars is the planet our solar system has studied most. Many probes have flown there to seek life and to study the rocks and land. The best-known trips use robotic rovers. In 1996 the United States sent the Pathfinder probe. It reached Mars on July 4, 1997. Two days later, the six-wheeled rover Sojourner began to wander the surface. What Sojourner found changed a view. Mars was more like Earth than scientists had first believed. Spirit and Opportunity reached opposite sides of the planet in 2004. They were more complex than Sojourner. The plan called for ninety days of work. Spirit fell silent in 2010, and Opportunity fell silent in 2018. Curiosity carries a crowd of tools. There are two Chemcam units and two left navcams. Right navcams ride along. A left mastcam and a right mastcam ride along too. Six front hazcams cover the left and the right.

6Two pairs of rear hazcams, left and right, stay off one diagram. Three wheels sit on each side. If Mars holds life, this rover had a real chance to find it. In 2012 it was the smartest Mars rover yet, a full science lab on wheels. Work started at once. Dust covers popped off the cameras. The weather station switched on. First pictures were taken and sent home to Earth. New tools include 3D cameras, so scientists can see the landscape as if they stood on Mars themselves. A laser on Curiosity can blast rock. After the zap, gases shoot into the air, and special tools study those gases. A drill can grind pieces of boulder down to dust. Curiosity can read that dust and name the minerals and chemicals in it. It can also scoop Martian dirt and study the bits. The mission hunts the building blocks of life. The search list starts with carbon, then hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and further elements. Curiosity found those elements. It also found clues that liquid water was once on Mars.

7A fact card lists the basics. Launch day was November 26, 2011. The mission name is Mars Science Laboratory. Length, width, and height measure 10 feet, 9 feet, and 7 feet. Landing came at 10:32 at night, Pacific Time, on August 5, 2012. The rover weighs 2,000 pounds, or 900 kilograms, about as much as a small car. On Eastern Standard Time, that landing was 1:32 in the morning on August 6, 2012. Electricity from plutonium powers the rover. Nuclear plants use that same fuel. Home radios drew many Americans on the night of October 30, 1938. A shocking report said a huge flaming object had hit a farm in New Jersey. Martians, the report claimed, were invading. People in and near New York City panicked. They phoned the police, the newspapers, and the radio stations. They asked whether to flee town and how to stay safe. Worry was needless. Listeners had tuned in to a radio play, The War of the Worlds. A novel by H. G. Wells was its source.

8At the opening, the actor Orson Welles told listeners the invasion was not real. Many missed those first words. They truly believed Mars was attacking Earth. Some workers drive buses, and others drive taxicabs. Curiosity needs a driver too. Mars is about twice as wide as Earth's moon, yet the rover stays in one neighborhood called Gale Crater. A meteor carved that crater about three billion years ago. The hole matches Connecticut and Rhode Island laid side by side. A mountain inside it stands taller than Mount Rainier, the peak that towers over Seattle, Washington. Scientists believe this crater is the best place to seek signs of life. They think water once flooded Gale Crater. Clays and sulfates pack the ground there. Those minerals are leftovers of water. The rover studies the soil for any microbes hiding in it. Imagine steering a rover on another world from a couch at home. From March 2020 on, that is what the Curiosity team had to do. The COVID pandemic sent the scientists home to work. A photo can trace the rover's path across Mars.

9The driving job is hard, because one bad turn could doom the whole mission. Scientists and engineers choose the route together before anyone touches the computer that steers. The driver wears special glasses to study the 3D pictures sent back. A computer program then simulates the path. Hundreds of commands go in, and those commands steer the craft. Just after landing, Curiosity crept only thirty feet in a day. Temperatures on Mars can drop below minus 81 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 62.78 degrees Celsius. Heated liquid runs through the rover to keep it warm. Reaching Curiosity is harder than calling a friend on a smartphone. The rover can send a message straight to Earth. It can also relay a signal through three satellites that orbit Mars. Giant antenna dishes send and receive those signals, as a diagram can show. The dish system is the Deep Space Network. The dishes stand near Madrid in Spain, near Canberra in Australia, and in the Mojave Desert in California. Scientists will listen as the rover crosses the Martian ground, hoping to learn if anyone else is out there.

10This link is the MSL telecommunications network. An element is a substance of one kind of atom, and it cannot be split into anything simpler. A mission is a set purpose, a special task. To relay is to pass something on, such as news or a signal. Evidence is support for a theory or a claim. Extraterrestrial means existing or coming from beyond Earth or its air. Robotic describes a device programmed to do jobs for people. A rover is a vehicle that explores a surface in space, such as a planet or a moon. A laser throws a tight, strong beam of light whose waves are alike. Martian means having to do with the planet Mars. Anything that orbits Earth, or another body in space, is a satellite, whether nature made it or people did. Microbes are living things too small to see without a microscope. To simulate is to copy how something looks or how it behaves.

28. Deities of Ancient Greece and Rome

1The ancient Greeks told stories of great wars, of adventures, and of romance. They raised temples for their gods and goddesses, and they made great works of art. They believed these deities were like humans, only larger, stronger, and more beautiful. Above all, the deities were immortal. People called them Olympians because their home was Mount Olympus. A gate of clouds ringed the peak, and only gods and goddesses could pass through it. Fancy jewelry, art, music, and games pleased the Olympians. Ordinary mortals enjoy those same things. They fell in love, they married, and they had children. They even argued and fought among themselves. On visits to Earth, they sometimes disguised themselves as people or as animals. The disguise made humans think the deities were mortal. That trick was a test for humans. Heroes received help from the gods and goddesses. People who showed them honor were honored in return. People who did not were punished. These deities stood at the center of Greek religion and of Roman religion. The tales were more than good stories. Greeks prayed to these gods and goddesses, and they worshipped them. The Roman name of Zeus is Jupiter. His domain is the sky, and his symbol is the thunderbolt. His name is said ZOOS. King of the Olympians was the role of Zeus.

2He was also god of the sky and of the weather. He was the strongest god. Every other god had to obey him. Rule of the heavens had not always been his. Poseidon and Hades, his brothers, followed him into a fight. Kronos, their father, was one enemy. The other Titans were enemies as well. Poseidon is said poh-SY-dun, and Hades is said HAY-deez. Together they overthrew the Titans. After that defeat, the three brothers divided rule of the world. Zeus won the contest and became god of the sky. His weapons were thunder and lightning. Protection of Earth's kings and rulers was something the Greeks believed he gave. He watched over all people, upheld the law, and defended anyone who had been wronged. The Roman name of Poseidon is Neptune. His domain is the ocean, and his symbol is the trident. Poseidon ruled the oceans of Earth. The sea suited him, because his mood could change as fast as the water. Storms rose at his call when he was angry. Earthquakes rose too. The tool was his magic trident. With that same trident, he could quiet the waves. A golden chariot carried him across his kingdom. The horses that pulled it were shaped like waves. Demeter, goddess of the harvest, was someone he tried to impress.

3One tale says the first horse was made during that effort. Her request was for a new animal. She wanted it more beautiful than every other animal. The horse he made delighted her. It delighted him too, so much that he forgot Demeter and rushed off to make more horses. The Roman name of Hades is Pluto. His domain is the underworld, and his symbol is a helmet. Hades received the realm called the underworld, and there he ruled as god of death. He saw that the dead were buried in the proper way. Hidden riches of the earth were his as well, including gold, silver, and other buried treasure. Palaces were home to most Greek gods. Hades rarely came up out of the dark underworld. He asked Zeus for permission to marry the lovely Persephone. Zeus agreed, and Hades carried her down to his palace. Demeter, the girl's mother, threatened Zeus. Zeus then gave Hades an order. The daughter had to be brought back into daylight. Hades obeyed, but only after he offered Persephone food from his kingdom. She ate several seeds of a pomegranate. Those seeds meant she had to return to his realm for a few months every year. The Roman name of Hermes is Mercury. His domain is merchants, and his symbol is the herald's staff.

4His name is said HUR-meez. A son of Zeus held the role of god of merchants. That son was Hermes. Aside from Hades, he was the only god allowed into the underworld. When a person died, Hermes led that person to the realm of Hades. The likeness to Hades stopped there. Hades rarely spoke or smiled, while Hermes loved talk and loved tricks. As a baby, he slipped away from his mother and stole his brother's cows. He wrapped the cows' feet in bark so their tracks would not show. He tied brooms to their tails so the brooms would sweep the ground behind them. His quick wit and clever speech pleased his father. Zeus made him the messenger of the gods. Zeus also gave him winged sandals and a winged cap of gold, so he could travel faster. The Roman name of Hera is Juno. Her domain is marriage and birth, and her symbol is a peacock feather. Her name is said HAIR-uh. Hera, goddess of marriage and of childbirth, was the wife of Zeus and queen of the gods. Few were allowed to argue with him, and she was among that small number. A royal crown was on her head. Her scepter was tipped with a lotus blossom.

5Peacocks drew the chariot she rode. Greek women asked her blessing at weddings. As goddess of childbirth, she was thought to protect a mother during birth. In the seventh century bce, Romans admired the Greeks so deeply that they shaped their own society on the Greek model. The gods and goddesses stayed the same. What changed was the reach of each deity's personality. Some grew more warlike, and others grew less powerful. The Roman forms of these names are the names given to the planets of our Solar System. The Roman name of Artemis is Diana. Her domain is the moon and the hunt, and her symbol is a golden bow and arrows. Her name is said AR-teh-mis. Artemis was goddess of hunting, of the wilderness, and of wild animals. Still a child, she won a promise from her father, Zeus. The promise was that she could stay unmarried forever. Mountains and forests were where she would hunt through the day. Nymphs would look after her hounds. She both guarded animals and hunted them, which made her popular with people who hunted game. Rural worshippers favored her in a special way because she was tied to wild nature. Greeks and Romans honored her with music and with dance. She was a childbirth goddess as well, because she had helped her mother deliver her twin brother.

6Her role was not the same as Hera's. The mother was under Hera's protection. The newborn baby was under the protection of Artemis. The Roman name of Hephaestus is Vulcan. His domain is the volcano Aetna, and his symbol is fire and the axe. His name is said heh-FES-tus. Hephaestus was god of fire, of volcanoes, of crafts and craftsmanship, and of blacksmiths. A disability affected his legs from the time he was born. Hera, his mother, was deeply upset at the sight of him. She threw him off Olympus. The fall ended in the ocean far below. Sea goddesses found him there and gave him shelter. He stayed with them for nine years and worked as a blacksmith. In that time he became the most skilled craftsman of the Olympians. Gods, goddesses, and heroes prized the weapons, armor, and jewelry he made so finely. A marvelous throne of gold was his work one day. He sent that throne up to Olympus. When Hera sat down, hidden springs locked her in place. The throne was a trap, built to punish her for casting him away. The Roman name of Aphrodite is Venus. Her domain is love and beauty, and her symbol is a seashell. Her name is said af-roh-DY-tee.

7Love and beauty were the domains of golden-haired Aphrodite. She could grant beauty and charm to anyone who pleased her, and she could make any person fall in love. Her son was the mischievous child-god Eros, whom the Romans called Cupid. After the trap caught Hera, Zeus offered marriage to Aphrodite as the prize for whoever set his wife free. Hephaestus could not resist her loveliness. He climbed to Mount Olympus, freed his mother, and married Aphrodite. His wedding gift was a belt of metal. Precious gems were woven into it, and so was magic. The belt's power made her completely irresistible to gods and to men. The Roman name of Ares is Mars. His domain is war, and his symbol is a spear and a helmet. His name is said AIR-eez. Zeus and Hera had a son who became god of war. That son was Ares. Fierce and strong, he was a warrior. A gigantic spear was his weapon. He loved the destruction of war, and he loved its smells. In a battle, other gods and goddesses sometimes picked one side to support. Ares did not. He cared nothing about who was right or who was wrong. At times he even changed sides in the middle of a fight. He loved battle for its own sake.

8He got along poorly with many Olympians, and most of them hated his attitude and his violence. He was often beside his sister Eris, goddess of discord, who could stir a war into being. Aphrodite was also the one he loved. Her love for the handsome war god was greater than her love for her husband, Hephaestus. The Roman name of Athena is Minerva. Her domain is wisdom, war, and the arts, and her symbol is the owl. Of all the children of Zeus, Athena had the strangest birth. She sprang from his head, already grown, and already dressed in golden armor. She became his favorite child, and the only child allowed to use every one of his weapons. As a war goddess, she gave leaders wise advice. Greeks also credited her with many kinds of wisdom. They said she invented the arts of spinning, weaving, pottery, and cooking. Farmers received two inventions from her. One was the plow. The other was the bridle a horse wears. Justice and morality used her as a symbol because of those talents. Athens took her as its patron goddess. The city carries a name given in her honor. Each year the city held a festival called the Panathenaea, said pan-ath-uh-NEE-uh, to thank her. Greek and Roman names for these deities can be set side by side.

9Zeus matches Jupiter, also called Jove, and the Latin form is Iuppiter or Iovis. Hera matches Juno, and the Latin form is Iuno. Poseidon matches Neptune, and the Latin form is Neptunus. Athena matches Minerva, and the Latin form is Minerva. Hades matches Pluto, and the Latin form is Pluton. Ares matches Mars, and the Latin form is Mars. Hephaestus matches Vulcan, and the Latin form is Vulcanus. Aphrodite matches Venus, and the Latin form is Venus. Hermes matches Mercury, and the Latin form is Mercurius. Artemis matches Diana, and the Latin form is Diana. Ancient Greek society gave gods and goddesses a place at its center. Countless sculptures came from that inspiration. Temples came from that inspiration as well. Other artworks did too. Their influence did not stop when ancient Greece ended. Italy was nearby. There, the Romans used the Greek example as the pattern for much of their society. People today still look to ancient Greece, and they study its temples and statues for ideas. The first Olympic Games took place in 776 bce. The events were races on foot. They were held so the gods and goddesses would be honored. Those races grew into the Olympic Games of today. Some people call ancient Greece the birthplace of Western society.

10Ideas pictured in Greek mythology helped form the way people think and the way they treat one another now. A realm is an area under someone's rule. A monarch is one kind of person who may hold that power. A chariot is a two-wheeled carriage pulled by horses, used in ancient times mainly for racing and for battle. A scepter is a decorated rod that a ruler holds as a sign of power. Disguised means changed in appearance so that others will not know who you are. Temples are buildings set aside as places of worship. Immortal means not subject to death, so the being lives forever. Greek myths tell of the Titans. They were huge and powerful, and they ruled in the time before the gods and goddesses. A person who likes playful trouble can be called mischievous. Mythology is the set of myths of a culture or a group, and myths are old stories of heroes or of supernatural beings. A trident is a weapon shaped like a spear, but with three points. Greek myths send some of the dead to the underworld. Hades is the ruler of that place. Stories describe nymphs as spirits with the looks of young women. Their homes are mountains, forests, meadows, or water.

29. Downs, Yards, and the End Zone

1Super Bowl history remembers a moment called The Tackle as one of its most dramatic. This championship game is played on January 30, 2000. The Tennessee Titans meet the St. Louis Rams. They are playing in the Super Bowl, the greatest game in American football. The Rams are ahead by a score of 23-16. The Titans have the ball at the Rams' 10-yard line. Only six seconds are left in the game. Titans quarterback Steve McNair throws a pass. Wide receiver Kevin Dyson stretches out an arm for the ball. That arm stops just 1 yard short of the end zone. The gap equals 0.91 meters. The crowd roars. The Rams capture their first Super Bowl championship. Endings full of excitement make one point plain. This spectacular sport gives people a reason to cheer. No sport in the United States draws a bigger following than American football. More fans attend football games than games of any other sport. More fans also watch football on television than any other sport. About seventy thousand people come to each National Football League game.

2People call that league the NFL. The championship game of the NFL is the Super Bowl. Around the world, this game stands with the largest sports events. The Philadelphia Eagles run onto the field to face the St. Louis Rams. The stadium is Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia. About seventy countries around the world field American football teams. The sport is less widespread than some other sports. Interest in it keeps growing. Those nations belong to the International Federation of American Football. A map of the federation shows North America and South America. It shows Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia. It also shows the Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, and the Indian Ocean. The Equator is marked on that map. Canada's own kind of football goes back more than one hundred years. Canadian football is similar to American football. The size of the field is not the same. The number of players is not the same. Some rules are not the same. Arena football is an indoor form of American football.

3People have played it since the 1980s. The games are fast, and the playing field is small. In the late 1860s and the early 1870s, students at several schools in North America took up two games from England. One game was soccer. In parts of the world, people also call soccer football. Players mainly used their feet. The other game was rugby, short for rugby football. Players used their hands as well as their feet. People know Walter Camp as the Father of American Football. Yale, a school in Connecticut, was among those that played rugby. Walter Camp studied at Yale from 1876 to 1881. He offered changes to the rules of the game. Over the years that followed, modern American football came into being. Some people think the earliest American footballs were probably rugby balls. Makers stuffed inflated pig bladders into casings of pig hide. The balls had an oval shape. Throwers found them difficult to throw. Later, makers stopped using the bladder. They shaped balls with more pointed ends.

4Today the balls are made of leather from cowhide. Some people still call those balls pigskins. In college football and in pro football, the goalpost measures 18.5 feet across. That width is 5.6 meters. The goalpost stands 10 feet tall. That height is 3 meters. One way to score is a kick that travels above the bar and between the uprights. The end zone measures 10 yards from front to back. That distance is 9.1 meters. A touchdown counts when the ball is carried into this area. A touchdown also counts when a pass is caught in this area. A field diagram marks a distance of 160 feet, or 48.8 meters. It also marks a distance of 360 feet, or 109.7 meters. Hash marks sit 1 yard apart. A 5-yard line is painted on the field. The 50-yard line shows the middle of the field. That number means the line is 50 yards from either end zone. The 50 yards equal 45.7 meters. At the 10-yard line, an arrow points toward the nearer end zone.

5The field also has a goal line, an end line, and a sideline. American football carries the nickname gridiron. Yard lines and hash marks make a pattern. That pattern gives the game its nickname. A play diagram lines the offense up against the defense at the line of scrimmage. The quarterback is marked QB. The center is marked C. Each guard is marked G, and each tackle is marked T. The tight end is marked TE. Each wide receiver is marked WR. Each running back is marked RB. On defense, each defensive tackle is marked DT. Each defensive end is marked DE. Each linebacker is marked LB. Each cornerback is marked CB. Each safety is marked S. Each game has two teams. Each team tries to reach the other end zone with the ball. That is how points are scored. Each team fields two main platoons, and each platoon has eleven players. A third platoon handles the kicking. The offensive platoon tries to put points on the board.

6The defensive platoon tries to keep the other team from scoring. The platoons take turns on the field. When Team A controls the ball, its offensive unit plays Team B's defensive platoon. When Team B controls the ball, its offensive platoon plays Team A's defensive platoon. Each offensive platoon is led by a quarterback. A quarterback from West Virginia University stands ready to throw. He keeps a towel at his side. He wipes his hands with it so his grip on the ball stays firm. A player can carry the ball forward to get nearer the end zone. A player may also pass it, which means throwing it to a teammate. The ball has to be carried into the end zone or caught there. If a teammate catches the throw, the pass is complete. A catch by the other team makes the pass an interception. If no one catches it and it drops to the ground, the pass is incomplete. Teams have several ways to put points on the scoreboard. Picture Team A playing offense.

7Team A scores six points for a touchdown by running the ball into the end zone of Team B. A completed pass into that end zone is also a touchdown. Right after a touchdown, Team A tries to add extra points. A kick through the goalposts is worth one point. A run or a pass that reaches the end zone is worth two points. Team A can also score a field goal, worth three points. A field goal comes from a kick that passes between the goalposts. Team B, on defense, can try to take the ball away. Team B can then score points of its own. A North Carolina State quarterback wearing number 12 dives toward the end zone. He is playing against the Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets. On another play, the Northwestern Wildcats line up on offense and prepare to move the ball. The Notre Dame Fighting Irish line up across from them on defense. Play begins when the ball is kicked off to the offensive team.

8That team drives toward the other team's end zone. It must gain at least 10 yards, a distance of 9.1 meters. The offensive team gets four chances, called downs. Those four downs must bring the 10 yards, or else a score across the goal line. If it gains at least 10 yards inside the four downs, it keeps the ball. It then earns a fresh chance to gain another 10 yards. If it cannot move the ball 10 yards in the four downs, the other team takes over. Teams keep many special plays ready. A play is a plan for moving the ball down the field. Each time the two teams line up, the quarterback tells teammates which play to run. The defense has several ways to stop the offense from scoring. Defensive players try to knock the ball carrier to the ground. That stop is called a tackle. They may also force the carrier to drop the ball. They may catch a pass that was aimed at a player on the other team.

9Football gear protects the body. Players wear a chin strap and a helmet. They wear shoulder pads, a jersey, and gloves. They wear hip pads and pants. They wear thigh pads, knee pads, and socks. Their shoes are cleats. Extra pads under the uniform help players keep from getting hurt. Jerry Rice and Joe Montana stand among the greatest players in the history of American football. Both played for the San Francisco 49ers during the 1980s. Rice was the best wide receiver the sport has known. Many fans would call Montana the best quarterback the sport has known. The 49ers won the Super Bowl three times with those two leading the way. Tackle football is still very popular with players of every age. Those other forms bring the same amount of fun. They are easier on the body than tackle football. In touch football, a player only has to touch the ball carrier to stop the play. Those players may follow the main rules of tackle football, the rules of the NFL.

10They may choose not to follow those rules. Flag football is one more form of the game. A player stops the ball carrier by pulling off a piece of cloth fixed at the waist. Whatever form fans play or watch, they can count on a great time with this amazing sport. A championship is a contest that decides a winner. Defensive describes action meant to stop the other team from scoring. The end zone begins after the goal line. It stops at the end line. Play in soccer can start with a kickoff. American football can start the same way. Blockers on offense form the offensive line. Their blocks clear a path so the ball carrier can score. Platoons are groups of teammates who share one job, such as offense, defense, or kicking. The quarterback is the player who calls the plays and throws the ball. Spectacular means wonderful and impressive. A wide receiver is the player whose main job is to catch the quarterback's pass and run with the ball.

30. Dreams That Built Giant Works

1Crews dug tunnels for a path under the sea. That path is the English Channel Tunnel. People also call it the Chunnel. This book shows how people pick the biggest projects. It tells about the Channel Tunnel. It tells about the North Sea Protection Works in the Netherlands. It tells about the Canadian National Tower. It tells about the Panama Canal. It tells about the Golden Gate Bridge. It tells about the Burj Khalifa. It tells about China's South-to-North project for moving water. A closing and a word list come at the end. Egypt's Great Pyramids have not fallen. They are the only Wonders of the Ancient World that remain. Workers built them along the Nile River. The building took eighty years. Stone blocks in the biggest pyramid numbered 2.3 million. Writers of ancient Greece, long ago, selected seven great works. Creative people had built them. Those seven works are known as the wonders left by the ancient world. In their own time, the buildings and statues seemed impossible. Only simple tools were on hand. Today, humans seem able to create almost anything. Not long ago, engineers asked experts on modern building to choose seven new projects.

2The projects seemed almost too huge to picture. Each one is a massive feat of engineering. Each one beat an old limit of size, length, height, or nature. The Petronas Twin Towers rise in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. A skybridge joins the two towers. The walkway of that bridge is not fixed to either tower. The tall towers sway as the wind pushes them. The walkway can slide into the buildings and back out again. Napoleon planned an attack on the United Kingdom first. A treaty with that country came later. Digging beneath the English Channel was one of his plans. His army would walk through that tunnel. Other soldiers would strike from the sky. They would ride in hot air balloons. The United Kingdom lies about thirty-one miles from the coast of France. The English Channel is the water between them. Seas in the Channel can be stormy. They can be dangerous. Those seas have often helped keep armies from other lands away. In 1802 the French general Napoleon dreamed of a tunnel under the Channel. His soldiers would walk across through it. People laughed at the dream. Today the crossing is easy.

3You ride a train called the Channel Tunnel train. Trains move through this system of underwater tunnels. They go from 100 to 200 miles an hour. A fast train comes out of the Channel Tunnel. Vehicles ride on that train. Cars, buses, and trucks are the only load on some trains. During the ride, drivers stay inside their vehicles. Other trains carry passengers and nobody else. Those passengers sit in train cars that are comfortable. About 13,000 people built this huge project. They worked for seven years. They dug three enormous tunnels. Each tunnel is 32 miles long. They dug through chalk. They dug through clay. The chalk and the clay lie under the English Channel. The three tunnels run next to one another. One tunnel is for the trip that starts in England and ends in France. They come back in a second tunnel. The tunnel in the middle is for service. Crews use it when something needs repair. The Netherlands is a small country on the cold North Sea. A great deal of its land is lower than the sea. In storms, waves used to destroy homes. Floods used to destroy farmland.

4Lost farmland led to shortages of food. The Dutch people looked for ways to hold the sea back. They wanted to save their land. They wanted to save their crops. They wanted to save their people. The North Sea Protection Works got its start in 1927. They built dams on some parts of the coast. They left other parts open to the sea. Open water was kept for ships. It was also kept as a home for wildlife. One huge barrier against storm surges stands in the Netherlands. The barriers hold back very high tides. They stop floods from ruining land and crops. Low farmland across the Netherlands stays protected. Floodwalls and surge barriers do that job. To guide water and ships, the Dutch built a floodwall bigger than any other. Giant gates are set in the wall. When the sea is calm, the gates stay open. Ships can pass. Wildlife can pass. In a storm the gates shut. Shut gates stop the flood. New protected land came to the Dutch from this giant system. The protected land is over one-half million acres. People farm it. They raise livestock on it.

5They build homes on it. Visitors in Toronto, Canada, can stand high on a tower deck made for looking out. The tower is the Canadian National Tower. People call it the CN Tower. From the deck you can see Niagara Falls. The falls are about eighty-five miles away. A glass floor lets you look straight down. The city is far below. A helicopter lifted the pieces of the tower's tall antenna. Workers joined the antenna in 44 sections. When the antenna was done, the tower set a height record for that time. The CN Tower stood 1,800 feet tall. It rises high over downtown Toronto, Canada. Panama is a narrow country. Panama joins North America to South America like a land bridge. Until the 1900s, a ship going from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean had a long trip. It had to sail all the way around South America. People dreamed of a canal cut across Panama. The canal would join the two oceans. Work on the Panama Canal at last began in 1904. The canal runs 51 miles. It uses a line of chambers with gates. The chambers are called locks.

6Each lock fills with water. Water rising in a lock carries ships up from the height of one ocean. It sets them at sea level on Panama's other side. The ships seem to climb stairs. Then they seem to go down stairs. Each year the canal system is used by about 14,000 ships. The Golden Gate Bridge is 1.7 miles long. It crosses the mouth of San Francisco Bay. Building it took 83,000 tons of steel. That steel came through the Panama Canal on ships. The beautiful bridge stands for San Francisco, California. For many decades it was only a dream. People who lived nearby pictured a bridge over a narrow stretch of water. The water is windy. San Francisco Bay lies on one side of that water. The Pacific Ocean lies on the other side. Planning lasted sixty-five years. Crews finally started building in 1933. They worked on towers that rose 746 feet over the water. They hung thick cables in the cold. Fog was around them. Wind was around them. A fall was always a danger. Eleven workers fell and died while the bridge was built. Eleven workers lost their lives during the building.

7A net hung below the bridge. Nineteen more workers fell. The net caught those workers. The bridge opened in 1937. Vehicles crossing since opening day number more than a billion and a half. Thousands of tourists come each year. People on foot get a wide look at the bay. Lanes for cycling give a wide view of the city. Fame has made this bridge one of the best known anywhere. People know it for how big it is. They know it for its dark orange color. They know it for the spectacular place where it stands. Dubai is a rich city on the coast. It is in the United Arab Emirates. People shorten that name to UAE. That nation lies in the Middle East. Dubai has put up many of the biggest structures on Earth. One of them is the Burj Khalifa tower. The tower has 160 stories. It stands 2,716 feet high. It opened in 2010. Then it was the tallest thing humans had ever built. Parks surround the Burj Khalifa. Fountains are there too. The area includes the largest mall. Projects like these draw business. They draw tourists.

8Dubai has not stopped building. One big project is named Dubailand. Dubailand holds complexes made for entertainment. Amusement parks are part of them. An elevator in the Burj Khalifa travels farther than any other elevator. The tower measures 2,716.5 feet. In 2010 the Burj Khalifa became the tallest building on Earth. It rose past the Canadian National Tower in Canada. The difference was almost 1,000 feet. China has always struggled to manage water. Some places are too dry. Other places flood too easily. Big cities in the north need more water than rain can give. Beijing is one of those cities. A huge plan will move water from China's south to China's north. The plan's full name places South-to-North before Water Transfer Project. The water will travel on three different routes. It will leave rivers and lakes that have plenty. It will go to Beijing. It will go to other crowded places that do not have enough. A huge set of locks is part of the Three Gorges Dam. The transfer project uses dams. It uses canals. It uses tunnels. It uses pumps. The system runs for hundreds of miles. Some tunnels will send one river underneath a different river.

9This work makes China's earlier giant project look smaller. That earlier project is the Three Gorges Dam. It is the largest hydroelectric project anywhere. The dam stands on the Yangtze River. It is 600 feet high. The dam stretches farther than one and a half miles. Cities downstream are safer from floods because of the dam. No other plant that uses moving water makes as much electricity. Its reservoir may soon link to the South-to-North plan. So much moving water pushes hard. The pressure has shaken farm fields. It has changed their shape. It has cracked houses nearby. Both the water plan and the dam draw argument. Millions of people had to leave their homes. Reservoirs and canals needed the land. Some old historic places may end up under water. The aim is to send water to the places that need it most. Unusually large problems can spark the largest dreams. They can spark the most imaginative answers. The seven structures in this book have designs like no others. Those designs fixed problems. The problems sat in different countries. They sat in different environments. Even bigger projects are going up right now.

10Human imagination seems to have few limits. One car maker had a problem with space. The maker built a garage that stores cars straight up and down. Machines run the garage. The garage used 80 percent less ground than a normal design spread out flat. When people plan something very tall, very large, or never built before, they have many important choices to make. A canal is a waterway people dig across land. It can carry travelers or water for crops. Dammed means a barrier was made. The barrier stopped water from flowing. To dwarf something means to make it seem smaller or less important. An engineer designs machines, builds them, or repairs them. They also work on buildings, bridges, and other structures. A feat is an amazing act or a great success. Hydroelectric describes electricity made by moving water. Locks are gated parts of a canal or a river. Water in them is raised or lowered so ships and boats can pass. An observation deck is a high platform. People stand there to see the land around them. A skyscraper is a building that is very tall.

31. Drums That Keep the World's Beat

1Today, a drum shell is built from thin layers of wood. A picture shows a man forming a shell that way. Stop and listen. Is the wind tapping a twig on the window? Does water fall from the roof and land in a puddle? If you are near a beach, can you hear waves break on the shore? You are hearing rhythm. Rhythm is a pattern of pulses that repeats. Feel your own pulse. That life-giving rhythm comes from your heartbeat. A mate can be drawn by repeated sounds that animals make. A territory can be guarded with repeated animal sounds. Since ancient times, people have made rhythmic sounds with drums. Music is only one of the old reasons people beat drums. Crickets are known for a chirp that keeps a rhythm. A young girl enjoys the sound of drumming. Drum making has happened in every part of the world. Drum playing has happened in every part of the world. A drum is a percussion instrument. A percussion instrument must be hit to make a sound. The hits create rhythm. The hits create patterns. Not every drum is built the same way. A cylinder is the shape of some drums. A cylinder drum has a head at each end. The player hits the top head with bare hands.

2The player may use drumsticks instead. Sound bounces around inside with help from the lower head. Some traditional makers cut a piece from a tree trunk. They hollow that piece out. The head is animal skin. Nails can hold the head on the drum. Leather straps can hold the head on the drum. Drums in a modern drum set are cylinders too. Heads still sit on the top of those cylinders. Heads still sit on the bottom. Modern heads are plastic. Metal parts attach the heads. Many Native peoples play drums that belong to their own tribe or nation. Taos Pueblo Indians made the drums shown in one picture. They live in New Mexico. British soldiers of the 1800s rode drum horses and played kettledrums. No horses in the Army were larger than the drum horses. A picture shows a British kettledrum from 1805. A bowl is the shape of some drums. Some drums are shaped like kettles. Early kettledrums used a bowl of clay. Early kettledrums could also use a bowl of wood. The bowl might be small. The bowl might be very large. A single head was stretched over the opening. Brass kettledrums were a soldier's tool many centuries ago.

3The noise was meant to frighten enemies. Those drums were huge. They were so heavy that horses had to carry them. Elephants had to carry them too. The pounding could confuse an enemy. The pounding could throw an enemy off balance. The sight of elephants with drums could cause panic. The sound of those drums could cause panic too. By the 1600s, this kind of drum was played in symphony orchestras. It had become a musical instrument. Kettledrums are also called timpani. Orchestras still play them today. They are usually made of brass. They are usually made of copper. A picture shows a drummer playing timpani in an orchestra. A message goes out when a Ni-Vanuatu man strikes a tree drum. He stands on Ambrym Island. The island lies in the South Pacific. Uses for drums have piled up across the years. People once used them in war. People have also used them to talk with friends. Some people believe drums have power to heal. Drum messages were sent by Native peoples across many centuries. Island communities of the South Pacific once sent word with tree drums. They have phones now. Some of them still use tree drums. A tree drum is a hollowed-out log set on its end. Some tree drums are 20 feet tall.

4That height is 6 meters. A slit is cut down one side. The slit is about 4 inches wide. That width is 10 centimeters. The length of the slit changes the sound. People often carve faces into tree drums. They carve animals. They carve different shapes. Men of the Libinza tribe make mokoto drums from logs. The Libinza live in the Ngiri River area. Democratic Republic of the Congo is the country of that river area. Builders group tree drums so that several sizes sit side by side. The group can make many sounds. Different sounds can come from a single tree drum. The sound changes with the place the drummer hits. A beat pattern lets people of a tribe pass a message. They can receive a message the same way. Drums have also carried messages in war. Imagine you are an officer in a battle. You need to give orders to soldiers. Guns make a thunderous noise. Cannons make a thunderous noise. The noise is so loud that soldiers cannot hear your voice. Drums can carry the orders instead. Soldiers learned to hear certain beats as commands. One command means attack. One command means retreat. One command means regroup. Each army needed its own set of beats so the two sides would not match.

5The 78th Colored Troops Infantry included a young drummer named Taylor. A picture shows him with his drum during the Civil War in the United States. Outside a tipi, two Sioux men strike hand drums. The picture was made in 1908. Ancient tribes believed drums could help healing. A hunter might come home very tired. The hunt had failed. While he slept, someone played a drum softly over him. The soothing rhythms helped him heal. Drum therapy is used by some tribes today as a path away from trauma. Some Native peoples speak of a spirit power in drums. Warriors about to fight drew courage from that sound. Dancing to drumbeats gave some Native peoples a feeling of group strength. That dancing still does this at modern powwows. Today, more people are learning that drums can help healing. Drum groups are gaining many new members. An experienced drummer teaches patterns to the group. People feel satisfied when their drum makes a pleasing sound. They feel happy. Playing together can be very healing. Members forget the worries of everyday life while they play. They can feel the medicine of the drums. Central Park is the setting for a modern circle of drummers making music.

6Central Park is in New York City. The djembe is a hand drum. Say djembe as JEM-bay. People across West Africa use it. Makers form it from a hollowed-out log. The shape is like a drinking goblet. The top is wide. The bottom is narrow. It has a single head. Players usually carry it with a shoulder strap. Different peoples of West Africa played the djembe before battles. The sound gave courage to warriors. Dances are one use of the djembe. It is also known for healing rhythms. The talking drum is another drum of West Africa. Its shape is like an hourglass. The top is wide. The bottom is wide. The middle is narrow. A head covers the top. A head covers the bottom. People first used talking drums to send messages between villages. The player held the drum under one arm. The player squeezed the drum against the body while playing. The squeeze made the drum change its sound. People said the drum could talk. A curved drumstick hits the talking drum. One of the most popular drums of Latin America came from the Congo region of Africa. It traveled by way of Cuba. People call it a conga drum. People also call it a conga.

7The shape is a cylinder that gets thinner at the bottom. It has one head. The player hits that head with the hands. The player can sit. The player can stand. A seated player grips the conga with both knees. A stand supports the drum if the player is on their feet. Three sizes are made for the conga. One size makes a high sound. One size makes a medium sound. One size makes a low sound. Bongos are easy to play. Bongos are hard to master. Bongo drums are also called bongos. Latin American music uses them. Their shape is like a conga. They are much smaller than conga drums. A pair is formed by joining two drums that are not the same size. The player holds them between the knees. The player sits down to play. Hands can strike either head. Each head can be hit with the fingers. A joke asks a question about size. If taiko drums are the largest, what is the smallest? The joke answers with your eardrums. Battlefields of East Asia once rang with taiko drums. Taiko groups now perform for audiences in many countries. Carving usually starts with one log when a taiko is made. Gigantic size is true of some of them.

8The player may be smaller than the taiko drum itself. Taiko drummers must train hard. The training earns them a place in these groups. A modern drum set includes drums. It includes pedals. It includes stands. It includes cymbals. Today's look is not how drum sets always appeared. They have not always sounded the same either. The modern set grew as jazz grew in the United States. Jazz began in the American South near the end of the 1800s. Jazz blends many kinds of rhythm. Jazz blends many kinds of music. That blend included work songs sung by enslaved Black people. Religious songs were part of the blend. Rhythms from West Africa were part of the blend. Together they gave birth to jazz. By the 1920s, jazz had become very popular. Marching bands in New Orleans keep an old tradition alive today. Black brass bands marched through streets in New Orleans and similar cities. They played music similar to jazz. Many drummers marched in those bands. Each drummer played one drum. Early in the 1900s, inventions made it possible for a single drummer to handle many drums together. Those inventions led to the drum set. In 1909, William F. Ludwig invented a bass drum pedal. Simplicity set this bass drum pedal apart as the first of its kind.

9It was easy to use. One foot was enough to sound the bass drum. The hands were free for the other drums. The hands were free for the cymbals. Bass drum pedals today are easy to play. They are easy to adjust. A picture shows a hi-hat. A picture shows a bass drum pedal. By the 1920s, modern sets had gained the hi-hat as one more piece. At first, a hi-hat was a pair of boards joined by a hinge. A cymbal was attached to each board. One foot came down on the upper board. The two cymbals struck each other. A hi-hat today has a foot pedal. It has a stand. The stand holds a pair of cymbals. The pedal makes the cymbals strike each other. A drumstick can strike the hi-hat as well. Electronic machines for drum sounds spread widely in the 1980s. Popular music looked, for a brief period, as if machines might push older drums aside. That trend did not last long. Drummers prefer to play real drums. Art Blakey lived from 1919 to 1990. He was an American jazz drummer. He was a bandleader. Cindy Blackman Santana was born in 1959. She is an American drummer of today.

10She plays jazz. She plays rock. Ringo Starr was born in 1940. He is a British rock star. He is a drummer. The drum is the oldest musical instrument in the world. Thousands of years have passed without a change to the basic plan. During those years, a vast array of drums has grown up around the world. Some of those drums have done jobs other than making music. Nearly all humans share a feeling for rhythm. Studies show something more. Our skill at recognizing these patterns seems unique to our species. That skill is what lets us tap our feet. That skill is what lets us clap along. Somewhere far inside, people carry their response to a beat. As long as rhythm moves people, we will keep using drums. Drums help us keep the beat. The author's grandfather was a drummer. He got the author started on drums. A band works the way a team works. Everyone must work together if the team is to succeed. The author has played in bands since the age of ten. The author still loves playing drums. A photo shows the author's grandfather playing drums around 1945. A photo shows the author playing drums with a band.

32. Eight Bears and How They Live

1Contents. What a Bear Is. Growing Up. Kinds of Bears. How Bears Stay Alive. Word List. Topic List. People often call the koala a koala bear. A bear is not what the koala is. It is a marsupial. A marsupial is a mammal with a pouch. Australia has an especially large share of marsupials. In the Americas, the opossum is the lone marsupial. Bears are intelligent animals. They are curious. They are powerful. They have always fascinated people. They have thick fur. They have short legs. They have small ears. They have stubby tails. They have long claws. Their jaws can crush bone. Smell is a strong sense for bears. They can smell food that is packed inside plastic bags. They can find that food. No bear is smaller than the sun bear. A sun bear weighs 36 to 63 kilograms. That is 80 to 140 pounds. No bear is larger than the polar bear. A male polar bear's weight can reach 680 kilograms. That is 1,500 pounds. Hibernation is what many bears are known for. To hibernate is to sleep, and the sleep often lasts for months. Bears that hibernate do so for a reason. They must survive the cold winter. In winter there is not enough food.

2Warmer months are when they take in huge amounts of food. They store enough fat to last the winter. They can then go without food until spring. Bears are famous for hibernating.
