Even so, many bears do not hibernate. Even in warmer months, a polar bear cannot store enough food. A giant panda has the same problem in those months. Winter is not a season they can pass with no food. Sun bears live where food is plentiful all year. Sloth bears live in places like that too. Those bears also do not hibernate. A picture shows a mother bear with her cub. Most adult bears are solitary. Roaming alone is what they like. There are exceptions. One exception is the mating season. Another is a mother's time of cub care. Bears usually have one cub at a time, or as many as three. A newborn cub is very small. It is blind. It is helpless. A den is where cubs remain beside their mother. They stay for several months after birth. Raising cubs is not a job male bears take on. Sometimes a male kills the cubs. Sometimes he eats them. The mother bear must protect her cubs fiercely. She does this while they are young.

3She does this while they are weak. For as long as three years, cubs remain near their mother. Learning is their biggest task in that time. They must learn how to find food. After that, they live alone. Eight kinds of bears appear on the pages that follow. A drawing below compares their sizes. The list runs from the largest bear to the smallest bear. The polar bear is 2.6 meters long, or 8.5 feet. It weighs 318 kilograms, or 700 pounds. The brown bear is also called the grizzly. It is 2.1 meters long, or 7 feet. It weighs 250 kilograms, or 550 pounds. The giant panda is 1.8 meters long, or 6 feet. It weighs 113 kilograms, or 250 pounds. The American black bear is 1.5 meters long, or 5 feet. It weighs 113 kilograms, or 250 pounds. The Asiatic black bear is 1.5 meters long, or 5 feet. It weighs 113 kilograms, or 250 pounds. The spectacled bear is 1.5 meters long, or 5 feet. It weighs 113 kilograms, or 250 pounds. The sloth bear is 1.5 meters long, or 5 feet. It weighs 113 kilograms, or 250 pounds. The sun bear is 0.9 meters long, or 3 feet.

4It weighs 36 kilograms, or 80 pounds. Size puts the polar bear first among bears. It is also the largest carnivore that lives on land. No larger meat-eater walks the Earth. White fur makes a polar bear easy to identify. The fur may also be yellow-white. That color camouflages the bear in the snow. Polar bears are fantastic swimmers. Their front paws are partly webbed. Warmth comes from a thick fat layer. The fat works even in extremely cold water. The North Pole region is where polar bears live. They are powerful hunters. They eat mostly seals. They also eat walruses. Finding food can be difficult. A polar bear may go days at a time without a meal. Under the fur, a polar bear's skin is black. The black skin absorbs energy from the sun. That energy helps keep the bear warm. A picture shows a polar bear. Not every brown bear has brown fur. Brown bears are divided into ten subgroups. The subgroups are based on coloring. The color can be light tan. It can be reddish brown. It can be very dark brown. The grizzly bear is one subgroup people know well. The name comes from gray-tipped fur. The fur looks frosty.

5People also say it looks grizzled. The largest brown bear is the Kodiak bear. Alaska is home to the Kodiak bear. Brown bears have a wider range than any other kind of bear. Western North America is part of their range. They live in parts of Europe. They live across much of northern Asia. Brown bears are not all the same size. Size depends on where they live. It also depends on what they eat. Fish is a staple food for many brown bears. Salmon is an especially important fish for them. A grizzly eats a diet with huge variety. Few living animals eat a more varied diet. Grizzlies eat meat. They eat fish. They eat insects. They eat eggs. They eat berries. They eat roots. They eat leaves. They eat grass. A picture shows a brown bear. The giant panda is famous around the world. It is one of the best-known animals anywhere. People recognize it easily. Its fur is thick. The fur is black and white. Distinctive patches surround its eyes. Giant pandas live in China. Their home is the mountains covered by forest. They feed on bamboo almost exclusively. They depend on healthy bamboo forests. Without those forests they cannot stay alive.

6Giant pandas are extremely rare. Only about 1,000 are left in the wild. Each giant panda hand has an extra thumb. The extra part is not a true thumb. It is a special bone in the wrist. A pad covers that bone. The bone helps the panda grasp bamboo stems. A picture shows a giant panda. The American black bear is often black. Sometimes its coat is lighter. It has a muzzle that is light in color. Scientists sort American black bears into subgroups. The sort is based on coloring. One subgroup is the cinnamon bear. Its coat is reddish brown. Another is the Kermode bear. Its coat is white. Another is called the blue bear, the silver bear, or the glacier bear. Its coat is bluish black or dark gray. American black bears live across much of North America. Alaska is one place they live. They can be found in Canada. They can be found in northern Mexico. Black bears are true omnivores. They eat a wide variety of plants. They eat honey. They eat fish. They eat insects. They eat dead animals. They are very good climbers. A picture shows an American black bear. The Asiatic black bear is sometimes called the moon bear.

7Its coat is black. The muzzle is the exception, because it is light in color. A patch of light fur marks the chest. The patch is shaped like a crescent moon. The ears are unusually large. Mountain country is home to Asiatic black bears. Those regions are in many countries of Asia. These bears often anger farmers. They eat crops. They kill sheep. They kill goats. They kill cattle. Their diet is diverse. It also includes fruit. It includes insects. It includes small animals. A picture shows an Asiatic black bear. Spectacled bears have shaggy coats. The coat may be brown. It may be black. Light markings appear on their faces. Sometimes the markings look like eyeglasses. Eyeglasses are also called spectacles. This is the only bear native to South America. It lives in mountains covered by forest. It lives in grasslands. It lives in deserts along the coast. Like most bears, spectacled bears are omnivores. They will eat almost anything. They will even eat dead meat. They especially like fruit. They like sugarcane. They like corn. Spectacled bears often climb cacti. They eat the fruit that grows at the top. Each spectacled bear has a face pattern of its own. The eye markings are unique to that bear.

8A picture shows a spectacled bear. The sloth bear is one kind of small bear. It has a long coat. The coat is shaggy. Its face is lighter in color than the rest of its body. It moves slowly. It often hangs from tree branches. A tree sloth is a different mammal. The sloth bear hangs in a similar way. India's forests are home to sloth bears. They live in the grasslands of India. They also live on Sri Lanka, a neighboring island. Their favorite food is termites. The snout of a sloth bear is long. It uses the snout to suck termites out of their nests. These bears also eat fruit. They eat berries. They eat honey. Feeding brings a loud sucking sound from them. People can hear that noise from far away. A picture shows a sloth bear. Inside the bear family, the sun bear has the smallest body. Its coat is mostly black. A light patch of fur marks its chest. A rising sun is the shape of that patch. That patch gives the sun bear its name. Sun bears live in tropical rainforests. The forests are in the lowlands. The region is Southeast Asia.

9Sun bears feed on plants. They feed on animals too. They have tongues that are unusually long. The tongues help them pull insects from tight places. Those places are hard to reach. People sometimes call sun bears honey bears. The name comes from their love of honey. A sun bear likes honey so much that it will face angry bees. It fights the bees to reach the honey. It eats the bees as well. A picture shows a sun bear. Stories about bears that attack people are frightening. People are a greater danger to bears than bears are to people. Human activity is causing bear populations to shrink. Humans have destroyed bear habitat in huge amounts. More than half of all bear habitats in the world are gone. People cleared that land for farming. They cleared it for mining. They cleared it for forestry. Endangered status applies to five kinds of bears. The other three kinds are decreasing in numbers. Hunters are another threat. They kill bears for meat. They kill bears for sport. They kill bears so body parts can be used as medicine. Some hunters call bears pests, and that is why they hunt them. They believe the bears threaten crops. They believe the bears threaten livestock.

10Saving bears from extinction is the work of conservationists. Wildlife biologists are working toward that same goal. Protection for bear homes is a goal many people are working toward. They are trying to stop the hunting. They want bears to keep living in the wild. A picture shows a scientist placing a tag on a brown bear's ear. The tag lets scientists track the bear. It helps them learn about the bear's behavior. A carnivore is an animal that eats meat. A muzzle is the long front of an animal's head. It includes the mouth. It includes the nose. Comparative means using a comparison. It can also mean showing a comparison. An omnivore eats plants, and it also eats animals. Diverse means made up of many different things. Exclusively means completely. It can also mean entirely. Solitary means alone. It means without companions. Hibernating means sleeping deeply. The sleep can last for a whole winter. Topics in this book include the American black bear. They include the Asiatic black bear. They include the brown bear. They include the giant panda. They include the polar bear. They include the sloth bear. They include the spectacled bear. They include the sun bear.

33. Fire Mountains and How They Erupt

1Pompeii was a Roman city. During 79 CE, earthquakes failed to worry many of its residents. No one linked those quakes to smoke rising from Mount Vesuvius nearby. Trees covered the volcanic mountain. Flowers covered it. Grass covered it. A thousand years had passed since the last eruption. Dormant was how most people described Mount Vesuvius. A dormant volcano has stayed quiet across many hundreds of years. Other people thought it was extinct. Extinct means it has not erupted for thousands of years and shows no sign of erupting again. Everything changed on August 24. The change came around one o'clock in the afternoon. The ground shook from a giant blast. Dust blew from the top of the volcano. Ash blew out. Melted rock blew out. The sky grew dark. Stones began to rain on the city. Rocks covered the ground as far as 16 kilometers from the mountain. That distance is 10 miles. Ash covered the ground that far too. By three o'clock, lava began to pour from the volcano. Lava is melted rock that has reached the surface. The lava destroyed everything in its path. At six o'clock that cloud of dust and ash had climbed 32 kilometers. That height is 20 miles. Ash kept falling. A layer 1 meter deep lay on the ground. That depth is 3.3 feet.

2The stones were heavy enough to bring buildings down. Buildings fell under the weight of the ash. People tried to flee. The volcano was destroying homes. The volcano was destroying farms. The ash was very deep. The ash was very hot. Trying to walk through the ash cost many lives. Others were killed by stones that dropped from the darkened sky. Many people choked on air clogged with ash. Many people choked on air clogged with dust. Around midnight, things got even worse. A massive cloud hung overhead. It held ash. It held poisonous gas. It held dust that glowed with heat. It held smoke. The cloud grew too heavy to stay up. It collapsed. It raced down the mountain at speeds up to 500 kilometers an hour. That speed is 310 miles an hour. A picture shows Mount Vesuvius in the background. The ruins of Pompeii stand in front. Within moments, the first surge cloud burned people in Pompeii. It buried them. The same thing happened in Herculaneum. A surge cloud is a superheated cloud. It carries ash, gas, dust, and rock. It moves quickly along the ground. More dust poured from the volcano. More ash poured out. More surge clouds followed. Two cities lay fully buried after the eruption stopped. They were wiped from the face of the Earth.

3More than one thousand years passed before people uncovered them again. A picture shows a plaster cast of a person from Pompeii. That person died in the eruption. Pompeii lay near Mount Vesuvius. A surge cloud buried the city completely. Many people were killed. Ash and mud hardened around the bodies. As time passed, the bodies decayed. Pockets of air were left behind. Each pocket had the exact shape of a body. Plaster went into the holes at the hands of scientists. Each cast records a person's appearance at the moment of death. The story you just read is true. How could it happen? How could a blast become that violent? The answer is in the way different volcanoes form. Earth's hard surface is called the crust. Huge sheets of rock form the crust. Those sheets are called plates. Some plates form the continents. Other plates form the floors of the oceans. Extreme heat lies immediately beneath the plates. The heat is so high that rock melts. The melted rock is called magma. Magma is liquid rock under the surface. Sometimes magma flows upward. It pours out through cracks in the crust. A diagram shows vents. A diagram shows a magma chamber. A diagram names the plates of the crust. One plate is the Eurasian Plate. One plate is the North American Plate.

4One plate is the Pacific Plate. One plate is the African Plate. The Pacific Plate appears again on the diagram. One plate is the Indian Plate. One plate is the Nazca Plate. One plate is the Australian Plate. One plate is the South American Plate. One plate is the Antarctic Plate. One plate is the Scotia Plate. The equator is marked. Plate edges appear as dotted lines. Most volcanoes in the world are found along those edges. The plates float on thick liquid magma. Each plate can head a different way. Plates can crash into each other. Plates can pull away from each other. Plates can grind past each other. Moving plates release pressure. The pressure causes earthquakes. Earthquakes open large cracks in the crust. Magma sometimes breaks through those cracks. A volcano can form there. Active volcanoes worldwide number at least five hundred. Plate borders are the neighborhood of most of them. An active volcanic belt follows the rim of the Pacific Ocean plate. People call that region the Ring of Fire. Another active region follows the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The ridge is a chain of undersea mountains. It lies in the Atlantic Ocean. A pair of plates is separating at that ridge. Rising magma is able to break through the seafloor. The magma piles up.

5As it cools, it becomes solid rock. Over time, the magma builds mountains. Some of those mountains rise above the sea. Those peaks become islands. The country of Iceland sits on top of large volcanoes. Those volcanoes are part of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Distance from a plate edge does not stop every volcano from forming. Hawai'i lies amid the Pacific Ocean plate, not along its rim. These islands lie above a hot spot. At a hot spot, magma lies much nearer the crust than is usual. Another hot spot lies under Yellowstone National Park. Yellowstone National Park lies inside the North American plate, far from the rim. The hot spot borders underground lakes. Magma heats the ground around it. Magma heats the water. The heat creates geysers. A geyser is a hot spring that boils from time to time. A tall column of water mixed with steam shoots upward. The heat also creates hot springs. A diagram shows Kauai. A diagram shows Hawai'i. Arrows show the plate moving. A hot spot made the volcanoes of Hawai'i. Movement of the Pacific Plate carries it across the hot spot. Old volcanoes go extinct. New volcanoes form. Picture a sheet of paper moving over a burning candle. The candle burns a row of holes in the paper. A line of volcanoes can grow from a hot spot, much as those burned holes line up.

6Volcanoes do not all erupt in the same way. The place where a volcano formed changes the eruption. The way it formed changes the eruption too. Some volcanoes erupt in a gentle way. They erupt slowly. Others explode all at once. The force can equal many atomic bombs. A picture shows a shower of red-hot cinders. Mount Vesuvius is a composite volcano. You read about that mountain earlier. Composite volcanoes are explosive. Their eruptions can be violent. Their eruptions can be destructive. They are usually large mountains. The sides are steep. The peaks are even in shape. A bowl-shaped crater often sits at the top. The crater is where magma comes out. Hot gas comes out there. Ash comes out there. One picture shows Mount St. Helens before the eruption of 1980. Another picture shows Mount St. Helens after that eruption. Most composite volcanoes form from magma that is thick. The magma moves slowly. Magma travels in underground tubes called vents. A vent is an opening in the crust. Magma and gases can come out through it. Very thick magma can cool before it reaches the surface. It can harden. The hard rock plugs a vent. Once the vent is plugged, the magma below has no exit. Pressure builds.

7When the pressure is great enough, the volcano explodes. Sometimes the whole mountain is destroyed. In 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted in Washington State. Destruction removed the whole north face of the mountain. When a composite volcano erupts, it sends huge clouds into the air. The clouds hold ash. The clouds hold dust. The clouds hold smoke. The clouds hold hot gas. The clouds hold rock. The clouds turn the sky black. Ash rains onto the ground. When a cloud grows too heavy to stay up, it falls. The fall is a violent surge cloud. Ice can sit on many composite volcanoes because the peaks are so high. They are tall enough to carry snow. A hot blast can melt all the ice in an instant. A hot blast can melt all the snow in an instant. Water, mud, and rock then flood down the mountain. The flood can run at up to 100 kilometers an hour. That speed is 62 miles an hour. Melting ice and snow once caused a huge mudslide. The biggest clouds of volcanic ash can travel around the world. Those clouds can block sunlight over large areas. They can cool the planet. Tambora erupted in 1815. Tambora is a volcano in Indonesia. After that eruption, North America had a summer that was unusually cold. The summer was unusually snowy.

8A buried pool of magma may drain out of a composite volcano. A huge empty space is left below. The surface falls into the empty chamber. A large bowl-shaped caldera remains. A caldera can be as wide as 100 kilometers. That width is 62 miles. Calderas often fill with water. The water makes large lakes. Oregon is home to Crater Lake, a famous caldera. It formed when the volcano fell in on itself. Mauna Loa is a shield volcano in Hawai'i. Composite volcanoes can destroy forests. They can bury cities. They can even cause human deaths. Hundreds of years of quiet can pass from one eruption to the next. Neighbors can forget that an explosion is still possible. Film of lava leaving a volcano is something you may already have watched. You may have seen lava spraying. This lava is runny. It flows quickly. It travels far before it hardens. It travels fast before it hardens. The hardening lava slowly builds up. Lava of this kind comes from a shield volcano. A shield volcano usually has gentle slopes. The slopes are shaped like shields. A blast is not the usual way a shield volcano erupts. Roads can still be ruined by the flowing rock. The lava can still damage homes. The lava can still damage forests.

9Sometimes lava sprays high from the crater. The spray is a lava fountain. Quiet activity can go on for a long stretch. It can grow very large. No volcano on Earth stands taller than Mauna Loa. From the base on the seafloor up to the summit, the rise is 9,170 meters. That height is 30,080 feet. It is taller than Mount Everest. Olympus Mons is the biggest volcano anyone has found in our solar system. Olympus Mons is on Mars. This shield volcano on Mars rises 27 kilometers. That height is 17 miles. A view of Mars shows Olympus Mons rising there. The whole of Arizona could fit beneath it. Cinder cones stand on Mauna Kea. Mauna Kea is a volcano in Hawai'i. Some volcanoes do not grow into large mountains. Only a little lava is thrown upward. Small chunks of lava harden. Bits of ash harden too. They become light rocks called cinders. Cinders collect in a heap around the opening. The pile becomes a hill. A bowl-shaped crater sits at the top. Cinder cone is the name given to each of these hills. New volcanoes often make cinder cones. Older, larger volcanoes sometimes hold added cinder cones inside a crater. Other cinder cones form inside calderas. One eruption is the full history of most cinder cones. Loose stones are what a cinder cone is built from.

10Wind wears them away quickly. Rain wears them away quickly. Small, quick eruptions sometimes build lava domes. Slow, thick lava can seep from an opening. It hardens quickly. That is how a lava dome forms. Later lava may force a path out through the dome. The sides crack. Lava domes often form where other volcanic activity is already happening. Craters of big volcanoes are a common home for them. Lava domes often burst with great force, as composite volcanoes do. One photo, taken in Alaska, shows a lava dome seated over an opening. Inside a crater, a scientist keeps an eye on a lava dome. Volcanoes show that our planet is always changing. They are impressive examples of that change. Volcanoes also bring benefits. Lava makes new rock. Lava makes new land. Volcanic ash makes rich soil. Farmers use that soil. Some peaks built by volcanoes rank among the loveliest on Earth. Mount Fuji in Japan is one of them. Mount Rainier in Washington is one of them. Mauna Loa in Hawai'i is one of them. Choosing a home near a volcano is a decision many people make. Everyone should remember that volcanoes are dangerous. Some of Earth's most powerful forces live in volcanoes. A picture shows beautiful Mount Fuji in Japan.

34. Forests That Drop Their Leaves

1This book tells about a blaze of color. It tells about the temperate deciduous forest biome. It tells about climate and soil. It tells about plants. It tells about animals. It tells about people. It tells about grand beauty. A word list comes at the end. A Blaze of Color. Of all the seasons, fall feels special. The weather grows cooler. Many people feel better about being outside. Certain places offer something extra in this season, beyond weather that feels good. As the air cools, the first hints of autumn color show on trees. Soon, yellows cover the countryside. Golds, oranges, and reds join that show. For some people, these landscapes sit right outside the door. Other people travel by air across thousands of miles just to look. One thing is sure. This event should not be missed. Few shows on Earth match these bright fall colors. They are also a clear sign of temperate deciduous forests. A forest in Germany shows leaves turning color. A Word Note. Deciduous began as a word in Latin. It means to fall off. In winter, trees of this kind let their leaves fall. People sometimes call them leaf-shedding trees. Shed means letting something go during ordinary living. A snake sheds its skin in this way.

2A cat sheds hair in this way. Autumn leaves color the land in Quebec, Canada. Next comes the biome itself. Earth's surface holds many kinds of environments. A biome is a region together with the living things in it. Grasslands are one example of a biome. Deserts count as biomes. So do rainforests and oceans. Temperate deciduous forests are also biomes. Many factors help create Earth's biomes. Two important factors are latitude and elevation. Latitude is how far a place is from the equator. Elevation is height above sea level. Together, those two factors set how warm a place is. Climate is a building block of a biome. Land and water are building blocks too. So are plants and animals. This biome covers wide stretches of land full of trees that drop their leaves. Come fall, color shifts in the leaves of these trees. Winter brings those leaves down onto the soil. Forests of this kind cover about 7 percent of the land on Earth. Australia has some areas with deciduous trees. New Zealand has some of these trees. Southern South America does too. So does Washington State. Those places are not counted as part of this biome. These forests sit in the northern temperate zone.

3That band of latitude is in the Northern Hemisphere. The cold polar zone is on one side of this band. The hot tropical zone is on the other. In the United States, a large share of the eastern third belongs to this biome. A small part of Canada is in it too. Large areas also lie in Europe. Japan holds large areas of this forest. Eastern Russia does too. So do China and Korea. These forests may sit next to many other biomes. They may border grasslands. They may border semiarid deserts. They may border taiga, which means cold forests. They may border subtropical forests. Spring wakes a beech forest in Germany. Snow rests on bare deciduous trees in winter. Weather and the ground come next. These forests grow in places that get both very warm weather and very cold weather. Because of that, the biome has four seasons. Each season has its own character. Winters are cold. They often bring low precipitation. The amount still changes from place to place. Temperatures rise in spring. Precipitation rises then too. Both reach their high point in summer. Summer can be quite humid. Cool, crisp air marks the autumn. Precipitation drops in autumn.

4Through the year, temperatures generally stay between -30 degrees C (-22 degrees F) and 30 degrees C (86 degrees F). This biome has the second-highest precipitation each year of any biome. Only rainforests get more. Each year brings about 75 to 150 centimeters of precipitation. That equals 30 to 59 inches. In winter, that water often falls as snow. It may also fall as sleet or hail. By the end of fall, a layer of leaf litter lies on the soil. Soils here tend to be deep. They tend to be dark. They tend to be fertile. This happens because trees drop their leaves in autumn. Fallen leaves collect in a layer on the ground of the forest. They make a thick layer of leaf litter. Fungi break that leafy layer down. Bacteria do this work too. Other organisms under the ground do it as well. Their work lets nutrients go into the soil. A Fact to Know. Certain temperate places have soil with extra sand. Those soils hold fewer nutrients. Forests there often mix deciduous trees with evergreen trees. Weaker soils are places where evergreens are able to live. They lose leaves and grow leaves all through the year. They do not do this only once a year.

5When both kinds of trees stand together, people often say mixed forest. One picture shows a mixed forest in fall. Another shows a mixed forest in winter. Plant eaters digest these leaves with ease, thanks to the leaf shape. Their texture helps too. Plants. These forests are also called temperate broadleaf forests. Most trees here have wide, flat leaves. They do not have thin needles. The form of the leaf is an adaptation. It helps these trees stay alive. A wide leaf has a large surface. Photosynthesis gets a large share of sunlight from that wide surface. During photosynthesis, the plant makes its food. The inputs are sunlight, water, and air. They also use chlorophyll, which is a chemical. Plant growth in this biome is usually stacked in five levels. The canopy holds the tallest trees. Those trees get the most sunlight. Fertile soil feeds many hardwood trees. Those trees include oak, elm, and maple. They also include hickory, beech, and ash. The thick canopy still lets a share of sunlight through. That light lets many kinds of plants grow in the lower levels. In a forest in Wales, rhododendron shrubs thrive beneath the canopy. The level under the canopy holds shorter trees, such as dogwoods.

6It also holds saplings. A sapling is a young, slender tree. Under that is the shrub level. Rhododendron can grow in that shrub level. Sumac can too. Honeysuckle can too. Next comes the herb level. It holds ferns, grasses, and wildflowers. Mosses grow on the forest floor, which is the ground. Fungi and lichens grow there too. Tree trunks are another place they grow. Trees here have more adaptations than leaf shape. They drop their leaves and go dormant in winter. That lets them save energy. It also lets them stand the cold. Thick bark gives trees protection from low temperatures. A birch forest is a place where ferns grow. Plants in the lower levels have adaptations too. Early spring is when ferns shoot up fast. Wildflowers do the same. They do this before the canopy fills in and blocks too much sun. Why Leaves Change Color. Leaves of deciduous trees mainly carry out photosynthesis in spring and summer. Sunlight is one tool. Chlorophyll is the other. Chlorophyll is a chemical found mostly in leaves. Water and carbon dioxide gas become a sugar with help from that chemical. That sugar gives the trees energy. Leaves look green because they are full of chlorophyll.

7They also hold orange, yellow, or brown chemicals. The green chlorophyll hides those colors. In fall, the weather grows cooler. The trees get less sunlight. Photosynthesis slows down. Chlorophyll production in the leaves comes to a stop. They lose their green color. The hidden colors then start to show. When fall is cold enough, the temperature drops below freezing. Sap inside the leaves must not start to freeze. The trees let the leaves go before that can happen. The goal is to keep the tree from being damaged. Winter leaves these trees without a covering of leaves. Survival then depends on food saved during the warm seasons. When spring comes, temperatures warm up. A fresh set of leaves appears. Animals. Many kinds of animals live in these forests. One reason is the many kinds of plants they can eat. Another reason is the many watery habitats. Those habitats include lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams. Bobcats hunt in these woods. Foxes hunt here too. Mountain lions hunt here too. So do timber wolves and coyotes. White-tailed deer are among the large plant eaters. Moose live in some areas too. Smaller herbivores include rabbits, squirrels, and chipmunks. Omnivores include skunks, raccoons, and opossums. Black bears are omnivores too.

8Eastern gray squirrels feed on nuts of deciduous trees. They also eat buds and flowers. Snakes are common here. So are frogs, toads, and turtles. Woodpeckers, cardinals, hawks, and owls live here. Many other birds do too. Insects live here in large numbers. Spiders do too. Regal moths eat deciduous leaves before they become adults. Animals here have adaptations that help them through harsh winters. Staying warm costs them extra energy. Food is harder to find because the trees are dormant. Squirrels are one example of animals that put food aside ahead of winter. Others hibernate so they will not need as much energy. Black bears do this. American toads do this too. Another way to last the winter is to lose less heat. A thicker fur coat grows on red foxes. They often stay safe from the cold inside dens. Snow acts like a blanket that keeps mice warm. Other rodents do the same. On a cold winter day, a red fox keeps warm inside a den. Woodpeckers live in this biome all year. Most owls do too. Many songbirds live here only in the warmer months. When winter comes, they travel to places that are warmer. Food is more plentiful there.

9Woodpeckers live all year in deciduous forests of the eastern United States. Fall colors draw hikers in South Korea. People. Human life in these forests goes back many thousands of years. The original condition of most of this biome is largely gone. Use of its resources goes back at least five thousand years. Fertile soil is used to grow crops. Hardwood trees are used for fuel. They are also used for building. Few biomes on Earth hold as many people as these forests do today. People still use their resources. Regrowth of the trees has happened in some spots. These forests are popular places for recreation. Hiking brings people here. So do boating, fishing, and camping. Wildlife watching brings people too. The fall colors are a pull that is hard to resist. Grand Beauty. Every season gives these forests a look of their own. Bare woods become winter wonderlands once frost, snow, and sunlight arrive. In spring, dormant trees and flowers wake up. That waking is a welcome sign of new life. Heat plus rain in summer sets off a rush of green growth. Bright fall colors turn the land into works of art. If you can visit one of these forests, go. Fall is an especially good time.

10Looking at the bright trees is an experience you will not forget. A walk across crunchy leaves underfoot is just as hard to forget. Word List. An adaptation is a change in a living thing, or in a species, that helps it survive better where it lives. Dormant means not active, yet able to become active again. The equator is an imaginary line around Earth, halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. Fertile describes land that can grow many plants or crops. Fungi is the plural of fungus. These living things grow on material that was once alive, and they make spores. Herbivores are animals that eat only plants. Humid describes air that holds plenty of water. Landscapes are what you see when you look across a piece of land as one view. Mosses are plants that are small and soft. They can grow on trees. They can grow on rocks. They can grow on ground that is moist. An omnivore eats plants. It also eats other animals. Precipitation is water coming down to the ground. Hail is one form. Sleet, rain, and snow are forms too. Temperate describes a climate or region with moderate, or mild, temperatures.

35. Frederick Douglass Wins His Freedom

1Frederick Douglass was eight. He took a loaf from the kitchen, left by the back door, and set off on errands. He was enslaved, yet he knew his meals were fuller than those of some neighborhood boys. He traded bread for a skill he wanted even more, the skill of writing. Only a day earlier, Sophia Auld had grabbed a newspaper out of his hands. He had been trying to read it where no one would see. Sophia was the wife of the man who enslaved him. All he wanted was an education. In the 1820s, teaching an enslaved person was against the law. The white boys he knew might be poor, but school had been open to them. He teased them by claiming he knew more alphabet letters than they did. Then he scratched a few letters in the dirt. The boys wrote the letters they knew, and Frederick learned each new one. Now the bread bought him proper lessons in reading and writing. Ahead, a friend waited with a lesson.

2Frederick hurried over. He would skip lunch every day if the lesson continued. His birth fell in February, either in 1817 or in 1818. He never learned the day of his birth. He knew his father was a white man, but he never learned the man's name. His mother was Harriet Bailey. His grandmother, Betsey Bailey, raised him. At eight he was sent to work for relatives of his enslaver, the Auld family in Baltimore, Maryland. At first Sophia Auld helped him learn the alphabet. She gave several lessons before her husband made her stop. He said education and slavery were incompatible. He believed a reader would grow unhappy with slavery and would want to be free. Time proved Auld right. The more Frederick read, the clearer his situation became, the more he hated slavery, and the sadder he felt. For a while the word abolition puzzled him. If an enslaved person ran away, people blamed abolition. They blamed it too when an enslaved person did something an enslaver called bad.

3Frederick checked a dictionary. It said only that abolition was the act of abolishing. He still wondered what was being ended. In 1831 a newspaper story answered him. It described the abolition movement and the people fighting to end slavery. He understood at last that some white people wanted slavery abolished too. He also learned that some states let Black people live free. Escape became his dream. Years later he wrote that learning to read leaves a person free from that day forward. He saw education and freedom as partners. He started lessons for other enslaved people, until enslavers shut down his Sunday school. Enslaved people came to see him as a leader. Enslavers came to see him as a troublemaker. For years he had lived in the city. At fifteen he became a field hand on a farm run by Edward Covey. Covey was known for beatings that forced enslaved people to obey. The loan to Covey may have been Auld's punishment for the teaching.

4Covey nearly broke Frederick's spirit. Six months of abuse passed. At sixteen, Frederick had taken enough. Covey came at him again. Frederick fought back, and the struggle lasted two hours. Covey never tried a beating again. After that fight, escape plans began. One try failed, and he was caught. He still dreamed of freedom and kept building his literacy. He joined a debate club called the East Baltimore Mental Improvement Society. Anna Murray, a free Black woman, was someone he met in that club. The two of them planned the escape together. Her savings paid for his train ticket. She also stitched a sailor's uniform for him. The sailor's uniform was on his back, and a freedman's passport was in his hand. His route ran through Delaware, then Pennsylvania, then New York. Less than twenty-four hours passed before the escape was finished. Later he wrote that this one day held more living than a full year in slavery. Speaking years afterward, he told crowds he stood before them as a thief and a robber.

5He had taken his own head, limbs, and body from his enslaver and run away with them. Reaching a free place did not make him truly free. Life in a free state could look like freedom. Capture could still drag that person back to a slave state. Frederick sent for Anna. They married in 1838. Because he was a fugitive who might be forced back into slavery, the couple took the name Douglass. They settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, and they had five children. In the 1800s, abolitionists built a secret network to help people who escaped. People came to call it the Underground Railroad. Stops with food, clothing, and shelter were safe houses, or stations. Many fugitives walked. Conductors, also called stationmasters, aimed to place a station every fifteen miles. That distance is 24 kilometers. Douglass stayed in safe houses right after his escape. Rochester, New York, is where he later served as a stationmaster.

6He and Anna helped fugitives get to Canada. One such safe house stood in Ripley, Ohio. Meetings against slavery soon had a new speaker. Before long, Douglass was the voice of the abolition movement. Enslavers said enslaved people were not intelligent enough to live as free citizens in the United States. Every speech he gave answered that claim with eloquence. His skill with words made some white listeners deny that slavery had ever held him. In his life he wrote three autobiographies. Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass was the title of that first book, out in 1845. Critics called the book fake, and they called Douglass fake too. They said no enslaved person could be smart enough to write that well. The book succeeded at once. It convinced many readers that an enslaved person could have a great mind. The pages also held details that could have brought his arrest as a fugitive. To stay free of capture, he left the country for a speaking tour of two years.

7He was a powerful speaker, and in England he was a star. Fans there raised the money to buy his freedom, a purchase called manumission. He came back to the United States in 1848 and founded a newspaper. He wrote thousands of speeches and editorials that called for slavery to end. He said he laid slavery open in this country because showing it would destroy it. He called slavery a dark monster that dies when truth shines on it. A famous speech of his carries the title What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July? He gave it on July 5, 1852, and he startled the crowd. He asked what Independence Day meant for people still enslaved and for people who had been enslaved before. He asked what he, and the people he stood for, had to do with the nation's independence. He pointed to the Declaration of Independence and its great principles of political freedom and natural justice. He asked whether those principles reached his people.

8When the Civil War came, no Black man in the United States was better known than Douglass. In 1863 he advised President Lincoln on the Emancipation Proclamation, the order that freed most enslaved people. Over and over he pressed Lincoln to name emancipation as a stated aim of the war. Some historians think his words helped inspire the Gettysburg Address. He also persuaded Lincoln to let Black soldiers fight for the North. Two of his own sons stood among those soldiers. Guards from the 107th United States Colored Troops appear in a wartime photo. Lincoln and Douglass did not always share one view. After Lincoln's death, Douglass gave the main speech at a memorial for him. The crowd rose in a standing ovation. Mary Todd Lincoln, the president's widow, gave Douglass the walking stick Lincoln had liked best. The gift showed her thanks. That stick still rests in Douglass's house. Slavery's legal end came with the Thirteenth Amendment after the Civil War closed in 1865.

9His writing and speaking helped bring that change. Citizenship for people who had been enslaved arrived three years later, in the Fourteenth Amendment. The year 1870 brought the Fifteenth Amendment. Every male citizen, Black men included, gained the vote. Douglass also fought for women's right to vote. Universal suffrage means every adult may cast a ballot. He fought for that right until death, without living to see it. Women gained the vote in 1920, when the states ratified the Nineteenth Amendment. A photograph from the 1870s shows Douglass in those later years. Black people, women, Native Americans, and immigrants were all part of the free country he wanted the United States to be. He said he would stand with anybody who did right, and with nobody who did wrong. Equality remained his fight until his life ended. He died on February 20, 1895. The civil rights movement often names him as its father. He changed American ideas about slavery and about race.

10The words he left still inspire, including a motto that right belongs to no single sex and truth belongs to no single color. Abolition means doing away with something or ending it, and here it means making slavery illegal. Enslaved means held in slavery, owned by someone or forced to work for that person. An amendment is a change or an addition to a document or a law. A fugitive is a person running away, usually from the law. Autobiographies are true life stories written by the people who lived them. Incompatible means unable to exist together without trouble or conflict. To inspire is to move a person to act. Civil rights are the legal, social, and economic rights that promise freedom and equality to all citizens. Literacy is knowing how to read and write. Editorials are newspaper or magazine articles that give the publisher's opinion. Principles are the basic values or ideals that guide a choice. Eloquence is writing or speaking that is clear and strong.

36. Freedom Written into the Highest Law

1A photo shows Mary Beth Tinker on the right. Her mother, Lorena, stands with her. A younger brother stands with them too. Mary Beth had been suspended for a black armband worn at school. The family is reacting to news from the Supreme Court. These pages start with that story. They then explain the top law that governs the whole country. They tell how the Bill of Rights was added. They list what those rights protect. They look past the first ten changes. They show that the fight for rights still goes on. A conclusion and a word list come last. In 1965 a school district in Iowa punished five students. The students had worn black armbands to school. The armbands protested the Vietnam War. That war lasted from 1955 to 1975. A lawsuit against the district was filed by three of the students. Their parents joined that lawsuit. The U.S. Supreme Court decided the case in 1969. Wearing the armbands was a right the students held. The ruling rested on an amendment to the U.S. Constitution. An amendment is a change or a correction. The Court called the armbands a form of speech. The First Amendment protects that speech. The First Amendment sits inside the Bill of Rights. The Bill of Rights is a list of ten amendments.

2They are the first ten added to the U.S. Constitution. Freedoms of citizens are what that list protects. The Bill of Rights belongs to the U.S. Constitution. The Constitution is the country's first law. It is also the highest law. Every other law has to follow the ideas in it. The United States began as thirteen colonies. Those colonies stood on lands taken by force. Native peoples had held the lands. Great Britain took them. Colonists believed their rights were ignored. The ruler they blamed was King George III of Britain. A revolution for independence began in 1775. The colonists who helped form the United States of America are called the Founders. During the war they built a weak central government. They refused to give leaders the powers of a king. Most powers went to the states instead. A photo shows the original U.S. Constitution on display. The place is the National Archives Building. The city is Washington, D.C. That display includes the Bill of Rights. After the war, the Founders saw that the system worked poorly. Fifty-five men gathered in 1787. Their task was a set of rules for a new system. The city was Philadelphia. The state was Pennsylvania. They hoped the central government would gain power. That central government is also called the federal government. They did not want people's rights taken away.

3They did not want people's freedoms taken away. The goal was a democracy. In a democracy, citizens hold the power. They also hold the right to pick leaders. Elections are how that choice is made. The Haudenosaunee inspired the Founders. That group is made up of Native nations. The nations formed a government together. Each nation also kept a government of its own. September 1787 is when the new constitution was complete. By the middle of 1788, only two states had not approved it. From then on, the Constitution stood as the country's ruling law. The opening words are We the People. The rights in that document were not granted to enslaved people. They were not granted to Native peoples. They were not granted to most women. Later amendments widened those rights. Later laws widened them too. North Carolina refused the Constitution without a bill of rights. Rhode Island refused it too. Neither would join the government without that addition. Some Founders feared a written list. People might think any right left off the list had no protection. James Madison was a leading Founder. He shared that fear. Thomas Jefferson was another important Founder. He said a bill of rights was necessary. He said the rights of citizens had to be spelled out.

4Madison agreed in the end. He drafted a bill of rights. His draft held twenty amendments. Congress reduced the number to twelve. By the end of 1791, three quarters of the states had accepted ten of the twelve. The Bill of Rights is the name those ten amendments received. A picture places James Madison on top. Thomas Jefferson is shown below him. Many women helped build the United States. Women wrote essays about politics. They hosted talks on political issues. They organized political rallies. Abigail Adams was one of the most important of those women. She was the wife of the Founder John Adams. She was also his close advisor. One letter asked him to remember the ladies. At that moment his work included the writing of the new constitution. The First Amendment protects five important rights. Freedom of speech is one of them. Citizens also receive the right to gather. A protest is one reason they may gather. A photo shows members of the Lakota nation. The place is North Dakota. The year is 2017. They are protesting an oil pipeline. The pipeline was planned through their lands. Freedom of the press is another First Amendment right. Reporters may share news with citizens. They may share thoughts with citizens. Newspapers are protected. Books are protected. Radio is protected.

5Television is protected. The Internet is protected. Many countries keep one official religion. The First Amendment says the United States cannot do that. Americans may practice any religion they choose. They may practice no religion at all. The Second Amendment gives citizens a right to own weapons. It also gives a right to use weapons. Some people think the right was meant only for militia groups. The National Guard is one example of such a group. Other people think every U.S. citizen has the right to own weapons. They think every U.S. citizen has the right to use weapons. The Third Amendment blocks a certain government act. People cannot be forced to house soldiers. Private homes could be taken over by British soldiers before the Revolutionary War. The Fourth Amendment limits police. An officer cannot search someone without a good reason. An officer cannot arrest someone without a good reason. The reason must be a belief that the person has done a crime. A court must give permission first. That permission is required before a search of a house. It is required before a search of a car. Four amendments guard people charged with crimes. The Fifth Amendment requires a trial. Punishment for a public crime cannot come unless that trial happens. Punishment for a crime against a state cannot come unless that trial happens.

6The charge has to be proved in court before any punishment. The Sixth Amendment sets rules for the trial. The soonest possible time is when it must happen. It must be public. It must be fair. A jury must be present for it. The Seventh Amendment covers a civil crime. A civil crime is a wrong against a person. It can also be a wrong against a company. A jury trial is a right in that case too. The Eighth Amendment limits punishment. A punishment cannot be cruel and unusual. A photo shows a crowd in Great Britain. The crowd insults men locked in wooden stocks. The stocks were a punishment for crimes. The last two amendments guard rights that were not already written down. The Ninth Amendment makes a limit clear. Listing some rights does not erase other rights people have. The Tenth Amendment limits the government. Only powers named in the Constitution belong to it. A power that is not listed belongs to the states. It may belong to the people instead. A timeline lists key moments in the story of the Constitution of the United States. In 1775 the American Revolutionary War began. In 1776 the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence. In 1781 the American Revolutionary War ended.

7In 1787 the U.S. Constitution was written. In 1788 the U.S. Constitution was approved. In 1791 the Bill of Rights was added. Those are the first ten amendments. In 1865 the 13th Amendment abolished slavery. In 1868 the 14th Amendment granted rights of citizenship. The grant covers every person born in the United States. It also covers every person who is naturalized. In 1870 the 15th Amendment gave the vote to all male citizens. Color did not matter. Race did not matter. Women gained the right to vote from the 19th Amendment in 1920. In 1971 the 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to 18. More amendments followed the Bill of Rights over the next two hundred years. The Constitution now holds twenty-seven amendments. Two later amendments stand among the most important. They are the Thirteenth Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment. Both passed after the Civil War. That war lasted from 1861 to 1865. Slavery in the United States was outlawed by the Thirteenth Amendment. The Fourteenth Amendment made once-enslaved people into U.S. citizens. The right to vote is one of a person's most important rights. At the start, most people in the country could not vote. Most Black men could not vote until the Fifteenth Amendment. That amendment passed in 1870. The Nineteenth Amendment gave women the vote.

8It passed in 1920. A photo shows protesters marching. They marched in support of votes for women. The case called Brown v. Board of Education turned on the Fourteenth Amendment. Racial segregation in public schools of the United States ended mainly because of that amendment. In the 1940s Oliver Brown wanted a nearby school for his daughter. Topeka, Kansas, was home to this Black man. The nearby school was for white students. The school refused her. She would have had to attend a school for Black students. That school was farther from her home. Brown took the problem to court. The case reached the Supreme Court in 1954. All nine judges agreed on the ruling. The Fourteenth Amendment was violated by racial segregation in public schools. The schools for white children were not equal to the schools for Black children. The decision is counted among the Court's most important rulings. Every American's rights are now supposed to sit under the Constitution's protection. A fight for those rights is still required at times. Alondra Jones, an honor student in California, was in school in 2000. Her high school did not have enough textbooks. It did not have any computers. The buildings were filthy. Rats filled them. One day she visited a different high school. Students there had books.

9They had computers. The buildings were clean. The buildings were safe. She realized her own school received far less money. Other schools in her state received more. She joined a lawsuit with almost one hundred other students. The case changed how her state funded public schools. The court said the state was failing to give equal protection. The Fourteenth Amendment requires that protection. A photo shows Alondra speaking at a conference in 2006. A teenager named Samantha Elauf put in a job application in 2008. The job was at a clothing store. The store would not hire her. She wore a head covering. Many Muslim women wear that kind of covering. The store said the covering broke its dress code. Samantha sued the store. The store lost in a Supreme Court ruling in 2015. The store had discriminated against her. Religion was the reason. A photo shows Samantha with her mother. The Supreme Court building is behind them as they stand. A photo shows different groups of people. Those groups have kept fighting for their rights. When the Constitution was written, protection left out most people in the country. Protection did not include them. Since that time, people have fought to gain the rights the Constitution promises to U.S. citizens. They have fought to protect those rights. Work for equality under the law still continues.

10Work for protection under the law still continues. Freedom of speech is the right to share opinions in public. An amendment is a change or an addition to a document or a law. Bill of Rights is the name for the earliest ten amendments in the United States Constitution. Those amendments guarantee certain rights. Freedoms are political rights. They are also powers to act as one wishes. They include the power to think as one wishes. A citizen is an official member of a country. A citizen can also be an official member of a state. A lawsuit is a legal process. A court uses it when people disagree. A court uses it when groups disagree. The Constitution is the written set of rules and principles behind United States laws. Force is how a revolution takes a government out of power. Another government takes its place. Excluded means kept from being part of something. A right is a freedom a person can justly claim. A right can also be a power of that kind. The Founders are the men who helped set up the United States. They also helped set up its system of government. Slavery is the condition of being a slave. A slave is the property of another person.

37. Giants of Ice on the Sea

1A glacier in Alaska breaks at its end and falls toward the sea. Soon that ice will be an iceberg. A painting shows the ship Titanic as it goes down. The ice that brought the ship down stood 15 to 30 meters tall. That height is about 50 to 100 feet. The same iceberg stretched 61 to 122 meters in length. That length is about 200 to 400 feet. Newspapers in 1912 printed those estimates. Sailors crossing cold seas have feared icebergs for hundreds of years. The fear has a good reason behind it. In 1912, the ship Titanic set out on its first voyage. The ship struck an iceberg. The blow came near Canada, along the coast on the northeast side. Less than three hours later, the ship sank. About 1,500 people went down under the icy water. An iceberg can rise from the sea like a mysterious white whale. It can also look like a mountain made of snow. Icebergs are amazing to look at. The part a person sees is only a small piece. That piece is the part that floats above the surface. The visible tip only hints at the huge mass of ice. Most of the ice stays hidden under the water, out of view. Icebergs begin at the far ends of Earth. Antarctica, in the south, is one source.

2The Arctic, in the north, is the other. Ice sheets form there when snow falls. Glaciers form in the same way. Over thousands of years, the snow compacts. The ice moves slowly downhill. When it reaches the sea, it breaks off. People call that break a calving. Once the ice separates from the land, it is an iceberg. Under the set meaning, floating ice is called an iceberg. It must rise at least 5 meters above the sea surface. That height is about 16 feet. Ice floats because of a change that happens as water freezes. Freezing water forms crystals. The crystals spread the same water over a larger space. Because of those crystals, ice has about 10 percent less density than water that is still liquid. The portion above the waterline is only near 10 percent. A picture may look like one iceberg plus a mirror image. It is really two views joined into a single picture. One view shows the ice above the water. The other view shows the ice below the water. Many icebergs near Antarctica are broad and flat, like the top of a table. Flat ice sheets are the parent ice they split from. Huge size is common for them too. The largest known iceberg was called B15. B15 was 295 kilometers long.

3That length is 183 miles. It was 35 kilometers wide. That width is 23 miles. B15 had enough room for every person on Earth to stand on it. Arctic icebergs are smaller. A pointed shape is common. They follow valleys downhill until they meet the sea. Icebergs come in many sizes, and some size names are a surprise. A growler is about as big as a grand piano. A bergy bit is as big as a garage. A small berg is as big as a mansion. A medium berg matches a ship of large size. A large berg is as big as a stadium. A very large berg is as big as a building of 23 stories. Some very large bergs are bigger still. Most icebergs look white because air bubbles sit inside the ice. The air inside is packed very tightly. Pressure in those bubbles can reach twenty times the pressure in a car tire. A melting iceberg can fizz in a way that sounds like soda. The sound is old air slowly getting out. That air can be ten thousand years old. Blue icebergs are made from old ice. The old ice has squeezed the air bubbles out. Blue ice can also form after ice melts and freezes a second time. Green icebergs are rare. They hold organic matter locked in the ice.

4Organic matter is material from animals or plants that once lived. One iceberg near Antarctica shows stripes of green and blue. The colors come from different layers. Each layer formed under different conditions. Stripes of blue are the most common. Ice in a home freezer is much softer than iceberg ice. The ice is packed so tightly that it can sink a ship. A ship sinks if it hits that ice. Ships had already been sunk by ice before the Titanic went down. From 1882 to 1890, icebergs caused the loss of fourteen ships. In those same years, icebergs damaged forty ships. After the Titanic was lost, nations decided to act. The United States joined a handful of other nations. In 1912, they formed the International Ice Patrol. People also call this group the IIP. On the North Atlantic, the season of ice lasts from late winter into late summer. In that season, icebergs break away from glaciers in Greenland. The trip from Greenland takes several months. This route crosses busy ship traffic in waters named the Grand Banks. This is the only place on Earth where icebergs threaten a major shipping route. From an airplane, an IIP officer looks over the sea below. The officer records the place where each iceberg is seen.

5Keeping watch on the Grand Banks is the task of the IIP. Airplanes help the patrol find icebergs. Reports sent in by ships help too. Images from satellites are a third tool. Together, these tools are used to draw maps. The maps show places where icebergs have been seen. In a typical year, the patrol spots about six hundred icebergs. Some years bring far more. In 1984, spotters recorded two thousand icebergs, a record. Other years bring none at all. Spotters found nothing in 1966. Why the yearly totals swing so much is still unknown. Since the IIP began, one safety fact stands out. An iceberg has never struck a ship that obeyed those warnings. Some captains still take a chance. Several ships sank after a captain tried a shorter route through the ice. Most icebergs stay inside a normal range. That range includes waters near Greenland. It includes the North Atlantic Ocean near Canada. Europe and the United States lie outside the usual path. The Grand Banks sit inside the normal range. The place where the Titanic sank is in that same region. Now and then, an iceberg drifts far past the normal range. Of those long travelers, three went farther than the rest. Icebergs might also be useful. Glaciers and ice sheets hold almost 70 percent of the fresh water on Earth.

6The water in them is very pure. This ice took shape thousands of years before dirty air was a problem. It also formed before pollution reached the water. Dry regions might one day receive water carried in from icebergs. The Middle East is one of those places. Southern California is another. The hard part is moving an iceberg to the people who need the water. Icebergs can be towed. Workers on oil platforms catch icebergs with a rope loop. They tow the ice away from the platforms. If an iceberg is moved into warm water, it melts. People are still looking for a way to insulate the ice on a long trip. They want the ice to stay frozen during the trip. A workboat pulls an iceberg clear of a nearby ship that drills for oil. The scene is near Newfoundland, Canada. Another plan uses tankers. A tanker is a ship made to carry a large load of liquid. Workers could fill tankers with chips of iceberg. Melted chips could then cross the ocean by ship. Like towing a whole iceberg, this plan still costs too much. It is not yet practical. A good-sized iceberg holds about 76 billion liters of fresh water. That amount is about 20 billion gallons. Imagine 1 million people. Suppose each person uses about 38 liters of water in a day.

7That daily amount is about 10 gallons. Water from one iceberg of this size would last 2,000 days. Pure water taken from icebergs goes into goods made by some companies. Skin-care products are one example. Before that can happen, somebody has to catch and control the ice. Workers in Canada, called iceberg cowboys, take on that job. These cowboys round up icebergs. The ice they gather is not headed for a hot place. They do not have to worry about the ice melting on the way. Taking ice from the sea is still risky. A berg can flip onto its side. A rolling iceberg can crush a ship. Sometimes an iceberg draws a crowd of admirers. In April 2017, the town of Ferryland, Canada, became a magnet for tourists. An iceberg 46 meters tall had grounded just off the shore. That height is 150 feet. Scientists pay attention to icebergs as well. They join the companies and the cowboys in paying attention. Some scientists want to know how a melting iceberg may change ocean currents. They also ask how those currents may change the iceberg. A big iceberg can drift through the ocean for ten years. Tides pull it along. Deep ocean currents pull it as well. It may break into pieces along the way.

8A break can happen when it hits another iceberg. A break can also happen when it hits an ice shelf. Most icebergs melt once their drift carries them into warmer seas. Arctic seals use icebergs as a refuge from predators. A seal may also give birth on an iceberg. Polar bears hunt Arctic seals. For that reason, polar bears spend time on icebergs too. Twenty polar bears, or even that many, were living together on a single iceberg. That iceberg floated off the coast of the Canadian Arctic. Near Russia, a mother polar bear travels on a drifting iceberg. Two cubs travel with her. A sled is pulled by two scientists as they cross the iceberg under study. They named that iceberg Chip. Today, ice in the Arctic is shrinking. Ice in the Antarctic is shrinking too. The cause is a warming Earth. More icebergs are calving as a result. One group of scientists stepped onto an iceberg to watch the melting closely. They wanted a clearer picture of how the melting works. In February 2017, a different team flew over Antarctica. The team photographed a rift in an ice shelf. A rift is a crack. People use ice shelf for a large sheet of ice. The sheet stays attached to land. At the same time, it sits in the water.

9In July of that year, the cracked shelf split away from the land. The break created an iceberg named A68. A68 was almost as large as the United States state of Delaware. On average, an iceberg travels more slowly than most people walk. Satellite pictures from 2017 show A68 separating from Antarctica. One picture is dated July 12, 2017. Another is dated August 5, 2017. A third is dated September 16, 2017. A68 ranks among the biggest icebergs ever recorded. That split changed the shape of the Antarctic Peninsula forever. Right after a break like A68, the sea does not rise very much. Most of that ice is already under the water at the moment it breaks free. Calving of an ice sheet does speed up a different movement. It speeds the flow of glaciers off the land. Glacier ice that enters the sea makes sea level rise much more. Higher seas flood coasts around the world. This is one reason scientists study icebergs. They hope to predict how far the sea will rise in the future. They also hope to help people plan for that rise. Icebergs have troubled people since the first ships sailed through chilly water. The way people relate to icebergs has changed. Today, more worry centers on coastal cities.

10People ask what melting icebergs mean for those cities. Less of the worry is about sailors out on the sea. We may come to depend on these giants of nature. Fresh drinking water is one possible use. Some other use may appear that no one has dreamed of yet. Research is still going forward. What people know about icebergs today may be only a small hint of the whole story. A man paddles a small boat past an iceberg. The place is Kenai Fjords National Park in Alaska. Calve means ice splits away from a larger frozen mass. To compact means to press parts together until they are denser and tighter. A current is water that flows in a set direction. Dense describes something whose parts are crowded close together. To endanger means to put a person or a thing into a harmful situation. A glacier is a large body of ice plus compacted snow. A glacier lasts through the whole year. It moves slowly downhill. An iceberg is a large piece of ice that has broken from a glacier and floats in the sea. To monitor means to watch or check how something changes over time. A satellite circles Earth, or it circles another object out in space. A satellite may be natural, or people may have made it.

38. Helping Wild Animals Heal

1Along the ground, a baby bird is hopping. No parent can be seen. What should you do if the baby bird seems to have no parents? What should you do about a rabbit that cannot seem to hop? What if you find a raccoon that walks in a strange way? Many people do not know what to do when wildlife may be in danger. They also do not know what not to do. Some people have special training. They do know what to do. Leaving the raccoon alone is what they know to do. The raccoon is probably sick. They can judge if help for the rabbit is possible. They know how to return the rabbit to the wild afterward. A look at the baby bird tells them which care, if any, is needed. You can learn how to help from these people. Tell an adult at once when a wild animal seems to be in trouble. A phone book is the next step if no trusted adult is nearby. Look under Wildlife Rescue. You can also look under Animal Rescue. Topsy is a female great horned owl. She is three months old. People rescued her. A windstorm knocked her from the nest. She had an injury to her neck. She had an injury to her back. People who help sick wildlife are called rehabilitators. People also call them rehabbers. They help injured wildlife. They help orphaned wildlife. To rehabilitate is to bring health back.

2Rehabbers rescue wild animals. They care for the animals while they heal. A return to the wild comes after recovery, whenever that return can be done. Rehabbers have special training. They know how to care for wild animals. They know how to feed them. They know how to house them. Many can treat sickness. Many can treat injuries. Safe handling of wildlife is part of their training. They avoid hurting the animals. They avoid hurting themselves. A sea turtle receives treatment from animal caretakers. The turtle has injuries to its right flipper. Rehabber Lisa treats Tripod. Tripod is a young javelina. A car hit Tripod. Tripod lost one back leg. Need for rehabbers grows as people settle in places that were wild. A habitat is the natural home of an animal. Those places once held only wild animals. Farming uses the land. Houses use the land. Businesses use the land. Homes of wild animals are destroyed. Wild animals lose the places they find food. Orphaned animals become more common once people enter wild areas. They are more likely to be injured. They are more likely to be killed. People and human activities cause most wildlife injuries. Cars and other vehicles hit animals. Animals hit objects such as windows. Poisoning hurts animals. Illegal hunting hurts animals. Litter hurts animals. Pollution hurts animals. Other animals attack them. How can you tell that an animal needs rescue? Always follow two rules. Do not touch the animal.

3Call an adult right away. The adult can phone a wildlife rehabber. That rehabber is trained in wildlife rescue. Watching from safety is a way you can help. Watch where the animal hides. Rescuers can then find it quickly. A box with small holes can cover a small animal. A laundry basket can cover it too. Other animals are kept off until help comes, because of that cover. A panther kitten is checked by a wildlife worker. Stay away if you see certain behaviors. Sickness may be what those clues point to. A sick animal may be dangerous. Stay away from a bat on the ground. Stay away from a wild animal that seems tame. Heavy drool is a reason to keep your distance. Stay away from foam around the mouth. Stay away from an animal that cannot move. Extreme anger in an animal is a reason to keep back. A nocturnal animal is normally active at night. Stay away if that animal is active during the day. Take extra care with a raccoon in daylight. Take extra care with a skunk in daylight. Take extra care with an opossum in daylight. Take extra care with a fox in daylight. Take extra care with a bat in daylight. Hurt and frightened animals can be injured if they are held the wrong way. They can die from the wrong hold. The wrong kind of cage can injure them. The wrong kind of cage can kill them.

4Wild birds may break bones while trying to escape a wire cage. They may damage feathers in that struggle. Parents may quit caring for a baby that smells like a person. This is more true for mammals than for birds. Smell is sharper in mammals. Pain can make an injured wild animal afraid. They may bite. They may kick. They may scratch. They may peck. They may stab. They are trying to defend themselves. They do not know that people want to help. Wild animals may carry diseases. Those diseases can pass to humans. Those diseases can pass to pets. Rabies shows up in bats more often than in many other wild animals. Coyotes are more likely to carry rabies. Raccoons are more likely to carry rabies. Foxes are more likely to carry rabies. Skunks are more likely to carry rabies. Rabies is a deadly disease. Every warm-blooded animal can catch it. Humans can catch it. Treatment must start at once for anyone rabies may have reached. People remove many baby animals that were never in danger. A hop on the ground does not prove a young bird has lost its parents. It might only be learning how to fly. Baby birds often hop as they practice moving. The practice comes before flight. Parents usually watch from somewhere nearby. The parents can be easy to miss. People sometimes rescue baby rabbits that are not in trouble. People sometimes rescue baby seals that are not in trouble.

5People sometimes rescue fawns that are not in trouble. Quiet rest is normal for these babies. They may rest on a beach. They may rest in the grass. The mother is eating nearby. Human help is a question only people trained in these animals' natural ways can answer. If the babies do not need help, taking them from the mother hurts their chance to survive. A baby animal that is not wounded does not need rescue. Taking a wild animal home feels helpful to many people. Love for animals is not enough. You cannot care for a wild animal just because you love animals. Wild animals need much more training than dogs need. Wild animals need much more training than cats need. Taking a wild animal home is against the law. Think of yourself after an accident. You would not want just anyone to care for you. You would want a trained helper, such as a doctor. You would want a clean place. You would want the right equipment. You would want the right medicine. Wild animals deserve that same level of care. Veterinarians examine a red panda. Wildlife rescue has its busiest season in spring. Spring is the season when wild animals have their young. Babies are weaker than adults. Babies often cannot survive alone. A car that hits a mother can leave her baby orphaned. A baby may be orphaned if a hunter kills its parents.

6A baby may be orphaned if a predator kills its parents. At a rehabilitation center, animals get a checkup. They get first aid. Doctors must treat broken bones first. Doctors must treat diseases first. A newly rescued animal is put in its own cage. It is kept apart from other animals. Separation keeps it from making others sick. Rehabbers write detailed notes about each animal. The notes show whether the animal is getting better. People frighten most wild animals. Stress rises when an animal is far from home. A wild animal can die from stress that is too high. Protection from stress is a rehabber's goal. They try to limit contact with people. The rescued black vulture is named Igor. He was fed birdseed. He needed meat for good health. His bones became fragile. His bones broke during the rescue. Rehabbers try to keep noise low. They cover cages with towels. The animals then do not see the people around them. Rehabbers avoid staring at the animals. In the wild, a stare is a signal. It means an animal is being hunted. A puppet acts as a substitute mother for a young condor. The puppet keeps the condor from getting too used to humans. Early in life, a baby animal imprints on its mother. Daily watching of its mother teaches a baby duck what kind of bird it is. Rehabbers take special care with baby birds. They do not let the babies imprint on humans.

7Those babies would grow up believing they were people. Humans, not their own kind, would be who they looked for. Danger in the wild can come from birds that imprinted on people. A hiker may be approached because the bird wants attention. The hiker may not know the birds are used to people. The hiker might get hurt in that meeting. The bird might get hurt. For this reason, those birds often cannot return to the wild. Meat-eating animals at a rehabilitation center need to eat meat. Meat helps them heal. Meat helps them grow strong. Rehabbers pick up animals that cars have just hit along roads. They also pick up animals that trucks have just hit. People call those animals roadkill. The centers use roadkill as animal food. They keep freezers full of frozen mice. Workers call the frozen mice mouse-cicles. Some centers raise their own animal food to save money. They raise quail. They raise mice. They raise rats. They raise rabbits. An adult red-tailed hawk is given a mouse by a volunteer. Almost no sight remains in this hawk. Each animal must get food similar to its natural food. Sickness can come from the wrong foods. Some foods can stop normal growth. Many baby animals are badly harmed by the cow's milk that grocery stores sell. That milk can kill them. Rescued animals must eat natural foods. Natural foods let them survive in the wild later.

8Natural foods matter most for orphaned animals. Those orphans grew up in a rehabilitation center. Starvation in the wild can follow a habit of eating human food. Starvation can also follow if they never learn how to locate food. A flight cage is where healed birds practice in the air. Release can wait until healing is far enough along. Choosing a release site is required once a rescued animal can live wild again. The search for a good place starts long before release day. The place needs plenty of food. The place needs plenty of water. The place needs plenty of shelter. The place must be safe from contact with humans. The animal must be healthy enough to release. It must be able to run without problems, or climb, or fly. It must be able to see. It must be able to hear. It must be able to find food. Animals that would eat it must be something it knows how to stay clear of. Life among others of its kind is a skill it needs. A Tasmanian devil is examined before release. An outdoor pen or cage is the first move toward release. Others of the same kind share that outdoor space. Outdoors, the animal gets used to the weather. It gets used to less contact with people. Time spent outdoors at the center leads to the day of release. Some young animals are released slowly. Orphans are often released this way.

9A safe wild spot is chosen for a pen. The door is left open. The animal can come back to the pen. Rehabbers give the animal food until it is clear the animal can feed itself.
