Adults that were rescued are released much faster. Young animals that never lived on their own in nature need more time. The spot where an animal was found is the preferred area for release. A bald eagle is set free by a wildlife rehabber. Return to the wild is impossible for about half the animals at these centers. They are too sick. They are too badly injured. Many have lost limbs. Many have lost beaks. Many have lost wings. Many have lost eyesight. Poor healing in a wing would stop a bird from flying free. Poor healing in a wing would also stop that bird from hunting free. A bird with only one eye could not fly in the wild. A bird with only one eye could not hunt in the wild. Survival in the wild is sometimes clearly impossible. Sometimes it will never survive at a center either. Rehabbers then face a hard decision. When pain will not end, a fast death without pain is sometimes the kindest choice. That choice ends the suffering. She is female. She is a great horned owl. She is fully grown. Her flight is not quiet. Her injured wing makes noise while she flies. The noise warns the animals she must hunt.

10Because of that noise, she can never be released. Children learn about local animals with help from this bird. Animals that must stay are often used by rehabbers to teach. Children learn to respect wildlife. Adults learn to respect wildlife. They learn about wildlife that lives in their area. They learn to respect the land. Respect for the land lets wild animals keep finding food. Respect for the land lets wild animals keep finding shelter. Rehabbers do important work. They care for injured wild animals. Many of the animals do go back to wild places. You can help by respecting wildlife. A call to a rehabber is help you can give for an animal in trouble. A single phone call might open a chance for a wild animal. The animal might grow up. The animal might live a free life. The animal might live a healthy life. A wild animal in trouble needs a trained person, not a quick grab. Tell an adult. Do not touch the animal. A rehabber can rescue it and care for it while it heals. Finding food and going back to a safe wild place is possible for some animals. Some animals are too hurt to go back. Those animals can still teach people to respect wildlife. Respect for animals and for the land keeps homes and food in place. One phone call can give an animal the chance to live free.

39. Holidays from Many Cultures

1Special holidays are loved by people in every part of the world. When a month ends, we turn our calendars. We search the new month for holidays that are coming. No time of year seems to hold more holiday excitement than the months from November to March. That stretch is a season of holidays. Festive holidays fill those months. This book starts with an introduction. Then it tells about Ramadan. It tells about Hanukkah. It tells about Christmas. It tells about Kwanzaa. It tells about Chinese New Year. It tells about Holi. It tells about the New Year. A closing and a word list come last. Holidays in this season are usually full of traditions. A tradition is an action kept because earlier people did it too. Traditions are passed from one generation to the next. Holidays are usually happy times. Friends meet at holidays. Families meet then too. People celebrate with song. They celebrate with dance. They celebrate with lots of good food. The pages ahead describe many holidays that are not all the same. Kids just like you celebrate them. Those kids live all around the world. This holiday season is when they hold their celebrations. A family gathering is part of most of these holidays. In Nigeria, Muslim girls spend Ramadan reading the Quran. Followers of a faith called Islam keep one full month each year for a special purpose. They use that month to observe Ramadan. Islam uses a calendar that follows the moon. Ramadan is month nine on that calendar.

2It begins when people see the new moon. Reading fills much of the month. The book is the Islamic holy book. That book is the Quran. They pray. They fast. A fasting Muslim takes no food while the sun is up. A fasting Muslim takes no drink while the sun is up. Islamic tradition gives a test for when eating must stop. People must not eat while enough light remains to tell two threads apart. One thread is black. The other thread is white. Most people take a small meal in the morning, before sunrise. At sunset the fast often ends with a fruit. That fruit is dates. Sunset prayer comes next. Dinner follows the prayer. Friends often share the meal. Relatives often share it too. Celebration is largest once Ramadan's final day has passed. Families and friends meet for large meals. Cities hold festivals. Before sunrise in Ramadan, a Muslim family eats together. Fasting in this tradition has many purposes. It reminds fortunate people of Islam that some people are always hungry. It reminds them to be thankful for what they have. It reminds them to be generous. They are reminded to share their good fortune with people who have less. During Ramadan, people look closely at the way they live. Helping others with good deeds is part of this time too. One Ramadan custom began with a king. The king went out to search for the new moon that starts the holy month. Children went with the king. They carried lanterns of many colors.

3They sang songs so the group could find the way. Today, in some places, children walk at night with lanterns of many colors. They sing songs when Ramadan starts. In the Philippines, Muslim women note when Ramadan has ended. They mark it with prayers at dawn. A Jewish family enjoys a meal at Hanukkah. Jewish people celebrate Hanukkah. They practice a faith called Judaism. Judaism is said JOO-dee-is-um. Judaism has a calendar of its own. Hanukkah comes in the third month. The holiday lasts eight days. The start falls late in November, or else in December. People know Hanukkah as the Festival of Lights. On each of the eight nights, Jewish families light candles. The candles are held in a special holder. The holder is called a menorah. Menorah is said meh-NOR-ah. The whole family gathers every night. They gather to light the menorah. A menorah holds nine candles. Eight of them stand for the eight nights. The ninth candle is used to light the other eight. That ninth candle is called the shamash. The shamash sits higher than the rest. On night one, only one candle is lit along with the shamash. On every night after that, one more candle is lit. On the final night, every candle is burning. Giving gifts is also part of Hanukkah. So is receiving gifts. The gifts continue through all eight days. Usually a child gets one small gift each night. The child also gets a little money each night. Children are urged to pass along some of that money, or even more than some.

4It should go to people who are less fortunate. An evergreen tree comes indoors in most homes that keep Christmas. They do this one week before Christmas Day, or sometimes two weeks before. They decorate the tree with lights. They add ornaments. Bright gifts in wrapping are placed under the tree. Some families open the gifts on the night before Christmas. Other families open them on Christmas morning. People hang small lights inside their homes. They hang lights around their homes too. Red is one color they use. Green is another. White is another. Trees and lights brighten many Christian homes at Christmas. Christmas brings many traditions. It also brings many activities. Giving is at the heart of the Christmas season. People give to friends. They give to family. They also give to people who are poor. They give to people who are in need. Toys are collected. Clothing is collected. Food is collected. These things are given to people who have very little. Many cities hold fairs. Towns hold celebrations. Places hold parades. On Christmas Day, Christians visit family. They visit friends. They open presents. They eat special foods. Sweets are a big part of the meal. Church is where many Christians go when Christmas Day arrives. Others go on the night before Christmas. They sing songs. They pray that other people will be safe. They pray that other people will be healthy. They pray that other people will be happy in the holiday season.

5Each year, many African Americans celebrate Kwanzaa. Kwanzaa runs from December 26 to January 1. It is not linked to one certain faith. It celebrates African-American history. It also celebrates what Africans have given the world. It celebrates what African Americans have given too. Many Kwanzaa customs come from harvest celebrations. Those celebrations belong to the continent of Africa. Kwanzaa is seven days long. At the beginning, families set out a table or a shelf. On it they put a special mat. They put candles. They put a bowl of vegetables, or sometimes a basket. The vegetables stand for a good harvest. They also stand for other things people achieved that year. Families show one ear of corn for every child. Homes are dressed with streamers. They are dressed with balloons. They are dressed with flowers. The colors used are black, red, and green. A Kwanzaa table may hold the kinara. It may hold the unity cup. It may hold vegetables from the harvest. Night by night, a single kinara candle is set alight. Someone in the family lights that candle. Often the youngest child does it. The candles stand in a special holder. The holder is called a kinara. Kinara is said KEE-nah-rah. The candles are red. They are green. They are black. The colors match the flag of Africa. On day six, family and friends gather. They share a large meal. A special cup is passed around the table. Before each person takes a sip, the family speaks.

6Sometimes the family tells an old story from African-American life. Sometimes they tell a piece of African-American history. They may share something about African-American culture. Gifts are often traded. A child usually receives a book. A child may receive a toy. A child may receive a video. The gift teaches something important about life. Many Chinese people celebrate a holiday called Chinese New Year. The holiday lasts for fifteen days. It follows the Chinese calendar. It opens on the new year's earliest new moon. During those fifteen days, people do many things. They hope the things they do will bring good luck in the year to come. They clean the whole house, from the top all the way to the bottom. They decorate with flowers. A tray set aside for candies is put on display. Red envelopes of money are a part of the holiday. Red is a lucky color at Chinese New Year. Orange is a lucky color too. People wear red clothes. They eat foods such as oranges. They hang red pieces of paper in their homes. Good-luck sayings are printed on the paper. They give money as a gift. The money sits inside red paper envelopes. Night number fifteen brings the biggest celebration. In cities, people play games. In towns, they play games too. They light fireworks. Dancers wear costumes and perform the Lion Dance. The dance is flashy. Friends visit one another. They wish one another well for the year ahead. The Dragon Parade closes the celebration.

7Everyone gathers to watch. People sing. People dance. At the parade's end, a dragon dances down the street. The dragon is beautiful. People say the dragon is lucky. The dragon is made of cloth. The Lion Dance looks wild. It is full of bright color. A family enjoys Chinese New Year together. Families do not all celebrate Chinese New Year in the same way. Some families honor people in the family who have died. A big dinner is made in honor of family members who have died. The dinner is also for people who are still living. The meal is a way to honor family unity. Every festival and custom of Chinese New Year welcomes the coming of spring. Many communities in East Asia have a new year celebration. Many other Asian communities do too. Their celebration starts with the first new moon on their calendar. People often call this holiday Lunar New Year. Some of these celebrations share customs with Chinese New Year. They happen around the same time. Other cultures celebrate Lunar New Year in their own ways. Holi is a holiday for people of the Hindu faith. Hindu is said HIN-doo. India is the country where most Hindus live. Holi is celebrated in the first part of March. The date is the day that follows the full moon. People call Holi the festival of colors. It marks the return of spring. The holiday is full of games. It is full of sports. It is full of mischief. Rules may be broken by anyone during Holi.

8Everyone may play pranks. Everyone may have fun. Bright colors matter a great deal at Holi. The colors cover everything you can see. People wear clothing in bright colors. Colorful cloth is hung up to dress their homes. They use powders. They use dyes. Family members decorate one another for the Holi festival. A Holi celebration can turn very bright with color. On the night before Holi, people build large bonfires. They sing. They dance. All through Holi, children play rowdy games. Adults play those rowdy games too. People chase one another. They try to spray one another with colored powder. They try to spray colored water too. Boys form one group. Girls form another. The groups hold contests. Many people wear white clothes. White makes the splashes of color easy to see. Enemies try to set their fights aside. They try to be happy together. Fireworks greet the new year. People in every country celebrate the new year. The religion you follow does not change that. The new year is when you mark the end of the old year. It is when you mark the start of the new one. Many people refuse to sleep on New Year's Eve until midnight comes. They want to greet the new year. They count the last seconds before the old year ends. Exploding fireworks greet the new year. Shouting greets it. Songs greet it. All sorts of merriment greet it. Parties for New Year's are common in many places. Colorful bits of paper are thrown into the air.

9People use noisemakers. People wear hats. People sing songs. They wish friends luck in the year that is starting. People also make resolutions at this time. A resolution is a promise you make to yourself. The promise is to do something good for your health. It is also for your wellbeing. Holidays of many kinds are kept in places all over Earth. The place they come from can differ. The faith can differ. The culture can differ. Even so, holidays share many things. They celebrate family. They celebrate friends. They celebrate sharing. They celebrate love. In Bolivia, people hold a traditional celebration at sunrise. It marks the winter solstice. The same sunrise also opens the new year. The winter solstice is a celebration in many other cultures too. On that day, the sun is as far south in the sky as it goes. In the Northern hemisphere, that day is the shortest of the year. In the Southern hemisphere, that day is the longest of the year. Native Americans celebrate the winter solstice. Ancient Europeans celebrate it. Hundreds of other cultures celebrate it too. They do this as a way to honor the cycles of nature. Chinese New Year arrives at the year's earliest new moon. The people who celebrate it are Chinese. They wear red. They decorate with red. They set off fireworks. They hold parades. Christmas falls on December 25. The faith is Christianity. People decorate a tree. People give gifts. People give to those who have less.

10Ramadan is the 9th month on the Islamic calendar. The faith is Islam. People fast in the daytime. People give to those who have less. New Year falls on January 1. It is for everyone. People stay awake until midnight. Fireworks, songs, and noise are part of it. Kwanzaa begins on December 26. People of African ancestry celebrate it. They light the kinara. They tell stories. They give gifts. Hanukkah falls on the 25th day of the Jewish month of Kislev. Kislev falls late in November, or else during December. The faith is Judaism. People light the menorah. People play dreidel. People eat foods made with oil. Holi comes in March. The faith is Hinduism. People wear bright colors. People play games. People play pranks. A dreidel is a top with four sides. It is used in a Hanukkah game. A generation is all the people born and living at about the same time. Parents are one generation. The children of those parents form the generation that follows. A kinara is the special holder for Kwanzaa candles. Merriment means fun. It also means happiness. A menorah is the special holder for Hanukkah candles. It holds eight candles plus the candle that lights the others. Ornaments are small decorations that hang. Resolutions are promises you make to yourself to do good things. The shamash is one candle in a menorah. It is the candle used to light the others. Traditions are customs passed along from older generations to younger ones.

40. Hoops, Speed, and the Court

1A Navajo boy sends a shot toward the basket in Monument Valley. That valley is in Utah. A New York Knicks player tries a three-point shot. Seconds are all that remain against the Houston Rockets. Basketball is full of excitement. Action on the court can change very fast. Those final seconds showing on the clock may be all a team needs. In that short time, a team can turn a loss into a win. A final shot from far away is as thrilling as the game gets. At that moment, every person watches the ball. People wonder whether the ball will sail through the net. It might strike the rim and bounce away. It might be an air ball and miss the hoop completely. Basketball is a global sport now. It began as a small game in 1891. Dr. James Naismith was a teacher who had been born in Canada. He taught in Massachusetts. He worried about his students during the cold winters. He wanted them to get enough exercise. He wanted a new sport for play inside a building.

2He tested a few ideas first. Then he nailed a peach basket high on the wall. He gave the new sport the name basket ball, written as two words. The game raced across the country. Schools picked it up quickly. Part of the appeal was how simple it was to begin. Players needed a ball. They needed a basket. They needed a court. In 1892, schools began basketball for men. Women's basketball started in schools in that same year. Dozens of United States schools fielded high school teams by the 1920s. Canada was the birth country of James Naismith. He studied physical education before he moved. Then he moved to the United States to teach. Women compete in the Women's National Wheelchair Basketball League. One of those games took place in 2016. The sport quickly became popular across many cultures. College basketball first included Black players in 1916. From that time, basketball became more than a game or a sport for Black people. Black culture came to hold basketball as an important part.

3The sport also mattered to Native peoples. Native children were placed by the United States government in schools that played basketball. Over time, the sport turned into a style many Native peoples call rez ball. Rez ball is short for reservation ball. That style of play is especially fast. That changed in 1949, when the National Basketball Association began. People call that league the NBA. Basketball then became the major-league sport it is today. In the United States, professional players of every age take part. Amateur players of every age take part too. The NBA has thirty teams. The WNBA has twelve teams. WNBA stands for Women's National Basketball Association. The count of national college teams is more than three hundred. A team for this sport exists at almost every high school. Basketball camps are open for younger students. Nearly every park that has a court also has regular pickup games.

4Manute Bol was one of the two tallest players ever in the NBA. Gheorghe Muresan was the other. Each man stood 7 feet 7 inches tall. That height is 231 centimeters. Muggsy Bogues was the shortest player in NBA history. He stood 5 feet 3 inches tall. That height is 160 centimeters. Members of the 1992 Men's Olympic team posed with their gold medals. They were in Barcelona, Spain. Soccer still has more fans than basketball. The sport is still growing around the world. A tipping point came in 1992. The Olympic Games that year included the Dream Team from the United States. Until then, college players usually filled Olympic basketball teams. College players of that time could not also be part of the NBA. Never before had NBA players formed an Olympic team, until the Dream Team. The whole world watched some of the greatest players ever. Those players won the gold medal. Basketballs were not always the orange balls used today. Before the 1950s, the balls were brown. NBA star Yao Ming began his career in China.

5In pictures he wears red. He was later chosen to play with the Houston Rockets. China plays more basketball with each passing year. India does too. Australia does too. Fans in the Philippines have loved this game for a great many years. The largest basketball building in the world is the Philippine Arena. Fifty-five thousand fans can fit in that arena. Khahi Rhodes dribbles during a game in 2017. Those courts stand on West 4th Street in New York City. Alyssa Thomas puts up a shot during a WNBA game in 2019. A basketball game uses two teams. Each team has five players. Play takes place on a court. A hoop is set at each end. Each hoop is attached to a backboard. The backboard hangs 10 feet above the floor. That height is 3 meters. The aim is to throw the ball into the hoop of the other team. A team earns two points for a made shot. A team earns three points for a shot from behind the three-point line.

6One point is the reward for each foul shot. A game is split into four quarters. In the NBA, each quarter lasts twelve minutes. The play is fast. A team is on offense while it controls the ball. It is on defense while the other team controls the ball. The ball can move only when a player dribbles it. A dribble means a bounce. The ball can also move when a player passes it. A pass means a toss to a teammate. A pass to a teammate in the right place at the right time can set up a basket. Moriah Jefferson dribbles the ball during a WNBA game in 2020. Kobe Bryant passes the ball during an NBA game in 2011. A diagram of the court names the main spots and roles. It shows the shooting guard, the power forward, and the point guard. It shows the center and the small forward. It shows the opposing team. It shows the midcourt line and the baseline. It shows the free throw line and the center circle.

7It shows the top of the key and the basket. It shows the key, the 3-point line, and the sideline. Teams often keep the same players in the same roles. Control of the ball belongs to the point guard. That guard works to get the ball to the right teammate at the right time. The shooting guard takes the long shots while the team is on offense. Speed helps the small forward take the ball from the opponents. That same speed helps the small forward score close to the basket. While the team attacks, the power forward faces away from the basket. The power forward stays open so a teammate can pass. The center uses height to score while on offense. On defense, the center uses that height to guard the basket. Referees make sure the players follow the rules. They call a foul when a player makes contact that is not fair. Many professional players have exciting personalities. Many of them have broken records. Those stars make professional basketball even more fun to watch.

8One player did more than any other to shape modern basketball. In the 1950s, George Mikan showed great skill at the sport. He stood 6 feet 10 inches tall. That height is 208 centimeters. The age of the big men opened with him. The big men changed the game. Basketball had been a sport of small, quick players. It became a sport of giants. Michael Jordan broke many records. Magic Johnson broke many records too. Shaquille O'Neal broke many as well. LeBron James also broke many records. Jordan picked up the nickname Air Jordan. He jumped high into the air for his famous slam dunks. Johnson moved the ball to teammates in surprising ways. The passes were full of skill. They looked almost like magic. People know O'Neal as Shaq. Shaq stood just over 7 feet tall. That height is 2 meters. During games, Shaq was a force. James ranks as an all-time high scorer. People speak of Lisa Leslie as a mother of the WNBA. She ruled the court at the 1996 Olympic Games.

9She went on setting records all through the 2000s. Maya Moore soon became a star WNBA player. People counted her among the best female athletes in the sport. Breanna Stewart has been a member of the United States team four times. She was a star at the University of Connecticut. More than one Player of the Year award has gone to her. Four gold medals for national teams of the United States came with her help. Members of the women's team from France hold up their silver medals with pride. They won those medals at the 2012 Olympic Games. Every player has to work with the rest of the team. Together they find the balance that leads to success. Fans pack basketball arenas because they want to see a team move like a smooth machine. The stars of tomorrow are practicing right now. They practice on courts in many parts of the world. Some of them compete in school leagues. Others only shoot hoops with neighbors at the park. Playing more often helps them improve.

10A person who wants to play can pick up a ball. That person can then look for the closest hoop. Amateur means not professional. An amateur takes part as a hobby. A court is a rectangular area used for ball games such as basketball or tennis. Defense is the effort to keep the other team from scoring. The word also means the players who do that work. A foul shot is a free throw taken from the foul line. A player receives it after another player has broken a rule. Offense is the effort to score against the other team. The word also means the players who try to help their team score. Opposing relates to a contest or a conflict with someone or something. A pastime is a hobby or an activity people enjoy. Personalities are the sets of qualities that make one person different from another. They include ways of behaving. Pay for taking part is what the word professional means. The person does not do it only for pleasure.

41. How a City Outline Grew

1A construction worker perches on a beam in 1930. He fastens beams that form the skeleton of the Empire State Building. In a lower picture, a Port Authority policeman watches traffic. He rides in an electric patrol car. The place is the Holland Tunnel in New York City. This book has these parts. Introduction. Growing the Big Apple. Building Skyscrapers. Twin Giants Rise, Then Fall. A Tower After the Loss. Words to Know. Introduction What would Paris be if the Eiffel Tower were missing? What would Dubai be without the famous Burj Khalifa tower? Structures like these are iconic. The buildings around them matter too. Together they draw an outline on the sky. That outline is a skyline. A skyline marks a place as one of a kind. Fingerprints mark you in that same one-of-a-kind way. Fingerprints do not change. A skyline does not stay fixed forever. It grows. It changes. Pictures can set Dubai, Paris, and New York side by side. Look at Manhattan for a clear case inside New York City. Its outline has shifted slowly at times. It has also shifted fast. The change has been dramatic. Buildings have gone up. Buildings have come down. Buildings have gone up again. The skyline of New York has kept evolving. An illustration from 1884 shows the skyline of Manhattan Island in that year.

2Growing the Big Apple In the nineteenth century, the famous skyline of New York City began a rapid rise. The population rose rapidly too. The people were diverse. The Civil War ended. Many people who had been enslaved traveled north. They came looking for work. Immigrants arrived from Ireland. Others arrived from Poland. Others arrived from Italy. A great number of these travelers settled on Manhattan Island. Late in the 1800s, no city in the country packed people more tightly than New York. By 1925, no city in the world did either. New residents needed homes. They needed workplaces. They needed shops. Little by little the city spread north. More stores went up. More factories went up. More homes went up. Only about 23 square miles make up Manhattan Island. That area is 59.6 sq km. Outward growth had no room left. Up was the only direction. New ways of building had to be used. Until then, walls carried a building's weight. Walls on the ground floor had to bear every floor above them. They had to bear the roof as well. That method capped how tall a building could be. No practical wall could be made thick enough for dozens of floors.

3A new method used a steel frame. The frame, not the walls, held the structure up. Gigantic steel beams were locked together. They formed a skeleton. Walls were then hung from the beams. They hung the way curtains hang from a rod. The foot of each wall was fixed to the floor. Walls on upper floors no longer loaded their full weight onto lower walls. The steel beams spread that load. Steel frames let buildings climb to new heights. As the twentieth century began, huge structures already stood in New York City. People began to call them skyscrapers. Soon one skyscraper followed another. Builders competed. Architects competed. Each side wanted the tallest building on Earth. Skyline Buildings Park Row Building was ready in 1899. It reached 391 feet (119 m). It had 29 stories. The Singer Building opened in 1908. It reached 670 feet (204 m). It had 37 stories. The Met Life Tower opened in 1909. It reached 700 feet (213 m). It had 50 stories. The Woolworth Building opened in 1913. It reached 792 feet (241 m). It had 55 stories. The Chrysler Building opened in 1930. It reached 1,048 feet (319 m). It had 77 stories. The Empire State Building opened in 1931. It reached 1,454 feet (443 m).

4It had 103 stories. The World Trade Center opened in 1970. The North Tower reached 1,727 feet (526 m). It had 110 stories. One World Trade Center opened in 2014. The tower itself reached 1,776 feet, or 541 m. Counting the spire, the full height was 1,792 feet, or 546 m. It had 104 stories. Raising Skyscrapers Late in the 1920s, the outline against the sky stood higher than before. Two of the best-known structures rose in that stretch of years. The Chrysler Building has seventy-seven stories. In 1928 its builder set a goal. He wanted the tallest building on Earth. The contest for the title was fierce. A tall spire was sneaked onto the roof. The hidden plan succeeded. The year 1930 made the Chrysler Building Earth's tallest structure. Nothing else yet cleared 1,000 feet. That line is 305 m. The reign was short. Blocks away, a steel-framed giant was climbing. The crown would pass to the Empire State Building. Ground was first broken in January 1930 for the Empire State Building. The job ended just 410 days later. Steel and granite formed the building. It held 103 floors. Height passed 1,400 feet. That is 427 m. More than three thousand workers brought skill to the job.

5They brought labor too. Sixty-four elevators worked in the finished tower. A ride to the 80th floor took less than one minute. An outdoor observation deck sat on the 86th floor. An indoor deck sat on the 102nd floor. Both opened panoramic views of the city. One picture shows the building while it was still going up. Another shows it finished. Crews added four-and-a-half stories each week. New York City took the tower as a symbol. It was added to the list called the Seven Wonders of the Modern World. Books featured it. Movies featured it. It kept the title of tallest building on Earth for nearly forty years. The title later moved to a pair of giants going up in Lower Manhattan. Two Giants Up, Then Down Skyscraper work slowed once the Empire State Building was complete. Mammoth buildings cost a great deal. The American economy was in trouble. The skyline did not grow taller again until 1970. During the 1960s, city officials studied an idea. They pictured a world trade center. It would be a hub for trade between nations. Lower Manhattan was the chosen ground. Running the project fell to the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. The designer was architect Minoru Yamasaki. Twin towers were his proposal.

6They would belong to a complex of many buildings. Offices would fill the complex. Storefronts would fill it. Each tower would rise 110 stories. New building ideas would be part of the plan. About That Agency The year 1921 is when this organization was formed. Its name is the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. Its job is to develop trade and transportation facilities. It also updates them and runs them. New Jersey receives the service. New York City receives it as well. Much of the World Trade Center complex is still owned by this agency. It still manages much of it. The site covers 16 acres (64,750 sq m). Building the George Washington Bridge was also this body's job. The bridge links Manhattan and New Jersey. One new idea replaced steel-frame construction with tube-frame construction. Each tower was like a hollow square pipe. Columns stood close together around the outside edge. With main supports on the outer edge, more of each floor could be used. Another new idea was the sky lobby. A taller building needs more elevators. Yamasaki shaped the elevators after the city subway. Express elevators ran in the towers. Local elevators ran there too. Who Was Elisha Otis? People needed a way to reach the top floors.

7Climbing hundreds of stairs was a poor choice. Elevators were required. Early elevators were not as safe as they needed to be. Elisha Otis fixed that problem. In 1854 he designed the first safety elevator. If the cable snapped, the platform dropped only a few inches. Engines that powered the car were part of his design too. His full name was Elisha Graves Otis. Tall buildings needed his invention. The next time you step into an elevator, look around. The name Otis may appear somewhere inside. At the busiest point, more than 3,500 workers helped raise the twin towers. An express car could carry a rider to a sky lobby. That lobby was on floor forty-four. Floors one through forty-three were skipped. The rider then changed to a local elevator. The local car stopped at every floor. An office on the forty-eighth floor could be reached that way. People could move straight up and down in a new way that saved time. Fewer elevator shafts were needed. The year 1966 started the tower work. December 1970 finished the North Tower. Its spire topped out at 1,727 feet. That is 526 m. Meals were served in a restaurant named Windows on the World. The view belonged to diners high in the North Tower.

8The view was breathtaking. The South Tower reached 1,362 feet (415 m). It was finished seven months later. A parking garage sat under both towers. As many as two thousand vehicles could park there. Under the garage were stations for railroads. Subway stations lay there too. The Twin Towers made a striking mark on the skyline. They stood apart from the city's other tall towers. They dwarfed the buildings around them. On Manhattan Island, no structures stood out more. For thirty years, New York had no taller buildings. Disaster came next. Morning came on September 11, 2001. Hijackers aimed two jets, both full of passengers, at the towers. Less than an hour later, the South Tower began falling in on itself. The fall ended in rubble on the ground. Thirty minutes after that, the North Tower came down too. Disbelief stunned the people of New York who watched. Burning rubble was all that remained of the huge buildings. The attack killed nearly three thousand people. That same morning, two planes under terrorist control struck the Twin Towers. A Tower After the Loss The loss at the World Trade Center devastated New York. The rest of the country felt the devastation too. Neighbors were mourned. The landmark was mourned as well.

9They also promised a new building on the same ground. Workers needed time to clear what the old towers left behind. Years passed while people argued over plans. Opinions differed widely. Many designs were turned in. Argument and controversy were strong. At last the Port Authority revealed a design for the new complex. A park of memory was set on one part of the ground. It honors the people who died that day. The footprints of the original buildings are reflecting pools now. Waterfalls pour down them. A memorial museum holds objects from the old towers. The two pools hold a record. No other waterfall made by people in the United States is larger. A new tower of 104 stories now stands nearby. People nicknamed it the Freedom Tower. The rise is an astonishing 1,776 feet. That equals 541 m. The number matches a year. That year is when British rule ended and the United States became independent. Glass panels cover the tower. The form is a twisted octagon. The shiny face mirrors shifts of light all around it. A spire crowns the top. A beam of light on that spire can be seen for miles. More tall buildings are going up on the same ground. The complex planned six new towers.

10By 2021, four of them were finished. The memorial was done. A museum was done. The skyline of New York keeps changing. It will keep showing a city that adapts and grows. One World Trade Center tops either original twin by more than 400 feet. The gap is 122 m. Words to Know Architects are people who design buildings. A behemoth is a person or a thing of immense size or power. A complex is a group of buildings set close together for one shared purpose. Dwarfed means something was made to look smaller or less important. Iconic describes an important symbol. It means famous and easy to recognize. Innovations are new ideas, new products, or new ways of doing a job. A landmark can be a building or a site with an important history. It can also be a land object that shows where a place is. Panoramic means a view that is complete in every direction. Perimeter measures the outside rim of an area. It can also measure the rim of a surface. Prominent means easy to see, standing out, or important. A skeleton is the supporting frame of a structure. A building is one kind of structure. Vertically means straight up and down.

42. How Animals Use Color to Survive

1A picture shows a chameleon. Most animals have enemies. They must defend themselves in order to survive. Some animals use speed to survive. Some animals use strength to survive. Alligators use powerful jaws. Alligators use sharp teeth. Rattlesnakes use venom. Black widow spiders use venom. Turtles have hard body coverings. Other animals must rely on color to survive. The pattern on the body covering is what some animals must count on. Coloring can disguise an animal. Patterns can disguise an animal. Coloring can conceal an animal. Patterns can conceal an animal. This use of color and pattern is called camouflage. Survival for many kinds of animals depends on camouflage. A predator is an animal that hunts. Predators use camouflage to sneak up on prey. They stay unseen. Prey use camouflage to hide from predators. Prey are animals that get eaten. The patterns on a snake can help it hide. The color of a snake can help it hide. Camouflage comes in many forms. Some animals have color patterns that stay the same. Those patterns help them hide. Seasonal shifts can change the color patterns of some animals. The surface under an animal can change that animal's color pattern. Some animals have patterns that change at different stages of life. Sixty miles is as far as a polar bear can swim before it must rest. Surroundings and polar bears share a matching look. A joke tells of a student and an art project. White paper with nothing on it was the student's project.

2The teacher asked how that sheet could be called art. According to the student, the page was a polar bear lost in blowing snow. Blending coloration can be seen in the polar bear. Its white fur blends well with snowy surroundings. Hunting goes better for the polar bear because of that blend. The bear is less visible. It can sneak up on seals. It can sneak up on walruses. It can sneak up on other animals that it hunts. Nature is full of blending coloration. Many creatures of the desert match the sand. Snakes of the desert do this. Lizards of the desert do this. Desert foxes do this. The sand color matches their surroundings. Many insects are green. The green matches the plants they live on. The green matches the plants they eat. Lions match the dry grasslands where they live. Those grasslands are the plains of Africa. Other big cats have color patterns. Leopards blend with the light and the dark of a woodland home. Cheetahs blend that way. Tigers blend that way. A picture shows a snake whose color matches the rocks. A special kind of blending happens in one kind of animal that lives in many places. Earless lizards are the example. White sands in New Mexico are matched by white earless lizards. Black volcanic rock nearby is home to other earless lizards. Those lizards are almost black. Still other earless lizards live in nearby desert areas. They are light yellow. The yellow blends well with sand.

3A picture shows earless lizards. A picture shows Arctic foxes. Their color changes for winter. Their color changes for summer. Many animals have fur that blends with their environment. Many animals have skin that blends with their environment. What happens when the color of the environment changes? Colder climates hold some animals whose color shifts as the seasons turn. Summer fur on an Arctic hare is brown. Arctic hares have white fur in the winter. Summer fur on an Arctic fox is brown. Arctic foxes have white fur in the winter. The change helps them hide all year. When the land is white, they are white. When the land is dark, they are dark. Arctic birds change color with the seasons too. Ptarmigans do this. Say ptarmigan as TAR-migans. Snowy owls do this. Spring is when ptarmigans begin growing a speckled brown coat for summer. The males stay white longer. The longer white coat makes them more visible to predators. Predators chase the more visible male. Her nest is the female's hiding place during that chase. She warms her newly laid eggs. Pictures show ptarmigans in summer. Pictures show ptarmigans in winter. A picture shows that chameleons can change color. Color change is famous in the chameleon more than in almost any other animal. Many people believe chameleons change color in order to hide. Most chameleons change color to show emotions to other chameleons. Green is the color of many chameleons. Many happen to be brown.

4Many happen to be gray. Those colors hide them well in nature. Chameleons have the widest color range of all animals that change color. They change color because of temperature. They change color because of mood. They change color to communicate with other chameleons. Color change is also a famous skill of the octopus. It can change the color of its skin. It can change the texture of its skin. A rock becomes the color match once an octopus climbs onto it. Its skin becomes bumpy. The bumps match the surface of the rock. A picture shows an octopus blending with its surroundings. Crab spiders change color too. They can match a white flower. They can match a pink flower. They can match a yellow flower. They sit on the flowers. They stay almost invisible. A beetle may come for a sip of nectar. A fly may come for a sip of nectar. A bee may come for a sip of nectar. The visitor does not expect an attack. The crab spider then attacks. A picture shows a white weasel. The weasel blends with the snow. Some animals have camouflage patterns while they are young. They lose those patterns later. They lose them when they are big enough to outrun enemies. They lose them when they are strong enough to outrun enemies. Parents have to go off for a while and leave small young on their own. The parents go to find food. If the young are camouflaged, a predator is less likely to eat them while the parents are away.

5Young deer have spots. The spots help them blend with the leaves. A picture shows a young deer. Similar light-colored spotting occurs in young tapirs. A tapir is a hoofed mammal. Similar spotting occurs in young wild boars. Young topi antelopes match the sand of the African desert. Black markings appear once they are strong enough to run from enemies. Even some young predators use camouflage to hide. Lion cubs have spots. The spots help them blend in. Some animals are camouflaged even before birth. Many animals risk being eaten while they are still in the egg. Ground nests put birds in serious danger. Leaving the nest can give a thief a chance at the eggs. Pebble color is the color of oystercatcher eggs. Those pebbles lie along the beaches where the birds live. Some other birds build their nests right on the ground. Their eggs carry streaks. Those eggs have blotches. A blotch is a dark patch. The streaks and blotches break up the egg-shaped outline. The broken outline helps the eggs blend with their surroundings. A picture shows speckled eggs. The speckles blend well with the rocks. Many insects look like parts of plants. Another form of camouflage is disguise. Looking like a different animal is what disguise can do. A disguised animal may look like an object instead. Few animals disguise themselves better than leaf insects and stick insects. Leaves are what the wings of a leaf insect copy.

6A stick insect looks so much like a stick that the two are almost impossible to tell apart. The insect rests on the stick. Some insects have the shape of flowers. Some insects have the color of flowers. An orchid is what the body of a tropical mantid copies. The praying mantis is one kind of tropical mantid. An insect can be swallowed the moment it comes close. That insect thinks it is about to taste nectar. What you can see on the body is what disguise uses. Trickery uses behavior. Some animals try to fool other animals. They may pretend to be dead. They may use some other trick. Fear can make a chameleon lie still on the ground. Dead wood is what the still chameleon resembles. A disturbance makes many small beetles act as if they were dead. They fall to the ground. They look like grains of soil. Birds that might eat them are fooled. A picture shows a chameleon. Many hunters will pass by a creature that has already died. Fresh meat is the only meal they want. Many prey animals play dead so they will not be eaten. When a hognose snake is threatened, it turns upside down. It throws its head back. It holds its mouth open. It pretends to be dead. The trick can make the predator leave it alone. A picture shows a hognose snake playing dead. A picture shows fireflies. Mates are drawn by the light of a firefly.

7A very clever trick is something fireflies do especially well. When a firefly wants a mate, it flashes its light. The flash pattern belongs to one species and not another. A female may copy a flash that belongs to a different species. She uses the copy to trick males of that other species. She flashes their signal. A male arrives. She eats him. Disruptive coloration is a further kind of camouflage. This camouflage breaks up an animal's outline. It hides the animal's true shape. The stripes of tigers are one example. The stripes of zebras are another example. Two antelopes of Africa also have stripes that break up their outlines. Shadows are what those stripes match. The blend makes the animals less visible. A picture shows zebras with disruptive coloration. A picture shows an Io moth with eyespots. Up to now, the talk has been about color and behavior that make animals less visible. Being easier to see is how some animals stay alive. A startle can be the way an animal gets away from a predator. To startle is to scare something in a sudden way. Some animals make a sudden noise. Some animals bare their teeth. A bright color is flashed toward the predator by others. That flash is called flash coloration. A related kind of camouflage uses eyespots. An eyespot looks like the eye of a much larger animal. Some moths have these spots on their wings. Eyespots flashed by the moth can give a predator a shock.

8The moth gains an extra second or two. In that moment it can fly away before it is eaten. A picture shows a poisonous frog. Other animals have bright coloring as a warning. The colors warn that the animal tastes bad. The colors may warn that the animal is poisonous. Predators remember a bad experience. The bright colors bring that memory back the next time they see one of these animals. Fish use warning coloration. Frogs use warning coloration. Snakes use warning coloration. Warning coloration appears on many kinds of insects. Survival for a few animals comes only from looking like a different animal. That other animal tastes bad, or it is poisonous. They use the same colors as a disguise. The colors keep predators away. Black stripes and yellow stripes mark the bodies of some flies. Some moths have those stripes. The stripes look like the stripes of stinging wasps. The stripes look like the stripes of bees. A bee-like buzz is another trick some of these insects use. Warning coloration is famously shown by the monarch butterfly. It is bright orange. It is black. A bird that eats a monarch often throws up because the taste is so awful. The viceroy does not taste bad. The viceroy has developed similar markings. It looks like the monarch. Predators are more likely to leave the viceroy alone. They leave it alone because it looks like the bad-tasting monarch. A picture shows a viceroy.

9A picture shows a monarch. A picture shows eggs hidden by camouflage. Small changes show up as living things produce the next generation. The changes are in physical traits. Colors are one kind of trait. Patterns are one kind of trait. Sometimes babies are born with features that are slightly different. Survival can be easier if that difference helps the new animal. It may be faster. It may have a color that blends better with its surroundings. It may have a pattern that blends better with its surroundings. Survival grows more likely once the animal has that advantage. It is more likely to produce its own babies. Those babies are likely to have the same trait. Their chance of survival is higher. A predator eats the animal if the camouflage fails. Offspring come from the animals whose traits work best. Offspring are the young that come from those animals. Parents often pass those same traits to the young. Working camouflage is handed on as each new generation is born. This process works for predators too. Predators with the best traits get regular meals. They stay strong. They are more likely to survive. They are more likely to reproduce. Their traits then pass to their offspring. Those young also have a better chance to live. Those offspring are also more likely to reproduce. Over thousands of years, weak animals failed to survive. Animals with weaker protection did not live on. Life continued for the animals whose traits gave the best protection.

10They could reproduce. A picture shows a polar bear. Camouflage is unnecessary for only a small number of animals. Natural enemies may be missing for these animals. Their meals are plants, and plants cannot run away. Humans are the sole threat these animals face. Natural enemies are not a reason for elephants to hide their bodies. Rhinoceroses do not need to do this. Hippopotamuses do not need to do this. A picture shows a rhinoceros. Camouflage is not required for the rhinoceros. Certain huge whales are the only ocean animals that can skip camouflage. Those whales eat plankton. Camouflage matters a great deal for the rest of the animals. Staying alive is a struggle, and this tool helps. Try a color test with your clothes. For one whole day, dress in neutral colors. Spend the day on normal tasks, including a trip to school. Do ordinary activities, such as going to a store. Count the people who notice you. On another day, dress in bright red. Do similar activities. Notice whether the bright color brings more attention. Try a second test outdoors. Take a family member with you into a natural place. Choose clothes colored only in green shades or brown shades. Take a place at the center of the woods. See whether your companion can spot you from 20 paces. Then put on a bright T-shirt you brought with you. Stand the same distance away. See whether your companion spots you now.

43. How Halloween Grew from Old Festivals

1An 1890s picture shows a group of children. They use jack-o'-lanterns to scare an adult away on Halloween. These pages open with a holiday that is both fun and scary. They tell about the Celts and Samhain. They tell how Halloween began. They cover costumes and trick-or-treating. They cover jack-o'-lanterns. They look at traditions from the past. They look at Halloween today. They show people celebrating in a crowd. The closing pages set old customs beside new ones. Hard words come last. Halloween is a colorful holiday. It is a delicious holiday too. Most of the celebrating happens in the United States. Canada celebrates it. The United Kingdom celebrates it. Ireland celebrates it. Ireland is where it first began. Streets fill with trick-or-treaters when October 31 arrives. Halloween parties leak a creepy kind of music. It oozes from haunted houses too. People dress in all kinds of costumes. Monsters join the night. Ghosts join it. Superheroes join it. Princesses join it. Every age celebrates together. A 1929 photo shows three girls in Cincinnati, Ohio. They are showing off Halloween costumes. A boy in one photo shops for a costume in Montebello, California.

2Today the United States may hold the holiday's greatest popularity. The holiday matters there in culture. It matters there in business. Hollywood movies pick it up. Popular songs pick it up. American stores do big business from it. People buy Halloween candy every year. People buy costumes every year. What people celebrate now belongs to a tradition of great age. It began with the Celtic peoples. Celtic is said like KEL-tik. They lived in Great Britain about two thousand years ago. They lived in Ireland. They lived in northern France. A photo shows modern-day druids at Stonehenge. Stonehenge is in southern England. They are performing a blessing. The Celts held a harvest festival each fall. The festival was called Samhain. The name is said like SOW-in. Samhain shared some features with New Year celebrations. It also shared features with Halloween. October 31 closed the year on the Celtic calendar. The celebration that day said farewell to the old year. Samhain had a supernatural side as well. On Samhain's eve, the Celts believed, certain doorways stood open. The living world's side and the dead world's side met at those doorways.

3People who had died in the past year could send their spirits across. Their destination was the underworld. The dead could appear. They could communicate with the living. Celts lit bonfires to help the dead on the journey. They sacrificed crops. They sacrificed animals. Priests, they also believed, could glimpse what was coming during the festival. Predictions made at Samhain mattered for planning the new year. Christianity later spread through Europe. Traditions of its own were what the Catholic Church hoped would stand in Samhain's place. One example was All Saints' Day on November 1. People also called that day All Hallows Day. October 31 is the day before All Hallows. All Hallows Eve became its name. The name was later shortened to Halloween. Many older Celtic traditions lived on inside the new holiday. What lived on most strongly was belief in supernatural activity that night, October 31. The Halloween traditions known today have several roots. The Celts are one root. The Catholic Church is one root. Legends from medieval Europe are one root.

4A photo shows Catholic churchgoers in a town in Poland. They are walking on All Saints' Day. The custom of costumes has changed many times across the centuries. The Celts are the likely start of Halloween costumes. They dressed like animals during Samhain. Costumed people walked England's streets in medieval times. Some dressed like fairies. Some dressed like witches. Some dressed like ghosts. The hope was to frighten those creatures away. The practice was called mumming. People often gave mummers food. They often gave mummers drink. An offering, people thought, would send the spirits off without trouble. Trick-or-treating is the form that practice takes for us now. Adults give candy to children. A child who gets a treat will, people hope, move on. No trick gets performed. A photo shows a modern druid in an animal costume. The event is a Samhain celebration in England. Many people make jack-o'-lanterns each Halloween. A face or a design is carved into a pumpkin. A candle or another light goes inside. The light makes the carving glow. The custom comes from an Irish story. The man in the story is named Stingy Jack.

5Tricks on his friends were his pleasure. After Jack died, darkness was where his spirit had to wander. The darkness was punishment for his mean personality. A turnip got a carved hole so his path could be lit. He placed a candle inside that hole. The Irish, for this reason, gave him the name Jack-of-the-lantern. Later they called him Jack-o'-lantern. His legend started one large Halloween tradition. Scary faces were once carved into turnips by people in Ireland. People in England did the same. Beets were carved too. Potatoes were carved too. Candles were set inside to make a jack-o'-lantern. Stingy Jack's terrifying face was the look those carvings copied. They were also meant to frighten him away. The 1800s brought many Irish people to North America. They brought the jack-o'-lantern tradition with them. Using pumpkins for these lanterns began in the United States. The time was the mid-1800s. Pumpkins make great jack-o'-lanterns. All kinds of designs fit on them because of their size. Fall is a season when finding them is easy. Today the celebration gives an important place to making them.

6Displaying them is an important part too. Turnips are still carved for Halloween by some people. Children in the United States appear in a photo, bobbing for apples. The time is the early 1900s. Certain once-popular Halloween traditions draw less notice now. Several of those traditions come from an old Celtic custom. The custom was fortune-telling at Samhain. Bobbing for apples is a classic party game. Fortune-telling was the form it had at the start. An apple sitting in a water tub is what players try to grab. Only the mouth may be used. Marriage was supposed to come first to whoever got an apple first. Many Halloween games today no longer include fortune-telling. A fortune-teller may still appear at a Halloween party. A fortune-teller may still appear at a haunted house. The modern celebration is fairly new. Older traditions are often mixed into it. North America is where that mix shows up most. Wide celebration there waited until the 1800s. Many early settlers from Europe in the New World met the holiday with a frown. The Puritans are one example.

7They discouraged people from celebrating it. The holiday grew much more popular later. The United States received huge numbers of Irish immigrants during the 1800s. They brought Halloween traditions with them. Jack-o'-lanterns were part of what they brought. Mumming was part of what they brought. Bit by bit, more Americans celebrated Halloween. Halloween night grew full of pranks once the celebrations gained popularity. By the 1930s those pranks were a major problem. Some city governments tried to reshape the night. They wanted a family holiday. Children's trick-or-treating events belonged to that plan. In the 1930s, trick-or-treaters received cookies. They received fruit. They received toys. They received pocket change. The same treats showed up in the 1940s. A photo shows American children in Halloween costumes in 1898. Trick-or-treating sped up in the 1950s. Candy turned into a favorite treat. Today's little Halloween candy bars waited until the 1970s to appear. Years have brought changes in the treats. Kids' enthusiasm has not changed. More than 41 million children in the United States alone went trick-or-treating during 2014. Costume ideas come from several places. Other sources account for 10.1 percent.

8Pop culture accounts for 13.6 percent. Online sources account for 31.4 percent. Friends or family account for 18.1 percent. A store accounts for 26.8 percent. A few lively numbers stand out. People in the United States ate 4.2 pounds of fresh pumpkin per person in 2013. Among dedicated Halloween fans, 5 percent start shopping before September. The United States spent 6.89 billion dollars on Halloween in 2015. Halloween's popularity is growing. The growth is especially clear in the United States. It is especially clear in Canada. More people celebrate it every year. Community trick-or-treating is held by some cities. The sites include malls. They include churches. They include community centers. Street traffic is a danger these events help trick-or-treaters avoid. The crowds are not made of kids alone. Adults are celebrating in growing numbers. In 2015, plans called for more spending on adult costumes than on costumes for children. Many adults host Halloween parties. Many adults go to Halloween parties. Many adults dress in costume. Halloween is fun for kids. Adults definitely do not want to be left out. A photo shows children trick-or-treating at an event.

9Today's Halloween does not much resemble how the 1950s marked it. The 1800s marked it in a different way. The ancient Celts' Samhain festival looked unlike it. The traditions are still changing. Old ways mix with new ways. Several different cultures now supply the many traditions inside Halloween. People of every age can enjoy them. Two girls in Halloween dress appear in an 1898 photo from the United States. Halloween candy supports an entire industry. Costumes are part of that industry. Party supplies are part of it. A survey in 2015 asked Halloween shoppers about their plans. The survey came from the National Retail Federation. It found that 93.7 percent planned to buy Halloween candy. Shoppers planned to spend 2.1 billion dollars on candy alone. They planned to spend about 28 dollars on costumes per household. Pet costumes were in the plans of many shoppers. A total of 44.8 percent of people celebrating planned to decorate their yards. Shoppers making up 31.5 percent planned either to give a Halloween party or to attend one. People who celebrated spent 74.34 dollars on average.

10Celtic describes ancient peoples. Their homes included Ireland. Their homes included Scotland. Their homes included Wales. Their homes included western Europe. A British Protestant religious group supplied the people called Puritans. They opposed the Church of England. Religious freedom was what they sought by coming to North America. Enthusiasm means strong excitement or interest. Rich can describe a person or a thing that has plenty. An immigrant is a person who arrives to live in a country that is new to them. Settling there is a common purpose. Roam means moving about with no set plan. Medieval relates to the Middle Ages. That period in European history runs from the year 500 to 1500. Supernatural means beyond what natural laws can explain. It often relates to religion. A tradition is a belief handed along as years pass. A custom can be handed along that same way. It also passes from generation to generation. Pranks are tricks or practical jokes. A prediction is a guess about a future event. Some myths send dead souls to a place called the underworld.

44. How Long Different Lives Last

1A group of rabbits uses every sense while it searches the area for danger. Quahogs make their home on the bottom of the North Atlantic Ocean. The quahog in view is old enough to make a person wonder. Try to guess the age of this clam. In 2006, scientists carried out a research project. The project took place off the coast of Ireland. From the ocean floor, the team lifted a quahog. A quahog is a clam. People say the name with the sounds KOH-hog. The researchers froze the clam after the catch. At a later time, they studied the clam with a microscope. Each year of growth leaves a new ring on a quahog. Many trees also add one ring for each year of growth. The scientists counted the rings on this clam. The count showed that the clam had lived 507 years. No one can say how many more years the clam might have had. The catch ended a life that was still going on. Giant tortoises rank among the longest-lived animals that have backbones. How long a life lasts is not the same for every kind of living thing. Life span is the name for the most years a species is able to last. Two weeks may be the whole life of a worm. One hundred years is possible for a tortoise.

2A few kinds of organisms even seem to stand outside the usual limits of time. Most living things slowly lose health after they reach adulthood. That slow loss is a natural result of aging. People still ask what aging really is. People also wonder why the years of some animals far outlast other animals. A chart of animal lives shows just how wide the range can be. More than one cause sits behind aging. Cells play a part in some of those causes. Every living body is made of tiny blocks called cells. Over time, cells replace themselves. The replacement happens through a process called cell division. Cell division lets a cell make a copy of itself. The older cell then dies off. The new cell takes the place of the old one. As a living thing gets older, this replacement slows down. A mistake during copying can leave the new cell damaged. Even a perfect copy may not work as well as the older cell did. Oxygen from breathed-in air can harm cells little by little. Water and oxygen can make iron rust in a similar way. In time, old damaged cells cannot keep a body healthy. At that point, the living thing gets sick and dies. This cell is almost finished making a copy of itself through cell division.

3Some worms have bodies made mostly of cells that cannot divide. Some flies are built in that same way. Bodies like these wear out even faster than the bodies of other animals. Knowing how cells work explains why every living thing dies. It does not, by itself, explain the big differences in timing. For some living things, old age and death arrive much earlier. Several factors work together to create that difference. A photo shows Jeanne Calment at age 120. Jeanne Calment lived in France. Her death came in 1997. Her birth came in 1875. Those dates mean she lived for 122 years. The world record still belongs to her. That record names the human who lived longest and whose date of birth is proven. She outlived her child. She also outlived her grandchild. At the age of 100, she was still riding a bicycle. Another photo shows Jeanne Calment at age 20. A big body can be a shield that keeps some animals safe from predators. A single kick by a giraffe is enough to end a lion's life. Long ago, people noticed a pattern about size and life. A bigger animal often outlasts a smaller animal. An elephant's years far outlast the years of a mouse. A whale's years far outlast the years of a rat.

4How large an animal grows changes its chance of being eaten. A horse can hold off a predator far better than a small animal can. Giraffes can do the same. Because the risk is lower, large animals have evolved in a certain way. They mature at a slow pace. Having young also happens slowly. A birth often brings a single baby, though sometimes there are two. A gap of several years can fall between one baby and the next. Even that unhurried pattern is enough. Their group size stays steady because they last long enough. Small animals lack that kind of safety. In general, predators threaten them much more. An end of life can arrive at a moment nobody expects. They need to grow up as soon as possible. They also need to breed as soon as possible. Mice need many babies very quickly if the population is to stay steady. Rabbits have the same need. In a single year, a rabbit may have babies as many as twelve times. One litter can hold up to fourteen rabbits. That is a large bunch of bunnies. Short lives are also the rule for Labord's chameleons. They hatch in November. That month falls in the rainy season in Madagascar. Four months to five months covers their whole life.

5Growing up does not take them long. They reach adulthood in just two months. As soon as they are grown, they have young. After that, the adults begin to die off. They place their eggs down in the soil before death comes. They do this ahead of the dry season. The timing helps the species stay alive. In Madagascar, one Labord's chameleon clings to a branch. A Cecropia caterpillar can grow to 11.4 centimeters long. That length equals 4.5 inches. An adult moth of this kind can have a wingspan of 15.2 centimeters. That wingspan equals 6 inches. Insects, more than other animals, fit a whole life into very little time. A mayfly begins life under the water. At that stage, it is called a nymph. Once it grows up, it leaves the water. Then its time is nearly finished. Most adult mayflies live for under twenty-four hours. Five minutes is the whole adult life of females in one kind. In that brief time, the female must find a partner. She must mate. She must also lay eggs. The path of the Cecropia moth is much like the mayfly path. The young spend a season as a caterpillar. Then the adult moth comes out. Five days is the whole adult life of these silk moths.

6Finding a mate is the single task they have. They must mate. The egg count can reach one hundred. They do not even have mouthparts. Without mouthparts, they cannot eat. A Major Mitchell’s cockatoo appears beside a mole. A smaller animal does not always live a shorter life than a larger one. Cockatoos are fairly small birds. A life past one hundred years is still possible for these birds. Brandt’s bats are tiny creatures with high energy. Forty years is not the upper limit for these bats. Some tortoises grow to a huge size. Some smaller tortoises can still live for a century. A life of six years, or even seven, is possible for some moles. A span like that may seem brief. It is about 50 percent longer than the lives of most animals their size. A large dog often lasts from ten years to twelve years. A smaller dog may last as many as fifteen years. Evidence suggests a reason for the difference. While they are puppies, large dogs get big at a much faster pace. Cells in a large dog keep the marks of that fast early growth. As they age, large dogs face a much higher risk of cancer. They also face a higher risk of other health problems. Several body changes for survival belong to naked mole rats.

7Those adaptations help them reach impressive life spans. One explanation fits some small animals that live a long time. Extra defenses are one result of change in some small animals. A tortoise is protected by a strong shell. A bird can fly away from danger. Gathering in a group gives bats safety. Moles are great at digging. They hide in tunnels. Some animals of similar size still age at very different rates. Animals that share a habitat can differ in the same way. The difference usually comes from a way of keeping cells healthy longer. Cockatoos have special body processes that cut down damage to cells. Other parrots have those processes too. A useful protein is found inside naked mole rats. The protein can quickly find problems in cells. It can also repair those problems. Thanks to this protein, a naked mole rat may last thirty-one years. That span is decades longer than their size alone would suggest. Adaptations let animals live in different environments. The environment can also change how long an animal lives. Cold oceans, far below the surface, hold many of the animals that last the longest. Bowhead whales often live well past 100 years. At least one bowhead has lived past 200 years. Greenland sharks cruise slowly through the Arctic Ocean.

8These sharks are giants. One of them reached an age of 392 years. Extreme cold is the setting these animals have changed to fit. Their heart rates are slower. Their metabolism is slower too. Metabolism means the chemical reactions inside the body. Evidence suggests that slower body processes also slow aging. Some plants outlive most kinds of animals. They do so by centuries. African deserts are where the plant Welwitschia grows. Say the name as wel-WITCH-ee-uh. Clues suggest a life past 1,000 years is possible for Welwitschia. Its taproots are how it gets water from far below the surface. Openings in its leaves can pull in moisture. The moisture comes from a rare morning fog. California's White Mountains are the home of bristlecone pines. The soil there is rocky. Water is scarce. Those hard conditions make growth slow. An age past 5,065 years belongs to one tree growing there. A few creatures can do more than simply live a long time. A few creatures can manage acts that are truly special. Shallow pools are where the African lungfish makes its home. It breathes air at the surface. This fish can delay death when a dry spell comes. It burrows into moist mud. Inside the tunnel, it turns around. It places its head and its tail just inside the entrance.

9Next it wraps itself in a cocoon made of mucus. A small hole remains so it can breathe. Inside the cocoon, the lungfish does not need to drink. It does not need to eat. It can last this way for months. It can even last for years. The return of rain is when the fish leaves that cocoon. The cocoon has been a sticky safety net. The lungfish then goes on with life in a muddy pool. Stranger still is the jellyfish called immortal. Danger can push this jellyfish to switch its body form. A full-grown adult can become a cluster of polyps once more. The polyps pop off the group. In time, each one can become an adult jellyfish on its own. No single jellyfish of this kind lives forever. The species has still found a kind of immortality of its own. Alaska's arctic sea is where a bowhead whale leaps clear of the water. Aging is a subject scientists still need to study much more. They also have much to learn about life spans. Many striking cases of long lives and short lives fill the animal kingdom. Those examples show that several things each play a role. Cells play a role in how long an animal lives. Body size plays a role.

10Metabolism plays a role. Adaptations play a role. The environment plays a role too. Studying the life spans of animals can help people understand aging. Many factors contribute to aging. One day, that knowledge may help people live longer lives. It may also help people live healthier lives. To adapt means to change so that a living thing fits a new situation. It can also mean fitting a specific environment. Aging is the process of getting older. One hundred years make up one century. Decades are periods of ten years. An environment is the set of conditions around organisms in a certain area. Those conditions include plants and animals. They also include water, soil, and weather. Landforms and air are part of an environment as well. To evolve means to change or develop over time. A factor is a fact that contributes to a result. A factor can also be a circumstance that contributes to a result. Immortal describes something that lives forever. An immortal thing is not subject to death. To mature means to become grown. It also means to become fully developed. Organisms are living things. Postpone means to push an event off to a moment that comes later. A predator is a hunter that eats other animals. They eat those animals so they can survive.

1Many people enjoy video games. Some may spend too long trying to win the game. A girl runs across a field of grass. She is dressed in a black helmet together with a purple backpack. They show up in almost every place between those two. The daily time a person spends looking at screens has a name. People call it screen time. Some families set strict rules about how long children may use screens. Other families have fewer rules. People ask why any of the rules exist. Are adults only trying to spoil the fun? Or is there a good reason to limit screen time? Screen questions have been around for a long stretch of years. 3Those studies looked at how television affects people. Scientists still research how screen time affects people. They look at health. They look at relationships. They look at the way the brain develops. Technology changes quickly. A fair share of devices, apps, and games has not been around very long. Because the tools are so new, researchers struggle to gather results they can trust. A survey in 2017 asked families across the United States about screens. The survey focused on households that include children younger than eight. In 98 percent of those homes, there is a smartphone or a tablet. Children under eight spend a little more than two hours a day with screens. The screens include TVs, computers, and tablets. Children from eight to eighteen spend even more time. They spend more than seven hours a day using screens. People often fail to notice how much time has passed. Games and social media make the minutes slip away. A boy stays up late to play video games. He gets out of bed late the following morning. The bus is nearly gone when he arrives.

4His mother sets a fresh rule. Screens go off before bedtime under that rule. She is aiming for real rest for her children. Turning on the TV before sleep is a common habit. Checking social media just before sleep is common as well. They believe this will help them relax. They believe they will fall asleep more easily. Most researchers suggest a different habit. They say to turn electronic devices off before bedtime. The stop should come an hour or two before sleep. Light from a phone, a tablet, or another screen tricks the brain. The brain decides that it is still daytime. Falling asleep at night then becomes harder. Looking at a screen before bed leads people to sleep less. It also leads them to wake more often in the night. Too little sleep can change a person’s mood. It can make it hard for a student to pay attention at school. It can lead to other problems with health. 5Reading can help the mind and the body get ready for sleep. Too little sleep is linked to obesity, the problem of weighing far too much. It is also tied to screen time. Heavy TV watching usually means long periods of sitting without moving. A person who plays many video games does the same. More hours with a screen may mean fewer hours of activity. It may mean less exercise. Sometimes a screen makes a person miss the signals of the body. A person may snack while watching TV. That person may not notice the moment of feeling full. The result can be eating too much. The result can be becoming overweight. Being around other people does not stop the habit of staring at screens. Picture a family eating dinner together. Mom answers email on her phone. A movie plays for the children. Their father sets a fresh rule. Dad's new rule bans screens while the family eats. He wants the family to talk to one another for real. In many ways, screens help people communicate. They help people stay connected. Social media, apps for messages, and video calls keep people in touch.
