6The contact can be almost constant. Screen time can also help a person build a new relationship. People share videos, images, or music. They leave comments on those posts. They can meet others who like the same creative things. Video games can be social too. A person who likes games often becomes friends with other players. They may play together after that. They may watch games together. Some adults worry about young people and screens. They worry that young people stare at screens for too long. They worry that real-life time with other people is too short. They fear a result of that imbalance. Young people might not learn to understand emotions well. They might not build strong relationships. Researchers think screen time is healthiest when people interact. The interaction can happen online. It can also happen in person. Two people can watch one video together. They can read one article online together. The pair can speak and can put questions to one another. The talk helps them understand the piece more clearly. Two people can play one video game together. They can team up to beat the game.

7Many people think time on screens can harm eyesight. Across fifty years, myopia became twice as common in the United States. They have doubled in Europe as well. Myopia means nearsightedness. Many researchers link myopia to too little sunlight. A child who stays indoors a great deal may miss that light. The eyes may not get enough sun to develop in a healthy way. A mother keeps watch while her children have their time on screens. Each child stares at a different screen. To her, they look like zombies. She asks herself whether so many screens might be bad for their brains. A fresh rule follows from her. Starting then, every minute of screen time must be educational. Students can benefit from quite a few kinds of time spent with screens. Some shows can help them learn. Some games can help them learn. Students may use a screen to grow their creativity. They may practice making videos. They may practice editing photos. A video game can teach a person to react quickly. It can teach strategic choices. It can teach problem solving. Students may even learn coding. Coding means writing programs for a computer.

8They may learn how to fix a technical problem. Social media, movies, and research online can introduce people who are different. Students may also meet ideas they have never considered. That experience can help them welcome new people. It can make them more willing to take part in their communities. Tablets and computers are school tools for a great many students. Some teachers say the devices help students work as a team. Some researchers think screens change the brain. The change is in the way the brain handles information. Some researchers have tied screen time to lower scores on tests. They have also tied it to a shorter span of attention. Scientists do not yet know every way a screen affects the brain. They do not yet know every effect on learning. They describe the healthiest screen use as active use that stays engaging. Active use can mean making something creative. It can mean playing a game that asks the player to solve problems. Simply watching videos is a less active kind of use. Some activities on a screen help people spend time together. Those activities can build relationships.

9For many years, scientists offered a daily limit. They said children should use screens for only one hour or two hours. Many researchers now say something else. The number of hours may matter less than the activity itself. What children do with a screen matters more. They argue that active time on a screen can be healthy. Interactive time on a screen can be healthy too. Screen time turns into a problem in one kind of case. It is a problem when it blocks important parts of life. Health is one of those parts. Relationships are another. Schoolwork is another. Future years will still find scientists examining what screens do to people. Parents will likely keep making rules that limit it. Students at school will keep playing games. They will keep using social media. Many people will look at a screen every day. A great deal of good can come from all of this screen time. It is still wise to pay attention. Each day, children and adults alike should notice how long they face a screen. They should notice how that time affects health. They should notice how it affects relationships and learning.

10Stopping in time for dinner is always a good idea. Many researchers suggest that families pick screen-free times. A meal can be free of screens. Bedtime can be free of screens too. Those breaks help keep screen time in balance. A smartphone is a mobile phone that has computer features and access to the Internet. Challenging means a job is tough or asks a lot. Electronic describes a device made of many tiny electrical pieces. The name social media covers for sites and programs built so people can share news, pictures, or other material. Engaging means something interesting enough to hold attention. Strict means insisting that rules be obeyed, or that certain behaviors be followed. Interacting means speaking with others or doing things with them. Technical refers to the skills and know-how of one kind of work. Obesity means body weight high enough to harm health. A relationship is the way living beings get along when more than one is involved. Technology means machines or tools that people develop by using scientific knowledge. Researching means studying or investigating, especially in order to learn something new.

46. January on Both Sides of Earth

1On Chile's Rio Valdivia, fishing boats sit on the water. This book packs you for a trip at 40 degrees of latitude. It shows seasons that are opposite. It visits New York City in the United States. It visits Beijing in China. It visits Madrid in Spain. It explains currents and peninsulas. It visits Wellington in New Zealand. It visits Valdivia in Chile. It tells the secret of the seasons. A word list and a topic list come at the end. At any time of year, the season at 40 degrees north is the opposite of the season at 40 degrees south. Can you find the labeled places as you read? This expedition sends you around the world twice. One trip follows 40 degrees north latitude. The other follows 40 degrees south latitude. You travel in January. Packing is difficult. Your trip takes you into two different seasons.

2You need clothes for summer. You need clothes for winter too. Earth takes one full year to orbit the Sun. Earth is tilted in space. The seasons come from that tilt. The tilt stays the same while Earth travels around the Sun. Because of the tilt, some places get more sunlight in a day than others. In January the Northern Hemisphere leans away from the Sun. Winter comes there. Meanwhile the half of Earth south of the equator leans sunward. Summer comes there. In June, the pattern flips. Which season does Australia have when June arrives? A girl blows snow off her hands. The day is cold in New York. A heavy coat is a good thing to have packed. New York City feels cold when January comes. The city sits at 40 degrees north latitude. Temperatures are in the twenties. The scale is Fahrenheit.

3People bundle up in heavy coats. They wear hats. They wear scarves. City streets are full of sounds and smells. You hear many different languages. Food smells from many countries fill the air. Lunch could be kebabs from Lebanon. It could be egg rolls from China. It could be sushi from Japan. It could be tacos from Mexico. New York is a city in the United States. Home for people from every land is still this city. Finding sushi in New York City is simple. Kebabs are easy to find there too. A walk takes you to Central Park. People there skate on the ice. You ask the man who rents the skates about June. He says the weather is hot then. People ride bikes in the park. People eat picnics in the park. In winter, people like skating on the ice in Central Park.

4Snow lies over Beijing's Forbidden City. You get on a plane for a long flight. Your destination is Beijing. Beijing is China's capital. Beijing sits at 39 degrees north. January there is very cold as well. People across Tiananmen Square are wrapped in warm clothes. Tiananmen Square lies south of the Forbidden City. The Forbidden City is an old Chinese city with walls. Workers built it in the 1400s. You take a short drive outside Beijing. A trip to Longqing Gorge brings you to the Ice and Snow Festival. At the gorge you see fireworks. You see shows made of light. You see sculptures made of ice. The scene is a winter wonderland. The festival runs every year. It runs from January to March. Visitors love the amazing ice sculptures at Longqing Gorge. Steps on China's Great Wall lie under snow. No trip to Beijing is complete if you miss the Great Wall.

5People first built the Great Wall about 2,000 years ago. No structure on Earth is longer. Builders ran it across mountains. They built it to hold back invaders. You ask a guide for a trip out to the wall. He agrees, but he warns you. It is very cold. It might be snowy. He says summer is a better time. Summer is much warmer. From Beijing you follow 40 degrees north latitude into Europe. You arrive in Madrid, the capital of Spain. Madrid is also the heart of Spanish culture. You walk along the Gran Via, one of the main streets. You want to see its famous buildings. The January day is sunny. Many people are outside. You sit down at a cafe outdoors. You order several tapas. Tapas are foods small enough for one bite. Bacon-wrapped dates are one kind.

6Chicken with leeks is another. You take your coat off. A winter day can feel very pleasant here. Madrid is warmer in winter than New York City. It is also warmer than Beijing. Winter temperatures sit in the 40s and the 50s. Those numbers are on the Fahrenheit scale. Snow hardly ever falls. Sometimes the air is warm enough for sitting outside. On a mild winter day, people sit outdoors. They eat tapas and other foods. Their seats are in a Madrid plaza, in Spain. One reason for the milder winter is the North Atlantic Drift. That drift is a current in the ocean. It carries warm air to Western Europe. The current makes climates in Western Europe warmer than you would expect. This is true around 40 degrees of latitude. It is also true around 50 degrees. Another reason is Madrid's place on the Iberian Peninsula.

7A peninsula is land with water along three sides. Big areas of water make a climate milder. Winters in Madrid stay cool. They do not get too cold. January leaves Wellington Harbor warm, with sun overhead. Now you feel January at 41 degrees south latitude. No capital city on Earth is farther south than Wellington, New Zealand. Wellington stands on Cook's Strait. Cook's Strait is a narrow channel of water. New Zealand's two main islands are split by this water. Summer air is about 75 degrees Fahrenheit. A cable car takes you up into the hills above the city. From there you look out over the view. Ships fill the harbor. People crowd the beaches. This January day would be well spent at the beach. Cable cars in Wellington give visitors wide views of the city. A riverboat sits docked in Valdivia, Chile.

8Valdivia is the following stop south of the equator. Valdivia is at 39 degrees south latitude. Three rivers meet the sea at Valdivia. Those rivers flow into the Pacific Ocean. You board a riverboat to cruise the water. You want to see what is left of Spanish forts. People built the forts in the 1500s. Just as you step onto the boat, sea lions appear. Each one can weigh 2,000 pounds. They flop their way down the street. Lunch is waiting at the fish market by the river. Other sea lions rest in the sun on rafts. They wait for leftover food. In Valdivia, a fisherman offers food to a sea lion. For tourists, sea lions are now one of the favorite sights in the city. Kayakers enjoy summer weather in New Zealand. Your January tour followed 40 degrees north latitude and 40 degrees south latitude.

9You saw for yourself how a season works. The month matters. The place matters too. In the same January week you felt winter's cold. That cold was in the Northern Hemisphere. You also felt the warmth of summer. That warmth was in the Southern Hemisphere. January finds the northern half of Earth tipped away from the Sun. The Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. The reason the seasons change is no longer a secret to you. Where would you rather spend January? Aromas are pleasant smells that are easy to notice. A hemisphere is one half of Earth. The equator splits Earth into a northern half and a southern half. A line through the poles splits Earth into an eastern half and a western half. A channel is a wide path of water that joins two bigger bodies of water. Invaders are people who force their way into a country.

10They want to conquer its people, weaken them, or harm them. Culture means the ideas of a group of people. It also means their customs. A peninsula is a long piece of land. Water goes almost all the way around it. A current is air or water moving one way. A gorge is a long, deep valley with higher land around it. A strait is a narrow path of water. It links two large areas of water. Topics in this book include New York City and the Northern Hemisphere. They include the Southern Hemisphere and Tiananmen Square. They include Valdivia, Chile, and Wellington, New Zealand. They include Beijing, China, and Cook's Strait. They include the Forbidden City and the Gran Via. They include the Great Wall of China and the Iberian Peninsula. They include Longqing Gorge and Madrid, Spain.

47. Learning Space at Camp

1Contents. From Camp to Space. Space Camps Around the World. A Day at Camp. Astronaut Training. The Multi-Axis Trainer. The One-Sixth Gravity Chair. The Space Shot and the G-Force Accelerator. Practice Missions. Astronauts of the Future. Word List. Kate Rubins was a sixth grader in 1990. She went away to camp in Huntsville, Alabama. Campfires were not the point. Canoes were not the point. The camp was about space. The program looked deeply at the science of space exploration. It also shared how exciting that work can be. She had already told her parents her dream. An astronaut came first. A biologist came next. A geologist came after that. In Huntsville, Alabama, campers sleep in a place called the habitat. The camp name is United States Space Camp. In July 2016, Takuya Onishi flew toward the ISS. Anatoly Ivanishin flew on that same trip. Kate Rubins flew with them. Twenty-six years after her own camp, young trainees sat down in an IMAX theater at the same site. Awe filled them. Live video filled the screen. The picture was a real launch of a giant rocket from Russia.

2Supplies rode on that rocket. So did a new crew for the International Space Station. People call the station the ISS. Its orbit is more than 322 kilometers above Earth, or 200 miles. The launch meant a great deal to these trainees. Doctor Kate Rubins was one of the three astronauts aboard. She was the girl who had come to this camp years before. Biology was her work for a long time. Training with NASA came later. NASA is the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. At last the launch was hers. A four-month mission on the ISS was her job. The childhood wish to be an astronaut had come true. A shuttle model stands on permanent display near the Alabama camp. Its name is Pathfinder. Space camps teach participants about space science. The history of exploration is part of the teaching. Hands-on projects look at technology made for space. Astronaut training is part of camp too. Campers test gear that astronauts use while getting ready for a mission. Camps like this now exist in many places.

3Huntsville's camp sits beside a center named for United States spaceflight and rockets. The center's full name is United States Space and Rocket Center. Giant rockets can be seen there. Space capsules can be seen there too. Those craft helped NASA astronauts land on the Moon in 1969. Attendance since the 1982 opening is more than 750,000 trainees. All fifty states have sent campers. More than sixty other countries have sent them too. While school is on break, some museums and some universities inside the United States host space camps. Texas has one at the Frontiers of Flight Museum. Florida has Camp Kennedy Space Center. Washington, D.C., has several summer day camps from the Smithsonian Association. The activities are about space. Kindergarten is young enough to join. Camps are popular far beyond the United States. Quebec, Canada, has the Cosmodome, which runs camps of three days. Many other space programs are offered there too. Space Camp Turkey stands in Izmir, among Turkey's largest cities. Russian Space Camp includes talks on the country's record in space. That record is amazing. Yuri Gagarin is honored at the center.

4He was the first human to fly in space, in 1961. A world map of camps lists six sites. Dallas, Texas, is one, in the United States. Huntsville, Alabama, is another. Merritt Island, Florida, is a third. Laval, Quebec, is in Canada. Izmir is in Turkey. Star City is in Russia. Almost anyone who is interested can find a camp. Younger children at some camps may come with family. Older campers are placed in groups by age. Some sessions welcome trainees who have special needs. A visual impairment is one example. A hearing impairment is another. History, science, and the technology of space travel are the main focus. Rocketry is studied at many camps. Trainees build small rockets. They launch them. Other camps study how a spacecraft is designed. Trainees then build a ship of their own for a mission. One sample day runs like this. From 8:00 to 9:00 in the morning, campers dress and eat breakfast. From 9:00 to 10:00 they ride simulators. From 10:00 to 11:30 they practice leadership and team building. Lunch in the crew galley lasts from 11:30 until noon.

5An astronaut-training simulator fills 12:30 to 1:30. Rocket building fills 1:30 to 3:00. A movie fills 3:00 to 4:00. A practice mission fills 4:00 to 5:00. Dinner is from 5:30 to 6:00. Spaceflight history fills 6:30 to 7:30. An engineering workshop fills 7:30 to 8:30. From 9:00 to 10:00 at night, campers phone home and prepare for bed. Camps about robotics draw many people. Robotics now matters a great deal to space exploration. Two prime examples are the rovers Opportunity and Spirit. Mars is where those rovers have explored. Trainees in robotics build machines. The machines answer problems from the real world. A contest may close the camp, with teams facing one another. Adults come too, from many countries. Fun is not only for children. Some of the adults are science teachers. They want fresh lessons for their classes. Those lessons can energize students who may explore space later. A picture shows a NASA astronaut beside an educator. They try out a robot rover made in a camp class. The Multi-Axis Trainer has a design goal.

6Riders should not feel sick. They should not feel dizzy. At some camps, simulators are a favorite. An astronaut has to practice every problem space might bring. Trainees get a taste of those problems on the machines. Counselors watch them the whole time. The Multi-Axis Trainer, called the MAT, goes back to the early 1960s. The first astronauts were tested on it. The task was to take back command of a capsule. The capsule was tumbling and out of control. A large metal ring sits inside a still larger ring. Straps hold the trainee in a seat at the center. Both rings then spin hard. Each ring spins its own way. A bounce like one on the Moon is what the one-sixth gravity chair offers. Moon gravity is one-sixth of gravity on Earth. The chair lets a body feel much lighter than normal, so movement can be practiced. An older chair is the model for this one. Astronauts trained for moonwalks in that earlier chair. Try this math. A person who weighs 27 kilograms on Earth, or 59.5 lb, would weigh how much on the Moon?

7The result is 4.5 kilograms, or 10 lb. Roller-coaster riders will know the feeling of the next two machines. The Space Shot throws people upward at four g's. Four g's is four times the pull of Earth's gravity. Picture a body of 23 kilograms, or 50.7 lb. On the ride, that body feels like 92 kilograms, or 202.8 lb. The G-Force Accelerator spins. Speed creates a force that presses on the body. The force reaches three g's, three times Earth's pull. A rocket launch presses astronauts with that same force. Riders on the Space Shot climb 42.7 meters in 2.5 seconds. That height is 140 ft. Inside some simulators, trainees work the controls. The controls make the ride feel like flight aboard a shuttle. Practice missions are another high point. Real astronauts need teamwork. They need leadership. Simulators let trainees practice both. Some camps make the practice feel like a video game. One mission starts with a shuttle launch. The crew flies toward the ISS. Then the craft docks there. Duties differ from person to person.

8Headsets carry the talk. Checklists are read, just as a real crew would read them. The lists keep every step in order. They also keep the timing clear. Some trainees play the astronauts. Others take the Mission Control jobs. That room stands in for the command post on Earth. A Hubble Telescope model is repaired by campers during one simulation. Some practice trips are mock voyages to the Moon. Others happen on models of a space station. Fast thinking is required. The machine may invent an emergency. An engine may fail in the simulation. A sudden shower of meteors may arrive. Older trainees at a few camps practice the future. A trip to Mars is one example. In Alabama, crews use life-size models. One model is the Orion capsule. The other is a lander for Mars. On the real voyage to Mars and back, astronauts will live aboard Orion. The lander will carry them down to the Martian surface. They will then go back up to Orion, which waits in orbit. Several astronauts and scientists are tied to these camps.

9Some finished a camp themselves. Others have backed programs that teach young people about space. Doctor Leroy Chiao once flew for NASA. He now leads a Houston group for space and science education. Its name is the Houston Association for Space and Science Education. Students and trainees around the world join him in live-streaming visits. Bobak Ferdowsi engineers aircraft and spacecraft. A future mission he is planning would send a robot probe to Europa. Europa is a moon of Jupiter. Samantha Cristoforetti came through space camp. She later flew as a fighter pilot in Italy's air force. Her time on the ISS in 2014 and 2015 lasted 199 days. Robert Gibson, known as Hoot, strongly supports these camps. Five shuttle missions are in his past. They took place in the 1980s and the 1990s. Michael E. Lopez-Alegria flew four shuttle missions. He has spoken at Space Camp Turkey. Trainees in camps today may fly tomorrow, much as Doctor Kate Rubins did. NASA is working with other space programs on a Mars mission. The hope is to go as early as the 2030s.

10If the plan holds, some of today's trainees could ride Orion. They could be first to press footprints into the soil of that Red Planet. Humanity's reach toward the stars would continue. Word List. Aeronautics is the science of flight and the practice of it. Mock describes a drill that is not the real event. People use it to practice. Counselors are the people who supervise a camp. Rovers are vehicles that explore the surface of a planet or a moon. Exploration is travel through land or space that is not yet known, in order to learn. Simulators are machines that copy how something looks or feels, usually so people can practice. G's are units of force equal to the pull of gravity on an object at Earth's surface. A spacecraft is a vehicle for travel in space. Impairments are conditions that damage an ability or keep it from working well. Technology is scientific knowledge, or the tools used to make or do something. Leadership is the skill of guiding other people. Trainees are people being taught a certain job.

48. Life Between the Two Rivers

1People kept records on a clay tablet. They carved the pictures into the clay. They used a sharp tool. A map shows ancient Mesopotamia from 5000 to 2150 bce. The Black Sea is on that map. The Caspian Sea is on that map. The Mediterranean Sea is on that map. Europe is marked on the map. Africa is marked on the map. The Fertile Crescent is marked. Akkad is marked. The Tigris River is marked. The Euphrates River is marked. Mari is marked. Babylon is marked. Umma is marked. Lagash is marked. Uruk is marked. Ur is marked. Land between two rivers is the meaning of the name Mesopotamia. The two rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates. The first civilizations started to form about 6,000 years ago. City life for at least some people is part of a civilization. Those people do specialized jobs. Civilizations have governments. They often have writing. They often have arts. They often have science. They often have trade. They often have monuments. Ancient Mesopotamia held one of the earliest civilizations. The modern lands of Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Kuwait cover old Mesopotamia. Historians say civilization was born in this land between two rivers. A civilization is an organized society. It has a steady food supply. It has a government. It has a social structure. It has a culture.

2It has written language. It has religion. The clay tablet and the sharp tool were tools for memory. Cities and special jobs were part of this new way of life. Ancient Mesopotamian civilization started between two rivers. The rivers were the Tigris and the Euphrates. People later called that region the Fertile Crescent. The first people there settled the southern part. Today that area is Iraq and Kuwait. In modern times, people found ancient stone tools near the Euphrates. They found bricks. They found pottery. These items told stories about early lives. Farming settlements, researchers found, had an early start. The time was as early as 5000 bce. They named these settlers the Ubaid. The find-site gave these settlers their name. A musical instrument may once have sat in a small box. The box shows life in early Mesopotamia. Sumer's first settlers were the people called the Ubaid. Before their settlements, they were nomadic hunters. They were gatherers too. Their life was a move from one place to another. They were searching for food. They were searching for water. Later, the Ubaid learned how to remain settled. They drained marshes. Rich soil was where they raised their crops. They built canals. The canals brought water to drier areas. River clay became their pottery. Plant stems were woven into baskets. The stems grew in shallow water.

3The river met their own needs. The river also gave them goods to trade. Asia's trade routes crossed the rich plains of Sumeria. Trade routes from Europe went through those plains too. Traders brought items the Ubaid could not grow. Traders brought items the Ubaid could not make. A lion's head comes from a famous Ubaid site. Nomadic means moving from place to place. Nomadic people have no permanent home. Farming at 5000 bce began a more settled life. Canals, clay pots, and baskets all came from the river lands. Over the years, more settlements grew in the Fertile Crescent. Some grew into true cities. A number of them became city-states. The most important city-state was Uruk. Uruk is modern-day Warka, in Iraq. Uruk's population once reached as high as eighty thousand. More than 2.6 square kilometers of ground lay inside the city. That area is 1 square mile. Mud bricks formed its large buildings. A huge ziggurat stood there. A ziggurat is a temple. It was a center of worship. One drawing pictures a ziggurat of ancient Mesopotamia. Uruk's ziggurat still has its stone base on the original spot. A tablet from about 2350 bce uses cuneiform script. It shows grain amounts for each month. Uruk is where Mesopotamian pictographs first appeared. Writing symbols of this early kind are called pictographs.

4This early writing grew from trade. It also grew from business. Uruk was a center of both. People marked simple images on clay tablets. The marks added up workers' pay. The marks also recorded goods. Over time, pictographs changed into cuneiform. Cuneiform symbols stood for sounds. They did not stand only for objects. Any language could be written with these symbols for sounds. A city-state is a city that acts as its own country. A ziggurat is a rectangular building. Steps go up its sides. A temple sits at the top. Cuneiform is writing made of wedge-shaped marks. This writing was used across areas of the old Middle East. Pictographs are pictures that stand for words or ideas. Eighty thousand people once filled this city of mud brick. The old temple base is still in its original place. This sound-based system had advantages. It had advantages over a system of pictures. The same symbols could be rearranged. Rearranging them made different words. So fewer symbols were needed. The system also made abstract ideas easier to write. Those ideas would be hard to show as pictures. Clay tablets with cuneiform told about Sumerian life. Mesopotamian society had three main classes. One class was free people. One class was semi-free people. One class was enslaved people. Rights for semi-free people were greater than rights for enslaved people.

5They had fewer rights than free people. A priest-king stood at society's highest rank. The lower classes of Sumer left few clear records of daily life. Most written records come from businesses. Wealthy people owned those businesses. Most Sumerian women were wives. Most were mothers. They took care of their homes. They took care of their families. School was closed to most girls. Girls from a wealthy family were the exception. Later Mesopotamian cultures gave women fewer rights than Sumer did. They could own property. They could run businesses. They could act as judges in court. They could act as witnesses in court. They could become priestesses. They could become scribes. They could become physicians. King Gilgamesh ranks among the best-known rulers. In Sumerian, his name is Bilgames. People believe he ruled Uruk around 2700 bce. Songs turned him into an epic hero. He became a hero of legend. Poems were written about his rule. The poems say the rule lasted 126 years. Stories called him a demigod. A human king was his father. His mother was a Sumerian mother-goddess. Gilgamesh is known for building a huge wall. The wall protected Uruk. That wall still stands today. A tomb was found by German scientists in 2003. The tomb was in a Euphrates riverbed. They thought the tomb belonged to Gilgamesh.

6The epic describes a tomb much like the one they found. Old Mesopotamian poems gathered together make the Epic of Gilgamesh. It tells of a king's battles. It tells of his victories. People think it is the oldest epic in history. Stone tablets of the poem date to about 2100 bce. A picture shows Gilgamesh with a lion. Abstract means the idea is not a physical thing. In myth, a demigod has a human part and a god part. Phonologic means related to speech sounds in languages. The Sumerian city-states grew. They thrived. Control of the region became the reason for their fights. Battles grew steadily more common. The earliest detailed war record is from 2525 bce. It shows a battle between Lagash and Umma. Both were city-states. Figures stand on an upright stone post. The post is called a stele. Say it like STEE-lee. The figures show soldiers. The soldiers carry swords. They carry spears. They carry shields. Trade routes supplied materials for weapons. Blacksmiths learned something important about metal. Copper is a soft metal. Tin is a soft metal. The two metals could be combined. Together they made a harder substance. That metal is called bronze. Bronze was used in swords. Bronze was used in spear tips. Tin was rare. Traders were the only source for it. Those traders came from central Asia.

7They also came from Europe. Blocking a trade route kept weapons away. An opposing army then had a harder time getting them. A piece of a stele is a very old historical document. The fight of Lagash against Umma is what that carving records. A tall stone slab or column set upright can be a stele. It is usually carved with designs or words. The carving remembers a person or an event. Constant fighting among Sumerians stopped for a time. King Sargon of Akkad took control. Akkad was in southern Mesopotamia. He took control in about 2340 bce. He united the city-states. They became the Akkadian Empire. Sargon kept order in a careful way. Powerful jobs went to allies he trusted. Later followers of the king kept using that same practice. 2150 bce is when the Akkadian Empire came to an end. At the high point, its lands ran between Arabia and the Mediterranean Sea. Iran and the land now called Turkey marked its other span. A map of Sargon's empire shows the Caspian Sea. It shows Syria. It shows the Mediterranean Sea. It shows Akkad. It shows Egypt. Sumerian was not the speech of the Akkadians. They still used Sumerian cuneiform. They used it to write their own language. Sumerian languages were used only in important ceremonies.

8The earliest named poet in the world was Enheduanna. She was Sargon's daughter. Her role in the city of Ur was high priestess. Many of her poems praised Inanna. No goddess in Mesopotamia was more popular than Inanna. An empire is many nations or peoples under one rule. Change followed the peace of the Akkadian Empire. The change came to Mesopotamia. Under Akkadian rule, people created the first mail system. They marked clay tablets with cuneiform messages. Then they wrapped the tablets in clay envelopes. A seal was pressed into the envelope. The seal showed the sender. The envelope also carried the name of the receiver. It carried the place where the receiver was. Someone had to break the clay envelope. Breaking it was the way to reach the message. Then no one but the receiver could read it. Laws were enforced by a central government. It carried out regulations. Trade grew. Trade expanded. Business deals used cylinder seals. A cylinder seal is a carved tube. People pressed the tube into clay. Pressing a seal into clay was like signing a name today. Mesopotamians developed numerical place value. Our clocks still follow this ancient way of counting. We use number bases to count certain things. Counting eggs by the dozen uses base twelve. Twelve eggs equal one dozen. Time uses a system from ancient Mesopotamia.

9That system is base sixty. One minute holds sixty seconds. There are sixty minutes in one hour. The earliest pottery wheels have been found in Sumer. Sumer is also where the oldest transport wheels have turned up. Modern life still depends on wheels. Around 3500 bce, Sumerians used a round, flat device. The device helped them make clay bowls. The potter's wheel sat level on an axis. When it spun, the potter could shape a bowl. The bowl could have even edges. The bowl could have even surfaces. Three hundred years later, Sumerians used wheels in a new way. The wheels made it easy to move objects. The wheels made it easy to transport people. After many trials, they tried a new build. A single axle got one wheel on its left and one on its right. The cart could then carry loads easily. Across the ground, the cart could roll. It took little effort. The design may have been copied by other civilizations. Soon, people in many lands were using wheels. The clay envelope kept a message private. A pressed seal worked like a name. Base sixty still sets the clock. The potter's wheel and the cart wheel both began in Sumer. About 2150 bce marks the finish of the Akkadian Empire. A severe drought was one cause. An invasion was another cause.

10The invaders were the Gutians. Say the name like GOO-tee-uhnz. Northern mountains were the home the Gutians left. Outer parts of the kingdom suffered their raids again and again. Travel became unsafe for Akkadians. Work in the fields became unsafe too. Akkad later fell to the nomads known as Gutians. The Akkadian Empire collapsed. Canals were allowed to break down under the Gutians. A terrible famine followed. Their rule of Sumer lasted 125 years. People later named that period the Dark Age of Mesopotamia. Mesopotamia later returned as a thriving empire. The empire was called Babylonia. The return came in the seventeenth century bce. A statue shows Gudea. Gudea was a Gutian prince. Lagash was under his rule from 2144 to 2124 bce. A raid is a sudden invasion. It can also be a surprise attack. The drought and the Gutian invasion ended Akkad's power. Broken canals helped bring the famine. The Dark Age lasted through 125 years of Gutian rule. Babylonia was the later empire that thrived again. Gudea's years at Lagash were 2144 to 2124 bce. The land between the rivers had risen. Then it fell into a dark age. Later it rose again as Babylonia. The dark age is where this empire's story closes. The story closes on a fallen empire and a later return.

49. Life on the Galapagos Islands

1A Galapagos tortoise lives on these islands. A marine iguana lives here. A Galapagos penguin lives here too. Picture thousands of black lizards lying on rocks of lava. They take in the morning sun. Picture giant tortoises eating cactus. Those cactus plants grow as large as trees. Picture an island that sits on the equator. Penguins swim in the water there. Fur seals rest on beaches of coral. These are the Galapagos Islands. People have been fascinated by the islands since the first visitors came. That first visit was in 1535. Strange landscapes stir our imaginations. The animals do too. The islands were born from fire. They remind us how powerful our planet is. They also remind us of wild places that are vanishing quickly. In those places, nature is still mostly left alone. Building and machines have barely changed them. This book tells where the islands are. It tells how the land was made. It tells about the first people who saw them. It tells about the visit of Charles Darwin. It tells about the animals. It tells about the plants. It tells about dangers to their survival. A closing, more ways to learn, a word list, and a topic list come later. The Galapagos Islands lie in the Pacific Ocean. They belong to the country of Ecuador. They sit along the equator. They are about 966 kilometers from the coast of South America. That is 600 miles. Five islands are the major ones. Many smaller islands of different sizes are there too. For a place on the equator, the climate is surprisingly cool.

2A cold-water current is the reason. The current flows north from Antarctica. That cold water explains a puzzle. Animals that usually need a colder climate can live here. Penguins live in the Galapagos. Sea lions live here too. The rough coast is one thing that draws people to the islands. Volcanoes made the Galapagos Islands. The islands are still some of the most active volcanic islands on Earth. Scientists think the islands sit over a hot spot. The hot spot is under the crust of the earth. A hot spot holds more heat than the areas around it. The heat melts rock. Melted rock rises through the crust. It comes up as lava. Lava spills onto the floor of the sea. There it hardens into solid rock. As time passes, the rock stacks higher. It rises above the water. An island is the result. The Galapagos Islands were first found in 1535. The bishop of Panama was on a ship bound for Peru. Wind blew the ship off its course. The bishop wrote down what he saw. A letter to Spain's king carried what he had written. No people lived on the islands then. In the 1700s and the 1800s, the islands became a refuge. Pirates hid there. Whalers stopped there. They came because the islands were so far away. Giant tortoises were a food the sailors liked best. These gentle animals were simple to catch. They were simple to keep alive. Once there were several hundred thousand of them.

3By 1800 only about 15,000 were left. Ships that hunted whales often stopped at the islands. Charles Darwin came to the islands when he was 24. The visit helped him shape the theory of natural selection. Of all the visitors, Charles Darwin is the most famous. He was a naturalist from Britain. He sailed to the islands in 1835. He gathered many specimens of wildlife. He wrote careful reports of what he saw. The variety of life amazed him. Variety is another word for diversity. He saw that similar species were not the same on every island. A species is a kind of animal. Similar kinds grew different traits on different islands. Because of his work, variety in nature is much clearer to us. Scientists are amazed by how many native animals and plants live here. Tourists are amazed too. New species are often found on the Galapagos Islands. In 1996 an expedition sent scientists far under the water. They studied the sea around the islands. They found many species no one had named before. They found jellyfish. They found moray eels of the deep sea. They found sea cucumbers. They found a red octopus that lives in deep water. On nearly every day of the trip, they found a new kind of marine life. The 1996 team used a special craft. The craft was built for studying the deep ocean. Reptiles are some of the best-known animals on the islands. The islands got their name from the giant tortoise. That tortoise is one of the most famous reptiles.

4These animals are herbivorous, said ur-BIV-or-us. They eat only plants. They can live 150 years or even longer. A male's length can reach 1.8 meters. That is 6 feet. A male can weigh as much as 300 kilograms. That is 660 pounds. There used to be fourteen kinds of Galapagos tortoises. Some kinds have died out. The kinds that remain are protected now. The tortoises fall into two groups. The shape of the shell sets the groups apart. The shell is called the carapace. One group has a shell that is round like a dome. That group has a short neck. It has short legs. The other group has a shell shaped like a saddle. The front of that shell is raised. That group has a long neck. It has long legs. The marine iguana is another famous reptile of the Galapagos. Some people say these lizards look like small dragons. Their skin is like leather. Their claws curve. Spines stick up along their backs. These lizards of the tropics can grow to 1 meter. That length is 3.3 feet. No other lizard on Earth spends part of its life in the sea. Red algae is their main food. Green algae is their main food too. They can stay underwater while they eat. They can stay down for as long as an hour. Special glands help a marine iguana. The glands connect to the nostrils. They let the iguana get rid of extra salt. The salt comes from seawater that the iguana drinks. The animals may look as if they sneeze often.

5They are only pushing salt out. Marine iguanas crowd together on the shore. Dark skin helps them soak up heat from the sun. They need that heat after swimming in cold water. They also shift their bodies to control how warm they are. In the morning, as the sun comes up, they often lie on lava rocks. When the heat grows too strong, they push up on their legs. The lift keeps their bellies off the hot rocks. Air can then move around them. Night finds them piled together once the cold sea day is over. Huddling helps them hold on to body heat. Many mammals of the Galapagos are animals that usually live far from the equator. Sea lions here are like gymnasts of the sea. Their playful tricks make tourists smile. Sometimes a sea lion gives a person a friendly nip. Sea lions live in big colonies. A female sea lion is called a cow. Cows gather on the beaches to sleep. An adult male is called a bull. Bulls guard their own area. During mating season they are very aggressive. Fur seals of the Galapagos are rarer than the sea lions. Hunters nearly wiped the fur seals out. Their thick fur was worth a lot of money. Fur seals, unlike sea lions, live in smaller groups. They like steep shores made of rock. They are afraid of humans. Getting close to them is hard. Among island animals, birds are some of the ones that interest people most.

6Few birds anywhere catch the eye the way frigate birds do. A frigate bird can stand up to 1 meter tall. That is 3.3 feet. Its wings can spread as wide as 2.1 meters. That is 7 feet. Hundreds of males come together when it is time to mate. Each male hopes a female will notice him. He puffs his bright red throat sac until it looks like a balloon. He spreads his wings. He shakes them. He calls out with sharp cries, again and again. A male can inflate that throat sac until it is as big as a soccer ball. The Galapagos penguin surprises many people. Most of us picture penguins living near Antarctica. This penguin lives farther north than any other penguin. Its weight is only from 2 kg up to 2.5 kg. That is 4.5 to 5.5 pounds. It stands 40 to 45 cm tall. That is 16 to 18 inches. Staying cool in tropical heat is one of its hardest jobs. It holds its wings out from its sides. Air can then pass along its body. It may keep its feet in the shade. It may also slip into the cool sea. Under the water these penguins swim very fast. Their wings work like propellers. Their feet work like rudders. They eat small fish. They hunt the fish in groups. They live in colonies. A pair stays together for life. The plants of the Galapagos are as remarkable as the animals. About 560 kinds of plants are native here. Almost one-third of them grow nowhere else on Earth.

7The scalesia tree grows only in the Galapagos. Say scalesia as ska-LEE-zee-yuh. It is part of the daisy family. It can reach 24 meters. That is 78 feet. It grows where the air is humid. Those places are higher up. Flowers called orchids often cover the tree. On many of the islands, the prickly pear cactus stays low to the ground. On Santa Fe, that cactus grows into trees. Land iguanas love to eat it. They eat the pads. They eat the flowers. They eat the fruit. Often they roll a pad on the ground first. Rolling knocks the spines off before they take a bite. These iguanas often wait under a tree. They wait for a pad to fall. A prickly pear can stand as tall as a tree. Nearly every chain of islands on Earth has lost many native plants. Many native animals have been lost too. So far the Galapagos have lost few of their native living things. Serious threats are still here. The worst problems come from species that are not native. Humans brought them. People brought cats. People brought dogs. People brought pigs. People brought goats. People brought horses. People brought donkeys. People brought cattle. People brought rats. Many of these animals became feral, which means wild. Their numbers grew very fast. Cows and other animals from outside disrupt the native ecology. Feral animals eat the eggs of tortoises. They eat baby tortoises. They eat other native animals. Plants needed by native animals are eaten by them as well.

8The islands run many programs to remove the animals that do not belong. The goal is to bring the native ecology back. Scientists raise tortoises in captivity. They want tortoise numbers to rise. They want more of the young to survive. More people on the islands are another serious problem. Some of those people live there. Others are visitors. Island residents in 1940 numbered only 600. In 1949 a major earthquake struck Ecuador. The quake was followed by a move of many people onto the islands. In the 1980s, tourism in the Galapagos grew extremely fast. More people came to live there. Many more people came to visit. By 1997 the population was about 15,000. More people bring more risks. Harmful new species are more likely to arrive. More wood and other materials are taken for building. More wood is cut for fires. More animals are hunted on land. More animals are hunted in the sea. Boats that carry tourists add more pollution. Supply boats add pollution too. In 2001 an oil tanker became stuck. It was in shallow water off one island. A huge spill of oil followed. Experts from many countries joined a giant cleanup. They worked with Ecuador's government. They worked with local scientists. Other people helped too. The tanker was named Jessica. Ecuador moved to protect the islands in 1959. A national park was declared on 95 percent of the land. In 1986 a law guarded the ocean around the islands. The protected ocean covers 69,930 square kilometers. That is 27,000 square miles.

9Strict laws now limit how many visitors may come. Every visitor must travel with a guide. The guide is trained to think about conservation all the time. Visitors may not bring food. They may not bring drinks. Food or drink could carry seeds of plants that are not native. It could carry insects. It could carry bacteria. The laws also shield animals and plants from people getting in the way. Visitors must not touch the animals. They must not feed them. They must not leave litter. Boat tours are watched carefully. That care helps keep the wildlife safe. Scientists clean a bird that was saved from the oil spill of 2001. The Charles Darwin Foundation began in 1959. It helps Ecuador's government choose wise ways to conserve the islands. Charles Darwin Research Station is operated by the foundation. The station is on Santa Cruz Island. Scientists can keep studying these amazing islands there. The public can learn there too. Many programs teach people about saving the Galapagos. Some of the programs are on the islands. Others are in places around the world. The islands are rugged. They are far from other lands. That distance may help keep their ecology one of a kind. Today many kinds of animals around the world are close to disappearing forever. Many kinds of plants are too. Few places on Earth still hold so many rare living things in so small a space. These islands are such a place. Many of these living things exist nowhere else. Scientists are working so the islands stay safe.

10Other people who care about nature are working too. They want future generations to have these islands. The islands are a treasure of nature. People must keep them whole. People must keep them safe. A librarian can help you find books about the Galapagos Islands. Some books are full of photographs. Some tell the history. Some explain modern science. Some are about one plant from the islands. Some are about one animal. Travel books may be there too. In them, people tell about their own trips. Some of those books were written long ago. You can also look up the word Galapagos. Read the results that seem interesting. Then look up other names. Try Charles Darwin. Try the Galapagos tortoise. Try the frigate bird. A carapace is the upper shell of a tortoise. A naturalist is a scientist who studies nature. A current is water flowing, as in a river or an ocean. A refuge is a safe place. Diversity means a wide mix of many different things. A species is a group of living things with similar bodies. Members of a species can reproduce. Ecology is the environment of a place together with its organisms. Specimens are examples kept for study. Feral means an animal left human control and now lives wild. Territorial describes actions used to guard a territory or to defend it. Herbivorous means eating plants only. Topics you can look up include Charles Darwin and the frigate bird. They include lava, the scalesia, and the tortoises.

50. Little Horses of the Sea

1A pair of pygmy seahorses rests in Indonesia. Their bodies blend in with the plants around them. What You Will Read. Strange Animals. An Odd Sort of Fish. Homes Along Warm Coasts. Bodies Made for This Life. Fathers Who Have the Babies. Life Against the Odds. A Closing Look. Words to Know. A pair of seahorses remains together for a whole life. Strange Animals. A strange sea creature hides in beds of seagrass. It is a fish that dances. It is a fish that can barely swim. It is an animal that can look forward and backward at one time. The animal is the seahorse. It is a delicate marvel of the ocean. It is unique. Scientists call the seahorse hippocampus. Two words from ancient Greek were joined to make the name. Hippos means horse. Kampos means sea monster. harlequin ghost pipefish. Honshu pipefish. An Odd Sort of Fish. Seahorses are close relatives of pipefish. Pipefish are skinny fish with long snouts. The two share some features. Both have small fins. Both have eyes that move on their own.

2Neither one has teeth. In other ways, these fish cousins are quite different. Pipefish look like skinny tubes. A pipefish is longer than it is tall. Pipefish hold their bodies level, the way most fish do. Seahorses do the opposite. They hold their bodies upright as they move through the water. Another big difference explains their name. Bumps called spines run along the top of the head. The spines also run along the back of the head. The spines look like a horse's mane. The snout looks like the muzzle of a horse. It also looks like the nose of a horse. Seahorses have a long tail as well. Parts of a Seahorse. More than forty kinds of seahorses all use this same body plan. Their size is not the same. About 2 centimeters, just under 1 in., is the length of a tiny pygmy seahorse. A Pacific seahorse may reach 31 centimeters, or 1 ft. Seahorses also come in different colors. The colors range from purple to gold to white. Color often shifts on these fish too.

3The body labels are the eye, the coronet, the pectoral fin, the snout, the keel, the dorsal fin, and the tail. Homes Along Warm Coasts. ASIA. NORTH AMERICA. EUROPE. PACIFIC OCEAN. ATLANTIC OCEAN. AFRICA. SOUTH AMERICA. INDIAN OCEAN. AUSTRALIA. The shaded area is the seahorse range. The Pacific Ocean lies on both sides of the map. Warm water in most regions of the world is home to seahorses. Seahorses live in warm water along coastlines around the world. They nest in kelp forests. They nest in beds of eelgrass. They choose places that have steady currents. Tiny plankton fill these weedy spots. They are full of shrimp larvae too. Seahorses like to eat those foods. Moving water brings the food to them. That matters, because they cannot swim far to hunt. During storms, seahorses sometimes move into deeper water. They go there to avoid rough waves. Usually, though, they stay inside a set area. A female may claim as much as 100 square meters (1,076 sq. ft.). The male stays in a much smaller area. A Denise's pygmy seahorse is one of the smallest kinds of seahorses.

4It is found in Indonesia. Bodies Made for This Life. For a fish, the seahorse body is strange. It has an exoskeleton. An exoskeleton is a hard covering, like armor, with skin on top. The exoskeleton helps the seahorse defend against predators. It protects the internal organs from harm. A small dorsal fin is attached to the back. The fin flutters as fast as the wings of a hummingbird. That fluttering fin is not strong enough for a fast escape. It cannot carry a seahorse away from hungry crabs quickly. It cannot carry a seahorse away from sea rays quickly. Seahorses are not fast swimmers. In fact, the tiny pygmy seahorse is among the slowest fish on Earth. In a full hour it covers only 1.5 meters (5 ft.). For the most part, seahorses drift. Ocean currents carry them along. A prehensile tail helps these animals that live in seaweed. A seahorse can wrap the tail around an object. It can grip the object the way a hand can.

5Seahorses use the tail to hold themselves in one spot. A grip on seagrass keeps them from being swept off. Swift currents would carry them away without it. Camouflage is an important part of how a seahorse stays safe. Seahorses have adapted so they can survive. They use color to blend in with what is around them. Seahorse skin has special groups of cells. The cells are called chromatophores. The cells change color when the body sends signals. Two cousins of the seahorse have leafy growths. The cousins are the leafy seadragon and the weedy seadragon. The growths look like leaves. In a kelp forest, those growths hide them very well. The leafy sea dragon comes from Australia. It is a master of camouflage. Seahorses have good vision. They can see objects as far away as 4.6 meters (15 ft.). Hunting is easier because of the eyes. The eyes work independently. They can look in two different directions at one time. The snout swings toward the prey as soon as the seahorse sees it. It uses the snout like a straw and sucks the food in.

6A seahorse can swallow only what fits through that thin snout. It has no teeth. It cannot chew. Small Bites, Often. A seahorse can take in only the tiniest bits of food. So it must eat often. It may eat up to fifty times a day. A pair of tiger-tail seahorses comes together to mate. Fathers Who Have the Babies. Seahorses are unique in the way they look. They are also unique in the way they reproduce. Males and females take roles unlike those of other animal species. The male seahorses give birth. Males are also called stallions. No other animals give birth this way. Only seahorses and pipefish do. First, a couple pairs off. They dance together for several days. In this mating dance, they may circle each other. They may swim side by side. They change colors as a way to communicate. They may hold each other with their tails. Some pairs bond for life. A stallion has a pouch. The pouch is not unlike the pouch of a kangaroo.

7At the right moment, eggs from the female go into the pouch. She may place as many as 1,500 eggs. The stallion fertilizes the eggs. About forty-five days pass while the eggs stay in his pouch. The female visits him while he carries the eggs. She wants to be sure all is well. A male with a pouch full of eggs guards his territory. He puffs himself up so he looks as large as he can. The big shape can scare off predators. The eggs slowly become baby seahorses. The babies are called fry. The fry look just like their parents. The stallion pushes the ready fry from his pouch. They enter the water. After that, each baby swims away alone. The count of babies depends on the species. One birth can include more than a thousand babies. Only about one in twenty will survive long enough to become adults. An adult life may last about five years. A male seahorse gives birth. Life Against the Odds. Few of the fry ever become adults. That number may not be enough to keep seahorse populations going.

8Adult seahorses face danger from natural predators. They also face danger from humans. Boats are a real threat to seahorses. Boats used for commercial fishing are a special threat. These boats may drag nets across the ocean floor. They may drag anchors too. The dragging pulls up sea plants. Those plants matter to seahorse survival. The anchors may also destroy seahorse habitat. Lost habitat brings their numbers down. Seahorses do not swim long distances. Their ranges are limited. Once a home is destroyed, they are less likely to look for a new one. Hunters are a second danger. People pull them in with nets. Seahorses are wanted for several reasons. They are used in traditional medicine. They are collected and sold as ornaments. People bring them to shore. People set them in the hot sun so they dry out. Their bodies are sold to companies. The companies use the bodies as decorations. Live seahorses are sold as pets too. Their unusual looks make them a popular addition to aquariums. Seahorses do not last long in home fish tanks.

9Most die within weeks. Stress is one cause. Disease is another cause. Conservationists say the best help is education. People need to learn about seahorses. They are beautiful creatures. They also matter to ocean ecology. The way they feed helps keep sea life in balance. That balance is around coral reefs and grass beds. A City for Seahorses. Roger Hanson was a retired schoolteacher. He often dived off the California coast. He wanted to study the seahorses he saw. He wanted to protect them too. He built a seahorse city on the ocean floor. He used pine branches and palm leaves. He placed this safe spot far from the beach. Seahorses could live there with less risk of being trampled. Daphne is a Pacific seahorse that lives in Roger Hanson's habitat. The small picture shows Roger Hanson. Look, but do not touch. A scuba diver watches a long-snouted seahorse with care. The animal is near Singer Island, Florida. A Closing Look. Seahorses are amazing animals of the sea. They are shy.

10They hide among the weeds. They try to stay out of sight. You may be lucky and spot a seahorse in the wild. If you do, move slowly. Do not disturb it. Take a quiet moment to admire its unique beauty. Then go on your way. These beautiful animals are a delight to see. They live in oceans all over the world. Their nature is gentle. Their traits are unusual. Those qualities make seahorses some of nature's most unusual treasures. Words to Know. Adapted: changed in order to suit a new place to live. Camouflage: body colors, patterns, or shapes that let an animal blend into the background or stay hidden. Conservationists: people whose work is to protect the natural world. Currents: air or water moving along one path. Delicate: able to be broken or hurt with little force. Habitat: the natural home of a plant or of an animal. Kelp: a big brown seaweed that lives in the sea. Marine: having to do with the sea. Prehensile: able to seize an object by curling around it.

51. Living Cities in Warm Seas

1Hiding places on a reef are many and good. A moray eel uses one. An opening starts this book. Then it asks what coral is. A busy community under the water comes next. Where the reefs are comes after that. Threats follow, and so does protection. A word list ends the book. Corals of many kinds live on these reefs. Other animals of the sea share that home. In warm oceans, huge communities lie a short way down from the top. Coral reefs is the name for them. Wonder and beauty fill these places. Life there comes in an incredible variety. Thousands of living organisms make a reef home. Food is something they need from one another. Shelter is needed too. Safety is needed too. Thousands of animals keep swimming, whether it is day or night. Hunting happens. Eating happens. Avoiding being eaten happens. Almost one quarter of the ocean's plants and animals live around reefs. Fish live there. Sea turtles live there. Sea stars live there, along with lots of other animals. Seabirds visit. Dolphins visit. A first look can mistake coral for rocks of an odd shape. Spiny plants are another easy mistake. Polyps are what corals really are, and polyps are tiny animals. Say the word PAH-lips. Very small is the usual size. A pinhead is one end of the range.

2A pea is the other. Thousands of these tiny polyps can live on one branch, or on one mound. A tube is the shape of the body. Tiny tentacles ring the mouth. Eating machines is a fair name for polyps. Night is when the tentacles open. Tiny animals are caught. Nutrients are taken in. A polyp stays on one surface. Forever is how long it stays. Hundreds of coral kinds live in the ocean. Two types hold most of them. Hard corals are also called stony corals. Hard skeletons are what they form. Millions of those skeletons pile up over time. Reefs are the result. Most stony corals live with algae that seem like plants. Say algae AL-jee. Food for the corals comes partly from the algae. Food for many reef fish comes from them too. Elkhorn coral looks like the wide antlers of an elk. Horns are not what elk have. Sea pens shrink if a creature comes too close. Sand is where they hide. Sea fans spread up and out, wide like fans. The shape traps tiny organisms for food. Soft coral is the second common type. Flexible woody cores are what they grow. Hard skeletons are not. Trees, bushes, or other plants are what they often resemble. Currents can bend them.

3Algae grow inside some soft corals. Other soft corals have none. Golden butterflyfish pass soft corals in one picture. Red bigeye fish pass in a school as well. Egypt's Red Sea is the place. Bright fish are what most people picture when reefs come to mind. The reason is a good one. Fish species on reefs number over four thousand. Food is one gift of the reef. Protection from predators is another. Algae and plankton feed some fish. Other fish that live there feed some. A few fish even eat the coral. Shrimp treat the reef as a favorite place to dine. Lobsters do. Crabs do. Clams hidden in the branches are caught by sea urchins. Smaller shellfish are caught by sea stars. Sea anemones wave like graceful flowers. Shallow openings hide them. The next meal is what they wait to see drift past. Eels use large holes as homes. The holes are hiding spots too. A busy reef wastes no space. Thousands of species are not the only thing reefs support. Shorelines gain protection from floods. Storms are blocked in the same way. Erosion of the coast goes down because of that protection. Property damage goes down. Loss of human life goes down. Animals that supply much of the world's seafood are fed by reefs.

4They are sheltered too. Economies of many countries gain from that. Diets gain too. Diving tours bring visitors near reefs. Sport fishing brings visitors. Income comes with them. Medicines use reef plants. Medicines use reef animals. A valuable natural resource is what a coral reef is. A reef in the Caribbean Sea, like others, protects the land. Medicines have already been made from reef organisms. More are likely. A substance from corals is now used against asthma. Arthritis is treated with it too. Several kinds of cancer are treated with medicines that come from reefs. Other reef organisms are under study. Skin conditions may be treated by them. Infections may be treated too. A map of the reef zone names North America, Asia, and Europe. It names the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. It names Africa and the equator. It names South America, the Indian Ocean, and Australia. Coral reefs, land, ocean, and Antarctica are marked. NOAA made the map in 2017. The equator is where most reefs are found. Warm tropical water close to shore is the usual place. Warm currents leaving the tropics can grow reefs too. Florida is one such place. Parts of Japan are another. Best growth comes in warm water. The range is 21 to 29 degrees Celsius. That is 70 to 84 degrees Fahrenheit.

5Sunlight is what algae need in order to make food. So most corals stay near the surface. Even then, many areas cannot keep a reef alive. River mouths are a poor place for growth. Dirt, trash, and fresh water enter the sea there. Corals can die if fresh water reaches them. Dirt can hurt a reef. Trash can hurt a reef. Smothering is possible too. Growth is very slow. Getting bigger takes a long time. Healing from damage takes a long time. Growth for some reefs still living started twenty-five million years before now. Three reef types exist. Fringing reefs are the first. Close to shore is where they sit. They usually trace the land's edge, the fringe where shore meets sea. Barrier reefs are the second. A deep lagoon is what they create between reef and shore. A lagoon is an area of water. The Great Barrier Reef, off Australia, is the largest barrier reef on Earth. Length is 2,300 kilometers, or 1,429 miles. Reefs and islands in it number over three thousand. Fish species there number nearly two thousand. That reef's age falls between six thousand years and eight thousand years. Coral growth at this location goes back about five hundred thousand years. Sea level changed many times in that span.

6Low seas killed earlier reefs. Higher seas let new reefs form. The time after the last ice age is included. The reef standing there today, scientists think, is number six or later. Atolls are the third type. A circle is the pattern. A sinking island can sit in the middle. An aging island volcano can too. As an island sinks, leftover land slips under the ocean surface. An old volcano can break apart the same way. The growing reef then rings a lagoon in the center. The Maldives, in the Indian Ocean, is a country built of twenty-six atolls. A reef can die quickly from pollution. High ocean temperatures can kill it too. Fragile is the word for coral reefs. Damage can come from many causes. A hurricane's large, powerful waves can destroy a reef. A tsunami can too. Say tsunami soo-NAH-mee. People cause most of the damage. Dirty water that people pollute is one likely reason coral gets sick. Weeks can be enough for those diseases to wipe out an ancient reef. Higher ocean temperatures are another likely factor, and people cause those too, through global warming. Global warming is a rise in how warm Earth's air and oceans are, on average. The rise is big enough to change weather patterns that last a long time.

7Human activity is the main cause today. Land is cleared for farming. Industrial processes run. Coal, oil, and gas are burned. These acts release a great deal of carbon dioxide gas. The gas enters Earth's atmosphere. Heat is trapped close to the surface. Many problems follow. Wildfires are among them. Extreme weather is among them. Reefs and other natural communities are threatened. Scientists expect worse problems unless the activities that make so much carbon dioxide are reduced. Bleaching is another killer of corals. Ocean water that gets too warm is the most common cause today. Algae inside the polyps go through a chemical change. The polyps are harmed. Algae are expelled so the harm will stop. Food for the polyps comes from algae. Color comes from algae too. Losing algae means losing the main food. Starvation begins. Color goes too, so the coral looks bleached. Recovery from bleaching can happen. If the cause keeps going, corals die and the reef dies. Three quarters of reefs are affected by bleaching now. White reefs, from bleaching, are showing up around the world. The same human acts load Earth's atmosphere with too much carbon dioxide. Oceans get too much of that gas as well. Ocean water turns more acidic. Calcium carbonate is then hard for corals to take in. Healthy skeletons depend on it.

8Instead, stony skeletons that hold corals up begin to dissolve. Reef skeletons dissolve too. Other human harm exists. Fishing with poisons has destroyed reefs. Fishing with explosives has too. The Philippines lost more than half its reefs to those methods. Coastal homes create soil erosion. Other buildings do too. Fresh water pours into the ocean. Coral is damaged by fresh water. Chemicals may ride in that water. Waste may ride in it. Scars in Florida's barrier reef have come from ships. Smaller boats have left scars too. Breaking chunks off a reef is another danger. Accident is one way it happens. Purpose is the other. Some pieces go home to be kept. Some go home to be sold. Since 2011, threatened reef area has grown by 30 percent. Stopping global warming now would still leave a hard prediction. More than 90 percent of reefs will die by 2050. Doing nothing could mean losing every one. Boaters damaged one elkhorn coral. Many countries have begun to preserve reefs nearby. A government group in the United States draws maps of the reefs. Pictures from satellites let scientists spot problems. Floating buoys measure sea level. They measure water temperature. They measure wind speed. They measure air temperature. Reef damage is easier to understand with all of that information.

9Reducing the damage becomes possible. Healthy coral can be grown in nurseries, piece by piece. Boat damage is one place a piece may be rescued from. Coastal construction is another. Bars can hold the hanging pieces. Baskets can hold them. Stands on the ocean floor can hold them. Later the pieces move to reefs that are damaged. Health can return with that help. Florida law forbids removing fish, plants, or coral from places set aside for protection. The same rule holds on the Great Barrier Reef. People may not go near many fragile reefs. Boats may not go near them. The work done so far is just the beginning. Half the world's reefs are already destroyed. Most of the rest are threatened. All of us share the job of keeping reefs alive. An ocean nearby is not required. Reducing global warming is a way to help. Use less energy. Walk more, or bike more. Recycle all you can. Each year, divers who volunteer pull trash off reefs. Mangrove trees are planted by people in Indonesia. Nearby reefs gain protection from those trees. Learning how communities support resilient reefs is another way to help. Health can hold when climate-related challenges arrive. Recovery can happen too. Crops planted by community members shade the reefs. Cooler water is the result.

10Other plants are grown to slow erosion. Pollution is kept from entering the ocean. Some people protect fish. A balanced ecosystem on the reef depends on those fish. There is a helpful act for every person. This natural wonder can stay beautiful for centuries ahead. Which part will you take? A word list follows. Bleaching means color goes away, the way coral goes white once its algae are gone. Erosion is rock or soil carried off by moving water, by wind, or by ice. Flexible means able to bend and not break. Carbon dioxide is an invisible gas formed when organic substances break down or burn, and fossil fuels are one example. Fragile means easy to damage or break, and delicate. Resilient describes a thing that can get well again after harm. Coral reefs are ridges in warm sea water. Outer skeletons of tiny sea animals, the polyps, build them. Skeletons are hard frames that support and protect some animal bodies. Tropical means the region around the equator, hot and humid. Dissolve means to break down, usually after touching a liquid. A tsunami is a set of large ocean waves that destroy, set off by an underwater earthquake, a landslide, or a volcanic eruption. An ecosystem is living things together with the habitat they share.

52. Love Lives in Animals

1A reader meets five parts after this opening. One part is an elephant facing a hard choice. One part is penguin parents. One part is a pair of malamute dogs. Then come a closing, a word list, and a topic list. A pet owner and a scientist may not see the same thing. Can an animal feel love? I say yes. Other emotions are real for them too, in my view. People who keep pets often share that view. So do many people whose work is with animals. A lot of scientists will not accept the idea. I use the word emotions for what animals show. Those scientists use the word instincts. An instinct is an act done with no thought behind it. Staying alive is what instincts are built for. Stories in this book still surprise me. Instinct is not a full explanation, as I see it. You will meet loyalty here. Friendship is here too. Tenderness is here. Compassion is here. A parent's care is here. While you read, picture a person in a moment like that. I expect the last page will settle the question for you.

2Love is something animals can feel. They do feel it. In one picture, Echo stands among the other elephants of her herd. She was the female who led a herd of African elephants. Her new baby was a boy. Very soon, a problem showed. The calf had no way to get upright. Bent wrists held his front legs in the wrong shape. Those legs would not go straight. Again and again he rose on the legs at the back. The front pair still failed. Her trunk made a try at lifting him. Walking was still impossible for him. The female at the head of an elephant herd is the one the others follow. Food was running short, so the herd had to leave. Echo hated the thought of being left behind by the others. Leaving her new son was something she would not do. The son's name was Ely. Days can pass with elephants taking no food. Days can pass with no water too. Even so, a long stay in one spot is dangerous. A choice sat in front of Echo. Go with the herd, or remain with her son.

3A picture shows elephants walking onward. Another shows a baby asleep below the mother. Most of the other elephants went away. Their search was for a fresh watering hole. Echo remained beside Ely. Enid, her daughter, remained too. Heat pressed on them. Food ran out. Water ran out. They got Ely as far as a little mud hole. Water went onto their own bodies. Water went onto the calf. Echo made another try to raise Ely. A scream came from him. Nursing the right way needs standing, and he could not stand. Starvation was getting close for the small calf. She refused to abandon him. Two full days passed, and the calf was still alive. Day three brought a change. The bottoms of his feet met the ground. Standing became his goal. Up, down, and up again he went. At last, walking was possible for Ely. The three of them located the rest of the herd. They became part of it once more. A picture shows elephants at a watering hole. Ely may have been a very big baby before birth. Inside his mother, those front legs may have locked in a position that was not natural.

4Echo seemed to understand the need. Time to stretch was what those legs required. Time to move the right way was required too. Love from a patient mother showed in what she did. She put her own life at risk so the calf could have that time. Survival depended on it. My own view is clear. Love for her son was real in Echo. A later picture shows Ely in the year 2000, when he was 10. Owen and Mzee can look like a mother with a baby. They are not that pair. In 2004 a tsunami struck Asia. A young hippopotamus lost contact with his mother during it. The hippopotamus was Owen. Waves of the ocean took him a long way from home. Rescue came from a wildlife ranger. The ranger set up a move to a wildlife park. His mother was missed. A tortoise named Mzee became the mom he turned to. Mzee had lived 100 years. Devotion grew between this unlikely pair. Nothing split them. A picture shows emperor penguins on the way to a nesting ground. Antarctica is where emperor penguins live.

5Few climates on Earth are as harsh. March is when they migrate. The trip is one hundred miles. The nesting ground is the goal. Walking is one way they go. Sliding on the belly is the other. Once there, the colony packs into a huddle. Freezing temperatures are easier to survive that way. High winds are easier too. A mate is chosen by each penguin. Snow is the name we will use for the female. Her egg comes in May, or early in June. She sets that egg on her feet. Ground contact is what she prevents. Freezing is what she prevents too. Ice is the name we will use for the male. The moment Ice sees the egg, singing starts, and it is ecstatically happy singing. Snow adds her voice. An hour can pass while the two of them sing. Their eyes stay on the egg. A picture shows an emperor penguin with an egg on the feet, held off the ground. After the song, Snow passes the egg to Ice with great care. His feet become the support. A flap of skin from the belly covers it.

6Warmth comes from that flap. Harm is kept away by Ice. Snow may travel as far as 50 miles. The ocean is where she goes to feed. Nearly four months pass with Ice eating nothing. A brutal winter is what he endures. The egg stays balanced on his feet. Motion from him is almost none. August is when the egg hatches. Snow comes back from the sea and sings. Finding Ice makes her dance. The peeping of her chick excites her even more. Onto her own feet the chick goes, and quickly. Ice heads for the ocean. Babysitting through that long hard winter earns him a good meal. Hatchlings stay warm with emperor penguin parents. They stay safe too. Snow and Ice show what it means to go a very long way for a child. In the months after that, the mother and the father trade trips. Each trip is to the ocean, for food.
