One parent is always with the chick. The watching is full of love. Keeping the chick safe, all the time, is how they show that love. Tika had a gentle nature.

7This part is about two malamute mates. Kobuk and Tika had been champion show dogs of the malamute kind. Breeding was their role as a pair. Retirement, in a dog's quiet way, was what they were enjoying. The male was Kobuk. Dominant was his manner. Attention from Anne was something he demanded. Anne owned him. His needs came out fast. A scratch on the belly might be the need. A meal might be the need. A trip outdoors might be the need. The female was Tika. Quiet was her way, much more than his. Passive was her way too. Any attention aimed at Tika was taken by Kobuk for himself. First through the door was his rule on daily walks. A knock-down often followed if Tika blocked him. A picture shows Kobuk, worried, beside his companion. A tumor on Tika's leg was what Anne found one day. Malignant was the word for that tumor. Kobuk understood, somehow. At once, the way he treated Tika changed. Day and night, her side was where he stayed. Grooming of her face happened often. Grooming of her ears happened often too. Amputation removed the leg, and with it the cancer.

8After the operation, his watch over her was attentive. Worry in Kobuk was plain to Anne. Tika's suffering was hard for him to see. Urgency was in Kobuk one night when he woke Anne. His run took him to Tika. Both dogs went outside with Anne. A swollen belly was what she found on Tika. Huge is the word for it. Air had filled the stomach. Deadly is what air in a stomach can be. An emergency veterinary clinic is where Tika's life was saved. The warning from Kobuk, given in time, is the only reason she lived. Recovery followed the surgeries. Three legs became enough for her to walk. Kobuk turned rambunctious again. That return came only after his devotion to his mate was proved. A picture shows Tika getting about on those three legs. Another picture shows Marc with two dogs. Jethro is the one on the left. Zeke is there as well. A big heart is the subject of this dog's story. Large and gentle describes Jethro. The Humane Society is where he came from, on his way to his owner.

9Marc Bekoff was that owner. Chasing animals was not Jethro's habit. For most dogs, chasing is an instinct. A peaceful watch of the world around him was what he preferred. A baby rabbit arrived one day, carried by Jethro to Marc. No parents were left to care for that rabbit. Two weeks of nursing followed, done by Marc. The box that held the baby had Jethro beside it the whole time. His watch over her did not stop. Release into the wild came later. For months, Jethro kept running back to one place. That spot was the release place Marc chose for her. A reunion was what he hoped for, with the rabbit he had saved. Only a handful of stories sit in this closing. Love and devotion in animals have inspired many more. Meetings of this kind happen constantly among animals. People are often not there to see them. Evidence comes from each meeting. The evidence says love is possible for animals. It says they do feel it. Next time animals are together in front of you, see them as family to one another. Words of love, the kind people speak, are beyond them.

10The feeling those words carry can still be there. Loyalty makes the case. Devotion makes the case. Compassion between them makes the case. Love is within what animals can do. A short word list follows. To abandon someone is to leave that one behind. Evidence is news that shows a claim is true, or shows it is false. Amputated describes a part that has been cut off. Instincts are behavior patterns animals follow with no thinking. Compassion is caring about another creature's suffering, plus a wish to help. Loyalty is the state of being committed. Devotion is love that is great, joined with commitment. Malignant describes something dangerous and deadly. Ecstatically describes a joy that is extreme. Passive describes a manner that is not active. Eventually means at last, once a long delay has passed. Rambunctious describes a noisy, active manner full of excitement. A topic list includes illness and an orphan. A penguin, a rabbit, temperature, and a tortoise are on it. Africa, Antarctica, and Asia are on it. A dog, a disability, an elephant, and a hippopotamus are on it.

53. Machines That Work Without Rest

1Contents. Workers That Do Not Tire. What a Robot Is. Simple Robots and Complex Ones. Places Too Dangerous for People. Robots That Go Exploring. Very Small Robots. Robots Shaped Like People and Animals. How Smart Robots Can Be. What Comes Next for Robots. Word List. Imagine a job where you pick up nails. You put the nails into boxes. The boxes move past you on an assembly line. Imagine that this one job fills your whole day. It fills your whole night too. You never get a break for a meal. You never get a break for sleep. You never get a break to use the bathroom. Work that repeats is called repetitive work. Repetitive work makes it hard to stay focused. After a while you would feel tired. You would feel cranky. You would feel exhausted. Every time, a robot finishes this job without a mistake. A robot does the job without complaining. A picture shows robotic arms. Factories often use those arms on assembly lines. A picture shows a robot that swims the way a fish swims. A video camera sits inside that robot. Robot began as robota, a word from the Czech language.

2Robota means forced labor. Forced labor is hard work that is also boring. Factories are where a large share of today's robots work. Many of them are simple robot arms. Some arms can grip pieces of metal. Other arms weld the pieces together. Still other arms drill parts. Some arms spray paint onto parts. A gentler robot arm is able to sort small items. The items might be chocolates. The items might be tiny screws. A robot is a machine with a mechanical body. It has sensors that take in information. It has a computer brain. Most robots can move. Others have parts that move. Some robots look like people. Robots also come in many shapes. They come in many sizes. Some walk on legs. Others use wheels to move. Some use tracks to move. Some robots fly the way insects fly. Some swim the way fish swim. Some even crawl the way snakes crawl. Before a baby dinosaur robot can work, it must have many parts. A color camera helps it see. Motors control how the head moves. Motors also move the neck, the legs, and the tail.

3A computer brain guides the robot. A microphone lets it hear. Speakers let it make sound. A rechargeable battery gives it power. An infrared sensor helps it notice things nearby. Floor sensors read the ground under it. Many robots use video cameras as their eyes. They use microphones as their ears. A robot is programmed to do certain tasks. It may do those tasks on its own. It may do them by remote control. Every step of the task is laid out in the program. If a task was never programmed, most robots cannot do it. The science of robotics covers how robots are designed. It is also the science of building them. It is also the science of operating them. Some schools offer programs in robotics. Some summer camps offer them too. Students in those programs work together. They create robots of their own. Each year, high school teams from many countries enter contests. The contest asks which team can build the strongest robot. A picture shows the robot SpotMini. SpotMini is a complex robot. It moves the way a dog moves. An arm on its back can open doors.

4That same arm can handle objects. A simple robot can perform a basic task. One basic task is moving car parts along an assembly line. For that job, the robot needs only one arm. A sensor must report the location of each part. A program must tell the robot how to move. A more complex robot has to carry a larger set of programs. Those programs are stored in their computer brains. Builders usually give a robot skill in just a few jobs. Ten separate robots, one for each job, are easier to build. It is harder to build one robot that does all ten jobs. A picture shows the Mini Mambo robot. People used Mini Mambo to inspect flooded buildings. The buildings belonged to a nuclear power plant that had been damaged. Some robots go into places where a human would not be safe. In Japan, an earthquake wrecked a nuclear power plant. Officials sent robots in to check the damage. Any living creature would have died from the radiation of that nuclear accident. No living creature could have entered that damaged plant and lived. A volcano can be just as unsafe.

5Eight scientists lost their lives during a volcano study. The volcano was in South America. The year was 1993. A robot was built to collect samples of gases in a safe way. They may also respond with flashing lights. A picture shows a robotic dog called AIBO. Faces of people are something AIBO is able to learn. AIBO can play games. 54. Marie Curie, Pioneer of Rays

1A photo shows Marie Curie's laboratory packed with scientific instruments. Her husband, Pierre, invented some of those tools. Others were invented by Pierre's brother, Jacques. These pages call her a trailblazer. They cover her early years. They cover her long preparation. They follow her arrival in Paris. They explain two kinds of rays. They list her honors. They tell of dark days and further fame. They follow her to the battlefront. They tell of her later life. They end with gifts she left the world. Hard words come last. She studied at a leading university. She followed her scientific interests anyway. Obstacles seemed to meet her wherever she turned. She was the first woman awarded a Nobel Prize. No other person has ever received Nobel Prizes across two different scientific fields. That groundbreaking scientist was Marie Curie. A family photo places Marie Curie in the center. Her brother and sisters stand with her. Zosia stands at the left. Hela stands next. Joseph stands next. Bronya stands at the right. She was born Maria Sklodowska. The date was November 7, 1867. The city was Warsaw. The country was Poland.

2As a child she was called Manya. The family had five children. She was the youngest one. Their father taught math at a boys' high school. He also taught physics there. Her oldest sister died in 1876. Her mother died two years after that. Manya was a bright child. She was a curious child. Schoolwork showed her to be an outstanding student. She graduated from high school in 1883. She was fifteen. She earned top honors. Few universities in the world ranked as high as the Sorbonne. It still is. More study was the wish of Manya. It was the wish of her sister Bronya too. The University of Warsaw did not admit women. Leaving Poland was the only path. Money for that path was missing. The sisters went to Warsaw's floating university. Polish teachers offered free classes there. The classes were held in secret. Those classes could not match the finest universities in Europe. They did keep Manya current on scientific discoveries. Both sisters wanted the Sorbonne in Paris. The cost was too high. They made a deal. Manya would earn the money for Bronya's schooling.

3After Bronya earned a degree, she would return the favor. Manya worked as a tutor for five years. She also worked as a governess. Free hours went to science. They went to literature. They went to other subjects. Once her sister's schooling was paid, Manya's own turn arrived. Paris became Manya's home in 1891. She enrolled at the Sorbonne. She took the name Marie at that time. Marie is the French form of Maria. Two years later she finished first in her class. The degree was a master's in physics. The next year brought a second master's. That degree was in math. A commission asked her to study steel. The question was the magnetic properties of that metal. She needed a laboratory. Another scientist introduced her to Pierre Curie. Pierre was a physics professor. He arranged lab space for her where he worked. A photo catches the pair soon after they wed. Pierre Curie stands with Marie Sklodowska Curie. Over time the two fell in love. They married in July 1895. A daughter, Irene, arrived two years later. Marie stayed deeply involved in her work. After that research ended, she chose a new goal. A doctorate from the Sorbonne became her next aim. Wilhelm Roentgen's discovery of X-rays came in 1895.

4Physics went through a revolution because of it. She needed a topic for the doctoral research. Two big physics discoveries were still recent. In late 1895 Wilhelm Roentgen found X-rays. He was a German physicist. Early the next year, Henri Becquerel made his own find. He was a French physicist. Rays also came from the element uranium. Those rays were weaker than X-rays. Marie chose uranium rays as her subject. She studied how those rays affected air. She measured electric currents in air that uranium rays had blasted. The currents were barely noticeable. She agreed with Becquerel on one point. Uranium gave off electricity in any form. She agreed on a second point. More uranium meant stronger rays. She also showed something further. The rays belonged to uranium's structure. They were not just a matter of its physical state. They were not just a matter of its chemical state. Another element gave off rays as well. That element was thorium. During Marie's time, scientists already knew about atoms. Atoms are the smallest particles of things. People then believed an atom had no smaller pieces inside it. Her uranium work led to a new idea. A huge store of energy sits inside atoms. That idea changed how scientists understood atoms. A new field grew from it.

5The field is atomic physics. She kept testing materials for rays. One mineral she tested was pitchblende. Pitchblende contains uranium. The rays from it were too strong to come from the uranium alone. She supposed a second radioactive element was hidden in it. Scientists did not know that element yet. In 1898 Pierre joined the search. Long research produced two new elements. One was polonium. The name honors Marie's homeland. The other was radium. Latin supplied the name, from its word for ray. Pierre also proved a danger. Radium's radioactivity could harm living flesh. His proof opened the door to treatments. Cancer was one illness those treatments could face. Other illnesses could be faced too. Illness often struck Marie during the work. Illness often struck Pierre too. The cause was not clear. Overwork was one possible cause. Radiation was another. Marie would not accept radiation as the blame. Today we know radiation can cause illness. It can cause death. June 1903 is when her Doctor of Science was earned. No woman in France had received a doctorate before her. No woman in Europe had received a doctorate in science before her. Charge of the physics research, even the part shared with Pierre, belonged to her. Even so, the Nobel Prize nearly passed her by.

6The reason was that she was a woman. The Nobel Prize is one of the world's most respected awards. Pierre Curie's name was placed on the nominee list for the physics Nobel of 1903. At first his was the Curie name listed. Henri Becquerel was nominated too. Pierre called it terribly unfair to leave Marie off. Her name was added to the list. In December 1903 she and Pierre won together. Becquerel won with them. The award honored their pioneering work on radiation. No woman had received a Nobel Prize before. Fame came to the Curies at once, all around the world. The Sorbonne gave Pierre a stronger post. Marie received a salary. She became chief of laboratory. The attention excited her. The new duties excited her. A second daughter, Eve, was born in 1904. A new laboratory from the Sorbonne reached the Curies around then. A photo shows the move in 1904. The new laboratory finally had more space. Success was bright when tragedy struck. In 1906 a horse-drawn wagon ran over Pierre. He was killed instantly. The whole world soon heard that he had died. Shock left Marie completely numb. She later found the strength to continue. She was given Pierre's teaching post at the Sorbonne. No woman had been a Sorbonne professor before her.

7A second Nobel Prize came in 1911. This prize was in chemistry. It honored her work in radioactivity. It honored her discovery of radium. It honored her discovery of polonium. No scientist before her had received two Nobel Prizes. Even now, no one else holds prizes across two different areas of science. A photo shows French soldiers on October 31, 1914. They gather around a mobile X-ray truck. The truck used Marie Curie's equipment. Many wounded soldiers of World War I lived because of those machines. Late July 1914 is when World War I began. Germany attacked France only a few days later. Most of Marie's staff left to fight. The research she was doing in science could not continue. She looked for ways her science could help the war effort. She supplied portable X-ray machines. Wounded soldiers on battlefields could be treated with them. X-ray stations under her setup numbered more than two hundred. She learned how to run X-ray equipment. She taught herself to drive. Driving let her run the machines herself. A timeline lists the marks of her life. In 1867 she was born in Warsaw, Poland, on November 7. In 1883 she graduated from high school. In 1891 she moved to Paris to attend the Sorbonne.

8In 1893 she earned a master's degree in physics. In 1894 she earned a master's degree in math. In 1895 she married Pierre Curie. In 1897 she began her study of Becquerel rays. Daughter Irene was born that year. In 1898 she announced the discovery of polonium. She announced the discovery of radium. In 1903 she earned a doctorate in physics. She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1904 daughter Eve was born. In 1906 Pierre died. She became the Sorbonne's first female professor. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry came to her in 1911. In 1914 she set up portable X-ray machines for World War I. In 1918 World War I ended. She opened the Radium Institute. In 1934 she died on July 4. A photo shows a 1921 trip. Marie Curie stands in the center. Her daughters Irene and Eve traveled with her. The destination was the United States. After World War I, Marie worked without pause. Her aim was the Sorbonne's Radium Institute. Her hope was a top-rank home for research on radioactivity. Her daughter Irene later shared a prize with Irene's husband. The prize was the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The year was 1935. The celebration with them came after Marie's life had ended. Radioactive substances are very dangerous.

9That danger was not known during her life. She died on July 4, 1934. Her age was sixty-six. The illness is one often caused by long years near radioactivity. She was buried next to Pierre. Their remains changed resting places in 1995. The new place was the Panthéon in Paris. France buries its most brilliant citizens there. Burial there for a woman's own achievements began with her. She was the only woman buried there for that reason. Science's view of atoms shifted in a huge way because of her work. Medicine gained new treatments from it. It led to radiocarbon dating. Ancient life forms can be dated by that method. She showed what careful scientific research can do. It can yield amazing breakthroughs. She showed how to stay strong. Difficult obstacles do not have to win. Her own words carry that lesson. She said life is hard for every one of us. She asked people not to be stopped by that hardness. She said perseverance is necessary. She said confidence in ourselves matters above everything else. She said we must believe we are gifted for some purpose. She said that purpose has to be attained. A researcher in one photo uses carbon dating. The goal is the age of scrolls. An ancient Roman library is where the scrolls were found.

10The technique was made possible by Marie Curie's discoveries. Nominated means put forward as a candidate. The opening may be a job. It may be an award. It may be a position. Atoms are the smallest parts of elements. Perseverance means staying determined and committed. Challenge or delay does not end that commitment. Breakthroughs are important advances in knowledge. They can also be important events. A commission is a task somebody asks for. It can also be a project somebody authorizes. Physics studies matter in a scientific way. It studies motion. It studies energy. The top degree a university can give is a doctorate. It is a Ph.D. Radioactive describes something that produces radiation. Radiation is a dangerous type of energy. An element cannot be split into any simpler substance. Only one kind of atom makes it up. The Sorbonne is a university in Paris, France. It is famous for high academic standards. X-rays are invisible energy. They can pass through many solid substances. A Nobel Prize is one of six prizes given each year. One field is chemistry. One field is economics. One field is literature. One field is medicine. One field is physics. A prize also goes to work that advances world peace.

1Six parts shape this book. Humble beginnings come first. Camp Shriver comes next. Then come the Special Olympics Games, Coach Pat, and an oath. A community champion closes the story. 56. Mustangs Running Free

1A government agency handles most of the West's wild horses. That agency is the Bureau of Land Management. It also cares for the wild lands where most of those horses live. In 2020, about 95,000 wild horses and burros roamed public lands. Burros are wild donkeys. That total is more than triple the number the lands can support. A 2020 count from the same agency lists wild horses by state. Montana had 170. Oregon had 6,162. Idaho had 664. Wyoming had 8,706. Nevada had 46,974. Utah had 5,316. Colorado had 2,116. California had 8,702. Arizona had 558. New Mexico had 200. The map of these western lands labels Washington and the Pacific Ocean. Immense herds once raced over those wide lands. The setting was the American West. There may have been millions of horses, enough that early maps simply labeled the region Wild Horses.

2Thousands still run free. Herds are how they travel the West. People are usually far away. People call these wild horses mustangs. Wild horses had a home in North America between two million and four million years ago. A land bridge then joined North America to Eurasia. Eurasia included the lands now called Asia and Europe. The familiar story says the horses crossed that bridge into Eurasia. The same story says North America lost its horses later, during the last Ice Age. The bridge is the Bering Land Bridge, also called Beringia. In parts of Wyoming, wild horses still run much as they did ages ago. Spanish colonizers returned horses to North America in the 1500s, millions of years afterward.

3Native peoples tell a different history in their oral traditions. Those traditions say the horses never left North America. Scientists have found some evidence that fits these traditions. Artwork is one kind of evidence. The pictures show horses and were made after the Ice Age but before the 1500s. Scientists are now testing DNA from living wild horses. The comparison uses DNA from horses of the Ice Age. It also uses DNA from horses of later times. If horses had remained in North America the whole time, the Spanish still added more. Some of the new horses were left behind. Others ran away. Life as wild animals was something horses learned again on the American plains. Some of those horses were tamed by Native peoples who lived on the plains.

4Cowboys used horses to drive cattle over the land. White settlers moved west into country where Native peoples had long lived. Those settlers used horses while they built homes. Once more, many tame horses escaped. When people had no more need for them, other horses were left behind. These animals joined the wild herds. Taming a wild horse is the act shown in a painting of an Osage Nation member. In Montana, a wild stallion gets ready to charge. A stallion that steps into another stallion's territory is often met with a charge. Wild horses live in herds, also called bands. Each herd has a leader. That leader is an adult male called a stallion. He is the mate of several females, called mares, and the mares remain with the herd.

5A wild pinto foal grazes beside its mother. In Spanish, pinto means spotted. The word names the white pattern on the coats of both horses. Young horses are called foals. After a few years, the foals leave and join another herd. Young males play together, and that play teaches them how to become stallions. Those stallions can then start herds of their own. Young females leave as well. They become mates of the new stallions. Grass is the main food of wild horses. At times they also browse for leaves. One mare guides the herd to food, to water, and to shelter. The stallion comes behind her and watches for danger. The herd stays together to raise its young and to help the group. Wild horses also have homes on islands.

6Those islands lie off the eastern coast of the United States. Two herds live at opposite ends of Assateague Island. That island lies off Maryland and Virginia. Ocean life is hard. These horses eat tough plants from the marsh. They also know how to live through stormy weather. People in the West once depended on tame horses. As settlers built more homes, towns and cities grew. Some people, by the early 1900s, had started calling wild horses pests. People killed wild horses so cows and sheep could have more grass. Other wild horses were sold to be used as meat. In 1971, a law made it illegal for people to harm wild horses. This law is known by the name Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act. Burros are wild donkeys.

7A 1976 photograph shows Velma Johnston standing with a mustang. Thousands of children were asked by her to write letters. The letters urged a change in the law about wild horses. The count of wild horses running free has become twice as large in the United States since the law passed. Thousands now roam freely in ten western states. Many Native peoples of North America give wild horses an important place in their cultures. Sanctuaries give horses safety and land where they can roam. Native people run many of these places. Other people who want to protect the animals run them too. A 2019 photograph shows a rescued wild mustang. Night Hawk Flying is the person with that horse. The place is Stoney Brook Farm in Connecticut. In Colorado, a helicopter drives horses toward a fence.

8Using helicopters for roundups is a question experts still do not settle the same way. U.S. law protects wild horses, yet a herd can grow too fast. Hundreds of horses are caught every year, at least for now. They are then removed from wild land. People who will give care adopt some of the horses. Horses that are not adopted at once may wait in fenced corrals. Others move to sanctuaries, where wide land is still open to them. A map shows the sanctuary. Its name is Black Hills Wild Horse Sanctuary. North Dakota, Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Nebraska lie nearby. Dayton Hyde, a rancher from Oregon, bought land in 1988. The land was near Hot Springs, South Dakota. He then persuaded the Bureau of Land Management to send him horses that nobody would adopt.

9That federal agency is in charge of wild horses. Adoption was not a fit, he said, for animals that were too old. The same was true of animals he called too ugly or too independent. He gave them a wide new home in the Black Hills. Other sanctuaries around the country protect wild horses as well. Many offer tours, and the ticket money helps pay for the horses' care. Every four years, a wild herd can grow to twice its size. A special shot from scientists limits how many foals a wild mare will have. The shot may hold herd numbers down, so fewer horses have to be taken from the wild. One picture shows mares back on their Wyoming range after receiving that shot.

10Some people call wild horses invasive pests. Others want at least some of them to run free forever. Their home can still fill with the thunder of beautiful herds. That home is the American West, at least for now. A herd is a group of large land animals, especially animals with hooves. In western North America, the small wild horses are called mustangs. A pest is an insect or another animal that harms people. A plain is a broad stretch of land that is flat or rolling. Trees are usually scarce there. Another name for this land is prairie. A sanctuary is a safe place. Tamed is the word for an animal brought under people's control. It also fits an animal made less wild.

57. Nelson Mandela's Long Road

1A map of this life marks Zimbabwe, Botswana, Mozambique, and Namibia. It marks Johannesburg, Swaziland, and Lesotho. It marks South Africa and the childhood home at Qunu. The Indian Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean appear on it. Fort Hare and Robben Island appear too. Europe lies far north of these lands. Hard ground on Robben Island was where Nelson Mandela sat. A pile of rocks waited in front of him. A guard gave him a hammer. The guard ordered him to smash the rocks into gravel. Rows of other prisoners sat nearby. Speaking to one another was not allowed. Mandela was forty-four years old. A court had sentenced him to life in prison. South Africa's coast has a small island called Robben Island. All day, the prisoners broke rocks. Their food was bad. Their cells were tiny. The guards treated them poorly. Without newspapers or radios, prison life was sealed off from the wider world. His children were on his mind, and so was his wife, Evelyn. Every six months the prison allowed him one short letter. Guards opened the letter and censored it. A visitor could come only once in each six-month stretch. The visitor had to talk to him through a glass window. Sitting in the dirty yard, he longed for the open fields of childhood. He longed for the freedom of those years. How had this prison become his life? Nelson Mandela was born in 1918. The country then was very different from South Africa today. Centuries earlier, the Dutch and the British had colonized the land. Control was forced on millions of Black South Africans. Diamond mines and gold mines made the country rich. Those riches were not shared with everyone. White people, a small minority, laid claim to 90 percent of the land.

2Chief Henry, Nelson's father, belonged to a royal family among the Thembu people. You say Thembu as TEM-boo. Chief Henry had helped advise the Thembu rulers. A local British official grew angry at him. The official took away his title and his money while Nelson was still a baby. A village near his mother's family was home for Nelson and Nosekeni Fanny. Three other wives kept houses where his father often stayed. At birth the boy was named Rolihlahla. In the Thembu language that name means one who shakes the tree. Tree shaker means a person who causes trouble or sudden change. Picture someone shaking an apple tree so all the fruit tumbles down at once. At age seven, Rolihlahla started school. His teacher gave him the British name Nelson. Many people now know him as Nelson Mandela. Play with other boys made Nelson happy. Herding sheep and cattle made him happy. School made him happy too. Then his father died. Nelson was nine, and the free-roaming life ended. His mother woke him early one morning. She told him to pack all he owned into a bag. They set off on a long walk down dusty roads. The family's round hut, made of mud, was behind him, and he turned to look. He feared that home was gone for good. Late that evening they reached the home of Chief Jongintaba. He was the leader of the Thembu people. Nelson had never seen a place like the Great Place. Grand houses stood there. Large herds of cattle stood there too. Friendship tied Chief Henry to Chief Jongintaba. Raising Nelson was the chief's wish. His mother agreed and left the boy there.

3Nelson was lucky to live at the Great Place. He made friends with the chief's son, Justice, and went to school with him. They sat in meetings and listened. Arguments among the people were settled by Chief Jongintaba. Nelson watched the chief hear both sides before he chose. Nelson heard stories of the people who came before him. He learned the ways of his own people. He came to believe he could be a leader. Strong schoolwork earned Nelson a place at Fort Hare. Chief Jongintaba sent him there. There he found his first real trouble. Poor food at the college set off a student protest. Nelson quit the student council to show he stood with the protest. The head of the college offered a choice. Nelson could rejoin the council and show support for the college. Or he could be sent away. Nelson would not give in. He was sent home. By 1935 his world had changed fast. Johannesburg, South Africa's biggest city, replaced village life for him within a few years. Chief Jongintaba grew angry and decided both young men should marry. Justice and Nelson were shocked. They did not want the girls the chief had picked. Money for the escape came from selling one prize ox that belonged to the chief. Then they ran away to Johannesburg. Justice became a mine clerk. Nelson became a security guard. Soon the chief located the pair. He ordered both of them back. Justice went back. The big city is where Nelson chose to remain, on his own. He made friends and moved into a tiny room. He finished his college degree by mail. A new friend found him work at a law office. Clerk work at that office ran alongside his study for a law degree.

4That friend also brought him into the African National Congress, the ANC. Equal rights for Black people were the ANC's cause. Soon Nelson joined his first protest march. The march tried to stop a rise in bus fares for poor workers. People boycotted the buses and refused to ride. After only nine days, the fares went down. The success excited Nelson. The year 1944 saw him help start the ANC Youth League, called the ANCYL, inside the ANC. The youth league wanted bigger protests and bigger boycotts. A few years later, the reasons to protest would be greater than ever. Voting in South Africa was closed to everyone who was not white. The 1948 vote made D. F. Malan president. He led the Afrikaner National Party. That party believed in apartheid. You say apartheid as uh-PARtide. Apartheid gives more rights to white settlers. It limits the rights of people who are not white. Malan supported this policy. In Afrikaans, apartheid means apart-ness. Descendants of the first Dutch settlers speak a language called Afrikaans. In the Johannesburg of the 1950s, signs in English and Afrikaans kept whites away from other races. Those signs stayed for decades after. Whites, called Europeans on the signs, were labeled ladies and gentlemen. Other races did not receive those titles. A 1946 count of ethnic groups in South Africa lists four groups. Black people numbered 7,832,000, or 68.6 percent. White people numbered 2,373,000, or 20.8 percent. Coloured people, a name for mixed race, numbered 928,000, or 8.1 percent. Indian or Asian people numbered 285,000, or 2.5 percent. When apartheid took effect, white people were only one-fifth of the population. Black people were two-thirds of it. Fewer rights fell to Black people than to any other group.

5Every Black man had to carry a pass in order to travel. Training for better jobs was closed to Black people. Every person received a race label: Black, white, Coloured, or Indian. Marriage across race lines was forbidden. Living areas were split so each race stayed in its own. Labels often came from a person's looks. Lighter skin could put members of one family into different groups. Split families could not share a home. Parks and other public places were segregated, so split families could not meet there. Mandela was married by then and had children to care for. The law office kept him at work for long hours. As life grew worse, he fought harder for justice. In 1951 he became president of the ANCYL. Part of a train car labeled For Europeans Only was taken over by Black protesters. They shouted the slogan Africa. Thirty-four of them were later arrested. A year later, the African National Congress told people to ignore the apartheid laws. Black people burned their travel passes. They sat in Whites Only sections of buses. Whites Only fountains were used for drinking. Whites Only parks were used for play. Thousands of protesters heard Mandela speak. Arrest followed. The law then banned him from travel, speeches, and public office. He kept working for the ANC in secret. He helped open South Africa's first Black law office. The office served people hurt by apartheid. Another arrest came in 1955. The charge was treason, a name for trying to bring down the government. He left jail for a time, but the bans on speech and travel stayed. His wife was unhappy with the risks and the dangers.

6She divorced him. The trial lasted four and a half years. Through it, Mandela kept up his secret work with the ANC, while conditions grew worse. Police opened fire at a 1960 protest. The protesters were peaceful. Sixty-nine of them died. The ANC was then outlawed. A picture shows a woman weeping after she viewed her husband's body. He was one of those sixty-nine people shot by police. Soon the trial ended, and Mandela was found not guilty of treason. He knew another arrest would come unless he quit the fight for equal rights. He would not quit, so he went into hiding. He felt the long years of peaceful protest had failed. He believed the ANC had to try a new path. In 1962 he left South Africa and asked leaders in other countries for help. Some gave money for the fight. Others offered training for war. For the first time he learned to shoot a gun and to make a bomb. A picture shows him in London during that time away in 1962. People often set Nelson Mandela beside Martin Luther King. King led the civil rights movement in the United States. Both men fought so their people could have equal rights. King watched his country move forward. Mandela watched South Africa move the other way, as rights for nonwhites kept disappearing. King did not turn to violence. Mandela at last decided violence was needed to force change. He described the choice this way. At first his group broke the law without using violence. Officials then made that peaceful form illegal. The government used a show of force to crush people who opposed its policies. Only after that did his group decide to answer with violence.

7In the end Mandela saw the South Africa he had dreamed of, a land without apartheid, united and at peace. A year later he slipped back into the country. A new ANC branch took the name Spear of the Nation. People shortened it to MK. The MK wanted the people in power to listen. The plan was sabotage, such as bombs at buildings or at power stations. People died because of those bombings. Mandela laid his plans at a secret MK hideout. He traveled in disguise. Fame came to him as the Black Pimpernel, a Robin Hood sort of figure who slipped past traps set to catch him. In 1962 he was caught and sent to prison. Police then found the hideout and the plans. Conspiracy to bring down the government was the new charge. Death was a possible punishment. The verdict came quickly, and it was guilty. Mandela would rather die than give up the fight for justice. He wrote the words he might say last, in case he was hanged. The judge chose prison for life instead. Those words said he had given his life to the struggle of the African people. They said he had fought white domination and had fought Black domination too. They said he held dear the dream of a democratic, free society. Harmony would mark that society, and every person would have an equal chance. He hoped to live for that dream and to reach it. If he must, he was ready to die for it. A 1964 picture shows him waiting after the guilty verdict. He did not yet know if the end would be life or death. The first years in prison were hard for Mandela. Prisoners were forbidden to speak to one another, yet they found secret ways.

8Notes hid under rocks. Other notes were taped under toilet seats. Mandela demanded rights for the prisoners. He demanded that every race be treated with dignity. In time the guards respected him. Food improved. Books arrived so the men could study. Talk became freer. Mandela grew into a leader among prisoners of many races. He used the listening skills learned in childhood, so each man felt his own side was understood. Many Black people believed South Africa should belong only to Black people, because they had been there first. Mandela once believed that too. He later saw that a truly free country should welcome every race. Family and friends made sure the men on Robben Island were not forgotten. They led protests and boycotts. They worked beyond the country's borders so Mandela's name spread everywhere. The government grew still more violent. Protesters were murdered, or they simply disappeared. Children were attacked for protesting school rules. Those rules forced the Afrikaans language on them instead of their own language. Other countries boycotted South Africa by refusing to trade. The 1980s brought a worldwide demand for apartheid to end. Hoping he would cooperate, the government shifted him to a better mainland prison. Freedom was offered if he would speak against violence and against the MK. He refused unless apartheid itself was cast off. During a 1990 visit by South Africa's president, protesters gathered in front of the White House. In 1989, F. W. de Klerk was elected president. Within months he released Mandela and let the ANC meet. Nelson Mandela was seventy-one. Twenty-seven years passed before he could walk free again. In 1993 he and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize, yet the work was not finished.

9Mandela turned to the job of free elections. A picture shows the two men with gold medals and diplomas from the prize. Great strides toward peace are what this prize recognizes. Another picture shows lines of voters stretching for miles. South Africa's first elections open to every race, in 1994, drew those long lines. The country's first free elections came that same year. Thousands stood in line for as long as five hours so they could vote for the first time. Nelson Mandela was elected president. He did not want hate and fear to fill the country because of the past. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, known as the TRC, was one project he helped start. Someone could confess apartheid-era acts to the TRC. That confession brought no criminal charge. A timeline records 1918, when Nelson Mandela was born. It records 1928, when his father died and Chief Jongintaba became his guardian. It records 1940, when Mandela was suspended from college and went to Johannesburg. It records 1944, when the ANC Youth League was founded. It records 1948, when apartheid became South Africa's official policy. The old laws had hurt many people, and some of them finally heard the hard news. Disappeared friends and relatives were sometimes accounted for at last. Some people thought the TRC process was unfair. Crimes from the apartheid years were not punished, and nobody paid for them. Mandela retired after one term as president. He moved back at last to the village of his childhood. Helping his people did not stop. He met world leaders to push his country forward and to push peace in the world. Children were the focus of a new project, the Nelson Mandela Children's Fund.

10A long illness ended with his death in 2013. He believed in talking with every side, not only one. That belief helped build a country where the law could treat all people as equals. Freedom for all people still has his life as a lasting symbol. The timeline also marks 1956, when he was charged with treason. It marks 1960, when the ANC was banned. The year 1964 marks another treason trial. The sentence was life in prison. It marks 1990, when he left prison. It marks 1994, when he was elected president of South Africa. It marks 1999, when he retired and moved back to where he started. It marks 2013, when he died. Apartheid was an official policy of racial separation in South Africa. It has ended. People who were not white were the ones the policy harmed. A minority is a small group inside a larger population, less than half. Protesting means showing strong disagreement or disapproval. A boycott means staying out of a purchase or a role so that a point is made or a change is forced. Reconciliation is how two or more people, or groups, settle a fight and grow friendly again. To censor is to remove words or other content seen as threatening or offensive. Sabotage is planned destruction, or interference that keeps something from working. To colonize is to set up a place that another country rules or owns. Segregated means kept apart by group differences such as race. A conspiracy is a secret plot by two or more people to do something illegal or harmful. To be sentenced is to receive a formal punishment from a court. Dignity is a worthiness of respect or esteem.

58. Nikola Tesla and Electric Power

1Crowds at Chicago's World's Fair in 1893 were stunned by electrical displays from Tesla and from Westinghouse. One day, a man asked a group of visitors into his laboratory to watch an experiment. The visitors took their seats. The man was Nikola Tesla. He walked calmly onto a wooden stage and sat down in a chair. Beneath the stage sat a powerful electrical generator. Tesla flipped a switch. Wild streaks of light leaped across the room, and some of them hit Tesla. When the display ended, he stepped down unhurt. The crowd burst into applause. One picture shows artificial lightning filling the laboratory. Tesla sits quietly there with a book. Tesla was a scientist, not a magician. He had just proved that a newly found kind of electric current was safe. That current is called alternating current, or AC. The discovery changed the world. In time it would run modern industry and bring light to whole nations.

2His public tests of new technology were often a spectacular sight. Tesla was born in 1856, during a lightning storm, in Eastern Europe. His urge to invent came from his mother. In her spare time she built small machines for the house. He grew up wanting to study electricity. After years of school and work, he found a safe way to produce electricity. The method used alternating current. In 1884, at age twenty-eight, he moved to the United States. Day two in America took him into a New York office. That office belonged to Thomas Edison. The letter in his hand came from a European friend of Edison. The writer told Edison that he knew two great men. Edison was one of them. The young visitor was the other. Thomas Edison was an inventor, and he was a sharp businessman too.

3By then, Edison already carried the name father of the electrical age. His lighting system used lightbulbs. The stations that fed it ran on direct current, called DC. Edison hired Tesla. He offered the young engineer $50,000 for a harder job. Tesla would have to raise the power of the DC system in New York City. Tesla accepted. Edison's first successful lightbulb shone with the light of sixteen candles. Charged particles called electrons are what flow when there is electricity. That flow can take two paths. One path is alternating current, and the other is direct current. Direct current travels one way, in a straight line. Sending it a long distance without losing energy is difficult. Raising or lowering its voltage is not easy either. In alternating current, electrons rush back and forth. They reverse direction sixty times each second. This current can be shifted to a lower or a higher voltage with ease.

4It can also travel long distances without losing much energy. Tesla worked long hours, slept little, and ate little. A few months later, he reported success. Edison still refused to pay the $50,000. He claimed the offer had been only a joke. Tesla was furious. He quit and stormed out of the office. News of his skill spread anyway. Soon a group of businessmen asked him to invent a better lightbulb. The new bulb made those men rich. Almost none of the money reached Tesla. Broke at last, he dug ditches. The work was for the light company Edison owned. The wage was two dollars a day. Luck changed after a meeting with A. K. Brown, who worked at the Western Union Company. Tesla explained his plans for alternating current. Brown was impressed and gave him money to develop the ideas. Tesla's design for an AC power station was made only a few blocks from where Edison worked.

5He also built every part that the station needed. Tesla was born on July 10, 1856, at midnight, while a lightning storm raged. In 1873, at age 17, he caught cholera and nearly died. His father promised an engineering school if the boy recovered. Tesla reached America on June 6, 1884. In March 1885, he founded the Tesla Electric Light Company. In 1891, he built a special coil that made alternating current at high voltage and high frequency. On May 1, 1893, his AC generators lit the Chicago World's Fair. In 1895, he tested radio waves. In 1898, he showed the first robot, a boat steered from a distance. On January 7, 1943, Tesla died at the age of 86. George Westinghouse, a wealthy inventor, believed alternating current was the future. He paid $60,000 for the right to use Tesla's inventions.

6That sum is about $1.4 million in today's money. Tesla also received a share of ownership in the Westinghouse company. He spent the payment quickly on a new laboratory. Together, the two men began carrying electricity to many parts of the United States. Edison grew angry as Westinghouse set AC generators in rural places. The DC system could not reach those places. Westinghouse sold the power at a low price so he could cut into Edison's trade. Edison risked losing a great deal of money. He spoke against Westinghouse and warned people that alternating current was dangerous. Westinghouse soon had a chance to answer that warning. Chicago's World's Fair was the event he was hired to light. The year of that fair was 1893. He asked Tesla to supply the AC generators. On opening day, U.S. President Grover Cleveland pressed a button.

7One hundred thousand lightbulbs blazed on, and the crowd was delighted. People called the fair the City of Light. The display showed that AC power beat DC power. It also showed that AC was less dangerous than Edison had claimed. Years of conflict with Edison had nearly emptied the Westinghouse company of money. Tesla destroyed the signed contract so the company could survive. Over the years that followed, his generous choice cost him millions of dollars. Large AC generators were his designs for Westinghouse. One picture shows machines of that kind. A modern Tesla coil can push electrical power through the air and light a neon tube. After winning the war of the currents, Tesla hunted for a way to push electricity through open air. He wanted to do it with no wires. For that purpose he built a special coil of wire. With the coil he created new kinds of lightbulbs.

8With it he also made the first X-ray photographs. November 1890 was when the coil let him do a thing many people had called impossible. He pushed AC current through open air. A lightbulb then glowed. Soon he turned to experiments with radio waves. Early in 1895, a radio signal of fifty miles was within his reach. West Point, New York, would receive the signal. New York City would send it. An accidental fire then destroyed the laboratory, and years of work vanished. Guglielmo Marconi, an inventor in England, drew on many ideas that belonged to Tesla. The year was 1901. The Atlantic Ocean was crossed by a radio signal that Marconi sent. The feat made him a huge star. Money for a radio company came to Marconi from several people. Tesla's rival, Thomas Edison, was one of them. Credit for inventing the radio went to Marconi, not to Tesla.

9A 1901 photograph shows Marconi surrounded by early radio equipment. Tesla died in 1943 at age eighty-six. Westinghouse paid for the hotel room where Tesla was living. After his death, the U.S. government at last ruled that radio was his invention. It called him the father of radio. He had poured his wealth into one failed project after another. He never received the credit his research and inventions deserved. Even so, his work deeply shaped technology and the modern world. Alternating current powered modern cities. It also transformed life in rural places that had gone without electricity. Wireless tools, X-rays, radar, radio, and robots were all part of his tests. Those tests pointed toward the future. A love of making new things placed him among the giants of modern science. Nothing pleased him more than the thrill of a first success, when an invention worked.

10A coil is made when rope, wire, or something like them is bent into one loop or into several loops. Two or more people can write down a formal deal. If the law can stand behind that deal, it is a contract. Current is the flow of electrical energy. Electricity is energy produced by charged particles in motion. An engineer is a person who plans machines or fixes them. The same work can cover buildings, bridges, and other structures. Experiments are tests carried out for science. Motion goes into a generator, and electricity comes out. A generator is that kind of machine. Inventing is the work of making a thing no one had made before, by creating it, planning it, or building it. When people use what science knows, or use tools, to make a thing or do a job, that use is technology.

59. Nine Innings on the Diamond

1A player for the New York Mets steps across home plate and scores a run. This book follows the big ideas of the sport. One part shows that the game belongs to everybody. Another part shows how people around the world love it. Later pages explain the rules. They look back at earlier times. They visit famous major league parks. They introduce well-known players. They tell why the sport feels timeless. A list of hard words closes the book. George H. Hastings painted a crowd of spectators. The crowd is watching the Boston baseball club. People also called that club the Boston Beaneaters. The scene is their play in the 1880s. A Game Anyone Can Start You need a bat. You need a ball. You need a glove. You need four bases. You need an open field. With those pieces, a game can start. For hundreds of years, people have played other forms of this sport. Colonists in early America played games much like the one known today. Stool ball was one of those games. Town ball was another. Rounders was a third. Many rules in those older games matched each other. Some rules did not match. In 1845, fresh guidelines were written down. The place was New York. The writers were a group called the Knickerbockers. They hoped to change some older rules.

2For the rest, they hoped to set a formal code. A great many of those rules still shape the game played today. Loved in Many Places Today, this sport is still a favorite in North America. Paid players compete on thirty teams. Together those teams are Major League Baseball. People often shorten that name to MLB. Each year the teams hope to win one championship. Fans know that championship as the World Series. Another 240 paid teams play below the MLB clubs. Those clubs make up the minor leagues. Minor league play lets athletes build their skills. The hope is a later jump to the major leagues. Love for the sport reaches far past North America. Play goes on in more than one hundred countries. Millions of fans like to watch it in places all over the world. In a number of countries it counts as a major sport. Canada is one of them. The United States is one of them. Argentina is one of them. South Korea is one of them. Taiwan is one of them. Japan is one of them. The field has many named spots. Center field is part of the outfield. A center fielder covers center field. A left fielder covers left field. A right fielder covers right field. A shortstop works in the infield.

3So does a second baseman. So does a first baseman. So does a third baseman. The pitcher throws from the pitcher's mound. A coach's box sits close to the action. Home plate is the base where a run counts. The on-deck circle is the waiting spot beside it. The catcher plays just behind home plate. Each base sits 90 feet from the next base. That span equals 27 m. Home plate sits 60.5 feet from the pitcher's mound. That span equals 18 m. Nine players take places on the field. Four infield bases together make a diamond. Outfielders are the players spread across right field, center field, and left field. Those players must run quickly. Quick feet help them catch fly balls. Their throws must be accurate. The throw goes to an infielder. An infielder is also called a baseman. A good throw can record an out on the opposing player. How a Game Works People sometimes name the field a diamond. The name comes from the field's shape. A pitcher's mound is one part of the field. Four bases are another part. An infield is another part. An outfield is another part. A full game holds nine innings. An inning is one basic unit of play. Two halves make up each inning. Players call the opening half the top.

4That label means the top of the inning. Players call the later half the bottom. Two teams take part in every game. Each of those teams uses nine players. One team stays out in the field. The other team sends hitters up one by one. Each hitter strikes the ball with a bat. Hitting continues until three batters are out. The club in the field has to make those three outs. Fielding the ball calls for great speed. It also calls for strong concentration. The ball may be up in the air. The ball may zoom along the ground. A runner might choose to take a risk. That choice is to steal a base. The runner goes while the pitcher stays busy. At that moment the pitcher is throwing to a batter. One youth game shows a player stealing second. Visitors hit before the home club. Their turn is the top of an inning. The home club hits in the bottom half. After a hit, the batter heads toward first base. A ball that gets to the outfield can send the runner onward. Second base may be the next try. Third base may be the try after that. Home plate may be the last try. Fielders rush to reach the ball. They may tag the runner.

5They may tag the base instead. The tag has to happen before the runner arrives. That tag counts as an out. Reaching home plate gives the team a run. A ball hit past the outfield fence can count as a home run. A ball hit past the wall can count as a home run too. The landing spot must be fair territory. The batter then circles every base. A step on home plate finishes the score. At the end, the side with the higher run total is the winner. Years When the Game Changed Long ago, major leagues would not let African Americans play next to white players. African Americans had no league of their own then. Their games were on small black teams. A different future was the aim of Rube Foster. He had been a pitcher on a black team. The league he founded was the Negro National League. Later years brought still more Negro Leagues. Talented athletes filled those leagues. In time, major league clubs that were white asked Negro League players to come aboard. Interest in the Negro Leagues then dropped among fans. Slowly, those leagues faded. Hundreds of teams played in the Negro Leagues at some point. The span ran between the 1880s and the 1950s. The total is only an estimate.

6Millions of men left the United States to fight in 1943. That war was World War II. Baseball players were part of the group that left. While the war went on, very little professional baseball was played. Philip Wrigley was owner of a major league team. He chose to organize a women's league. Its full name was All-American Girls Professional Baseball League. The short name is AAGPBL. Thousands of people came to watch the women. The players numbered more than six hundred. Fifteen women's teams carried those players. Their seasons fell in the 1940s. Their seasons also fell in the 1950s. Major league men started coming home once the war ended. The pull of the women's games began to fade. One final AAGPBL season took place in 1954. Young women today play in programs run by Little League. High school teams include them. College teams include them too. Some people expect the major leagues to open to them. In that view, the wait is only a matter of time. Parks That Hold the Crowds The East Coast was the center of baseball in North America for a long stretch of years. The Brooklyn Dodgers used Ebbets Field as their home. That stay lasted from 1913 until 1957. Growing popularity brought more fans than Ebbets Field could seat. A move came in 1957.

7The Dodgers took a larger park. Los Angeles was the city of that park. The New York Giants changed cities in 1957 too. Their new city was San Francisco. The sport kept spreading across the country. Bigger parks went up to match the larger crowds. Boston is the city of Fenway Park. It opened during 1912. No major league park in the United States is older than Fenway. The Boston Red Sox still play there. Its seats hold a crowd of 37,673. Wrigley Field belongs to Chicago. Only Fenway is older among stadiums in America. Work on Wrigley ended in 1914. Home games there belong to the Chicago Cubs. Plenty of fans treat Wrigley as a baseball treasure. Nine decades of rich history sit inside that park. Walls there wear a coat of ivy. Fly balls into the outfield meet those walls. The ivy seems to gobble the balls up. The seat count is 41,072. Devoted fans fill those seats. Some parks use a roof that can pull back. Pictures show the SkyDome with the roof open. Pictures also show that roof closed. Wowser! A roof of this sort helps in places where weather might delay play. It helps where weather might cancel play too. Toronto, Canada, is the home of the SkyDome. It was the earliest park built with a roof like that.

8Cold days were one reason for the roof. Snowy days were another reason. The goal was to keep the game going. Phoenix, Arizona, has a park called Chase Field. Air conditioning in that park pushes back the desert heat. Names Fans Still Say Most people place Babe Ruth at the top of baseball history. Some even call him the best player the sport has ever seen. His club was the New York Yankees. With that club he helped capture four titles. Each of those titles was a World Series win. Across twenty-two seasons, he broke every home run record. Attendance records fell to him as well. No earlier pro season had drawn crowds of that size. Jackie Robinson played a smart game. He was a fearless competitor. His skills with a bat and a glove were remarkable. He was an African American. His earlier clubs were in the Negro Leagues. The Brooklyn Dodgers had a general manager. That manager was Branch Rickey. Rickey convinced Jackie to enter a major league team. Until then, that level of the sport had been all white. Jackie was the first player to take that step. The date was April 15, 1947. On that day he appeared in a Dodgers game. The majors had never included an African American player before him.

9The country came to see him as a hero. Another great was Roberto Clemente. His birthplace was Puerto Rico. He was raised in Puerto Rico as well. From 1955 through 1972 he wore the uniform of the Pittsburgh Pirates. The 1971 World Series lasted until Game 7. A home run by Roberto in that game took the championship. The winning club was the Pirates. Death came later in a plane crash. Roberto was traveling to lend help. An earthquake had hurt people. Those people lived in Nicaragua. Derek Jeter stands as a hero of the modern game. He once played shortstop. His club was the Yankees. He ranked as a leader for hits. He ranked as a leader for runs. Those totals were in the American League. Five times he was a World Series champion. October 2014 was the month he retired. He spoke about what matters most to him. He hopes to be remembered as a Yankee. Little League gives young players a way to practice skills. It is also a way to make friends. It is a way to learn about teamwork. A Season That Keeps Returning A long winter comes to an end. Spring arrives. Warm weather comes with that season. That is the moment the baseball season begins.

10Each return to the season can carry fans into old memories. Some memories are of childhood. Some are of players they once rooted for. Some are of players they loved. For many fans, the sport is a wonderful pastime. Life is the picture some people use for the sport. Each person has a position that must be played. Every player must work with the others. Success comes only when they do. Words to Know A competitor is a rival you face in a game. The rival might be one person. The rival might be a whole team. Fielding means being out on the field while the game is played. The infield is one section of the field. Home plate sits in that section. Three bases sit in it too. A league is a group of sports teams. The teams in it play one another. Minor means less important than something else. It can mean secondary. It can mean not serious. The outfield is the section past the infield. Foul lines mark its sides. A pastime is a hobby. It can be some other activity as well. Professional means pay is earned for the activity. Pleasure is not the only reason for doing it. Titles are championships a player or team has won. Titles can also be other awards.

60. One Long Walk on the Eastern Ridges

1I hiked through many kinds of land. Some parts were steep mountains. One part was the rolling fields of Pennsylvania. I am Ben. In 2015, my job as a therapist overwhelmed me. An extra-long rest was what I needed. I chose to follow a dream from childhood. The dream was to hike the whole Appalachian Trail. People also call this path the AT. Nearly a hundred years have passed since the AT began. It links the Appalachian Mountains in the eastern United States. It follows their highest ridgelines. Workers finished the trail in 1937. It then became the world's longest footpath meant only for hiking. It still holds that title. The AT starts on Springer Mountain in Georgia. It goes north for over 2,000 miles (3,000 km). It ends on Mount Katahdin in Maine. The path goes through fourteen states in the United States. The ground includes farmland. The path runs beside rivers. The path travels above the trees. The path even goes through backyards. A footpath is a narrow trail made for people on foot. My walk crossed steep slopes and gentle fields. Pennsylvania's rolling fields were one of those lands. The long break from my therapist work made the dream possible. The highest ridges carry the path through the eastern mountains. From Georgia to Maine, the trail stays a hiking path. No other hiking-only footpath was longer when the AT was finished. None is longer now. A canoe is required for the crossing at the Kennebec River.

2That river crossing is in Maine. Mount Katahdin stands in Maine. Canada lies beyond the northern end. The path also crosses Vermont. Mahoosuc Notch is in southern Maine. It has jumbled boulders. The boulders are slippery. No other mile on the trail was harder than that notch. The path crosses New Hampshire. The path crosses New York. The path crosses Massachusetts. The path crosses Connecticut. The path crosses Pennsylvania. The rocky part in Pennsylvania hurt to hike. The path crosses New Jersey. My sneakers wore out just before New Jersey. A fresh pair replaced the worn shoes before New Jersey. The path crosses Maryland. The path crosses Virginia. The path crosses West Virginia. I did not forget to brush my teeth. I brushed them even while I was on the move. The path crosses Tennessee. The path crosses North Carolina. I stood at Springer Mountain in Georgia on April 4, 2016. Thru-hiking is the name for finishing a long trail inside one year. Thousands of people try an AT thru-hike each year. Only a few hundred finish. I was one of the people who finished. Most thru-hikers start in spring. Most of them hike north. I did the same. Spring is already warm in the south. Springer Mountain is mile zero of the AT. I took my first step there on April 4, 2016. Those following days ranked among my hardest. My body had to get used to the daily work.

3My mind had to get used to it too. The trail is 2,190 miles (3,524 km) long. A thru-hike takes about five million steps. The highest point is Clingman's Dome. Clingman's Dome is on the border of North Carolina and Tennessee. It stands 6,643 feet (2,025 m) above sea level. The total climb up and down matches a huge task. A sea-level start up Mount Everest, then back down, matches that total of ups and downs. A hiker would do that climb sixteen times. The first thru-hiker was Earl V. Shaffer. He is also the oldest thru-hiker in this record. He first finished in 1948. He was thirty years old then. He finished again in 1998. He was eighty years old then. The fastest AT thru-hike took 45 days, 22 hours, and 38 minutes. The United States holds this long path from Georgia to Maine. I spent several months getting ready in a serious way. I walked wherever I could. I wore my heavy pack on those walks. I often walked in poor weather. An outdoor store gave me a job. Hiking supplies were what I hoped to understand better. I tried to save money. The Brooklyn Bridge was where I did one practice hike. My backpack was full of supplies on that hike. Inside my apartment, I rehearsed putting up my tent. I packed a sanitary kit. I packed a toothbrush and toothpaste.

4I packed a towel. I packed a hat. I packed gloves. I packed a bandanna. I packed underwear. I packed long underwear. I packed a T-shirt. I packed shorts. I packed pants. I packed a long-sleeved shirt. I packed a balaclava. I packed hiking sneakers. I packed camp shoes. I packed camp socks. I packed sock liners. I packed wool socks. I packed gaiters. I packed a headlamp. I packed a smartphone. I packed headphones. I packed a GPS tracker. I packed backup batteries. I packed a backpack. I packed a tent. I packed trekking poles. I packed a sleeping bag. I packed a sleeping pad. I packed a sitting pad. I packed a down jacket. I packed a rain jacket. I packed a poncho. I packed a rain skirt. I packed a pack cover. I packed waterproof bags. I packed a food bag that was also a bear bag. I packed rope. I packed a camping stove. I packed fuel. I packed a lighter. I packed water bottles. I packed a water filter. I packed purification tablets. I packed a first aid kit. I packed a repair kit. I packed a mini pocketknife. I packed earplugs. My average pack weight was 21 pounds (9.5 kg). That weight included food for a day. It included some stove fuel. It included a liter of water. All the gear cost nearly $2,500. Months of practice made the heavy pack familiar. The store job taught me about the supplies I would carry.

5Saving money was part of getting ready. The Brooklyn Bridge walk was one practice with a full pack. Setting up the tent at home was another practice. On the AT, no spot is photographed more than McAfee's Knob in Virginia. The trail community had interested me since I was a kid. Picture a whole community on the move. People in it travel at different speeds. They spread along 2,190 miles (3,524 km) of trail. The trail is one continuous path. It is only a few feet wide. People of all ages choose this hike. People of many cultures choose it. People of many abilities choose it. Healing after a tragedy is why many people take this hike. Some people I met were families walking the entire trail as a group. Every person I met was on the AT for a reason. Some thru-hikers walked with a group. Most of my miles were walked without a partner, by my own choice. I liked meeting new people. I liked keeping my own schedule. When I felt lonely, I looked for friends among other hikers. The hardest part was hiking every single day. On a usual day, I woke with the Sun. Walking stopped once the day's distance goal was met. I arrived at camp a little earlier than sunset. Most thru-hikers eat food that costs little. I did too. The food is light to carry. The food is easy to prepare.

6The food will not spoil. Weather decided how far I could walk on a given day. My miles also depended on the ground. My own goals changed the miles too. How tired I felt changed the miles too. I tried to stay at camps with a lean-to shelter. I looked for a water source at camp. I looked for an outhouse at camp. My small tent was the shelter when that kind of camp was missing. Shelters were usually small. One small shelter was in Pennsylvania. Shelters were also crowded. One crowded shelter was in the Smoky Mountains. A small shelter with a roof that slopes is called a lean-to. Rocks, posts, or trees hold that roof up. The moving community stays strung along a path only a few feet wide. I could find company when the days felt lonely. Sunset was my usual time to stop at camp. A free spot inside a shelter was not always there for me. Then I set up my tent. One night, I slept in a forest in Vermont. A nearby town was my stop after every few days. In town I filled my food supply again. I took a shower. I did my laundry. I learned that real rest mattered as much as hiking. Filling my supplies again mattered just as much. On rainy days I planned around the shelter. I needed to arrive in time to get a spot.

7Shelters can fill up fast in bad weather. Sometimes rain fell without a stop for several days. Full dryness had to wait until a town. My hike took about six months. In that time I covered about 365 miles (587 km) each month. Safety was the most important concern. I met black bears on the trail. I met venomous snakes. I met ticks that can carry disease. Knowing what to do around these animals is critical. I tried to stay calm. I tried to act with respect. I tried to keep a safe distance. I filtered all my water. I was careful about staying clean so I would not get sick. I stayed dry to prevent a dangerous drop in body heat. I stayed warm for the same reason. The right shoes helped me avoid injuries. Paying attention to my limits also kept injuries away. I kept my gear in good order. Then I was ready if an emergency came. Staying in touch with people I love mattered to me. Hikers hang anything that smells like food on bear poles. This keeps bears away from camp. High heat dried up most water sources in New York. So I filtered water from puddles. To filter means to pass a liquid through a device. The device takes out what you do not want. Clean habits are part of staying healthy. A dangerous low body temperature is called hypothermia. The forest in Vermont was one of my tent nights.

8Town days gave me food, a shower, and clean clothes. Happiness filled most of my days on the hike. Even so, hiking was not always fun. I was often hungry. I was often exhausted. I was often sore. Sometimes I was even bored. The best help was the people around me. I leaned on them for support. The end of the hike was hard. The beginning had been hard too. Fall was fully here. Nights were getting cold. Never before had I felt hunger like that. Northern New England's mountains gave me the hardest climbs. Southern Maine slowed me to half my usual speed. I was crossing rocky ranges there. After nearly six months, I reached the top of Mount Katahdin. The date was October 1, 2016. Those last days were not like my first days. I felt like a different person from the one who started. I had never felt so strong. I had never felt so confident. I had never felt so accomplished. Sports were rare for me in childhood. Athlete was a word I could use for myself for the first time. I had hiked more than 2,000 miles (3,000 km). I was skinnier than when I began. I was dirtier than when I began. People asked about my favorite memories after I finished. My dearest memories were hard moments that became beautiful. At first the challenge had seemed impossible to overcome.

9One night I camped alone on a mountaintop. The top had no trees. Strong winds hit my tent. Heavy rain hit it too. The tent fell down. I became frustrated. I became afraid. At 3:00 a.m. I gave up on sleep. I packed my things. I ate breakfast. I started hiking. The sunrise that followed was the most amazing one I had ever seen. I was all alone on a mountaintop. A challenge that seemed impossible became something incredible. People ask how I did it. I say I did it the way you do anything. I did it one step at a time. People also ask why I did it. After my hardest night, I saw beautiful views. Those views were in the Roan Highlands in Tennessee. To reach a summit means to reach a mountain's highest point. To traverse means to move across an area. The rocky miles of southern Maine cut my speed in half. Beautiful places from the walk often come back to my mind. Mount Katahdin in Maine is one of them. The reasons I kept going changed. They were not the same reasons I had at the start. Love and support surrounded me on the trail. Love and support also came from home. I never wanted to stop. This book comes several months after my thru-hike ended. Pain from those five million steps is still in my knees. Six months went by far from the people I love.

10You might ask if it was worth it. I followed a dream. I took one step after another. Those steps added up to five million. Nobody can remove that accomplishment from me. Careful preparation took months. Failure always felt close. I faced many dangers. I faced many challenges. I planned. I saved money. Living with very little spare money was a skill I learned. Each thing in my pack became precious to me. My life depended on that gear. The friends I made came from many countries. I grew closer to people who cheered from home. Thru-hiking was still a priceless experience. The challenges did not erase that. Acclimate means becoming used to a situation you did not have before. It can also mean getting used to a new climate. Natural features of the ground are what terrain means. It is the ground you walk on. Thru-hiking means walking a long trail from start to end. The walk fits inside one hiking season. To replenish means to fill something up again. Insurmountable means impossible to overcome. It can also mean impossible to achieve. Looking back, the love around me kept me moving. Six months away did not erase the five million steps. The hurt in my knees is a reminder of that distance. A tight budget was part of making the dream work. Friends on the trail and people at home both mattered. The accomplishment is mine to keep.

61. Opening the Road: Heroes of American Sport

1Contents. Jim Thorpe, Greatest Athlete of His Century (1887-1953) 4. Thorpe Becomes a Pro 6. Mildred Didrikson Zaharias, Called Babe (1911-1956) 7. Any Game at All 8. Jackie Robinson, Baseball's Bold Star (1919-1972) 9. Althea Gibson Leads On (1927-2003) 11. Jesse Owens, Quickest of All (1913-1980) 14. Olympic Glory That Lasts 15. Great Names 15. Glossary 16. Jim Thorpe, Greatest Athlete of His Century (1887-1953). Who was the greatest American athlete of the last century? Basketball fans might name Michael Jordan. Tennis fans might name Billie Jean King. Baseball fans might name Babe Ruth. Those stars set record after record. They revolutionized their sports. Any of them could hold the number one spot. One man was still placed above them. People called him the greatest of the great. That man was Jim Thorpe. Thorpe was a Native person. His nation was the Sac and Fox Nation. Oklahoma was his birthplace. His birth year was 1887. He played professional baseball. He was the top football star of his day. Track and field brought him win after win. College crowds already knew his name.
