That fame came before the 1912 Summer Olympics. He earned All-American honors. He played halfback. His blinding speed thrilled the crowds. His strength thrilled them too. He starred on the school baseball team. He starred on the school basketball team. He played golf. He played tennis. Many other sports filled his time. Do You Know? He was born inside the United States. He was not officially a citizen. Most other Native people of that time lacked citizenship too. A 1924 law finally changed this. The law was the Indian Citizenship Act. A picture shows Jim Thorpe. The Olympics of 1912 put Thorpe on a national team. He represented his country there. That country was the United States. He entered the two hardest tests in track and field. One test was the pentathlon. Five events make a pentathlon. The other test was the decathlon.

2Ten events make a decathlon. He needed only a few days. Four of his pentathlon events ended in victory. His decathlon total set a world record. A gold medal was his in the pentathlon. A gold medal was his in the decathlon. Sweden's king called him forward for the prize. The king was Gustav V. The king said no athlete alive was greater. Do You Know? Those Olympic tests call for many skills. Joined together, they measure all-around ability. The pentathlon starts with the long jump. The javelin comes after that. The discus comes after the javelin. The 200-meter run comes next. The 1,500-meter run closes the pentathlon. The decathlon starts with the 100-meter run. The long jump follows that sprint. The high jump follows the long jump. The shot put follows the high jump. The 400-meter run follows the shot put. The 110-meter hurdles follow that run. The discus follows the hurdles. The javelin follows the discus. The pole vault follows the javelin. The 1,500-meter run closes the decathlon. A picture shows Jim Thorpe in the middle of those Games. Thorpe Becomes a Pro. Pro baseball started for him in 1913. His team was the New York Giants. He was good at baseball. Football was the sport he liked more. A football team signed him in 1915. The team was the Canton (Ohio) Bulldogs. He led that team to the 1916 championship. He led that team to the 1917 championship. He led that team to the 1919 championship. Summer months were still for baseball. In 1920 he took the president's chair of a new group. No one had sat in that chair before. The group was the American Football Association. Years later the group gained a new name. The new name was the National Football League. The Football Hall of Fame keeps a statue of Thorpe. It honors the top athlete of the twentieth century. That statue greets people who come to visit.

3Do You Know? His Olympic medals were taken from him. His records were struck down too. The International Olympic Committee did both. People also call that body the IOC. Two summers were the cause. One summer was 1909. The other summer was 1910. He played minor league baseball then. Amateurism rules were broken on a technical point. Other athletes had played in the same way. Those athletes kept their amateur standing. Fake names hid them on the lists. Thorpe told the Olympic Committee he was sorry. The rule had been unknown to him. The committee refused to bend. A late repair came in 1983. The IOC gave his family replacement gold medals. His scores never went back into the official record. Mildred Didrikson Zaharias, Called Babe (1911-1956). Some people rank Thorpe as the top athlete of the twentieth century. Sports lovers can still weigh a second choice. Her nickname was Babe. Her full name was Mildred Didrikson Zaharias. She was an all-around athlete. Three sports showed that power. She dominated women's basketball. She dominated track and field. She dominated golf. Her power covered the 1930s. It covered the 1940s too. It covered the 1950s too. Babe was a serious competitor. Her style was rough-and-tumble. Women then were told to seem modest. Women then were told to seem polite. Texas was the state of her birth. The year of her birth was 1911. High school came after that. Volleyball was one sport on her list. Baseball was on her list too. Tennis was on her list too. Basketball was on her list too. For women, basketball was the favorite sport then. Her high school basketball team never tasted defeat. Thirty points was a sum she often scored alone. A full team total of twenty was already strong. She lifted weights in training. Few women did that kind of training then. Hard workouts showed their worth in July 1932.

4Sharp skills showed their worth then too. The stage was a national track meet. She entered eight events. She won five of them. She took the meet with no team beside her. Every rival side had twenty members. A picture shows Babe shooting free throws. The Summer Olympics came a few weeks later. Gold was hers in the 80-meter hurdles. A world record was hers in that race too. Gold was hers in the javelin. A world record was hers in the javelin too. Gold was hers in the high jump. A world record was hers in the high jump too. Any Game at All. Her real fame had not arrived yet. Golf was the sport that brought it. A club was new in her hands at age twenty-one. Her first championship arrived one year after that. The year of the win was 1935. Eighty-two tournaments fell to her after that start. The span was the next twenty years. Seventeen of the wins stood back to back. One year in that run was 1946. The next year in that run was 1947. Bad health news came in 1953. The illness was cancer. Babe was the one who learned it. Doctors believed she was done with play. An operation came next. Only four months passed. Then the pro tour had her back. Death came the following year. Her family was crushed. Her fans were crushed. Her age was forty-five. A life of sports achievements opened two halls. One hall honors golf. The other hall honors track and field. She blazed that path. Many great female athletes used it. Do You Know? Female athletes had a fierce advocate on their side. Babe filled that role. She stood up for them. She pushed for their rights. Her push for equality skipped some peers. Some of her remarks were racist. People of color were the ones she spoke about. One incident is remembered as infamous.

5She hurled ice water. The water came from a pitcher. Black women were the people she hit. They ran on the Olympic track team. That team carried the United States. No Black women had made that team before them. No one could doubt her prowess in sport. Her character did not equal that prowess. Jackie Robinson, Baseball's Bold Star (1919-1972). Picture Major League Baseball today. Frank Thomas is one of its superstars. Derek Jeter is another. Alex Rodriguez is another. Picture the Hall of Fame. Hank Aaron has a place there. Willie Mays has a place there. Roberto Clemente has a place there. So do many other brilliant Black ballplayers. So do brilliant Latino ballplayers. The scene might have looked very different. Jackie Robinson and his courage changed that. His determination changed it too. The year of the change was 1947. He began to play in Major League Baseball. No Black player had done that before. People of color met unfair walls in many parts of life. In sports, they were discriminated against. The Major Leagues allowed white players only. Black players then built leagues of their own. Branch Rickey led the Brooklyn Dodgers. His post was general manager. He saw a clear wrong in the game. Good players of color were kept off those clubs. He wanted those players added. He knew the work would be hard. Jackie Robinson was the player he found. The time for that find was right. A picture shows Jackie Robinson. With a bat, he matched the best. On the bases, he matched the best. In the field, he matched the best. His daring on the bases stirred the fans. It put opponents on edge. A short bunt could beat the other side. A long blast could beat them too. Character did the most important work. The minor leagues held him for one year first. He then joined the Brooklyn Dodgers. Trouble filled that rookie season.

6Players on other teams shouted insults. Pitchers aimed throws at his body on purpose. Fans booed. Even some teammates treated him badly. Quiet dignity was how he carried himself. Determination stayed with him too. His temper never broke loose. His fists never flew. Solid hits marked his rookie year. He stood first in the league for stolen bases. Rookie of the Year was the prize he took. The National League batting crown came in 1949. Most Valuable Player was his title that year too. By 1950 his pay was the top sum on his club. The club was the Brooklyn Dodgers. He was that team's leader. He made a plain truth clear to all. Skill was the thing that counted. Other clubs soon brought in Black players. Latino players came onto those clubs too. Baseball is the national pastime. In the United States, every race now takes part. Players show this mix. Management shows it across every nationality. Althea Gibson Leads On (1927-2003). Jackie Robinson broke the color barrier. Baseball was the sport he opened. Tennis still kept its door shut. A Black woman forced that door. Her name was Althea Gibson. Her parents worked as sharecroppers. South Carolina was their home. Her birth year was 1927. The family moved when she was three. Harlem was the new home. Harlem is a neighborhood. The city around it is New York City. Althea grew tall as a girl. She grew athletic too. Street games showed her gift. Kids in her neighborhood played them. A citywide win came when she was twelve. The game was paddle tennis. Sport mattered more to her than class. She left school in grade seven. Extra time to play was her reason. Tennis came into her life next. Two young Black doctors noticed her game. Robert Johnson was one doctor. Hubert Eaton was the other. They backed her growth in tennis. They also got her through high school.

7A picture shows Althea Gibson in 1956. She is at the U.S. National Championships. She climbed to the top of one group. The group was the American Tennis Association. Its short name was the ATA. The ATA was an all-Black group. The National Indoor Championships came in 1949. She played in that event. No Black woman had played in it before. A ban struck her in that same year. The closed meet was the U.S. National Championships. Today people call that meet the U.S. Open. Ethnicity was the reason given for the ban. An invite came from the U.S. Open the next year. An invite came from Wimbledon the year after. No Black player had been invited to Wimbledon before. Wimbledon stands in the United Kingdom. Few tennis championships in the world are larger. Off the court, her classes went on. An athletic scholarship covered college. Florida A&M University was the school. Tallahassee was the city of that school. She played tennis for her college. She played basketball for her college. She played golf for her college. A degree was complete in 1953. Physical education was the subject. Her big tennis breakthrough came in 1956. She won a Grand Slam. No Black player had won a Grand Slam before. A Grand Slam is a set of four events. Those events are the leading ones in tennis. One year had to contain every win. A doubles crown came along as well. The doubles event was for women. The place was Wimbledon. Singles glory followed in 1957. Wimbledon was the place again. Queen Elizabeth II handed her the prize. A parade met her when she got home. New York was the city of that parade. She closed the year with one more win. That win was the U.S. Nationals tournament. Another year brought both big titles back to her. She won Wimbledon once more. She won the U.S. Nationals once more. Sports Illustrated put her face on a cover.

8Time magazine put her face on a cover. The Associated Press picked a yearly winner. Female Player of the Year was the name of the honor. She received that honor across two straight years. Tennis ended for Gibson after those wins. Sport itself did not end. The year 1964 took her into golf. She joined the LPGA. The long name of that group is the Ladies Professional Golf Association. No Black member had joined it before her. Golf clubs in many parts of the country set harsh limits. Black golfers could not join those clubs. The courses were closed to them too. A few courses did let Gibson play. The clubhouse was still often closed to her. The bathrooms were often closed to her too. Insults came from the crowds. Death threats came from the crowds too. Gibson would not quit. Some clubs still tried to block her entry. Players in the LPGA took a vote. They dropped any course that left a player out. Every player had to be welcome. The clubs then gave way. Talent pulled her through the wall. Determination pulled her through too. A color barrier fell because of her. It fell in two sports. She paved a road for great Black tennis players. Those players came later. Arthur Ashe was one who followed. Venus Williams was one who followed. Serena Williams was one who followed. A picture shows Althea Gibson. Jesse Owens, Quickest of All (1913-1980). Jesse Owens drew wide notice while still a boy. He was in junior high school. The city was Cleveland. The state was Ohio. A world record in the high jump fell to him. The mark counted only athletes his age. A world record in the long jump fell to him. That mark was for his age too. The high school track coach wanted Jesse. He asked Jesse to join the team. Work waited for Jesse after school.

9The job helped support his family. Afternoon practice was impossible for him. His training hour was 5:00 a.m. He rose at that hour to meet his coach. A national meet for high school track came next. In the 100-yard dash he tied a world record. A new world record in the long jump was his. College brought a championship meet in 1935. A new world record came in the 220-yard dash. A new world record came in the long jump. A new world record came in the 220-yard low hurdles. He matched a world record in the 100-yard dash once more. The clock showed 9.4 seconds. A picture shows Jesse Owens in a race. He runs ahead of every other runner. The race is at the 1936 Olympic Games. Olympic Glory That Lasts. The year 1936 carried Owens to the Summer Olympic Games. Berlin was the host city. Germany was the host country. World War II had not started. The war was very close. Owens was not welcome in that city. Adolf Hitler held power over Germany. He was the leader of the Nazis. Nazis taught that Aryans ranked above every other group. To them, an Aryan was a white person. An Aryan also had to be non-Jewish. Black people received a cruel word from them. That word was primitive. Hitler showed a cold attitude. Threats were in the air around Owens. Owens felt no fear of the attitude. He felt no fear of the threats. Berlin's track is where he proved it. Four gold medals came from those races. No person before him had four in the Olympics. Records list it as a first in Olympic history. He left Germany when the Games ended. Cheers waited on his return. A parade waited too. A title arrived with that welcome. America's Ambassador of Sports was the title. The government granted him the title. More years passed after that honor. The Presidential Medal of Freedom became his.

10Great Names. Pro sports passed through an amazing age. That age was the twentieth century. Hugely talented people filled the playing fields. A small band of athletes still rose above the crowd. Their abilities astonished the world. Their sports were changed for all the years after. Society was changed for the better. They held the top level of play open. Every person with skill could compete there. Memory will keep each of these athletes. People will know them as American sports legends. Word meanings are listed below. Glossary. achievements (n.) page 8 means successes earned by hard effort. dignity (n.) page 10 means a calm worth that merits respect, and honor too. barrier (n.) page 11 means a block in the way of progress. The block may be a rule. It may be an obstacle or a problem. discriminated (v.) page 9 means given unfair treatment. Race can drive that treatment. Age can drive it, and so can sex. Religion or some other difference can drive it too. blazed (v.) page 8 means went first. A mark stayed so later people could follow. dominated (v.) page 7 means rose far past the rest of the field. The edge may be success. The edge may be influence or power. The place may be a sport or a competition. championships (n.) page 6 means contests that settle first place. opponents (n.) page 10 means people lined up against you. You may meet them in a game. You may meet them in a fight or a discussion. competitor (n.) page 7 means a rival across from you. The rival might be one person. The rival might be a whole team. represented (v.) page 5 means acted as the symbol for a group. determination (n.) page 9 means a steady will toward a hard goal. Commitment is part of that will. revolutionized (v.) page 4 means brought enormous changes.

62. Paintings Hidden under the Ground

1A cave map marks the entrance and the Painted Gallery. It marks Lascaux cave. It marks Great Hall of the Bulls. It marks the Chamber of Engravings and the Shaft of the Dead Man. It marks the Lateral Passage and the Main Gallery. France and the Vezere River sit beside Lascaux Cave on the map. The Chamber of Felines is marked. Spain and the Dordogne River are marked. Discovery in the woods is the first part. Exploring the cave comes next. More questions and more exploration follow. Then the book asks about the painters, and about their method. Understanding the art comes last. A word list closes the book. More than 100 prehistoric sites lie by the Dordogne River and the Vezere River. A walk can end with a stumble over a hole that feels mysterious. Did you pause? Did the dark below make you wonder? Four teenage boys lived that moment. Lascaux manor, in southern France, was nearby. Say Lascaux as la-SKO. September of 1940 was warm that day. Marcel Ravidat was among the boys. Say his name RAH-vee-dah. Three friends came along. A dog came along. Woods around Montignac were where they explored.

2Say Montignac as MON-tee-nyack. The hole was found then. Years earlier, lightning had hit a large pine. The tree fell. A wide entrance opened. What waited inside ranks among the most interesting treasures history holds. Can you picture the find waiting for Marcel and his friends? Excitement made the dog bark. Knees hit the ground. Eyes went into the hole. No light meant the space below stayed hidden. Hollow, and thrilling, was still the feeling. A burrow did not match the feeling. A mole tunnel did not match it. A groundhog tunnel did not match it. Excitement was almost too much to hold. A cave, maybe? A tomb buried long ago, maybe? Instincts told them to go on. Exploration would continue. A later return was planned, with light and with shovels. Days later, the hole had the boys again. A lantern came with them. Fast digging made the hole bigger. In they went, one after another. A pile of rocks caught them. Looking around came next. Dim was the light. Minutes passed before eyes grew accustomed to that underground dark. Another entrance showed itself. It was nearly a doorway into shadow farther on.

3Rocks blocked the front of it. Looks passed between them. Nods followed. Shrugs followed. The lantern went higher. A large dark space took them in. Deeper and deeper the boys went, still together. A passage stopped them. It was deep, narrow, and too tight for the whole group. Talk led to a plan. Marcel would go on by himself. The lantern would go with him. The passage would be widened. Then he would come back. Lantern, shovel, and rope were what he carried. Squeezing and digging, he moved ahead. Later the rope went down. A shaft dropped him into a room that was cavernous. The lantern rose. Walls around him came out of the dark. Animal pictures in bas-relief covered those walls. Bas-relief means a carving raised up from the surface it is cut from. Closer he moved. Horses, cows, stags, and bison covered the stone. Each one seemed to dance, to gallop, and to swim. Holding still was almost impossible. Out of the room he hurried. Up he climbed. More pictures showed on the passage walls as he returned to his friends. Largest of the rooms at Lascaux carries the name Great Hall of the Bulls.

4Its walls carry paintings from the Stone Age. Bull paintings are why that hall carries its name. Horses and stags appear more often in the cave. One image is a stag wearing antlers. Another is a horse. Morning brought the news through the whole village. Villagers came down to the cave. More rooms held carvings that were new and exciting. Very, very old was plain to see. Archaeologists arrived before long, ready to study. Scientists of that kind study ancient cultures. Objects people leave behind are their evidence. Careful looking followed. Questions grew the longer they looked. The cave entrance at Lascaux appears in a picture. One painted scene has a title, Scene of the Dead Man. A man is in it. A bison is in it. A bird is in it. A spear is in it. A rhinoceros runs away toward the left. Who made these mysterious paintings? What age were they? Underground caves are an odd place for paint. Why there? Large birds and animals, horses and bulls among them, are almost all the artists painted. Snakes and fish, the small creatures, were ignored.

5Why? Perfect art in so much dark is hard to explain. How? Tiny holes mark the wall about halfway toward a high ceiling. What were they for? Old, clearly, is what the paintings are. The exact age was the puzzle. Dating the pictures was the first job the archaeologists set. Several methods were tried. The paintings themselves were where many scientists began. Dyes, paints, and other color materials were analyzed. Charcoal, if the artists used it, might allow a radiocarbon date. A date can come from carbon, once someone measures the change in it. These pictures, the scientists found, could not be dated that way. A scientist cleans a mammoth tooth before a radiocarbon date. Mammoths show up in the art at Lascaux. Tools in one picture may be like tools the Lascaux artists used. Answers required the scientists to look down. Flint lay on the ground under the pictures. Bone fragments used for carving lay there. Pigments for color lay there. Like fossils, those materials were sealed in ground layers. Long study finally named the find. Stone Age people made the wall pictures. About 17,000 years earlier is when those people lived.

6Back-to-Back Bison hang in the Main Gallery. Three-dimensional art was what the Lascaux artists were trying for. Secrets remained in this cave. Nearby caves held secrets too. Who the artists were was still unknown. Far underground is a strange place to carve and paint. Why go there? By 1940, Stone Age life was already well known to scientists. Hunters is what the men were. Large animals, bison among them, were killed and eaten. Magical powers were believed to sit in their leader. Shaman is the name of that leader. Could a Shaman have carved and painted the Lascaux walls? That mystical leader may have gone under the ground to reach spirits. Those spirits would be people who had lived earlier. A successful hunt may have been the reason for the pictures. Or the hunters may have made the pictures themselves. Luck on the hunt may have been the aim. Footprints in other nearby caves include small ones and large ones. Help from children is one possible meaning. A visit to the Shaman, children with parents, is another. Stags in the Main Gallery look as if they swim across the wall. Sight itself befuddled the scientists.

7Deep in the cave, dark was total. Carried lighting, for Stone Age people, was something nobody believed in. Did Stone Age people arrive first, and painters much later, after fire was known? Accident solved a question that seemed to have no answer. A hollowed piece of sandstone turned up. One side held the hollow. Leftover carbon sat in that circle. Analysis and dating of the carbon found animal fat. The fat burned inside a scooped early lamp, and Stone Age people used it that way. Light in the cave came from it. Light was no longer a mystery. Lamps of animal fat lit the workspace of Stone Age artists. Other questions stayed open. Glorious pictures sit high in the Painted Gallery. Carving and painting up there is hard to explain. Very, very high is the ceiling. Reaching it seems impossible. Holes halfway up the wall may be the clue. A painting shows scaffolding that would let artists reach high places. Artist size was estimated. Distance from the artists to those high pictures was guessed. The deduction followed. A temporary scaffold used the holes. They painted from that scaffold, either climbing it or standing there.

8Shapes in the Main Gallery use red, yellow, and violet. Stone Age artists themselves are the next puzzle. What were they like? Color was made somehow. Tools were used somehow. Thoughts sat behind the work. Clues of many kinds were left on the ground under the masterpieces. Stone walls inside the cave were carved with tools. Can you guess which ones? More than one kind was used. The rock decided the tool. Very soft rock took a stick. A finger could do it too. Very hard rock took a stone tool that had been carved to a point or a round end. That tool cut the rock face. Some rock faces could not be carved at all. Paint was the only choice. Red pigment and black pigment cover most pictures. Minerals and metals from the earth make those pigments. Seventeen thousand years is how long the colors at Lascaux have stayed on the rock. Scientists came to understand why. Why the colors did not fade is a question you can try. The closing gives the answer. Other caves add to the story. France's Dordogne region holds the Cussac cave.

9Engravings there might be older than the ones at Lascaux. Near Vallon-Pont d'Arc, another French cave shows animals gone from that area now. A reader can look at each image and name what lives in it. Meaning is the next question. Do the carvings and paintings tell us what they meant? One message is clear. Drawing has always belonged to men, women, and children. It always will. These caves were not homes for Stone Age people. Down into the earth they went. Pictures there stood for something in their lives. Drawing alone may have been the reason. Nearness to ancestors may have been the reason. Help from a Shaman may have been the reason. Knowing may stay out of reach. Art was still what they made. Only one rhinoceros appears in all the Lascaux art. During the Stone Age, rhinos lived all over France. Here is the answer about the colors. Minerals are what the pigments were made from. Inside the cave, weather stayed away. Rain stayed out. Wind stayed out. Snow stayed out. Sun stayed out. That protection is why the colors held. Paintings from fifty years ago raise a question.

10Can we tell what the artist thought? A painting made today raises the same question. Do we need the answer? Or can a person simply look, and call the picture beautiful? A word list follows. Accustomed means a person grew familiar by use or by practice. Masterpieces are works of art that stand out as exceptional. Methods are orderly, planned ways of doing a job. Analyzed means looked at closely. Bas-relief is sculpture raised a little from a surface, while still attached to it. Mysterious means hard to understand. Mystical means a spiritual or supernatural power past what humans can grasp. Befuddled means confused. Cavernous describes a big empty space underground, dark and deep and hollow. A passage is a route or a channel a person or a vehicle can travel. A discovery is the first time something is found, or uncovered. Radiocarbon is a radioactive form of carbon. A scaffold is a short-term platform that holds workers while they build, repair, or decorate. Exploration is travel through land you do not know, in order to learn. Instincts are strong feelings that come naturally, not from reasoning. Treasures are things with value.

63. Paths Cut Through Rock and Water

1This book names six tunnels. One is the Channel Tunnel in France and the United Kingdom. One is the Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland. One is the Lærdal Tunnel in Norway. One is the Marmaray Tunnel in Turkey. One is the Seikan Tunnel in Japan. One is the Stad Ship Tunnel in Norway. A world map around them shows the Arctic Ocean. It shows the Atlantic Ocean. It shows the Pacific Ocean. It shows the Indian Ocean. It shows Asia, Europe, Africa, and Australia. Water runs through Hezekiah's Tunnel under the ground. It is in Jerusalem. The likely date is the eighth century bce. For much of history, travelers met obstacles. Mountains were one kind of obstacle. They had a choice. They could go around. They could go over. Both choices were difficult. Then someone decided to go through. Today, tunnels allow safe passage through hills. They allow speedy passage through mountains. They also let people pass under cities. They let goods pass under cities. They pass under rivers. They pass under seas. The largest tunnels show what modern engineers can do. An obstacle is something that gets in the way.

2It blocks progress or movement. Engineers are people who design or build structures. They also repair machines, buildings, and bridges. Going through became a third choice beside around and over. Jerusalem's old water tunnel shows how long people have dug. Tunnel building by people goes back thousands of years. Danger filled most of those years of tunneling. Hard work could stretch across many years. The 1860s made tunnel building much less difficult. Alfred Nobel created dynamite. Dynamite was easy to use. It was safer than other explosives of that time. Dynamite let people blast through rock in moments. Since then, technology has kept advancing. Tunnels have grown larger. Tunnels have grown more amazing. Inventions brought Alfred Nobel great wealth. Dynamite was one of those inventions. After his death, that money funded a prize. The prize is the Nobel Peace Prize. In 2016, almost 2 billion people rode the subways of New York City. If those tunnels were laid end to end, they would reach far. Chicago, Illinois, would be the far end if the tunnels began in New York City.

3Rock mountains now have tunnels carved by workers. They have carved tunnels under large bodies of water. They have carved tunnels below busy cities. Before a tunnel is built, engineers study the ground. They look at soil samples. They look at rock samples. They drill test holes. The holes show the type of rock they must dig through. With that information, they can design the tunnel. They design it so it will not collapse. Blasting is the use people give this explosive material called dynamite. An explosive is a substance that can blow up. The blast is a sudden release of energy. Technology means putting scientific knowledge, or tools, to work. Falling apart, or falling down, is what collapse means. Nobel's blast tool changed a slow and dangerous job. Test holes tell builders what kind of rock awaits. Three basic steps are the usual path for tunneling. The first step is to dig. The second step is to support. The third step is to line. Digging part of the tunnel is the opening step. They may use tools. They may use machines. They may use explosives.

4Once part of the tunnel is cleared, support begins. Any unsteady ground must be made stronger. The goal is to prevent a collapse. The method depends on the material ahead. Once the tunnel is stable, workers build the lining. The lining is the inside of the tunnel. To line a tunnel means to cover that inside. Stable means balanced or steady. It means unlikely to change. These three steps have been used all over the world. People have built amazing tunnels with them. Road tunnels in Norway number over 900. They go through mountains. They go under water. The Lærdal Tunnel is about 25 kilometers (16 miles) long. Say Lærdal like LAR-dahl. No road tunnel in the world is longer. Norway's mountains are what it cuts through. A trip from Borgund to Flåm is longer without the tunnel. Say Borgund like BOR-gund. Say Flåm like FLAWM. Without the tunnel, the drive is 84 kilometers (52 miles). Using the tunnel leaves a route of only 56 kilometers (35 miles). The tunnel saves 28 kilometers (17 miles). Workers used a huge amount of explosives on the Seikan Tunnel.

5They used more than 2,540 metric tonnes (2,800 tons). The Seikan Tunnel connects two islands in Japan. One island is Honshu, the main island. The other island is Hokkaido. The tunnel is 54 kilometers (34 miles) long. Only one tunnel in the world is longer. Tons of hard rock had to be blasted by the workers. In 2016, a record railway tunnel opened in Switzerland. It is the Gotthard Base Tunnel. It is the world's longest railway tunnel. It is also the world's deepest railway tunnel. It travels beneath the Swiss Alps. Its length is 57 kilometers (35 miles). Dig, support, and line are the three steps to remember. Norway's many road tunnels include the long Lærdal route. The distance saved from Borgund to Flåm is 28 kilometers (17 miles). May 2014 was when workers placed explosives. They were starting the Brenner Base Tunnel. It is a train tunnel in Austria. Small holes come first when workers plan to blast rock. The type of rock sets how deep the holes must be. The type of rock also sets how far apart the holes must be.

6Explosives are then packed tightly into those holes. After the explosives go off, workers haul away the broken rock. That broken rock is called muck. Muck is the broken material a blast makes. Workers must remove it. A 2008 picture shows a worker cutting a rock bolt. The bolt had held a weak section of rock. A train tunnel's roof was where that rock sat. The tunnel was in New York City. Tunnels of solid rock often need no extra support. They are already sturdy. Broken rock still has to be held in place. Workers may install long bolts. Workers may spray the area with concrete. They need to be sure the rocks will not move. The work on the tunnel continues after that. One picture imagines the future look of the Stad Ship Tunnel. The first tunnel made for ships is what Norway plans to build. Its planned length is almost 2 kilometers (1 mile). Small holes, packed charges, and hauled muck are the blast steps. Solid rock can hold itself. Broken rock needs bolts or sprayed concrete. A ship tunnel would be a new kind of passage.

7The Stad plan would give Norway that first ship tunnel. Moles is another name for tunnel-boring machines. Some rock tunnels are built with these huge machines. At the front is a plate shaped like a circle. The plate contains disk cutters. The plate rotates. It carves into the rock. It grinds into the rock. A belt receives the scooped muck. Toward the tunnel entrance, that belt carries the load back. These machines make tunnel building easier. They make it faster. They cost millions of dollars. If they break down, repairs can take a long time. Repairs can take months. Repairs can even take years. A tail shield section was put in place by workers in 2016. That machine was built for light rail running under the ground. The place was Los Angeles, California. Boring here means able to make a hole. The tool spins or twists to do it. Building through soft ground can be dangerous. Sand is one soft ground. Gravel is another. The earth can collapse easily. To stop a collapse, workers use a steel cylinder.

8The cylinder is called a shield. Support comes from pushing the shield forward into the earth. Then they dig out the material inside the shield. Next they install a liner. The liner is often made of steel. It is often made of concrete. With the liner done, they push the shield farther ahead. Then they repeat the process. Marc Brunel invented this method. He invented it to build the Thames Tunnel. That work was in the 1840s. A spinning plate full of disk cutters chews into rock. A steel shield holds soft earth while workers dig inside it. Brunel's shield method is still the idea behind that soft-ground work. The Marmaray Tunnel is in Istanbul, Turkey. A map shows the Bosphorus River. It shows a train station. It shows the Asian side. It shows the European side. It shows the Marmara Sea. Building a tunnel under water adds more challenges. In many cases, workers make a trench. At the same time, they build tunnel sections aboveground. When the trench is done, the sections are sunk. The sections are connected together. Pumping removes the water after the seals are complete.

9The Marmaray Tunnel was built with this trench method. It connects the European side of Istanbul with the Asian side. Workers used huge barges. The barges carried tunnel sections into the sea. The sections were sunk into place. A trench is a long ditch. Sealed means closed tightly. Nothing should pass through or leak. The Channel Tunnel uses a different method. It crosses under the English Channel. The Channel lies between England and France. Eleven tunnel-boring machines started the work. They started from both sides. Two years later, the meeting point was the middle. The tunnel opened four years later. The opening year was 1994. A map of this route shows the United Kingdom. It shows Dover. It shows Folkestone. It shows Calais. It shows France. Each day, about four hundred trains use the Channel Tunnel. The trains carry passengers. The trains carry cars. The trains carry freight. Sunk sections joined under the water made the Marmaray Tunnel. Machines from both shores met to make the Channel Tunnel. Daily trains move people, cars, and freight through that tunnel. Tourists ride through the Bund Sightseeing Tunnel.

10The tunnel is in Shanghai, China. They ride in self-driving cars. They see strange images on the way. These amazing tunnels help huge numbers of people move. They help tons of goods move. The movement happens each day. It happens all around the globe. People keep making newer ways to travel. They keep making faster ways. They keep making better ways. They still meet the same obstacles. New tunnels will be needed. The goal is to get people where they are going faster. Technology now allows longer structures. It allows deeper structures. It allows wider structures. The work can be easier than before. The work can be safer than before. The next amazing tunnel is still an open question. A sightseeing ride in Shanghai shows images inside a tunnel. Self-driving cars carry the tourists through. Goods and people already depend on tunnels every day. Mountains, cities, and water are still in the way. Longer, deeper, and wider tunnels are more possible now. The next great tunnel is still to be chosen. Safe passage through obstacles remains the reason to dig.

64. Penguins of the Southern Seas

1When an Adelie penguin feels threatened, it sends a warning call. This book looks at a bird that is not like other birds. What bird cannot fly at all? What bird has strong flippers where wings would normally grow? What bird spends each day swimming or else walking? That bird is a penguin. Strong flippers do the job of wings for this bird. Its life stays in the water or on land. People like to watch penguins. Dark feathers cover the back. White feathers cover the belly. Those colours make the bird look dressed for a fancy party. Most penguins are clumsy on land. They walk with a waddle that looks strange. In the water, these birds become swift. In the water, they become graceful too. A movie stirred great interest in emperor penguins. Sixteen other types of penguins exist along with the emperor. Later pages tell more about these birds. Where might these gentoo penguins be going? King penguins near the Falkland Islands at times live beside herds of sheep. Every penguin has its home in the southern hemisphere. Many live where cold weather is the rule. Four species stay on the ice that surrounds Antarctica. No spot on Earth is colder than Antarctica. Three further species live on islands close to Antarctica. Not all of these birds live in cold or harsh places. Coasts in Australia and in New Zealand are home to the little blue penguin. In those places, forests come down to the ocean. Ice fields do not. Galapagos penguins live in the sea west of South America. The country nearby is Ecuador. That country sits on the equator.

2Picture yourself in a spaceship far above Antarctica. Looking down, you can view the south of Africa. You can view the south of Australia. You can view the south of South America. A large map drawn from that height shows where most species live. Small maps show only where Galapagos penguins live. Place names on the large map include Africa and the Atlantic Ocean. They include South America, Antarctica, and the South Pole. They include the Antarctic Circle, the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific Ocean. They include Australia, New Zealand, the equator, and the Galapagos Islands. Penguins do not live the way most birds live. Most of a penguin life is spent in the ocean. A streamlined body lets the bird move through water with ease. Webbed feet help that swim. Over a short distance, some penguins reach 40 kilometers per hour. That speed is the same as 25 mph. Long feathers do not cover penguin wings. Powerful flippers stand in their place. The flippers of seals are much like them. The flippers of dolphins are much like them. The flippers of sea turtles are much like them. The bird rows with its flippers as if they were boat oars. Those flippers push the water. The penguin then moves forward. The feet are used for steering. The tail is used for steering too. Flippers send this king penguin racing through the water. Two feather layers cover a penguin. The outer layer is stiff. The layer beneath it is soft. Outer feathers are small. They are also stiff. They sit packed close together. An oil gland lies at the base of the tail.

3The beak rubs that gland. Oil is then spread on the outer feathers. The oily coat keeps water out. The oily coat keeps heat in. Down lies under those outer feathers. Down is warm and fluffy. It holds warm air next to the skin. Fat adds another insulating layer. The fat layer is thick. A penguin that gets too hot fluffs up its feathers. Body heat can then escape. A hot penguin may swallow snow to cool down. Eating that snow also supplies water for the body. Most penguins molt once in a year. Molting puts new feathers in place of old feathers. Near the age of two, young penguins grow adult feathers. Lines in the snow show where a penguin slid. A slide on the belly is faster than walking. Penguins feel awkward on land. Legs attach at the rear of the body. Smooth walking is hard for that reason. Long trips on land are still common. Tired birds drop down and slide on the stomach. That slide is known as tobogganing. Why do the feet avoid freezing on ice? Warm blood stops the feet from freezing. Fat holds the core body temperature up. Feathers do the same for that core. A foot may sit only slightly above the freezing point. The core stays warm anyway. Blood moving toward the feet is warm. Blood on the way back to the heart is cold. The two flows pass very close to each other. Heat shifts from the warm blood across to the cold blood. Core temperature stays out of the danger zone. Scientists group penguins by their feathers and their markings.

4Letter codes name each home. ANT stands for Antarctica. NANT stands for near Antarctica. GI stands for the Galapagos Islands. AFR stands for South Africa. ANZ stands for Australia, New Zealand, or both. SAM stands for southern South America. Crested penguins show yellow feathers or orange feathers on the head. The erect-crested penguin measures 67 cm, or 26 inches. Its home is ANZ. The fiordland penguin measures 55 cm, or 22 inches. Its home is ANZ. The macaroni penguin measures 70 cm, or 28 inches. Its home is NANT. The rockhopper penguin measures 52 cm, or 20 inches. Its home is NANT. The royal penguin measures 70 cm, or 28 inches. Its home is ANZ. The Snares Island penguin measures 50 cm, or 19 inches. Its home is ANZ. Banded penguins show black stripes across the upper chest. The black-footed penguin is also called the African penguin. It measures 68 cm, or 27 inches. Its home is AFR. The Galapagos penguin measures 49 cm, or 19 inches. Its home is GI. The Humboldt penguin measures 70 cm, or 28 inches. Its home is SAM. The Magellanic penguin measures 70 cm, or 28 inches. Its home is SAM. Brush-tailed penguins are known for long tails. The Adelie penguin measures 70 cm, or 28 inches. Its home is ANT. The chinstrap penguin measures 74 cm, or 29 inches. Its home is ANT. The gentoo penguin measures 80 cm, or 31 inches. Its home is ANT. Giant penguins are the largest of the penguins. The emperor penguin measures 120 cm, or 4 feet. Its home is ANT. The king penguin measures 90 cm, or 3 feet.

5Its home is NANT. Some penguins match none of the groups above. The little blue penguin is also called the fairy penguin. It measures 43 cm, or 17 inches. Its home is ANZ. The yellow-eyed penguin measures 55 cm, or 22 inches. Its home is ANZ. No penguin is smaller than the little blue penguin. It is close in size to a large duck. No penguin is larger than the emperor penguin. An average third grader matches it in height. An average third grader matches it in weight. South of the equator, spring begins late in September. Most penguins come onto land at that time. They start their families then. Nests are built inside huge areas made for nesting. A rookery is the name for one of those areas. One rookery may rest on snowy ice. Another may rest on a rocky cliff. Another may rest on a hillside. The species decides which of those places is used. A rookery full of penguins looks busy. It looks crowded too. Birds that nest in one shared place form a colony. Hundreds of a single species may fill a colony. Thousands of a single species may fill one too. The birds let out grunts. They let out croaks. They let out hisses. They let out trumpeting sounds. Some birds stretch their bodies. Some birds bow. Some point a beak up toward the sky. Such a colony is very loud. It is dirty as well. A lot of activity fills the colony. The noises help penguins choose a mate. The movements help them choose too. A pair of birds builds the nest as a team.

6Grass, moss, feathers, or pebbles may form that nest. Emperors do not build a nest of that sort. Kings do not build a nest of that sort. Their feet serve as the nest. The egg sits on top of the feet. The egg must keep its warmth. If the warmth is lost, the egg will not hatch. Smaller Antarctic penguins remain on the eggs. They do this for about five weeks. An emperor egg needs about eight weeks before it can hatch. A king egg needs about eight weeks before it can hatch. Across those weeks, heat from the parent wraps the egg. King mothers and fathers take turns sitting with the egg. The emperor father stays with the egg. The mother leaves so she can find food. Four months may pass before that father eats. His mate returns when the wait is over. She cares for the chick once it has hatched. During the wait he faces weather that is very harsh. Other emperor males face it too. That weather is among the harshest found on Earth. A skin flap on this king penguin lies over the egg. The flap holds heat against the egg. This gentoo chick feeds on food from a parent. The parent brings that food up from the stomach. A chick leaves the egg with a coat of down. It cannot swim in those first days. Waterproof feathers have to grow before swimming is safe. The chick must stay on land until then. Food for penguins is not found on land. One parent stays and cares for the chick.

7The mate swims in the ocean in order to feed. Food from that swim is carried back to the chick. An older chick leaves its nest. It lives among other chicks in a group. The chicks press close so the group stays warm. Parents still carry food to the group. A chick knows the voice of its own parent. Thousands of penguins may share one colony. The calls around them are very loud. The chick can still pick out its parent call. Then the parent and the chick find each other. Adult feathers mean the young bird can head to sea. It can hunt its own food after that. The young birds eat plenty. They put on size quickly. From two years of age until eight, these birds raise their own chicks. Penguins are animals that eat meat. Fish is one part of the diet. Squid is one part of the diet. Crab is one part of the diet. Other ocean animals are part of the diet too. Tiny krill are one favorite food. Shrimp are the group that krill belong to. Emperors and kings are larger than other penguins. They eat fish and squid more than other foods. That food fills them more than krill would. Most penguins find meals near the surface. Larger penguins may dive deep to reach food. A penguin does not grow teeth. Other birds do not grow teeth either. Spines form a fringe inside the mouth of some seabirds. Penguins have that kind of fringe. The spines take hold of food that is slippery. Such food may be trying to get free. This rockhopper shows spines running down each side of its mouth.

8Leopard seals get most of their meals from penguins. Sharks hunt penguins. Orcas hunt penguins as well. Leopard seals cause the most danger. A leopard seal swims at high speed. To get away, a penguin must leave the water fast. It dives down first so it can build speed. Hard paddling comes after that. The bird shoots out of the water and onto land. The leap can look like a shot fired from a cannon. Adults on land have few enemies. They do not need to fly in order to get away. Chicks in Antarctica must be kept safe from other birds. Smaller birds may take the eggs for food. Larger seabirds may take eggs too. Those larger birds may attack the chicks. A healthy adult penguin is not hunted by any bird. A penguin has no way to fly. Hunters on foot or in boats cannot be escaped. Sailors long ago caught penguins and ate them. That hunting still happens in some areas. People also kill penguins to use the bodies as fishing bait. Huge crowds gather at set places in order to breed. Those crowds need a large supply of food. People fish on a large scale in many of those same waters. Penguins then have to compete with people for ocean food. When the food supply is not dependable, fewer adults survive. Fewer chicks survive for the same reason. A fishing net can trap a penguin. Trapped penguins die. Conservation groups ask large fishing companies to catch less fish. They want that change in waters near rookery sites. They want it during the season of breeding.

9The great auk lived in the northern hemisphere. The great auk could not fly. It was a bird much like a penguin. Hunting in the 1800s made the great auk extinct. Galapagos penguins can be seen out fishing. Oil pollution adds one more threat. It puts the safety of penguins at risk. Penguins spend so much time in the water that spills reach them often. Most other birds are less likely to meet a spill. Penguins cannot fly over dirty water to see it and keep clear. Spill oil can coat the feathers of a bird. The natural insulation then stops working as it should. The bird gets cold much too fast. A thick layer of fat sits under the skin. That fat gives extra protection against cold. People sometimes rescue these birds and wash them. The fat lets washed penguins last more often than birds of other kinds. Even so, deaths outnumber the birds that people can save and wash. This Magellanic penguin is covered in oil. People are washing that oil away. Warmer ocean water has shifted the food of black-footed penguins to the south. Those birds must cover more distance when they swim for food. Fewer black-footed penguins survive as a result. Global warming has opened new dangers for penguins. Air over the Antarctic region is warming. Water in that region is warming too. The mass of ice then becomes smaller. In a normal winter, algae gather on top of the ice. Spring warmth makes the ice melt. Krill eat the algae once the ice is gone. Less ice leads to less algae.

10Less algae leads to less food for krill. Less krill means fewer Antarctic penguins can survive. Scientists are looking at other effects of global warming on penguins. Many species have dropped by nearly half in number. That change happened over the past fifty years. Polar regions make the effects of global warming easiest to see. In the northern hemisphere, polar bears send a message of the same kind. Penguins send word that the planet is in trouble. Penguins need help from us so they can survive. Every other bird needs that help too. Wildlife of every kind needs that help too. These terms have set meanings. Algae are living organisms. They grow in water. They make their own food. They are not plants. Conservation includes protection of natural resources. It also includes preservation of natural resources. Insulation is material that holds heat inside. It blocks warmth from getting out. It blocks cold from getting in. Pollution is what we call harmful substances put into air. The same word covers harmful substances put into water. It also covers harmful substances put into soil. A species is a set of living things that are much like one another. Those living things can have babies with each other. Streamlined describes a shape that moves smoothly. The movement may be in water. The movement may be in air. A waddle is clumsy walking. The steps of a waddle stay short. The body sways from side to side. Index topics are Antarctica and eggs. They also include feathers and global warming. They also include krill and oil pollution. They also include rookeries and seals.

65. Pirates and the Kings Who Hired Them

1What do you picture when you think of pirates? Do you picture buried treasure? Do you picture ships with mighty sails? Do you picture a black flag marked with a skull and crossbones? Have you ever wondered what a pirate's life was really like? Pirates seemed to love adventure. Often they were vicious men and women who robbed and killed. Movies and books sometimes make pirate life look glamorous. In truth they were scoundrels, and their days were not pleasant. The way they lived often brought great discomfort, and it could bring death. One picture shows the ships of Bartholomew Roberts off the coast of Africa. Eleven captured merchant ships are part of that scene. All through history, pirates have sailed seas in every part of the world. Many famous pirates raided during those years. The span ran from the 1500s through the 1700s. Ships were targets, and so were ports. The sea was the Caribbean. People call that era the Golden Age of pirates. A map of the region shows North America and South America. It shows the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. It also shows the Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, and Puerto Rico. In 1669, the privateer Henry Morgan and his crew of buccaneers assaulted Gibraltar, a settlement in Venezuela. During the Golden Age, Spain built colonies across large parts of Central America and South America. Spaniards wanted the spices, the gold, and the silver of the Americas.

2To get those treasures, they enslaved Native people. They forced those people to work in mines and to gather spices. Gold was taken from the Native people as well. Silver was taken too. Royalty in England and in France learned how rich Spain was growing from American gold, silver, and spices. They wanted gold for their own empires. At the same time, many sailors had no jobs. Those sailors wanted adventure, and they wanted a chance to grow rich. The Queen of England formed a plan to seize some of the wealth Spain was hauling across the Atlantic Ocean. She would hire sailors who had no work, give them ships, and send them against Spanish vessels. England called these sailors privateers. Spain called them pirates. Many treasure-laden ships leaving the Americas passed through the Caribbean Sea. That sea is full of small islands, so it was an ideal place for pirates to wait. Spanish ships moving among the islands could be attacked from there, which made the spot ideal for a launch. Sir Francis Drake takes Spanish treasure ships in one picture. The Queen of England was the ruler he served, and his role was privateer. Another picture shows Henry Morgan attacking a ship. Pirates soon became known as ruthless villains. Sailors on other ships felt fear when a pirate ship drew near. They had heard stories of pirates and of the cruel things pirates did.

3Most of the ships under attack were cargo ships, and those ships had few weapons for a fight. The crews knew they could do little to stop the raiders. Some pirates used smaller, faster boats and struck at night. They slid up beside a cargo ship in the dark, seized it quickly, and killed many of the surprised crew. Small, fast ships were the ones pirates liked best. A sloop was one such ship, able to catch nearly any vessel marked for capture. A cannon fired a warning shot first. Boarding came after that shot. They hoped the captain and crew would hand over the cargo with no fight. Cannon fire was also used to smash the other ship's masts and rigging. Next, the pirates tossed smoke bombs onto the deck to confuse the crew and frighten them. Grappling hooks then let the pirates climb aboard. Once on the ship, they used many weapons to take control. A cutlass was one of the most common. A cutlass is much like a small sword, and it served for close, hand-to-hand fighting. Pirates also carried guns, including flintlock pistols and flintlock muskets. A musket fired a ball made of lead. Each ball was loaded into the barrel alone, then blasted out by exploding gunpowder. Sometimes the raiders built crude grenades for the attack.

4One picture shows Roche Brasiliano holding a cutlass. Pirate fights left many people wounded or dead. At times the victors took hostages. Members of a captured crew might even be forced to join the pirates. More often they tied up the crew and the passengers, then carried every valuable thing to their own ship. Now and then, pirates in small boats hijacked a whole ship and used it to attack other ships. A drawing shows Captain Kidd hiding his treasure. Most pirates stole because they loved gold. The rulers who hired them, both queens and kings, felt that same push. They stole many other valuable goods as well. Silver was often aboard the ships they hit. Precious gems were aboard too, emeralds and pearls among them. Tobacco was on those ships as well. So were wine, brandy, coffee, tea, and spices. Expensive cloth, such as velvet and linen, was aboard too. Most of the goods were sold or traded. Some goods stayed with the pirates for their own use. To some people, pirate life looks exciting. It was not very glamorous. People hated these criminals as much as they feared them. They had to stay on guard at all times, and often they could not trust even their own crew. The labor was hard and dangerous. Fierce fights cost many pirates a leg, an arm, a finger, or an eye. Some of those fights cost a life.

5Their quarters were unpleasant too, often dirty and foul-smelling. In a violent Caribbean storm, a mast sometimes snapped. Crew members then had to climb into dangerous rigging and cut the broken mast free, or it could capsize the ship. Making and mending sails was one of the special jobs on a pirate ship. Flags were also made and mended by the sailmaker. Each pirate was given a particular job. One person always stood watch, clinging to rope ladders high over the deck. That lookout searched for enemies and for ships worth raiding. A helmsman steered, using a lever called a tiller. The cooper made every barrel on the ship, and he also repaired and sealed them. Those barrels held most of the food. They held most of the drink too. If a barrel was poorly made or poorly sealed, the food or drink could spoil. Other work included mending sails, cooking for the crew, and caulking the wooden planks of the deck. Someone also had to pump water out of the bottom of the ship. When the work ended, there was time to eat, to drink, and to play. Meals were shared by the crew. The drink was liquor or wine. They played dice and cards. They played instruments, sang, and danced. At meals they were often lively and rowdy. Like other sailors, they lived packed into small spaces with little privacy.

6They slept in hammocks. Personal things, such as shaving kits and clothes, went into sea chests. One picture shows pirates celebrating. One picture shows Captain Edward England. Pirates often stole clothing from people on the ships they captured. Crew dress was not the same as the captain's dress. A sailor needed clothes that were comfortable and practical. A typical pirate wore plain shoes and pants, a sash at the waist, and a jacket with buttons of wood or bone. Many crew members covered their heads with scarves. Captains usually dressed in a much fancier way. Silk pants appealed to some of them. So did shirts that had lace at the cuffs and buttons made of gold. They often chose shoes with silver buckles. Many captains grew their hair long and tied it with ribbon so it looked like a gentleman's wig. Not every pirate was a man. A few women became pirates too. Most crews banned women from the ship, so a woman pirate had to disguise herself in men's clothes. On many ships the crew had a real voice in how things were run. They voted on rules, and they helped decide how raid treasure would be split. The captain always took the largest share. Other shares followed the importance of each person's duties. In some crews, the sailors even elected their captain. One picture shows Mary Reade fighting an opponent.

7Many pirates grew famous, and stories about them have been retold for years. Blackbeard's real name was Edward Teach. England was his birthplace, and he became a notorious pirate. He began as a crewman under a pirate captain named Benjamin Hornigold. Ships around the Caribbean were among their targets. Port towns were targets too. Blackbeard came out of that time with a name as a fierce fighter. Later he captained a ship of his own. Few captains sailing that sea were feared more than he was. He would not wait for a victim to remove a ring and hand it over. He cut the finger off instead. He stuck burning, smoking cord into his beard so black smoke rose around his face. People thought he was mad, and that fear made him even more frightening. The year 1718 took him and his crew north. They followed America's Atlantic coast and entered North Carolina. North Carolina was then part of the British colony. He followed coastal rivers inland and raided wealthy plantations. Frightened and angry, people wanted him and his pirates gone. Help was requested from the British Navy. A navy captain and his sailors fought a fierce battle against Blackbeard and his crew. Blackbeard was killed in that fight. Twenty wounds from a cutlass, plus five shots, is what legend says it took to kill him.

8One picture shows Robert Maynard fighting Blackbeard. Anne Bonny was one of the few women who became pirates. Ireland was where she was born. While she was still a young girl, her family moved with her to South Carolina. A lawyer was her father. A maidservant was her mother. A sailor won her love. She ran away with him. Their destination was New Providence, in the Bahamas. Calico Jack, a pirate, was the man she met there. She joined the crew he led. Men's clothing was her disguise. In a fight, she showed great toughness. Most people never learned she was a woman. Ship raids with Calico Jack continued until 1720. The British Navy captured them, and a court in Jamaica put them on trial. The judge first ordered that Anne be hanged. The navy learned of her pregnancy before any hanging could take place. Her sentence was changed to life in prison. Pegleg is another pirate people still remember. A French king used him as a privateer. What people remember most is a wooden leg. François le Clerc was the name he was given at birth. He did not wear a wooden leg. After he lost a leg in battle, he used a wooden crutch. Movies and books, including Treasure Island, often show pirates with wooden legs, probably because of Pegleg. One picture shows the body of Captain Kidd on display as a warning.

9Another famous pirate from England was Captain Kidd. Capture led to his death. The authorities then ordered the body hung beside the harbor, in sight of everyone. They hoped the sight would turn other people away from piracy. Sir Francis Drake was another privateer, and he was English. He went to sea at just 14. Cousin John Hawkins took him on the first voyages. Hawkins violently seized people in Africa. He then sold those people into slavery in the Americas. In 1570, Sir Francis took command of his own ship. Spanish vessels were his targets. Large stores of treasure from those attacks went to Queen Elizabeth of England. He did not keep his raids to the ocean. Spain was hauling more riches from Panama's mines by mule train. Once he learned that, he left the coast and went inland. Those mule trains came under his attack. He even took the central town of that mining region. Attacks on ships and on mule trains made him a rich and successful pirate. Queen Elizabeth rewarded him for the treasure he brought England, and she made him a knight. A cruel fate often waited for the captain once pirates had taken the ship. During piracy's Golden Age, safety did not exist for any ship on the sea. Pirates gathered in many places, and the Caribbean Sea was among the most notorious.

10Waters far from that sea were sailed by pirates as well. Theft and robbery were the living of many of them. They were lawless, and they were vicious, both the men and the women. Others were former sailors hired by greedy kings and queens who wanted still more wealth. Pirates still roam the world's seas today. They no longer rely on slow wooden sailing ships. They use high-powered speedboats. Small pleasure boats come under attack. Larger ships do too. Stolen goods are then sold on the black market. The black market is a network for trade that breaks the law. Caulking means packing gaps and cracks with a sealant that keeps water out. A cooper is a person who makes barrels. A cutlass is a sword that is short and curved. Glamorized means made to seem more fascinating and more attractive than the real thing. Grappling hooks are anchors that carry several hooks and are tied to a strong rope. A helmsman is the person who steers a ship. To launch something is to start it or to set it going. A maidservant is a woman who does the work of a household. A privateer is an independent pirate. The work is done under a license granted by a king or a queen. A rough person can be called rowdy. So can a person who is loud, excitable, quarrelsome, or aggressive.

66. Polar Bears on Thinning Ice

1A map shows where polar bears live. This book opens with an introduction. Next comes winter and summer on the tundra. Then a body built to survive. Then shrinking ice. Then other problems. A closing follows. A word list comes last. Home for a polar bear is the tundra of the north. Most living things find the wide northern Arctic tundra harsh and unfriendly. The polar bear is one of the most magnificent animals on Earth. It managed to thrive there. That success held until now. Tundra is a word from a language of several thousand Native people. Their home is the far north of Europe. The word means a plain without trees. Winter and summer are very different on the tundra. Through a large part of the year, readings stay far below the freezing point. Winter runs longer than six months. During several of those weeks the Sun stays below the horizon. Soil just under the surface never thaws.

2No trees stand in the way of the cold wind that crosses this icy land. The place becomes even harsher because of that. Frozen tundra soil is called permafrost. The word joins permanent with frost. Winter here is not a friendly season. Summer brings mosquitoes and plovers. Low plants appear too, including lichen, mosses, and shrubs. The summer Sun stays up for several weeks. Often it only peeks above the horizon. Average temperature in this season stays over freezing. Snow gets a chance to melt. Low plants grow. Mosses are among them. Lichens are among them. Grasses are among them. Small shrubs are among them. Millions of insects hatch. Air fills with them. Ground fills with them. Pools of water fill with them. Huge numbers of birds arrive because of those insects. The birds migrate here and spend the summer. Mammals that went south to escape winter come back as well. They feed here each summer. All year, the polar bear stays.

3The tundra suits it. Recent years have been a struggle for survival. Harsh tundra weather is not the cause. Fast change on Earth is the cause. Some scientists think a polar bear hides its black nose under a paw. The goal would be to stay harder to see while hunting seals. A picture shows bears covering their noses that way. Survival is built into the body. Arctic life is what these bears are adapted for. Water does not soak the fur, so a swim in icy water does not chill them. Each hair is actually clear. The bear still looks fully white. Snow camouflage comes from that white look, and stalking prey gets easier. The fur also holds warmth during an icy swim. A chart sets males beside females. A male's height is 2.5 to 3.5 meters, or 8 to 11 feet. A female's height is 2 to 2.5 meters, or 6 to 8 feet. A male's weight is 225 to 450 kilograms, or 500 to 1,000 pounds.

4A female's weight is 180 to 320 kilograms, or 440 to 700 pounds. Coat color is off-white. Seals are the main food. Fish, seabirds, and berries are eaten sometimes. Baby counts do not apply to males. A female has 1 to 3 babies every 28 months. A typical life runs 25 to 30 years. Smell is very sharp. A dead seal that is rotting can be smelled from 32 kilometers away, or 20 miles. Seals matter greatly in what these bears eat. Seals are the main meal. Walrus is also eaten. Smaller whales are eaten. Some land animals are eaten. Most seal hunting happens in winter, once ice covers the Arctic Ocean. White fur can vanish into the snowy scene. A seal may miss a bear that is ready to pounce. The wait beside an ice hole can last hours. That hole is where a seal comes up to breathe.

5A paw can measure up to 30 centimeters across, or 12 inches. Claws, pads, and hair on the paw keep the bear from sliding on ice. A great amount of food is required for an adult to live. Fat is stored for the seasons when hunting stops. The stomach is large. One meal can reach nearly 45 kilograms, or 100 pounds. Picture 400 hamburgers of a quarter pound each, eaten at a single sitting. Very cold air is blocked by two fur layers. A thick fat layer blocks it too. Even the underside of the big paws carries fur. Swimming is a strength. Hunts for seals have been seen as far as 80 kilometers from shore, or 50 miles. The head stays above the water. The stroke is the paddle a dog uses, faster than 9 kilometers each hour, or 6 miles each hour. Huge paws work like broad paddles. Thick blubber helps the body float. A math task.

6Average speed is five kilometers each hour. The bear leaves shore for an ice floe, then continues to four more floes. Each floe gets a rest of 10 minutes before the next swim. On the final floe, the bear waits beside a breathing hole until a seal comes up. Total swimming distance is 30 kilometers. How long from the shore departure until the last floe is reached? The picture shows a bear swimming. The answer is 6 hours and 40 minutes. Humans are the polar bear's only enemy. Hunting by people is not the greatest threat. What people do to the environment is the greatest threat. Scientists know the planet keeps getting hotter. That heating is called global warming. Pollutants sent into the atmosphere cause it. Each year more pollutants go up. A growing human population burns more gasoline. It burns more oil. It burns more coal. Car engines that burn gasoline send pollutants into the air. Factories send pollutants into the air as well.

7Plants and animals worldwide face harder lives because of the changes global warming brings. In polar bear country, the ice is melting. Some animals might not suffer much from that melt. Polar bears do. These bears need the sea frozen through most of the year. Once it freezes, they walk out on the ice. They look for holes a seal is likely to use for air. A longer freeze means a longer hunt. More eating means more fat stored for the short summer, the season when they fast. For Inuit people of the Arctic, polar bears are an important food. They are important clothing too. Weather shifts threaten that way of life. So does a smaller bear population linked to global warming. A shorter hunt means less fat can be stored. Scientists estimate a lost week costs 10 kilograms of summer fat, or 22 pounds. The problem is serious, because more polar ice melts every year.

8The cut in hunting time is why deaths among these bears have become alarming. An estimate says they could be extinct by 2100. Rising oceans have more than one cause, and melt of the polar ice caps from global warming is one of them. In time, long stretches of coast in many regions will flood. Scientists think many coastal places will lie underwater if that polar ice melts fully. Churchill, in Manitoba, draws hungry polar bears. Lower weight in females means fewer cubs are born. The problem is very serious. A typical span of 28 months brings this animal only two young. Summer hunger also sends bears into human towns. In some places the bears are caught and held in compounds until winter ice returns. Release comes next, so they can hunt and rebuild their fat. Human activity harms polar bears in more ways than global warming. Many pollutants in air and water are toxic. Seal blubber often collects those pollutants.

9A bear that eats the seal eats the toxins too. The path of that pollution has three steps. Toxic chemicals arrive in Arctic air and in Arctic water. Seals then eat fish whose bodies carry high levels of those pollutants. Bears then eat the seals, and the seals' fat holds the stored poison. Planet Earth is shared by many creatures, and you are one of them. List every action you can take to slow global warming and to help the bears' environment. Then think what happens if other people join you. An oil rig in the Arctic drills for oil. Fuel demand that keeps rising is another threat. Firms that sell oil, and firms that sell gas, hope to drill in the bears' Arctic home. Much of that drilling would sit where females dig dens and give birth. Survival could be hurt by that drilling. A frozen sea is what these bears need when they hunt seals.

10The world population of polar bears is shrinking. That fact is not in doubt. Western Hudson Bay, in Northern Canada, shows a steep drop by itself. The year 1995 had over 1,200 bears there. The year 2021 had fewer than 620. Worry about this plight has moved many groups to act. They are trying to protect these magnificent animals before the chance is gone. Word list. To fast is to eat very little, or to eat nothing. Global warming is the rise in average temperature of the air around Earth and of the oceans. To insulate is to hold heat inside. To migrate is to travel from one region to another. A plight is a terrible situation. A pollutant is dirt or debris. It may float in the air. It may lie on the ground. Prey is an animal hunted to be eaten. To thrive is to grow and stay healthy. Toxic means poisonous, and dangerous to life.

67. Puerto Rico, Island of Many Stories

1The San Sebastian Street Festival fills Old San Juan with dancers in a parade. Hold a picture of a warm island paradise in your mind. Picture palm trees that sway. Picture beaches of sand. Past the shore, misty peaks of mountains rise above green slopes. Calls of wildlife that stays out of sight drift on the warm air. You have arrived at Puerto Rico. The United States counts Puerto Rico as one of its territories in the tropics. A locator map shows Florida beside the Atlantic Ocean. It shows North America and the Pacific Ocean. Cuba and South America appear on the map. So do the Dominican Republic, Haiti, and Jamaica. The Caribbean Sea and Venezuela are marked as well. Navio Beach is a beautiful shore on Vieques, an island of Puerto Rico. Say Vieques like vee-AY-kayss. Puerto Rico lies where two great waters meet. One is the Atlantic Ocean. The other is the Caribbean Sea. The island sits 805 kilometers north of Venezuela. That distance is 500 miles. Venezuela is in South America. A little more than 1,609 kilometers separates Puerto Rico from Florida. That distance is 1,000 miles, southeast of Florida. Florida is part of the United States. Puerto Rico has never been one of the states, though Florida has. It is a protected territory of a kind called a commonwealth. Puerto Rico has a government of its own. It has a flag of its own. Its people are considered citizens of the United States. A Puerto Rican who travels abroad carries a passport of the United States. Lots of people think of this commonwealth as only a single island. It is really an archipelago.

2An archipelago here is a cluster of islands, cays, and atolls. The cluster contains 143 of them. Only the three largest islands have people living on them. Those islands are Puerto Rico, Vieques, and Culebra. Puerto Rico is the largest of the three. Most of the people live there. The main island is around 161 kilometers long. That length is 100 miles. It is 56 kilometers wide. That width is 35 miles. Jamaica and the main island are close to the same size. Jamaica is a neighbor to the west. Long beaches line this island, just as long beaches line Jamaica. It also has mountains. The coastline runs for 438 kilometers. That length is 272 miles. Hundreds of beaches line that coast. The Cordillera Central mountains cross the island. Say the first half of the mountain name as kor-dee-YAIR-ah and the second half as sen-TRAHL. These mountains split the island into a north and a south. The two parts have climates that differ a little. Rain falls often on the northern side. Rivers in the north flow through the whole year. The southern side receives less rain. In the hot summer, rivers of the south often go dry. Atolls and cays are pieces of land found in tropical water. Coral builds them. An atoll takes the shape of a ring made from coral reef. A lagoon lies in the middle of that ring. A cay is the low sandy island of the pair. This low sandy island sits on top of a reef built by coral. The first people known to live here were the Taíno. Say Taíno like tah-EE-noh. During the final years of the 1400s, Taíno communities lived on many Caribbean islands.

3Cuba was one of those islands. Jamaica was another. Hispaniola was another. Hispaniola is the land of Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The Taíno also lived on the Virgin Islands. They lived in settlements. They farmed the land. Their crops included cassava, yams, and beans. The water around Puerto Rico gave them fish. Other food from the sea was theirs as well. The year 1493 brought Christopher Columbus to this island. He was an explorer from Italy. He supported Spanish plans to colonize new lands. Columbus gave the island the name San Juan Bautista. Say Bautista like bou-TEEstah. The name honored Saint John the Baptist. Spanish colonists declared that they owned the islands. They also declared that they owned all the peoples there. Soon, people found gold in the rivers of the island. The Spanish gave the island a new name, Puerto Rico. The name means rich port. San Juan, the main city, became the capital.
