Interviewer: What does climbing a mountain mean for you? Erik: The scene around me is exciting. Sound is part of that. So is the feel of rock under my hands. So is sun on my face. So is the changing ground under my feet. So is the changing feel of ice and of snow. Challenging that environment with my team is exciting.

3Skill is one tool. Endurance is another. I take situations I cannot control and bring them under control. Erik stands on the right with other climbers on Mount Ama Dablam. That peak is in Khumbu, close to Mount Everest. Pointed boots are on Erik's feet. He carries a pole. An ice ax is in his other hand. Both help on ice and on snow packed hard. Interviewer: On a mountain, how do you tell where to go? Erik: Climbing has more than one part. On a hike I follow a person whose pack carries a tied-on bell. Long trekking poles let me feel the ground ahead. When a foothold feels right, I lean on one pole and step. Then the other pole sweeps the next spot. People expect this to be slow. It is not. My hiking pace matches anyone's. Nearly vertical snow fills deep gullies. Those gullies are called couloirs. I kick boot toes into the snow. Each step is single. An ice ax is swung into the snow. The way up is felt slowly, the same way the others feel it. Vertical ice is a frozen wall that looks like a waterfall. Crampons let me kick into it. Those are sharp points fixed on the boot toes. I rise high onto those toes. Ice tools are swung into the ice. Then I hang on the tools and pull my body up. Seeing the swing is not required. Climbers who can see hunt for blue ice, since white ice is rotten. A tap of the tools tells me if the ice is rotten. I listen for the sound. I notice the vibration. A picture shows Erik on an ice cliff. Interviewer: Can you be the lead climber on a mountain?

4Erik: The leader's work is to carry the rope upward, clipped to a harness. Metal pieces are jammed into the crack. The rope is then clipped to that gear. Everyone stays safer because of it. Touch is enough for me to lead on rock. I do it on a vertical crack. I do it on pockets. Interviewer: Crevasse crossings are different. You do not lead there? Erik: Snow bridges over crevasses can be very narrow. Lining up the best route would require sight. On a big peak I am usually tied by rope to two partners, and I follow one of them. Interviewer: How can you tell a narrow snow bridge will hold? Erik: It has to be tested. The rope team is the reason a test is possible. If the first person drops through, the other two drop their bodies onto the snow. Their ice axes are jammed into the ground. The fall stops. The fallen climber hangs on the rope until a slide up the rope lets him pull himself free. Interviewer: What climb moment made you laugh the most? Erik: We were about thirty minutes from the top of Mount McKinley when we called the village by radio. At the top, a small plane circled above us. My dad was aboard. My wife was aboard. Both of my brothers were aboard. Ski poles waved. Every suit was red. We looked the same as one another. I asked a friend whether the plane would know I had arrived. He said yes, because my ski pole was the only one waving the wrong way. The joke was affectionate. It showed love. It was not cruel. Interviewer: What climb moment scared you the most? Erik: I want a climb to stay boring.

5Collapsing snow bridges have dropped me into crevasses. I simply jumped to the far side. Once, while I led, a piece of gear left the rock. That gear is what ties the rope to the stone. I dropped about 25 feet and hung at the rope's end. Another time a gully of loose rock began to slide under me. I jumped aside and the rock passed by. Once I hung on ice while an avalanche poured over my head. Chunks of ice struck me. A helmet was on my head. Nothing I have lived through is what I would name a near-death experience. One photo puts Erik on the summit of Everest. A smaller photo shows base camp at Everest. Interviewer: What is the summit of Mount Everest like? Erik: Arrival means the climb is finished. It is over. Planning is what excites me. Building the team excites me. Preparing as fully as I can excites me. I like settling small choices, such as the spot for my gloves. Food and water go where my hands can reach them fast. Knots are a skill I enjoy learning. Little time gets wasted in the mountains because of skills like that. Little energy gets wasted too. Preparation itself is the fun. Twenty minutes is the longest you stand on the summit. Sound changes up there. Sky is over you and all around. Vibrations of sound travel on without end. My hand meets the snow. The wind's howl is clear. The highest point feels wonderful. The hard work starts after you leave it. Edmund Hillary was first to reach the top of Mount Everest. His view was that the climb counts only when you return. Tired legs make a trip and a fall more likely.

6On the descent, 90 percent of climbing accidents occur. Another photo shows Erik and the team on the summit of Elbrus. Try a sound test that Erik describes. Ceilings are something I hear. Walls are something I hear. Other objects are too. Vibrations leave us, strike an object, and return, in the way a bat uses echolocation. Any person can do this. Ceiling height can be heard. A wall can be heard. Test it in a hallway with closed eyes. An open door changes the sound, and that change tells you the door is there. During Primal Quest, Jeff Evans is on the right, steering the tandem bike Erik rides. Interviewer: Are other extreme sports part of your life? Erik: Tandem biking is one, and I sit in the rear seat, of course. Adventure races are another. Those races include mountain biking, kayaking, and rafting. They include rock climbing, hiking, and canoeing. One race crossed Greenland in five days. Another covered 460 miles in the Sierra Nevada of California. The ground there is as hard as any terrain I can picture. Primal Quest is the world's hardest adventure race. Our team was among 42 that finished. The start line had held 80 teams. Interviewer: Is there a guide dog? Erik: Yes. Three German shepherds have been mine. Wizard was first, when I was 16. Seigo was second, a dog as big as a bear, and he is retired now. Willa is third, and she has been with me about a year. A gentle dog was the goal, because my daughter is four. Willa is small and a bit timid. I sometimes have to urge her on and tell her she is able. She then chooses well, because she is smart.

7Leave a movie theater and tell her to find the car, and she walks straight to ours. A lot of 100 cars does not confuse her. One photo shows Erik with Wizard, the first of his three German shepherds. Another shows him with his daughter, Emma. Emma is the reason he later chose a guide dog that does well with toddlers. Climb notes are typed on a Braille word processor. The machine speaks back the words he typed. Interviewer: Tell us about the Tibet trip that is coming. Erik: Sabriye Tenberken, a woman from Germany, went to Tibet. She met blind children who were four and still could not walk. A school for the blind was her next step. Thirty-nine children study there now. Six or seven years earlier, those children were outcasts. Families would not take them outdoors. Now they walk Lhasa with canes. Braille in three languages is part of their study. Six students will climb Lhakpa Ri. From the left they are Tashi, then Kyila, then Sonam Bungso. Then come Tenzin, Kienzen, and Dachung. Interviewer: Were these children treated as if blindness meant they were not smart? Erik: Some places treat an imperfect birth as a sign. People may believe demons live inside the child. Sabriye's teaching changed that. These children are now the smartest in their villages. Respect replaced rejection. Six of her strongest and most motivated students seemed right for a peak. The chosen peak is Lhakpa Ri. It lies just to the north of Mount Everest. Spring training lasted three weeks. The journey itself was planned for a month. Interviewer: Describe the training. Erik: Mountains were the classroom. Experienced climbers held the rope with them. Crampons went on their boots. One day crossed a high pass at 17,500 feet.

8No path exists there. The ground is awful. A storm was underway. Every child shivered. One child vomited. One child fell into a river. The day was a test and a push. Every child passed, so readiness seems real. Toughness is obvious. Leaders can grow from this project. The children can feel that a life holds many possibilities. The world can also hear a message about human ability. One photo shows Erik at the front of Climbing Blind Tibet 2004. Another shows him talking with a group about reading and writing in Braille. Interviewer: Aside from peaks, what work fills your time? Erik: Schools often hear me speak. Our film about Everest is part of that visit. I read aloud from my book. Quite a few schools are already using it. Leadership is a large part of the book. So is loss, and the gain that can follow loss. So is stepping into the unknown. Climbing blind is a theme, and it is wider than a blind person on a peak. It means going ahead when you doubt that you have enough. Fear and doubt can block a goal, and the book is about moving through them. American Foundation for the Blind counts me as a literacy champion. Educational groups hear me talk about a need. Blind children need Braille, just as children who see need print. The program spreads a second need. People must learn to turn books into Braille. Raised dots in patterns are what Braille uses. Fingers do the reading. Interviewer: Which goals come next? Erik: Hard climbing should continue for four or five more years. The goals do not run out. The list of climbs keeps growing. Ice faces in Alaska are on it.

9Rock faces in Canada are on it. The Alps are on it, both for rock routes and for ice routes. Chile is on it. Peru is on it. The Himalayas are on it. More peaks follow those. A photo shows the trek toward Everest base camp. A summit already reached does not close his climbing life. This photo catches Climbing Blind Tibet 2004 in a celebration. Interviewer: What would you tell someone who faces a hard challenge? Erik: Proof that a blind person can climb is not my reason. I climb for the pleasure of it. Still, a blind person on a summit makes others question their old limits. Doors open, in my view, because of that sight. People spend less thought on inability. They spend more thought on what might be possible. A life does not have to follow only our own expectations. It does not have to follow only what others expect. Children will start things we cannot yet imagine. Society can be nudged forward in many ways. People, and children most of all, dismiss their power to change the world. Extraordinary power still sits in each person's two hands. Interviewer: Before this book ends, is there more you want readers to hear? Erik: Mountains taught me that leadership does not require being the quickest. It does not require being the brightest. It does not require being the best liked. It does not require the sharpest eyes. Some skill is needed. A picture of who you are is needed. A picture of the person you hope to become is needed. Courage in large amounts has to carry that picture through. Plans and speeches are how many adults try to lead. Actions lead better, in my view.

10Climbers name that choice the rope's sharp end. It means you actually go out and climb. Leadership, for me, is that sharp end. It appears in choices, not in talk. Erik keeps climbing, and that is how he takes the rope's sharp end. Teams that believed in Erik were with him on every one of the Seven Summits. Interviewer: People follow the person who acts. Talking them into line behind you is not what moves them. Is that your point? Erik: Yes. A strong team that trusts you still has to be gathered. What pushes the world ahead, though, is a person willing to step forward and take the sharp end. Read his book to learn how he pushed past limits that blindness placed on him. The title is Touch the Top of the World: A Blind Man's Journey to Climb Farther Than the Eye Can See. Word list. An avalanche is a huge slide of snow and ice down a mountainside. Echolocation finds an object by sending sound and timing the return bounce. Braille prints for blind readers by using a raised dot for each letter. Endurance is lasting through pain and through strain. A couloir is an open, deep gorge or gully, and snow or ice usually fills it. Genetic refers to heredity and to how living things vary. Crampons are metal spikes on boot soles so a walker can stand firmly on snow or on ice. Outcasts are people society has pushed away. A crevasse is a deep crack, most often in the ice of a glacier. Terrain means the character of a piece of land. A documentary is a film that presents real events with dramatic force. Vibration is a quick movement that goes back and forth.

75. Skates, a Stick, and a Puck

1Children play hockey on a rink that belongs to their community. This book walks through the sport in several parts. One part tells of a famous Olympic game. One part shows how clubs chase a win. One part maps hockey around the globe. One part tells how the sport began. One part explains play on the ice. One part names great players. One part shows how a beginner can join. A word list comes last. Joy fills Team USA after a win that few people saw coming. The loser that day was the Soviet team. The stage was the 1980 Winter Olympics. An Upset on the Ice The date to remember is February 22, 1980. The site is Lake Placid, New York. The setting is the Winter Olympic Games. A national team from the United States meets a national team from the Soviet Union. Gold had gone to the Soviet team in six Olympic Games out of the seven before this one. Nearly all watchers expect the Soviet team to win. Ten minutes remain on the clock. The United States is in front by a score of 4-3. Al Michaels is a newsman on television. He counts the closing seconds.

2He asks if anyone believes a miracle is taking place. He answers that question with a strong yes. The United States team defeats the Soviet team. The same team then defeats Finland. Gold at the Olympics comes from the win over Finland. Wins of this kind give off a powerful energy. Speed is part of what makes the game thrilling. Player talent is another part. Together they make hockey a thrilling sport all over the globe. Playing for a Cup Another name for the National Hockey League is the NHL. The league's first year was 1917. Only five teams took the ice then. Every one of those teams was Canadian. The league now fields thirty teams. About one fourth of them are based in Canada. In North America, team sports have a popularity list. Hockey sits in sixth place on that list. Clubs in the NHL play for a shot at the men's top award. That award is called the Stanley Cup. Separate leagues exist for women. Canada is home to the Canadian Women's Hockey League. The league dates from 2007. A second women's league was formed in 2015. The country that formed it was the United States.

3Its name is the National Women's Hockey League. One picture shows the Los Angeles Kings. They are holding the Stanley Cup. The club they beat was the New York Rangers. That final was played in 2014. A map shows the parts of the world where hockey is played. Europe appears on the map. North America appears there too. Asia appears on it. Africa appears on it. South America appears on it. Australia appears on it. The Atlantic Ocean is labeled. The Pacific Ocean is labeled. The Indian Ocean is labeled. The equator is marked as well. Players live in hot countries. Players live in cold countries too. Far from Home More than seventy countries have hockey. By 2013, the world count of players stood above one and a half million. Canada has many more players than nearly every other nation. The United States has a huge number as well. Ice for most games is indoors. An indoor rink can keep the ice frozen for the full year. Outdoor games still happen where the weather stays cold. Frozen ponds can hold those games. Frozen lakes can hold them too. Men first took part in Olympic Winter Games play in 1924.

4The women's event joined that same Olympic program in 1998. Before Today's Game A hard rubber puck is what players use now. The game is played on ice. It did not start in that form. A ball was the old object of play. Using a ball made the sport dangerous. Players found a ball hard to guide. The trouble showed up on the ice. The earliest rules came out of eastern Canada. A landmark day was March 3, 1875. The city was Montreal. That day brought the first game played with a puck. The sport quickly became popular across Canada. South came next. The United States took up the sport after Canada did. Victoria Skating Rink hosted the early games that used a puck. Montreal is the city of that rink. The rink's province is Quebec. The country is Canada. The page picture is a hockey rink. What Happens on the Ice This team sport is fast. It is also exciting. Play takes place on a smooth ice rink. A rubber puck is in use. So is a stick that is long and thin. Stickhandle is a word for controlling the puck with that stick.

5The same stick can pass the puck. The same stick can shoot it. Picture those moves while the skates fly. A skater may hit 20 miles per hour. The same speed is 32 kmph. Some skaters go faster still. The puck must enter the net to become a goal. The net belongs to the other team. More goals than the other side means a win once time runs out. Each club wants the puck in its control. Control is the path to a goal. The club with the puck is playing offense. The club without the puck is playing defense. Good play depends on strong stickhandling. Pads of a special kind cover the goalie's legs. Gloves are part of the goalie's gear too. One glove is the blocker. It sits on the hand that grips the stick. The other glove is the catching glove. It is made to catch pucks that come in very fast. Speed for a puck can pass 100 miles per hour. The same speed is 161 kmph. Blue lines, two of them, cross the ice. Three zones are created by those lines. The center zone is known as the neutral zone.

6A defending zone belongs to each club. One zone lies at each far end of the rink. An attacker may not skate in early. First the puck has to cross the blue line. Only then may that attacker enter. The space ahead is the other club's defending zone. A usual shift puts six players on the ice for one club. The goalie is the player who guards the net. Stopping the other club is mainly that player's job. Hands may stop the puck inside the crease. Only the goalie is allowed to do that. The goalie may also use other parts of the body there. The remaining five players roam the full sheet of ice. Scoring is the main job of the center. It is also the main job of the two wings. The two defensive players focus on blocking the other club. All five still chase the puck whenever the other club has it. Offense and defense trade places as the puck changes hands. The club that holds the puck sets that trade. Face-offs can be won in many different ways. A game is built from three periods. Each of those periods runs for twenty minutes.

7Shorter periods are used in youth hockey. A tied score after the third period brings extra time. One overtime period may be added. Further overtime periods may be added too. Scoring first in overtime makes a team the winner. Play in each period opens with a face-off. The face-off circle at center ice is the spot. Inside that circle stands a referee. One player from each club stands there as well. Down goes the puck from the referee's hand. The two players then battle until one controls it. More face-offs arrive at other moments. One follows a goal. One follows a penalty. Nine dots on the ice can host any of those later face-offs. Penalties come when play gets rough. Poor behavior is a common cause. A fight can bring a penalty. So can a jab from a stick into another player. An elbow can bring a penalty. A knee can bring one too. Stopping someone with a stick can bring one. Stopping someone with a body part can bring one too. The player who is called must get off the ice. A seat in the penalty box is where that player waits.

8The club goes on with fewer skaters. The wait lasts until the given time is up. Gear is worn so players can avoid injuries. Shoulder pads sit on the upper body. A helmet covers the head. A face mask is fixed to that helmet. A mouth guard protects the mouth. Elbow pads cover the elbows. Pants may be padded. Shorts may be padded instead. Gloves cover the hands. Shin pads cover the lower legs. Steel blades run under the skates. Stiff boots protect the feet. Those boots support the ankles as well. A hockey stick is carried by each player. A puck is the object they chase. Greats of the Game Few would argue if Wayne Gretzky were called the best player ever. His talent was so rare that a nickname stuck. People knew him as The Great One. He took the ice starting in 1979. He led his club, the Edmonton Oilers, to the Stanley Cup. Those Cup wins came in four seasons. One season was 1984. The next was 1985. Later cups came in 1987. Another came in 1988. Record books changed often across his career. Hayley Wickenheiser was fifteen years old during 1994.

9During that same year she made Canada's team. The team was the National Women's Team. She has guided it to seven medals. The matches that awarded them are the Women's World Hockey matches. Olympic medals on her record number five. Her work also helped the women's game draw more fans. You might want to try this sport yourself. A youth league may already exist in your city. It may exist in your town. Some skills at the start are useful. Starting with no skills is fine as well. Most leagues run programs that fit all ages. They run programs for every level of skill. A team is open to you once you feel ready. A coach will help with the rules. Skills get stronger as the days pass. New friends show up along that same path. Action fills this sport from end to end. Speed matters. Skill matters. Quick thinking matters. Teamwork matters. Only two words are needed to name the feeling. The words are nonstop fun. A junior team listens to its coach in the middle of a match. Connecticut is where that match is being played. Words to Know The crease is a marked patch of ice by the goal.

10It can sit directly in front of the goal. It can also wrap around the goal. Lacrosse uses the same word for a similar patch. Dangerous means something is able to cause harm. It can also mean harm is likely. Defense is the work of blocking a score by an opposing team. The word can also mean the players who do that work. Neutral means a person or spot supports neither side. It can mean there is no link to either side. That can be true in a conflict. It can be true in a contest. Offense is the effort to score on an opposing team. The word can also mean the players who try to score. Penalties are the punishments handed out when rules are broken. The puck is a small disk. Hard rubber is what the disk is made from. Hockey is the sport that uses it. A referee is the person who judges the game. The same role exists for a match. That person checks that the rules are followed. Zones are marked areas. Each one has a special purpose. Each one can carry its own rules.

76. Small Germs: Help and Harm

1Sneezed air may leave the mouth at 120 kph (75 mph). Order: introduction, microbes, immune system, bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, infection spread, outbreaks, epidemics, vaccines, antibiotics, conclusion, glossary, index. Night coughs, sneezes, sleepless tiredness, heat then cold, and a sore throat are symptoms. A caught bug is a disease from a tiny microbe, a germ. Unstudied illness was blamed on punishment, mistakes, or a witch's curse. Prevention was unknown, and so was any cure. Germs called microbes cause disease. What they are, where they live, and if all are bad may aid prevention. In 1799, first United States president George Washington caught a throat infection. Leeches did common bloodletting and removed five pints of his blood that day. A body holds at most 12 pints. Treatment killed him. The disease did not. Microbes are tiny organisms visible only by powerful microscope. Air, surfaces, skin, clothes, and our insides hold helpful and harmful kinds. Some cause disease. Others help prevent or cure it. Pictures: a flu virus, strep bacteria, and a yeast fungus, plus Ophryoscolex protozoa.

2Louis Pasteur (pass-TUR) supplied the Germ Theory of Disease. It links disease to contact with harmful microbes. Medicine still uses that proof. Sealed-canister food, heated at a set temperature for a set time, lost many organisms. Call that heat pasteurization. Fresh milk and canned food both receive it. Compare 145 degrees Fahrenheit (62.8 degrees Celsius) for 30 minutes with 163 degrees Fahrenheit (72.8 degrees Celsius) for 15 seconds. How many seconds quicker is the hotter way? The body is a warm, moist, food-rich microbe home. Friendly microbes give help and receive a place to live. Too many friendly microbes, or harmful ones that enter and multiply, can harm health. Some double every 20 minutes. From 1 microbe, how many exist after 4 hours? At 0 minutes there is still 1. Harmful microbes damage the cells that build body parts and the immune system. Muscle, skin, bone, blood, stomach, and other cells, trillions of them, build and protect. One blood drop holds from 7,000 up to 25,000 white blood cells.

3Some send antibodies that block a microbe's chemicals. Others enclose the microbe and destroy it. Full skin cover blocks many troublemakers. Guard-like white blood cells in the vessels destroy millions daily with friendly help. Together this is a healthy immune system. It knows good from bad, remembers what worked, and fights a return. After mumps, another sickness is unlikely. Say bacteria back-TEER-ee-uh. Each simple cell needs a powerful microscope, and it may help or harm. Kinds of bacteria outnumber every other organism. One intestinal kind breaks food down for digestion. Some good bacteria help white blood cells kill harmful bacteria. Several kinds turn milk to yogurt and also to sour cream. They consume lactose, the sugar in milk. They give off lactic acid. Milk curdles, thickens, and turns tangy and sour because of that acid. Some bacteria cause food poisoning. Good bacteria help make dairy foods. Harmful bacteria cause strep throat. Strep brings pain, swelling, fever, headache, stomachache, swollen neck glands, and white pus. A food-safe gel dish lets scientists grow strep for study.

4Careless handling or cooking of raw food lets those bacteria cause food poisoning. Wash hands before preparing food. Cook hot enough to kill them. Vomiting, diarrhea, and an upset stomach often follow. Salmonella causes many cases. Viruses, said VY-russ-es, are smaller than bacteria. Human and animal cells house them. Outside a creature they die. Inside, they multiply from cell to cell and cause infection. A cold lacks headache and chills, and fever is absent or mild. Flu has headache, chills, and a high fever of 102 to 104 degrees Fahrenheit for days. Muscle aches and tiredness come sometimes in a cold and always in the flu. Sore throat, runny nose, and sneezing mark a cold, sometimes the flu. Both bring coughing. A virus may sicken someone or may kill. Mutation changes its identity, dodges notice, and makes finding it harder. The body kills it by destroying host cells. Separate viruses lie behind flu, behind chicken pox, and behind the common cold. An influenza virus can be magnified 295,000 times. Athlete's foot is fungus on skin.

5Fungi, said FUN-guy, seem plantlike but cannot produce food. Many-celled mushrooms may be edible or poisonous. Yeast has one cell and makes bread rise. Many fungi are parasites, absorbing needed energy from other living things. Ringworm, from harmful fungi, is a red worm-shaped ring on the skin. Athlete's foot hits soles and between toes, so skin may itch, crack, and peel. Protozoa, pronounced pro-toe-ZOE-uh, have one cell and are very small. Streams and ponds hold them often. Some birds and fish eat them. Dirty untreated water holds them too. People may get stomachaches, diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting. Malaria comes from a dangerous protozoa in an infected mosquito's saliva. A bite carries it into the blood. The illness is serious. High fever, delirium, and weakness follow, mostly in the hot tropics. A million deaths worldwide each year are tied to malaria. Mosquitoes move malaria and West Nile virus between people. Germs spread easily in saliva, in blood, and in nasal mucus. Sneezes, coughs, and contaminated objects pass them on.

6Dozens may touch a doorknob each day. Blowing a nose then touching the knob leaves microbes from the nose-to-hand path. Eyes or a sandwich can let the next person take the germs in. Speech, coughing, or sneezing while sick sends microbes through the air. Other paths: air, dirty surfaces, spoiled food, polluted water, or infected animals. Infected mammals, including dogs, raccoons, and skunks, can give people rabies. Chickens, other birds, fish, and reptiles may hold Salmonella. Infected mosquitoes can pass malaria and West Nile virus. Sick birds can pass avian flu. Ticks can pass Lyme disease. An outbreak is one disease in a small local group. An epidemic is a fast spread to many people. A pandemic is a fast spread to groups worldwide. Airplanes cross the world within hours, and a sick traveler can infect contacts. A new patient can start an outbreak elsewhere on the trip. The United States CDC monitors infections worldwide. CDC stands for Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. One area's sickness can endanger distant people.

7Vaccines train the immune system to spot and fight a harmful microbe. Some are chemicals for weak defenses. Others are tiny bits of virus or bacteria. England, two hundred years ago, imagined one virus blocking a worse virus. Doctor Edward Jenner saw mild cowpox keep farm workers free of smallpox. Thousands died of smallpox, one of the deadliest diseases. He called them cousins and trusted the mild illness to block the worse. His test gave healthy people mild cowpox. Immune systems beat it, learned the virus, and recalled the defense later. Deadly smallpox missed them, sparing many thousands of lives. A vaccine may be a shot or swallowed. Europeans and Africans brought smallpox microbes into the Americas. Native Americans lacked exposure and immunity, so millions died. South and Central America's largest native cities lost nine people in ten. Some microbes kill other microbes and spare healthy cells plus helpful microbes. Antibiotics, once called magic bullets, hit the chosen infection and spare nearby healthy cells. Most microbes behind a disease die from an antibiotic.

8The strongest may live and change enough to slip past. Overuse and misuse created resistance. Newer antibiotics are needed for deadlier microbes. In 1928 Doctor Alexander Fleming saw common bread mold kill bacteria. Penicillin followed. It was the first antibiotic and is the most widely used. When sick, stay home, rest, and keep apart. Rest helps the body's fight. Distance keeps others safe. For a cold or a cough, cover nose and mouth with tissue, then discard it. Do not leave it out for germs to ride on. No tissue means cupped hands, then a quick wash. While ill, keep food, cups, and plates to yourself. Crowds make germ travel easy. Fruits, vegetables, nutritious food, lots of water, outdoor air, exercise, and enough sleep strengthen the immune system. Soap and water clean knives and cutting boards after raw meat. Keep raw meat off cooked food. Skip dented or swollen cans and floor food. Soap plus water is the best microbe defense. Touch spreads eighty percent of diseases when hands are dirty.

9If everyone washed, spread would shrink. Wash after the bathroom and after animals, and before and after cooking and eating. Twenty seconds of soap, about two Happy Birthday hums, covers hands and nails. Rinse and dry on a clean towel. Brush and floss teeth clear of leftover food. Cavities come from bacteria in the mouth, which feed on rot. Infection can enter the blood through the mouth. A doctor visit once a year helps even well people and can stop trouble early. Get every shot. Leave wild animals alone. Bites, scratches, or disease-carrying bugs may occur. Camping or hiking needs insect repellent against mosquitoes and ticks. Drink only purified and chlorinated water. Microbes are inside, on, and around nearly everything. Most bring no harm, but some bring disease. Wash before food is eaten or handled, and after bathroom use. Two hundred years of discovery, research, and modern medicine produced vaccines and antibiotics. Countries, organizations, and doctors unite to control and eradicate diseases. Harmful microbes remain, but people can learn to battle them and live healthier.

10Antibiotics: microbe-made drugs against infections from different microbes. Cells: smallest self-working units in organisms. Contaminated: covered by harmful microbes. Disease: a change in normal body function. Epidemic: fast disease spread in a community. Eradicate: destroy completely. Immune system: moves antibodies through the body against infection. Infection: sickness from microbes. Invade: push in to conquer, weaken, or hurt. Microscope: a tool that shows tiny objects. Mutate: a lasting change. Organisms: living things, including people, animals, plants, and microbes. Outbreak: disease that spreads fast. Pandemic: fast spread of disease over the whole world. Parasites: creatures that take survival needs from others. Resistance: power to push back. Symptoms: signs of illness. Vaccines: a weak disease that trains the body against stronger forms. Index: antibiotics, bacteria, blood, chicken pox, contaminated, cowpox, epidemic, Alexander Fleming, food poisoning. Also: fungi, germ theory of disease, immune system, infection, Edward Jenner, malaria, microbes. Also: microscope, organisms, outbreak, pandemic, Louis Pasteur, pasteurization, penicillin. Also: protozoa, ringworm, salmonella, smallpox, strep throat, symptoms, vaccines, viruses, West Nile virus.

77. Spinning Storms from the Sea

1The picture is a Hurricane Hunter plane, a C-130. These parts follow. A storm is on the way. What this storm is. How it grows. Where it grows. How the storms are sorted. How people study them. How people forecast them. How to get ready. A closing. Ways to learn more. A word list. A word finder. News reaches a small cafe in Florida by radio. The report comes from the National Hurricane Center, which is in Miami. A hurricane watch covers the east coast of Florida. Florida City is one end of that stretch. Flagler Beach is the other end. Hurricane Frances sits about 555 miles from Palm Beach, in an east-southeast direction. Its track is toward the west-northwest. Speed is about 14 miles each hour. Outside, the cafe guests see a warm day with sun. They look toward the sea for the coming storm. No sign is there. On television, a satellite picture shows a huge storm in a spiral. Dots trace where the hurricane has been heading. A shaded wedge marks coast that the storm might strike. One hurricane has already hit these people this season. They know preparation cannot wait. Extra boards for windows are what some of them buy. Grocery supplies are what others gather. Water is one supply. Food is another. Batteries are another. A picture places Hurricane Frances just north of Puerto Rico. Miami flooded in September 1945 when high waves came with a hurricane. Morning brings faster wind. Clouds cover the sky. Farther along the coast, some people evacuate. That word means they leave home for a safer place. Wind reaches hurricane strength and bends the palm trees.

2Roofs are torn off buildings. Objects flying through the air can kill. Low coastal ground floods under high waves and rising water. Power lines break when trees fall. People who stayed sit in dark houses. Battery radios tell them how the storm is moving. At last the storm goes inland and the wind eases. Heavy rain is still there. Floodwater is still there. Sun returns the next day. Cleanup begins, and it costs a great deal. Wind and rain are familiar. A hurricane is not the same kind of storm. These storms are huge and round. Width can reach hundreds of kilometers. The Pacific Ocean name for them is typhoon. The Indian Ocean name is severe tropical cyclone. The Atlantic Ocean name is hurricane. Only the name changes. Death can follow from the heavy wind, the heavy rain, and the high seas. Damage can reach billions of dollars. Satellite pictures reveal the shape. Cloud arms spiral outward for hundreds of kilometers from the middle. People call that middle the eye. From the outer edge inward to the eyewall, the wind grows more fierce. A picture shows a hurricane eye. A picture shows the storm once it is fully formed. At the eyewall, wind that has been rushing inward suddenly climbs. The air loses heat very quickly. Rain starts. Most of the rain falls in the eyewall. One hour can bring 20 millimeters of rain, which is 0.78 inches. Over several days, one area can receive about 15 to 30 centimeters, which is 6 to 12 inches. Calm and sun are common inside the eye. Width of most eyes is 30 to 60 kilometers, or 20 to 40 miles.

3That peace ends soon. The eye moves on. Then the far side of the storm hits with sudden force. A drawing sets three sea levels side by side. One is a pleasant day. One is a rainy day. One is during a hurricane, and that rise is labeled storm surge. Near shore, strong wind joins with low air pressure. The sea around the storm is pushed higher than usual. Scientists gave this rise the name storm surge. It reaches for miles around the storm's middle. Any low land on the coast can flood. A large share of hurricane property damage comes from that flooding. Tropical oceans around the world are where these storms begin. They tend to arrive in a season. Summer in the Northern Hemisphere is a usual time. Summer in the Southern Hemisphere is a usual time. Sun energy warms sea water near the equator, and that is how the storm starts. Warm moist air leaves the ocean by evaporation. Cold dry air sits above it, and the warm air weighs less. The warm air forces its way up through the cooler air. Cooler air sinks and fills the space the warm air left. The result is a low-pressure zone called a tropical depression. North of the equator, the winds of these storms spin counterclockwise. South of the equator, those winds spin clockwise. Rising warm moist air cools and condenses. Clouds form in that change. Heat energy is released too. Giant thunderclouds appear before long. Wind starts to spin around the low-pressure zone. The blow grows harder. About 62 kilometers each hour is the next step, and that is 39 miles each hour.

4The tropical depression is then a tropical storm. More heat from the warm ocean can let a tropical storm become a hurricane. Some storms never gather enough energy for that change. Extra energy makes the wind faster. Thick cloud bands in a spiral spread away from the middle. Official hurricane status starts when wind passes 119 kilometers each hour. That rate is 74 miles each hour. The naming happens at the moment the storm reaches official hurricane rank. Each region of the globe has a yearly list of names. Many nationalities appear on those lists, because many countries feel these storms. Atlantic names for 2010 were these. Alex came first, then Bonnie, Colin, Danielle, Earl, and Fiona. Then came Gaston, Hermine, Igor, Julia, Karl, and Lisa. Then came Matthew, Nicole, Otto, Paula, Richard, and Shary. Tomas, Virginie, and Walter finished the list. A usual track north of the equator runs west, and then north. After that the storm turns northeast. The track leaves the equator behind. It also leaves the warm sea water that feeds the storm. A usual track south of the equator runs west, and then south. After that the storm turns southeast. Warm sea water is left behind on this track too. Cooler water takes away much of the storm's energy. Land does the same. Wind eases. In time the storm disperses. A diagram draws the common tracks. Hits come almost every year to Central America. They come almost every year to Caribbean islands. The eastern shore of the United States is struck almost yearly. The West Coast of the United States is rarely hit. Atlantic storms of this kind begin southeast of the Caribbean Sea.

5In the Pacific, typhoons most often strike Asia and Indonesia. Australia feels the severe tropical cyclones of the Indian Ocean. They reach the Middle East. They reach parts of Asia. They reach Africa's eastern coast. Six months or more can pass in a hurricane season. Through that time, meteorologists watch systems hundreds of kilometers from shore. Tropical depressions are watched. Tropical storms are watched. The question is which ones will grow into hurricanes. Sorting comes next. Sustained wind of a tropical storm runs from 62 to 119 kilometers each hour, or 39 to 74 miles each hour. Pass 119 kilometers each hour, or 74 miles each hour, and the storm is classed as a hurricane. Intensity is how meteorologists sort hurricanes. Their tool is the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Scale. Numbers on it run from 1 to 5. Each number describes the damage and the danger of that group. Category One wind runs from 119 to 153 kilometers each hour, or 74 to 95 miles each hour. Buildings get little damage. Plants get minor damage. Dolly, a Category One storm, left the damage in the picture. Category Two wind runs from 154 to 177 kilometers each hour, or 96 to 110 miles each hour. Roofing is ripped away. Doors and windows of buildings are damaged. Plants are pulled out of the ground. Boats that lack shelter often break free of docks. Category Three wind runs from 178 to 209 kilometers each hour, or 111 to 130 miles each hour. Small buildings take damage to their structure. Mobile homes are destroyed. Land lower than 1.52 meters above the sea, or 5 feet, may flood.

6The water may reach 13 kilometers inland or farther, and that is 8 miles. Pigs left with nowhere to go appear in a picture from a Category Two storm. Katrina ranked high in Category Three. Flooding was massive. Deaths numbered 1,800. Category Four wind runs from 211 to 249 kilometers each hour, or 131 to 155 miles each hour. Walls of buildings fall. Beaches erode in a major way. Land lower than 3 meters above the sea, or 10 feet, may flood. Huge evacuations may be needed as far as 9 kilometers inland, and that is 6 miles. Charley, in 2004, was an intense Category Four storm. Thousands of homes were destroyed. Category Five wind is greater than 249 kilometers each hour, or 155 miles each hour. Houses take damage across a wide area. Industrial buildings do too. Low ground within 8 to 16 kilometers of the shore may need a huge evacuation, and that span is 5 to 10 miles. Andrew, in 1992, was a Category Five storm. Its wind caused crippling damage across a wide area. History holds storms that did the most harm. They were powerful. They also moved slowly. Major cities in their tracks were destroyed by many of them. Famous hurricanes, typhoons, and cyclones include the ones below. India, on the Indian Ocean, lost 70,000 people in 1864 in a storm labeled Calcutta. The storm itself had no name. The label is the place hit hardest. The United States, on the Atlantic, lost 6,000 to 8,000 people in 1900 in a storm labeled Galveston. That storm had no name of its own either. The label is the place hit hardest.

7Japan, on the Pacific, lost 5,000 people in 1958 to Vera. Bangladesh and India, on the Indian Ocean, lost 300,000 to 500,000 people in 1970 to a storm labeled Bangladesh. That storm had no name of its own. The Philippines, on the Pacific, lost from 5,101 people to more than 8,000 in 1991 to Thelma. The Caribbean and Central America lost 11,000 to 18,000 people in 1998 to Mitch. The Central Gulf Coast of the United States lost more than 1,800 people in 2005 to Katrina. Study of these storms uses satellites. Far at sea, satellites locate tropical depressions. They locate tropical storms. They locate hurricanes. They follow all three. High above Earth, the satellites take pictures often. Scientists compare one picture with another. Movement of the storm shows up in the differences. Intensity shows up too. Inside a strong hurricane, high clouds look colder on satellite pictures than the air around them. The boldest tool is called the Hurricane Hunter. This aircraft is built for a special job. It flies into the eye. It measures temperature directly. It measures moisture. It measures how fast the wind is. It measures which way the wind blows. A C-130 Hurricane Hunter is in the picture. Storm tracking also uses Doppler radar. Television weather reports use it to show rain nearby. As a hurricane nears land, wide-range Doppler radar shows how fast its wind is. Short bursts of energy waves leave a Doppler station. Rain sends the waves back. Clouds send them back too. Waves returning from hurricane rain that is moving toward land are not the same as waves from rain moving away. A computer reads those differences and builds a model of the storm.

8Speed can be shown from that model. Direction can be shown from it. Forecasts of where a hurricane will go come from computers. Supercomputers receive thousands of typed measurements. The aim is to say where the storm is headed. Better computers will improve the forecast of a landfall. Lives can be saved that way. Evacuations that are not needed can be cut. Perfect accuracy, a full 100 percent, will never come from computers. Weather systems are chaotic. They are often hard to forecast. People who follow a hurricane's track tell others when to evacuate. Some researchers think a hurricane could be stopped before it forms. They think its path could be turned. Cloud seeding over wide birthplaces of these storms is one idea. Planes would spray a fine mist made of salt powder. Water would condense out of the air more easily because of that powder. Many small clouds would form and spend the energy. A single huge storm might have used that energy to grow into a hurricane. Seeding would have to cover an area as big as Texas or it would not work. A plan that truly blocks a hurricane from forming has not been made yet. Getting ready can protect both lives and property. A family needs an evacuation plan. The plan should name the time to leave. It should name the destination. It should name the way you will travel. It should say what to do if the family is split up. Emergency supplies should be kept on hand. A first aid kit is one. A flashlight is one. Drinking water is one.

9Canned food is one. A radio that runs on batteries should be ready if the power fails. Each time the warning level rises, follow what that radio tells you. The car should have a full tank of gas, in case leaving becomes necessary. If the hurricane is aimed at you and time remains, protect the house. Cover windows by nailing plywood over them. Tie down objects that are loose outdoors. When an order to evacuate comes, leave right away. Closing. These storms are an awesome show of the power in nature. Satellites reveal a lot about them. One fact they can give is the direction of travel. Another is which areas should be emptied. A future path may be forecast. Stopping the storms is unlikely to be something people can ever do. Protection is still possible. Choose with care the place and the way a home is built. Keep emergency supplies. Be ready to leave if you must. More to explore. The topics in this book can be looked up. Useful search words are hurricanes, storm surge, and typhoons. Words from the word list and the word finder are useful too. Word list. Air pressure is how hard the air in the atmosphere presses. A hurricane watch is an official notice that hurricane weather might occur inside the watched area. Caribbean describes the Atlantic region that lies between North America and South America. Intensity means how strong a force is. Chaotic means random, with no tidy pattern. A satellite is a craft that travels in orbit around Earth. To condense is to turn from a gas into a liquid, or to become more dense. A storm surge is a fast rise in sea level.

10During a hurricane it comes from strong wind and from falling air pressure. To disperse is to break apart or to scatter. Structure is how the parts of something fit as it is built. To evacuate is to move people away from danger. Sustained means continued without a stop. An eye is a center, and a hurricane has one. Tropical means belonging to the tropics, or taking place there. An eyewall is the cloud-and-rain wall that rings a hurricane's eye. A tropical depression is a weather system with low pressure. Its spinning winds, kept up steadily, stay under 62 kilometers each hour, or 39 miles each hour. A tropical storm is also a low-pressure system. Its steady spinning winds run from 62 to 119 kilometers each hour, or 39 to 74 miles each hour. Word finder. Topics in this book include Africa and air pressure. They include Asia, the Atlantic Ocean, and Australia. They include batteries, the Caribbean, and Central America. They include how storms are classed, damage, and death. They include direction, Doppler radar, and energy. They include evacuation, the eye, and the eyewall. They include floods and both hemispheres, Northern and Southern. They include the Hurricane Hunter, the Indian Ocean, and Indonesia. They include the Middle East, names, and the National Hurricane Center. They include the Pacific Ocean, the path, and prediction. They include protection, rain, and the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Scale. They include satellites, seeding, and the severe tropical cyclone. They include speed, storm surge, and structure. They include the tropical depression, the tropical storm, and the typhoon. They include the United States and wind.

78. Sticks, Nets, and a Fast Ball

1High school players scramble for the ball during a match in Oregon. In a match with Syracuse University, a Cornell University player carries the ball at a run. Lacrosse brings together the teamwork of basketball. World Cup soccer lends its excitement to this game. It brings the speed of ice hockey. Fans agree that watching this sport is an amazing experience. They say the same about playing it. New teams are appearing in more and more places. Growing popularity sends a clear message. Lacrosse, an ancient game, has not gone away. It will stay with us for a long time. Lacrosse began in the St. Lawrence River Valley, in the land that is now Canada. First Nations people of that region played it. First Nations people are also called Native people. In time, the game spread to tribes living west of the valley. It spread to tribes living south of it as well.

2Different groups used different names for the game. The old form was very unlike modern lacrosse. A side rarely fielded fewer than one hundred players. A side could field as many as one thousand. The field, the space they played on, could stretch for miles. Even so, the way they moved the ball was almost the same as today. Curved sticks were the usual tool for most tribes. Each stick measured 3 to 4 feet, or 0.9 to 1.2 meters. A net was fixed to each stick. Players passed the ball with those sticks. They carried the ball with them. They shot the ball with them too. Early contests were huge, and a match could last as long as three days. Artist H.W. Hall sketched a crowded game in Canada. The sketch shows First Nations players and other players, with many watchers around them. The game mattered deeply to First Nations people.

3They believed it pleased their creator. Many tribes called it the Creator's game. Play made young men brave, and it made them strong. At times they played to settle an argument. At other times they played to celebrate a friendship. French settlers in the land now called Canada watched games played by First Nations people. Before long, Canada had lacrosse clubs for white players and clubs for First Nations players. George Beers put the rules on paper in 1860. Today's game rests on those rules. Because of that, people call Beers the father of modern lacrosse. Schools in the United States started playing lacrosse in the 1870s. Most of the play was in private schools and in colleges in the Northeast. People treated it as a gentleman's sport, played for love of the game. Many athletes who might have excelled at it showed no interest.

4They wanted sports that could bring fame. They wanted sports that could bring fortune. A shortage of sticks also held the sport back in the United States. Players call the sticks crosses. Until the 1970s, only certain First Nations tribes made the sticks. They made those sticks by hand. Then cheaper sticks of lightweight metal reached the shops. After that, lacrosse began to take off. Players reach for the ball in a 1926 practice photo. The match was for the women's national championship. People in lands across the world enjoy the sport now. Outdoor teams often play their games in football stadiums. A second form, called box lacrosse, is played indoors. The Federation of International Lacrosse runs World Championship games for men and for women. Those championships come every four years. North America has two pro leagues. Major League Lacrosse is the outdoor league. The National Lacrosse League is the league for box lacrosse.

5Both men's teams and women's teams play the sport at colleges across the United States and Canada. In North America, the fastest growth is among young players. Youth teams are growing. Junior high teams are growing. High school teams are growing. As more young athletes discover the game, college play is sure to grow. Play at the national level is sure to grow too. In earlier years, only small pockets of lacrosse sat outside North America. Those pockets were in Australia and in England. Across the last thirty years, the sport has grown through Europe and through Asia. It has grown in other parts of the globe as well. Someday lacrosse may become the next huge international sport. The Summer Olympics included lacrosse twice, in 1904 and again in 1908. A photo from 1908 shows the Canadian winners. The most special piece of the game is the crosse, the stick every player uses.

6With it, a player can cradle the ball, catch it, pass it, and shoot it. Cradling is the back-and-forth rocking of the crosse head. That motion keeps the ball from falling out while the player runs. Only the goalie may touch the ball with the hands, a limit much like the rule in soccer. From end to end, a crosse shaft measures 2 to 5 feet. That is 0.6 to 1.5 meters. A curved head sits at the top, and a net is fitted into that head. Gear for men and for women can include a crosse, an eye mask, a helmet, and a mouth guard. It can include shoulder pads, gloves, rib pads, arm protectors, and cleats. Goalkeepers add throat protectors. They also wear more padding on the chest. A women's lacrosse field carries fewer markings than a men's field.

7Men's sides place ten players on the field, and women's sides place twelve. The field is about as large as an American football field. In the men's game, an X marks the center. Opposing players face off on that X at the start of every period. They face off there again after each goal. Three attackers stay on the other team's half of the field. Three defenders stay on their own half. Three midfielders range over the whole field. Each side also has a goalkeeper. Goalies must be fast and brave, because the shots they face are powerful. Their crosses have larger heads than the sticks of their teammates. A team wins by scoring more goals than the other team. A goal is a shot that enters the other team's net. A full game lasts one hour. The men's game uses four quarters of fifteen minutes each.

8The women's game is split into two halves. Speed is the most exciting part of any lacrosse match. Fast running and complex teamwork make the play amazing. A shot on goal can easily pass 100 miles an hour, or 161 kilometers an hour. Watch out. Oren Lyons grew up on a reservation. He played goalkeeper for Syracuse University, and he was an All-American athlete. His most important work came after the playing days ended. He is a great humanitarian. He helps lead organizations that speak for people in many places. Not long ago, Syracuse University asked him to throw the ball in before a game. Many people know Jim Brown as a legend of American football who won many awards. Far fewer people know that lacrosse was his first love. A great many fans call him the greatest lacrosse player America has ever had.

9He believed this game fit his athletic gifts better than any other. Over the years, he told people it was his favorite sport. Jen Adams grew up in Australia, then came to America for college lacrosse. She broke a long list of records. Many people call her the greatest female player the sport has seen. She was fast, she played fair, and she was a strong teammate. Today she coaches college lacrosse. As recently as 2009, she represented Australia at the Women's Lacrosse World Cup. Lacrosse is catching fire more strongly than at any earlier point in its long history. The strongest spark is among young players. Pace, excitement, and a rich history all draw young athletes to the game. Some fans love hockey for its speed. Some love soccer for its complicated teamwork and for the way players pass the ball. Others love basketball for plays that look acrobatic.

10In years ahead, fans may find all of those joys inside this one spectacular sport. High school sides meet in a match run by the Oregon High School Lacrosse Association. The sport is more popular now than it has ever been. Acrobatic describes leaping, tumbling, or other skilled body movement. Call something ancient when it comes from a very long time ago. Athletic relates to speed, strength, skill, or sports. To cradle means to hold or support someone or something in a gentle way. To exceed means to go past a limit. A goalie is the defensive player who keeps the ball, or the puck, out of the team's goal. A humanitarian is a person who helps others, often by easing pain and suffering. A thing has popularity when many people like it and support it. A reservation is land the government sets aside for Native Americans.

79. Storms That Touch the Ground

1These pages open with a short introduction. They then explain how a tornado forms. They show how strength is measured. They tell where these storms take shape. They give steps for staying safe. A conclusion follows the safety steps. Hard words are explained last. One photo shows a violent tornado in St. Louis, Missouri, in 2011. That storm nearly destroyed a home. It also flipped an SUV in the driveway. Roofs can be lifted off buildings by these storms. Houses can be swept into the air. Trees can be ripped out by the roots. Tornadoes are able to do all of that. Sizes differ a great deal. Some are narrow. A narrow one may be only a few feet across. That width is about 1 meter. Others stretch more than a mile across. That width is about 2 kilometers. Almost 3 miles was the span of the widest tornado ever recorded. That width is about 4 kilometers. Oklahoma was where it struck, in 2013.

2Some tornadoes touch down for only a short time. Others travel for hundreds of miles. Everything in the path can be destroyed along the way. Houses can be carried for long distances. Cars can be carried for long distances too. Scientists still cannot say for sure what causes a tornado. The strongest ones come from huge thunderstorms. The most violent ones come from those same storms. The storms are called supercells. A supercell can be built by warm moist air that climbs into the atmosphere. Cold dry air sits higher in the sky. The two kinds of air mix. A photo shows a supercell moving across Nebraska. The month was June 2004. In some supercells, scientists think the warm air climbs very fast. Cold air then rushes in to take its place. The rush makes the air rotate. Clouds get pulled into a funnel shape by that spin. The funnel cloud stretches downward. Winds inside it can reach 300 miles per hour.

3That speed is 483 kilometers per hour. Touching the ground is the moment it officially becomes a tornado. One photo shows a funnel cloud over Kansas in 2004. That funnel later became a strong tornado there. A diagram lays out the steps in order. Cool air spins inward. The storm is a supercell thundercloud. Warm air rises. Inside the thundercloud, that spin goes on. Rain begins to fall. Hail begins to fall. A funnel cloud appears. The funnel touches down. It then travels over the land. Anything in the path can be damaged. Debris flies through the air. Some scientists think tornadoes act to balance the air. Temperature is one thing brought into balance. Moisture is the other. A chart called the Enhanced Fujita scale rates the storms. People shorten that name to the EF Scale. Gusts of 65 to 85 miles per hour match EF-0. Those gusts are 105 to 137 kilometers per hour.

4Gusts of 86 to 110 miles per hour match EF-1. Those gusts are 138 to 177 kilometers per hour. Gusts of 111 to 135 miles per hour match EF-2. Those gusts are 179 to 217 kilometers per hour. Gusts of 136 to 165 miles per hour match EF-3. Those gusts are 219 to 265 kilometers per hour. Gusts of 166 to 200 miles per hour match EF-4. Those gusts are 267 to 322 kilometers per hour. Gusts of 200 miles per hour or more match EF-5. Those gusts are 322 kilometers per hour or more. Causes are still being researched. A rating system for strength already exists. T. Theodore Fujita built that system. The Enhanced Fujita scale is his way to rate strength. Wind speed is the basis of the rating. Getting close to a tornado is hard. Damage is what scientists study instead. Wind speed is estimated from that damage. EF-5 marks the most powerful tornadoes.

5Their winds are greater than 200 miles per hour. That figure is 322 kilometers per hour. A portrait shows T. Theodore Fujita. Measuring a tornado is hard. Scientists still have a solid idea of where one will occur. A tornado can strike any place in the world. Most of them happen in the United States. The country's middle region gets more than one thousand of them each year. That region is called Tornado Alley. Parts of South Dakota lie inside it. Parts of Nebraska lie inside it. 82. The Alamo and Texas Freedom

1The year was 1836. People now call that region Texas. Mexico's army kept the Alamo under a siege. Mexican troops raised a red flag. They flew it from a church. The church stood in the town of Béxar. The flag carried a hard message. Fighters inside the Alamo should expect no mercy. That church is San Fernando. A mission stands with it in Béxar. Texan rebels held out for thirteen days. Mexican soldiers faced them the whole time. The Mexican force was much larger. Colonel William B. Travis asked for more troops. The requests were urgent. Few soldiers arrived to help. Travis saw the likely end. He and his men would probably die. Death would come while they defended the Alamo. A legend is told about March 5. On that day, Travis spoke to his men. He called the situation hopeless. He marked a line in the dirt. His sword made the line. He asked each man to cross the line. A man who crossed would stay. He would fight the Mexican army. He might die in that fight. All the men but one crossed. They stayed to fight. A map of Texas helps show the places. It marks San Antonio de Béxar. It marks the Alamo. It also marks Gonzales and Goliad. San Jacinto is marked too. The Gulf of Mexico appears on the map. The clock read about 3:00 a.m. The morning was March 6. Mexican soldiers moved without speaking. They made a ring around the Alamo. Every soldier took a spot in that ring. Dawn was close. Then the attack started. A few hours went by. Almost every person inside was dead by then. The siege took many lives. The battle took many lives too. About 200 Texans died. Mexican losses were 400 to 500 soldiers. Bigger wars have happened in later years. Even so, this fight holds a key place. The place is inside United States history.

2Looking back shows the reasons. Mexico's first people were Native tribes. They lived in this region for thousands of years. The early 1500s brought the Spanish into Mexico. They came looking for gold. Spain turned Mexico into a colony. Spanish leaders worked to convert Native people. They wanted those people to follow Christianity. Starting in the late 1600s, Spain built missions. The missions spread over a wide region. Part of that region is now Mexico. The other part is the southwestern United States. The year 1718 came next. Spain set up two places beside a river then. One place was a fort. The other place was a mission. The river is the San Antonio River. The two places stood on facing banks. In 1731, Spanish settlers began a town. They called the town San Antonio de Béxar. A river lay between the town and the mission. A small map shows the layout. It shows the Alamo fort and the mission. It shows San Fernando mission. It shows the river and the town. A map from circa 1833 shows the wider region. The United States is on it. Mexico is on it too. Texas is marked. The Alamo is marked too. The Florida Territory is marked. The Oregon Country is marked. Some land is shown as disputed. Other land is shown as territories. The Gulf of Mexico is drawn. The Pacific Ocean is drawn too. In 1801, the Spanish military changed the old mission at Béxar. Soldiers began to use it as a fort. People renamed the fort. The new name was the Alamo. In the Spanish language, Alamo means cottonwood tree. Settlers from the United States reached Texas in 1821. Stephen F. Austin led the first group. Many more families came after that group. At that time, the frontier in Texas was wide open. Its land was rich. Farmers could work that land. Ranchers could work it too.

3Leaders in the United States had a large hope. They wanted the country to grow. They wanted the growth to reach the Pacific Ocean. Mexico rose up against Spanish rule. In 1821, the revolt made Mexico independent. Texas then belonged to Mexico. Spain no longer held Texas. In 1824, Mexico formed a republic. It adopted a constitution at that time. The new constitution was like another famous one. That other one was the U.S. Constitution. A picture from these years shows Mexico's flag. Anglo settlers were the largest group living in Texas. They had come from the United States. Some Tejanos lived in Texas too. Tejanos were settlers born in Mexico. Most Anglos farmed the land. They had taken Mexican citizenship. They stayed loyal to Mexico. They felt grateful for the chance to settle. By 1830, Anglo numbers had climbed. The count was at least 20,000. Mexico's government grew worried. Leaders feared Mexico was losing its control of Texas. A new law tried to block further Anglo moves into Texas. The government also outlawed slavery. Anglo settlers grew angry at that ban. They wanted plantations. They wanted enslaved workers on those plantations. The new laws divided Texans. Some wanted Texas linked with the United States. A second group wanted a fully separate Texas country. A third group wanted a different result. They wanted Texas to be a separate state. The state would remain inside Mexico. Over time, more Texans rejected Mexican rule. Mexico's leaders would not give up Texas. Mexico had let thousands of Anglos settle. Those settlers lived inside its borders. The settlers then grew angrier. Leaders feared the United States might send force. That force could take Texas away from Mexico. Soldiers went out to block the plan. Mexico sent weapons for the same reason. In 1833, Mexico gained a new president. General Santa Anna took the office. The next year, he changed the system. He ended the democracy.

4A dictatorship took its place. Texans became even more determined to leave Mexican rule. The opening battle came in early October 1835. That battle started the fight so Texas could be independent. The town of the battle was Gonzales. Texans won. Hope for independence grew after the win. New fighters joined the rebels. Most of them were volunteers. The volunteers came from the United States. In late October 1835, rebels closed a ring around the Alamo. Mexican troops were trapped inside the fort. The rebels kept them under siege. The Texan attack date was December 5, 1835. Mexican troops had more men. They had three men for every one Texan. The Texans still captured the fort. They took it from Mexican General Cós. Fighting went on for four days. While the fort was surrounded, Texan leaders met. The meeting town was San Felipe. They discussed what should happen to Texas next. They created a government for an independent Texas. Henry Smith was chosen as governor. Sam Houston was chosen to lead the rebel army. After the win, many Texan troops left the Alamo. They went to fight in other parts of Mexico. About 100 men remained. Colonel James C. Neill commanded them. Winter was near. The men were low on food. They were low on supplies too. Neill sent a letter to General Sam Houston. The letter asked for more troops. It also asked for more supplies. Houston did not think the fort could be held. He sent Jim Bowie out with 30 troops. Bowie was told to move the men away. He was also told to destroy the fort. Mexican soldiers must not use the fort later. Neill persuaded Bowie to change the plan.

5Neill argued that the Alamo had value. He said defenders ought to hold the fort. A letter from Bowie went to Governor Henry Smith. Smith agreed to send more troops. He agreed to send weapons too. Colonel William Travis came with 30 soldiers. Davy Crockett arrived soon afterward. Crockett had once been a soldier for the United States. He brought a group of volunteer riflemen. Not long after Crockett arrived, Neill departed. Neill's wife was ill. Neill left Travis in charge of the troops. Bowie was the commander picked by the volunteers. The two commanders often did not get along. They still both worked to strengthen defenses. They also kept calling on Texan leaders to send aid. Santa Anna meant to retake the Alamo. Soldiers were to take spots in a ring. The ring went around the Alamo. They walked into place without noise. They waited there until dawn was near. A bugle then sounded the call to arms. Rooms for officers are labeled. The entrance is labeled. The diagram also marks north. The town on the diagram is San Antonio de Béxar. Santa Anna sent still more soldiers. Sharpshooters inside the walls shot many of them. The Mexican troops fell back so they could regroup. Santa Anna sent them forward again. They climbed the walls. They swarmed over the compound. The Texans then fought up close. They fought hand to hand. Rifles no longer helped them. The rifles were useless. The Texans kept fighting with courage. They already knew the result was hopeless. The fighting stopped sometime after 6:30 a.m. It stopped before 9:00 a.m. Almost all of the Texan men were dead. A few still lived. Those few were executed not long after. Nobody knows the exact number of dead. Belief puts the Texan dead at 190 or more. Belief also says the Texan dead stayed at or under 260. Mexican dead are put at 400 or more. They are put at or under 500. Some people were spared. The spared group included women. It included female children. It included two enslaved people. Santa Anna did not stop at the Alamo. He still planned to end the rebellion. The rebellion was Texas seeking independence. His army won a further battle. The place was Goliad. After that win, he thought the revolt was over. 7News of the Alamo spread. Sympathy for Texans grew inside the United States. Many people wanted revenge. Anglo Texans felt that wish. Citizens of the United States felt it too. The wish was for men Santa Anna's troops had killed. Houston launched a sudden strike. He chose April 21, 1836, for the strike. The Mexican camp sat at San Jacinto. Houston's army was not expected there. Texans rushed the camp. During the rush, they shouted a cry. The cry was Remember the Alamo. The fighting ended after 18 minutes. Mexican dead numbered more than 600. Many other Mexican soldiers were wounded. Still others were taken prisoner. Texas lost only nine men in the fight. The next day, troops captured Santa Anna. Many Texans wanted him put to death. Houston would not allow that. Houston spared him. Freedom for Santa Anna depended on terms. Santa Anna had to recognize independence for Texas. He also had to take every one of his troops away. The troops had to leave Texas. Santa Anna accepted both terms. Mexico's government later rejected them. It would not agree that Texas was independent. Texans paid no attention to that refusal. They believed they were free. They elected Sam Houston as their president. He led the Republic of Texas. Right away, Texas asked the United States for statehood. Statehood waited on one task. Texas needed its own stable government. Statehood came in December 1845. Until that month, the United States treated Texas as its own nation. Many countries in Europe did the same. A map shows divisions after September 1848. It shows land the United States had acquired. It shows the Republic of Texas. Mexico is on the map. The Gulf of Mexico is on it. The Pacific Ocean is on it too. A photo shows the Alamo in the present day. Texans and U.S. citizens fought there for many reasons. Some wanted to become rich landowners.

8Others wanted to hold enslaved workers. Most believed the cause was freedom. Anglo families lived in Texas. Tejano families lived there too. Most people in both groups wanted independence. They wanted to leave Mexico's dictatorship behind. Across the United States, people remember the battle as a symbol. The symbol stands for heroism. That heroism sits inside a struggle. The struggle's goal was freedom. In Mexico, people see the battle as one piece of a campaign. The aim was to steal Mexican land. The full story is rarely simple. Right and wrong are not the whole story. People need every viewpoint. Only then can they see what really happened. All of this happened at the Alamo fort. The first life story is Stephen F. Austin. He lived from 1793 to 1836. In 1821, he guided settlers into Texas. The settlers were from the United States. His command of the rebel Texas army lasted only a short time. He then left to ask the U.S. government for help. The help was meant for Texas independence. After independence, he served as secretary of state. He died later that same year. He also gained money by forcing travel on enslaved people. Texas became his home late in the 1820s. Mexican citizenship came after the move. His wife was a daughter in a prominent family. That family was Mexican. In 1833, disease killed his wife. The same disease killed his in-laws. He afterward joined rebels who wanted Texas free. He was killed at the Alamo. Davy Crockett lived from 1786 to 1836. While young, he learned how to stay alive in wild country. At age 25, he entered the army of the United States. He gained fame for bravery. He also gained fame for rifle skill. He served in the state government of Tennessee.

9Later he served in the Senate of the United States. In 1835, he lost his place in Congress. He traveled to Texas to seek land. He hoped to find money there too. He got to the Alamo only weeks before the siege began. Santa Anna led that siege. Crockett then joined rebels seeking Texas independence. He was killed at the Alamo. Three early marks belong on the time line. In 1801, Spanish troops began fort use of the Alamo. The use was military. In 1821, Mexico became a republic on its own. In 1830, Mexico's government passed a blocking law. New Anglo settlers were stopped. They could not move into Texas. Sam Houston lived from 1793 to 1863. His fighting record includes the War of 1812. He held a seat in Congress for the United States. He also served as Tennessee's governor. His Texas years began in 1832. Joining Texas to the United States was his goal. He was the Texas army's commander in chief. His men beat Santa Anna in the San Jacinto fight. After Texas was independent, voters made him president. After Texas became a state, he took a Senate seat for Texas. Later he served as governor again. Antonio López de Santa Anna lived from 1794 to 1876. During the 1820s, he was a hero in Mexico. Mexico was struggling to leave Spain. The goal was independence. He took the presidency in 1833. He then ruled as a dictator. He fought hard to keep Texas under Mexico. He lost that effort. Loss forced him to resign. He held the presidency again in 1841–45. He held it again in 1853–55. William Barret Travis lived from 1809 to 1836. He left Alabama because of debt. He also left because of an unhappy marriage. Soon after reaching Texas, he joined a group of men. The men wanted statehood for Texas inside the United States.

10The Texas army gave him the rank of colonel. He commanded during the siege at the Alamo. He commanded during the battle there too. He was among the earliest Texans killed in that fight. His death came at the Alamo. More marks belong on the time line. Santa Anna became Mexico's president in 1833. In October 1835, Texans won a battle at Gonzales. It was the first battle of their break from Mexico. In December 1835, Texans attacked the Alamo. They captured the fort in that attack. On March 6, 1836, fighters clashed at the Alamo. Another clash came on April 21 of that year. Men under Houston beat the troops of Santa Anna. San Jacinto was the site of the win. In 1845, the United States took Texas in as a state. Texas was state number 28. These words have plain meanings. An Anglo is a white person whose roots are European. Plantations are crop lands that need a large work force. A call to arms is a signal. A bugle sounds it. Sharpshooters are people very skilled with a gun. A colony is land run by a different country. A siege means an enemy is surrounded for a long period. Attacks often come during a siege. Food and other supplies are blocked too. Defiant describes bold resistance to an enemy. A dictatorship is rule by one leader. That leader takes total control. The people have not approved it. Spared means saved from being killed. A frontier is wild country along an outer edge. That edge is a country's official border.
