84. The Biggest Lizards on Earth

1This book has these parts. Real Dragons. Built to Fight. Island Home. Dragon Food. Dragon Babies. Saving Dragons. Monster Lizards. Words to Know. Real Dragons People read stories about dragons. In those stories a dragon is huge. It is fierce. It is a reptile. Often it breathes fire. Its body is powerful. Its claws are sharp. Some readers think dragons live only in storybooks. Those readers should look again. The Komodo dragon is a living animal. It is a lizard. No lizard on Earth grows larger. Hold a dragon story next to this animal. Almost every detail lines up. One detail does not. This lizard cannot breathe fire. Its bite comes close to that same deadly power. See the Size Set a Komodo dragon beside a person. The dragon can be 10 feet (3 m) long. The dragon can weigh 176 pounds (80 kg). The person may stand 6 feet (1.8 m) tall. The person may weigh 176 pounds (80 kg). On this chart the two weights are equal. The lizard stretches farther than the person stands high. Length is the first number to compare. Weight is the second.

2The picture is there so you can see the difference in size. Male dragons battle one another. The fight is over females. Built to Fight Among lizards, Komodo dragons are the heavyweights. Their bodies are made for combat. A dragon seizes a rival with its front legs. It tries to slam that rival onto the ground. A muscular tail keeps the body balanced. Balance matters most when the dragon rises upright. Two males need that balance in a fight. Bony plates cover the skin. The plates block bites from a rival. They block scratches too. The teeth are sharp and jagged. The claws are huge. Teeth help during battle. Claws help during battle. Teeth also help when a dragon kills prey. Claws help with that kill as well. Is This Lizard a Reptile? The skin feels rough. It can be black. It can be yellow-gray. Bony plates lie in the skin. About sixty teeth fill the mouth. Each tooth is sharp. The teeth tear flesh. The tail is long. Strong muscles run through the tail. The tongue splits into a fork. The claws are long.

3Each claw curves. Every reptile has a backbone. Every reptile has scales or bony plates. Lungs are how every reptile breathes. Eggs are what most reptiles lay. Most reptiles are cold-blooded. Where These Dragons Live A map of the region shows Asia. It shows Indonesia. It shows the Indian Ocean. It shows the Lesser Sunda Islands. It shows the Flores Sea and the Savu Sea. The island names include Komodo, Flores, Padar, and Rinca. Gili Motang is marked. Gili Dasami is marked. One shading shows where dragons live now. Another shading shows where they lived before. Homes on the Islands Five small islands are where these dragons live. The islands are part of Indonesia. Indonesia is a country in Asia. Hills cover the islands. Forests grow there. Grasslands grow there too. The weather stays hot. A rainy season arrives. A dry season arrives. On two of the islands the dragons are much smaller. On the other three islands the dragons are larger. The smaller body is an adaptation. Less food is one cause. A harsher climate is another cause. These animals swim with real strength.

4A dragon can cross from one island to the next. Most of them never leave the home island. They often stroll the beaches. They search for dead fish. The waves have carried those fish onto the shore. A burrow is often only just wide enough for the animal inside. In the heat of day, the giant lizards slip into burrows to cool off. At night the same holes help them hold warmth. A dragon may dig the burrow itself. It may move into a burrow another dragon already made. A dragon usually keeps to itself. It hunts on its own. It eats on its own. It naps on its own. Humans carried three main prey animals to these islands. The three are the Timor deer, the water buffalo, and the wild pig. Dragons now live where those animals were brought. Dragon Food Meat is the only rule for a Komodo dragon meal. The kind of meat can vary. These lizards hunt. They also feed on animals that have already died. Deer are a main food. Wild pigs are a main food. Water buffalo are a main food.

5Rats get eaten too. Snakes get eaten. Bird eggs get eaten. Dead fish get eaten. An adult will even eat a young dragon. A dragon can sprint after prey. An ambush is more common. The dragon then overpowers the animal. Hiding spots line the trails. The dragon waits for an animal to pass. Then it strikes. The hunted animal is not usually killed on the spot. A bite may land. The wounded animal may escape. Death still usually comes quickly. It can also come within a few days. More than one path leads to that death. The open wound may drain the animal of blood until it dies. Harmful bacteria live in the dragon's mouth. Those bacteria may start a deadly infection. After a bite, prey may stand in dirty water. The dirty water may start an infection of its own. That infection can kill. Not long ago, scientists found a surprise. Komodo dragons carry venom. Venom is a poison. The bite puts it into the prey. Further study is still needed. Researchers need to learn the part venom plays in these deaths.

6They also need to learn the part bacteria play. Top speed is 13 miles per hour. The metric figure is 20 kmph. Dead animals leave a trail a dragon can follow. The tool is a forked tongue. The tongue tastes the air. Next the tongue taps a special organ. The organ sits on the roof of the mouth. It picks out tiny odor particles floating in the air. One tip of the tongue may carry more particles than the other tip. The heavier tip points toward the prey. The dragon heads off in that direction. A meal waits somewhere along that line. These lizards usually share a kill. Mealtime is still dangerous. Fights flare between dragons over the food. At hatching, a baby measures a bit past one foot. That is 0.3 m. Dragon Babies A female may dig a nest in the ground. She may place a nest on a hillside. Some females skip both choices. They use a mound a bird already built for its own eggs. One nest holds from ten to thirty-five eggs. Six to nine months pass before the eggs hatch.

7Through all those months the female stands guard. She keeps predators away from the eggs. The eggs open when the rainy season is nearly over. The month is April. Insects are plentiful then, and the babies need that food. From the first day, the babies must manage alone. They climb into trees. Tree branches keep them safe from adult dragons. Other predators have a harder time reaching them up there. Two years in the trees is common for the young. Some stay as long as four years. Insects are on the menu. Geckos are on the menu. Rodents are on the menu. Birds are on the menu. Later, the young feed on leftovers. The leftovers come from meals the adults have left. Adult dragons weigh too much to climb after the young. The young stay in the trees so they will not be eaten. A Komodo dragon becomes an adult around the age of seven. A male may reach the age of sixty. A female may live only half as long. Scientists see a reason for the shorter female life. Nest building spends extra energy.

8Laying eggs spends extra energy. Guarding the eggs spends extra energy. One meal can be enormous. In one feeding, an adult may take in over three-quarters of what it weighs. An extra hinge sits in the lower jaw. The hinge lets the mouth gape wide. Food bigger than the head can go down in one swallow. At times the young roll around in droppings from their own bodies. The scent can turn adults away. Those adults may then skip a hunt for the young. Keeping Dragons Alive A count of wild dragons comes to only 3,000 on the low end and 5,000 on the high end. Female lives are much shorter. Females that can breed may number only 350, or even fewer. The animals are listed as vulnerable. Vulnerable means they stand at risk of becoming endangered. People clear wild land. Dragons lose homes when that land goes. A dragon may attack livestock. Villagers may kill the dragon for it. Poachers kill dragons. Poachers also kidnap them. The stolen animals are sold as pets. In some areas, food runs short. Dragons must compete with humans for it.

9They must compete with wild dogs too. Scientists in many countries are working so these lizards do not go extinct. Some of them study dragons in Indonesia. They learn the animals' habits. They learn what the animals need. Conservation groups join with schools. They join with communities. They teach people ways to help protect the dragons. Zoos have raised Komodo dragons and succeeded. The work has continued since 1992. Some of the zoos are inside Indonesia. Some are outside it. Many different zoos now take part in keeping dragons alive. A dragon tastes the air with its tongue. The taste offers clues about prey. Monster Lizards No lizard in the world is bigger than a Komodo dragon. These animals are fierce. They hunt with clever skill. A long list of adaptations helps them stay alive. Teeth are one tool, and they are sharp. Claws are another sharp tool. The body is huge. The body is strong. A body like that can overpower almost any rival. More than seventy zoos, spread around the world, keep these lizards. One day you may be lucky and see one.

10You may admire how these heavyweight wrestlers are put together. You may look on in awe. Dragons are not trapped inside storybooks. Living dragons share our world. Words to Know An adaptation is a change in one living thing, or in a whole kind of living thing. The change helps it survive more easily in its home. To ambush is to burst from a hiding place and strike by surprise. Bacteria are tiny one-celled living things. At times they cause infection and disease. Conservation is the care of wild land. It is also the care of the living things found on that land. Muscular describes a body that has large, strong muscles. An organ is one body part with its own job. The kidneys are organs. The lungs are organs. Poachers are people who kill wild animals when the law forbids it. Reptiles are animals that are cold-blooded and have a backbone. Scales or plates cover their bodies. Venom is a poisonous liquid. Some animals kill prey with it. Some defend themselves with it. A bite usually carries it. A sting can carry it too.

85. The Branch That Writes the Laws

1This book tells about the United States Congress. It tells how the Constitution sets up the government. It tells how Congress works. It tells the steps that turn a proposal into law. It tells what members of Congress do. That includes committees, speeches, getting elected, and voting. It tells how power is shared. It tells about the duty of Congress. A word list comes at the end. The United States Congress. During summer 1964, members of Congress in the United States discussed a proposed law. People of color would share schools with white people under the Civil Rights Act. It would also open the same libraries, restaurants, and swimming pools. A long speech came from Senator Robert Byrd. His state was West Virginia. His aim was to stop the Civil Rights Act. The House of Representatives had already said yes to the act. The Senate is the other half of Congress. It still had to agree. Long speeches came from a group of senators. They spoke on the floor of the Senate. They were trying to stop a vote from happening. The longest of those talks ran fourteen hours and thirteen minutes. Once that speech ended, the Senate at last voted yes on the Civil Rights Act. Later, President Lyndon Johnson put his signature on it and made it law. This act shows only one way that Congress does its work.

2Members of the Senate sit in Congress. House members have seats there as well. Within the legislative branch, this is the main body. Members of both parts represent citizens of the United States. They are responsible for writing the laws of the country. Changing those laws is part of the duty too. They have other important duties as well. How the Constitution Sets Up the Government. The Constitution was adopted in 1788. The plan it sets is a blueprint for government in the United States. Government is split into three parts. Each part is called a branch. The executive branch is led by the president. Most day-to-day government work sits under this branch, along with the departments. The Senate belongs to the legislative branch. The House of Representatives belongs to it as well. It represents citizens in government. It also makes laws. Courts of the United States sit in the judicial branch. At times, the branches work together. Disagreement shows up at other moments. Creating new laws is a right given to the legislative branch in Article I. It also gives that branch the right to change laws that already exist. No other part of the government can do this. Many further rights and duties of Congress also come from Article I. Since the Constitution was adopted, twenty-seven amendments have been made. An amendment is a change.

3Thomas Jefferson was the third president of the United States. A contest to design the Capitol Building was held by him in 1792. How Congress Works. Work for senators and for House members happens inside the Capitol Building. The two groups have different numbers of members. Each state gets two senators. The size of the state does not change that number. Population does not change it either. The Senate has one hundred senators. A senator's term lasts six years. Some jobs the president fills need a yes from the Senate. Supreme Court judges are one example. Treaties with other countries also need a yes from the Senate. Population sets how the House of Representatives is filled. It has 435 members. Each member is elected to a term of two years. Those seats are shared across the fifty states. The split follows each state's total population. No state in the United States has more people than California. That is why its group in the House is the biggest. States with smaller populations have fewer. Delaware has only one representative. Delaware sends just one person to the House. Her name is Representative Lisa Blunt Rochester. In Oregon, during a meeting called a town hall, a man puts a question to his representative. Members of the House elect their leader. That leader is called the Speaker of the House. The Speaker would take over if the president could not serve.

4The same is true if the vice president could not do the job. The Speaker would then take over the presidency. That duty is why the Speaker's job carries so much power. Citizens who dislike the way the country is run can reach their representative. Politicians also lead town hall meetings that any person may attend. At those meetings, people can talk openly with their representatives about government matters. Rules for a Seat in the Senate or the House. A Senate seat requires an age of at least thirty. The person must have been a citizen of the United States for the last nine years. The person must live in the state he or she wants to represent. A House seat requires an age of at least twenty-five. The person must have been a citizen for at least seven years. The person must live in the state he or she wants to represent. The Path From a Bill to a Law. Making a new law takes many steps. Writing the bill is step one. Anyone can do this. A person in the public may write a bill too. A member of Congress must then offer the bill and act as its sponsor. The offer can go to the Senate. It can go to the House. It can go to both.

5The bill then goes to one or more committees in the Senate or the House. The committees review it. Committee members research the bill. Choosing which laws need a look is part of their job. They recommend what to do next. Hearings are part of committee work. Experts are questioned about the bill during a hearing. They try to find answers to any problems. In the Senate, a scientist speaks during a hearing held by a committee. A subcommittee is the next group to review the bill. Subcommittees research the bill further. A hearing comes next. A vote comes too. A yes from most of the subcommittee sends the bill back to the full committee. The full committee then holds a hearing and a vote. Talk on the bill stops when a majority of the full committee refuses to support it. Members of Congress can bring bills back many times. They often do. Support from most of the full committee puts the bill onto the official calendar. That calendar belongs to the Senate or the House. Bills that matter most are decided at once. A wait of many months is possible for the rest. A large share are never taken up. An illustration made in 1850 shows members of Congress arguing fiercely over slavery. Bills That Die. Each term in Congress runs two years. When the term ends, bills that did not pass are called dead.

6Some of those bills cleared the Senate or the House alone. They did not clear both. Bills that cleared both houses also count if the president never signed them. A Math Minute. Most bills that are proposed never become laws. The count of bills put forward from January 2011 through January 2013 was 6,845. Only 561 of those bills passed and became laws. What number failed to become law? The answer is 6,284. On the day set for a bill, debate opens in the Senate or in the House. Changes are allowed at that stage. Then that house votes on the bill. Majority approval sends the bill across to Congress's other chamber. It is debated again. It may be changed again. Once each house has a majority in favor, the bill goes to the desk of the president. One choice is a signature from the president. If that happens, it becomes a law. There is another way for a bill to become law. The president can let ten days pass. It then becomes law on its own. The president can also veto the bill, which means reject it. The bill then goes back to Congress. A bill may still turn into law even if the president withholds approval. Two-thirds of the Senate must vote to override the veto. Two-thirds of the House must vote the same way.

7What Members of Congress Do. A member's schedule is usually packed. Some pieces of that work are described below. One piece of the work is committee service. Senators receive posts on committees and on subcommittees. Members of the House receive those posts as well. Some committees in Congress are permanent. Examples include committees for education and the workforce, for agriculture, and for the budget. These are called standing committees. A different committee may study a single problem, and only for a limited time. Certain tasks are handed to smaller groups that a committee creates. Speeches. A senator may speak on a bill with no time cap. A time limit can change that. Often just a handful of senators stay on the floor while a bill is discussed. Other senators are busy with committees. Others are busy in their offices. A ringing bell calls senators in so a vote can be taken. There are many more representatives than senators. Because of that, rules limit how long representatives can speak about a bill. The rules also cap how many edits they may offer on a bill. Getting Elected. Campaign work fills much of the schedule for members of Congress. They also spend a lot of time fund-raising. A new election for representatives comes every two years. Keeping the job depends heavily on raising money.

8In a year with an election, raising money can fill four hours of a representative's day. The money pays for advertisements. It pays for travel, posters, stickers, and stamps. Phone calls are one tool members of Congress use when they seek votes. They also use speeches and interviews. They talk about what they have done for the people they represent. They talk about what they plan to do. During a 2018 rally, a senator presents Representative Ayanna Pressley. She is from Massachusetts. Voting. Casting a vote means being inside the Capitol Building in person. A House member votes by sliding a card into a machine. The House has forty-seven voting stations for this. Senators have three ways to vote. In a roll call vote, a clerk calls each name. The senator then votes aloud. During a voice vote, senators call out their choices as one group. Exact numbers are not counted. A division vote has another name, a standing vote. Each spoken choice is then counted on its own. How Power Is Shared. Those who wrote the Constitution wanted no branch to misuse the power it holds. The branches are legislative, executive, and judicial. The Constitution contains a system known as checks and balances. It makes sure power is spread fairly among the three branches. Two limits let the legislative branch restrain the executive branch. People named by the president for certain jobs need its yes.

9It approves treaties the president makes. Names the president picks for judge jobs need a yes from the legislative branch. That is one check on the judicial branch. Congress can also propose amendments to the Constitution. Those amendments could overturn decisions made by judges. The other two branches can check the legislative branch as well. The presidential veto is one check by the executive branch. Most of Congress can back a bill, and the president can still block it. Congress may still vote to override that veto, which keeps power from tipping too far. Two-thirds of each house must vote to accept the bill. By way of the Supreme Court, the judicial branch can limit the legislative branch. The Court may throw out a law that won approval from Congress and from the president. It does this if it decides the law is unconstitutional. The Duty of Congress. A statue named Freedom rises above the dome. The building under that dome is the Capitol. Both lawmaking houses gather inside that building. The figure is a woman. She wears a helmet. A sword is in her grasp, and so is a laurel wreath. Peace is her wish. If the nation's freedom must be defended, she is prepared to fight. The statue nudges politicians who speak for the American people to remember the nation's purpose.

10The legislative branch can write laws. It can also change laws. That makes it an important part of the government. A voice for every citizen is what senators and representatives work to protect. They work so each citizen has fair standing in the government. Bronze is the material of the statue. The figure's weight is about 15,000 pounds, which is 6,804 kg. Word List. Override means to take over, cancel, or replace something else. Amending means making a change in order to improve something. Permanent means lasting, or meant to last, with no change. Committees are groups of people who consider a course of action or decide on one. Recommend means to suggest. Debate means a long, careful talk about a subject that matters. Research means looking into a question, often to uncover facts or information not known before. Fund-raising is collecting money from people or groups to support a cause or a goal. Congress has two houses that write laws. The Senate is one. It has two members from each state. The House of Representatives is the other lawmaking house. The number of members from each state is based on population. A sponsor is a person who supports another person, an idea, or a thing, and accepts responsibility for it. Legislative is the word for the branch whose job is writing laws.

86. The Cold Plains Without Trees

1Wildflowers color the tundra inside Denali National Park in Alaska. Extremes of every kind mark the tundra. Howling winds cross it. Temperatures there drop to freezing cold. Vast empty plains stretch out, and no trees grow on them. Moss hugs the rocks. Snow lies over the ground during part of each year. In late spring, the tundra bursts into brilliant color. Summer brings the same burst when wildflowers bloom. Great stretches of this land have never been walked by explorers. Its remoteness is one reason. Its unique challenges are another reason. Even so, living things have found ways to survive in this harsh world. Plants have done so. Animals have done so. Humans are among those animals. Sami speech is the likely source of the word tundra. The Sami live in northern Scandinavia. They also live in northwestern Russia. In that language, the word can mean elevated wasteland. It can mean marshy plain. It can also mean a hill with a high top. Different kinds of environments cover the surface of Earth. Biome is the word for a region plus the communities of life in it. A desert is one example of a biome. Grassland, a rainforest, and the ocean count as biomes as well.

2The tundra is a biome as well. Many factors help create the biomes of Earth. Latitude is one important factor. Latitude tells how far a place is from the equator. Elevation is another important factor. Elevation is the height of a place above sea level. Both latitude and height change whether a place feels warm or cool. Climate is an important part of a biome. Land and water matter too. Plants and animals matter as well. The tundra biome sits in the cold parts of the world. Its land is flat, or it rises in gentle hills and valleys. No trees stand on the ground. The ground is bare and rocky. Low plants grow in patchy areas. Other plantlike organisms grow there too. Only a limited set of animals lives in this biome. Musk oxen are animals of the tundra. Most of the tundra on Earth is in the Arctic. The Arctic lies north of the Arctic Circle. High mountain country also holds tundra, and that kind is called alpine. An alpine setting is high on a tall mountain. About one-tenth of the land on Earth is tundra. About one-third of that tundra is the alpine kind. Most of this biome lies in the Northern Hemisphere.

3One reason is that far less land lies near the South Pole. Ice covers most of Antarctica. Antarctica is mainly thought of as a cold desert. A few tundra plants still grow on Antarctica where the coasts are milder. Northern Canada is among the chief regions of Arctic tundra. Alaska, Russia, and Scandinavia hold Arctic tundra too. Parts of Greenland and Antarctica do as well. Alpine tundra is found mainly in Asia and Europe. It is also found on the western side of North America. The western sides of Central America and South America have it too. In some Arctic tundra places, summer brings a Sun that never goes down. Tundra climate can shift a great deal from one area to another. The Arctic tundra is the colder of the two kinds. In summer, temperatures there can reach 4 degrees Celsius. That is about 40 degrees Fahrenheit. In winter, temperatures can fall to minus 32 degrees Celsius. That is minus 25 degrees Fahrenheit. The alpine tundra has milder temperatures. Summers there are usually from 3 to 12 degrees Celsius. That range is 37 to 54 degrees Fahrenheit. Winters are rarely colder than minus 18 degrees Celsius. That temperature is 0 degrees Fahrenheit.

4Both kinds of tundra get little precipitation. The yearly amount is up to about 25 centimeters. That is about 10 inches. About two-thirds of this precipitation falls as rain. Snow can still build up. Wind is usually lighter across the Arctic tundra than across alpine tundra. The Arctic tundra also receives more precipitation. Sometimes permafrost shows along a river. It can also show near a road. A frozen layer under the top soil is a key mark of the Arctic tundra. That layer is called permafrost, and it stays frozen all the time. Each summer the top soil melts. Each winter that top layer turns solid again. Ice underneath can hold water in place. Trapped water cannot drain away. Low Arctic tundra ground turns swampy once summer comes. Soil that is soaked with water can slide down a slope. The alpine tundra has no layer of permafrost. Its soil still freezes and thaws as the seasons change. Surface water there usually drains quickly because the land is steep. The frozen bodies of dead plants and animals stay inside permafrost. Those remains store large amounts of carbon. Carbon stays locked in place while that deep layer remains frozen. If the permafrost thaws, gases leave the ground and enter the air.

5Carbon dioxide is one of those gases. Methane is another. These gases make global warming worse. Melting is underway in permafrost across the southern Arctic. The cause is climate change. A diagram can show the cycle. Carbon dioxide from the thaw rises into the air. Cold forests border a lot of tundra country. Those forests are called taiga. Wind shapes how plants grow in the tundra. Cold temperatures shape growth too. Permafrost limits growth. Surface soil that is poor in nutrients limits it as well. Because of these limits, the growing season is short. It lasts fifty to sixty days. Trees do not grow on the Arctic tundra. Frozen ground is part of the reason. Roots cannot grow deep into that soil. A plant here must have shallow roots if it is to grow at all. In the alpine tundra, trees fail for a different reason. High winds and cold temperatures stop them. Several important adaptations let plants live in the tundra. Plants usually stay low to the ground. Other plantlike organisms do the same. Staying low protects them from high winds. The low growers include lichens. Say lichens like LY-kunz. Mosses grow this way.

6Herbs, grasses, and dwarf shrubs grow this way too. Arctic poppies bloom in the tundra. Tundra plants grow during only two to four months of the year. They have adapted by finishing a whole life cycle in a short time. Many plants open flowers within just a few days of the snow beginning to melt. Some plants need only one month to form seeds that are ready. Many tundra plants gather nutrients for several years. They store the nutrients before they make seeds. Woolly lousewort is one plant of the tundra. High in the alpine tundra, the air holds less carbon dioxide gas. The air is thinner there. Plants in that thin air have adapted. During photosynthesis, they use carbon dioxide in a more efficient way. Some animals of the Arctic tundra change color in winter. The arctic fox is one of them. The new color lets the animal blend with the snow around it. A small variety of plants limits which animals can live in the tundra. Fewer kinds of food are available. Cold temperatures challenge the animals. High winds challenge them too. For the animals that do live here, body features help them survive. Musk oxen grow a thick winter coat that holds in warmth.

7Reindeer grow a thick winter coat too. In North America, people call reindeer by the name caribou. Hooves help these animals walk on slippery ground. Hooves also help them dig through snow to reach food. Arctic foxes have compact bodies. Hares have compact bodies too. Short ears help them hold body heat inside. Short tails help in the same way. Polar bears stay warm with fur. They also have a thick fat layer called blubber. The way an animal behaves can also help it last on the tundra. Grizzly bears hibernate so they can survive the winter. Arctic ground squirrels hibernate too. Lemmings are small rodents. Voles are small rodents too. They store enough food to last through the coldest months. Snow over a nest acts like a warm cover. Snow also helps keep their tunnels warm. Some tundra animals leave during the coldest part of the year. Reindeer are among the animals that leave. Snow geese leave too. These animals travel toward warmer lands that offer more to eat. Many alpine animals make their seasonal trip by heading downhill. In winter they travel to forested land below the high slopes. Wildcats make this trip. Some kinds of birds make it.

8Mountain sheep make it too. Marmots hibernate through the winter. Ground squirrels hibernate as well. Pikas are tiny relatives of rabbits. A pika stays awake all winter. It eats food it stored, and it keeps eating until spring. People have kept a life here across a great many thousands of years. Early on, some groups had no fixed home. They moved as the seasons changed. Their livelihoods included hunting. Fishing was part of life too. Herding was part of life as well. For most of these groups, daily life is no longer what it used to be. Towns, and villages too, are where many of them live now. They still work to keep their traditions alive. New towns of a modern kind have shown up on parts of this land in recent years. A search for oil is one reason. A search for gas is another. A search for minerals is a third reason. Many people also visit the tundra for time outdoors. Skiing draws them. Hiking draws them. Wildlife viewing draws them too. A child of the Nenets people is shown in Siberia, Russia. More than forty native groups carry a long history on this land. The Inuit of Greenland are one group.

9Inuit people also live in the Canadian Arctic. The Aleut live in Alaska. The Inupiat live in Alaska too, along with other groups. The Innu live in northern Labrador and in Quebec, Canada. Russia's far northern Arctic is home to the Nenets. The Sami live in Scandinavia's north and also in northwest Russia. Norway's bare open tundra is a feeding ground for a reindeer. A visit to the tundra in the colder months can make the land look empty. It can look like a wasteland. Empty frozen flatlands run for miles, whichever way you look. Barren slopes full of wind do the same. The tundra still has a beauty of its own. A close look at the tiny plants is worth the time. They look fragile. These plants are sturdy enough to keep living where Earth is at its harshest. Animals of the tundra must be tough as well if they are to make a home here. Lemmings are part of that tough group. Caribou are part of it too. The wonder of this place is the way life continues. The wonder is the set of amazing survival paths used by plants and by animals in this wide frozen land. An adaptation is a change in an organism or in a species.

10The change raises the odds of survival where that life makes its home. Alpine refers to high mountains. It can also describe land above the tree line. Fragile means easy to damage or break. It can mean delicate. Global warming is a rise in the average temperature of Earth. The rise can be large enough to change the climate. To hibernate means to enter a deep sleep. The sleep often comes in winter. Lichens are crusty organisms. They grow on rocks and on trees. To migrate is to shift from one home region to another when the same season returns. The move comes at a set time each year. Nomadic describes moving from place to place with no permanent home. Permafrost names a soil layer in a cold place that does not thaw at any time of year. Photosynthesis is the process plant cells use to make food. Plant cells use chlorophyll so that light, water, air, and nutrients become food. Precipitation names rain, snow, hail, or sleet coming down from the clouds. Hail, sleet, rain, and snow are forms of it. Remoteness is the state of being far away or isolated.

87. The Country of Spain

1Dancers in Maryland move in a traditional Spanish style at a festival. Contents. Finding Spain. The People. The Land. The Past. Festivals. Meals. Closing. Word List. A map of this country marks the Bay of Biscay and France. It marks the Pyrenees, the Atlantic Ocean, and Barcelona. It marks Madrid, the Balearic Islands, and Portugal. It marks Valencia, Córdoba, and Granada. It marks the Mediterranean Sea and the Strait of Gibraltar. It also marks the Canary Islands, Cueta, and Melilla. Spain lies in the southwest of Europe. The Iberian Peninsula is the land it sits on. The Pyrenees, said PEER-uh-neez, rise north of Spain. Spain's land runs south to a narrow body of water. That water is the Strait of Gibraltar. France is the neighbor on the northern side. Portugal is the neighbor on the western side. Spain's land also takes in the Balearic Islands. Those islands form a beautiful string. They sit off the eastern coast.

2The sea around them is the Mediterranean. The capital of Spain is Madrid. The city holds about 3.3 million people. About 6.5 million people have homes or jobs in the area around the city. A raised plateau is where Madrid sits. That plateau is about 640 meters above sea level, or 2,100 ft. Madrid ranks among Europe's oldest cities. Some of its buildings go back to the 1500s. Madrid's Royal Palace is among the grandest buildings in Europe. Inside are 2,800 rooms. The state now uses the palace for special parties and events. Spain's royal family once lived there. They now stay outside Madrid, in a palace that is much smaller. The picture shows that Royal Palace, one of Europe's finest. Olive growers in Spain raise more than two hundred kinds. In 2014, Spain moved past Italy. It became the top maker of olive oil in the world. About forty-eight million people call Spain home.

3Most of them live in cities. Madrid, Barcelona, and Valencia are examples. Tourism is a major part of life in Spain. About two million people have jobs in that industry. Making cars is also one of the biggest sources of work. Other jobs are in food, clothing, shipbuilding, and medical equipment. No other country makes more olive oil than Spain. Spain is a member of the European Union, called the EU. Five countries started the EU. They were Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, and Luxembourg. The EU asks countries to face shared problems as a group. Trade is one of those problems. Security is another. So are the rights of citizens. By 2024, twenty-seven nations belonged to the EU. The official language of Spain is Spanish. Other languages are spoken in some regions. One picture shows a woman buying fruit at a market. Another shows workers getting clothing ready for stores. A landform map names the Pyrenees and the Meseta Central.

4It names the Sierra Morena and the Sierra Nevada. It also names the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts. Spain's land is not all the same. High plateaus fill some areas. Dry places that seem like desert fill others. Central Spain has a plateau called the Meseta Central. About half the country lies under that plateau. At its southern edge rise the Sierra Morena. Those mountains are beautiful. Silver, lead, and copper are mined there. Farm animals are raised there too. The craggy Sierra Nevada also stands in the south. In the north, the Pyrenees form a solid line between Spain and France. Mountains and many beaches make the landscape beautiful. The Pyrenees chain stretches 434 kilometers, or 270 miles. It begins on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea. It ends at the Atlantic Ocean on the west. A high wall of mountains stands between France and Spain. The chain has three zones.

5They are the eastern zone, the central zone, and the western zone. People live in each zone. Weather is different in each one. Animals differ too. One rare bird there is the bearded vulture. A goat-antelope lives there as well. It is known for how well it climbs. The picture shows these mountains on the border of France and Spain. Granada has a castle that was built in the 1300s. Around 800 bce, settlers from the Middle East came to southern Spain. They sailed with great skill. Shipbuilding was one of their skills. Glassmaking was another. Greek traders arrived too. They carried olive trees with them. They carried grapes. The Romans came several hundred years after that. They laid many roads. Bridges linked the towns. They dug canals, which are ditches. River water traveled in those canals to nearby cities. Germanic people from the north came after the Romans. They made jewelry that was colorful and beautiful.

6Moorish people arrived from northern Africa in the 700s ce. Some of their buildings remain. The palace still standing in Granada is one of them. Power came to King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella in the 1400s. They ruled Spain together. They paid explorers to search for new trade routes. Christopher Columbus was one of those explorers. Spain built colonies in the New World. Today that New World is North and South America. Gold came back to Europe from the colonies. Silver and spices came back too. Enslaved people were sent back as well. Much of the wealth was later spent fighting other countries. Spain's riches started to fade. Its power faded with them. In the 1800s and the early 1900s, rich people and poor people were far from equal. That gap led some people to try to overthrow the elected government. The try failed. Fighting then broke out in the Spanish Civil War.

7The war began in 1936. It went on until 1939. Francisco Franco became leader once the war was over. His death came in 1975. In 1978, Spain set up a different form of government. A monarchy stayed in place, so there is still a king or a queen. Elected officials hold the power to rule. They also hold the power to pass laws. Spain is still led by that government. La Tomatina may be the largest tomato fight on Earth. Truckloads of tomatoes are thrown from person to person. The throwing is just for fun. Local holidays in Spain are called fiestas, or festivals. Dancing is part of a fiesta. Singing is part of it. Fireworks are part of it too. April 23 is Saint George's Day. Loved ones receive books on that day. They also receive red roses. July in Pamplona brings the festival called San Fermín. People try to dodge bulls during the festival.

8The bulls run down Pamplona's streets. The run is short, about three minutes or four. Excitement is still high. Danger is high too. October 12 is National Day. The date recalls Spain's arrival in the Americas. Spanish people use the day to remember how Spain has shaped the wider world. Three meals a day is the pattern for most people in Spain. Breakfast is often a sweet roll. Milk or hot chocolate goes with it. The largest meal is lunch. Soup may be on the table. Salad may come next. A main dish may follow, and then a sweet dessert. Dinner is often salad and sandwiches. Each region cooks in its own way. Seafood is the usual food beside the sea. Beans and lentils are common in central Spain. Lamb and pork are common there too. Warm months bring gazpacho. Gazpacho is soup that is served cold. Tomatoes and other vegetables go into it. Tapas are foods you eat with your fingers.

9Olives can be a tapa. Nuts can be a tapa. Meats can be a tapa. Some tapas are cold. Some are hot. Shrimp and squid are served along the coasts. Sausages are served inland. Tapas come in many bite-size pieces. In Spanish, the word tapa means lid. A church in Barcelona was designed by Antoni Gaudí. Work started in 1882. The building is still going up. Many people in Spain feel proud of what their culture has given the world. The story of Spain is long. It is also complex. Culture from Spain has touched many parts of the world. Actions from Spain's past have touched the world too. The land takes your breath away. The fiestas are full of fun. Living in our world is more interesting because Spain is part of it. Spain statistics for 2022 come from World O Meter. The population is 46,785,909. The land covers 498,980 square kilometers, or 310,052 square miles.

10Madrid is the capital. The primary language is Castilian Spanish. About 74 percent of the people speak it. The primary religion is Roman Catholic. The currency is the euro. Word List. Cultural describes the beliefs, the customs, the language, or the arts of one group of people. Industry means the businesses that make or sell one kind of product or service. Monarchy means rule by one person who was not elected, such as a king or a queen. Peninsula means a long stretch of land with water on nearly every side. Plateau means a wide area of flat land that is raised up. Region means one particular place or area. Security means being kept safe from danger, from loss, or from threat. Strait means a thin channel of water that joins two large bodies of water. Tourism means the work of serving people who travel for pleasure.

88. The Flu and How to Fight It

1Has your throat ever felt sore? Have you had a headache with a fever? Was the pain so strong that sleep was all you wanted? Flu germs may have been in your body. Learning about the flu helps you fight back. Learning about the flu helps you stay healthy. This book tells what the flu is. It tells what causes the flu. It tells what the flu feels like. It tells how to treat the flu. A picture shows a boy who has the flu. A picture shows an avian influenza virus. The flu is also called influenza. Say influenza as in-floo-EN-zah. A virus causes it. Tiny size is what makes a virus a microorganism. A microorganism is a microbe. A microbe is a germ. Unaided eyes cannot see a virus. Only a powerful microscope lets scientists view a virus. The microscope can magnify a virus to a thousand times its size. The head of a pin has room for hundreds of thousands of these microbes. Small as they are, viruses are dangerous. They can move fast between separate living things. Viruses are everywhere. Only certain kinds of viruses harm humans. Harmful viruses include influenza. Human cells are the place these viruses go into. Then they make copies of themselves at a rapid pace. Person-to-person travel is how influenza viruses get around.

2That movement is how the flu spreads. Washing your hands can help stop the spread. A hand or arm over a cough can also slow the spread. A cough sends germs into the air. People who breathe those germs in can get infected. One drawing explains the path a virus takes inside a body. A virus invades a cell. The virus takes over that cell. The virus makes copies of itself. The copies break out of the cell. The copies start invading other cells. A diagram labels the nose. It labels the mouth. It labels the pharynx. It labels the windpipe, also called the trachea. It labels the larynx. It labels the lungs. The respiratory tract is the target of flu viruses. The respiratory tract is the path air takes when you breathe. That path runs through the nose, the mouth, the throat, and the lungs. Different viruses cause the many kinds of flu. One kind of flu feels much like another. This illness infects the respiratory tract. The whole body can feel the effects. An achy feeling is a usual result. It makes you feel feverish. It makes you feel tired. It makes you feel sick to your stomach. Influenza has three basic types. One type is Influenza A. One type is Influenza B. One type is Influenza C. Humans can become seriously ill from Influenza A.

3It can cause serious illness in other animals. It is usually the type behind large outbreaks. Influenza B is milder. It causes smaller outbreaks. It affects only humans. Most of those humans are children. Influenza C usually causes only a mild illness in humans. A sneeze fills the air with saliva. A sneeze fills the air with mucus. A healthy person can catch any type from someone who is already sick. The virus can travel through the air. The virus can travel on things such as cups. The virus can travel on things such as forks. An infected person's saliva carries the flu virus. An infected person's mucus carries it too. A sneeze can send it into the air. A cough can send it into the air. Wild birds often pass viruses to chickens. People meet chickens more often than they meet wild birds. A picture shows both. Viruses can change. That change is called a mutation. Most other viruses change less often than flu viruses do. A new strain is born with every mutation. Microbes of one type, grouped together, form a strain. Wild animals are the starting point for many influenza viruses. They often start in birds. Farm ducks can catch strains that these viruses become after they change. Farm chickens can catch strains that appear after further change.

4Once farm birds are infected, the viruses can change again. The new strains can infect pigs. The new strains can infect humans. Viruses can spread among many different animals. A virus can still pass between animals as unlike as a dog and a whale. Farms keep humans and other animals near one another. Death can follow when viruses spread and mix in that setting. Sometimes a virus takes a shortcut. In 1997, an avian virus passed from birds directly into humans. A sample chain in a diagram shows a wild duck. The chain shows a chicken. The chain shows a human. The chain shows a pig. A diagram shows white blood cells. It shows a cell infected with flu virus. It shows antibodies. It shows viruses. Flu viruses can be fought by the human body. The immune system protects us from harmful microbes. It makes chemicals called antibodies. Antibodies travel in the blood. They look for microbes that do not belong there. An attack begins once one of those microbes is found. They destroy any cell that contains the virus. A weak immune system changes the fight. Copying then outruns the antibodies that try to destroy the viruses. Flu symptoms show up in the body. The feeling of sickness keeps growing in people who are infected.

5A doctor visit may become necessary. Common sense can help keep a flu virus out of your body. Get plenty of rest. Eat well. Leave alone any item a sick person used while eating. Leave alone any item a sick person used while drinking. Wash your hands often. Fingers should stay away from your mouth. Avoid people who show flu symptoms. Sneezing is one of those symptoms. Coughing is one of those symptoms. A picture shows hands being washed. Frequent washing helps you avoid the flu. Scientists study ways to help the body fight the flu. Even very careful people can still get infected. Fortunately, scientists invented vaccines. Takeover of the body by a flu virus can be blocked by a vaccine. Some vaccines are weak flu viruses. Some vaccines are dead flu viruses. A flu shot injects them into a person. These weakened viruses make the body produce many more antibodies. Success against stronger viruses comes once antibody numbers are high enough. Defense is stronger if the flu shot comes before illness starts. The defense is ready if flu viruses arrive later. Each strain needs its own vaccine. Sometimes one shot holds several strains. Each strain makes the body build one particular antibody. Doctors choose strains they think may show up in flu season. After that shot, the body is ready for many of those strains.

6Vaccines usually prevent illness 80 percent of the time. That means a vaccinated person stays well 80 percent of the time. The protection is against a strain in the vaccine. Eighty percent is high. It is not perfect. Illness is still possible. If you had the vaccine, the symptoms are milder. You will not ache as much. Your fever will be lower. Risk of catching this illness is not equal for every person. The sickness hits some people harder. People who are very young are more likely to catch it. People who are very old are more likely to catch it. A person who is already ill has a higher chance of catching it. A picture shows a swine flu virus. Some groups face a higher risk. People over 65 are in that group. Babies are in that group. Very young children are in that group. Pregnant women are in that group. People with diabetes are in that group. People with heart disease are in that group. People with lung disease are in that group. Exhausted, ill people belong in the higher-risk group. Healthcare workers are in that group. Many vaccines are grown in chicken eggs. The number of eggs is in the hundreds of millions. The eggs are grown for this special use.

7That many eggs would fill about fifty football fields. The work starts when scientists and doctors sort viruses apart. They isolate the virus they selected. They kill that virus, or they weaken it. Two additional dead strains are blended in. Those other strains were grown in chicken eggs in a similar way. Then the dead viruses and the weakened viruses are combined. The mix becomes a vaccine. The vaccine protects you from each of those strains. You cannot always stop the flu. If viruses infect your body, you can still act. Aches can be eased by certain medicines. Certain medicines can lower a fever. Drinking lots of fluids can help. Water is one useful fluid. Juice is another. Get plenty of rest. Fighting viruses takes a great deal of work from your body. A picture shows a doctor in 1941. The doctor is giving a child a flu vaccine. Many influenza outbreaks have happened through history. Some were mild. Those mild outbreaks affected only small groups. Others were severe. Millions of people worldwide have died in the severe outbreaks. A flu virus can start in a few people. It can then spread rapidly. A rapid spread inside a community is an epidemic. Haskell County, Kansas, saw people grow very sick early in 1918. The same symptoms soon appeared in many soldiers at an Army base close by.

8Forty-eight soldiers were dead at the base hospital after only a few weeks. No one knew the cause at first. Scientists later learned that a strain of influenza virus caused the illness. More than six hundred thousand people in America died from the strain known as the 1918 flu. Worldwide deaths reached twenty-five to forty million. An outbreak of that size is a pandemic. Rapid spread across the world is what makes a disease a pandemic. A map shows Russia. The map shows Mongolia. The map shows China. The map shows Japan. The map shows the Pacific Ocean. The map shows India. One map gives a sample of a pandemic moving out from a single area into many more. The flu of 1957 to 1958 is the example. History holds other major influenza outbreaks besides the one in 1918. About seventy thousand people in the United States died in the flu pandemic of 1957 to 1958. It first appeared in China. June 1957 was the month it arrived in the United States. Hong Kong, China, was the first place another flu strain was noticed. Another pandemic began in 1968 from this virus. Deaths in the United States from it numbered 34,000. A small city holds about that many residents. H1N1 swine flu turned into a pandemic in 2009.

9Forty-one years had passed since the previous flu pandemic. More than seventy countries had people who caught it. A chart lists historic influenza pandemics. From 1917 to 1919, the 1918 flu was the deadliest influenza pandemic ever. It killed more than twenty million people. Southwest China saw a new flu in February 1957. The outbreak is counted from 1957 to 1958. It then spread through the Pacific. It affected 10 to 35 percent of the population. Deaths were far lower than in the 1918 flu. Worldwide, a new flu from 1968 to 1969 took 700,000 lives. It took 34,000 lives in the United States. In 2009, H1N1 swine flu became a pandemic. Other influenza outbreaks caused worldwide concern. They did not become pandemics. The Russian flu of 1977 was one of them. The avian flu of 1997 was one of them. The avian flu of 1999 was one of them. China was the starting country for both avian flu strains. They spread to other countries. Doctors are always watching for major influenza outbreaks. If they spot an outbreak quickly enough, they can often stop a pandemic. A mask over the mouth lowers the chance of catching the virus. A mask over the nose lowers that chance too. A mask also lowers the chance of spreading the virus. Thousands of years have passed with influenza still present.

10Flu viruses can change. They can develop into new strains. A full end to influenza may never come, because the virus keeps changing. When you have the flu, take care of yourself. That is the most important step. Try to keep other people from getting sick. Wash your hands often. Be careful not to cough on other people. Be careful not to sneeze on other people. Drink a great amount of water. Sleep for a long time. Get a vaccine if you can. Most of all, remember to fight back. Healthy cells get help from good food as they fight. Rest helps those cells win too. The flu starts with a virus too small to see. Coughs and sneezes can carry it from person to person. The three types do not all hit with the same strength. Viruses can mutate into new strains. Antibodies in the blood fight cells that hold the virus. A vaccine made from weak or dead viruses can prepare that fight. Rest, fluids, and medicine can help a sick person. Huge outbreaks have spread across the world. The years 1918, 1957, 1968, and 2009 mark some of the largest. A mask, clean hands, and care around other people slow the spread. Good food and sleep help the body fight back.

89. The Great Arena of Old Rome

1A map places Rome in Italy. Italy sits near Europe, Asia, and Africa on that map. The Adriatic Sea is beside Italy. The Tyrrhenian Sea is beside Italy. The Mediterranean Sea is nearby too. A huge building rose with the labor of thousands of enslaved people. They built it out of stone. They built it out of concrete. That building is the Colosseum. Think of a big stadium. You might go there to watch football. You might go there to watch baseball. Remember how it feels when your team comes onto the field. Picture a time almost two thousand years earlier. The time is the Roman Empire. Picture yourself seated among ancient Romans. You are in a sports arena. It was the world's largest sports arena. It is the oldest. It is the most famous. People call it the Roman Colosseum. The stone and concrete still speak of those builders. Enslaved workers raised this huge place for games. A modern stadium can help you picture the crowd. The feeling of a team walking out is the feeling to imagine. Ancient Romans sat where fans sit today in your mind. Almost two thousand years separate that crowd from now. The Roman Colosseum was their great arena. Emperor Caesar Augustus was the ruler at the start of the Roman Empire.

2The year was 27 bce. The empire ended in 476 ce. At one point it covered much of Europe. It also covered the Middle East. It covered parts of North Africa. Ancient Rome still affects the world. Many countries shape their laws after Roman laws. Roman ways of building still affect designs today. Romans got very good at using concrete. Concrete is a strong building material. People still use it. Today Rome is also called the Eternal City. Rome is a busy place. Visitors come from across the globe. They enjoy its museums. They enjoy its monuments. They enjoy its food. The Colosseum is a ruin. Even so, it remains amazing architecture. Rome counts it as a major landmark. Rome is the capital of Italy. Europe has few cities larger than Rome. Fame puts the Colosseum among the best-known monuments anywhere. Ancient Rome's glory is what this building represents. Many lands appear on a first-century-ce map of the empire. Those lands include Britain. They include Gaul. They include Spain. They include Macedonia. They include Greece. They include Asia Minor. They include Syria. They include Arabia. They include Egypt. They include parts of Africa and Asia. The Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea appear on that map.

3Builders made the Colosseum to be a huge theater in the open air. People called this kind of building an amphitheater. An amphitheater is round or oval. Seats rise in curved rows. 3The legs join this front section. The rear section holds the glands that make silk. Coffee-colored hairs cover the body. Dark brown hairs cover the long, thick legs. Her body is the bigger one. Eight eyes sit on these giant spiders. Sight is still poor. Light and dark are all the eyes sort out. Fine detail stays out of reach. Special hairs blanket the body. The spider relies on those hairs. The hairs notice prey that comes near. They pick up the slightest vibration on the ground. They pick up vibration in the air. A mouse or another small animal may crawl past. The attack hits at once. A spare set of short limbs grows near the head. Those limbs clamp the victim. 4They haul it toward the fangs. Spider Checklist Legs join the front body section. That front section carries the eyes. It carries the fangs. It carries the mouth. It carries the stomach. Pedipalps sit near the head. Silk glands fill the rear section. Fangs are the tool spiders use to push poison into hunted animals. Every spider has eight legs. Every spider has jaws that bear fangs. Most spiders produce venom. Silk comes from glands that every spider has. A hard outer skeleton is the protection around every spider. Eyes are part of every spider. Eight is the usual count. Hairs that sense the world grow on the body. Rainforest Homes Heat and damp air mark the rainforests where Goliath spiders live. Those forests stand in South America. Homes are burrows under the ground. Homes are also gaps under rocks. Many spiders spin a web. Goliaths do not. They still produce silk. The silk is used inside the burrow. Tropical rainforests are crowded with living things. Bats live there.

5Butterflies live there. Birds live there. Big cats live there. Lush plants fill the space. Life in these habitats is rich. Only about 6 percent of Earth's surface is rainforest, or maybe 7 percent. More than half of the world's plant species live in them. More than half of the animal species live in them too. Where These Spiders Live The range sits in South America. The map shows the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. It shows Guyana, Suriname, Venezuela, French Guiana, and Brazil. A Goliath often drags prey back to the burrow. The meal happens there. Out Hunting Tarantulas are nocturnal. The word means daytime is for hiding in the burrow. Hunting starts after the Sun goes down. Skill at hunting is high. Crickets count as food. Beetles are on the menu. Frogs are on the menu. Bats count as food. Mice count as food. Other small animals do too. Now and then a small bird is eaten. Birds with feathers are not a usual food.

6The fangs of these tarantulas are extra large. They are hollow. Venom fills them. A mouse or another small animal may come close. The spider pounces. Legs seize the prey. Fangs drive venom into the body. Venom strikes the nervous system. Small prey becomes paralyzed. The dose is not strong enough to cause serious harm in a human. A bite can still bring swelling. It can bring pain. The feeling is like a bee sting. It is also like a wasp sting. The mouth is an opening shaped like a straw. Sucking is all it can do. Food has to be liquid first. The spider sprays strong juices onto the paralyzed animal. Those juices turn flesh to liquid. About thirty-six hours is enough for a large tarantula to break a mouse down. Hair and bones are left in a little heap. Tissue breaks down. The spider sucks up what is left as liquid. Stiff hairs can be shot in a cloud at an attacker. Tiny hooks cover the hairs.

7The hooks cause tremendous irritation. A spider wasp may haul a paralyzed tarantula along. The trip ends at the tarantula's own burrow. What Eats a Giant Spider? These bird-eating tarantulas are giants among spiders. Enemies still find them. To frighten a predator, a Goliath may rise on its hind legs. It may hiss loudly. The hiss comes from rubbing leg hairs together. Hawks sometimes eat these spiders. Owls sometimes eat them. Skunks sometimes eat them. Snakes sometimes eat them. One of the deadliest hunters is an insect. One name for it is spider wasp. Another name is tarantula hawk. A female may find a tarantula and drive in her sting. Paralysis follows. Death does not. It does not kill the spider. She digs a hole. She sets the paralyzed spider inside. She lays an egg on it. The egg hatches. The larva bores a tiny hole into the spider. It crawls inside. Then it feeds on the spider. Becoming an Adult These spiders keep to themselves. Mating season is when they come together.

8A female also stays near her young while she guards them. Females grow bigger than males. A female's life is much longer. Captive females have lasted past twenty-five years. Molting is part of life for these tarantulas, as it is for spiders in general. Molting happens when the hard outer covering is outgrown. That covering is called an exoskeleton. The old skin is left behind. Under the old skin, a fresh covering grows firm. An adult Goliath molts once a year or twice a year. Spiderlings are the young. They molt more often. A picture may show a tarantula just free of its shed skin. The empty skin lies beside it. A mother tends her young. Color will change as those young grow older. After mating, the female lays about fifty eggs. A sac of silk holds the eggs. She keeps the sac in her burrow. She guards it until the eggs hatch. About six weeks pass before hatching, or sometimes seven. For a few weeks after that, she watches the tiny spiderlings.

9They stay through the first molt. From then on, each young spider faces life alone. A Wild Fact Like many spiders, this bird-eater has forty-eight knees. Six joints bend on each leg. Explorers in the 1800s gave the animal its name. They came upon one that was eating a hummingbird. Weight slows these spiders when they climb. Most other spiders climb faster. Why Spiders Matter Goliaths have lived on Earth for millions of years. Across that long time they have changed very little. Sheer size has always drawn people's interest. Learning about them still goes on. One question is how the venom works. Another is why females outlive males. Like every living thing, these spiders fill an important role. The role belongs to the habitats they occupy. They help hold rodents in check. They help hold insects in check. They help hold other prey species in check. Other animals eat them in turn. A forest without these hairy giants would be a less interesting world.

10Words to Know Appendages are parts on the outside that project away from the rest of the body. An arm is one. A leg is one. Burrows are holes dug in the ground. An animal uses the hole as a home. Captivity is the state of being confined. Freedom is missing. Glands are organs that make substances a body process needs. They release those substances. To molt is to drop an outside layer. Skin can be that layer. So can hair, feathers, or a shell. A fresh layer takes its place. Nocturnal means busy at night instead of during the day. Paralyzes means it leaves one or more body parts unable to move. To sense is to take in news about the world. Sight can do it. Touch, taste, smell, or hearing can do it. Venom is a poisonous liquid. Some animals kill prey with it. Some defend themselves with it. A bite usually delivers it. A sting can deliver it too.

Sound is still detected, because the legs feel vibrations. A photo shows large items held in the mandibles. The brain sits in the head. The eyes sit in the head. The antennae sit in the head. Hundreds of lenses sit in each eye. Many separate images become one picture inside the brain. Three small sensors sit on the head of some ants. The sensors are called ocelli. The word is said like oh-SELL-eye. Light is what those sensors notice. Dark is what they notice too. Taste is one job of the antennae. Smell is another job. Hearing is another job. Weather is one danger it blocks. Predators are another danger it blocks. Four ants in a photo press their antennae together to share a message. Ants pass news in three ways. Touch is one way. Sound is one way. Smell is one way. Heads meet heads when a message is sent by touch. Antennae meet antennae for the same kind of message. Sound can be made by rubbing the legs together. The food can be found because of it. The way home to the colony can be found because of it. Getting lost is avoided. A trail grows stronger as more ants use it. The nest gets its protection from them too. The ants you notice above ground are usually these ones. Older ants are usually the ones in that outside work. Building the nest is a job for other ants. Thousands of eggs can leave her body in a single day. A lifetime of that laying can produce millions of ants. Short worker lives are why so many young are needed. Crops get protection because ants eat flies. Caterpillars are eaten too. Other pests are eaten too. Soil for plants improves because of their digging. Pause and watch one trail. 94. The Hive Path to Honey

1The book order starts with amazing honey, bee types, and foraging. It continues with passing nectar, drying, capping, honey types, helping bees, and word meanings. Honey stands among the most useful foods. Honey also stands among the most delicious foods. People spread honey on bread. People pour honey in tea. Honey sweetens cakes and cookies. Bears, raccoons, skunks, and opossums use honey as an important food. Humans have loved honey for a very long time. Nine thousand years, or even longer, is the length of that love. Ancient Egypt preserved mummies with honey. Honey is eaten together with many different foods. Bees do not make honey so other animals will benefit. The young of the hive are fed honey. Cold winter months create another need. Bees cannot find flowers in those months. Honey is kept as a guaranteed food for winter. The bees need honey in order to survive. Honey is critical to them. Some people call honey bee vomit. That claim is wrong. Some people call honey bee poop. That claim is also wrong. An amazing process lets the hive produce honey. The process takes much hard work.

2Every member of the hive must share the work. Their cooperation makes the honey. Three types of bees live in a honeybee hive. Workers are female. Drones are male. The queen is the third type. A single day can bring as many as two thousand eggs from the queen. Mating with the queen is the one reason drones are in the hive. Jobs for workers change with each stage of development. Inside the hive is the usual place for a worker during her early half of life. Her inside jobs include nurse, guard, and queen attendant. Older workers become foragers. Flowers give the foragers both nectar and pollen. Nectar is a sweet substance made from sugar and water. Honey cannot exist when nectar is missing. A typical hive has only one queen. Drones there can number up to five hundred. Workers there can reach as many as sixty thousand. A hive view shows the worker, the queen, and the drone. The usual nectar search stays within 2 kilometers, or 1.25 miles, of the hive. If needed, she may travel two times the usual distance.

3She may even travel three times the usual distance. Her long, pointed proboscis sucks nectar out of a blossom. That hollow mouthpart works like a straw. Two stomachs are found in each honeybee. Nectar goes into the special honey stomach. Another name for it is crop. The second stomach is used for digesting food. A nectar load can weigh close to the bee herself. A plant picture shows her sucking up nectar. One pound of honey takes a flight of almost 90,000 kilometers, or 55,000 miles. Two million flowers are visited for that same pound. Yearly honey from one colony can weigh 27 to 45 kilograms, which is 60 to 100 pounds. Bumblebees and some other insects make honey or a food much like it. Those insects do not keep large stores. Honeybees do keep large stores. Across her lifetime, one honeybee makes about 0.4 milliliter of honey, or 1/12th of a teaspoon. Pollen from other flowers covers a honeybee on an African daisy. She spreads the pollen onto the daisy. Travel from flower to flower is for more than nectar. A little pollen clings to her feet at each landing.

4Blossom by blossom, she carries pollen onward. The pollen comes from male flower parts. She delivers it to female flower parts. Flight can shake some pollen loose. Wind may carry the loose pollen to flowers. People call this transfer pollination. Fertilization can happen because of pollination. Plants can produce fruit after fertilization. Plants can produce seeds after fertilization. Bee pollination accounts for thirty percent of foods people eat. The list includes blueberries and strawberries. It continues with apples and beans. It also includes lettuce and onions. More foods are included as well. The honeybee diet needs pollen as well as nectar. Some bees gather pollen but skip nectar. Other bees gather pollen along with nectar. Leg parts made for this job hold the pollen. The pollen is carried back to the hive. Other bees then receive a share. A waiting house bee takes nectar from a forager. The nectar leaves the forager stomach and enters the house bee mouth. While foragers search for flowers, enzymes mix with nectar in the honey stomach. The enzymes begin moving the nectar toward honey.

5As many as five hundred flowers may be needed to fill the honey stomach. She flies home once that stomach is full. A processor bee, also called a house bee, is waiting. Up comes the nectar solution, and it enters the processor mouth. In a group, processor bees hand nectar from one mouth to another. The handoff helps turn the nectar into honey. Foragers leave again to hunt more nectar. Processors stay with the liquid. Each handoff adds more enzymes. Those enzymes break the complex sugars apart. Two simpler sugars remain. Honey is the result of the chemical change. Inside the warm hive, bees spit the nectar up again and again. Some water evaporates each time warm air touches it. A good nectar find is shared by dance. The dance shows other bees the location. Waggles, runs, and turns shape the dance. Other movements are included as well. One view shows a honeybee about to load a cell. She will place one drop of nectar in the honeycomb. The next view shows nectar filling the cell. About half an hour of passing must happen first. Then the nectar is ready for the honeycomb.

6Every honeycomb cell is a perfect hexagon. Beeswax is what the cell is made of. Six equal sides form that hexagon. Glands on the abdomen produce the beeswax. Thin wax sheets leave the body. Those sheets are called scales. The hexagon uses the least beeswax of any cell shape. It still makes the strongest honeycomb. It also makes the most compact honeycomb. Bees spread the nectar solution thinly in the cell. Water keeps evaporating from that thin layer. Wings fan the liquid at top speed. The rush of air thickens the liquid. More water evaporates while air moves around the cell. Worker bees work as a group to cap filled honeycomb cells. Enough water has now evaporated. The honey has the correct thickness. Bees can cap it. A beeswax cap covers each filled cell. The cap keeps the cell clean. The cap also keeps the cell airtight. Stored honey waits for winter, when the bees need it. Humans may harvest honey from the cells. Other animals may enjoy it too. Sealed honey can stay fresh for a very long time.

7Archaeologists dug at the famous pyramids of Egypt. They found pots of honey. An ancient tomb held the pots. The honey is about three thousand years old. It is the oldest known honey sample in the world. It had been preserved. It was still edible. An Egyptian tomb held a drawing of a bee. Different flowers make honey look different. Different flowers make honey taste different. Flavor follows the flower that gave the nectar. Color follows that flower. Thickness follows that flower. France often chooses lavender honey. Greece often chooses wild thyme honey. In the United States, clovers lead all other plant groups in honey production. Only a little water is in honey. The sugar level is high. The honey is slightly acidic. Because of those three traits, bacteria cannot grow in honey. Other germs cannot grow in honey either. When honey is mixed with water, hydrogen peroxide forms. That chemical kills germs. Honey is useful for treating wounds because of this. Manuka honey is better for wound care than other kinds. It comes mainly from New Zealand. A special chemical in manuka nectar is the cause.

8Making honey is hard work for bees. Foraging for nectar is one hard step. Processing the nectar is the next hard step. Drying the honey comes next. Storing the honey comes last. The honey holds nutrients bees need. Those nutrients help the bees survive. People have discovered many ways to use this sweet treat. Even so, people do not rely on honey as honeybees do. People do need bees to pollinate food crops. A large share of human food depends on bee pollination. Crops that feed other animals depend on bees too. Almonds make the need easy to see. Of all almonds on Earth, eighty-five percent grow in California. Pollinating those orchards takes 1.7 million hives each year. Hot, dry weather leaves bees thirsty. People may set a water dish outside. Bees stop at the dish for a drink. Flowers that bees like can be planted to help them. Wildflowers and native plants are special favorites. Using fewer chemicals against bugs will help. Using fewer chemicals against weeds will help. Many of those chemicals harm bees. Choose local beekeepers when you buy honey. Those beekeepers nurture their bees.

9In summer, a saucer of water can help a thirsty worker. A stone or a pebble gives the bee a place to stand. She can take a water break there. People can protect the bees. People can protect their environment. The bees can then keep making delicious honey. The honey is for them and for us. Humans use several bee products besides honey. Beeswax is used to form honeycombs. Beeswax is used to cap cells. Long ago, beeswax served as sealing wax. Candles have been made from beeswax. Cosmetics have been made from beeswax. Archery bows have used beeswax. Sewing thread has been strengthened with beeswax. Shoelaces have been strengthened with beeswax. Some cosmetics include royal jelly. People take royal jelly as a dietary supplement. People also use royal jelly as medicine. Any benefit for humans remains unproven. Worker bees produce the royal jelly. All larvae eat it during the opening three days of life. Venom from the honeybee stinger makes a sting hurt. Venom is used for certain medical problems. Arthritis is one problem venom is used to help. These word meanings belong with the honey facts.

10A forager is a person or an animal that gathers food or other needed things. An abdomen is the rear section of an insect body. Reproductive organs and digestive organs sit inside the abdomen. A gland is an organ that makes substances and gives them off. Body processes need those substances. Capped can mean covered. Capped can also mean limited. Cooperation is joint work aimed at one goal. To nurture is to give care and food to a living thing. That support helps the living thing develop and grow. If something is critical, it is very important. Digesting is the body turning food into energy. Pollen names the male cells of a flower. Those cells often appear as fine yellow powder. When a liquid evaporates, it turns into a gas. A substance is a single kind of physical material. Fertilization combines male cells with female cells. A new animal can come from that joining. A new plant can come from that joining. The honey story ends on the same hive work. Bees still make honey for themselves and for people.

95. The Island Gate into America

1Many immigrants put on their best clothes for the journey. They were going to Ellis Island. What You Will Read. A Gate into the Country. Who Came Through the Island. Crossing to the Island. A Check of Their Health. The Flow of People Slows. The Museum on the Island. Words to Know. A Gate into the Country. Today, a large share of the United States comes from several groups. Indigenous peoples are one group. Immigrants are another. Descendants of immigrants are part of the country. Descendants of enslaved peoples are part of it too. Some people move from one country to another because they choose to. Those people are called immigrants. For many years, newcomers had to pass an immigration station. Only then were they allowed into the United States. From 1892 to 1924, one station processed the most people. Ellis Island, just outside New York City, was the site of that station. Each year, Ellis Island draws millions of visitors. Where Is Ellis Island? Some experts offer an estimate. Almost half of all Americans can trace a family tree back to Ellis Island. An ancestor in that tree passed through the island. From 1892 to 1954, workers on the island cleared people to enter.

2They cleared more than twelve million immigrants into the United States. Many of those immigrants stayed in New York City. Many stayed in nearby areas. Others ventured farther into the country.
