Some went to the Midwest. Some went to the West. Immigrants packed lightly. They carried only as many bags as they could hold. The belongings of two young women from Poland are in their arms. They are leaving Ellis Island in 1910. The picture above shows them. Children spent long hours waiting with their families. The picture on the right shows that wait. Home Countries in 1907. Russia, 19 percent. Italy, 15.5 percent. Austria, 15 percent. Hungary, 8 percent. Germany, 6.4 percent. Canada, 5.7 percent. England, 4.1 percent. Ireland, 3.6 percent. Mexico, 2.7 percent. Sweden, 2.4 percent. The rest, from more than 35 countries, made up 17.5 percent. The numbers come from the 1910 U.S. Census. Who Came Through the Island. Most people who passed through Ellis Island had crossed the Atlantic Ocean. They came on giant steamships. Their home countries were many and different. Europe was the starting place for most of them.

3In the late 1800s, the numbers grew large. People left Ireland by the thousands. People left Italy and Russia by the thousands too. Their reasons were not all the same. They hoped to build new lives in the United States. Some wanted adventure. Some wanted a fresh start. Others fled hunger. Others fled violence. Others fled religious persecution. Others fled other dangerous situations. A Fact to Know. The first person processed at Ellis Island was a teenage girl. Her name was Annie Moore. Ireland was behind her. She was moving to the United States. Her two younger brothers came with her. A statue shows Annie Moore. Families often arrived at Ellis Island together. Other immigrants traveled by themselves. Many families could pay for only one steamship ticket at a time. Often the father went first. Sometimes a teenage son went first. He traveled to the United States to find a job. Then he sent money home. The family used the money to buy tickets. In the late 1800s, a ticket across the Atlantic had a set price. It cost around 20 or 30 dollars. In 2024 money, that is about 700 and 1,000 dollars.

4The sum was about half of one year's pay. A worker in a country such as Ireland might earn that pay. The deck of the SS Patricia is packed with immigrants. The steamship has come from Europe. It arrives at Ellis Island in 1906. Crossing to the Island. The ocean trip took European immigrants about two weeks. They sailed from Europe to Ellis Island. A ticket did not end the trouble. Immigrants still faced many challenges on the way. At the ship, they had to answer twenty-nine questions. The questions asked about work they had done. Some questions covered relatives who might already live in the United States. The questions asked about similar topics. For most immigrants, the Atlantic crossing was hard. One Boy's Hope in America. Osman Lewis was a thirteen-year-old orphan from Belgium. In 1921, he slipped onto a ship as a stowaway. He reached Ellis Island sick. He stayed in the hospital there. A woman in the U.S. Army heard his story. She adopted him. Osman Lewis hugs Helen Bastedo in 1921. She is the woman who adopted him. Life on the giant steamships was not equal. It depended on the price a person could pay.

5First-class passengers had private rooms. Second-class passengers had private rooms too. They enjoyed fresh air on deck. Third-class passengers had to stay low in the ship. They stayed in a large open room called steerage. They had little time on the main deck. Hundreds of people shared close quarters. The air on the lower decks smelled bad. The air could carry disease. Many travelers became ill. Sickness made a hard trip even worse. After two hard weeks, the immigrants at last reached Ellis Island. Most steamships were too big to dock at the island itself. First-class passengers had a short health check on the ship. Second-class passengers had that check too. They also had a short interview. Then they boarded smaller boats and entered the United States. Just before arrival, the immigrants saw the Statue of Liberty. The statue is a symbol of freedom. Third-class passengers had a longer path. They faced a series of checks on Ellis Island. They faced interviews there too. Small ferry boats carried them from the ships to the island. About five hundred workers greeted the crowds. Thousands of immigrants arrived each day. The process could frighten many of them.

6They were terrified of being sent back home. Most of the workers had once been immigrants themselves. Many spoke the languages of the new arrivals. The workers had many different jobs. Some asked the same twenty-nine questions from the ship. The new answers had to match the old ones. Workers also checked two practical needs. The immigrants had to be able to find work. They had to be able to find a place to live. The U.S. government wanted one outcome. Immigrants should not need government help in order to survive. Long lines often filled the Great Hall. People waited there to speak with workers. A Check of Their Health. Workers also examined the health of the new arrivals. The ships were overcrowded. Sanitation was poor. Medicine was scarce. Those conditions helped disease spread. Workers wanted to keep illness out of the United States. Training taught them how to spot illness. One of the worst diseases was trachoma. The word is said truh-KOH-muh. The disease affected the eyes. It could cause death. Doctors pulled back the eyelids of every arriving person. They looked for the disease. Some doctors used hooks.

7Some used their fingers. One nickname for the island was the Island of Hope. Most immigrants were allowed to enter. The other nickname was the Island of Tears. Some people were sent back to their home countries. Most often, an illness was the reason. The illness did not get better. Families who had traveled together faced a hard choice. They could all go back. Or they could leave the sick person behind. Being sent back was rare. About twelve million people came to Ellis Island. Around 1 percent were refused. That share was 120,000 people. Children on the Island. Sometimes a child traveled to Ellis Island alone. Sometimes a child stayed for weeks. Workers were still deciding if the parents could enter. The island had a playground. It had a school. It had places for children to sleep. Around 1900, children are at play on Ellis Island. People Arriving from 1893 to 1925. 110,000 in 1917. 50,000 in 1919. 510,000 in 1921. 300,000 in 1923. 150,000 in 1925. 350,000 in 1893. 195,000 in 1895. 190,000 in 1897. 270,000 in 1899. 350,000 in 1901. 610,000 in 1903. 730,000 in 1905. 1,100,000 in 1907. 570,000 in 1909.

8680,000 in 1911. 900,000 in 1913. 150,000 in 1915. The counts come from yearly reports of the commissioner general of immigration in Washington, D.C. The Flow of People Slows. Arrivals at Ellis Island reached a peak in 1907. More than one million people came through its gates that year alone. People moved because the economy of the United States was booming. Immigrants needed jobs. They wanted to build lives for themselves and for their families. In that same year, many Jewish people fled attacks. The Russian government carried out those attacks. After World War I began in 1914, fewer people reached the island. Travel across the ocean was dangerous. At times, that travel was impossible. New laws in the United States also changed the numbers. Some immigrants had to pass a reading test. Some had to pass a writing test. Some even had to solve a puzzle. They needed to learn English before they arrived. One test was a wooden puzzle. The pieces fit together into the shape of a human head. The travelers were exhausted. Some were sick. Tiredness and sickness made the tests harder. Many failed because they were nervous. Many failed because they misunderstood the directions.

9The United States also passed laws about China. Those laws limited how many people could come from China. Then a law in 1924 changed the whole system. It changed the way people entered the United States. It banned immigrants from Asia completely. People could now apply while they were still at home. Ellis Island was no longer needed. Other immigration stations were no longer needed either. During the 1930s and the 1940s, the numbers fell. The island was used in a new way. Prisoners of war were held there in World War II, from 1939 to 1945. Some of the people held there had spoken against the U.S. government. Others were suspected of being spies. The Museum on the Island. The number of immigrants kept falling. Ellis Island closed at last in 1954. Large steamer ships were no longer the way people arrived. Airplanes had taken over that travel. Many years later, a museum opened on the island. The year was 1990. Today, visitors can learn the history of Ellis Island. They can learn about immigration to the United States. People can do research on the island. They can search for relatives who came through the station.

10The island is only a small piece of land. It has played a large part in the history of the United States. For millions of immigrants, Ellis Island was the first United States soil under their feet. Those people became Americans. They worked hard to build better lives in the new country. At the museum, visitors can read thousands of names. The names belong to immigrants who passed through the station. Words to Know. Ancestor: a person in your family who lived long before you. Dangerous: able to hurt someone, or likely to do so. Descendants: children and later family of a person or a group from the past. Economy: the way money moves through work, trade, and finance in a country or a region. Exhausted: extremely tired, or worn down. Persecution: cruel unfair treatment of a group, often because of religion, politics, or race. Quarters: the rooms where people live, especially workers, soldiers, enslaved people, or ship passengers. Sanitation: the actions, steps, or equipment that keep a place clean or take waste away. Ventured: went into a place even though it might be dangerous.

96. The Jaguar Steps Back North

1A camera that senses motion took a nighttime picture of El Jefe. During autumn 2015, a huge cat with spots passed a camera that people had hidden. That camera was placed among mountains in the south of Arizona. That walk carried the cat into history. The recording was the first video footage of its kind. The video showed the one wild jaguar known to live inside the United States. Some lands that now belong to the United States were once home to jaguars. Old reports place jaguars in California. Old reports also mention Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. Since 1997, jaguars have roamed north out of Mexico. The ground under their paws today is land their ancestors used long ago. Scientists say that all seven of the animals people have sighted are males. A male jaguar is the one that typically looks for a new territory. He looks for a place where he can start a family of his own. That plan depends on females following him. Students at a middle school in Tucson, Arizona, held a vote. Say Tucson like TOO-sahn.

2The mascot of the school is a jaguar. The students chose a name for the big cat on the camera. They settled on the name El Jefe. Say El Jefe like HEF-ay. In Spanish, those words mean the boss. Within months, the video of El Jefe had spread around the world. More than twenty million people had seen it. He was a star. Some jaguars have black fur. The pigment in that fur is different from the pigment of other jaguars. Pigment means coloring. Wild cats of the world have only two kinds larger than the jaguar. No other wild cat in the Western Hemisphere is larger. Lions are larger. Tigers are larger as well. A jaguar has thick legs. It has a large chest. Its jaws are strong enough to crush a skull. That crushing bite is often the way a jaguar kills prey. The fur is a yellowish color. Groups of spots called rosettes cover the fur. People often mix up jaguars and leopards. Telling the two cats apart is not hard. A jaguar has spots in the middle of its rosettes.

3A leopard does not have a spot in the middle. In a side-by-side test, pattern A belongs to a jaguar. Pattern B belongs to a leopard. Jaguars can climb trees. They do not lift a kill up into a tree. The top hunter of the Americas has no need to stash a meal up in a tree. No other animal is likely to steal the meal. A jaguar can weigh from 150 pounds to 250 pounds. That range is 68 to 113 kilograms. From the nose to the tip of the tail, a jaguar can measure 7 feet. That length is 2 meters. Even with that size, a jaguar is stealthy. It is fast. Climbing trees is something this big cat handles pretty well. These traits make it a perfect predator in the wild. Jaguars that are breeding still live across a wide range. Breeding here means the cats are having cubs. The range covers eighteen countries. It runs from Mexico to Argentina. North America and South America both hold parts of this range. The Atlantic Ocean lies along one side of these lands.

4The Pacific Ocean lies along the other side. They are gone from close to half their former lands. These cats need travel paths that stay safe and open. The routes let them travel between areas of good habitat. Human actions can block that travel. Cutting down forests is one of those actions. Building walls along a border is another. Fences can stop the cats too. A map can mark where jaguars lived in the past. The same map can mark where they live now. Once, the wild held over four hundred thousand of these cats. Their range reached through forests and swamps. Those forests and swamps were in South America and Central America. That old range also took in drier country in the south of the United States. Through roughly the last hundred years, jaguar numbers have fallen. People caused most of the fall in numbers. At times the killing was intentional. Hunting is one example. People have long hunted jaguars for their beautiful fur. Scientists offer an estimate for the 1960s and the 1970s. During the 1960s and the 1970s, yearly killings could reach fifteen thousand of these cats.

5The Fish and Wildlife Service of the United States stores items that were taken illegally. One stored item is a cape made from jaguar fur. That cape was seized from travelers on their way into the country. Other people kill these cats for a separate reason. They sometimes dislike jaguars. They may dislike other large predators as well. Bears, wolves, lions, and tigers are among those animals. Part of the dislike comes from fear. Predators also need to eat. Sometimes they take an easy meal from livestock. Cows are one kind of livestock. Sheep are another kind. Some ranchers worry that a jaguar might kill their animals. Ranchers need those animals in order to make a living. Even people who do not mean to kill jaguars can still cause their deaths. Cutting a forest for some other use is one example. That cutting destroys the places jaguars need. Just fifteen thousand of these cats are left anywhere on Earth. Scientists say the number keeps dropping. After officials tried to restore wolves, a protest sign appeared in New Mexico.

6The sign showed that some local people did not want wolves nearby. A jaguar eats many different animals. The diet depends on the place where the jaguar lives. In Brazil, a jaguar has brought down a snake called a yellow anaconda. Views of jaguars have changed as scientists have learned more. Views of other large predators have changed in the same way. Scientists have taught people that nature needs jaguars for an important job. As a top predator, a jaguar helps keep other animal numbers in balance. That balance helps leave enough food for every species. Inside the United States, protection for jaguars started in 1972. The protection treats them as an endangered species. Killing them is illegal. The government must protect the cats. The government must also protect their habitat. In 2014, the government of the United States named a large area as critical habitat. The area covers 750,000 acres. That area is 3,035 square kilometers. The land lies in Arizona and New Mexico. People must take extra care with this land if they plan to change it.

7In Mexico, scientists study the Northern Jaguar Reserve. From 80 to 120 is the estimate for how many jaguars live in that reserve. The reserve is a tough land of mountains. It lies about 150 miles south of the border with the United States. That distance is 241 kilometers. Every so often, a jaguar from that Mexican group walks north. It enters the United States. Scientists placed video cameras in certain wild spots. When something moves nearby, a camera starts to record. Cameras caught El Jefe on video in 2015. Since then, cameras have caught other male jaguars as well. Those males were in the mountains of Arizona. Meet Mayke. She is a dog that detects scat. She first trained for police work. Mayke scares easily. Loud sound is more than she can stand. Training began again for a new task. Her second training taught her to smell fresh jaguar droppings. Scat is another word for poop. She found a great deal of it. Those finds showed scientists good places to put wildlife cameras. Schoolchildren near the Arizona cameras have named other recent jaguars besides El Jefe.

8They named one cat Sombra. In Spanish, Sombra means shadow. They named another cat Yo'oko. Yo'oko is the Yaqui word for jaguar. Say Yaqui like YAH-kee. Each time a jaguar shows up in a photo, scientists study the picture. They do the same with a video. They look closely at the spots. They want to know whether the spots match a jaguar they already know. They also study the shape of the skull. They study the size of the cat. Those clues help them decide whether the cat is male or female. March 2014 brought these cats some habitat protection under the United States government. A map of critical habitat shows part of the United States. The map area includes Arizona and New Mexico. Tucson is marked on the map. Mexico lies to the south. Cameras have caught jaguars inside this mapped area. Sombra is one of those cats. El Jefe is another. Yo'oko is another. Saving the places a species needs is a major piece of saving the species itself. Jaguars wander over a very wide area.

9These wide-roaming cats use more land than people can set aside. A trap ended Yo'oko's life late in the year 2017. He had wandered back into Mexico. A mother jaguar gives birth to two cubs, or as many as four. Full size arrives for the cubs after about three years. So far, cameras in the United States have caught only males. Females may not have reached the United States so far. Another, simpler idea is possible too. It is possible that no female has ever passed in view of a camera. Either way, people who advocate for jaguars share a hope. They hope female jaguars will come into the United States. They hope those females will start a family. Jaguars will count as set up again in the United States only after that happens. Someday the number in the United States may grow large enough for a change in status. The cats might no longer be listed as endangered. Not everyone wants large predators roaming free. Almost nobody would call these cats dull. Excitement spreads because these cats have come back to the United States.

10People who care deeply about big cats feel that excitement. Many hope to see jaguars again on some of the lands they used to occupy. For now, only a few are here. Someday there could be many. A wall painting in the center of Tucson, Arizona, honors El Jefe coming to town. It also celebrates other jaguars that may travel north. An advocate is a person who actively supports a cause. Ancestors are members of a family from long ago. Critical habitat is land the government protects so that an endangered species living there can be helped. Declined means to have become fewer, smaller, or worse. A species called endangered is an animal or a plant with a serious chance of vanishing forever. Footage is film or video that has captured pictures or action. Reestablished means set up again, started again, or made to exist again. A reserve keeps wild plants safe, and it keeps wild animals safe too. A territory is an area of land or water that an animal, or a group of animals, defends and lives in.

97. The Kingdom of Morocco

1Contents. Finding Morocco. The People. The Land. The Past. Animals. Meals. Closing. Word List. A map marks Spain and the Mediterranean Sea. It marks the Strait of Gibraltar, Salé, and the Bou Regreg River. It marks the Atlantic Ocean, Casablanca, and Rabat. It marks Algeria, the Canary Islands, and Western Sahara. It marks Mauritania, plus parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa. Morocco lies in Africa. Spain is a little larger than this country. The location is the northwest of Africa. Algeria lies just to the east. Western Sahara follows the southern border. One coast faces the Atlantic Ocean. Another coast faces the Mediterranean Sea. A narrow channel links those two waters. The channel is the Strait of Gibraltar. Spain sits just across it. The nearest point is only about 13 kilometers away, or 8 miles. Morocco's capital is Rabat. Rabat stands where the Bou Regreg River flows out to the Atlantic. Rabat is old. People have lived there since the 1100s.

2In earlier times it was a major port for Morocco. Pirates lived in Rabat from the seventeenth century into the nineteenth. They also lived in Salé, the sister city nearby. Their ships ranged widely. The route ran from North Africa to the coasts of Spain, Italy, England, and Ireland. More than half a million people live in Rabat. Old parts of the city sit inside ancient walls. Donkeys are shown pulling a farmer's plow. A little more than thirty-three million people live in the country. Most of them descend from Berber people or from Arab people. Berber people were the original residents. Cities hold almost two-thirds of the population. Rabat is one of those cities. Casablanca and Tangier are others. Tourism is a huge business. Mining gives many people work. Manufacturing and communications do too. Farming is the work of about one-third of the people. Crops grow well in many places. The climate is mild, and the soil is fertile.

3Other places do not give farmers enough water. Most people find city life comfortable. Social life is a large part of the culture. Many men like cafés. Soccer is what they watch there. No sport is more popular. City people also enjoy movies. They enjoy restaurants. They enjoy shopping. The official religion is Islam. Muslims are 99 percent of the people. Islamic law matters deeply in society. Some laws were changed by the government in 2004. Women gained more rights from those changes. Women's equality is more accepted here than in some other Arab countries. Arabic, Berber, and French are the languages people speak. The Princess Lalla Meryem School posts its sign in all three languages. A daughter of a Moroccan president is the person the school was named for. A landform map marks the Mediterranean Sea and the Rif Mountains. It marks the Atlantic Ocean, the Bou Regreg River, and Rabat.

4It marks the Atlas Mountains, Ouzoud Falls, Mount Toubkal, and the Sahara Desert. Mountains fill much of the country. One major range is the Atlas Mountains. Another major range is the Rif Mountains. The Atlas range runs from north to south through the middle. The Rif range follows the Mediterranean coast. The highest peak is Mount Toubkal. Its height is 4,165 meters, or 13,665 ft. Rain falls heavily in the mountains. Snow falls heavily too. Streams are common because of that water. Coastal temperatures stay between 18 and 28 degrees C. That is 64 to 82 degrees F. Inland, the temperatures swing wider. Summers inland are hot. The reading is often above 35 degrees C, or 95 degrees F. Winters can freeze. When spring is nearly over, or when summer has just begun, a hot wind comes north out of the Sahara Desert. People call that wind the sharqī, said shar-KEE. Temperatures climb when it blows.

5Heat waves can reach 41 degrees C, or 106 degrees F. Climate shapes the landscape. Mild places grow beautiful forests. Some high mountains are forested with argan trees. Nowhere else grows the argan tree. Its nut makes it valuable. Cooks use the nut for oil. Other products are made from it too. Where the land belongs to the Sahara, it looks nothing like those mild forests. Almost no plants grow there, except in oases. Several oases are found in Morocco. One picture shows Ouzoud Falls. Another shows goats up in argan trees, eating the fruit. King Idris I traveled from the Middle East to Morocco. His aim was to found a Muslim dynasty. More than twelve hundred years have passed since then. Later Muslim kingdoms from this region held parts of today's Spain. That hold lasted until 1492. European countries started gaining power here in the 1800s. Spain took control along the coast in 1884.

6France took the rest of the country in 1912. Civil unrest came before that French control. France made a promise at the time. It would share its military strength. It would protect the standing of the royal house. Freedom from France came in 1956. Moulay Idriss was Morocco's first Islamic city. Idris I is the founder. Today the country has a king. It also has a prime minister. In the 1970s, Spain gave Morocco the desert called Western Sahara. Mauritania received that desert too. Armed fights over that land followed. Algeria has been one opponent. Western Saharan groups have been others. The land is a harsh desert. Valuable minerals lie under the barren ground. The country that controls them could grow rich. Morocco claims most of Western Sahara. It also controls most of it. Many people still question the claim. Flamingos gather along the waterways. Huge flocks of birds pass through, especially in winter. Herons are among them.

7Flamingos, ducks, and storks are among them too. The waterways are places they enjoy. Single-humped camels do well here. They matter to the tourist industry. A visitor can ride one through the countryside. The Barbary macaque, said muh-KAK, is a monkey that also lives here. Forests are its home. The same monkeys live in Spain, on the far side of the Strait of Gibraltar. No other monkey lives in Europe. Large ears help the fennec fox let body heat out, which keeps it cool. These foxes live in the deserts. They are the smallest foxes on Earth. Daytime is for sleeping. Night is when they come out, which helps them beat the heat. An unusual spider lives in the Sahara. Its way of moving is strange. Danger makes it fling itself end over end. The move is called flic-flac. The spider can go forward this way. It can go backward. It can even go uphill.

8The speed is 2 meters each second, or 6.6 ft. That is twice its usual speed. Flipping costs so much energy that only a couple of flips can happen in a day. More than that would kill the spider. A picture shows this Moroccan flic-flac spider. A special clay pot is sometimes used for cooking. Food from Morocco is famous worldwide. Cooks draw on Spanish tastes. They also draw on French, Berber, and Arab tastes. Couscous is a popular food. It is pasta in tiny round bits. Vegetables show up often. Tomatoes are common. Onions, peppers, and eggplant are common too. Fruit of many kinds is common too. Garlic flavors many dishes. Olives, lemons, and spices do too. Kebobs are well liked. So is a stew of lamb. That stew is served for Ramadan, a Muslim holiday. Pigeon meat is enjoyed as well. People especially like it inside a light pastry with sugar on top. The pastry is called b'stillah, said buh-STI-lah.

9Fish is eaten often along the coast. Sweet mint tea is a common drink with meals. Black coffee is another. Shoppers fill a Moroccan market. Many people treat this country as a gateway between Africa and Europe. Its history is long. Its land takes many beautiful forms. Mountains wear snow. Beaches are sandy. Forests are lush. Dunes cross the desert. Interesting animals find homes on these lands. Rabat and the other coastal cities have mild weather. Ocean breezes keep the air fresh. Many city people live in comfort. They take part in many activities. They also eat the famous foods of their homeland. The Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook for 2016 gives these facts. The population is 33,322,699. The land covers 446,300 square kilometers, or 172,317 square miles. Rabat is the capital. Arabic and Berber are the primary languages. Islam is the primary religion. The currency is the dirham. Word List.

10Barren describes land with almost no plants. Oases are watered, fertile spots inside a desert. A café is a small place that sells drinks and light meals. A port is a waterside place. Ships can shelter there in a storm. Ships can also take cargo on or off. Culture means the ideas and customs of one group of people. A prime minister is the government leader in most lands that use a parliament. A dynasty is a line of rulers who come from one family. Industries are sets of businesses that make or sell the same kinds of goods or services. A strait is a narrow water path linking two large bodies of water. Islam is the religion followed by Muslims. It rests on what the prophet Muhammad taught. It worships one God. Tourism is the work of serving people who travel for pleasure. Landscape means the features you can see across an area of land.

98. The Leader Who Took Back Jerusalem

1A map shows the Middle East in the years 1137 to 1193. The Caspian Sea is marked. The Tigris River is marked. The Euphrates River is marked. Aleppo is marked. The Mediterranean Sea is marked. Tikrit is marked. Baalbek is marked. Damascus is marked. Baghdad is marked. Hattin is marked. The Syrian Desert is marked. Jaffa is marked. Jerusalem is marked. The Persian Gulf is marked. The Arabian Desert is marked. Cairo is marked. Asia is marked. Europe is marked. Egypt is marked. Africa is marked. The Red Sea is marked. Today the name Middle East covers a wide region. Turkey is part of that region. Cyprus is part of it. Syria is part of it. Lebanon is part of it. Iraq is part of it. Iran is part of it. Israel is part of it. Palestine is part of it. Jordan is part of it. Egypt is part of it. Sudan is part of it. Libya is part of it. Kuwait is part of it. Oman is part of it. Qatar is part of it. Saudi Arabia is part of it. The United Arab Emirates is part of it. Yemen is part of it. These pages begin with the holy city of Jerusalem. Early years come next. Then a leader rises. Then war begins.

2Europe fights back after that. Life after the truce follows. A final section remembers him. Hard words close the book. Jerusalem is one of the world's oldest cities. Nearly nine hundred years ago, the Middle East was home to a Muslim boy. His name was Yusuf. His faith mattered deeply to him. Grown up, he became one of history's most famous Muslim leaders. People know him as Salah al-Din. Three religions hold Jerusalem holy. Jews visit many special places there. Christians visit many special places there. Muslims visit many special places there. Muslims had held Jerusalem for over four hundred years. People of all religions lived in the city. In 1099, Christians from Western Europe conquered it. Safety for every person in the city had been promised. They killed many people instead. Salah al-Din's birth happened inside the world just described. The city would be his to recover on a later day. His birth came in 1137 or in 1138. The place was Tikrit. Tikrit lies in modern-day Iraq. It lies far from Jerusalem. His father was a wealthy chief. The family moved to Syria while he was still a baby. That area belonged to a Turkic Muslim empire. His father began work for the ruler when the boy was six.

3The ruler was Sultan Zengi. The family later moved to Damascus. School began there at age seven. He learned the religion of Islam. He studied science. He studied math. He studied poetry. He studied the history of his people. Learning interested him more than soldiering. The words Salah al-Din are a title. The meaning is a person who honors the faith. Yusuf was the name he was given. Islam has five duties, called pillars. The first duty is faith. A Muslim states that Allah is the only God. A Muslim states that Muhammad is his messenger. The second duty is prayer. Prayer is done facing Mecca. It happens five times each day. One time is dawn. One time is noon. One time is afternoon. One time is evening. One time is night. The third duty is fasting. Muslims refuse food from dawn to dusk during Ramadan, the holy month. They do not drink from dawn to dusk. The fourth duty is almsgiving. A share of income must go from Muslims to people who need it. The fifth duty is pilgrimage. If possible, a Muslim travels to Mecca once in a lifetime. Sultan Zengi died in 1146. Nur al-Din was the second son. He received part of that kingdom. Salah al-Din's father became governor of Damascus.

4Army leadership came to his uncle Shirkuh. At fourteen he entered the army led by Nur al-Din. A few years later he became Nur al-Din's main helper. The new sultan was rich. He was powerful. He still led a simple life. He ruled fairly. That kind of man was the model he hoped to follow. Egypt was his destination years later. By then his age was the late twenties. He made the trip several times. His uncle Shirkuh went with him. The aim was to keep Egypt out of Christian control. The uncle ended up as Egypt's ruler. He died nine weeks later. Salah al-Din was thirty-one. The year 1169 made him the ruler who came next. He also commanded Egypt's Syrian army. He announced a plan. He would free Jerusalem from Christian control. Egypt gained many schools from his building. Scholars came to them from Europe. Scholars came from Asia. A huge palace could have been his home. He chose a small, simple house instead. Most of his riches were given to others. People followed him because he was firm. They followed him because he was gentle. They followed him because he was generous. Crusades were wars ordered by popes. Christians were called by the popes into a fight in the Middle East.

5The aim was to take Jerusalem from the Muslims. Surrounding areas were part of that aim. The First Crusade was ordered in 1095 by Pope Urban II. A picture shows Pope Urban II. Salah al-Din ordered a citadel built in Cairo, Egypt. That fort is named Citadel of Salah al-Din. Work ran from 1176 to 1184. The fort was meant as protection from the Crusaders. The year 1174 was the year Nur al-Din died. In his own view, nobody was better suited to rule. Syria was where he led an army. He fought Nur al-Din's brothers for nine years. During those years he ordered respectful treatment of enemies. His men never burned villages. They never stole from villages. Captured soldiers were never treated without mercy. The fighting ended in 1185. Lands between the Nile and the Tigris River came under his control. A war against the Christians was opened by Salah al-Din in 1187. The goal was to take Jerusalem back. Earlier years had the Christians fighting one another. The fight was over who should rule Jerusalem. A man named Raynald gained power over trade routes. He did not like Muslims. A French knight named Guy became king. Before that time, Arab traders passed peacefully through Christian lands. Christian traders passed peacefully through Arab lands.

6Treaties with Salah al-Din were broken once Raynald held power. He attacked Muslim towns. He attacked Muslim traders. Salah al-Din decided the time for war had come. In July 1187 his army trapped Guy's soldiers. The trap was on two hills. The hills are called the Horns of Hattin. The Christians were badly beaten. A picture recalls that Muslim victory. For the Crusaders, the loss was a hard one. King Guy was captured. Freedom was given to him later by Salah al-Din. Raynald was killed. Peace between the Christians and Salah al-Din had been wrecked by Raynald. In September the army surrounded Jerusalem. The holy city fell two weeks later. The date was October 2, 1187. The Christian takeover of 1099 had killed thousands. Salah al-Din did not do that. No Christian holy place was destroyed. Even Christians reported that nobody was treated badly. Holy places in the city stayed open to Christian visitors after the victory. His goal was met. Jerusalem was back under Muslim control. A battle map covers the years 1187 to 1192. Tyre is on it. The Syrian Desert is on it. Acre is on it. The Sea of Galilee is on it. Hattin is on it. Tiberias is on it. The Mediterranean Sea is on it.

7Jerusalem is on it. The Arabian Desert is on it. The Dead Sea is on it. Europe was shocked that Muslims had taken Jerusalem. Leaders called for another war. Several European kings raised armies. England's King Richard I was among them. People also call him Richard the Lionheart. The armies wanted the holy city back. In the end, Richard led them. Salah al-Din tried to capture Tyre. He did not succeed. Tyre was the strongest Christian city still standing. King Guy was set free by him around then. Acre was the city Guy went to. His supporters went there too. Muslims controlled that city. Guy's group surrounded it. Help arrived in the form of Crusaders from Europe. The Muslims at Acre stayed surrounded by the Christians for 638 days. For those same days, Salah al-Din's army surrounded the Christians. In the spring of 1191, leaders from Western Europe arrived with their armies. Philip Augustus of France came first. Richard the Lionheart came a few weeks later. Richard was a brilliant commander. Acre had to be given up by the Muslims because of him. The fall came only a month after he arrived. Christian soldiers were marched by him toward the coast in August of that year. He captured cities along the coast.

8Salah al-Din could not stop them. He moved his army to Jerusalem instead. He strengthened the city against Christian soldiers. The Christians never attacked. Richard saw that his army was not strong enough. It could not take the holy city. It could not hold the holy city. A picture shows Richard the Lionheart. On September 2, 1192, a truce was agreed. Salah al-Din's brother made the agreement with Richard. Christians could keep parts of the coast. The rest of the land would be Muslim land. Jerusalem was included in that Muslim land. Christians could still visit holy places. The battles were over. The Christian world gave Salah al-Din lasting respect. The reason was his fair conduct. Damascus was the home he returned to once the truce had been signed. Only six months after that, his life ended. The date was March 4, 1193. His age was fifty-five. Money had never mattered much to him. He had given everything away. No money remained to bury his body. His son later built a building in Damascus. Salah al-Din was buried there. His family kept ruling Egypt after his death. They also ruled nearby lands. That rule lasted until 1250. Another empire gained power then. A photo shows his tomb. The building that holds the tomb was built in 1193.

9It was restored in 1898. A statue of him on horseback stands in Damascus today. The city is in South Syria. He was a great leader. He was kind to his enemies. After he took Jerusalem back from the Crusaders, Christians could still visit the holy city. Some of the land the Christians had taken was left in their hands. His age in history was known for fierce battles. People remember him, among that age's most respected leaders, because he was fair. His oldest son heard his words just before death came. He said gentleness had won men's hearts. He said kindness had done the same. He said that was why he had grown as great as he was. Many people think he set an example. The example is a leader who is fair. The example is a leader who is good. He still sets that example today. A timeline sets out how Salah al-Din lived. In 1137 or 1138 he was born in Tikrit. The region was called Mesopotamia. From 1152 to 1169 he served under the Syrian ruler Nur al-Din. In 1169 he became ruler of Egypt. He also became commander of Egypt's Syrian troops. In 1174 Nur al-Din died. Uniting the Muslim states became the effort he began then.

10In 1185 he succeeded in uniting those states. On July 4, 1187, the Battle of Hattin was fought. On October 2, 1187, he recaptured Jerusalem. The battle for the city had lasted two weeks. In 1189 the Third Crusade began. On July 12, 1191, the battle in Acre ended. On August 4, 1192, the Battle of Jaffa ended. On September 2, 1192, he and Richard the Lionheart made a truce. On March 4, 1193, he died in Damascus. Brilliant means extremely intelligent or talented. An empire gathers nations under one ruler. It can also gather people under one ruler. A governor leads an area in politics. A colony is one such area. A state is another. Holy means related to a god or a religion. Sacred is another word for it. Mercy is forgiveness. It is also gentle handling of a person who deserves to be punished. A follower of Islam may be described as Muslim. A Muslim country may be ruled by a sultan. The role is similar to a king or an emperor. A treaty is a formal peace agreement. It can also be a formal agreement of friendship. They bind two nations or groups. A truce is an agreement not to fight.

99. The Lives of Monkeys

1This book moves through these parts. It opens with an introduction. Then come primates. Then monkeys are set beside apes. Then New World monkeys are set beside Old World monkeys. Then comes group life. Then come kinds of monkeys, first New World and then Old World. Then come babies. Then come monkeys and humans. A closing follows. A word list comes last. At the Bronx Zoo, visitors stand and watch a monkey. People feel nearer to monkeys than to the other animals. Hear someone say you act like a monkey, and that remark is probably close to fair. A monkey exhibit often holds a crowd longer than the other exhibits do. The silly actions catch people. Laughter follows. The show feels entertaining. A likely reason is how much monkeys resemble people. Monkeys are mammals, and their larger group is the primates. That group splits two ways. Anthropoids are one branch. Prosimians are the other. The primates most people recognize are the anthropoids. Monkeys sit in that branch. Apes sit in it. Humans sit in it. Prosimians are the less familiar branch. The lemur is the prosimian people know best. Ring-tailed lemurs belong with the prosimians. Hands set primates apart from other mammals. The fingers are well formed. A thumb faces those fingers and bends toward them. People call that thumb opposable. Small objects can be gripped hard because of that thumb. Other mammals lack this advantage. Tree life is the daily life of many primates. Branches can be grasped because of the thumb.

2Climbing is easier because of it. Orangutans are great apes, and an opposable thumb is part of their bodies. Among apes, chimpanzees rank with the most intelligent. Plenty of people treat apes as oversized monkeys. A gorilla is an ape. An orangutan is an ape. A chimpanzee is an ape. None of those animals is a monkey. A tail is missing on an ape. A tail is present on most monkeys. Intelligence is usually higher in apes than in monkeys. Body size is larger in apes too. Extra weight leads most apes to scramble along a branch and to climb along it. Monkeys can swing between branches. They can jump between branches. Home region splits monkeys into two groups. Central America and South America are home to the New World monkeys. In that New World, the only primates of this set are monkeys. Apes are absent. Prosimians are absent. Asia and Africa are where Old World monkeys are found. Apes belong among Old World primates. Prosimians belong there too. Monkeys belong there too. Four clear differences separate the two monkey groups. Noses are the first. New World nostrils sit wide apart. Old World nostrils sit near each other and aim downward, in the human way. The left animal is a golden lion tamarin, and it is a New World monkey. Look at its nostrils. On the right, study the Japanese macaque, an Old World monkey. Tails are the second difference.

3A prehensile tail lets some New World monkeys grip an object. Old World monkeys lack that ability. A grown spider monkey can seize a rope with that kind of tail. Hair is often missing on a prehensile tail. A human palm is bare in a similar way. Teeth are the third difference. A count of 36 teeth fits most New World monkeys. A count of 32 teeth fits most Old World monkeys, the same count humans have. Time spent in a place is the fourth difference. Trees are home for every New World monkey. The ground takes much of the day for many Old World monkeys. Group life comes next. A monkey lives with others of its own type. People call that group a troop. Fewer than 24 members is the usual size of a New World troop. Old World troops can grow far past that. A baboon troop can pass 100 members by a wide margin. One adult male is the only grown male in some troops. Several females and their young share that troop. Many adult males share other troops. Ground-living monkeys keep tighter groups. Enemies are more common on the ground, so these monkeys rely on one another more for safety. A threat brings the adults together. As a group they push the attacker off. The picture is a baboon troop. A young hamadryas baboon is in the picture. Arms on a monkey are long and strong. Legs are long and strong too. Leaping through trees is easier because of them.

4Swinging through trees is easier too. On the ground, those same limbs make a fast run possible. Fingers, like human fingers, grow on a monkey's hands. Objects can be grasped with them. An opposable thumb appears on some Old World monkeys. Small objects can be held with it. Small objects can be handled with it. A thumb that works only partway appears on some New World monkeys. Other New World monkeys have no thumb. A fifth finger takes its place. Each foot has five toes. On some kinds, the big toe can oppose the others and act as a thumb. Feet can then grip an object. Play between a young vervet monkey and its mother is shown here. Waking hours for young monkeys go largely to play, the way kids play. Food is what fills an adult day. Searching is part of that day. Eating is part of it. Grooming one another is part of it. Almost any food will do. Plant parts are eaten. Fruits are among those parts. Nuts are among them. Leaves are among them. Roots are among them. Flowers are among them. Animals are eaten too. Insects, frogs, and birds are among them. A baboon may even attack a small hoofed animal and eat it. A baby antelope is one example. Eggs are also food for most monkeys. Voice is one way monkeys send messages. Body language is another. A stare can be a threat.

5Bared teeth can be a threat. A head that bobs back and forth can be a threat. Hands send messages too. A chest may be beaten. The ground may be slapped. Danger brings a voice warning. Finding food brings a voice signal. A few monkeys even have words for things they know well. The vervet (VUR-vit) does not stop at one all-purpose alarm. Snake has its own call. Eagle has its own call. Leopard has its own call. Territory is defended by howler monkeys with shouts and howls that keep other monkeys out. A black howler is shown shouting at an intruder. More than 150 kinds of monkeys exist. A few are tiny. Leave off the tail, and a pygmy marmoset is only about the length of a new pencil. The mandrill is the largest monkey. Stand an adult mandrill up, and the height matches a kitchen counter. New World monkeys include the spider monkey. Its prehensile tail works like one more hand. The animal hangs from a branch with that tail. It lifts objects with that tail. Thumbs are absent, which sets spider monkeys apart from most other monkeys. Say marmoset as MAR-mo-set. These monkeys rank among the smallest. Most measure under 30 centimeters, or 1 foot. Nails cover the fingers of most monkeys. Claws cover the fingers of marmosets. Above, a black howler monkey is shown. At the right, a golden lion tamarin is shown. The howl of a howler is famous and loud.

6A listener 3 kilometers away can hear it, and that distance is 2 miles. Among New World monkeys, howlers are the largest. Their tails are long. Their faces are black. Adult howlers wear a beard on that face. Say tamarin as TAM-ur-in. These monkeys are small, usually about 30 centimeters, or 1 foot. More than one color shows on most of them. Long hair grows on the tops of many heads. A mane on the golden lion tamarin gives it the look of a little lion. A chart on this page sets monkeys side by side. The columns are type, size, life span, food, and habitat. Howler, New World. Chart size: 6.8 kilograms, or 15 pounds. Chart life span: 20 years. Chart food includes flowers, fruit, and small animals. Spider monkey, New World. Chart size: 8 to 9.5 kilograms, or 17.6 to 21 pounds. Chart life span: 33 years. Chart food: fruit and nuts. Marmoset, New World. Chart size: 300 to 500 grams, or 10.6 to 17.6 ounces. Chart life span: 12 years. Chart food: fruit, sap, small animals, and insects. Tamarin, New World. Chart size: 410 to 560 grams, or 14.5 to 19.8 ounces. Chart life span: 15 years. Chart food includes fruit and small animals. Mandrill, Old World. A female weighs 13.6 kilograms, or 30 pounds. A male weighs 27 kilograms, or 60 pounds. Beside the male weight, the chart lists 46 years. The food list is fruit, nuts, vegetation, and leaves. Baboon, Old World.

7A female baboon weighs 12 kilograms, or 26 pounds. A male baboon weighs 20 kilograms, or 45 pounds. The life span is 37 years. Food is fruit and plants, and also small animals and insects. The baboon habitat is the forest floor and the plains. The floor in Africa is part of that habitat. The proboscis monkey is an Old World monkey. Size is 8.2 to 23 kilograms. A weight of 15 to 50 pounds is on that same line. The life span is 13.5 years. Food is pedada leaves, animals, and insects. The habitat is mangrove forests and rainforest in Borneo. The colobus is an Old World monkey. Size is 13.6 kilograms, or 30 pounds. The life span is 29 years. Food is fruit, leaves, flowers, and buds. The habitat is the space above the forest floor in the forests of Africa. High elevations are part of the colobus habitat as well. Rainforest canopies in South America and Central America are the spider monkey and howler habitats. A height of 3 to 9 meters goes with those tree homes. Brazil and Ecuador, and rainforests in Brazil, are the marmoset and tamarin habitats. Tropical forest in central Africa is the mandrill habitat. Old World monkeys include the baboons. These large monkeys grow long, sharp canine teeth. Most of their hours are spent on the ground. The African plains are home to many baboon types. The olive baboon is one of those types. A mandrill is a kind of baboon, and mandrills are the biggest monkeys. Color on the male face is well known.

8Color on the male rump is well known too. Cheeks are blue. Noses are red. The rump repeats those same colors. Say colobus as CALL-ah-bus. These monkeys are medium in size. Length runs from 45 to 75 centimeters, or 1.5 to 2.5 feet. Strength and a stocky build are typical. Color is not the same on every animal. Some are black all over. Some are black and white. Some are red and olive green. Say proboscis as pruh-BOSS-kiss. The long nose gives these monkeys their name. In Latin, proboscis means nose. Males call with that nose. Body length, tails left out, runs from 70 to 100 centimeters, or 2 to 3 feet. Swimming is something they do very well. Most monkey mothers have a single baby each time. Once born, the baby gets every bit of food from its mother. It gets every bit of care from her too. Mother's milk is the baby's food, as with every mammal. Nursing time changes with the kind of monkey. Two weeks can be enough. Two years can be the long end. Fur is what the baby holds. The belly is the first place it clings. Later it rides on her back. It keeps holding on until its own travel is safe. Marmosets are one species in which the male cares for the young. He carries the baby through the day. At nursing time he passes the baby to the mother. A baby yellow baboon is shown clinging to its mother's back.

9In 1961 a chimpanzee named Ham is pictured getting ready to go into space. Movies have starred monkeys and their ape relatives. Circuses have starred them too. Many television shows have used them. Many books have been about them. Some have even ridden rockets into space. Similarity to humans is why people have used monkeys in medical research. Using monkeys that way draws objections from many people. Using other animals that way draws objections too. Still, new medicines have taught us a great deal through monkeys. Humans did not have to be the first test. Monkey meat counts as a delicacy in some cultures. Monkey brains are eaten by some people. Capture has been the fate of many monkeys. Zoos around the world hold them. Display cages hold them too. Today's zoos have tried to give monkeys a setting like a wild habitat. At the Bronx Zoo, ebony leaf monkeys live in a habitat built to feel natural. Pets are another life for many monkeys around the world. Because monkeys are clever and can handle objects, trainers have taught some of them to assist people who are unable to move. Paralyzed people get help with their work. They get help cooking. They even get help brushing teeth. A boy from Bolivia is shown beside his pet monkey. Wild monkey numbers are threatened because people destroy habitats. Hunters are another threat, since many people want monkey meat to eat. In many places, work is underway to help those populations survive.

10Monkeys show up in many places. Cartoons give them roles. Movies give them acting parts. Almost every zoo has them on view. A pet monkey may belong to someone you meet. A helper monkey may belong to someone you meet. Love for monkeys is easy to understand, because they resemble humans so strongly. They are primates with strong minds. An opposable thumb is part of them. Objects are something they can use. Words are something they can use too. Difference is real as well. Humans do not come in a crowd of species the way monkeys do. No other primate has more species than monkeys do. Funny, smart, beautiful, and useful are fair words for them. Protection and respect are what these animals should receive. One tantalus monkey grooms another. Grooming here means cleaning. Word list. Anthropoids are the primates that include monkeys, apes, and humans. A habitat is the land and the surroundings where an animal lives. North America and South America are the continents meant by New World. Asia, Europe, and Africa are the continents meant by Old World. An opposable thumb faces the other fingers and bends toward them. Prehensile describes a foot, a tail, or another limb that can grip or lift the way a hand can. Primates take in monkeys, apes, humans, lemurs, and more. Prosimians are the smaller primate set that includes lemurs. A troop is monkeys of one species sharing a life together.

100. The Long Path of a Meal

1This book starts with the moment we eat. It then tells about ingestion. It tells about absorption. It tells about elimination. It closes with ideas to think about. A word list comes at the end. Each meal sends food on an amazing trip inside the body. Let's Eat. A catchy line goes like this. Food crosses the lips, moves past the gums, and aims for the stomach. The line tells the path of every bit of chicken once it is in the mouth. It captures every piece of cheese and chocolate too. Getting chewed is only the start. Getting swallowed is only the start too. Every bite takes a long trip along the digestive system. The ride is messy. It is slow, like a roller coaster in slow motion. From the top downward, organs join in an astonishing network that digests food. The organs work together. What we eat gets broken into tinier bits. Work continues until molecules from food become energy. Digestion also supplies raw material used to build the body. Those materials build bones and muscles. They build skin and eyeballs. They build toenails, nose hairs, and spit. They build everything else. Eating itself is something people already understand. What follows is told from the upper end downward. Ingestion. Picture a fresh pizza just coming from the oven. Think of another favorite dish. Smell from a favorite food can set the mouth watering.

2There is a very good reason. The body is preparing to ingest. Ingest means to eat. A tasty smell switches the digestive system on before the first bite. Glands in the mouth begin to ooze saliva. Saliva is another word for spit. Water makes up nearly all of that spit. Molecules known as enzymes are in it as well. Those enzymes start breaking food down. Teeth work like a shredder so digestion is easier. Slicing is the job of sharp teeth at the front. They can slice into an apple or a sandwich. Harder foods, including nuts, are ground by strong flat teeth at the back. All the while, saliva softens every mouthful. Starchy foods are what these enzymes break apart best. Bread is one of those foods. Crackers and potatoes are others. Many germs riding in food are also killed by saliva. It does this before the germs can make us sick. Flavors are enjoyed by way of taste buds sitting on the tongue. Now the tongue has another job. The tongue pushes that mashed glob of food into the throat. That glob is called a bolus. Bolus is said as BOH-luhss. The trip keeps going once swallowing happens. Digestion is the next stage. The swallow sends the bolus into the esophagus. Esophagus is said as ih-SOF-uh-guhss.

3From the rear of the mouth, a tube called the esophagus leads down toward the stomach. A flap with a leaf-like shape sits high on the esophagus. It is called the epiglottis. Epiglottis is said as eh-puh-GLAH-tuhss. The flap shuts to block food from the breathing tube. Drinks are blocked from the lungs too. Have you gulped water and then begun to cough? Some of the water dribbled down the wrong tube. An epiglottis that failed to shut soon enough was the cause. A chart of the digestive system can show many parts working together. Those parts are the esophagus, the liver, and the gallbladder. They include the stomach, the pancreas, and the small intestine. They include the large intestine, the appendix, and the rectum. As a group they turn food into separate things the body must have. The esophagus measures about 25 centimeters. That is 10 inches. It follows a downward path behind the throat. It sits behind the windpipe. Muscles line the esophagus. Those muscles drive food in the direction of the stomach. The trip from the esophagus to the stomach usually takes two to three seconds. The stomach is where the breakdown keeps going. Picture a rubbery sack bent like a comma. It produces gastric juices. Acid plus enzymes make up most of those juices. Gastric mucus covers the inside of the stomach. That slippery coating guards the stomach against acid made inside it.

4Trouble With Lactose. Some of us have trouble digesting certain foods. Many people have a digestive disorder called lactose intolerance. Lactose is the main carbohydrate in milk. It is also in cheese and other dairy products. The disorder appears when too little lactase is made. Lactase is an enzyme. Lactase digests lactose. It breaks lactose into glucose and galactose. Those are two sugars the body can use. Lactose remains whole when lactase is too low. That can make people feel ill. It can make them feel gassy. Lactose intolerance is common. Some version of this problem shows up in about 75 percent of people worldwide. Food comes apart faster because of gastric juices. Churning is how muscles wrapped around the stomach lend help. They turn solids into mush. As many as five hours may pass before a meal is fully broken down and ready to leave. The digestive system works extra hard to fight germs that might make us ill. Bacteria that bring sickness can be destroyed by these juices. Those bacteria might have ridden in on our food. Victory over those germs is not guaranteed. The body may notice germs in food that could cause harm. An illness that bothers the stomach lining may be the other cause. The body may then send a signal that the stomach must empty.

5A muscle above the stomach squeezes down. That muscle is the diaphragm. Diaphragm is said as DY-uh-fram. Muscles across the abdomen tighten as well. The contents of the stomach may then leave quickly as vomit. Vomiting is never pleasant. It is still another way the digestive system protects us. Success leaves the stomach with a nutrient-rich smoothie. The chicken, the cheese, or the chocolate now belongs to a gloppy mess. The mess is called chyme. Chyme is said as KYM. Muscles drive the mixture forward to the following stop. That station is the small intestine. The digestive system turns food into nutrients. The brain gets fuel from carbohydrates. They power muscles. They help the body fight disease. Fats help the body absorb vitamins and minerals. They support healthy blood. They help build cells and muscle. Calcium, iron, zinc, and other minerals belong in this group. Teeth and bones get built with calcium. It keeps them strong. Iron supports healthy blood. Zinc helps the body ward off illness. It helps cuts and bruises heal. Green leafy vegetables supply minerals. Many other foods do too. Proteins are the body's building blocks. They support growth. They help the body gain strength or keep it. Proteins sit in every cell, including muscle, bone, and hair. Vitamins help fight illness and disease. They support healthy eyes, skin, and bones.

6They can ease depression. Vitamins fill fruits, vegetables, and eggs. Water is a nutrient the whole body needs in order to work. Six glasses a day are advised for ages nine through thirteen. A diagram places the stomach and the pancreas with the liver. It also places both intestines and the gallbladder. Most of a meal's time in the body is inside those two intestines. The small intestine is not actually small. Most adults have a coil that measures 6.1 meters. That is 20 feet. The name comes from its narrow width. Side to side, it is about 2.5 centimeters. That is 1 inch. Its main job is absorption. A sponge absorbs by soaking up spilled water or another liquid. The intestinal walls take nutrients from arriving chyme in a similar way. Duodenum names the opening section of the small intestine. Say it doo-AH-dih-nuhm. Two ducts, which are openings, deliver bile and digestive enzymes. Those chemicals keep digestion going. The liver makes bile. The gallbladder stores it. Bile helps split fats. It also helps split vitamins. The pancreas makes digestive enzymes. Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are all broken apart by those enzymes. Nutrients are then ready for absorption. Most absorption happens in the small intestine. The lining is only one cell thick. Nutrient molecules pass through it easily and reach the blood. Blood carries them where they are needed.

7Running, thinking, and carrying a backpack all require energy. Food supplies that energy. The body turns food into molecules. Glucose is one of those molecules. It is a simple sugar, yet it holds a lot of power. Some glucose is used right away. Extra glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and the muscles. Say glycogen GLY-kuh-juhn. If that extra sits unused too long, the body stores it as fat. Blood leaving digestion carries nutrients and chemicals. The liver filters that blood. Arteries and veins serve the liver. The liver also clears harmful chemicals, like a filter. It sends some nutrients on to other organs and to other cell groups. Other vitamins and important sugars wait in the liver until needed. Those sugars are the body's main fuel. Every usable nutrient gets used. The rest is stored. Anything still unabsorbed moves on. The large intestine receives it. Too much glucose, also called blood sugar, can harm health. Insulin is a hormone. It helps the body use glucose properly. It helps the body store glucose properly. Some bodies make insulin poorly. Some use it poorly. Those people can develop diabetes. That disease brings serious health risks. Elimination. Last among the organs of digestion is the large intestine. In adults its length is about 1.5 meters, equal to 5 feet. Its distance around is about 7.6 centimeters, or 3 inches.

8Food that the stomach has not digested ends up here. So does food that the small intestine has not absorbed. More water may still leave the digested food by crossing these walls. Some leftover vitamins may be drawn off too. Some leftover minerals may as well. Salt is one of those minerals. Crossing the walls, these nutrients enter the blood. The same thing happens in the small intestine. What remains is prepared here so it can leave the body. That waste is feces, better known as poop. A chart can show the large intestine, also called the colon. It can show the rectum and the anus. This is the final chance for nutrients to be pulled from food already digested. Microbes in huge variety mainly live here too. Most of them are bacteria. These microbes are not merely good to have inside us. They are vital. They fight harmful germs. They also produce vitamins. Gut microbes make vitamin K, as one example. Vitamin K builds stronger bones. It builds healthier blood. Strong muscles around this organ finally press the poop ahead to its final stop. That stop is the rectum. Nerves in that spot announce the moment for poop to leave by way of the anus. What is actually in our poop? Water makes up the largest share. A portion is waste left from food.

9Bacteria account for about one third of the solids inside feces. Those bacteria come from the small intestine and the large intestine. Most of the gas that leaves us also traces back to these bacteria. Bile that stayed with the waste is what makes the usual brown shade. The digestive system has completed the work one more time. Washing your hands after you use the bathroom removes germs. It helps keep you healthy. It helps keep other people healthy too. You can care for your digestive system so it can care for you. Three suggestions make the work easier for the stomach and the intestines. First, eat real food. Cut back on junky grub. Foods full of sugar may taste good. Foods full of salt, also called sodium, may taste good. The body is not well served by them. A snack package with a very long list of unfamiliar chemicals is a cue to pick something else. That choice is better for digestion and for overall health. Second, eat more fiber. Good foods to eat more often include oatmeal. Beans belong on that list. So do nuts. So do seeds. So do vegetables. Lots of fiber works like a scrub brush inside the system. Third, slow down and chew. Teeth and saliva mash the mouthful more when you go slowly.

10Digestion gets easier. Absorption gets easier. Slower eating cuts indigestion, belching, and gas. Mess is part of this system. Smell is sometimes part of it. A biological assembly line is a fair picture of the work. Food travels from the top of the body to the bottom. Strength, health, and energy are supplied on the way. The system is one of the body's true marvels. A few words name the parts. An enzyme is a protein, in a plant or an animal, that starts certain natural chemical reactions. The abdomen runs from the chest down to the hips, and most digestive organs sit there. Gastric means related to the stomach. Absorption means soaking something up or taking it in. Microbes are organisms too small to see without a microscope. The digestive system is the body parts that break food down and take in nutrients for living and growing. A molecule is the tiniest bit of a substance that is able to exist alone. Atoms, one or several, build each molecule. A nutrient is a substance life needs for living, for health, and for growth. Dissolving means a thing comes apart, and a liquid is usually what causes it. Saliva is mouth liquid that mixes with food and helps digestion start. Elimination means removing something or taking it away. Vital means necessary for success or for survival.

101. The Mystery in Loch Ness

1An opening starts this book. Then comes the loch called Ness. Sightings of a monster follow. A part asks whether the tale is fact or fiction. A closing and a word list finish the book. Loch is a word for a lake. It can also mean a thin reach of seawater that runs in from the coast. Scotland's own language is the source of the word. Scottish Gaelic is that language. Say it GAY-lick. Myth or legend: which one is the Loch Ness Monster? People tell of something strange rising out of dark water. The water is Loch Ness, in Scotland. Old accounts of dragons come to mind. Sea serpents come to mind too. Dark is the body. Long is the neck. The head looks like a sheep's head. Two humps, or more, sit on the back. Nessie is the monster's name. The name comes from the loch, the lake, that holds it.

2Legends, myths, and stories in many places tell of strange sea creatures. A water spirit in Scottish myth is called a kelpie. A horse is what it looks like. Sailors who first went past the sight of land spoke of monsters. Some, they said, were big enough to swallow a whole ship. Legend gives those enormous, awful beasts a job: they guarded treasure. The sea bottom is where that treasure lay. Might Nessie belong with those monsters of myth, or of legend? The picture shows a legendary beast whose home was called the Sea of Darkness. Large is the water said to hide the legendary Loch Ness Monster. No other freshwater lake in the British Isles is larger. Length is 24 miles, or 39 kilometers. Width is only 1 mile, or 1.6 kilometers. Depth in some places is over 800 feet, or 244 meters.

3Seas around the British Isles are not this deep. The last ice age is when Loch Ness formed. Scotland, as the land is called now, split in two. A trench was made by earthquakes. Ice from glaciers lay over that trench. The cover lasted to roughly 12,000 years before now. Melting ice filled the trench. A loch was the result. A map names the British Isles and the Atlantic Ocean. It names Northern Ireland, Loch Ness, and Scotland. It names the North Sea, Ireland, and the Irish Sea. It names Wales, England, and the Celtic Sea. It names the English Channel and France. Very cold is the water in Loch Ness. Peat is dead plant material in a layer. That layer is thick in this water. Light gets down only a few yards because of the peat. Sunlight cannot warm the water.

4Swimming is too cold for people. Summer warms the top 100 feet, which is 30.5 meters. The warm level is 54 degrees Fahrenheit, or 12 degrees Celsius. Everything deeper stays at 42 degrees Fahrenheit, or 6 degrees Celsius, all year. Life in the loch, for that reason, stays near the surface. Fish do. Seals do. A gray seal, seen in a loch, might be taken for a monster. More than 1,400 years have passed with curious people treating Nessie sightings as serious. NASA computers have been used by scientists. Underwater cameras and other gear have tested the loch. The 1970s are when that testing began. Earlier eyes had already seen the monster there. The first written sighting is from the year 565. Saint Columba, an Irish missionary, is the source. He asked a servant to swim the loch. A boat was the errand. A creature rose.

5A roar came. The mouth opened. Columba ordered it back. Quiet was ordered. Touching the man was forbidden. The creature obeyed. Sightings after that one have all been quiet and peaceful. One man said he had seen Nessie. He said a film was made too. Urquhart Castle stands above water in Loch Ness that ranks among the deepest anyone has measured. Say the castle name ER-kert. Sightings stayed quiet until the 1930s. Cameras grew popular then. Hunting for Nessie took off in a flash. A picture, at least, was what people hoped to catch. Thousands who live nearby have signed a statement. The statement promises they have seen the monster. Most sightings sit near the ruins of Urquhart Castle. Midpoint of the loch is where those ruins stand. Deepest water is there. Strange water creatures are reported in other places too, not only at Loch Ness.

6Lakes and rivers that have such reports number at least 265, around the world. A saltwater mammal is one guess. A fish is another. A prehistoric reptile is another guess for the Nessie reports. Survival across millions of years is the idea. The trench of the last ice age, some say, trapped a prehistoric beast. A whole group of beasts may have been trapped, landlocked. A link to the plesiosaur is what some people believe. Millions of years ago is when the plesiosaur lived. Extinct is what it is now. Boats in a line across Loch Ness were used by Operation Deep Scan. Evidence of the legendary monster was the search. Fact or fiction is the question of this part. Some people take the Nessie reports as fact. Believers point to descriptions that match one another. They point to how many eyewitness reports exist. Possible sonar evidence is another point.

7Other people call the reports legends. Children, those legends would say, should stay away from water that is deep and cold. Nonbelievers point to missing proof. Hard scientific evidence that Nessie is real has not appeared. Hoaxes have been built so the world would believe. Tricks of that kind keep the Loch Ness Monster legend alive. A newspaper printed a photograph in 1934. Later, the picture was shown to be a hoax. Photos are the basis of several hoaxes that became very well known. Three humps in one photo were taken for the real monster. Three bales of hay were the truth. Black tar covered them. A famous 1934 photograph was fake as well. A toy submarine carried a made-up sea-serpent head. Another 1934 hoax stirred excitement. Mud on the banks held a giant footprint. A stuffed hippopotamus foot was the tool a man used to press it.

8Scientists stepped in despite the hoaxes. Real or not: that was the question they wanted settled. An end to the mystery was the hope. Consistent evidence remained, and people could not explain it. Sonar, for example, found a long object. It moved at a depth of 480 feet. Most fish cannot live that deep. A map of the whole loch became the plan. The year 1987 is when scientists launched Operation Deep Scan. Twenty-four boats took part. Sonar gear mapped the bottom. It mapped the sides. Sound is what sonar uses to name the shapes of objects. A sonar machine sends a sound out. An echo comes back when the sound hits something. Time for that bounce is what scientists measure. A picture can be built from the time. Objects hidden by murky water show up on a sonar machine in the loch.

9Some sounds in Operation Deep Scan were echoes off steep sides. At least one echo stayed unexplained. Large and moving is how that object was described. Two hundred feet down is where it was. Nobody knows for sure what it was. Could it have been Nessie? Divers send a creature camera into Loch Ness. The hope is a photo taken under the water, showing the monster of the legend. Other findings have come from study of the loch. The year 1981 brought a fish find by the Loch Ness Project. Red-bellied Arctic char is the fish. Say Arctic as ARK-tick. Depth of the living place was 700 feet, or 213 meters. More than 12,000 years, back to the last ice age, is how long they had lived there. Experts had thought life could not last below a few hundred feet, because of the cold.

10Surprise followed the find of red-bellied Arctic char. One picture asks whether you see Nessie. Legendary status may leave the Loch Ness Monster someday. A new species of fish is one possible identification. Say species as SPEE-sheez. For now, mystery is what Nessie remains. Appeal may be greatest because of that mystery. Imaginations keep getting caught by the legend. A word list follows. Bales are bundles wrapped tight. Hoaxes are tricks that push people to accept a fake thing as real. A legend is an old story people hold as true, even though proof is missing. Peat is brown material like soil, used in gardens and burned as fuel. Sonar finds objects under water and measures how deep water is, by sending sounds and timing the echoes that return. A species is a group of animals alike enough that they may have babies together.

102. The Nation's Great Library

1A photograph shows the Library of Congress. Someone took that photo in 1902. By then, one fire had already damaged the building. A second fire had damaged it too. Both fires came before the picture. In 1804, two explorers set out. They crossed North America. Meriwether Lewis was one leader. William Clark was the other leader. The United States had acquired land. The explorers went to study that land. Along the route, they drew maps. The maps were thorough. Settlers who came later could use them. The maps offered those settlers aid. The nation planned to expand. Growth would go westward. The maps supported that plan. One map guided the men each day. People still call the journey historic. Today the guiding map is kept safe. Workers there guard that map. While the group traveled, Lewis added notes. He made corrections as well. He updated the map during the trip. This library holds major American documents. Those papers record the nation's history. The explorers' map is one of the papers. Visitors can tour a famous room. People call it the Main Reading Room. This library is the national library. It serves the United States. No other library anywhere is bigger. A local library is very different from this one. Books are stored here. Artifacts are stored here too.

2Documents are stored here as well. Many of these items exist in no other place. In some ways, the building is like a museum. At the start, the shelves held 740 books. Only three maps were there then. The book total is now more than 38 million. The map total is over five million. Photographs are part of the collection. Newspapers are part of them too. Letters are included. Films are included. Diaries are included. Still more kinds of items are kept. Together, the items form the collection. The total is more than 168 million items. The items use 470 languages. Growth has not stopped. About 12,000 items are added every day. Shelves run more than 830 miles. The same length is more than 1,335 km. Compare the shelves with a trip between two cities. One city is Washington, D.C. The other city is Jefferson City, Missouri. The shelves are longer than the trip. People who founded the United States saw a need. Libraries mattered to them. They believed books were necessary. They believed knowledge was necessary too. A democracy must have both if it is to succeed. In 1800, Congress held a vote. Congress is part of the U.S. government. Its job is creating laws. The vote chose a new capital. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, had been the capital.

3Washington, D.C., became the capital. It is still the capital today. President John Adams gave support. Congress then voted to build a library. The library would stand in Washington, D.C. Its chief purpose was a work place for members of Congress. They needed a place for research. They also needed a place for writing. The writing would become the nation's laws. A photo from 1891 shows the library while it was under construction. Thomas Jefferson helped the library live again. He served as president number three. The country was the United States. The first building was ruined in 1814. The first collection was ruined that year too. Jefferson's part in the rebirth was a major one. Soldiers from Britain arrived in 1814. They attacked the capital. The capital was Washington, D.C. They burned many buildings. Fire destroyed the White House. Fire destroyed the Capitol Building too.
