The original library was inside the Capitol. Jefferson owned 6,487 books. In 1814 he sold that personal library. The buyer was Congress. Visitors can still see his book collection. It remains on view at the library. Jefferson cared about many subjects. History was one subject he valued. Science was another subject he valued. He believed wide knowledge was important. People could use such knowledge to create laws.

4Staff still follow this belief. It guides each new item they add. A time line tracks the growth. In 1800, the library was established. President John Adams supported the start. During 1814, British soldiers struck Washington, D.C. Flames ruined the Capitol Building in that attack. The library's rooms were in that building. Also in 1814, Jefferson sold Congress the books he owned. The books were his own collection. The sale helped build the library again. In 1851, a fire began by accident. The date was Christmas Eve. Much of the collection was lost. By 1873, growth had filled the space. The collection no longer fit. Leaders held a competition for an architect. The winner would design a new building. Work on that building lasted seven years. In 1897, the doors opened. The public could come in. In 1939, workers added a second building. More growth made the extra building necessary. In 1980, workers added a third building. People named it the James Madison Building. The 1897 building received a new name later. The name honors Thomas Jefferson. People named the 1939 building for John Adams. Lawmakers are not the only people this library serves. It collects records of American lives. It also collects records of American accomplishments. Books are one kind of record.

5Some items may surprise a visitor. Board games sit in the collection. Musical instruments sit there too. A lock of hair is stored as well. The hair belonged to Thomas Jefferson. Many books stand on the shelves. That is true of other libraries too. A large share of the books are rare. Rare means only a few copies exist. Most libraries do not hold so many rare books. The rare-book group here is the largest one in North America. Only a handful of libraries anywhere keep these same titles. The smallest book has a name. The name is Old King Cole. Each side is 1/25 inch long. The matching metric size is 1 sq mm. Picture a period that ends a sentence. This book is about that tiny. The largest book has a long name. The name begins with Bhutan. The rest calls the work a visual odyssey. The subject is a trip across the Himalayan kingdom. The book is 5 feet tall. The metric height is 1.53 m. The book weighs 130 pounds. The metric weight is 58.9 kg. Some adults are about this large. The oldest printed book here was made in 770 ce. Its age is more than a thousand years. Some books here were written by hand. Those go back further than the printed ones.

6The oldest item with writing is a tablet. The writing on it is cuneiform. Ancient Mesopotamians invented that writing. It is among the earliest ways of writing. The tablet goes back to 2040 bce. A tablet of this kind is kept for visitors to learn about. Key papers from the United States are here too. One paper is a rough draft. The draft is an early writing of the Declaration of Independence. James Madison was president. His own copy of a famous paper is here. The paper is the Bill of Rights. A world map made in 1507 is here too. People call the map America's Birth Certificate. The name America is printed on it. No older document shows that name. Comic books fill many shelves. Nearly every superhero appears in those comics. This comic group is the largest one on Earth. Personal items of famous Americans are here. Some belonged to presidents. Some belonged to explorers. Some belonged to artists. Some belonged to inventors. Susan B. Anthony wrote diaries. The library keeps those diaries. She worked so women could vote. The vote was the right she sought. Wilbur Wright left notebooks. Orville Wright left notebooks too. Their photographs are stored beside the notebooks. One photograph shows a flight. It was the first flight that succeeded.

7People remember it as the first working airplane flight. Abraham Lincoln died in 1865. Items from his pockets that night are on display. The library shows them to visitors. Not every item here comes from long ago. In 2010, leaders made a decision about social media. They called social media important. Social media counts as communication. From it, people can learn about society today. From 2010 to 2017, workers saved public posts. Each saved post was a tweet. The posts came from Twitter. They dated from 2006 onward. Every public tweet from that span was saved. The first three years produced a huge number. The number was 170 billion tweets. More than three thousand workers have jobs here. The Librarian of Congress leads them. This leader makes important decisions. Some decisions guide the way the library runs. Other decisions choose what the library collects. The president picks the librarian. A term lasts ten years. A few leaders stayed much longer than that. George Herbert Putnam stayed the longest. He led as head librarian. The job lasted forty years. It started in 1899. It ended in 1939. In the library's first two hundred years, only thirteen people held the post. A fourteenth leader was chosen in 2016. President Barack Obama made the choice.

8He selected Carla Hayden. She was the first woman in the post. She was also the first African American in the post. Art covers the Great Hall. Learning is a common theme in that art. Knowledge is a common theme too. One well-known artwork is a mosaic. The mosaic shows Minerva. She was the Roman goddess of wisdom. The library now has three buildings. Each one carries a former president's name. Tourists visit one building in Washington, D.C., more than the others. That site is the Thomas Jefferson Building. Visitors treat it as a popular attraction. Inside it, one room is the main room. People know that room as the Great Hall. More than fifty artists worked on the room. Some made sculptures. Some made paintings. Some made mosaics. The room displays art of the United States. It also displays the nation's culture. The pieces come from the country's early years. In those years, the country was still new. Members of Congress still study here. They study subjects tied to new laws. The laws are ones they are writing. Only some people may take items out. People in Congress may do so. Other government members may do so too. They must have special permission. Anyone may visit, even without that permission. A visitor can read books.

9A visitor can do research. A visitor can view exhibits. A visitor can take a tour. The tour costs nothing. Hundreds of thousands of people come in a year. In 2018, the visit count was nearly two million. One exhibit is about early Native American culture. Guests can walk through it. The exhibit stands in the exhibit hall. Millions of collection items are now digitized. People far away can see those items. They can study them on a screen. A journey to Washington, D.C., is not required for that. One building is the main home of this library. People call that building the Thomas Jefferson Building. The first job of the library was service. The service was for Congress. Today the library matters to every American. Its role in their lives is important. It helps preserve the nation's history. It helps preserve the nation's culture too. Many items are one of a kind. No other place in the world has them. The items help tell how the country grew. They also help tell how the country changed. That change covers a long span of time. Here, the items stay protected. Future generations can still use them. Acquired means got something. It can also mean learned something. Documents are things people wrote or printed.

10A document can give a record. It can give information. It can give proof. Appointed means chosen for a certain job. A draft is an early version. It is not the finished work. The work may be a piece of writing. The work may be a drawing. Artifacts are old objects. Humans made them or used them long ago. An attraction is something people enjoy. It may be a person. It may be a thing. It may be a kind of entertainment. Exhibits are displays open to the public. A display might hold one object. It might hold many objects. Museums often set up exhibits. A collection is a set of items kept as a group. The items go together. A person may choose to save them. Mosaics are pictures built from tiny colored bits. A bit might be paper. A bit might be tile. A bit might be glass. Communication means sharing information. People may share with words. They may share with pictures. They may share with gestures. They may share in other ways. To preserve something is to take care of it. It also means to save it for later people. Research is careful study. The study looks hard at one subject. It may discover new information. It may also find facts.

103. The Plan That Governs the Nation

1This book tells why a constitution was needed. It tells about a historic meeting. It tells what is in the Constitution. It tells how the document stays alive. It tells about the legacy of the Constitution. A word list comes at the end. British forces surrendered at Yorktown in 1781. That surrender closed the final big campaign in the Revolutionary War. Why a Constitution Was Needed. Independence from Great Britain came to the United States in 1783. The war had lasted seven years. Americans were happy to have their own country at last. They soon realized a different kind of government was required. From 1781 onward, the states shared an agreement and tried to work as one. That agreement was called the Articles of Confederation. It was not working. Under the Articles, most power sat with the states. The Continental Congress was the nation's first government. It had very little power. A single state saying no left the congress nearly powerless. By 1786, the need for a stronger government at the center was plain. At the Constitutional Convention, George Washington was the president. This role came before his later election as the nation's president. A Historic Meeting. Summer 1787 brought delegates together in Philadelphia. They came to create a new constitution, which is a plan of government.

2Washington was one person in that group. It included Benjamin Franklin. James Madison was part of the group. He did the main writing on the Constitution. George Washington directed the delegates. Talks focused on the shape the new government ought to have. All through that hot summer, they laid their ideas out. They argued about those ideas too. The result was a government built from three branches. The legislative branch is Congress. The executive branch is the presidency. The judicial branch is the federal courts. Opening the Constitution are three words: We the people. Those words have come to stand for the central idea of democracy. The finished plan was built to endure for hundreds of years. No other law in the nation ranks above the United States Constitution. No older written plan of government remains in use anywhere. Early in 1789, yes votes had come from eleven states. It became law. The final two states added their approval near the close of May 1790. Those states were North Carolina and Rhode Island. February 1789 was when voters chose George Washington as the first president under this plan. A new age had begun. What Is in the Constitution?

3The opening of the Constitution explains the goal of the document. The goal is a society that is just, peaceful, safe, and prosperous. In that society, the blessings of liberty are meant for the people. Seven articles, also called sections, form the main body. How the three branches are set up is told in the first three articles. Article I deals with Congress. Congress is divided into two parts. One part is the House of Representatives. The other part is the Senate. Passing new laws is the chief work of both houses. Tax collection is another power the Constitution grants to Congress. Congress also receives the power to see to national defense. The executive branch is the subject of Article II. Certain powers are handed to the president in that article. The president is placed at the head of the nation's armed forces. It also explains who may run for president. That person must be a natural-born citizen. That person must have reached the age of thirty-five. A chart shows how power is split. The legislative branch makes laws. It includes the Senate and the House of Representatives. The executive branch carries out laws. It includes the president, the vice president, and the Cabinet. The judicial branch rules on the ways laws may be used and the ways they ought to be used.

4It includes the Supreme Court and other federal courts. Under the system in the Constitution, Americans do not vote directly for their president. Their votes go to people known as electors. State legislatures choose those electors. Those electors are the ones who then choose the president. This system is called the Electoral College. It is supposed to keep a popular but dangerous person from becoming president. People still use this system now. It is now combined with a popular vote. A republic needs a short explanation. Democracy is the system used in the United States. It is not a pure democracy, which is also called a direct democracy. Under a pure democracy, proposed laws receive votes straight from citizens. The system here is a representative democracy. Another name for it is a republic. In a republic, citizens choose others who will act in their place. Those people sit in a national lawmaking body. In America, Congress is the body that does this. The bills passed by elected officials turn into laws for the nation. Those officials are senators and representatives. A simple chart compares the two ideas. In a democracy, people vote on laws.

5In a republic, people vote for representatives, and the representatives vote on laws. Federal courts are the topic of Article III. The article says the judiciary includes courts at a lower level. It also includes a Supreme Court. In cases under federal law, the last decision belongs to the Supreme Court. The other articles deal with how the states relate to one another. They deal with the procedure for amending the Constitution, which means changing it. They also deal with national debts and treaties. The writers wanted checks and balances to limit each part of government. Each branch finds its power held in check by this system. No single branch is supposed to hold too much control over the rest. A major worry of the states was this. They were afraid the federal government might hold too much power. The Constitution answers that fear by setting federal powers apart from state powers. Rights held by every citizen are also guarded in the Constitution. Someone accused of a crime does not lose life until a fair legal process takes place. Liberty is protected the same way. So is property. A trial by a judge is one such process. A trial by a jury is another.

6Cruel and unusual punishment is banned as well. Free speech gets protection, and so do other liberties. Ways to Change the Constitution. Two groups can suggest a change. States may suggest a change when two-thirds of them gather for that purpose. The other path needs a two-thirds yes in the House and the same share in the Senate. Two groups can approve a change. One way to approve a change is a three-fourths yes from states gathered for that purpose. The other path is three-fourths of the state legislatures. A Living Document. Because it can be amended, people call the Constitution a living document. As times change, the document can change too. As needs in American society shift, the document can shift too. The Constitution was amended before every state had approved it. Some states worried that the first seven articles did not protect the rights of citizens well enough. James Madison responded by writing out new amendments. Late in 1789, the first Congress said yes to twelve amendments from his list. They were sent to the states. The states said yes to ten amendments from that group. They became part of the Constitution. The name for those ten amendments is the Bill of Rights. Of all additions, the First Amendment matters most.

7It guarantees freedom of speech. It guarantees freedom of religion. It guarantees freedom of the press. It guarantees freedom of assembly. Free speech lets people share their opinions in the open. They may do this even if the views criticize the government. Free speech still has some limits. Threatening to harm someone is not protected. A lie told under oath during a court case is not protected either. On religion, the First Amendment says Congress may not make a law that sets up a religion. It also may not make a law that stops people from practicing religion freely. People may follow any religion they want. They may follow none at all. Government and religion have to stay apart. Thousands of Americans gathered in peace in 1963. They came so they could listen to Martin Luther King Jr. as he spoke. During a briefing inside the White House, reporters are using a free press. A free press means journalists may do their work without being blocked. They can report on wrongdoing by the government. They can criticize the government. Because assembly is free, citizens may come together without violence. This freedom lets Americans hold protests. It lets them hold rallies for a cause or against a cause.

8More key protections are written in the Fourth Amendment. The Fifth holds some too. So does the Sixth. The Fourth Amendment stops police from searching a home without a sound legal reason. It stops other government agents in the same way. People facing a criminal charge find protections written in the Fifth Amendment. The Sixth Amendment does this too. Any power not handed to the federal government belongs to the states. That is what the Tenth Amendment says. This is why so many laws differ from one state to another. Laws for public education are one example. Laws for state taxes are another. Seventeen further amendments joined the document as time went on. Some of those amendments ended slavery. Some granted the vote to African Americans. Some granted the vote to women. One created a federal income tax. Just one amendment has later been wiped off the books. The Twenty-First Amendment, passed in 1933, undid the Eighteenth Amendment. The Eighteenth Amendment was adopted in 1919. It made the manufacture of alcoholic beverages illegal. It also made their sale illegal. It also made their transport illegal. When the Eighteenth Amendment passed in 1919, a time called Prohibition began. The Twenty-First Amendment ended that period.

9The year 1915 shows women marching through New York. They march for the right to vote. Ratification in 1920 of the Nineteenth Amendment finally gave women that right. The Legacy of the Constitution. Writers of constitutions in many lands have looked to this one as a guide. It is not without problems. A serious flaw was the choice to let slavery go on. Slavery came to an end only once the Civil War was over, and only by an amendment. Another point draws argument from some people. They call it unfair that each state, no matter its size, gets two Senate votes. In their view, less populated states receive a congressional voice much larger than their numbers justify. The Electoral College draws a further complaint. Winning the presidency requires a majority among the electoral votes. This way of electing a president has a result. A candidate can win the popular vote and still lose the election. Five presidential elections have turned out that way. One case was the election in 2000. Another was the election in 2016. A copy small enough for a pocket is what some people keep with them. Given their own time, the writers produced the best plan they could. Problems and all, their document has lasted well past two hundred years.

10Even now, daily government in the United States still follows this Constitution. If the people's needs are not fully met, the people can amend the plan. Many hope this living document will steer the nation across future centuries. Word List. A confederation is a loose joining of states, provinces, or other groups. Its central authority stays limited. Federal describes a central government sharing power with states or regions that remain their own. A constitution is the basic law set that explains how a state or a nation runs its government. Liberty means a person may hold beliefs and act independently. A procedure is a set of actions followed to finish a specific task. Critical means showing disapproval or harsh judgments. Debts are amounts owed to another, and they are usually money. Prosperous means having success or wealth. Representatives are people picked to speak for others, to vote for them, or to act for them. Delegates are people chosen to represent others and act for them. Elected means a vote has placed someone in a government office. Lawmaking in the United States Congress happens in two houses. One house is the Senate. It contains two representatives for each state.

104. The Prize Alfred Nobel Left Behind

1These pages name the most famous prize in the world. They tell Alfred Nobel's life. They explain how winners are chosen. They introduce famous winners in the sciences. They cover economics. They cover literature. They cover peace. They take up controversies. A conclusion follows. Hard words come last. No honor in the world is more famous than the Nobel Prize. December 10, 1901, was the first day the prizes were given. Alfred Nobel's death had come five years before that date. He was the creator of the prizes. Between 1901 and 2015, the prizes went to 874 special individuals. They also went to 26 groups. For many years one field was physics. Another field was chemistry. Another field was physiology or medicine. Literature was a field too. Peace was a field too. Economics gained an award in 1968, the sixth of the set. Alfred Nobel's face appears on the front of every medal. The back of each category carries its own image. One back stands for peace. Another back is shared by physics and chemistry. Other medal backs stand for economics.

2One stands for literature. One stands for physiology or medicine. October 21, 1833, was Alfred Nobel's birth date. The country was Sweden. His father was an engineer. His father was also a businessman. Russia was the family's new home by 1842, after they left Sweden. Russia is where Alfred's excellent schooling took place. He learned Swedish. He learned Russian. He learned French. He learned German. He learned English. Chemistry interested him as well. In 1850 he was sent to Paris. The subject was chemical engineering. A very explosive liquid was the material he worked with. The liquid had been invented not long before. At that time people still thought it was too dangerous to use. Sweden saw the family's return in 1859. Alfred kept doing experiments there. His brother Emil also experimented with explosives. A tragic accident in 1864 took Emil's life. Alfred did not give up. An explosive of his own invention appeared in 1866. He named it dynamite. The invention made him rich. The invention made him famous. His death in 1896 left every bit of his money for the prizes.

3Alfred Nobel appears in a photo beside his brother Ludvig. The choosing process follows a yearly path. September is for preparations to receive nominations. February is the deadline for submission. Work starts from there. March through May is for preparing a short list. June through August is for adviser review. October is when the Nobel Laureates are chosen. December brings the Nobel Prize Award Ceremony. Winners are chosen with great care. Famous scholars make up the prize committees. Scientists sit on those committees too. The voting is top secret. December 10 is the yearly day winners receive the prizes. Some of the world's most important people are among the winners. Their work can go on with help from the award. Marie Curie was the earliest woman given this award in the sciences. The year was 1903. The field was physics. She shared it with her husband. She also shared it with another scientist. In 1911 she received the prize in chemistry. Only one other person shares Curie's record of Nobel Prizes in different areas.

4The Nobel Prize in Chemistry also went to her daughter Irène. No other mother and daughter have both won the prize. Few women have received Nobel Prizes. The gap is especially wide in the sciences. How far women scientists could advance used to be limited. New studies show a remaining problem. Qualified women scientists are still under-represented. The situation is changing, however. Three women, for example, took science Nobel Prizes in 2020. Many people know the famous formula E=mc2. That formula is Albert Einstein's theory of relativity. Einstein received the prize in 1921. The field was physics. Many top scientists of the twentieth century felt his influence. Scotland's Sir Alexander Fleming received a prize in 1945. The field was medicine. The work was his discovery of penicillin. The discovery saved many lives. It changed medicine forever. No Chinese scientist had won in physiology or medicine before Tu Youyou. She won in 2015. The work was a cure for malaria. Other cures for that deadly disease had stopped working.

5Mosquitoes are what spread the disease. After she found the new cure, she tested it on herself. Only then did she give it to patients. Millions of lives around the world have been saved by her discovery. Economics had never had a younger winner than Esther Duflo in 2019. Only one woman had won that prize before her. She worked with a small team. Together they won for their work on global poverty. Literature had never given the prize to a Black woman before Toni Morrison in 1993. The prize recognized a gift in her writing. A basic part of life in America felt alive in her writing. Viewpoints seldom seen in the books of that time showed up in her work. Beauty is what many people saw in her work. Many people found it important. Gabriel García Márquez was born in Colombia. He wrote with a remarkably distinct voice. He received the prize in 1982. The committee praised his novels. In those novels, fantasy and reality join. Together they build a full world made from imagination.

6These two writers are only examples. Literature winners have influenced other writers for years to come. One very famous peace winner was Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Another was Nelson Mandela. Dr. King tried to make life better for people hurt by injustice. Mandela had that same goal. In 1964 the peace prize honored Dr. King's fight for civil rights. The place of that fight was the United States. Nelson Mandela received the prize in 1993. It honored his struggle against South Africa's unfair political system. In 2011 the prize went to three women. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf was one of them. Leymah Gbowee was one of them. Tawakkol Karman was one of them. Liberia's president at that time was Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. Before that office, she had resisted the country's old dictatorships. She had fought for equality. She had fought for democracy. Leymah Gbowee works as a social worker. She educated herself. She led women in Liberia in a fight for peace. Bloody civil wars were the setting of that fight, across several years.

7Tawakkol Karman works as a journalist. She is Yemeni. She led sit-ins. She led protests. She pushed for democratic rule. She pushed for free expression. The youngest Nobel winner is Malala Yousafzai. She received the peace prize in 2014. She was seventeen. A political group in parts of Pakistan, her home country, forbid schooling for girls. Malala fought to change that ban. In 2012 she was attacked. She was nearly killed. She recovered. She bravely continues the fight today. Some prize winners cause controversy. American president Theodore Roosevelt received a peace prize in 1905. The reason was his help in ending a war. The war was between Russia and Japan. Many people objected to his selection. Some committee members objected too. They felt his military power should have blocked the award. That power was used to secure U.S. control over the Philippines. It was used to secure control over Cuba. It was used to secure control over Panama. Others grew angry when Henry Kissinger won in 1973. He was the American Secretary of State. Ending the Vietnam War was work he did.

8Attacks on Vietnam had involved him as well. He had been involved in attacks on nearby countries. Those attacks killed many people. Questions also met the 2009 peace prize given to President Barack Obama. Hope filled many people when a Black president was elected. Critics thought the prize came too soon after his election. He accepted at last on behalf of every person who strives for justice. He accepted it in the name of everyone who strives for dignity. He donated the 1.4 million dollar award to charity. Some people believe the selection process is itself controversial. A committee of Norwegian politicians awards the Peace Prize. Critics think that makeup could bias the committee. Nominees from some countries could face unfair bias. It could be unfair toward nominees from some fields. They think other people should make the selections. Historians are one group they name. People who study politics are another. People who research peace are another. The committee is made of politicians. Some worry the prizes might be given for political reasons.

9Another controversy concerns racial diversity. History's Nobel list holds 954 people. Only 70 of them have been Asian. Only 17 have been Black. Through 2022, the sciences had never given a Nobel Prize to a Black person. A photo shows Barack Obama. The entire world has felt a strongly positive influence from the Nobel Prize. Great minds all over the globe have their work shown by the awards. They show the dreams of those minds too. The money lets these amazing people keep working. The fame lets them keep working too. The prizes honor freedom. They honor peace. A better life for everyone is a goal they honor. The Nobel Foundation gives each winner a cash award. It gives a diploma. It gives a gold medal. Alfred Nobel's image is on that medal. Eight million Swedish kronor was the size of one person's prize in 2015. That sum was just under a million dollars in United States money. Shared prizes split that sum of eight million Swedish kronor into equal parts. The prizes are given at the Nobel Banquet.

10The banquet is held in Stockholm City Hall. There are speeches. There is dancing. There is a full concert. There is a fancy dinner. Committees are groups of people who consider a course of action. They may also decide on that course. A controversy is a clash about an idea. It can also be a clash about an issue. A democracy is a form of government run by the people. Free and frequent elections are how they run it. Economics studies the making of goods. It studies the making of services. It also studies how they are sold. It also studies how they are used. An engineer designs, builds, or repairs machines. An engineer may do the same for buildings, bridges, or other structures. Injustice means a person is treated unfairly. It also means a group is treated unfairly. Physics studies matter through science. It studies motion. It studies energy. Physiology studies the workings of living things. It studies how their parts work. Scholars are intelligent, well-educated people.

105. The School Bus System at Work

1Children at an army base in 1943 rode to school in a bus pulled by horses. During World War II, horses and wagons helped save gasoline. They helped save tires too. Contents. The Trusty Bus. From Taxes to Rides. A Huge Transit System. The Past. Safety. Yellow Buses Turn Green. Closing. Word List. Sarah's short morning walk makes her shiver. Winter that day is freezing. The bus stop is close. Her wait will not be long. A yellow school bus arrives right on schedule. She greets the driver while she climbs aboard. Once she is seated, she barely notices the ride. It is simply one piece of her day. Sarah is one of many students in the United States who need a bus to reach school. Almost nobody pauses to ask how the system runs. Even so, school buses in America form one of the country's most important mass transit systems.

2They also form one of the most complex. Thousands of people must work so students can be bused. Local school districts run the vehicles. They hire the drivers. They handle the rest of what the system needs. Local property taxes often pay for the buses. The tax is based on what a person's property is worth. Payment goes to local governments. Those governments spend it on services. Schools are one of the services. The buses serve the American public school system. That system promises an education to every student. Laying out the rides to school and back is an enormous job. No other American mass transit uses more vehicles. None moves more people. A typical day in 2023 put students on about 547,000 buses. Daily riders included slightly over half the students in public schools. Count the vehicles. This system has more than twice the number found in all other American mass transit systems put together.

3Size has several causes. The country itself is very large. So is the number of people. Many places have few other public ways for students to travel, so buses are needed. In rural places, the school bus may be the only public ride at all. Routes in the country tend to cover a lot of ground. Kingman, Arizona, is an example. Its rural bus area is bigger than the whole state of Delaware. Delaware covers 1,954 square miles, or 5,060 square kilometers. Among the fifty states, it is the second smallest. Arizona's Kingman Unified School District covers over 3,000 square miles, or 7,779 square kilometers. Here is a math question. Treat the district as 3,000 square miles. How many square miles larger is that than Delaware? The gap is 1,046 square miles, or 2,709 square kilometers.

4Planners try not to make the daily trip too long. Students should not spend too much time going to school and coming home. Stops are placed so they are not a long walk from home. Students can then reach the stop on foot. A common rule offers a ride to any student living more than 2 miles from school, or 3.2 km. A ride is also offered when the walk itself is dangerous. Crossing a highway is one example. Some children still make unsafe crossings on the way to school. Public schools in America started moving students in groups a long time ago. The 1800s brought many one-room schoolhouses. The areas around them were sparsely settled. Walking was how some students arrived. Horses or sleds carried others. Later, districts used wagons that horses pulled. Students were picked up. They were taken to school. Around 1910, a Colorado high school had a stagecoach out front that served as its school bus.

5Motor vehicles took the place of wagons as time passed. Districts drew routes for them. Pickup came before school. Drop-off near home came at day's end. Early student vehicles did not resemble buses of today. In the 1920s, one looked like a long car. A picture shows a bus from 1925. Bodies grew over time so more students would fit. Yellow paint was picked because other drivers could spot it easily. A bus that stands out is seen in time. Drivers stop, and students can board in safety. The law now names the color. The paint must be National School Bus Glossy Yellow. Bright paint helps drivers know a school bus at a glance. A later goal was school integration. Black children and white children were to share the same schools. Before 1954, segregation was common.

6Black students were kept out of white students' schools. The separate schools were not equal. Better chances to learn usually went to white students. More resources went to them too. In 1954 the United States Supreme Court ruled on the question. School segregation, it said, discriminated against black students. Integration of schools followed that ruling. A 1954 picture shows a woman with her daughter. The pair is seated on the Supreme Court steps in Washington, D.C. The woman tells her daughter about the ruling that would end school segregation. Buses mattered to integration for a while. Through the 1970s and the 1980s, schools sent students across old lines. Black students rode to schools that had been white. White students rode to schools that had been black. By the 1990s, most districts had quit that plan. Busing was no longer their tool for desegregation. A 1973 picture shows white children riding a bus in North Carolina.

7A 1979 picture shows black children riding a bus in Ohio. Closing schools in recent years has brought consolidation. Several small schools join into one bigger building. Costs of education can fall. Some students must travel much farther, though. Routes grow. They grow more complex. One rural route in Texas was extreme. In the mid-1990s, certain students rode about 100 miles each way, or 160 km. Time on that bus was longer than time in class. A school bus is forty times safer than a private car. Drivers get strict training in safety. Emergency exits are built in. Roofs are reinforced. Seats are shaped to protect students in a crash. The seats sit close together. Their backs soften a hit. A flashing stop sign may swing out. It warns that students are getting on or off. Cameras on some buses show the driver what is happening inside and outside.

8Traffic must halt when the stop sign is out. Both directions of cars have to wait. In a private car, seat belts make riders much safer. For a school bus, the answer is less clear. Bus safety rules are much tougher to begin with. A bus often carries more than fifty students at once. Checking every belt is then a hard task for the driver. Some districts are also changing buses to help the environment. One bus in New York runs on an electric engine. That engine does not dirty the air. About 120 miles, or 190 km, is as far as it can go before a recharge. Propane is another green choice. It costs much less than ordinary bus fuel. It pollutes less too. A hybrid bus burns fuel and uses electricity. The mix gives better mileage than a regular school bus.

9A bus is bigger than a car, so the same distance takes more gas. Count the riders, though, and a bus uses fuel far more efficiently. It pollutes far less. A chart lists gallons for a trip of 10 miles, or 16 km. 36 family vehicles use 14.4 gallons, or 54.5 L. A regular diesel bus uses 1.4 gallons, or 5.3 L. A hybrid that uses diesel plus electricity uses 0.8 gallons, or 3 L. Buses also cut pollution by standing in for private cars. Fifty-four students can ride one average bus. About thirty-six private vehicles then stay off the road. Newer, greener technology adds to that gain. The air can stay cleaner. The bus eases to a stop. Sarah picks up her things. She steps off. The bus leaves the curb. For now, the work is finished. Late in the day it will be there again.

10The same trip will start once more, this time in the other direction. Word List. Discriminated means a person or a group was treated unfairly over gender, race, age, religion, or some other difference. Integration is the process that opens schools, buildings, and the rest of society to every race on equal terms. Mass transit is public transportation that carries many people at once, by bus, subway, or train. Rural describes the country, as opposed to the city. School districts are the areas that contain every school run by local school leaders. Segregated means kept apart over a group difference such as race. Sparsely means in low numbers, or spread thin. The Supreme Court is the top court in the law system of the United States. Transportation is the act of moving people or things from place to place.

106. The Story of Speed

1This book asks what speed means. It asks which living things and machines are fastest. It looks at bicycles. It looks at boats. It looks at trains. It looks at automobiles. It looks at aircraft. A closing comes at the end. The peregrine falcon is the fastest living thing. Speed is how long it takes to cover a certain distance. For most things, speed is given in kilometers per hour. It is also given in miles per hour. Think of a speed of 16 kilometers an hour. That is 10 miles an hour. At that speed, something can cover 16 kilometers in one hour. People write the speed as 16 kph. They also write it as 10 mph. Other units can measure speed too. Meters per second is one unit. Meters per minute is another. Centimeters per second, per minute, or per hour can be used. Inches per second, per minute, or per hour can be used too. Faster objects are usually measured with bigger distance units. They are measured with shorter time units. Slower things are usually measured with smaller distance units.

2They are measured with longer time units. A snail might be timed in centimeters per hour. A glacier might be timed in meters per month. Nothing in the universe is faster than light. Light moves at 299,338 kilometers each second. That is 186,000 miles each second. The marlin ranks with the world's quickest fish. The sailfish is one of them too. Speed has always seemed to fascinate people. We seem to love whatever moves fast. A cheetah chasing a gazelle is one example. A horse racing around a track is another. Human runners sprinting to a finish line are another. We simply think fast things are cool. That may be why speed races have stayed so popular. From the first Olympic games onward, speed contests have been favorites. An early footrace was part of the Greek Olympic games. Women sprinters race in the 100-meter dash. At a track meet we cheer the quickest runners. We do the same at other sports. Next to many animals, humans are not very fast. The fastest people run only about 35.4 kilometers an hour. That is 22 miles an hour.

3A cheetah's run can match a car traveling the interstate. Speed helps most living things stay alive. The cheetah can run up to 113 kilometers an hour. That is 70 miles an hour. On land, no living thing is faster. The cheetah needs that speed to catch food. For many animals, staying alive means outrunning the animal that chases you. Fish swim much faster than people. Their bodies are more streamlined. The sailfish is the fastest fish. It shoots through the water at up to 113 kilometers an hour. That is 70 miles an hour. The fastest living thing travels through the air. It is the peregrine falcon. In a dive it reaches 435 kilometers an hour. That is 270 miles an hour. It dives to catch other birds while they fly. A sailfish is slow beside this falcon. A cheetah is slow beside it too. Our bodies do not set the limit on how we travel. We use our brains. We invent ways to go faster. Here are some of those ways. A lithograph shows a horse named Maud S.

4Maud S held the world trotting record in 1874. A man rides an early bicycle called the Accelerator. The year is 1819. Going uphill, the Accelerator matched a person who was walking. Going downhill, it matched a horse at a gallop. Humans alone build mechanical things. We keep finding new ways to go faster. Long ago, a bicycle could beat a horse that was walking. It could also beat a horse that was trotting. A bicycle needed less room than a horse. Nobody had to feed it. Nobody had to give it water. Nobody had to clean up after it. On a bicycle, the air ahead seems to push against you. That push is called air resistance. The faster you ride, the harder the air seems to push. Charles Murphy, a bicycle racer, thought of a plan in 1899. He would ride behind a train so the air would push less. Behind the train, Murphy reached 98.5 kilometers an hour. That is 60 miles an hour. Later, riders tried drafting behind race cars. They wanted still more speed.

5Some have gone faster than 241 kilometers an hour. That is 150 miles an hour. A rider on a bicycle follows a motorcycle. The motorcycle cuts the air resistance. The bicycle can then go faster. When people first used boats, a few things set the speed. One was how fast the river flowed. Another was how hard and how fast people paddled. Another was how hard the wind blew. Sails made boats faster than paddles could. Water pulls back on a boat. Sailors call that pull drag. Drag kept sailors from going as fast as they wished. Better designs made boats quicker. Wind speed and current speed were still the limit. The steam engine changed travel in a huge way. Ships began to use steam power. People could then go faster still. They could go faster than the wind. They could go faster than the water. They could head into the wind. They could push against the current. A steam engine powered the SS United States. No ocean liner had ever been faster. Its Atlantic crossing averaged 35 knots. The average equals 65 kph, or 41 mph.

6Its fastest speed was 44 knots. That top speed is also 80.5 kph. It is also 50 mph. Drag from the water on a boat's bottom slows the boat down. Racing boats today barely touch the water. They skim on top. This skimming is called hydroplaning. A hydroplane can reach 354 kilometers an hour. That is 220 miles an hour. The fastest boat on Earth is a hydroplane powered by a jet. It has reached 510.2 kilometers an hour. That is 317 miles an hour. One hydroplane runs on the St. Clair River. An early locomotive used steam. Steam engines first powered boats. They also powered tractors. After trains were invented, steam powered them too. Trains moved people faster than boats could. They moved people faster than wagons could. They moved goods faster too. Early trains reached speeds up to 65 kilometers an hour. That is 40 miles an hour. Some riders were used to carriages pulled by horses. Those carriages were much slower. At the new speeds, some riders fainted. For years, steel wheels on steel rails limited how fast a train could go.

7Magnetic trains fixed that problem. At high speed, a magnetic train does not touch the track. Newer trains are called bullet trains. Strong new engines power them. They travel at close to 320 kilometers an hour. That is 200 miles an hour. Even faster trains are planned. Those trains would run inside tubes. They would go over 800 kilometers an hour. That is 500 miles an hour. Japan runs a high-speed train. The first automobiles were very slow. They broke easily. The first car was little more than a small buggy made for a horse. It rolled on wheels taken from bicycles. A small noisy engine pushed it along. It was something like a golf cart that used a lawn mower engine. Some early cars ran on steam. Others ran on electric power. The first accepted land-speed record for a car came in 1898. An electric motor drove that car. It reached 63.13 kilometers an hour. That is 39.24 miles an hour. Picture a rough dirt road. Picture going almost 64.4 kilometers an hour in a golf cart.

8That is 40 miles an hour. The driver must have had a thrilling ride. A race of early cars took place in 1900. Sir Malcolm Campbell sits in a car from his Bluebird line. In 1934 he tried for a new world record on land. The beach was Daytona Beach in Florida. Cars gained speed as engineers, designers, and builders made them better. In the early 1900s, paved roads were not there for high speed. People found sand packed hard on ocean beaches. They drove on it when the tide was low. For many years the top records were set on beaches. Dry beds of desert lakes turned out to be fast places to drive. Those beds are in the desert. The Bonneville Salt Flats are in Utah. The Black Rock Desert is in Nevada. Both places are flat. They are open. They stretch for miles. Vehicles can be driven there safely at very high speed. A jet car holds the record for wheeled vehicles on land. Two engines from jet fighters power it. In October 1997, Andy Green made history.

9No person before him had gone faster than sound while staying on the ground. He reached 1,228 kilometers an hour. That is 763.035 miles an hour. The car was the Thrust SSC. From a full stop it hit 965.6 kph in 16 seconds. That is 600 mph. At 1,228 kph, Andy Green is at the wheel of the Thrust SSC. That speed is 763 mph. No jet airplane on Earth is faster than the Lockheed SR-71. People have always wanted to fly the way birds fly. Over many centuries, inventors tried all sorts of ways to fly. Propellers turned by engines powered the earliest airplanes. About 40 years later, someone invented the jet engine. Airplane speed jumped after that. The record for aircraft is now 3,367 kilometers an hour. That is 2,193 miles an hour. Picture a trip across the United States that lasts one hour and 15 minutes. A normal jet airliner needs five hours plus thirty minutes for that crossing. A Saturn V rocket lifts off with an Apollo mission. The mission is headed to the moon.

10If you want to move truly fast, become an astronaut. A rocket must break free of Earth's gravitational pull. To do that it must go faster than 45,062 kilometers an hour. That is 28,000 miles an hour. Cheetahs are not likely to run faster in the years ahead. Sailfish are not likely to swim faster. Falcons are not likely to fly faster. People will probably not add much speed to their running. People will still look for other ways to go faster. There was a time when people wanted to travel as fast as sound. Later, we built planes that beat the speed of sound. Today rockets leave Earth for space. They travel several times faster than sound. People will keep finding ways to pick up speed. They will go faster on land. They will go faster on water. They will go faster through the air. People probably will not feel finished until we move at the speed of light. Light-speed travel could loop Earth over seven times. We could do that in one second. Moving that fast is hard to picture.

107. The Town That Never Emptied

1Tourists who explore Castillo de San Marcos can see old relics. One relic is an old cannon, shown in the picture. What You Will Read. Founding the Town. Drake Comes to Attack. The Town Changes Rulers. The Town Today. Words to Know. Founding the Town. Florida's sunny east coast is where St. Augustine stands. In the United States, no older town of European and African origin has been lived in without a break. Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded it. His name is said DEH ah-vee-LESS. He founded the town in September of 1565. Jamestown, the English town, came forty-two years later. Jamestown was founded in 1607. Menéndez named the city for the Catholic saint Augustine. The founder's hometown in Spain looked to Augustine as its patron saint. Pedro Menéndez de Avilés. This city lies about 200 miles (322 km) east of Tallahassee. Tallahassee is the capital of Florida. Two months before the founding, Menéndez had left Spain. He traveled with soldiers and sailors. Enslaved African people and free African people came too.

2Women and children were in the group. Six hundred of them reached the shores of Florida. The new settlement struggled to feed itself. Food for the colonists came from the Timucua, a local Indigenous tribe. They gave help as well. Some Spanish men married Timucua women. The new town of St. Augustine became busy. Its residents soon included Spanish colonists. Indigenous residents were mostly women. They had married colonists and joined the Catholic faith. African people lived there, both free and enslaved. Germans lived there too. An engraving shows daily life in the first days after the town was founded. The Timucua People. The Timucua lived in what is now Georgia and northern Florida. When European settlers arrived in the 1500s, about 200,000 Timucua lived on that land. European forces killed many of them. European diseases killed many too. By 1800, no Timucua remained. Scholars study artifacts the Timucuan people left behind. They study those objects because no Timucua remain to tell their own stories.

3The first meetings of settlers and Timucua people were friendly. The friendship soon broke down. Diseases carried by the Spanish took many Indigenous lives. Sometimes a whole tribe died. The Timucua began to attack the Spanish settlement. They hoped to force the Spanish away. The city also had conflicts with other Europeans. Spain sent Pedro Menéndez to drive out French colonists. Those colonists had settled nearby a year earlier, in 1564. Their settlement was Fort Caroline. Fort Caroline was nearer present-day Jacksonville, up the coast from the new town. Spain wanted Florida for itself, as other European countries did. Spain was Catholic. Menéndez spared the French Catholics at Fort Caroline. He killed the French Protestants. Drake Comes to Attack. Sir Francis Drake was an English sailor. He was also a colonizer. He traded enslaved people. In 1585, Queen Elizabeth sent him against the Spanish in St. Augustine. Protestant England and Catholic Spain were in a growing conflict. By then the governor was the nephew of Pedro Menéndez. He had been warned about Drake.

4Twenty-three ships and two thousand men waited with Drake off the Florida coast. The governor had fewer than one hundred soldiers. He ordered the residents to leave the city. Sir Francis Drake. When Drake and his soldiers entered St. Augustine, the town was empty. Many residents hid in the nearby woods. A small clash with the British was led by Menéndez. Drake still took over the town. A map shows Drake's attack. No earlier map of the city is known. At that time, most buildings were wood and clay. Wood and clay burned easily. Drake burned the buildings. He burned the land around them. He took anything of value. He did not burn a nearby Timucua village. He wanted the Indigenous people to side with the British in later fights. Drake's men took what they wanted, burned the town, and then sailed away. The Spanish came back and rebuilt. They rebuilt mostly with wood and thatch. The town burned again in March of 1599.

5Severe flood damage followed a hurricane that September. The future of St. Augustine did not look bright. The Town Changes Rulers. In 1602, Spain had to choose a future for St. Augustine. Should Spain keep the town? Should Spain move it? Should Spain abandon it? The king of Spain decided to leave the town where it was. Later, Spanish leaders paid for Castillo de San Marcos. Work began in 1672. The stone fort would strengthen the city's defense. Even so, the town stayed poor for much of the 1600s. It stayed isolated. The Spanish crown ignored it while fighting various wars in Europe. Shipwrecks sometimes blocked aid and supplies. Indigenous uprisings hurt the town. Severe disease hurt it. Pirate attacks hurt it. England's power nearby was a threat that kept growing. Building Castillo de San Marcos took twenty-three years. The fort was completed in 1695. It is now a U.S. national monument. Spain controlled Florida. Britain controlled the colonies to the north. Spain wanted to make life hard for Britain.

6Spanish leaders made a safe place for certain enslaved people. If escapees reached St. Augustine, the governor let them stay free. They had to promise loyalty to Spain. The governor started the community of Mose in 1738. Mose stood north of St. Augustine. It was for certain enslaved people and for free Black people. British attacks on the town continued. Spain entered the Seven Years' War in Europe, fought from 1754 to 1763. Spain sided with France against England. When the war ended, the Treaty of Paris gave Florida to England. England gave Cuba in return. Many Spanish residents left Florida and moved to Cuba. Britain ruled Florida until 1783. The next agreement was the Second Treaty of Paris. England agreed that the United States was a country. Control of Florida passed to the United States in 1819. Florida became a state in 1845. Florida entered the Civil War with the Confederacy sixteen years after that. A Neighborhood Called Lincolnville. Mose supplied many Black soldiers to the Union side in the Civil War.

7Some of them settled in St. Augustine after the war. The Emancipation Proclamation was signed in 1863. Thousands of enslaved people in Confederate states gained freedom from it. More than 670 enslaved people met on January 1st, 1863. They met in a vacant lot later called liberation lot. These freed people founded the neighborhood of Lincolnville. The name honors the president. By the 1880s, many Black residents owned property. Homes, businesses, and churches rose from their own work. Public office included many of them up to the early 1900s. Then restrictive voting laws took rights from Black citizens. Other policies took rights away too. In 1991, the Lincolnville Historic District joined the National Register of Historic Places. The listing honors this historically Black neighborhood. The 1922 picture shows a wedding party in Lincolnville. Henry Flagler built the Flagler Memorial Presbyterian Church in 1889. Jenny, his only daughter, is remembered by this church. Twenty years after the Civil War, Henry Flagler had a plan for the town.

8He worked to make St. Augustine a vacation place for wealthy Americans. He built many hotels there. His railroad company linked the town to cities on the East Coast. The link brought opportunity. It brought political activity. The St. Augustine Movement was centered in the city from 1963 to 1964. Many people were arrested while they protested segregation. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was in the city during 1964. He worked to help pass the Civil Rights Act. The Town Today. In 2015, St. Augustine marked its 450th birthday. Residents and visitors could celebrate the town's rich history. Parties went on all year. The Look of the Town. Streets and buildings in St. Augustine show its Spanish origin. Many buildings with special designs rose in the late 1800s. The city grew more charming because of those buildings. The charm drew still more visitors. Today the Atlantic Ocean floods the city again and again. The water threatens the historic buildings. The floods are growing worse.

9They are growing more frequent as sea levels rise. The Villa Zorayda Museum looks much like the Alhambra. Spain is home to the famous palace called the Alhambra. Tourists ride in a horse-drawn carriage. Flagler College's Courtyard of Ponce de Léon Hall is on their route. Many cultures have shaped the city. You can see that mix in the buildings, the food, and the people. Today St. Augustine is a popular place for a vacation. Tourists can walk through Castillo de San Marcos. They can visit museums. They can spend time on the beach. They can admire the beautiful buildings. Wherever you go in St. Augustine, history fills the place. History of St. Augustine. 1565: St. Augustine is founded. 1607: Jamestown is founded. 1565 to 1763: Spain controls the area. 1738: The community of Mose is established by Governor Manuel de Montiano. 1763 to 1783: Britain controls the area. 1776: The Declaration of Independence is signed. 1783: Britain accepts the United States as a nation of its own.

10The United States takes control of Florida in 1819. 1845: Florida becomes a state. 1861 to 1865: the U.S. Civil War. 1863: The Emancipation Proclamation is signed, and newly freed Black residents gather in liberation lot. 1885 to 1913: St. Augustine becomes a vacation destination through the work of Henry Flagler. 1991: Lincolnville Historic District joins the National Register of Historic Places. Words to Know. Attack: to move against an opponent with force, often using weapons in a battle. Conflicts: fights, battles, or wars. Damage: harm done to a person or to a thing. Defense: a means that guards people or objects when harm or an attack comes. Indigenous: of the first peoples in a place, or related to those peoples. Isolated: set far from other people or from other things. Looted: stripped of belongings, often in a war, a riot, or another destructive event. Segregation: a rule that keeps groups of people apart, often because of race. Settlement: a place where people have started a community.

108. Three Dry Lands Full of Life

1Contents. A First Look. The Sahara. The Gobi. The Atacama. A Last Look. Word List. Topic List. Only a few deserts have sand dunes. A picture can show that fact. Shut your eyes. Picture yourself in the middle of a desert. Which sights are around you? You might see camels. You might see cactuses. You might see sand dunes. Most people picture those things when they imagine a desert. A real desert is far richer than that sandy scene. It is also more varied. In a desert, water that dries up is greater than water that falls as rain. To evaporate means to dry up. A desert can be hot. A desert can be cool. A desert can be cold. The North Pole is considered a desert. The South Pole is considered a desert too. All the water at the poles is frozen. Nearly a third of Earth's land is desert. They cover mountains. They cover canyons. They cover glaciers. Three amazing deserts have inhabitants that may surprise you. This book tells their stories. Their names are Sahara, Gobi, and Atacama. Many maps color the upper third of Africa yellow. On some maps that area is pale beige.

2That color marks the Sahara Desert, a huge dry land. The Sahara is far larger than any other desert in the world. Many of our pictures of the desert come from this place. Great landscapes of yellow sand dunes look like an ocean. One fifth of the Sahara is covered by those dunes. The Tuareg people wear blue robes that flow. They wear turbans. Camel caravans cross the sandy desert under their lead. They travel in order to trade salt. A picture shows that many people in the Sahara still rely on camels. Sand is only one part of the Sahara. A surprise waits inside this huge desert. A river that ranks among the world's longest flows here. Along the Sahara's eastern side, the Nile flows. It brings water that lets crops live. Cities along its banks depend on that water too. Ancient Egypt's great civilization lasted because of this river. Egypt's people lived among the dunes. In ancient Egypt, people carved irrigation channels. People still carve them today. These channels carried water out of the riverbed. The water went to thirsty crops. It went to animals. It went to people.

3One picture shows a pyramid. Ancient Egyptians built it. Deep under the Sahara, more water stays hidden. In some places, that water seeps close to the surface. The seep creates an oasis. An oasis is a little patch of land that stays green. Do not picture the Sahara as moist and pleasant. Years can pass in some areas with no rainfall. Heat there can reach 136 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 58 degrees Celsius. Powerful winds whip up dust storms. The dust can block the sun. Thorn trees grow in the Sahara. It is home to shrubs. It is home to grasses that grow low. Several kinds of antelope manage to live here. Many rodents survive here too. So do many birds and reptiles. One kind of reptile is a skink. People know the skink as a sandfish. It can move through the sand in a way that looks like swimming. A picture shows a worker walking through a plant in Algeria. The plant makes gas from oil. For centuries, people have made homes in the Sahara. Trade comes naturally to northern Africa. Traders come from Africa. They come from Europe. They come from Asia.

4Rich ancient cities survived on crops watered by channels. They also grew rich from goods that passed through. Those goods included spices. They included fabrics. They included precious metals and gems. In the Middle Ages, art had a center in northern Africa. It was a center of writing. It was a center of science. It was a center of learning. A treasure sits under the Sahara today. The desert holds the largest oil reserves in the world. Oil is a liquid. Many people depend on oil heavily. They use it for fuel. They use it for energy. Oil sales have made some Sahara countries extremely rich. They grew rich by selling oil. Sadly, wars between many nations have been fought for this valuable resource. One picture makes a contrast clear. The Gobi sits farther from other people than the Sahara does. Deep inside the huge continent of Asia are Mongolia and northern China. The high, dry Gobi Desert is in those lands. The cold of the Gobi may surprise you. Cold there can fall to -40 degrees Fahrenheit. That is also -40 degrees Celsius. Like the Sahara, traders often crossed the Gobi.

5They brought goods to Asia. They brought goods from Asia. Cities can survive in the Sahara. The Gobi is too harsh for them. It is also too remote. A lot of the Gobi sits at a high elevation. They are dry. They are mountainous. The soil is rocky. The soil is salty. Few plants grow there besides tough grasses and shrubs. Grazing animals can live on these grasses. Mongolian horses graze on them. Antelope graze on them. Gazelle graze on them. Many kinds of gerbils also feed on the grasses. The jerboa, another small rodent, also eats those grasses. One picture shows horses at a drink. The water is in Gobi salt pans. Salt that occurs naturally in soil usually dissolves in rainwater. Rivers then carry that salt to the ocean. Ocean water tastes salty for that reason. Desert rain is too scarce to melt the salt away. Desert rivers dry up before they reach the ocean. So most of the salt stays in the soil. Some rivers drop their salt in marshes that soon vanish. They may carry salt into lakes that do not last. Desert air dries those waters. Huge salty stretches remain.

6People call these salty stretches salt pans. A picture shows a Mongolian horseman. He herds his horses. Most of the people who live in the Gobi are nomads. A nomad is a person who keeps moving, with no settled home. They often move in search of food. Horses supply almost every need of some of these nomads. Horses give them meat. Horses give them milk. Horse hides are used for tents. Horses also provide transportation. These nomads live in Mongolia. They are excellent horse trainers. They rope horses. They race horses. A rodeo rider would not beat them at either skill. Oil and other natural resources are very scarce in the Gobi. It does hold a fascinating kind of treasure. That treasure is fossils. Delicate fossils have lasted for millions of years in this dry climate. The lack of humans has helped preserve them too. Scientists now come to the Gobi in large numbers. They come for new discoveries. Dinosaur eggs had their first discovery in this desert. A fossil of a feathered reptile was found here too. That fossil led scientists to believe something new. That find made them consider a link between birds and dinosaurs.

7One picture shows a dig in the Gobi. Archaeologists there are hunting fossils. One picture shows the Atacama. It ranks among the highest deserts. South America holds the Atacama Desert, and the Pacific Ocean is just west of it. No body of water on Earth is larger than the Pacific. The Pacific Coast is the Atacama's western edge. It is squeezed into a narrow band. The ocean is on one side. The high Andes Mountains are on the other side. The Atacama's temperatures feel pleasant. They stay between 50 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit. That range is 10 to 20 degrees Celsius. A person might think the nearby ocean would give this desert some moisture. Even so, Earth may have no drier place than this desert. Some Atacama places may have had no rain in all the years people can remember. The Atacama does get a little moisture at times. Spring melt comes from snow on the Andes. Rivers of that meltwater cross the desert. The rivers run to the Pacific. These rivers do not fill with water often. They are usually steep. They are narrow. They move quickly. The water never gets time to spread.

8It also never gets time to soak into the ground. Fog is the only other moisture people can count on. Cold ocean air pushes the fog inland. Many plants evolved smart methods for catching this fog. Droplets from the fog collect on some leaves. The leaves direct the droplets toward the roots. Along sheltered coasts, these plants form small cloud forests. Thick fog is what lets them grow. Aside from the cloud forests, the Atacama grows almost no plants. Some plants exist as dormant seeds. Dormant means inactive. A rain shower wakes these seeds. Ten years may pass before the next shower. Rodents and insects are almost the only animals in the Atacama. The chinchilla lives here. It is a popular new pet. Llamas can also be found. Alpacas can be found too. They are furry relatives of the camel. They live in damp areas near rivers. They also live high in the mountains. A picture shows llamas. The Atacama has few animals. It has many minerals instead. The Andes are volcanic mountains. Their volcanic activity brought copper to the surface. It brought nitrates to the surface.

9Nitrates are an ingredient in fertilizer. They are also an ingredient in explosives. Volcanic activity brought sulfur to the surface too. Salt is also abundant here. It collects in marshy lakes. Whole towns are built by mining companies so the workers have homes. The workers dig up these minerals. Cities with ports grow up on the shore. Ships leave those ports with minerals for lands far away. All food must be trucked in. All water must be trucked in. Some supplies are shipped by boat. The desert climate does not forgive people who are unprepared. That harsh climate is why miners are nearly the only people who ever settled in the Atacama. A picture shows trucks. Ore from an Atacama mine rides out on the trucks. A picture shows the city of Tucson, Arizona. Tucson lies in the Sonoran Desert. A desert can hold sights you did not expect. You might find lakes of salt. You might find dense fogs. You might find huge underground supplies of oil. You might find ancient civilizations. You might find expert herders of horses. You might find mining towns. Deserts may have seemed empty to you. You may have thought they were lifeless.

10For thousands of years, plants have treated deserts as sources of life. Animals have treated them as sources of riches. Humans have treated them as sources of wonder. Dormant describes something inactive that is able to become active again. When something evaporates, a liquid becomes a gas. It also means dries up. Irrigation means bringing water to land, or bringing it to crops. The water is supplied so growth can happen. Minerals are solid, natural materials. A plant is not their source. They do not come from an animal. Moisture is a small amount of water. It may be a liquid. It may be a vapor. A nomad is a person who keeps moving, with no settled home. They have no permanent home. Where a desert has water and fertile ground, that place is an oasis. A resource is a supply of something valuable. It can also be a supply of something very useful. Topics in this book include the Andes Mountains. They include camels. They include dunes. They include Egypt. They include fog. They include Mongolia. They include the Nile. They include oil. They include the Tuareg.

109. Two Years Under the Glass

1A map of this glass world shows the human habitat and the tropical rainforest. It shows the Landscape Evolution Observatory, known as LEO, plus the ocean and the South Lung. It shows the coastal fog desert, the Energy Center, Phoenix, the West Lung, Arizona, Tucson, and B2. That figure outside the rainforest is me, Birdie. Nearly one hundred kinds of plants grow in there. Hello, I am Birdie. I am ten, and I come from Tucson, Arizona. Sometimes I wonder what a trip to another planet would be like. I do not wonder only about the landing. I wonder about the days of travel. Would there be enough food to eat and enough air to breathe? Could the other people on the ship and I stay on friendly terms? One group of scientists lived the way people might live on a giant spaceship. On September 26, 1991, they stepped into Biosphere 2, or B2, and stayed for two years. The stay lasted 730 days. John points out the many structures that form B2. People call planet Earth Biosphere 1. B2 was built to work like Earth. It spreads across three acres inside a huge glass building, a sort of giant greenhouse set deep in the Arizona desert.

2Yearly visitors number one hundred thousand. Students make up about ten thousand of that crowd. Deputy Director John Adams recently led Mom and me on a tour past the public areas. John, Mom, and I head toward the Lung, and I want them to slow down so I can catch up. That Lung once held the air pressure in B2 at a normal level. On the walk to the dome, John told how B2 began. Moon landings in the 1960s left people asking a bigger question. How much farther into space could humans go? Fuel might carry astronauts to a far planet. Food and oxygen would still run out unless the crew could make more on the way. Could they? That question pushed the designers of B2 to start. Building began in 1987 and ended in 1991. With only three acres, B2 could not hold everything people on Earth take for granted. The designers had to choose. Their choices included a rainforest, plus an ocean, plus a desert, plus a farm. Goats, pigs, chickens, and bush babies were among the animals they chose.

3Last of all they picked eight people, four men and four women. Those eight had to grow their own food. John said moving every bite from the soil to the table was an enormous job. Not every crop succeeded. The crew fell short on calories and lost a great deal of weight. Life inside was hard for other reasons too. Earth does endless work for us. John calls that work natural services. We need it to stay alive, yet most of us ignore it until the moment we need it. Imagine pollinating every plant on Earth by hand, with no wind and no billions of insects to help. What a task. The first eight scientists entered in 1991 ready to test a new way to survive. A photo shows two of them cooking in the B2 kitchen. Every meal they ate was grown inside. In there, nobody could ignore the jobs nature usually does. Air was one of those jobs. B2 is among the tightest sealed buildings on Earth. Yearly air loss stays under ten percent. The 1991 plan counted on the plants to produce oxygen equal to the air beyond the glass.

4The oxygen level fell instead. The people inside grew exhausted. Walking became hard. Even remembering their own names became hard. Experiments stopped. Survival was the only job left. At last a big truck piped oxygen in, and the air problem eased. By then the residents were arguing. Stress was high, but they kept the original plan and stayed the full two years. The closed ecosystem was not flawless, as they had hoped. They still collected important data and learned how to do better next time. Numbers show the scale of B2. Sealed glass covers 7.2 million cubic feet, or 203,881 cubic meters, and the walls hold 6,500 windows. The top reaches 91 feet, or 27.7 meters. A welded stainless steel liner of 500 tons, or 453.6 metric tons, seals the building off from the earth below. Thousands of miles of wire, pipe, and ductwork run through it. When the two-year test ended, scientists still saw a rare chance to do research. They had to pick the question. Studies inside Biosphere 2 got their start from the University of Arizona in 2007. The focus left outer space and turned toward Earth.

5John said a few short steps would carry us all over the world. He asked if I was ready for the rainforest. I was more than ready. We passed trees so tall they brushed a ceiling 91 feet, or 28 meters, high. Brown roots of tropical vines hung in long strings and looked like spaghetti. John said this forest is not a wild rainforest. It is a lab, where scientists can control factors they cannot control outdoors. One quick phone call proved it. He said he could play the role of weather maker in B2. Minutes later, rain fell. Scientists here sample the soil and measure both the rain and the growth of roots. Rainforest research continues. Soon they will remove all the rain and give the forest a drought of three months. They predict dry spells like that as Earth grows warmer. Staging one here could show them what to expect. Much of today's science at B2 looks at changes in Earth's climate. I walked out of the warm rain toward the next biome without thinking of climate change or global warming.

6I wanted the ocean. We came into the ocean biome on a platform above 676,000 gallons of salt water, or 2.56 million liters. Warmth in the water reached nearly 80 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 27 degrees Celsius. Most living things at B2 today are plants, yet colorful fish still swam below us. We climbed a corridor and reached the beach. Soft waves, made by a machine rather than by wind, washed the shore. I saw small crabs, and I got to hold one. Past the beach, at the back of the ocean, a small mangrove swamp grows in the salt water. Humid air followed us until another door. Beyond it the air turned hot, dry, and familiar. We had returned to the desert. Workers are now reshaping this ocean biome so it will resemble the Gulf of California. That is the magic of B2. A turn of a doorknob carries you from one corner of the world to another. Our next stop was not a biome. It was a lung 50 feet, or 15.24 meters, high. Photos show the outside, and they show John and me inside. Two huge domes were built so the whole of B2 would not burst.

7Extra air pops a balloon. The same danger once faced B2, because hot days made the inside air expand and the pressure rise. Engineers had to control that pressure. A hatch labeled South Lung Tunnel led us onward. The huge room beyond threw echoes everywhere. While B2 stayed sealed, its two lungs, like the two in a body, kept the inside pressure even. The ceiling is a rubber membrane. Picture a circus tent of 40,000 pounds, or 18,144 kilograms, with no poles. Air pressure holds that ceiling up. By day the indoor air heats, expands, and pushes the membrane higher. At night the pressure drops and the membrane sinks. When John opened the door, air rushed out in a whoosh. We rushed out with it and went on. The room in front of us used to be the farm. Scientists study landscapes there now, under the name LEO. Early B2 work asked how people might live on other planets. The work now asks how to live on this planet as the climate changes. In the Landscape Evolution Observatory, that is the puzzle. We entered the old farm.

8Scientists there study how water meets land, and they do it in three phases. Phase one is underway now. Basalt, which is crushed volcanic rock, went onto three slopes. The load topped a million pounds. Rain can be made in this room too. Over time the basalt will become soil. The team wants to know how long that change takes and which conditions drive it. Phase two watches plants and water together, and it watches how plants change the way the land behaves. Phase three asks how shifts in air temperature, moisture, and carbon dioxide affect these huge slopes. John knows that crushing rock can look pointless. He said it is hard for people to see how the studies get used. The B2 scientists do see it. Once, the glass world gave them data on life inside a closed ecosystem. As Earth's climate keeps changing, the glass world shows them what life here may face. John said that if people can see a change coming, they can prepare, adapt, and change their behavior. He hoped that would let them survive. Climate has always shifted, so why does the present shift cause worry?

9Fossil fuels, when burned, release greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide is one, and these gases hold heat in the air. Many scientists say Earth has been warming for many years.
