Harsher weather may follow, including hurricanes and droughts. Wildlife may lose good places to live. A change in one place can trigger a change in another, because air, water, and land are linked. Melting ice, for instance, makes the seas rise. These changes are now faster, and larger, than anything modern humans have seen. The OmniGlobe sits in the lower habitat of B2, where Mom and I look it over. It shows how weather patterns affect every planet. I am only ten, so plenty of science is still ahead of me. I do know why experiments exist. They let us find out what we do not know yet. Any test can teach something. B2 taught a costly lesson. Spend as much money as you like, and we still cannot engineer a long-term system that supplies everything people need in order to live. Earth gives those services away for free. Take Earth for granted, and survival is at risk.

10B2 is a wonder. Nothing matches Biosphere 1. Air pressure is the push of air in the atmosphere. To engineer is to design and build with science and math. A biome is a community of plants and animals living in one kind of habitat. Factors are facts or conditions that help produce a result. Global warming is a rise in the average temperature of Earth's air and oceans, especially a rise big enough to change the climate. A biosphere is the surface and air of a planet where life can exist. Carbon dioxide is an invisible gas made when organic matter breaks down or burns, as fossil fuels do, and plants take it in during photosynthesis. A membrane is a thin sheet that can divide a space or line it. Natural services are the jobs Earth does so living things can survive. Climate change means lasting shifts in the weather of Earth or of one region. Oxygen is a gas without color, taste, or smell. Most animals need it, and plants and algae make it during photosynthesis. An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the habitat they share.

110. Warning Tails

1A resting rattler seldom bites. Most snakes cause people no harm. A few snakes can strike with a bite that kills. People often call rattlesnakes rattlers. Rattlers sit among the deadly snakes that people fear most. It is easy to form the wrong idea about them. A rattler does not roam in search of a person to bite. Most snakes would rather keep away from people. Rattlers feel the same way. Most people who receive a rattlesnake bite do not die from it. Later pages tell where these snakes live. They tell how a rattler hunts. They tell how a rattler moves. They tell about the babies and about the rattle. They name the types. They explain bites and safety. They look at what lies ahead for rattlers. Snakes fill an important role among living creatures. Rattlers eat rodents. Rats and mice are two kinds they eat. Many rodents carry diseases. Many rodents also destroy crops that people value. They can destroy property too. Rattlesnakes help humans by keeping rodent numbers under control. The next time you think only bad things about rattlesnakes, remember that help. A picture may show a rattler eating a mouse. Every rattlesnake in the world lives in North America or South America. Nearly every state in the United States has rattlesnakes in it. They live in every country of South America. They live throughout southern Canada. Many species share those two continents. A number marks the center of each territory. The Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnake is one of those species.

2The Timber Rattlesnake is another. So is the Eastern Massasauga Rattlesnake. The Banded Rock Rattlesnake is on the map too. The Sidewinder has a number of its own. The Western Diamondback Rattlesnake is marked as well. The Prairie Rattlesnake is included. The Pygmy Rattlesnake is included too. The Mexican West Coast Rattlesnake lives along that coast. The South American Tropical Rattlesnake lives farther south. Swamps, deserts, prairies, forests, and mountains all serve as home ground. The greatest numbers live in deserts and other dry places. Those dry places are in the southwestern United States and in northern Mexico. Rattlesnakes are reptiles. Like all reptiles, they are cold-blooded. Body heat in a cold-blooded animal rises and falls with the air around it. A rattler cannot keep its own body warm. In winter, rattlers hibernate in dens under the ground. Most of the time, a rattler lives alone. One winter den may hold hundreds of snakes at the same time. When spring starts, they crawl out of the dens. They bask in the sun. The sun warms their bodies. Warm rattlers become more active. Summer hunting is what they prepare for next. Sightings are most common in air of 21 to 30 degrees C. That is the same as 70 to 90 degrees F. Where the day grows truly hot, a rattler must find shade so it can stay cool. Rocks, bushes, cactuses, and trees are favorite shady spots. Pit vipers are the snake group that counts rattlers as members.

3A pit viper has deep pits below its eyes. The pits sense heat. They detect body heat from rodents, birds, and other prey. From 10 meters off, a candle flame is still warm enough for a rattler to notice. That distance is 30 feet. A rattler also smells with a forked tongue. The tongue flicks in and out of the mouth. Heat and smell together make rattlers strong night hunters. A dark spot sits above the mouth, and that spot is the pit. A drawing can show the fangs swinging down before a bite. A second drawing labels the parts that create venom and push it out the fangs. Blending patterns on the skin help a rattler hide. The snake waits near small trails or near holes. Rodents, lizards, and birds pass those spots. The strike comes as the prey passes. The strike uses long, hollow fangs. Most of the time the fangs fold back against the top of the mouth. At the moment of the bite, the fangs drop down. The jaws spread far enough for the fangs to pierce skin. The poison these snakes make is known as venom. The venom is made in glands behind the eyes. During a bite, tubes carry the venom into the fangs. Each fang acts like a doctor's needle. Venom enters the victim the way medicine leaves a needle. A snake can smell prey that is still in the air. After the bite, a rattlesnake lets go unless the prey might escape.

4An animal that can fly has a good chance to get away. The bitten animal runs off. It does not get far before the poison starts to work. The venom of a rattlesnake does its harm in two steps. Nerves and muscles feel the first effect. The victim then has trouble breathing and moving. Second, the venom starts to break down muscles and organs. Digestion is already underway when the snake comes back to feed. The tongue that smells leads the snake along the victim's trail. When the prey is found, the snake swallows it whole. The head goes in first. A rattler can separate the lower jaw from the upper jaw. That opening lets the snake swallow prey larger than its own head. A snake does not spend energy staying warm. Because of that, one meal can last a rattler for months. Hunting without legs sounds impossible. How do these snakes manage it? Rattlesnakes move in three ways. The most common way is the serpentine method. You say that word SERP-en-teen. The body moves in an S shape. Along each curve, muscles press the ground and drive the snake ahead. The same motion makes rattlesnakes excellent swimmers. Some snake skeletons contain very tiny leg bones. Those snakes have no legs you can see. The bones hint that snakes may once have had legs. A drawing of the serpentine motion shows the rattler moving forward. An arrow marks that forward direction. Sidewinding pushes the body sideways rather than forward.

5Only a few kinds of rattlers use sidewinding. Those kinds live in sandy deserts. To the eye, sidewinding resembles the serpentine motion. The push, though, sends the snake to the side. The third movement is called caterpillar locomotion. It uses the snake's scales. Wide, flat scales cross the belly. Muscles lift the edges of those scales. Muscles also lower the edges. The edges dig in and shove the body forward. Caterpillar treads shove a tractor forward in a similar way. Some tractors took their name from the way a caterpillar moves. A female rattler begins having babies when she is three or four years old. Most reptiles lay eggs. A rattler mother does something else. She gives birth to live babies. A birth usually brings 10 to 12 babies. After they are born, the babies do not need their mothers. They still tend to stay close for about ten days. After about ten days they shed the baby skin. Hunting starts after that shed. A baby may outgrow its skin quickly. Three or four sheds can happen in one year for a fast-growing baby. A picture can show the babies staying near the mother until that shed. A newborn rattlesnake can already deliver a poisonous bite. A baby has no rattle. It cannot sound a warning. How much venom goes in is harder for a baby to control. In these ways, a tiny baby can be more dangerous than a large adult. Many predators eat baby rattlers.

6Owls, hawks, ravens, and coyotes are on that list. Other snakes eat the babies too. A hawk is one hunter shown feeding on them. A rattler can warn other animals to stay back. No other snake carries a rattle like this one. Any animal that threatens the snake gets a warning from the rattle. A shed of the skin is called a molt, and it happens again and again. A hollow section is left behind on the tail. The section is made of material like a fingernail. The sections grow bigger as the snake grows. When the snake is afraid, it coils up. It shakes its tail. The hollow sections knock against each other. They make a buzzing sound. The buzz gave rattlers the nickname buzztails. Some people think you can read a rattler's age from the number of sections. The oldest pieces of the rattle snap away. A rattle usually has no more than ten sections. A rattler can live 25 years. In a single year the snake may molt 2 or 3 times. Losing old sections is probably a benefit. If they did not, an old snake might drag a huge rattle. That rattle could hold up to 75 sections. An old buzztail with a rattle of that size would be incredibly loud. A threatened rattler coils up and lifts its head. Bold patterns cover the eastern diamondback. Rattlers come in more than 30 types. Eastern diamondbacks grow larger than the other types. Some have grown to almost 2.5 meters, which is 8 feet.

7Western diamondbacks are slightly shorter. They can be thicker than eastern diamondbacks. They can be heavier too. A typical western diamondback reaches somewhere between 1 and 1.5 meters. That span is 3 to 5 feet. Diamondbacks get their name from a diamond-shaped pattern on the skin. Many wooded parts of North America are home to timber rattlesnakes. Southern Canada and northern Mexico mark the two ends of their range. A timber rattlesnake is about 1.5 meters long. That length is 4 to 5 feet. Sidewinders are another common rattler. They get their name from the way they cross desert sand. They use the sidewinder motion. A sidewinder is smaller than a diamondback. It is usually less than 1 meter long, or 3 feet. The banded rock rattler belongs with the smaller kinds. The pygmy rattler is small too. How do you think those two snakes got their names? One picture can show a banded rock rattlesnake. Another can show a pygmy rattlesnake. Except while hunting, a rattler bites only to defend itself. A picture may show the body held in a defensive posture. Bothering the snake is how most people get bitten. Others are bitten when they step on it by accident. A threatened rattler often gives a dry bite. A dry bite has no venom in it. Even a venom bite usually delivers only a small amount. The snake is not trying to kill a person. It is not trying to kill an animal that only threatens it.

8It wants to hurt that visitor just enough to make the visitor leave. It wants the visitor to stay away later. Most people who get bitten were trying to catch the snake, tease it, or kill it. Safety tips keep rattlers from being a danger to you. First, never bother a rattlesnake or any other snake. Snakes are wild animals. Catching a snake is not a safe plan. You should not try to touch them. Second, dress with care in wild places where snakes may live. Wear long pants. Wear boots that cover your ankles. A snake bites down low. Cloth over the skin can stop the fangs. Third, keep your pets on leashes. Do not let a dog get close to a snake. Do not let a dog chase a snake. Fourth, keep hands and feet out of hidden spots. Do not reach under rocks, logs, or bushes you cannot see. An object overhead makes a favorite hiding spot for a snake. Fifth, stop moving at once if you hear a rattle. Look around in a calm way. Use your eyes to find where the snake is. Move backward, slowly, until you are clear of the snake. The rattle is a warning meant for you. The snake does not want to bite if it does not have to. Heed that warning. Use the steps below if a bite hits you or someone you know. Use the same steps for a pet. First, keep the bitten one calm.

9Panic only makes the heart beat faster. Venom spreads faster when the heart is racing. Second, reach a doctor with as little delay as possible. Do not let the bitten one run. Do not allow any other exercise. If you can, have someone carry the person. Third, cover the bite with a cloth that is cool and wet. Leave ice out of the treatment. Ice can cause frostbite. Fourth, name the kind of snake you believe did the biting. Tell the hospital workers the same thing. Leave the snake where it is. Catching it is a bad idea. Do not kill it. Do not bring it to the hospital. Snakebites are treated with a medicine called antivenom. That medicine comes from horses. A small dose of snake venom is injected into the horse. The horse does not get hurt. Inside the horse, a chemical forms that blocks what the poison does. Doctors collect this chemical. People and other animals are protected by that same chemical. When Columbus reached the Americas, far more rattlers lived than live now. Many people fear these snakes. They do not understand the good the snakes do. They often kill rattlers when there is no need. Rattlesnake roundups drew big crowds in the recent past. During those hunts, people captured every snake they could find. The snakes were killed and then skinned. The meat was sold. Belts, wallets, and purses were fashioned from those skins. Many rattlers died because people wanted their beautiful skin.

10A close photo can show the pattern of the scales. Other threats stand in the way of rattlesnake survival. Warm roads draw rattlesnakes that want to soak up the sun. Cars kill many of those snakes. Trucks kill many of them too. People destroy rattlesnake habitat as they build larger cities. They destroy habitat when they build more highways. Some people are starting to take action so rattlesnakes can survive. Bans or limits now cover many of the old rattlesnake roundups. Drivers meet signs on roads where a sunning rattlesnake may lie. Protection now covers some places kept aside as snake habitat. If people respect these animals, the animals will not hurt them. Learning more about rattlesnakes shows why protection matters. The natural home of a plant or an animal is its habitat. Call an animal cold-blooded when its body heat follows the air around it. Fangs are long, hollow, sharp teeth. To hibernate is to pass the winter in a deep sleep. Snakes called pit vipers carry heat-sensing pits on their heads. Animals eaten by other animals are called prey. Serpentine describes an S-shaped motion. In that motion the snake pushes itself forward where the body bends. Sidewinding describes a fast, strong S-shaped motion that pushes the body sideways. Animals use venom, a kind of poison, both to kill prey and to protect themselves. Caterpillar, as a name for motion, means the edges of the scales catch the ground. Those edges then pull the body forward.

111. Wave Sliding Around the World

1In Cape Town, South Africa, surfers sprint toward the waves. Surfing already held a deep place in Polynesian life before anyone wrote history. People have surfed for hundreds of years. They may have surfed for thousands of years. Polynesian people who fished may have been the earliest to ride waves. They rode boards so they could move quickly through the waves. Settlers from Polynesia reached Hawai'i for the first time near the year 1200 ce. Love for wave riding came with those settlers. They called the sport he'e nalu. Say that like HAY-ay NAHL-oo. The words mean wave sliding. During the 1780s, the Sandwich Islands had a chief named Kana'ina. Say his name like kah-nah-EE-nah. The Sandwich Islands are the islands of Hawai'i. Chiefs had more free time for surfing practice than common people had. Many chiefs became talented surfers. To early Hawaiians, riding waves meant more than sport by itself. Wave riding held a key place inside their culture. Hawaiians carved boards called alaias. Say alaias like ah-LY-ahz. Those boards were shaped from Acacia koa wood.

2Surfers prayed to their gods. They asked the gods for protection. They asked the gods to send great waves. Chiefs of Hawai'i showed skill by riding huge boards of wood. They showed courage in the same rides. The best beaches were reserved for royalty alone. People in Europe first heard of wave riding late in the 1700s. That is when Captain James Cook, a British explorer, and his crew saw surfers. They saw them around Tahiti and around Hawai'i. In 1885, three princes from Hawai'i visited Santa Cruz, California. The princes took their boards out from the beach and rode. Soon, boys who lived nearby tried to copy them. Jack London was an author famous around the world. He visited Hawai'i in 1907. He put the surfers he had watched into written stories. One of those surfers was George Freeth. Freeth drew ideas from the Hawaiian people. He helped carry surfing across the mainland. He traveled to California often. He showed his skills there. At shows in Redondo Beach, California, people gave him a title.

3Crowds named him a fellow who seemed able to walk upon the sea. Duke Kahanamoku was a champion swimmer born in Hawai'i. Say his name like kah-hah-nah-MOH-koo. He won medals at the Olympic Games of 1912. He won medals again at the Olympic Games of 1920. Surfing was a skill he picked up as a Hawai'i boy. He loved to share the sport. His travels carried Kahanamoku through many parts of the United States. He became one of the most important early stars of surfing. He took part in the first surfing shows in Australia. He rode a board he had built himself. During the 1960s, California took up surfing with great enthusiasm. It was very popular in Hawai'i. It was very popular in Australia too. Hit songs celebrated the fun and the freedom of surfing. Movies did the same. Magazines and TV shows did the same. Plenty of people knew the surfing lifestyle without ever watching a live ride. People also call Duke Kahanamoku the Big Kahuna.

4By that decade, the sport already had a wide following. It is even more popular today. A set of old wooden boards shows how many sizes and shapes early boards had. Until the early years of the twentieth century, surfboards were solid wood. They were heavy. They were hard to steer. In 1926, a surfer named Tom Blake invented a board that was hollow. The hollow board was much lighter. It was also faster. Blake was the earliest builder to attach fins. Fins gave riders better command of a board. Makers in the 1940s switched to balsa, a wood that is light. Fiberglass and other new stuff later changed the boards once more. Boards today are light, strong, and buoyant. Surfboards come in many styles. The styles include the shortboard, the longboard, and the funboard. Each board has a nose and a tail. The nose and the tail help the board go faster. Fins on the bottom help the rider steer. A shortboard measures about 2 meters. That length is 6.5 feet. A longboard can reach 4 meters.

5That length is 13.1 feet. A funboard is a little longer than a shortboard. It is also a little wider. New surfers often find a funboard a good choice. A modern board has a leash. A leash is a rope for the leg. It keeps the board from being swept away. A leash also protects swimmers, since a loose board cannot slam into them. It matters most when the rider falls off. Boards in wide use now include the longboard and the funboard. They include the shortboard, the fish, and a board for a kid. They also include the gun and the Malibu. Skateboarding began under another name, sidewalk surfing. Surfers in California invented it. They wanted an activity for days when the waves were flat. The first World Surfing Championship took place in 1964. The beach was Manly Beach in Australia. Surfers came from Hawai'i. Others came from the continental United States, from Peru, and from Australia. More than 65,000 people watched them. Bernard Farrelly of Australia became one of the first world champions.

6Phyllis O'Donnell of Australia became one of the first world champions too. Modern surfing also includes contests on giant waves. Riders take on waves so large and so dangerous that rescue crews must wait nearby. The crews stay close on small fast boats. Pro surfer Sally Fitzgibbons cuts along the crest of a wave. The best surfers today compete on the World Championship Tour. The World Surf League runs that tour. One heat gives a rider no more than thirty minutes for catching waves. Every wave can earn a mark from one up to ten. A surfer may catch as many waves as possible during the heat. Judges keep the top two waves for each surfer. The highest possible total is twenty. Few surfers ever earn a perfect score. Once each year, dogs get a surfing contest of their own. Each year, Huntington Beach holds an event named Surf City Surf Dog Competition. The beach is Huntington Beach in California. Dozens of dogs take to the waves.

7Their humans go out beside them. Layne Beachley comes from Australia. During her career, she earned the title of world champion seven times. Points pile up from the skill a rider shows in contest heats. The riders with the highest points in a year become the champions. They are the champions of the World Surf League. Judges study five things when they score a ride. First, they look at how big the wave is, or how hard it is to ride. Second, they look at how creative the rider’s moves are. Third, they look at how many big moves the rider links on one wave. They also look at how well those moves flow from one to the next. Fourth, they look at how different the moves are from each other. Fifth, they look at how much speed and power the rider shows. Carissa Moore is a world champion of surfing five times over. Her full name is Carissa Kainani Moore. In 2022, she surfed in a final at Pipeline. The place was Haleiwa, in Hawai'i.

8The well-known rider Moore comes from Hawai'i. Her father was a swimmer. At age five, she got her first lessons from her father, who swam. Moore won surfing contests around the world. Readiness was already hers when 2020 arrived. That year brought the first Olympic contest in surfing. She won the gold medal. She was the first person to take the women's gold medal at the Olympics in surfing. Moore enters those contests for the United States. She does not wear the flag of the United States. The flag she puts on is Hawai'i's flag. The flag honors her Hawaiian roots. A leash on the leg holds a board firmly to the surfer. People can get hurt while they surf. Surfers need to take care. They need to avoid hurting themselves. They also need to avoid hurting people around them. A surfer needs to be a strong swimmer. Before going near the water, a surfer should check the weather. A surfer should check the tides too. A surfer should make sure the board is in good shape.

9A surfer should always use a safety leash. A surfer should never go out alone. A surfer should keep control of the board at all times. A surfer should wear sunblock. A surfer should wear a swim shirt. Together, these protect the skin from damage by the sun. They also protect the skin from rashes. A surfer should wear a wet suit so the cold stays out. An instructor teaches surfing at a surf school in Hawai'i. The lesson is at Barber's Point Beach. Surfing began in Polynesia. From there, it has spread to every continent. The spread includes Antarctica. Across every part of the world, people have learned what this sport can give. They have found it fun. They have found it healthy. They have found it exciting. When surfers say surf is up, they mean the waves are high enough to ride. Surfers have a slang of their own. Slang is a special kind of language. A wipeout is a fall from the board. Hang ten is a ride with every toe past the board's front end.

10The word cowabunga comes from a Hawaiian word, kupaianaha. Say that word like koo-py-ah-NAH-hah. It means surprising or wonderful. Buoyant means able to float. Champion means the one person who comes out ahead of every rival. A competitor is a person or a team that someone plays against. A competitor is a rival. Culture means the particular ideas and the particular customs a group shares. It can also mean a society that has its own ideas and customs. A heat is a single round inside a contest that runs for more than one round. The nose is the leading end of a board, and the same word fits a plane or a boat. Polynesian refers to ethnic groups that began on many islands of the Pacific. Surfing is riding a sea wave in toward land, most often while standing on a board. The tail is the rear end of a board, and the same word fits a plane or a boat.

112. Welcoming the New Year Around the World

1Contents. Introduction. Africa. North America. Central and South America. Europe. Southeast Asia. Closing. Word List. Red clothes mark the New Year for a boy in China. His snack is a stick of candied red berries. In the other picture, two children in Japan ring the year in. A new year does not fall on one date for every land. The customs are not all alike. Parties are the choice in some cultures. Other cultures pick fascinating traditions. Those traditions are unique. They usher the year in. Midnight brings fireworks in many cities. People make resolutions as well. A resolution works like a promise. That promise may stop a bad habit. It may start a good habit. Healthier foods can be one promise. Being a better friend can be another. Resolutions let people meet the new year in a hopeful, positive way. The map labels the Red Sea, Eritrea, the Gulf of Aden, Ethiopia, and Africa. Ethiopia and Eritrea share a New Year celebration.

2Its name is Enkutatash. September 11 is the usual date. Their calendar has a thirteenth month. Set beside calendars in many other countries, it runs seven or eight years behind. The rainy season ends as Enkutatash arrives. Torches are carried for the celebration. Those torches represent sunshine. Coffee brings families and friends together. Meals are shared. Gifts are exchanged. Children often bring daisies. A daisy is a symbol of the new year. Paintings the children made are gifts too. An Ethiopian girl is shown collecting flowers. A second map labels Canada, the United States, Mexico, the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Gulf of Mexico. Elsewhere in the United States, New Year's Eve may be only a small gathering. Family and friends may be the whole guest list. New York City has a packed square called Times Square. The crowd there is far bigger. An estimate puts that crowd at about a million people. They count down the year's final minute.

3Lights cover a huge ball. The ball falls from a high building. Television carries the scene to millions of viewers in many lands. When midnight strikes, cheers rise from the crowd. The picture shows a father celebrating there with his young daughter. In California, the Rose Parade floats are built from thousands of flowers. When the year turns, college teams in the United States play special football games. Pasadena, California, hosts the most famous of those games. That game is the Rose Bowl. Before kickoff, many viewers watch the Rose Parade. Floats in the parade are covered with flowers. Marching bands take part too. In many parts of Canada, people greet the New Year with a cold-water custom. It may be a Polar Bear plunge, a dip, or a swim. Brave people leap into freezing water on New Year's Day. The shock is one way to feel fresh as the year begins. Hoppin' John is a dish eaten in the southern United States.

4Rice and black-eyed peas make up the dish. Some people hold a belief about plain foods. They think plain foods on New Year's Day may bring success later in the year. Spain is where the New Year's Eve grape custom began. Central and South America keep that custom. People there eat twelve grapes. The grapes are eaten in the year's final twelve seconds. Colonists from Spain carried the custom into the lands they settled. One grape means one month in the year ahead. Finishing all twelve is a wish for good luck. Another favorite custom is a clean house before midnight. Good luck feels welcome in a clean home. A sweep clears out what is old from the past year. The map labels the Atlantic Ocean, Central America, South America, and the Pacific Ocean. In Uruguay, women throw water from a window. They hope it will bring New Year luck. Some people sweep coins into the house at midnight.

5Wealth is what they hope the coins will bring. Starting fresh and clean is a good idea. In many countries, water is poured from windows onto the streets. The pour says goodbye to bad luck. The act is a symbol. It washes the old year away. It welcomes a fresh start. Janus, an ancient Roman god, gives January its name. Doors were part of his role. Gateways were part of it. Beginnings were part of it too. Pictures usually give him two faces. The old year is what one face looks back at. The New Year is what the other face looks toward. Russia is where the statue of Janus in the picture was made. The map labels Finland, Scotland, Denmark, the Baltic Sea, the Atlantic Ocean, the Czech Republic, the Mediterranean Sea, Greece, and nearby parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa. For the New Year, people in the Czech Republic slice apples into halves.

6They study the pattern of the seeds. Bad luck is what a crossed pattern means. A star pattern is a promise of good luck in the year ahead. In Finland, tin is melted so people can guess fortunes for the next year. Love or marriage is the meaning of a heart shape. Good luck is the meaning of a circle. Bakers in Greece hide a coin inside a cake. Luck in the coming year should belong to the person who finds that coin. All year long, people in Denmark save broken dishes. New Year's Eve is when those dishes get broken. Dishes are smashed on the doorsteps of relatives and friends. Good luck is what a pile of smashed dishes outside the front door means. Hogmanay is what Scotland calls its New Year celebration. Homes are cleaned by midnight for Hogmanay. After dark, groups parade in the streets. Torches are carried. Balls of flame are swung. Some of the fireballs are giant.

7One can weigh as much as 9.1 kilograms, which is 20 lb. Midnight is when people sing Auld Lang Syne. Remembering old friends is what the song is about. At a Scottish New Year celebration, a man swings a fireball. The Southeast Asia map labels the Philippine Sea, Thailand, the South China Sea, Cambodia, and the Philippines. Round objects in the Philippines stand for coins. They symbolize good luck too. Polka-dot clothes are what Filipino people wear on New Year's Eve. The dots are a way to invite luck. People meet and eat round fruit. Twelve different types are eaten. Homes are also cleaned before New Year's Eve. Every window is opened at midnight. Good fortune is invited in through the open windows. Two girls in Cambodia pour water over a Buddha statue. Late March or mid-April is the traditional New Year in parts of Southeast Asia. That timing ends the dry season in Cambodia.

8It ends the dry season in other countries too. The season is very hot. Dust fills the air. Water festivals fit this time of year. Dusty Buddha statues are washed with water as people get ready. The water is saved for priests. A priest pours it gently onto someone's shoulders. Good luck is the aim of that pour. Songkran is the name of the water festival in Thailand. April 13 to 15 is the usual length of Songkran. Water sprays from parade floats onto the crowds. Children chase each other with water blasters. Water pails are used too. Heat in Thailand on New Year's Day can easily reach 38 degrees Celsius, or 100 degrees F. In heat like that, a water fight is a perfect celebration. In Los Angeles, California, a schoolboy blows a shofar. A shofar is a ram's horn. He honors the Jewish New Year. Buffalo are herded by people at an Islamic New Year parade in Indonesia.

9Some cultures move the New Year to a different time each year. Enkutatash is one example. Al-Hijra, said al HI-jruh, is the name of the Islamic New Year. A lunar calendar is its base. The Moon's cycles guide that calendar. About eleven days is how much shorter a lunar year is than a solar year. A solar year has 365 days. Earth's path around the Sun is what the solar year follows. Spring Festival is the name of the Chinese New Year. Rosh Hashanah is the name of the Jewish New Year. The solar calendar and the lunar calendar both guide those two New Years. Red clothes fill a parade in London, England. People there hold a dragon up high. The parade is for the Chinese New Year. Countries share many New Year traditions. Many cultures clean the house ahead of the New Year. Midnight fireworks are common in many cities. Resolutions for the year ahead are common too. These traditions share one wish, a fresh beginning.

10A wish to celebrate runs through them too. Music is part of that wish. Dancing and fun are part of it. What will your New Year celebration be like? Music and dance are how children in many lands greet the New Year. Word List. Buddha is the title of the person who began the Buddhist religion. Cultures are the ideas and the customs that belong to particular groups of people. Cycles are events that happen again, always in the same order. Exchange means giving something and receiving something back. Fortunes are guesses about later times, or about success and failure. Resolutions are choices or promises about things a person will do. Symbolize means using an object, a picture, or a sign to stand for an idea. Traditions are beliefs or customs handed on through the years and from one generation to the next. Usher means greeting a new start, or celebrating it.

113. Whale Sharks, Giants of the Ocean

1Thoughts of sharks often bring pictures of sharp teeth and of blood. There is no need to be afraid. The largest shark on Earth is also the largest fish, and it is a gentle giant. Swimming at its side is safe. The reason is the peaceful nature of this shark. This harmless animal is named for its size. Like a whale, it is big, and it is really big. A whale shark may reach 40 feet, or 12.2 m, in length. It may weigh 40,000 pounds, or 18,144 kg. A person who stands 6 feet tall is 1.8 m tall. A person who weighs 175 pounds weighs 79.4 kg. A whale shark has a wide, flat head, a blunt snout, and a huge mouth. It often swims with that mouth open. Like other sharks, it has rough skin and sharp scales. The back is dark, in a bluish, grayish, or brownish shade, with cream-colored spots and stripes.

2People often compare that pattern to a checkerboard or to a set of dominoes. Scientists do not know why the pattern looks this way. It might be camouflage. Hiding from predators is hardly needed once a whale shark is grown, because of its size. The pattern may help young whale sharks stay safe. It may also block some of the strong sunlight at the surface of the water. The huge mouth and the back pattern make a whale shark easy to recognize. A whale shark swims with its whole body. Other sharks drive themselves mainly with the tail and the rear of the body. This fish has a large fin on its back and a large tail fin. Five large gill slits open on each side. The mouth sits at the front of the head, not underneath the snout as on other sharks. Like every shark, it has a skeleton of cartilage rather than bone.

3Most fish have a backbone. Most fish breathe with gills and live in water. Most fish have tails and paired fins. Most fish are cold-blooded and have scales. Most fish lay eggs. Warmer water is where whale sharks live. Those waters lie in the Atlantic, the Pacific, and the Indian Ocean. They swim in the open sea, and they also swim close to shore. People often see these giants at the surface, and the sharks are known to dive deep as well. A dive can reach 6,000 feet, or 1,829 m, below the surface. Other whale sharks are not their usual travel companions. Other kinds of fish may stay near them. Groups of large fish sometimes move with them. Those fish feed in a similar way. Remoras, fish that have suckers, are often seen with them. A remora clamps onto a whale shark and eats parasites off the skin.

4In return, the remora gains protection. A map of their habitat and migration crosses many regions. It includes Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, North America, and South America. It includes the Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, and the Indian Ocean, with the equator running through the range. These sharks migrate over long distances. A common trip is more than 1,240 miles, or 2,000 km. One whale shark was tracked for 8,077 miles, or 13,000 km, across more than three years. Scientists cannot yet say why the journeys are so long. Breeding may be the reason, or the search for food, or something else. Whale sharks gather at certain places around the world. The largest gathering is called the Afuera, a Spanish word meaning out or outside. It lies off the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico. At one time, watchers have counted more than four hundred whale sharks in that place.

5The sharks were feeding on fish eggs in huge numbers. Unlike most sharks, the whale shark does not actively hunt, and it is not classed as a predator. Tiny animals of the ocean are its food. Those animals drift in the water or swim there. Favorite foods include krill. Krill are animals similar to shrimp. Small fish may be eaten too. So may squid, plants, and fish eggs. Now and then a larger fish is eaten. Each side has five large gill slits. They open and close while the shark takes water in and lets water out. The shark collects food by filter feeding. Food enters with the water when the mouth opens. As that water moves toward the gills, filter pads trap the small animals and plants. The water then leaves through the gill slits. A vacuum cleaner is a good picture of how suction feeding works.

6The shark opens its mouth and sucks hard, pulling in water and prey together. Whale sharks use two kinds of filter feeding, and either kind can be done lying level or hanging upright. Suction feeding means gulping or sucking in a large volume of water. It is useful when food is plentiful. A whale shark may cough to clear extra food that piles up on the filter pads. In passive feeding, the shark swims with its mouth open while its head bobs from side to side. It swallows whatever flows in, and that can include trash from the ocean. To dump the trash, it turns its stomach inside out through its mouth. Tiny teeth fill 300 rows in a whale shark's mouth. Eating is not what those teeth are for. It probably finds food by smell. Scientists reached that idea by studying where the nostrils and the eyes sit.

7The nostrils are near the top of the mouth, close to the food. The eyes sit farther back on the head, which suggests they matter less in the search for food. Across an open mouth, the measure can be 5 feet, which is 1.5 m. A person could fit in that opening. Sixty-six feet is the length of the longest whale shark ever measured. That is 20 m. A line made of one school bus plus half of another would match that length. In four hours, a whale shark can filter as much water as an Olympic-sized pool holds. That amount is 650,000 gallons, or 2,460,517 liters. A newborn's length, multiplied by twenty-five, may equal the length of an adult. Scientists once believed that whale sharks laid eggs. In 1995, they learned that the sharks give birth to live young. A pregnant female that had died carried more than three hundred babies, called pups.

8Length of those developing sharks ran from 16 inches to 24 inches. In centimeters, that is 42 to 63. Some pups were further along than the rest. Those pups would have been born sooner. Two snorkelers swim next to a young whale shark. Aside from size, a pup looks like an adult. Births are poorly understood, because nobody has ever seen one. Near shore is not where scientists think the births happen. They think the open ocean is the place. A young whale shark becomes an adult at about thirty years of age. Nobody knows the length of a whale shark's life. Sharks as a group live a long time. Given their great size, scientists think a whale shark might live one hundred years. Swimming with these animals is popular at the places where they gather. More than twelve thousand people, each year, swim with these sharks or dive with them.

9Tour companies set rules that protect both the sharks and the people. Divers are told not to touch the sharks and not to disturb them. One woman who swam with them said the first sight took her breath away. She called the swim an experience of a lifetime. Fear of these gentle animals, she said, has no basis. Seeing them up close, she said, is fully worth doing. Fear might seem certain if the planet's biggest fish is a shark. The whale shark is not that kind of animal. It is huge, peaceful, and slow. In parts of Asia, it stands for good luck. Many stars is the meaning of its name on an island off Africa's coast. In Vietnam, people call it Sir Fish and believe it offers protection. People who study whale sharks, and people who swim with them, agree that these enormous fish really are gentle giants.

10They travel slowly, at about 3 miles per hour, or 5 kmph. An animal can blend in, or hide, because of its colors, its patterns, or its shapes. That set of features is camouflage. A habit is a regular way of behaving. Migrate means an animal changes habitat or region. The change comes at the same time each year. A parasite is a plant or an animal that grows on another living thing or feeds from it. Passive means not active. A predator is an animal that hunts other animals and eats them in order to survive. Many fish, and many reptiles, are covered by thin, flat plates. Those plates are scales. An animal's nose, together with its mouth, is its snout. Suction is a sucking force that can pull something into a space or make it stick to a surface.

114. What Happens to Our Garbage

1A 1912 photo shows children in a garbage dump in Rhode Island. Thousands of years ago, people in the ancient city of Troy threw garbage onto their floors. Troy stood in the land now called Turkey. When a floor grew filthy enough, the people spread a fresh layer of earth over it and buried the mess. They stacked so many layers that the rooms changed, and they had to lift the roofs. You may laugh. What we do now is not very different. People in every age still face the question of where trash belongs. Europe's Middle Ages, about one thousand years ago, saw waste thrown into the middle of the street. They did not yet see the link between public health and garbage. The filth drew rats and fleas, and those animals spread a deadly disease. People called that disease the plague, and also the Black Death.

2It killed 75 million people around the world. Today most people do not dump garbage on the floor or in the street. They drop it in a trash can, a truck hauls it off, and they forget it. The question is where away really is. Trash that you throw out enters the waste stream, the flow of garbage toward its last stop. Most of that garbage ends in landfills, areas of land set aside so trash can be buried. Some garbage is composted, including food scraps and yard waste. The result is rich organic matter. Returned to the soil, it helps plants grow. Trash that cannot be recycled can be burned in a controlled way to make heat, electricity, or fuel. That burning, called combustion, also shrinks the amount of trash. Most of the ash still goes to a landfill. These facts come from the 2011 Municipal Solid Waste Characterization Report of the US Environmental Protection Agency.

3Each year the world makes more than 2.6 trillion pounds of trash, or 1.2 trillion kilograms. That mass is about the weight of 182 Great Pyramids of Egypt. Americans are only 5 percent of the world's people, yet they make 25 percent of the world's waste. An average American throws out 4.5 pounds, or 2 kilograms, every day. Paper and paper goods, such as cardboard boxes, make up a large share of what Americans toss. Figures for US trash from 1960 to 2011 come from that same 2011 report. A compactor truck can squash trash flat at a landfill. A garbage truck brings the load and dumps it into a cell, a storage space made for garbage. A heavy truck then drives across the pile. Spiky wheels mash the trash down. At day's end a bulldozer spreads dirt over the load, so weather can reach less of it.

4The dirt also keeps wildlife out and cuts the smell. Landfills come in many sizes. Workers usually dig a huge hole about 200 feet, or 61 meters, wide, and as much as half a mile, or 805 meters, deep. Garbage cannot go straight into bare ground, because some of it is toxic. As the trash breaks down, toxic parts mix with rain and form leachate. Liquid that has drained through the fill is called leachate. The word leached names that draining. The liquid is often poisonous. Think of the landfill as a giant pool. Leachate is the liquid in that pool. If it is not collected and treated, it will leak through the bottom or spill over the top. Machines unroll a liner across a new landfill. A thick plastic liner blocks the leachate so it cannot escape.

5Pipes running through the fill pull the liquid out. Sometimes the site itself treats that liquid. Often the liquid travels by sewer to the nearest plant that cleans water. Designers must also plan for landfill gas. Rotting trash makes methane. The gas has to be let out or burned, or it may explode. Methane from these sites can make electricity and can fuel vehicles. More than one million homes could draw power from current United States projects that turn this gas into electricity. The projects also stop methane from drifting into the air. That matters, because methane is a strong greenhouse gas. It holds heat in the atmosphere and adds to climate change around the world. A well can pull methane from garbage as it decays, and engines can turn that gas into electricity. A working landfill has labeled parts. They include the trash cell, the methane pipe, the plastic liner, and compacted clay.

6They include groundwater, the leachate pipe and pump, and the leachate pond. Trash sealed inside a landfill stays for a long time, shut away from air and water. Vegetables and other organic matter are biodegradable. Bacteria and other living things could break them down quickly, but those helpers need air and water, so they cannot work inside the seal. Plastic that people throw out is not biodegradable. It may take thousands of years to fall apart. A foam cup tossed out today could need more than a million years to become dust. Foam waste can litter a beach. Newer sites, called bioreactor landfills, help garbage rot faster. Pumps send air and liquid through the trash. Decomposers can then break the waste down. Faster rotting frees space for new loads. A bioreactor can add as many as twenty years to a landfill's useful life.

7New York City once sent all its trash to the biggest landfill on Earth, on Staten Island. That site closed in 2001. The ground is being made into a park of 2,200 acres, three times the size of Central Park. Filling a landfill can take thirty to fifty years. A full site is often capped with clay, then plastic, then soil so plants can grow. A closed landfill can become a park, a playground, or open land. Even with a cap, it cannot be forgotten. A 2008 study found leaks at 82 percent of the landfills it checked. No liner can block every drop from the ground forever. In time a liner wears out, rips, or cracks. The Environmental Protection Agency reports that fact. When the liner fails, poisonous liquid escapes and pollutes the soil and the groundwater.

8The United States has plenty of land, but a site for a new landfill is still hard to find. People often refuse one in their own neighborhood. They fear the noise, the pests, and the pollution. Some states ship trash across state borders to be rid of it. Open landfills in the country are growing fewer. There were 6,300 open sites in 1990. By 2021 only about 1,250 remained. The new ones are larger and better built, but the trash must travel farther. Each year the country burns more fossil fuel just to carry that trash to rest. A sign in Illinois speaks against a landfill that might pollute. Hauling trash across a state line fixes one problem and creates another. The longer the trip, the higher the cost. For years, New York City's garbage moved only a few miles, to Staten Island. Ohio, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia are among the states that now take the city's trash.

9It spends more than 300 million dollars a year to reach those distant fills. Moving so much trash so far also harms the planet. Each year those trips release carbon dioxide measured in the hundreds of thousands of tons. Carbon dioxide, like methane, is a greenhouse gas. Climate change is what it drives. No one knows how long our trash will take to break down, or how long the liners will hold. What is known is that each person chooses what to do with garbage. Recycling could keep about half of thrown-away things out of landfills. Buying less in the first place also cuts the daily pile. Floors may be clear of trash now, but thrown-away things do not vanish. What will future people say about the waste we leave? In a garden, a boy looks over kitchen scraps sitting in a compost bin.

10Garbage that would sit for ages in a landfill can instead break down by composting. Biodegradable describes something living things, such as bacteria, can break apart. In this story the elements are weather, including wind, rain, sun, and extreme heat or cold. Water held in underground soil or rock is groundwater. Springs and wells often draw on it. Landfills are places that store garbage and cover it with dirt. Methane is a gas you cannot see or smell, and it can catch fire. Another name for it is natural gas. Organic means tied to living things, or coming from them. To pollute is to make something unclean or unsafe, including the environment. Toxic means poisonous and dangerous to life. Treated means a substance, such as a chemical, was added to improve, protect, or clean something.

115. When Mud Races Downhill

1After a mudslide struck China in 2008, rescue crews hunted for people still alive. This book tells what happens when the earth moves. It tells how a mudslide builds up. It tells about the danger zone. It tells about the aftermath. It tells how people prepare. It tells why these disasters are hard to predict. A word list comes at the end. When the Earth Moves. December 1999 sent mud and debris racing down slopes above Vargas, Venezuela. Debris may be said as duh-BREE. Few mudslides on record were worse than this one. Soft, thick, wet mud is called sludge. It buried whole neighborhoods. Several mudslides hit the area. Flash floods hit it too. The trouble lasted three days. From high apartment buildings, people watched mud pour into floors down below. Days passed on the roof while they waited to be helped. All at once, over 150,000 people were left without homes. About 25,000 people lost their lives in the Vargas tragedy. Mud in that tragedy stood as high as 3.5 meters, equal to 11.5 feet. They left boulders on the second floor of a building.

2How a Mudslide Happens. A picture can show the original area and the land that moves. Soaked ground on a slope is how a mudslide begins. The land starts to shift. Later that mass breaks free and heads down the hill. Mudslides are also called mudflows. They are also called debris flows. This kind of event belongs with landslides. A landslide is a natural disaster. It happens when an event affects how stable a slope is. An earthquake can be that event. A drought can be that event too. For mudslides, a buildup of water makes the land on slopes unstable. Mudslides cause soil erosion. Erosion means land wears away little by little. Ground that begins shifting on a slope can turn into a disaster. Mudflows move downhill at fast speeds. They gain momentum quickly. Chaos often follows. Danger comes with it. A great deal of harm does too. The Buildup. Mudslides show how dangerous nature can be. They also show how unexpected it can be. Reasons for mudslides are under study by researchers. They also study ways to protect people if a slide starts.

3They have found that mudslides happen only under very specific conditions. A heavy load of water on the soil is the first requirement. This can happen during a heavy rainfall. It can also happen after one. Snow that melts fast can set a mudslide off as well. Every case starts the same way. Water soaks the ground until the soil comes loose. Then the soil shifts. Soil turns into a rushing mix of mud together with debris. That river is called a slurry. Little warning is typical, and the slide can form fast. They often come with little warning. A 2015 mudslide in California trapped more than one hundred vehicles. Homes in Colombia were wrecked by mudslides during 2017. Down a slope, the average pace is 16 kilometers each hour. That equals 10 miles each hour. Where the ground is very steep, speed can match an avalanche. The pace can climb to 130 kilometers each hour, or 80 miles each hour. Mudslides differ in how thick they are. Some are mainly watery mud. Other flows are mud so thick that rocks and boulders ride inside it.

4The mudslide travels a long way. It gathers trees, sand, and cars. Anything else along the route, materials or objects, gets picked up. A longer run usually builds a bigger slide. A mudslide can become so intense that its momentum destroys bridges. It can destroy other large structures too. The Danger Zone. Areas at risk for mudslides exist on every continent except Antarctica. The moment a mudslide will start cannot always be known ahead. The place cannot always be known ahead either. Some locations have a higher risk for this kind of disaster. Places that get hit usually have two traits in common. They have steep mountains. They have heavy rainfall. Being near a coast often adds to the risk. Japan is at high risk. Islands elsewhere in the Pacific Ocean share that high risk. Mudslides can occur in places with no seacoast too. No range of mountains on Earth rises higher than the Himalayas in Asia. The area is far from the coast. It is still at severe risk because a large amount of rain falls there.

5A map can show areas at risk that this book describes. A firefighter climbs a slope in California once a wildfire has passed. After that fire, a mudslide could strike the land more easily. Inside these danger zones, some spots carry the highest risk. Slopes belong on that high-risk list. The ground underneath them does too. They include the bottoms of canyons. They include places where mudslides have happened before. Streams and channels see mudslides as well. Those paths fill up quickly. Land burned by wildfires is especially risky. A big wildfire can strip the ground so nothing is left growing. Plant roots are gone, so they cannot hold the soil together. Soil is more likely to wash away after that. Collect enough water, and a mudslide can start. Places close to volcanoes carry risk too. Heavy rains often follow a volcanic eruption. Mudslides often come with those rains. The Aftermath. After a big slide, people are often moved away until the area is safe again. Shelters hold them for a span nobody can predict.

6Internet service may not work. Television may not work either. Survivors then listen to the radio for information. They may listen to emergency workers. Weeks can pass before news of their homes reaches them. Buildings in an area may remain intact. Even then, mudslides and what follows can disrupt infrastructure. Roads, bridges, and tunnels can be hit. Trains can be hit. Electric lines and gas lines can be hit. Water service can be hit too. A return to home or work often has to wait. Road repair in Austria begins after the mudslides of 2018. During 2018 in California, a search-and-rescue dog hunts for people who lived through a mudslide. After a mudslide, survivors may face more mudslides. They may face flooding that continues. This is especially true if rain keeps falling. On ground that is very dangerous or very sloped, water and moving earth can snowball. Rain builds up and causes a mudslide. Then water that was pushed aside builds up in a new place. That causes another mudslide. The chain can go on for quite a while. It is most likely during an intense storm.

7Fresh problems appear once the disaster has truly ended. Standing water from mudslides may stay for a long time. It can create mold. Mold can rot the walls of buildings. It can rot the floors. It can even spread disease. Sierra Leone's 2017 mudslide left mud running like a river. The mudslides in Vargas, Venezuela, led to extreme flooding. While the slides were moving, water collected. That water pushed the moving debris out over a wider area. The water seeped inside homes that had not been swept away. It seeped inside businesses too. August 2017 brought another disaster much like it. Sierra Leone, in West Africa, was the country where it took place. The mudslides themselves took five hundred lives. Disease-carrying insects arrived after the flash floods. Mosquitos were among them. The insects left survivors fighting malaria. Survivors also fought cholera and other deadly diseases. A Chinese town was struck by a mudslide in 2018. Rescuers looked for survivors there. Heavy rains and a mudslide made a river overflow in Switzerland. Part of a nearby town flooded in 2000.

8Preparing for Mudslides. Very little notice may come before a mudslide. It can happen with no warning. Early clues can still help people notice one before it arrives. Soil that stays dry most of the time may turn wet before a slide. It might be sunken. It might be full of holes that no one expected. A dangerous buildup of water can crack concrete. It can crack pavement on roads or sidewalks. It can also make bumps there. Huge amounts of water can make the ground shift. Foundations can shift too. Windows might tilt. Doors might tilt. They may stick and refuse to open. Water levels in creeks may rise quickly. They may fall quickly. Rivers may do the same. Sandbags went up in 2009 at a California house to hold floodwater back. Workers repair walls of sandbags in Sri Lanka in 2017. Walls can split under the hard push of a slurry. Steering the flow clear of buildings can stop harm. Sending it to a safer area works better than trying to stop it. Landscaping done with care can send a slide away from buildings.

9Stones, ditches, and walls can help too. Another step is to plant vegetation so soil does not erode. Local emergency departments help people in danger zones. They share safety measures. They share evacuation plans. Sandbags may be given out as well. The bags are staggered in a stack, in the same pattern people use for bricks. The stack makes a seal. People hope to steer both the water and the mud onto a different path. Disasters That Are Hard to Predict. Mudslides are natural disasters that are incredibly dangerous. They begin with one simple ingredient, which is water. Water that has piled up can leave the ground unsteady. It pulls more and more mud into its flow. It pulls in more debris too. Mudslides often strike with little notice. Knowing the warning signs still matters. This matters most in mountainous areas near coasts. Those places carry the greatest mudslide risk. People who live where mudslides are a risk need to be prepared. They need to stay alert. A great deal of damage remains once a slide is over.

10That damage is a reminder of the power of nature. China lost a wide stretch of land to a mudslide in 2010. Word List. Accumulation means material heaping higher as time passes. A natural disaster is a sudden event that forces of nature set off. It can bring damage across a wide area. It can also bring death. Dangerous describes something that can hurt people, or that is likely to. Saturated means completely full of moisture. Debris means leftover bits once the rest has been ruined or has vanished. Stability means staying set in place, steady, and not changing. Disrupt means to damage something, break it apart, or change it in a drastic way. Survivors are people who made it through something extremely hard, or through a threat to life. Evacuated means moved people out of danger. A tragedy is an event that brings huge destruction, deep suffering, or many deaths. Intense means extreme, forceful, or present at a very high level. Momentum is the push that keeps a thing moving, or keeps that motion growing, as minutes pass.

116. Why a Heavy Machine Can Fly

1Contents. Leaving the Ground. Two Brothers Named Wright. Facts About the Plane. The Big Question. Up Into the Sky. Word List. Topic List. A picture shows the inside of a typical passenger airplane used by airlines. Picture a walk along a narrow aisle. A short row of seats sits on each side of you. Each side has three seats. Some people stuff luggage into large compartments overhead. Others push things under the seats. You do the same. Then you slide into the seat. You buckle your seatbelt. You keep looking around. The walls, you see, bend upward. They curve toward the ceiling. A small plastic window sits beside you. The window has a thick shade. You can lift the shade. You can lower the shade. People keep walking down the aisle. They bring more and more luggage. Suddenly you wonder about this machine. It is a big metal tube. It is heavy. It holds all these people. It holds all this stuff. How will it ever leave the ground? The question under that wonder is a simple one. How does an airplane fly? All through history, people have asked how to fly. They wanted to soar through the sky the way a bird soars.

2The question has intrigued people. It has mystified them. Birds can fly. People asked why humans could not fly too. Some people built copies of bird wings. They attached the wings to their arms. They flapped their arms wildly. Those homemade wings, they learned, did not solve the problem. Those wings did not give humans flight. A way to fly finally appeared in 1783. Two brothers in France made the discovery that year. Cooler air weighs more than hot air. Hot air could be used to fill a giant balloon. Inside the balloon, the warmer air would go up. The cooler air outside would stay below that warmer air. The idea was ingenious. With this discovery, the brothers created the first hot-air balloon. Flight succeeded for the first time with this balloon. People went on testing ideas for several decades after that. They tried various methods of aviation. Bit by bit, the shape of these flying machines changed. They started to look like the airplane we know today. A drawing shows the hot-air ship of Henri Giffard. It was the first powered aircraft.

3A picture shows Wilbur watching. Orville is making the first flight. Science was not the job of Orville Wright or Wilbur Wright. Bicycles were the machines they understood best. Like many people before them, they were intrigued. They were drawn to the chance of being able to fly. A special sort of plane was the Wright brothers' goal. It would take off from the earth. Once aloft, it would stay in the air by its own power. They believed a new invention would be a key part of that dream. The invention was the gasoline engine. They hoped it would power a flying machine. Wilbur Wright lived from 1867 to 1912. Orville Wright lived from 1871 to 1948. They grew up in Ohio. They owned a shop that repaired bicycles. The shop was in Dayton, Ohio. People in the United States got their first look at this powered airplane from the brothers. They introduced it to people in Europe too. The day was December 17, 1903. The Wright brothers pulled their new flying machine onto a field. They called the machine Flyer. The field was in North Carolina. It overlooked the Atlantic Ocean.

4Toward the front, the odd machine carried a long pair of wings. It had a shorter pair of wings near the rear. Two propellers were part of the plane as well. One engine drove both propellers. Orville Wright lay face down. He lay on the lower wing. He started the engine. The propellers turned. Two small wheels carried the plane as it rolled ahead. Wilbur ran alongside. He held a wing so the plane would stay steady. Moments later, the machine left the ground. The brothers felt delight. Their invention was a success. Three further flights that day also worked. None of those flights lasted more than a minute. A picture shows a glider flight from 1911. In that 1911 glider flight, Orville Wright stayed up for 9 minutes plus 45 seconds. He set a record. The record lasted for more than 10 years. Changes to their flying machines kept coming from the Wright brothers. They continued to experiment. Other people also worked with that incredible design. They hoped to build flyers that were bigger. They hoped the flyers would be quicker. They hoped the flyers would be better.

5Later years brought airplanes with more complexity. They became more advanced. Even so, every airplane shared some basic parts. The planes could differ in size. They could differ in form. The shared parts were the ones on the brothers' first plane. Those parts were engines. Those parts were wings. Pictures show Charles Lindbergh and Amelia Earhart. After the airplane was invented, people began to challenge themselves. They challenged their aircraft too. Distance was the test they set for themselves. Charles Lindbergh was one famous early pilot. Amelia Earhart was another. In 1927, Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic Ocean alone. No person had done that before. His flight left from New York. He landed in Paris. Five years later, Amelia Earhart made her own solo flight. No woman before her had crossed the Atlantic alone in a plane. Every plane that powers itself must have an engine if it is going to fly. A car engine moves a car forward. An airplane engine moves the airplane forward in a similar way. Every airplane must also have wings. Wings are the part that truly raises the plane off the ground. Every airplane must also have moving parts on its wings.

6Those moving parts are called ailerons. Ailerons help control the airplane. Other parts also make flight possible. Those parts help pilots control the plane's movements. The rear of a plane is its tail section. The tail has a rudder. The rudder moves right and left. The tail also has elevators. The elevators move up and down. The pilot can move these parts. The controls sit inside the plane's cockpit. A picture shows a simple plane with a single engine. Each kind of airplane movement has its own name. Rolling is a tilt to either side. Pitching is a move of the nose up or down. Yawing is a move of the nose to the left or the right. A picture shows a stunt airplane. A car's controls feel similar, in some ways, to a plane's controls. There is one extra challenge. The pilot has another dimension to deal with. A person driving a car can make it go forward. The driver can turn it right. The driver can turn it left. A bike rider can do those same things. You can think of those directions as two dimensions.

7One dimension is what lies in front of you. The second is everything to your left and your right. An airplane can move forward. It can move right. It can move left. It can also move up. It can move down. The pilot can use the space below the plane. The pilot can use the space above the plane. From inside the cockpit, controls give the pilot help. With those controls, the pilot can travel through every one of these dimensions. The cockpit contains several instruments. Important facts reach the pilot through the instruments. A car's steering wheel is a close match for the control column. Turning the column to the right moves the ailerons. Turning it to the left moves them too. The ailerons on the wings go up or down. The plane then tips from one side toward the other. A pilot can also draw the control column backward. It can be pushed forward. That action moves the elevators on the tail. The elevators go up or down. A downward elevator tips the plane's nose toward the ground. An upward elevator tips the plane's nose toward the sky. A picture shows a pilot.

8He is monitoring his many instruments. Most planes also have pedals. The pedals control the rudder. The right pedal sends the rudder toward the right. Then the nose of the plane yaws to the right. The left pedal does the reverse. The plane yaws to the left. Flight depends most of all on an airplane's wings. Pilot control of the airplane is clear now. One big question still remains. How does an airplane fly? Compare the wings on different airplanes. You will notice something no matter which plane you study. Wing shape stays the same on every one of them. That wing construction is the secret of flight. That same shape is the science that lets an airplane fly. A curve runs along the top face of an airplane wing. The bottom surface is flat. The path over the top face is the longer one. Air that moves across the lower surface has a shorter path. Air over the top has to match the speed needed to stay with the air below. To keep pace, the air over the top must move faster. When air moves faster, it exerts less pressure.

9Greater pressure comes from the slower air under the wing. The lower face of the wing receives that push. The fast-moving air exerts less pressure on the upper surface. Stronger pressure from below forces the wing up. People call this upward push of air lift. The plane rises off the ground because of lift. Lift causes the plane to fly. A diagram can show lift. Over the wing, moving air covers more distance than the air underneath. That upper air also travels faster. A picture shows an airplane engine up close. Moving air is what creates these different pressures. Because of that, forward momentum is critical. The plane needs that momentum in order to fly. The forward motion makes air flow past the wings. The flow creates the differences in pressure. Those differences create the lift the plane needs. Lift lets the plane overcome gravity. The wings must keep moving forward fast enough. Only then do they generate lift. As long as they do, the airplane will remain airborne. Picture yourself sitting inside an airplane. You gaze out the window. Do not focus on the weight of the airplane.

10It is loaded with people. It is loaded with stuff. Look instead at how the wings are shaped. Think about the air flowing past those wings. The Wright brothers did that. They used speculation. They used experimentation. They worked on the shape of wings. They worked on engines. Because of that work, today's airplanes can carry us far. Almost any place in the world is now within reach by plane. Which place would you choose? A picture shows a line of airplanes waiting before take-off. Ailerons are hinged surfaces. An airplane wing carries them on its rear edge. Aviation means the flying of aircraft. Elevators are hinged flaps. Airplane tails are where they are mounted. Lift is an upward aerodynamic force. Gravity pulls down. Lift works the other way. A rudder is a steering device. Boats carry it near the rear. Ships and airplanes do too. Speculation means guesses. Ideas and unproven theories are the base of those guesses. Topics in this book include the hot-air balloon. They include Amelia Earhart. They include invention. They include the cockpit. They include the propeller. They include the contraption. They include yawing. They include dimension.

117. Why a Price Rises or Falls

1During the COVID-19 pandemic, shoppers hunted for toilet paper. They hunted for paper towels too. The store shelves were often bare. What You Will Read. Who Decides the Cost. The Push and Pull of Price. A Lunch Deal. When Buyers and Sellers Match. Feelings Change What People Buy. The Part You Play. Words to Know. Who Decides the Cost. Have you ever wanted something and then not bought it? Was the price too high? Maybe the item was new. It might have been a T-shirt with a movie character you love. You might have returned to the store later. By then the shirt was on sale. Did you buy it? Probably not. A shirt from a newer movie would interest you more. Some scientists study shopping and the brain. They say a purchase can make people feel excited. They say it can make people feel happy. Why does each thing cost what it costs? When you decide to buy, you join an exchange with the seller. Any meeting place of sellers and buyers has a name.

2It is called a market. In a market, buyers hand money to sellers. In return they receive goods, such as toys. They may receive services, such as haircuts. You have likely noticed a wide spread in prices. Goods and services can be cheap or costly. Even matching kinds of things can differ. Cars, clothes, and food can each be low in price or high. Sellers put up signs with large letters. The signs use bright colors. The signs pull people into a store. They pull people onto a website too. Economists try to explain how prices work. Economics is their field. It studies buying, selling, and wealth. The law they use is called supply and demand. The law describes how the cost of goods and services shifts. It describes why the cost shifts. Supply means how much of a good or a service exists. Demand means how much of it people want. Supply and demand set the price of everything. The same products do not keep one price.

3Popularity can change the price. Location can change it. Season can change it. Remember this. Prices move often because supply and demand never sit still. The link also runs the other way. A new price can change supply. A new price can change demand. Think of the movie on that T-shirt. Did the movie fail? Was it a great hit? How popular the movie is changes the price of goods tied to it. Supply, demand, and price keep shifting. Each one influences the others from one moment to the next. Buyers like you help decide a cost. You help decide what goods and services cost. A Lunch Deal. Picture this moment. Your stomach is grumbling. A nearby restaurant offers a lunch special on chicken sandwiches. You can buy two for the price of one. What a deal. In this case, the sandwich price fell. The lower price created a sudden rise in demand. Now look at the same sandwiches as the seller would. Why offer two for one?

4Maybe too many chicken patties were on hand. Maybe they had to be sold by a certain date so they would not spoil. The restaurant had more patties than people wanted to buy. That situation is called a surplus. When the market has a surplus, prices often drop. Scarcity Means There Is Little. The year 2020 brought the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. The price of toilet paper shot upward. Shops sold out fast. Some customers hoarded toilet paper. Other people could not find any to buy. A common item for the home had suddenly become scarce. Economists treat scarcity as the reverse of abundance. Abundance means a large amount is on hand. Sellers usually want the highest payment the market will allow. They try to make a profit. A profit means they sell goods and services for more than those things cost to make. Buyers usually want the opposite. They hope to pay as little as possible. The strain between the two sides helps keep supply and demand in balance.

5Here is how that balance can break. If a seller sets a price too high, demand often drops. Think again of the chicken sandwiches. Suppose you arrived and saw a shocking price. Each sandwich cost one hundred dollars. You would probably leave. You would eat lunch somewhere else. Demand for that sandwich would fall as the price rose. Popcorn costs shoppers more inside a movie theater than inside a supermarket. Supply, Demand, and the Price. Supply of products and services is always on the move. Demand is always on the move too. The lines below show how the two work as a pair. Together they change prices. If supply stays the same and demand rises, the price rises. If supply stays the same and demand falls, the price falls. If supply rises and demand stays the same, the price falls. If supply falls and demand stays the same, the price rises. A price can also be too low. Then demand is likely to jump. Imagine the restaurant again.

6This time each chicken sandwich costs one dollar. You would probably buy as many as you could eat. You might buy extra ones for friends. The restaurant would run out of sandwiches very fast. Neither buyer nor seller gains for long from either extreme. Buyers will do a great deal to catch a sale. Some will wait in line overnight. Some will wait even longer. When the sandwiches cost too much, demand drops. The restaurant earns nothing. The customer does not eat there. When the sandwiches are too cheap, the kitchen may run out. Many customers will likely feel let down. The restaurant probably does not earn enough. It cannot cover what it costs to make the sandwiches. Picking a price for one local sandwich may look simple. In truth, the choice is quite complex. The restaurant has to count the price of ingredients from suppliers. It has to count pay for the people who work there. It has to count the cost of keeping the place open. Energy bills are part of that cost.

7Rent is part of it too. Nearby places charge their own prices, and those prices matter. The restaurant must also judge what its customers will pay. Balancing every factor is difficult. Because of that, prices can fluctuate. Once a holiday is over, stores try to clear the special goods. They want the holiday merchandise gone. Prices Around a Holiday. The next time your area marks a holiday, watch the shops. Notice how some items are sold. Candy is a good example. Before the big day, holiday candy usually costs much more. After the day passes, it costs much less. You now know how supply and demand work. Can you guess why the candy price changes? A chart for chicken sandwiches shows the pattern. High demand is marked. Low supply and low demand are marked. Supply is marked. The market equilibrium price sits where the sides meet. When the Two Sides Match. Buyers and sellers both gain when a market is more even. An even match of supply and demand is called market equilibrium.

8In the sandwich example, equilibrium has a clear result. The price lets every sandwich sell. The seller never runs out. Customers want exactly the number the restaurant has ready. They do not want more. They do not want fewer. Now picture a band that tours every summer. Each year, more people like the band. The band keeps playing in the same stadium. The number of tickets stays fixed. The stadium has only so many seats. That seat count does not change. Here, a ticket's equilibrium price will probably go up. The band grows more popular.
